Article.Title: Temporal modulation of cortical parvalbumin and somatostatin neurons shapes network activation and adaptation during microstimulation
Article.Authors: Hughes, C. L.; Kozai, T. D.
Article.Abstract: Parvalbumin-positive (PV) and somatostatin-positive (SOM) inhibitory interneurons play distinct and critical roles in cortical sensory processing, yet their activation dynamics during patterned input remain unclear. This study used two-photon calcium imaging to measure how PV and SOM interneurons are activated and regulate layer 2/3 somatosensory cortical activity during prolonged, patterned input with 22 clinically relevant microstimulation patterns divided by temporal pattern (fixed, burst, or dynamic/biomimetic) and amplitude. Activation over time depended on the interaction between microstimulation amplitude, frequency, and duration. For fixed-frequency stimulation, PV neurons were generally more strongly activated than unlabeled neurons, while SOM neurons were more strongly engaged at higher amplitudes and frequencies, corresponding with greater suppression of surrounding populations over time. Burst patterns limited suppression by evoking stronger and more sustained activation than fixed-frequency patterns especially in PV neurons, potentially by reducing SOM feedback. Theta-burst stimulation (TBS) strongly activated and facilitated SOM neurons, which may underlie its therapeutic effects. Dynamic amplitude modulation preserved excitatory-inhibitory balance by eliciting brief, consistent responses that resemble natural sensory input while reducing long-term adaptation. Many findings fit a model in which PV provides fast-adapting feedforward inhibition and SOM provides slower-facilitating feedback. Supporting this model, distant PV neurons reached peak activation earlier than non-PV neurons, and SOM neurons later than non-SOM neurons during stimulation bursts. A simple computational model built on these dynamics reproduced observed responses, including distance-related effects. Neurons recruited directly bypass SOM input onto their dendrites leading to rapid PV-mediated depression but increasing activity across the stimulation pattern. Together, these results inform the design of microstimulation-based sensory restoration and clarify the circuit-level roles of PV and SOM neurons in transient and sustained inhibitory control of somatosensory cortex.

Article.Title: Oxytocin modulates behavioral economic and dopaminergic measures of motivation to seek intravenous oxycodone in rats
Article.Authors: Blount, H. L.; Gits, M.; Colley, E. A.; Kang, J.; Wilkinson, C. S.; Schwendt, M.; Knackstedt, L. A.
Article.Abstract: The opioid epidemic persists despite available pharmacotherapies for opioid use disorder (OUD), motivating interest in treatments targeting the motivational and neurochemical substrates of opioid seeking. Peripherally administered oxytocin (OT) attenuates drug seeking and consumption across substances and modulates the mesolimbic dopamine system, yet its effects on opioid seeking and its underlying neurobiology remain poorly characterized. Here we investigated the effects of OT on behavioral and dopaminergic measures of opioid reinforcement using in vivo fiber photometry with the dopamine sensor, GRABDA2m, in the nucleus accumbens (NA) core of male and female rats. Daily OT (15 IU/kg, IP) administered 30 min prior to operant sessions increased demand elasticity for intravenous oxycodone self-administration in males but not females. Acute OT (15 and 45 IU/kg, IP) increased GRABDA2m dopamine signal in the NA core in females, and potentiated oxycodone-evoked dopamine release in both sexes. In a high-effort task, NA core dopamine increased prior to lever presses, and acute OT (15 IU/kg, IP) produced sex-divergent effects on phasic NA core dopamine release during lever pressing, increasing peak signal and area under the curve measures in males. Support vector machine classifiers determined that features of dopamine transients (e.g., mean peak, standard deviation of the amplitude, peak-valley range) before an active lever press distinguished between treatment and sex. Thus, the ability of chronic oxytocin to reduce the motivation to self-administer oxycodone in male rats is independent of oxycodone-induced NA dopamine release but rather may involve dopamine transmission during lever pressing under high effort conditions.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: oxytocin; oxycodone self-administration; opioid use disorder; mesolimbic dopamine system; fiber photometry; nucleus accumbens dopamine; demand elasticity; sex differences

Article.Title: Three-dimensional object-based quantification of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit colocalization using Imaris
Article.Authors: Sitaula, A.; Zarin, A. A.
Article.Abstract: Neural circuit function depends not only on synaptic connectivity but also on the molecular composition and spatial organization of neurotransmitter receptors. Determining whether receptor subunits occupy shared or distinct domains requires spatial measurements capable of resolving sparse receptor puncta across neural tissue and, when needed, restricting analysis to defined cellular compartments. Conventional intensity-based colocalization metrics can be difficult to interpret for sparse, punctate signals and do not inherently provide object-level classification or cell-specific analysis. Here, we describe a three-dimensional object-based colocalization workflow for endogenously tagged nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) subunits imaged by Airyscan super-resolution confocal microscopy and analyzed in Imaris. Individual receptor puncta are segmented as 3D surface objects and classified as colocalized or non-colocalized using a control-defined spatial overlap criterion. The workflow supports analysis within a defined region of the ventral nerve cord neuropil or within genetically labeled motor-neuron dendritic compartments. For dendrite-restricted analysis, receptor puncta are first selected by their overlap with the dendritic surface before receptor-receptor overlap is quantified. The overlap criterion is empirically calibrated using positive and negative biological controls processed under the same imaging and analysis conditions, providing a reproducible alternative to arbitrary threshold selection. This approach enables receptor organization to be quantified within the neuropil and genetically labeled motor-neuron dendritic compartments and can be adapted to other epitope-tagged receptors, ion channels, and synaptic proteins.

Article.Title: A Mechanistic Theory Unifying Value and Schema in the Prefrontal Cortex
Article.Authors: Warren, J.; Jensen, K. T.; Behrens, T.; Whittington, J. C.
Article.Abstract: Animals exhibit behavioural flexibility by making reward-optimal decisions in unfamiliar situations. Computing value from minimal reward feedback requires leveraging known structure in the world. The Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) plays a pivotal role in both value computation and learning world structure, however mechanistic explanations for each---within the frameworks of Reinforcement Learning and Cognitive Maps---are largely distinct. We develop a mechanistic model of PFC that unifies value and structure through behavioural flexibility. In this model, value acts as a control signal that gates structured working memory representations of the current context in order to ultimately control behaviour. This is a significant departure from the conventional perspective of value, in which it is used for action readout. Critically, this model generalises to novel contexts without the need for additional synaptic plasticity. We demonstrate that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) meta-trained with either reinforcement learning or supervised learning recapitulate this exact model on various value-based tasks. These results not only provide a parsimonious explanation of both the value and schema frameworks of PFC function, but also propose a new mechanistic interpretation of the role of PFC in flexible decision making.

Article.Title: Phasic and tonic pain serve distinct functions during adaptive behaviour
Article.Authors: Tong, S.; Denison, T.; Hewitt, D.; Lee, S. W.; Seymour, B.
Article.Abstract: Pain drives self-protective behaviour, and evolutionary theories suggest it acts over different timescales to serve distinct functions. Whilst phasic pain provides a teaching signal to drive avoidance of new injury, tonic pain is argued to support recuperative behaviour, for instance by reducing motivational vigour. We test this hypothesis in an immersive virtual reality EEG foraging task where subjects harvested fruit in a forest: some fruit elicited brief phasic pain to the grasping hand, and this reduced choice probability. Simultaneously, tonic pressure pain to the contralateral upper arm was associated with reduced action velocities. This could be explained by a free-operant computational framework that formalises and quantifies the function of tonic and phasic pain in terms of motivational vigour and decision value. Additional analyses examined the relationship between model parameters, subjective ratings, and physiological and neural responses. Overall, the results show how tonic and phasic pain subserve distinct objective motivational functions that support harm minimisation during ongoing adaptive behaviour.

Article.Title: The Alzheimer's disease risk gene ABCA7 regulates microglial lysosomal and lipid homeostasis and promotes phagocytosis to maintain neuronal health
Article.Authors: Heuer, S. E.; Ahsan, F. M.; Terzioglu, G.; Misra, A.; Duong, D.; Katkar, C.; Giera, M. M.; van der Kant, R.; Seyfried, N.; Young-Pearse, T. L.
Article.Abstract: Background: Loss of function mutations in the lipid transporter ABCA7 have been linked to increased risk for late onset Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although rare and common variants in ABCA7 associated with AD alter the coding sequence and are predicted to impair protein function, the precise cell-type consequences of ABCA7 deficiency remain incompletely defined. Methods: We used CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) that were deficient for ABCA7 (ABCA7-KO) and their wild-type (ABCA7-WT) isogenic counterparts and subsequently performed unbiased proteomics on differentiated astrocytes (iAs), neurons (iNs) and microglia (iMGs). ABCA7 deficiency in iMGs produced the largest proteomic changes, so we therefore conducted additional functional analyses to define its effects on microglial lysosomal activity, phagocytosis, and lipid metabolism. In addition, we leveraged CRISPR/Cas9 to correct the ABCA7 rs3752246 AD risk variant in patient-derived iPSCs and compared proteomic and functional phenotypes between corrected iMGs and isogenic mutant carriers. Finally, we examined the functional consequence of ABCA7-deficient microglia on neurons. Results: ABCA7-KO iMGs were deficient for proteins involved in lysosome function, measured by down-regulated lysosomal proteomic signatures, as well as reduced DQ-BSA activity and reduced LAMP1+ area. Additionally, ABCA7-KO iMGs displayed impaired phagocytic capacity and increased inflammatory markers, including MHC proteins CD1A and CD1E, and IL-18. Multi-omic integration of lipidomic and proteomic profiles nominated a dysregulated metabolic network characterized by altered phospholipid steady-state metabolism and increased lipid peroxidation in ABCA7-KO iMGs. This was complemented by an accumulation of polyunsaturated triacylglycerols and lipid droplets, suggesting that ABCA7 deficiency disrupts intracellular lipid dynamics. This was supported by the alleviation of lysosomal and lipid droplet phenotypes through the inhibiting the synthesis of triacylglycerols. Concordantly, proteomic and functional analyses revealed lysosomal dysfunction in rs3752246-mutant iMGs, suggesting a shared ABCA7-dependent mechanism underlying AD risk. Tri-cultures of iNs, iAs and iMGs revealed that ABCA7 deficiency in iMGs worsened AD-relevant neuronal measures such as tau phosphorylation and synapse number. Conclusions: This work supplies evidence for the important role of ABCA7 in microglia and provides unique insights into the molecular and functional consequences of reduced ABCA7 function in lysosomal and lipid regulation, paving a path forward to a more comprehensive understanding of AD molecular subtypes and personalized therapeutics.

Article.Title: Responses to unannounced rule changes in adults with developmental disabilities: A community-based pilot study with consumer-grade EEG
Article.Authors: Jeong, Y.; Hyun, S.
Article.Abstract: Unannounced changes in rules or environments often precede challenging behavior and limit community participation for adults with developmental disabilities, yet their responses to change have rarely been quantified directly. We recruited adults with developmental disabilities, including those with intellectual disability, at a community day-service center. We administered a probabilistic reversal learning task and recorded resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) via a 14-channel wireless EEG system. Among the 12 adults who performed the task, total errors were comparable across participants (range 31-57), whereas a switch bias index, contrasting perseverative errors (persisting with the previously correct option) with regressive errors (failing to maintain the newly correct option), ranged from -0.96 to +0.91. In the 9 participants included in resting-state EEG analyses, a flatter aperiodic spectrum over the frontal cluster (preregistered, but selected as the focus post hoc) was associated with fewer switches after negative feedback ({rho} = .80) and more perseverative errors ({rho} = -.72). The preregistered parieto-occipital cluster showed the same direction ({rho} = .69, 95% confidence interval [-.11, .97], n = 8), which was opposite to the preregistered prediction. Frontal alpha peak amplitude was associated with accuracy ({rho} = .77), and the between-run reliability of resting-state measures was .82-.99. These findings provide preliminary evidence that EEG recorded in community settings can capture individual differences in how people respond to change. Field measurement that includes people with intellectual disability may help extend the evidence base for the Sustainable Development Goals of good health and well-being (SDG 3) and reduced inequalities (SDG 10).

Article.Title: Hidden Markov Modeling Reveals Altered Functional Network Dynamics in Multiple Sclerosis
Article.Authors: Hiremath, K. C.; Hobbs, D. A.; Hettish, D. M. R.; Khan, E.; Alias, B. P.; Lin, M. M.; Fox, P. T.; Chiang, F. L.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a neurodegenerative and demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Recent evidence suggests that localized gray matter atrophy in MS may be involved in distributed functional brain networks. However, the dynamic trajectory of functional network alterations in MS remains unclear. The current study extends prior network-mediated findings and aims to investigate the dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) and energetic landscape across an atrophy-prone network in MS. Methods: Twenty MS participants and twenty healthy controls (HC) underwent resting-state fMRI. The atrophy-based functional network (AFN) model was implemented, and time series from atrophy-prone regions were fit to a 12-state hidden Markov model. Each functional network state, a recurring pattern of activity across the AFN, was characterized by the AFN regions with the strongest activation. The states were then grouped into two metastates. Dynamic functional network metrics were compared between groups by permutation testing and correlated with disability and cognition. The energetic landscape of the network was mapped with a pairwise maximum-entropy model. Temporal irreversibility was also measured, which defines the arrow-of-time asymmetry of network dynamics. Results: People with MS showed lower occupancy of state 1, which peaked on the right middle frontal and anterior cingulate cortex. Occupancy and mean lifetime were higher in states 3 and 10 (p < 0.05). In state 3, cortical activity was below the network average, and state 10 peaked on the postcentral gyrus. At the metastate level, MS participants spent more time in metastate M1 and less in M2 (p = 0.04). Within the MS group, a longer interval between visits to state 3 was associated with greater disability (r = 0.57), and a higher switching rate in state 10 with poorer verbal fluency (r = -0.50). The energetic landscape was similar between groups. Temporal irreversibility was lower in MS, mainly across subcortical connections. Conclusion: MS participants dwelled longer in specific dFC states of the AFN, while the rate of transition between states did not differ from healthy controls. Dynamic functional network metrics were associated with disability and cognitive performance and may serve as functional correlates of clinical impairment. The states were similar between groups, whereas the directed drive between states was lower across subcortical connections. This pattern suggests altered network dynamics rather than altered network architecture in MS. Findings from this study characterize the functional network dynamics of neurodegeneration in MS, which may inform future development of network-based approaches for monitoring disease progression.

Article.Title: A Relational Code for Objects in Primate Frontal Cortex
Article.Authors: Watters, N.; Gabel, J.; Tenenbaum, J. B.; Jazayeri, M.
Article.Abstract: When we remember a scene, we recall both the locations of individual objects and their spatial arrangement. Yet, how neurons encode this arrangement alongside individual locations is unknown. In this work, we recorded large-scale neural activity from the frontal and supplementary eye fields of monkeys performing a two-object spatial working-memory task. Using a continuum of two object configurations, we tested whether neurons encoded individual object locations or the spatial relationship between them. Many neurons had well-defined position tuning when a single object was presented. With two objects, responses spanned a continuum from retinotopic to relational tuning. Surprisingly, most units were better explained by relational tuning than retinotopic tuning. Relational and retinotopic units encoded complementary dimensions of the stimulus, and their observed mixture supported near-optimal population decoding of object locations. Relational tuning was systematically aligned with single-object receptive fields, enabling a readout that produced repulsive biases resembling those observed in behavior. Standard multi-object models such as averaging and normalization failed to reproduce the observed continuum, whereas a model integrating receptive fields over potential saccades captured it. These findings show that the frontal oculomotor cortex represents not only where objects are, but also how they are arranged with respect to one another.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: supplementary eye field; spatial working memory; receptive fields; population decoding; saccade planning

Article.Title: A new Mmrn1-CreERT2 Mouse Model for High-Fidelity Labeling of Adult Lymphatic Endothelium
Article.Authors: Goelz, C.; Tavares, G. A.; Lubera, J.; Louveau, A.
Article.Abstract: Cell type-specific Cre driver lines are essential for studying organ-specific biology in vivo, but recombination in unintended targets can limit their interpretive power. The dural meninges harbor a distinct network of lymphatic vessels implicated in neurological processes ranging from neurodevelopment to neurodegeneration. Current lymphatic reporters, driven by Prox1, Lyve1 or Vegfr3, efficiently recombine in lymphatic endothelial cells, including in the dura, but are also expressed in other CNS cell populations, resulting in non-lymphatic recombination that complicates interpretation. Here, we identify Mmrn1 as a gene specifically enriched in lymphatic endothelial cells throughout the body, with no detectable expression in other CNS cells. We generated an Mmrn1CreERT2 mouse line and show that, in adult mice, it drives recombination restricted to lymphatic endothelial cells, with no detectable recombination in non-lymphatic CNS populations. A similar but less complete recombination is observed in developing mice. This tool offers the lymphatic field a new means to specifically manipulate lymphatic vasculature and study its cell-specific functions.

Article.Title: LATS2 modulates synaptic organization and function by regulating actin dynamics
Article.Authors: Wigerius, M.; Labana, P. K.; Diab, A.; Krueger, S. R.; Fawcett, J. P.
Article.Abstract: Recent work has highlighted the importance of core Hippo pathway kinases in cycling cells. Many of these kinases are also expressed in post-mitotic neurons, where they have been linked to synaptic function, and more recently a number have been shown to be dysregulated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimers disease. Despite this, little is known about the specific role or subcellular localization of the Large Tumor Suppressor kinases, LATS1 and LATS2, in postmitotic neurons. Previously, we demonstrated that LATS1 plays an important role in synapse development; however, the role of LATS2 remains poorly understood. Here, we examined the distribution and function of LATS2 and found that it is highly expressed in CA3/CA4 neurons of the hippocampus and localized throughout dendrites and dendritic spines. In contrast to LATS1, LATS2 expression remains stable throughout neuronal development. Furthermore, ectopic expression of LATS2 induces kinase-dependent structural spine defects, alters actin dynamics and reduces activity-dependent synaptic SEP-GluR1 fluorescence. Collectively, these findings reveal a unique distribution LATS2 in the hippocampus and demonstrate that LATS2 directly regulates actin dynamics and GluR1-containing AMPAR trafficking.

Article.Title: Cellular-resolution Three-photon Ultra-Deep Imaging (TrUDI) of neuronalpopulation activity at 2 mm depth in the mammalian brain
Article.Authors: Santra, K.; Logiacco, F.; Frechou, A.; Barber, K.; Bellafard, A.; Liou, J.-y.; Vaziri, A.
Article.Abstract: Extending the depth reach of multi-photon microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an exponentially hard problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain. However, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which the out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal arising from suboptimal optical design and acquisition conditions. Here, we demonstrate a Three-photon Ultra-Deep Imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI optimally matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and non-linear limits for safe laser exposure. At the same time, TrUDI remains compatible with the spatial and temporal requirements for single-cell resolution calcium imaging, and its parameters are tuned to the photo-physics of 3p excitation and the scattering properties of the mouse brain tissue. Our approach results in a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photons at the same laser power as in previous approaches. We use TrUDI to demonstrate in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 x 230 um2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: three-photon microscopy; neural population activity; hippocampus; mouse cortex; calcium imaging

Article.Title: Cognitive cartography of mammalian brains using meta-analysis of AI experts
Article.Authors: Luppi, A. I.; Ali, H.; Liu, Z.-Q. I.; Milisav, F.; Sala, A.; Annen, J.; Gozzi, A.; Bzdok, D.; Misic, B.
Article.Abstract: No individual mind can fully grasp the complexity of modern neuroscientific literature. Where human experts flag, the latest AI models excel. Here we show how frontier large language models can systematically and quantitatively summarise literature-wide neuroscientific knowledge about the cognitive functions and dysfunctions associated with each brain region. Meta-analysis of these AI experts reveals structure-function mappings to which existing meta-analytic frameworks are blind, demonstrated by causal manipulations including lesions and intracranial stimulation. It also unlocks the possibility of extending quantitative literature meta-analysis and decoding of brain maps to other model organisms beyond human. As proof-of-concept, we integrate LLM meta-analysis with species-specific transcriptomics and connectomics in human, macaque, and mouse, discovering that the human molecular circuit for cognition is evolutionarily conserved. Altogether, literature synthesis with AI experts can fundamentally catalyze neuroscientific discovery by overcoming the barrier of data aggregation from heterogeneous studies, finally bringing together a scattered literature to identify latent insights across disparate subfields, modalities, and species.

Article.Title: Retrospective attention strengthens a report-independent neural signature of visual perception
Article.Authors: Li, Y.; Wan, X.; Mao, M.; Jin, L.; Cai, Y.; Zhang, X.
Article.Abstract: Visual perception can remain modifiable after a stimulus has disappeared, but it is unknown at which processing stage a post-stimulus cue operates: on the lingering sensory trace, on the perceptual representation, or on later decision and report processes. We used masked retrospective cues to establish the behavioral effect and a Report/No-report EEG design to locate its processing stage. In Experiments 1 and 2, retrospective cues improved orientation discrimination even when masking reduced cue-location accuracy to near chance. In Experiment 3, valid cues increased EEG evidence for the target in a late interval, without the early enhancement expected from an early, additive sensory interaction. Without explicit target report, valid cues still strengthened the neural representation of the target, and a decoder trained only on no-report trials predicted trial-by-trial visibility and orientation discrimination in separate report trials, arguing against a purely report-contingent decisional account. When report was required, the cueing benefit appeared mainly in additional report-specific signals, which also predicted visibility most strongly. Retrospective attention thus strengthens a report-independent visual target representation, and explicit report can amplify this effect.

Article.Title: Layer 1 NDNF interneurons form distinct subpopulations with opposite activation patterns during sleep in freely behaving mice
Article.Authors: Brecier, A.; Mailhos, G.; Jarzebowski, P.; Li, Y.; Paulsen, O.; Hay, A.
Article.Abstract: Non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep facilitates memory consolidation by transferring information from the hippocampus to the neocortex. This transfer is thought to occur primarily when hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) and thalamocortical spindles are synchronized. However, the mechanisms underlying this synchronization remain unknown. In this study, we investigated the role of cortical layer 1 NDNF-expressing (L1 NDNF) interneurons in gating information transfer during SWR-spindle synchronization in NREM sleep. Using simultaneous cell-specific calcium imaging with a head-mounted microscope and local field potential recordings in freely moving mice, we compared the activity of L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons across vigilance states and during NREM-specific oscillations. Our findings reveal that L1 NDNF neurons form three distinct populations, assembling into cell networks tuned to specific sleep stages. REM active L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons exhibit opposite activation patterns during spindles. While L2/3 cells are mostly inactive during SWR, NREM, and REM active L1 NDNF cells inhibit the network upon SWR onset depending on their coupling with spindles. L1 NDNF neurons mediate slow inhibition primarily via GABAB receptors. Systemic application of a GABAB receptor antagonist resulted in decreased neuronal coupling of pyramidal cells but did not change the inhibitory responses during SWRs. Overall, these findings highlight the potential role of L1 NDNF neuron-mediated inhibition in the response to synchronized sleep oscillations, with potential implications for memory consolidation.

Article.Title: Sustained activation in basal ganglia and cerebellum after repetitive movement in cervical dystonia
Article.Authors: Kuster, J. K.; Levenstein, J. M.; Waugh, J. L.; Multhaupt-Buell, T. J.; Lee, M. J.; Kim, B. W.; Pagnacco, G.; Sapienza, S.; Bonato, P.; Makhlouf, M. L.; Sudarsky, L. R.; Breiter, H. C.; Sharma, N.; Blood, A. J.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: We previously observed abnormally sustained fMRI BOLD signal in the basal ganglia in focal hand dystonia (FHD) patients after they performed a repetitive finger tapping task. Focal hand dystonia is frequently a task-specific dystonia, where pathogenesis has been linked to excessive task repetition and aberrant sensorimotor plasticity. In the current study we asked if the effect of repetitive movement observed in FHD would be seen in other forms of dystonia where there is less known about the role of muscle use and repetition. Methods: We evaluated fMRI BOLD signal time courses before, during, and after the block design finger tapping task in cervical dystonia (CD) patients for comparison with our previous study of focal hand dystonia. To ask whether brain function differences in CD might be linked to aberrant cervical muscle function during the task, we acquired surface EMG (sEMG) from a subset of the CD patients and controls at a follow-up session. Specifically, we measured hand/arm and cervical muscle activity during the tapping task. Results: We observed abnormally sustained BOLD signal after tapping in CD participants in the left putamen and left cerebellum during non-dominant (left) hand tapping runs. BOLD signals in left putamen and cerebellum were also abnormally elevated in CD during the tapping task itself and escalated over time as the task was repeated. The laterality of sustained putamen signal was the same in CD as in our previously studied FHD cohort: patient/control differences were observed only in the left hemisphere. In contrast, there were no cerebellar BOLD time course abnormalities in the FHD cohort. sEMG signal across the left-hand tapping run bore strong resemblance to contralateral fMRI BOLD time courses at both the group and the individual level, including escalation of signal during tapping and sustained activity during rest blocks following tapping in CD. These effects were largest and most consistent in the right sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle. In contrast, task-related arm/hand muscle (flexor carpi radialis) sEMG was similar between CD and controls and did not escalate in either group. Discussion: Based on these preliminary, qualitative findings, we propose that future paired imaging/EMG studies in larger cohorts are needed to evaluate the link between brain abnormalities and aberrant, task-related function in the dystonic muscles. While the imaging findings are not inconsistent with sustained brain activity reflecting an endophenotype and/or hemodynamic abnormality in CD, the sEMG data support the additional possibility that in CD there is an amplified response to the normal mechanical demand of hand tasks on proximal/core body musculature.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: cerebellum; basal ganglia; cervical dystonia; focal hand dystonia; putamen; task-specific dystonia; finger tapping; repetitive movements; dystonia pathogenesis

Article.Title: Dynamic recruitment of PV interneurons in the somatosensory cortex induced by experience dependent plasticity
Article.Authors: Campos, B.; Yang, X.; Marmouset-de la Taille, I.; Dipoppa, M.; Zeiger, W. A.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive circuit plasticity plays crucial roles in the brain during development, learning, sensory experience, and after injury. During chronic whisker trimming, a well-studied paradigm for inducing experience-dependent plasticity, whisker representations in the somatosensory barrel cortex (S1BF) undergo remapping, with expansion of maps for spared whiskers and contraction of maps for trimmed whiskers. At the cellular level, excitatory pyramidal (Pyr) cells in Layer 2/3 shift their whisker tuning, increasing selectivity to spared whiskers and away from deprived whiskers. While these changes are well documented, the circuit mechanisms regulating experience-dependent plasticity remain incompletely characterized. Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons play important roles in regulating the spatial and temporal dynamics of sensory evoked activity in Pyr cells and have been implicated in the regulation of experience-dependent plasticity in other cortical regions. However, there is little evidence as to how the sensory evoked activity of PV cells changes in S1BF during whisker trimming or how those changes might affect cortical remapping. To address these questions, we used longitudinal in vivo two-photon (2P) calcium imaging of PV cells in S1BF before, during, and after inducing experience-dependent plasticity by whisker trimming. At baseline, we found that PV cells have spatially distributed responses to whisker deflections, responding best to the principal whisker of a given barrel and less frequently to surrounding whiskers in a distance-dependent manner. After whisker trimming, there is a substantial recruitment of PV cells responsive to the spared whisker in deprived, but not spared, barrels. Upon whisker regrowth, this recruitment is reversed, but changes in individual PV cell whisker selectivity can persist for weeks. To better understand how changes in PV activity might affect sensory-evoked responses in S1BF, we used chemogenetics to acutely manipulate the activity of PV cells and found that modulating PV cell activity strongly affects sensory-evoked responses in local Pyr and PV cells, as well as Somatostatin (SST) interneurons. Surprisingly, activating PV cell activity strongly suppressed sensory-evoked activity in all three cell types. Computational modeling of the effects of chemogenetic perturbation of PV cells reproduced observed effects on the S1BF microcircuit, underscoring that directly perturbing interneurons in one direction can paradoxically change their activity in the opposite direction due to network effects. Together, our results reveal dynamic changes in the spatial distribution and tuning of PV cells during experience-dependent plasticity and demonstrate that increased PV cell activity can profoundly alter microcircuit dynamics in the adult S1BF.

Article.Title: Supramodal Coding of Detection and Confidence in the Human Cortex
Article.Authors: Porte, P.; Robin, A.; Boscher, F.; Dezier, C.; Goueytes, D.; Mahdian, S.; Hoffmann, D.; Kahane, P.; Minotti, L.; Pereira, M.; Caron-Guyon, J.; Goupil, L.; Faivre, N.
Article.Abstract: Perception is inherently multisensory, yet it remains unclear whether the brain detects stimuli and evaluates confidence in these detections using circuits shared across senses or circuits specific to each modality. Prior evidence is limited: scalp electrophysiology cannot localize where a shared code operates, whereas functional imaging cannot resolve its timing. We recorded intracranial activity (stereoelectroencephalography) in eight patients with epilepsy who performed a near-threshold audiovisual detection task in which they reported, on each trial, whether a visual, auditory, or audiovisual stimulus was present and rated their confidence, both overall and separately for each modality. Analyzing high-gamma activity at the single-channel and region-of-interest levels, we found that stimulus detection involved a broadly distributed, largely supramodal set of cortical regions responding regardless of modality, including the insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and superior temporal gyrus. Multivariate decoders trained to distinguish detected from undetected stimuli in one modality generalized to the other modality, indicating a shared detection code within these regions. Confidence relied on a more mixed architecture but was also substantially supramodal. Finally, the auditory cortex encoded confidence information about its non-preferred (visual) modality, with a similar effect in the visual cortex for auditory confidence, suggesting that the involvement of sensory cortices in confidence is not confined to its preferred input.

Article.Title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression
Article.Authors: Dehnad, M.; Bjorness, T.; Kulkarni, A.; Thai, T.; Pandey, R.; Loer, S. A.; Konopka, G.; Greene, R.
Article.Abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

Article.Title: Selection vs. integration task demands shape the similarity of information neural coding
Article.Authors: Aguado-Lopez, B.; Palenciano, A. F.; Ruz, M.
Article.Abstract: Attention is a function that enables selection and integration of multiple sources of information. However, how these demands influence neural coding of information is not well understood. In this study we used EEG to examine how the selection vs. integration of stimuli shapes the content and geometry reflected on neural patterns, during both preparation and target processing. Participants performed a size judgement task in a cue-target paradigm that, depending on the block, required judging either the size of a selected item and ignoring the additional stimulus or integrating both to respond. Decoding analyses showed that under selection demands, categorical templates of the cued stimulus were active during preparation and target coding, contrasting with integration, where patterns linked to the cued category could be observed only during preparation. Notably, RSA suggested specific exemplar encoding during its processing, which was sustained also across the post-stimulus window during selection, yet was not observable under integration contexts. Our results also suggest that attentional demands shape the similarity between stimulus categories by increasing the distance between selected stimuli and distractors or by reducing it between to-be-integrated information. Overall, this study uncovers the dynamics of stimulus encoding under selection and integration demands, offering crucial advances to understand how top-down processes shape information representation in the human brain.

Article.Title: Entering and Exiting Awareness are Asymmetrical: Evidence from tracking Continuous Flash Suppression
Article.Authors: Phan, C. K.; Rideaux, R.; Alais, D.
Article.Abstract: This study provides a model for obtaining cleaner threshold estimates of entry into and exit from conscious awareness measured with the popular breaking continuous flash suppression (bCFS) and newer tracking CFS (tCFS) paradigms. In both, a suppressed target increases in contrast until it breaks into awareness. tCFS also measures exit thresholds by reversing the contrast change. Both CFS paradigms require a response when the threshold is reached and thus involve a reaction-time component. During this period, target contrast continues to change and threshold estimates are inflated (the "overshoot" problem). Here, we measure reaction-time components for both increasing (entering awareness) and decreasing targets (exiting awareness). We find overshoot is asymmetrical, being greater for stimuli entering (breakthrough thresholds) than for exiting awareness (suppression thresholds). To solve "the overshoot problem", we introduce a mathematical model that quantifies reaction-time components so they can be partialled out to produce clean breakthrough and suppression thresholds. The model can also be applied to previously published CFS studies. The model works for simple target detection and two-alternative target discrimination, even in the continuous tracking paradigm of tCFS. With the timing corrections applied, changes in pupil diameter around transitions in awareness are shown to align with the corrected time points, most clearly when targets exit awareness. Even after correction, the contrast decrease required for a target to exit awareness was greater than the increase required for it to enter awareness.

Article.Title: A systems approach uncovers drivers of the multifocal emergence of an astrocyte state contributing to cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease
Article.Authors: Comandante-Lou, N.; Lama, T. D.; Heuer, S. E.; Chen, K. W.; Kim, J.; Zhang, J.; Hu, B.; Liu, S.; Dey, S.; Brennand, K. J.; Schneider, J. A.; Barnes, L. L.; Zhang, B.; Wang, M.; Zou, H.; Friedel, R. H.; Fisher, T. L.; Mishra, V.; Balch, L.; Ma, Y.; Li, A.; Fujita, M.; Bennett, D. A.; Menon, V.; Klein, H.-U.; Zhang, Y.; Evans, E. E.; Zauderer, M.; Young-Pearse, T.; Taga, M. F.; De Jager, P. L.
Article.Abstract: Diverse cellular states have been mapped in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology, but their links to cognitive decline and the tissue signals driving their emergence remain unclear. We assembled a unified single-nucleus atlas from 867 diverse brains. Meta-analysis identified new cell-state associations with AD and prioritized a non-canonical reactive SLC38A2highSMTNhighCACNA1Dhigh astrocyte (Ast10) as a key link between neuropathologies and cognitive decline. To identify regulators of Ast10 emergence, we modeled ligand-receptor relationships. Independent datasets and two spatial modalities validated these drivers and revealed Ast10's multifocal distribution throughout the neocortex. Mechanistic validation in mouse and human astrocytes confirmed PLXNB1, JAM2 and SEMA4D as regulators. In cerebrospinal fluid from a SEMA4D-blocking antibody trial, Ast10 markers are pharmacologically modifiable, and their reduction tracks with cognitive stabilization. Ast10 may contribute to cognitive decline through disrupted presynaptic neurotransmitter release and may be a convergence point for AD and other neurodegenerative pathologies, a promising target for enhancing resilience to dementia.

Article.Title: Can We Really See the World in Three Dimensions? An Exploratory Study with Finger Alignment Task and Ponzo Illusion
Article.Authors: Mukherjee, A.; Paul, A.; Ghosh, K.
Article.Abstract: Stereopsis is the perception of depth when two 2-dimensional (2D) images of an object from slightly different angles align with corresponding retinal positions in both eyes. However, when we consider the blind spot (BS), a new set of challenges arises. In binocular vision, one eye's higher visual areas compensate for the other's non-receptive region. However, our brain only receives information from one image patch in the BS region, and another visual patch does not contribute to constructing a comprehensive 3-dimensional (3D) representation of the scene. This suggests that the brain adeptly manages this dimensional transition. We aimed to determine the extent to which we perceive 3D across our entire field of view (FoV). We employed the Ponzo illusion, a stimulus relying on visual depth cues (pictorial depth cues), and an eye-tracking technique to assess participants' accurate fixation and eye movement patterns. The participants attempted to align their index fingers before a chart paper to create a Horopter-like setup, supporting the hypothesis about our capacity for stereoscopic perception. The results of our exploratory pilot study with two specific tasks revealed that our ability to perceive depth diminishes beyond approximately 8$^{\circ}$ of retinal eccentricity (in the horizontal meridian) in both halves of the visual field centered around the fovea. This limitation is not apparent in our day-to-day experience.

Article.Title: Motivation to work for amino acids requires acute dopaminergic activity.
Article.Authors: Black, P. M.; Stapleton, K. T.; Lam, G.; Rodan, A. R.; Rothenfluh, A.
Article.Abstract: Aberrant motivation is a hallmark of many psychiatric disorders, and studying motivation in model systems can be useful to understand the neural mechanisms of these disorders. Having versatile, ethologically relevant assays with which to measure motivation is therefore important. However, motivational assays in Drosophila have not been able to measure willingness to exert effort to consume food. Here, we took advantage of the fact that flies prefer to feed on liquid over solid foods to develop a new assay using agarose as a barrier to feeding, which we termed the Fly Liquid vs Agarose Motivation Evaluation (FLAME). Unlike motivational assays based on overcoming bitterness, the FLAME measures willingness to work and is less confounded by deprivation acting on peripheral sensing of the modality to overcome. By depriving flies of specific nutrients and measuring their choice to overcome semi-solid agarose food to get those nutrients, we show that the FLAME is a versatile assay for measuring motivation. We show that flies choose to overcome agarose to consume sugar, salt, or amino acids, depending on the specific of prior deprivation. We then show that show that flies rely on acute activity in a subset of their dopamine neurons during the choice period in order to work for amino acids when deprived. The FLAME thus allows the investigation of specific neural mechanisms of motivation.

Article.Title: Distributed neural dynamics underlie the shift from movement preparation to execution
Article.Authors: Yin, Z.; Liu, J. K.; Kornysheva, K.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in non-human primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across the broader networks and support skilled memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography (MEG) during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that motor preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces - a separation that generalised across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatiotemporal transition across the brain: the state-shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 ms before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localised to the motor cortices alone.

Article.Title: An area postrema GLP-1R to NTS pathway dissociates semaglutide-induced satiation, nausea and reduced food motivation from satiety
Article.Authors: Jones, L.; Cross, E.; Song, Y.; Claxton, P.; Monaco, N.; Yu, Y.; Trapp, S.; Adriaenssens, A.; Brierley, D. I.
Article.Abstract: The GLP-1-based anti-obesity drug semaglutide lowers bodyweight primarily by increasing satiation and satiety, whilst also reducing motivation to consume high calorie foods, and commonly causing nausea. The brainstem dorsal vagal complex (DVC) has been identified as a key mediator of these phenotypic components of semaglutide's anorectic effect. However, which DVC neuron populations are recruited to mediate these components and whether they are dissociable, are translationally important but unresolved questions. We addressed these in mice using metabolic and behavioural phenotyping to resolve the distinct anorectic components elicited by the acute administration of semaglutide. We combined this phenotyping approach with activity-dependent genetic labelling to identify semaglutide-recruited neuron populations ('Sema-TRAP') and chemogenetic manipulation to interrogate their contribution to these effects. Semaglutide potentiated satiation and satiety, caused behavioural proxies of nausea, and suppressed motivation to consume high-fat, high-sugar Western diet, in a largely sex-independent manner. It activated a substantial proportion of GLP-1R-expressing neurons in the brainstem area postrema (AP), but surprisingly most semaglutide-activated neurons in the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) did not express GLP-1R. Chemogenetic reactivation of Sema-TRAP neurons in the NTS alone was sufficient to recapitulate the effects of semaglutide on satiation, nausea, motivation for Western diet, and bodyweight. Knockdown of GLP-1R expression in the AP prior to Sema-TRAPing prevented the recruitment of Sema-TRAP NTS neurons which elicited these effects on satiation, nausea and motivation. AP GLP-1R knockdown also abolished semaglutide's effect on satiation and motivation, while effects on satiety and bodyweight were preserved. These data demonstrate that semaglutide suppresses eating via distinct behavioural mechanisms, at least some of which are mediated by dissociable circuits. GLP-1R populations outside the DVC, or distinct subpopulations within the non-GLP-1R NTS neurons recruited downstream of GLP-1RAP, may therefore represent therapeutic targets to tune GLP-1-based obesity drugs towards a better-tolerated effect profile.

Article.Title: Curiosity shapes brain-like architectures and functions
Article.Authors: Poli, F.; Fakhar, K.; Mousley, A.; Klein, C.; Grosse Wiesmann, C.; Astle, D.
Article.Abstract: How does complex cognition emerge from simpler underlying processes? We show that two components are sufficient: infant-like curiosity and brain-like biophysical constraints jointly drive the emergence of complex neuronal architectures and cognitive abilities. We first tested curiosity-driven exploration in 275 8- to 15-month-old infants. We then implemented these mechanisms in artificial recurrent neural networks, letting them actively sample 20 cognitive tasks during training, while forcing the networks to operate under brain-like biophysical constraints. These two components were sufficient for a range of biological and cognitive phenomena to emerge: The resulting networks captured human synaptic development, the adult brain's architecture, and displayed compositional generalisation, a hallmark of human cognition. Curiosity, long viewed as a downstream consequence of complex brains, is also a driver of their complexity.

Article.Title: Aperiodic neural activity predicts cortical excitability in TMS-EEG
Article.Authors: van Hattem, T.; Hougland, J.; Gogulski, J.; Gordon, P. C.; Belardinelli, P.; Ziemann, U.
Article.Abstract: Background: Fluctuating cortical excitability states are inherent to and critical for brain function. They can be probed non-invasively using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) by measuring early local TMS-evoked potentials (EL-TEPs). Pre-stimulus periodic neural activity can predict fluctuating excitability states. To what extent aperiodic neural activity represents a marker of cortical excitability has not been explored. Objectives: We investigated the relationship between pre-stimulus aperiodic and periodic neural activity and EL-TEP amplitude in both the primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Methods: Single-pulse TMS was delivered to the left M1 or left DLPFC in 29 and 11 healthy adults, respectively, while EEG was recorded simultaneously. Pre-stimulus EEG was parameterized into aperiodic and periodic components to extract the aperiodic exponent (slope of 1/f-like activity), alpha power (8-13 Hz), and beta power (13-30 Hz). EL-TEP peak-to-peak amplitudes were extracted from approximately 20-65 ms after the TMS pulse. Results: Aperiodic exponent showed a strong negative relationship with EL-TEP amplitude in both M1 and DLPFC, with steeper 1/f-like slopes associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Inconsistent relationships were found between alpha and beta power with EL-TEP amplitude across the two regions. Conclusions: These findings indicate that pre-stimulus aperiodic neural activity influences cortical excitability in both motor and prefrontal areas. Notably, the aperiodic exponent exhibited stronger associations with cortical excitability compared to periodic alpha or beta power. Brain-state-dependent protocols may benefit from real-time extraction of aperiodic exponent as a target feature to improve the precision and efficacy of TMS.

Article.Title: Slow and steady: universal learnable structure in animal vocalizations
Article.Authors: DiTullio, R. W.; Wei, L.; Balasubramanian, V.
Article.Abstract: The discovery of universal structures in natural stimuli has allowed neuroscientists to make powerful normative statements about the organization of sensory systems. We sought such structure in animal vocalizations -- stereotyped sound patterns that are received, recognized, and responded to by conspecific and allospecific individuals. Across humans, macaques, and four evolutionarily divergent species of birds we found that: (a) Vocalizations have the majority of their power in low-frequency temporal modulations, (b) Most of this power arises from 9-10 ``slow'' auditory features, (c) The acoustic space spanned by the leading slow features is universal, up to a small rotation, across species, (d) The leading slow features span the same space as the features most predictive of the future time course, (e) A classifier can learn to discriminate vocalizations with high accuracy based on the 10 leading features. These results suggest a universal temporal structure in vocalizations that may be exploited in animal communication.

Article.Title: Active sensing explains cortical variability and improves visual information
Article.Authors: Ressmeyer, R. A.; Rowley, D. P.; Kothapalli, T.; Galor, D.; Wu, R.-J.; Rucci, M.; Mitchell, J. F.; Butts, D. A.; Huk, A. C.; Yates, J. L.
Article.Abstract: Active vision is often considered at the scale of saccades, with each fixation treated as a static visual sample. Yet the eyes continue to move during fixation, continually transforming the retinal input. Here we measured these movements at high precision while recording neuronal populations in the foveal primary visual cortex of awake marmosets viewing repeated flashed natural images. Fixational eye movements accounted for most conditional firing-rate variability and nearly all shared variability not explained by the trial-averaged response. An image-computable model captured this modulation largely from gaze-dependent retinal input; explicit eye-position and eye-velocity signals added little predictive power. Under natural viewing, retinal motion redistributed image power across temporal frequencies, and motion effects grew when this power engaged spatiotemporal tuning. In model-derived populations, fixational motion increased the spatial information carried per spike relative to stabilized input, with sharpening growing across successive nonlinear stages. Thus, activity commonly assigned to cortical noise is not just structured visual reafference generated by the movement of the observer, but is beneficial signal which sharpens spatial representations.

Article.Title: Heterochronicity shapes brain network formation
Article.Authors: Poli, F.; Oldham, S.; Mousley, A.; Bullmore, E. T.; Vertes, P. E.; Astle, D. E.
Article.Abstract: Brain network formation unfolds on a non-uniform developmental timetable, with different cortical regions generating connections at different developmental phases. Generative network models (GNMs) aim to uncover the principles underpinning the organisation of connectomes by creating synthetic networks according to simple computational rules. These models capture the connectome's topology, operationalised here as the cumulative distributions of network metrics (e.g., modularity, small-worldness, rich-club structure). However, GNMs typically ignore the differential timing of connectivity formation, and by omitting this temporal programme they often misplace topological features in physical space. Here, we add a heterochronous growth term to GNMs and use a new model fitness function that weighs topology and topography equally. Topography refers to the spatial embedding of the network - the actual anatomical positions of the axonal tracts. With these advances, we can generate synthetic networks that more faithfully reproduce the spatial layout of diffusion-MRI connectomes from two independent adult cohorts. Compared with classical, temporally agnostic models, heterochronous simulations improve model fit, accurately locate cortical hubs and modules across individuals, and converge on a single caudal-to-rostral gradient of brain maturation. Overall, integrating heterochronicity makes GNMs more faithful to brain development, and allows for better identification of individual differences in network formation.

Article.Title: From Consensus to Individual Differences: Typicality Links Brain and Behavior Across Naturalistic Contexts
Article.Authors: Zamberg-Elad, M.; Har-Shalom, I.; Jarbi, A.; Wilf, M.; Ramot, M.
Article.Abstract: Naturalistic behaviors largely lack objective measures of performance, making it difficult to quantify individual differences and establish links between brain and behavior. Here, we propose typicality, the degree to which an individual's response aligns with the group average, as a framework for identifying and relating stable individual differences across behavioral and neural domains. We propose that, when observers share similar objectives and constraints, convergence toward a consensus response may reflect convergence toward an effective or optimal solution, allowing typicality to approximate optimal processing even when objective ground truth is lacking. To evaluate this framework, we combined naturalistic movie viewing during fMRI with a behavioral battery across multiple tasks spanning social and non-social cognition. Behavioral and neural typicality proved highly stable within individuals while remaining sensitive to the specific computations engaged by different stimuli. Crucially, behavioral typicality was related to neural typicality across multiple domains, with different behavioral measures mapping onto neural systems relevant to the corresponding computations. Neural typicality also predicted objectively measured performance in motion prediction and face recognition tasks, extending the framework beyond consensus-based measures alone. Together, these findings establish typicality as a stable, computation-sensitive measure that links individual differences in behavior to the neural systems supporting them. More broadly, they suggest that the group consensus provides more than a reference for quantifying individual differences: under appropriate conditions, proximity to this shared response may provide an empirical approximation of optimal processing. Typically, therefore, offers a framework for linking brain and behavior in complex naturalistic contexts.

Article.Title: Stimulus category is associated with conscious access during motion-induced blindness
Article.Authors: Sarkozy, A. Z.; Gommlich, S.; Robinson, J. E.; Kovacs, G.
Article.Abstract: Stimuli from different categories, such as faces or letters, differ in semantic content and neural representation. How stimulus category relates to conscious access during perceptual suppression has been studied mainly with binocular rivalry and continuous flash suppression, in which suppression arises from interocular competition. Motion-induced blindness (MIB) is a form of perceptual suppression without interocular competition, in which a static peripheral target intermittently disappears from visual awareness in the presence of a continuously moving background. Here, we tested whether target category affects the temporal dynamics of MIB using human faces, familiar Roman letters, and phase-randomized noise images as targets. Faces disappeared more frequently than noise and showed shorter invisible and visible episodes, whereas overall invisibility fraction and latency to first disappearance did not differ reliably. Letters showed a smaller increase in disappearance rate relative to noise, with no reliable difference in invisible episode duration. These findings reveal systematic category-related differences in the temporal organization of MIB and identify associations between stimulus category and the dynamics of conscious access.

Article.Title: Neural correlates of ketamine-induced dilation of temporal expectation
Article.Authors: Waters, J. R.; Madeira, B.; Shadlen, M. N.; Shushruth, S.
Article.Abstract: Time estimation is critical to many cognitive operations, including decision-making, working memory, and action planning. Neural correlates of interval timing have been described across multiple cortical and subcortical networks, both at a single-neuron level (as ramping activity) and population level (as dynamical motifs). Low-dose ketamine, a dissociative anesthetic and potent antidepressant, is known to distort time perception, but how it affects these neural correlates is unknown. Behaviorally, ketamine caused monkeys to respond as though less time had elapsed than had actually passed under objective clock time, a dose-dependent dilation of time estimation. This behavioral change was accompanied by parallel effects on the neural representation of elapsed time. At the single-neuron level, ketamine flattened anticipatory ramping activity. At the population level, it induced a rotation of delay-period activity in neural state space, away from the pre-ketamine configuration. By linking a graded pharmacological manipulation to concurrent shifts in behavior and cortical neural activity, we show that ketamine dilates perceived time while reshaping LIP population dynamics. These findings offer a route to probe how cortical activity supports time estimation and point to a network mechanism that could contribute to ketamine's dissociative and antidepressant effects.

Article.Authors: Rhodes, E.; Deegan, T.; Alania, K.; Borella, J.; Sabathy, M.; Capstick, M.; Kuster, N.; Howard, J.; Bono, D.; Grossman, N.
Article.Abstract: Background Temporal interference (TI) is non-invasive, steerable deep-brain stimulation strategy using multiple kHz-range electric fields whose difference frequency ({triangleup}f) falls within the neural frequency range. Electroencephalography (EEG) measurement of the direct neural response to TI stimulation is critical for understanding its mechanisms and for closed-loop optimisations but has been limited by intermodulation distortion at {triangleup}f. Objectives To establish a method for recording EEG during TI without the {Delta}f artefact, and to test whether TI modulates neural activity at {Delta}f. Residual artefact was assessed per recording in stimulation-only blocks using a two-stage detection pipeline. Results On a resistive load, the filter suppressed the {Delta}f artefact below the noise floor. In vivo, residual artefact was confirmed in two participants and possible in two more; all four were excluded from EEG analyses. Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) amplitude at 11, 14.5 and 15.5 Hz predicted faster responses. In-phase 15.5 Hz TI increased 14.5 and 15.5 Hz SSVEP amplitude and shortened response times relative to sham and anti-phase TI, the latter not differing from sham. Conclusions With front-end filtering and per-recording verification, EEG can measure TI neuromodulation during stimulation and at {Delta}f, revealing phase-specific modulation of visual entrainment linked to behaviour.

Article.Authors: Heinrichs, H.; Glebowicz, D.; Spitschan, M.

Article.Authors: Cox, J. E. J.; Poljanska, E.; Ray, S.; Forsgren, M.; Ko, S.; Swiergiel, P.; Wright, Z.; Thomas, M. A.; Freeman, W. M.; Delpirou Nouh, C.; Rice, H. C.; Ocanas, S. R.

This finding provides insight into APP-associated biology beyond A{beta}, which may be obscured in AD models that rely on APP overexpression. DISCUSSION Together, these findings identify conserved regulatory networks that may contribute to female-biased microglial responses to AD pathology across mice and humans. Our results emphasize the importance of incorporating biological sex, aging, and human validation into preclinical experimental design and provide a translational framework for identifying mechanisms and therapeutic targets to improve precision medicine approaches.

Article.Title: Diminished ascending drive in transdiagnostic anhedonia shifts the cortico-subcortical hierarchy away from bottom-up dominance
Article.Authors: Roghani, P.; Vohryzek, J.; Kringelbach, M. L.; Deco, G.
Article.Abstract: Anhedonia, the diminished capacity to experience or pursue pleasure, is a core feature of mood and psychotic disorders, yet the large-scale brain dynamics underlying it remain uncharacterized. This shift recurred within the frontostriatal reward circuit and replicated across independent halves of each participant's data. Flow asymmetry also increased with subject-level severity. Decomposing flow into ascending and descending arms showed that both weakened in high anhedonia, but ascending subcortex-to-cortex and striatum-to-prefrontal drive fell more than the descending drive. These findings identify a reorganization of cortico-subcortical hierarchy in anhedonia and suggest that the previously reported prefrontal over-recruitment reflects diminished ascending drive rather than stronger cortical output.

Article.Title: Opioid addiction vs. sugar addiction: Mesocorticolimbic stimulation controls motivation for remifentanil or alternative reward
Article.Authors: Morales, I.; Berridge, K. C.; Nguyen, D.
Article.Abstract: Addiction is characterized by intense incentive motivation that becomes narrowly focused on particular targets. Laboratory studies have modeled intensification, directional targeting, and narrowing of the focus of incentive motivation using paired optogenetic stimulation of central amygdala CeA circuitry, which can create addictive-like motivation focused on either cocaine or on sucrose, as directed by experimenters. However, opioid drugs have been suggested to be different from cocaine in both reward and addictive effects, to be less dependent on mesolimbic incentive salience circuitry, and so may be potentially exempt from such control. To test if opoioid motivation is subject to similar control, CeA ChR2 rats were allowed to freely choose between intravenous remifentanil (2 ug/kg) or sucrose. One group had CeA stimulation selectively paired with earning sucrose, while the other group had stimulation paired with remifentanil. The sucrose-paired CeA ChR2 rats came to nearly exclusively pursue sucrose, ignoring remifentanil. By contrast, remifentanil-paired CeA ChR2 rats specifically pursued remifentanil, ignoring sucrose (control eYFP rats had no overall preference). To confirm whether CeA ChR2 pairing also intensified incentive motivation for remifentanil, as well as controlling its target, a separate CeA ChR2 group chose between two remifentanil options: one paired with CeA Stimulation, and the other unpaired. CeA ChR2 stimulation both focused pursuit specifically on laser-paired remifentanil, and escalated breakpoint for laser-paired remifentanil in a progressive ratio test of motivation intensity. Despite this ability to control motivation for opioid or sucrose, CeA ChR2 laser on its own had only low to moderate incentive value. For example, some CeA ChR2 rats above completely failed to self-stimulate CeA laser by itself. It appears that amygdala-related recruitment of mesocorticolimbic circuitry can transform the incentive salience of opioid drugs, similar to that for cocaine or sucrose, and gate the induction of intense but narrowly focused wanting in an addictive-like fashion.

Article.Title: Effects of Cyperus Esculentus Infused Diet on the Hippocampus in Rotenone-Induced Parkinson-like Disease Model in adult male Wistar Rats; a preliminary study.
Article.Authors: Dada, M. M.; ADELODUN, S. T.; AWOLUSI, O. E.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder contributing to cognitive decline and memory impairment beyond its characteristic motor deficits. Rotenone, a mitochondrial complex I inhibitor, reliably reproduces both the motor and non-motor features of Parkinson disease in experimental models. Tiger nut (Cyperus esculentus) is a commonly consumed plant known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties; however, its neuroprotective efficacy against rotenone-induced hippocampal damage is not yet fully elucidated. This study, therefore, evaluated the neuroprotective efficacy of tiger nut-infused diet on the hippocampus in a rotenone-induced Parkinson disease model using male Wistar rats. Thirty-two male Wistar rats weighing between 100 g to 150 g were obtained from the Animal Holding facility of Babcock University, Ilishan-Remo, Ogun State. The rats were randomly assigned into four groups (A, B, C and D) (n = 8). Group A served as the control and received normal rat chow and sunflower oil. Group B received tiger nut-infused diet only. Group C received rotenone (2 mg/kg) intraperitoneally. Group D received rotenone (2 mg/kg) concurrently with tiger nut-infused diet for 28 days. Neurobehavioral assessments were conducted using the open field test and Y-maze tests. Oxidative stress biomarkers, including malondialdehyde, catalase, and glutathione, were assayed from hippocampal homogenates, and gamma-aminobutyric acid was measured as a neurotransmitter parameter. Histological evaluation was performed using hematoxylin and eosin for general cytoarchitecture, Cresyl Fast Violet for Nissl substance integrity, and Luxol Fast Blue for myelin visualization. Data were analyzed using One-way ANOVA followed by the Student Newman-Keuls post-hoc test on GraphPad Prism 9.0, with significance set at p [≤] 0.05. Rotenone administration produced significant impairments in locomotor activity and spatial working memory, reduced catalase activity, and caused marked histopathological alterations in the hippocampus, including neuronal vacuolation, chromatolysis, and myelin disruption. Tiger nut-infused diet partially attenuated these effects, most notably by enhancing catalase activity and preserving hippocampal cytoarchitecture compared to the rotenone-only group. This study concludes that tiger nut-infused diet demonstrates partial neuroprotective potential against rotenone-induced hippocampal neurotoxicity, with implications for dietary intervention in Parkinson-like disease-related cognitive decline. Further studies involving phytochemical screening of the tiger nut-infused diet are recommended to identify and isolate the specific active ingredient responsible for its neuroprotective effects, enabling investigation of its mechanisms of action at the molecular level.

Article.Authors: Lopes Alho, E. J.; Friedrich, H.; Alho, A. T. D. L.; Alaminos Bouza, A.; Amaro, E.; Grinberg, L. T.; Oxenford, S.; Talamoni Fonoff, E.; Horn, A.; Heinsen, H.
Article.Abstract: Precise localization of human brain regions is critical in clinical practice and population neuroimaging, particularly in stereotactic functional neurosurgery, where small targeting errors may lead to treatment failure. Although MRI provides in vivo and postmortem brain parcellation, histology offers complementary mesoscopic and microscopic information. A major limitation of histological atlases for clinical use is accurate coregistration with in vivo imaging, since tissue processing introduces deformation. To reduce this problem, we sectioned an entire human brain using high-thickness slices, which are less prone to slice-level deformation. Histological sections were registered to the brain's own MRI and normalized to standard stereotactic space through a multistep transform chain. Users can apply MRI-to-MRI registration to transform the atlas into patient space and vice versa, with further nonlinear refinement using SwanWarp or WarpDrive tools. Segmentations and software are being prepared for open distribution. This resource may empower both clinical neurosurgical research and the broader neuroimaging field at large.

Article.Title: Neural populations in the dorsal and ventral cervical spinal cord share temporal dynamics during reach
Article.Authors: Smith, T.; Egawa, S.; Kosugi, A.; Maeda, K.; Sugai, c.; Yaron, A.; Seki, K.
Article.Abstract: Neural population dynamics provide a popular framework for studying motor cortex function. However, whether such dynamics reflect stage-specific computations or are shared across the input and output stages of a sensorimotor circuit is unknown. In the spinal cord, afferent inputs and motor outputs are segregated by anatomical depth. Here we developed depth-resolved Neuropixels recordings from the rat cervical spinal cord during targeted reaching behavior. Across our recordings, population activity was low-dimensional and organized into transient, rotational and target-specific dynamical motifs. Despite differences in single-neuron activity by depth, dorsal and ventral populations expressed nearly identical dynamics across targets and animals. The dominant target-invariant component was strikingly synchronized across depths, whereas other components, including the target-specific component, showed condition-dependent ventral-to-dorsal delays with timing consistent with movement-related feedback. Thus, cervical spinal population dynamics span sensory and motor territories, and may reflect shared coordination of activity rather than purely state-specific local processing.

Article.Title: Rationalizing sensorimotor deficits in autism spectrum disorder
Article.Authors: Chen, Y.; Noel, J.-P.; Schrater, P.; Angelaki, D.; Pitkow, X.
Article.Abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by socio-communicative, sensory, and motor anomalies. Recently, a host of probabilistic models have been proposed to account for the varied phenotypes observed in ASD. These computational psychiatry efforts, however, have (1) largely focused on simple tasks that artificially segregate action from perception, and (2) unequivocally assumed that both neurotypical and divergent populations attempt to optimize the same cost function. Here, we ask individuals with ASD and neurotypical (NT) controls to perform a task in virtual reality (VR): they should navigate to, and stop at, the position of briefly presented targets in a closed action-perception loop. First, we demonstrate that while summary task performance is insufficient to distinguish between ASD and NT individuals, data-rich virtual trajectories do differentiate these groups. This suggests that ASD and control participants use distinct navigational strategies and/or cost functions. Next, we leverage the theoretical framework of Inverse Rational Control (IRC) to interpret the sensorimotor anomalies present in ASD. IRC does not assume that agents are optimal, but rational: that is, agents attempt to maximize reward according to an internal model of the task, which may not match the true task and environment. Applying IRC to this VR navigation task revealed both sensory and motor differences between ASD and neurotypical participants. The sensory differences are consistent with Bayesian inference under altered weighting of sensory evidence. The motor differences manifest as more frequent and abrupt actions in ASD, which we explain by a reduced subjective action cost in ASD. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of model-based characterization of psychopathology and suggest that the computational study of ASD should consider not only perceptual anomalies, but also subjective costs.
