Article.Title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
Article.Authors: Gao, S.; Leong, Y. C.; Rosenberg, M. D.
Article.Abstract: Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

Article.Authors: Urrutia Desmaison, J. D.; Lena, C.; Popa, D.
Article.Abstract: Learning from experience to assess threat is crucial for survival and mental health. This function is known to involve several midbrain areas, notably the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey (vlPAG) and dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN). Recently it has been shown that fear learning involves projections from the cerebellar fastigial nucleus (FN) to the vlPAG. Here, we show using simultaneous single-unit recordings during fear conditioning that a subset of vlPAG/DRN and FN neurons acquire responses to conditioned cues following learning. Strikingly, these populations exhibit firing covariance and directional functional interactions consistent with their collaboration to the response to cues predicting threat. We also demonstrated the reciprocal monosynaptic connectivity between vlPAG/DRN and FN supporting the interactions between these structures. Together, our findings demonstrate shared dynamical activity within a network integrating midbrain and cerebellar computations during fear learning.

Article.Title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways
Article.Authors: Nuttin, B.; Sans-Dublanc, A.; Chrzanowska, A.; Liu, C.; Hanson, L.; Drakaki, Z.; Luyks, R.; Bruystreen, A.; Philipon, A.; Grillet, M.; Kuhn, N.; Goncalves, P.; Montaldo, G.; Bonin, V.; Urban, A.; Farrow, K.
Article.Abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

Article.Title: Task-general brain state dynamics relate to trial-to-trial performance and individual response strategy
Article.Authors: Yamashita, A.; Sawayama, M.; Amano, K.
Article.Abstract: Behavior fluctuates from moment to moment, yet individuals also show characteristic response strategies across tasks. Whether these two levels of variation relate to common brain dynamics is unknown. Using an inside-out approach across 10 cognitive tasks during fMRI, we identified recurring brain states and related their dynamics to behavior within and between individuals. Default mode network (DMN) dominant and action mode network (AMN) dominant states occurred in all tasks. Within individuals, momentary state identity (the state occupied at a given moment) tracked trial-to-trial performance. The AMN-dominant state was associated with slower, more variable responses across tasks, whereas its relationship to accuracy depended on the task. Across individuals, switching between the two states, but not time spent in either, showed cross-task consistency, and frequent switchers showed faster, less accurate responding. Thus, distinct aspects of the same task-general brain state dynamics, momentary state identity and state switching, relate to behavior at both levels.

Article.Title: Multi-timescale dynamics organize descending pain modulation
Article.Authors: Ashworth, C.; Martenson, M.; Shi, Z.; De Preter, C. C.; Heinricher, M. M.; Mancini, F.
Article.Abstract: Descending pain-modulatory circuits must coordinate rapid nociceptive responses with slower changes in physiological state, yet how their activity is organized across time remains poorly understood. We investigated this question in physiologically identified pain-modulating neurons of the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM). The RVM contains ON- and OFF-cells that exert descending control over spinal nociceptive transmission, regulating pain sensitivity and behaviors. By integrating neuronal recordings with probabilistic modeling, we show that unstimulated and stimulus-driven conditions give rise to distinct timescales of ON- and OFF-cell dynamics. During noxious stimulation, we find that population responses undergo rapid activation (<1 s) followed by superimposed slow (~ 100 s) and fast (<10 s) recovery dynamics. In the absence of stimulation, the same neurons exhibit slow quasi-periodic fluctuations in firing activity with a characteristic timescale of approximately five minutes. Gaussian-process models show that these slow dynamics are statistically predictable from past activity, indicating structured temporal organization beyond stimulus-evoked responses. Taken together, these results indicate that descending pain-control circuits exhibit structured dynamics encompassing rapid pain-related signaling and slower fluctuations consistent with ongoing physiological state.

Article.Title: Projection populations form a dorsoventral gradient of reward representations in the lateral septum
Article.Authors: Isaac, J.; Karkare, S. C.; Balasubramanian, H.; Olah, V.; Rowan, M.; Murugan, M.
Article.Abstract: Several decades ago, the septal region was identified as the most dependable location of intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS) in the brain, but the neural substrates that mediate septal self-stimulation are still unknown. One part of the septal region, the lateral septum (LS), contributes to a number of motivated behaviors and may promote reward-seeking. However, the LS contains different anatomical subregions, complicating the characterization of its reward representations. We examine the responses of LS neurons along its dorsoventral axis using cellular resolution calcium imaging during an operant assay. We find that a greater proportion of neurons are excited in response to sucrose reward in the dorsal LS, while a greater proportion are inhibited in response to sucrose reward in the ventral LS. Additionally, we identify two distinct LS projection populations, one to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and another to the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), which are located in the dorsal and ventral regions of the LS, respectively. These two projection populations also have opposing reward responses and their corresponding optogenetic manipulation supports ICSS. These findings demonstrate how LS projection populations contribute to its functional heterogeneity, especially as it pertains to reward-seeking behavior.

Article.Title: An organotypic hippocampo-prefrontal co-culture model for studying long-range connectivity and circuit plasticity
Article.Authors: Stoehr, P.; Grigoryan, G.; Lenz, M.; Vlachos, A.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampal projection to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is a key component of brain networks involved in cognition and emotion. Here, we establish and validate an organotypic entorhino-hippocampo-prefrontal co-culture model that enables experimental investigation of long-range circuit connectivity and plasticity under controlled in vitro conditions. Anatomical tracing, viral labeling, and ultrastructural analyses demonstrate hippocampal axonal projections and synapse formation within the mPFC. Functional connectivity was supported by hippocampal CA1 stimulation, which evoked postsynaptic responses in 90.6% of recorded layer 2/3 mPFC pyramidal neurons. Intrinsic membrane properties and excitatory synaptic transmission were largely preserved across culture configurations. To demonstrate the experimental utility of the model, we examined the effects of selective alveus lesion and global activity blockade. Alveus lesion produced no detectable changes in the examined synaptic or intrinsic properties of mPFC neurons, whereas tetrodotoxin-mediated activity blockade increased miniature excitatory postsynaptic current frequency and reduced membrane capacitance. Together, these findings establish a versatile experimental platform for investigating long-range circuit connectivity and activity-dependent plasticity, with potential applications in mechanistic studies of neuromodulatory interventions.

Article.Title: Gait transition mechanism from quadrupedal to bipedal locomotion in the Japanese macaque based on inverted pendulum
Article.Authors: Nishizaki, K.; Adachi, M.; Ambe, Y.; Tsuruse, Y.; Iba, R.; Oshima, H.; Suzuki, T.; Higurashi, Y.; Mochizuki, K.; Nakajima, K.; Aoi, S.
Article.Abstract: The ability of non-human primates to transition from quadrupedal to bipedal locomotion offers critical insights into both the evolution of human bipedalism and the principles of complex motor control. While quadrupedal and bipedal gaits in non-human primates have been studied, the dynamic mechanisms underlying the transition between these gaits remain poorly understood. Japanese macaques trained to walk bipedally have been reported to utilize inverted pendulum dynamics to achieve efficient bipedal locomotion. Given the intrinsic instability of inverted pendulum systems, which can induce large changes in movement with minimal control input, we hypothesized that this mechanism also contributes to the gait transition. To test this, we developed a neuromusculoskeletal model of the Japanese macaque that integrates a detailed musculoskeletal structure with a physiologically inspired motor control system. Through forward dynamics simulations, we generated a variety of movement patterns by systematically parameterizing motor commands, including failed transitions that are difficult to capture experimentally. We then applied dynamical systems analysis using on an inverted pendulum model to examine the underlying principles of the transition process. Our results demonstrate that successful gait transitions depend on generating an inverted pendulum motion through appropriate control of the forward step length of one hindlimb. These findings provide mechanistic insights into how Japanese macaques coordinate their complex musculoskeletal systems to perform skilled, full-body movements in the gait transition, offering a deeper understanding of both advanced motor control and the evolution of human bipedalism.

Article.Title: Neurexin mediates neuropeptide release from cholinergic motor neurons through dense-core vesicle localization
Article.Authors: Tikiyani, V.; Hart, M. P.
Article.Abstract: Neurexins are critical synaptic cell adhesion molecules that play many roles in modulating neurotransmitter release and synaptic function, and are high-confidence risk genes for neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism. Understanding the function of the neurexin superfamily has been challenging in mammalian systems that have 3 genes (NRXN1-3) that encode 2-3 major isoforms, which undergo extensive alternative splicing and generate thousands of transcripts. In contrast to mammals, C. elegans has a single gene, nrx-1, encoding only long alpha and short gamma isoforms. Neurexins canonically regulate synapse morphology and function in a neuron- and context-specific manner, through mechanisms related to release of chemical neurotransmitters and receptors. Whether neurexins (nrx-1) impact other secretory molecules such as neuropeptides (NPs) and NP containing dense-core vesicles (DCVs) is not well understood. Here, we report that nrx-1 regulates the release of multiple NPs from cholinergic motor neurons in C. elegans. Using tissue specific expression and degradation of endogenous NRX-1, we find that nrx-1 functions in NP release in a cell-autonomous manner and that the short gamma-isoform is required to regulate NP secretion from the cholinergic neurons. We confirm that loss of nrx-1 gamma-isoform impacts cholinergic active-zone number, but also find it regulates the clustering, distribution, and expression of the DCV protein, IDA-1 (PTPRN), and the DCV secretion regulator, UNC-31 (CADPS). We find that nrx-1 functions to maintain separation and juxtaposition of neurotransmitter and NP release sites and DCV localization. Loss of cholinergic excitation (unc-17) or GABAergic inhibition (unc-25) did not impact cholinergic NP release, but that the increased NP release upon loss of nrx-1 is dependent on the calcium channel unc-2. We find that neurexins can regulate NP signaling, a novel mechanism to modify circuits and behaviors, and of potential importance for NRXN1 associated human conditions.

Article.Title: Inferring structural complexity from dynamical measures
Article.Authors: Gaglioti, G.; Cattani, A.; Nieus, T.; Momi, D.; Comolatti, R.; Dalla Porta, L.; Sarasso, S.; Massimini, M.
Article.Abstract: Complexity, commonly defined as the coexistence of integration and differentiation, is a fundamental property of thalamocortical networks and is regarded as a prerequisite for adaptive brain function and consciousness. A variety of metrics have been developed to estimate neural complexity from recorded activity and are increasingly employed in both research and clinical settings. Yet, the extent to which these measures reflect specific architectural features of the underlying circuits remains poorly understood. Here, we used Wilson-Cowan mean-field equations to simulate neural dynamics across networks spanning a broad range of architectures. By systematically rewiring connectivity, we generated graded variations in the structural integration-differentiation balance and assessed a panel of complexity measures derived either from spontaneous activity (observational metrics) or from responses to external perturbations (perturbational metrics). Observational measures exhibited markedly heterogeneous behavior: some were primarily sensitive to network integration, others to differentiation, whereas some showed limited sensitivity to architectural manipulations. In contrast, perturbational measures robustly peaked at intermediate rewiring steps and scaled with small-worldness, consistent with architectures that combine local recurrence and distributed communication. Moreover, perturbational metrics proved robust to common-driver confounds and were highest in a wake-like regime near critical instability, declining as sleep-like dynamics became more widespread across the network. Taken together, these findings map widely used empirical complexity measures onto specific network architectures, reveal dynamical factors that can bias observational estimates, and provide guidance for inferring complexity in systems whose internal organization is inaccessible, unconventional, or only partially known, including brain organoids, non-human nervous systems, and synthetic neural networks.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: neural complexity; thalamocortical network; network architecture; small-worldness; spontaneous neuronal activity; brain organoids; criticality

Article.Title: Functional inertia reveals history-dependent organization of large-scale brain dynamics
Article.Authors: Wiafe, S.-L.; Calhoun, V.
Article.Abstract: The brain does not process the present in isolation. Its responses are shaped by the accumulating weight of prior states, yet existing frameworks treat large-scale brain dynamics as sequences of transient configurations, leaving the constraining influence of history implicit in how models are specified rather than measured directly. Here we define functional inertia as the rate of change of an accumulated latent state and make it measurable through an inertial state-space model. Applied to resting-state fMRI in 160 healthy controls and 151 individuals with schizophrenia, functional inertia organizes brain activity into three recurrent regimes, and patients redistribute their time across them in a way that tracks negative symptom severity. The same measure carries opposite consequences in the two groups, linked to better cognition in controls and to more severe symptoms in patients, because what inertia means depends on the accumulated configuration it operates from. The same contextual logic holds across circuits, where stronger inertia tracks greater symptom negative severity in integrative hubs and lower severity in sensory pathways, resolving the longstanding tension between reports of excessive rigidity and reports of excessive volatility in schizophrenia. These findings position functional inertia as a multilevel constraint on brain reorganization, and the accumulated past as a dimension of brain function that can be measured rather than assumed.

Article.Title: Emergence of long- and short-range functional connectivity parallels the development of neonatal brain gradients
Article.Authors: Chang, Q.; Oldham, S.; Fenn-Moltu, S.; Treder, N.; Arichi, T.; McAlonan, G.; Batalle, D.
Article.Abstract: The emergence of macroscale brain organisation during the perinatal period represents a critical but poorly understood process. Using resting-state fMRI in 325 term-born neonates within the first month of postnatal life, we characterised the early emergence of macroscale brain organisation with functional gradients. Neonatal functional gradients showed a distinct pattern compared with the canonical adult gradients: the principal gradient in neonates, separating the primary sensorimotor and visual networks, broadly corresponded to the secondary gradient in adults (sensorimotor-visual axis), whereas the secondary gradient in neonates, spanning from primary visual to association networks, aligned with the principal gradient in adults (sensorimotor-association axis). We found that the perinatal emergence of distance-dependent functional connectivity paralleled the development of neonatal functional gradients, potentially underlying the protracted development of the sensorimotor-association hierarchy in neonates. Regions with a higher proportion of short-range functional connectivity were more strongly associated with the sensorimotor-visual gradient in neonates, while regions with a greater proportion of middle- to long-range functional connectivity were more strongly associated with the sensorimotor-association hierarchy. Together, these findings highlight the critical role of short- and long-range functional connectivity, which showed a close correspondence with neonatal macroscale functional hierarchy. Disruptions to this process during the perinatal period may alter macroscale brain organisation and contribute to the early origins of neurodevelopmental conditions.

Article.Title: A sparse neural code for acoustic targets enables speech-like vocal flexibility in parrots
Article.Authors: Zhao, Z.; Plump, A. N.; Jones, C.; Teoh, H. K.; Kardon, B.; Goldberg, J. H.
Article.Abstract: English speech flexibly recombines 44 phonemes into >20,000 words and limitless phrases. Here we identify a novel neural code supporting combinatorial vocal control in budgerigar parrots. Deep learning based acoustic analyses show that both English imitated and natural warble songs are composed of subsyllabic acoustic elements that are flexibly reused across acoustic contexts, analogous to phoneme reuse in words. Such reuse poses a scaling problem for songbird-inspired timing-based codes, which require distinct neural sequences for distinct syllables even when syllables share acoustic components. We identified neurons in the parrot frontal cortical nucleus MO that exhibit sparse bursts locked to reused acoustic elements independent of syllable identity, timing, or surrounding acoustic context. These results provide the first evidence for a sparse, acoustically-grounded vocal motor code that can be flexibly reused to assemble a large and combinatorial vocal repertoire.

Article.Title: From labels to latents: revealing state-dependent hippocampal computations and non-spatial replay with Jump Latent Variable Model
Article.Authors: Zheng, Z.; Zutshi, I.; Huszar, R.; Zhang, Y.; Karadas, M.; Buzsaki, G.; Williams, A. H.
Article.Abstract: Neural activity is often interpreted by imposing external labels (e.g., position during locomotion) and decoding within that space (e.g. replay). While powerful, such supervision can mask structure in the data that do not correspond to the label. Unsupervised methods, in turn, often assume smooth latent dynamics and miss genuine discontinuities. We introduce a conceptually simple, computationally efficient latent variable model that infers both (i) the latent variables organizing population activity and (ii) whether their dynamics are continuous or fragmented in time. Fitting reduces to an expectation-maximization (EM) procedure that alternates two operations familiar to systems neuroscience - tuning-curve estimation and label decoding - without requiring external labels. Applied to rodent hippocampal recordings, our method identifies a continuity-fragmentation axis that characterizes population activity across sleep-wake brain states, modulated by cholinergic inputs. For a spatial navigation task, the model reveals distinct population patterns at the same physical position that supervised spatial decoding fails to detect. Moreover, the model enables replay analysis beyond spatial trajectories, and finds prevalent pre-play events associated with immobile and off-maze behaviors and post-task replay of locomotion. By not relying on externally imposed spatial labels, our approach exposes structure that supervised approaches obscure and provides a powerful tool for datasets lacking behavioral tracking.

Article.Title: Hippocampus-evoked polysynaptic responses in the medial prefrontal cortex are attenuated in aged rats.
Article.Authors: Srivathsa, S.; Vishwanath, A.; Garza, V. M.; Cowen, S. L.; Barnes, C. A.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampus-medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) circuit is critical for spatial working-memory and decision-making. Age-associated changes to these functions are attributed to alterations in this circuit, although the exact mechanisms remain unclear. These regions are connected via monosynaptic projections from the intermediate (iHC) and ventral (vHC) hippocampus to the mPFC. We examined the functional connection between these regions in young (10-12 months) and aged (23-26 months) male F344 rats. High-density Neuropixels probes were used to record mPFC field excitatory postsynaptic potentials (fEPSPs) and single-unit responses to electrical stimulation of iHC and vHC. We observed that hippocampal stimulation evoked both short-latency (5-35 ms) monosynaptic and long-latency (35-100 ms) polysynaptic responses across the dorsoventral mPFC axis. Monosynaptic fEPSP amplitude increased with mPFC depth for iHC and vHC stimulation sites. Age did not affect hippocampal-prefrontal monosynaptic transmission as measured by fEPSP amplitude and evoked neural firing. In contrast, polysynaptic responses, reflecting local mPFC circuit recruitment, were larger than monosynaptic responses in young but not aged rats. Polysynaptic fEPSPs increased toward ventral mPFC in young but not aged rats, and polysynaptic evoked firing was reduced with age, most prominently at ventral mPFC depths. Our findings demonstrate that aging preserves the functional direct synaptic transmission but impairs polysynaptic recruitment of local mPFC circuits, with ventral mPFC showing particular vulnerability. These circuit-level deficits may contribute to age-related impairments in cognitive flexibility.

Article.Title: Activation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons promotes the attribution of incentive salience to reward cues in male rats
Article.Authors: Rakowski, E. A.; King, C. P.; Mukherjee, A.; Holmes, E.; Hannan, L.; Loney, G. C.; Meyer, P. J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Reward-associated environmental stimuli (cues) can gain incentive salience in some individuals, thereby becoming attractive, reinforcing, and instigators of motivational states. In rodents, the tendency to attribute incentive salience can be measured using a Pavlovian Conditioned Approach (PavCA) procedure, in which approach to a food cue (sign-tracking), relative to approach to the food delivery location (goal-tracking) is the operational definition of the incentive salience attributed to the cue. Growing evidence suggests that acetylcholine promotes this process, thus the current study tested the effect of activating cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain on sign- and goal-tracking during PavCA. Methods: We injected a Cre-dependent virus with excitatory Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADDs) into the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca of transgenic rats expressing cre-recombinase in acetylcholine containing neurons. We then injected clozapine-n-oxide (CNO) before each of eight sessions of PavCA. On the ninth session, no CNO was given to test if any effects were immediately reversible. Results: We found that activation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons increased sign-tracking over time without an overall effect on goal-tracking, relative to a control group injected with a control virus. Changes in responding from the final CNO session to the saline test did not differ between virus groups. Conclusions: This effect demonstrates that acetylcholine promotes the attribution of incentive salience to a reward-related cue. Future studies should investigate the effect of inhibiting this area on sign-tracking as well as how activation of this area influences reactivity to cues associated with other rewards such as drugs of abuse.

Article.Title: Anterior hippocampal integration tracks the developmental emergence of flexible navigation through changing environments
Article.Authors: Varga, N. L.; Friend, O. W.; Dutcher, A. M.; Roome, H. E.; Schlichting, M. L.; Sherrill, K. R.; Coughlin, C. A.; Preston, A. R.
Article.Abstract: Flexible memory depends on cognitive maps that integrate spatial relationships and guide behavior as environments change. The anterior hippocampus is well positioned to support integration across broad spatiotemporal scales, but its late maturation may constrain development of flexible, map-based navigation. Here, we tested whether hippocampal temporal autocorrelation, an index of neural activity stability over time, tracks the development of spatial integration in humans. In a large resting-state fMRI sample (N = 382; ages 5-34 years; 174 females, 208 males), temporal autocorrelation increased with age in anterior, but not posterior, hippocampus. This anterior-specific pattern was replicated in an independent task-based fMRI sample (N = 83; aged 6-12 years and adults; 41 females, 42 males), wherein we linked hippocampal autocorrelation to dissociable components of spatial behavior. The navigation task separated memory for object locations from the ability to update and generalize knowledge across rotations of the distal reference frame and to new objects. Although all age groups learned object locations, only older participants showed evidence that prior spatial structure supported performance as the environment changed across runs. Critically, hippocampal autocorrelation related to behavior only when spatial knowledge was used across runs, rather than improved through within-run feedback, with the clearest profile emerging in adults. In adults, anterior and posterior autocorrelation jointly predicted precise object-location memory, whereas anterior autocorrelation uniquely predicted efficient navigation trajectories. These findings identify anterior hippocampal temporal autocorrelation as a later-maturing computation that supports the transition from local spatial learning in childhood to flexible navigation through changing environments in adulthood.

Article.Title: Constricted pupil states index neural replay during wakeful rest in humans
Article.Authors: Dash, D.; Claudino, L.; Sugata, H.; Iwane, F.; Cohen, L.; Buch, E. R.
Article.Abstract: Neural replay has been linked to skill consolidation during wakeful rest, yet its physiological context in humans remains poorly understood. In animals, hippocampal ripples and associated replay occur more frequently within intrinsically oriented brain states associated with constricted pupils, suggesting that pupil dynamics may index neural replay events in humans. Replay was indexed by smaller-pupil states, and replay timing clustered on the constricting phase of slow pupil fluctuations. More frequent replay accompanied larger cumulative offline gains during early learning, while smaller rest pupil was associated with better performance when practice resumed. Multivariate pupil features predicted replay-associated states across and within individuals while preceding pupil dynamics showed modest predictive ability to identify the precise onset of individual replay events. Here, we show that constricted-pupil states index neural replay during wakeful rest in humans, linking replay-associated physiology with early motor learning.

Article.Title: A Relational Code for Objects in Primate Frontal Cortex
Article.Authors: Watters, N.; Gabel, J.; Tenenbaum, J. B.; Jazayeri, M.
Article.Abstract: When we remember a scene, we recall both the locations of individual objects and their spatial arrangement. Yet, how neurons encode this arrangement alongside individual locations is unknown. In this work, we recorded large-scale neural activity from the frontal and supplementary eye fields of monkeys performing a two-object spatial working-memory task. Using a continuum of two object configurations, we tested whether neurons encoded individual object locations or the spatial relationship between them. Many neurons had well-defined position tuning when a single object was presented. With two objects, responses spanned a continuum from retinotopic to relational tuning. Surprisingly, most units were better explained by relational tuning than retinotopic tuning. Relational and retinotopic units encoded complementary dimensions of the stimulus, and their observed mixture supported near-optimal population decoding of object locations. Relational tuning was systematically aligned with single-object receptive fields, enabling a readout that produced repulsive biases resembling those observed in behavior. Standard multi-object models such as averaging and normalization failed to reproduce the observed continuum, whereas a model integrating receptive fields over potential saccades captured it. These findings show that the frontal oculomotor cortex represents not only where objects are, but also how they are arranged with respect to one another.

Article.Title: Dopaminergic reward signals shape foraging decisions through learned value expectations
Article.Authors: Kingsbury, L. E.; May, H.; Uchida, N.
Article.Abstract: A fundamental function of the nervous system is to direct animals towards life-sustaining resources and enable adaptive strategies for acquiring them. Foraging, the challenge of securing these resources from the environment, requires making decisions that balance local gains against costs, opening a window on value-based decision making in ecological context. Yet despite the centrality of foraging in life, the algorithms and neural mechanisms underlying foraging decisions are not well understood. We studied mice making stay-or-leave patch foraging decisions for water across poor- and rich-resource environments with dynamic local reward outcomes. We found that mice integrate immediate rewards, local reward history, and reward (i.e. value) expectations to guide foraging decisions, favoring greater time investment in rich-environment patches. Computational models revealed influence of a time-varying bias which mirrored the shape of a learned value function. Consistent with a reinforcement learning mechanism, dopamine in the ventral striatum signaled a temporal-difference reward prediction error, which could be used as a teaching signal to construct value functions, and calibrated optogenetic manipulation of dopamine to create fictive reward signals recapitulated the value-related decision bias. Taken together, our results shed new light on the neurocomputational basis of foraging, revealing a novel role for value expectations in dynamic environments. Further, they establish generalized function of biological reinforcement learning in ecological context, demonstrating a specific role for the canonical dopamine reward circuit in shaping temporally resolved value expectations to guide behavior and cognition. The unification of this framework with foraging opens a new avenue to elucidate principles of how animals learn and dynamically adjust cognitive strategies for real-world ecological problems.

Article.Title: Increased CA3 burst activity in Doc2α and Syt7 knockout mice
Article.Authors: Salaka, R. J.; Chapman, E. R.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampal CA3 subfield is central to associative learning and memory consolidation. CA3 pyramidal neurons execute these functions by generating hypersynchronous bursts that feed forward to the CA1. Extensive recurrent collateral connections within CA3 are crucial for the generation of this burst activity. Double C2 domain-containing protein (Doc2) and synaptotagmin 7 (Syt7) are high-affinity calcium sensors implicated in asynchronous release (AR) of neurotransmitter and in the exocytosis of dense-core vesicles (DCVs). Additionally, Doc2 is a sensor for miniature neurotransmission, whereas Syt7 is involved in synaptic facilitation and SV replenishment. Both Doc2 and Syt7 are expressed in the hippocampus, but their potential roles in spontaneously bursting networks, like CA3, remain unanswered. However, there was a marked increase in burst activity, originating in CA3, in all three KO conditions; this was not due to changes in AR or the intrinsic properties of CA3 pyramidal neurons. We propose that this novel burst phenotype in Doc2- and Syt7-KO mice is unrelated to changes in neurotransmitter release but might be mediated by changes in neuropeptide release from DCVs in the CA3 subfield, or along upstream pathways. Article.Title: New cerebellar nuclei evolve through diversification of excitatory progenitors
Article.Authors: Anant, M. M.-G.; Zuercher, E. C.; Lowman, M.; Shi, C.; Faltine-Gonzalez, D. Z.; Piacentino, M. L.; Fan, J.; Kebschull, J. M.
Article.Abstract: New brain regions have been proposed to evolve via the duplication of an existing region's complete set of cell types. Using developmental single-cell and spatial transcriptomics time courses in mouse and chicken, we show that formation of new nuclei is governed by changes to nucleus-specific excitatory progenitors. During development, excitatory neurons transcriptomically and spatially define cerebellar nuclei territories, with nucleus- and species-invariant inhibitory neurons incorporating into these territories only after they are established. Across species, evolutionarily conserved excitatory neuron progenitors can generate new nuclei by co-opting border formation gene programs to spatially sort their descendant neurons into distinct territories. While most new nuclei share a common developmental origin and the canonical olivocerebellar error-prediction circuitry, we find the higher order subnuclei of the ancient medial nucleus have a distinct origin and do not participate in the canonical circuit, suggesting a unique evolutionary innovation. Together, our findings suggest that new brain regions can evolve when conserved excitatory cell types first diversify and then spatially segregate, while generic inhibitory neurons are incorporated after regions have formed.

Article.Title: VO659, a CAG repeat-targeting antisense oligonucleotide, lowers multiple neurotoxic mutant huntingtin proteins in Huntington's disease
Article.Authors: Röttgering, B.; Weij, R.; Bijl, S.; Verheul, R.; Testerink, J.; Toonen, L.; Bragg, R.; Carroll, J. B.; Beekman, C.; Datson, N.
Article.Abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, encoding an elongated polyglutamine stretch in the corresponding mutant HTT (mHTT) protein. HD pathogenesis is driven by multiple neurotoxic mHTT protein species, including HTT1a and repeat-associated non-AUG translation (RAN) proteins, which increase in expression as mutant CAG repeats lengthen due to somatic expansion. VO659 is an investigational CAG repeat-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that lowers mHTT protein levels by blocking translation. Here, we show that VO659 allele-preferentially lowers levels of multiple neurotoxic mHTT protein species in a CAG repeat length-dependent manner, relatively sparing wild-type HTT, while becoming more efficacious as somatic expansion occurs. VO659's unique CAG repeat-dependent and allele-preferential mechanism of action holds promise for its therapeutic effect in HD patients by targeting multiple core neurotoxic proteins derived from (somatically) expanded mHTT CAG repeats, while sparing wild-type HTT expression.

Article.Title: A brain-behavior generative model links individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions
Article.Authors: Wang, C.; Yang, G.; Wang, S.; Luo, H.
Article.Abstract: Perceptual decision speed varies across individuals and trials. Explaining this variability requires linking individual brain anatomy, neural dynamics, and behavior, yet whole-brain models typically reproduce brain signals without behavior, whereas behavioral models lack anatomical constraints. Here we introduce a brain-behavior generative model in which whole-brain dynamics on each participant's structural connectome generate both single-trial electroencephalography (EEG) and reaction times. Fitted to 17 participants performing motion discrimination, the models reproduced individual event-related potentials and reaction-time distributions. Joint fitting enabled the models to predict whether held-out trials were relatively fast or slow within each stimulus condition. In silico silencing further predicted where, how, and when each person's brain controls decision speed. Sensorimotor regions affected decision speed consistently across most participants, whereas the same parietal region had opposite effects in different participants. These opposite effects reflected whether the region acted mainly through network dynamics or the decision readout. Temporal analyses suggested that early activity largely set decision speed, whereas late EEG mainly tracked the unfolding decision. These results show that brain-behavior generative modeling can link individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions and yield testable predictions of why decision speed varies across individuals and trials.

Article.Title: Multiquantal transmission supports dynamic synaptic strength in vivo
Article.Authors: Patel, P.; Higley, M.
Article.Abstract: In the central nervous system, synaptic transmission occurs through the probabilistic release of neurotransmitter vesicles following presynaptic action potentials (AP). Traditional models posit a single vesicle release event per AP, though experimental evidence indicates multivesicular release (MVR) may occur under some circumstances, greatly expanding the dynamic range and information content at single synapses. However, the quantal nature of synaptic transmission in the intact, waking brain is largely unknown. Here, we used two-photon imaging of iGluSnFR4f-expressing cortical axons and found that MVR dominates synaptic transmission at both layer 4 and layer 2/3 synapses, enhancing reliability and yielding non-binary signaling for single synaptic connections. Moreover, MVR in the presence of cholinergic modulation conveys behavioral state-dependent influence over synaptic potency. Overall, our findings demonstrate that MVR at central synapses in vivo contributes to the computational capacity of cortical circuits.

Article.Title: Contribution of the Late Positive Potential to Emotional Memory: A Joint Neuro-Cognitive Approach to Memory Prediction
Article.Authors: Hellerstedt, R.; Gunn, J.; Talmi, D.
Article.Abstract: Emotional events are better remembered than neutral events. Emotion-enhanced LPP did not covary with emotion-enhanced memory between participants or across lists within participants, but the early LPP specifically predicted memory for emotional items on a single-trial level. Third, we compared eCMR variants to test whether trial-level early LPP should scale learning for both categories or only for emotional items, and whether it could replace or complement a common learning-rate increase for all emotional items. The best-fitting model combined emotion-specific LPP scaling with the common learning-rate increase. The finding that early LPP predicted enhanced recall only for emotional items is difficult to reconcile with accounts on which the LPP reflects attention or stimulus significance more generally, which predict a relationship to memory for neutral items as well. These results pave the way to quantitative prediction of internal recall trajectories by individual participants without requiring behavioural output.

Article.Title: Withdrawal latency in a human hot plate analog tracks inter-individual differences in pain sensitivity
Article.Authors: Keuter, L.; Goltermann, O.; Jessberger, J.; Asan, L.; Büchel, C.
Article.Abstract: Pain research relies mainly on self-report in humans and nocifensive behavior in animals. Crucially, withdrawal latency tracked inter-individual differences in pain sensitivity: Participants who withdrew earlier reported higher pain in the separate task (48 {degrees}C: r = -.47 and -.50) and showed lower pain thresholds and higher suprathreshold sensitivity during calibration. After correction, theta suppression was not preserved, whereas a smaller low-gamma residual remained. Conclusions: ANT-DBS was associated with consistent acute scalp-EEG state signatures comprising raw gamma enhancement, lower aperiodic exponent and offset, and a modest residual low-gamma effect. These hypothesis-generating findings show that scalp EEG can capture acute ANT-DBS state changes, while larger prospective studies are needed to establish clinical relevance.

Article.Authors: Muldowney, J. J.; Umlauf, M. C.; Bocarsly, M. E.

Preceding cocaine exposure, application of leptin to fasted mice restored semaglutides regulation of cocaine. Our results exhibit a potential mechanism for semaglutide-induced cocaine reward inhibition, emphasizing the potential of central leptin signaling as a therapeutic target for CUD.

Article.Title: Progression of visual-stimulus-evoked blood velocity response timing across the vascular network measured with individual-vessel phase-contrast fMRA
Article.Authors: Hu, Z.; Hartung, G. A.; Proulx, S.; Varadarajan, D.; Bollmann, S.; Rosen, B. R.; Polimeni, J. R.
Article.Abstract: Most functional MRI (fMRI) studies of brain function aim to measure hemodynamic responses arising from the microvasculature within the tissue parenchyma, where spatial and temporal coupling with neuronal activity is thought to be tightest. However, the measured hemodynamic responses emerge from an interconnected vascular network that includes upstream feeding arteries, downstream draining veins, and the intervening microvascular compartments. Directly measuring and comparing vascular responses across multiple stages of this network may therefore provide more specific information about network-level hemodynamics--and how hemodynamics in one stage of the vascular hierarchy influence hemodynamics in others--that is not accessible from conventional fMRI signals alone. This can provide new insights into the relationship between the observed fMRI responses and the underlying neuronal activity of interest. This study extends our recently proposed dynamic phase-contrast functional MR angiography (PC-fMRA) method for tracking stimulus-evoked blood-velocity responses in large supplying arteries to enable concurrent hemodynamic measurements across multiple levels of the neurovascular complex. Here, we apply this method across several levels of the vascular hierarchy, from the basilar and posterior cerebral arteries to pial arteries, pial veins, and major draining venous sinuses such as the straight and superior sagittal sinuses. Stimulus-locked velocity increases were observed in individual vessels within each subject. Arterial responses occurred rapidly and nearly simultaneously across upstream and pial arterial segments, whereas venous responses exhibited temporal delays relative to the arterial responses. The average arterial-to-venous response time delay differed between the onset and offset phases, measuring approximately 4.1 s during response onset and 1.3 s during response offset, and also varied across different vessel segments. A simplified Windkessel model--used to interpret these findings--predicted similar inflow-outflow delays, suggesting that these temporal differences may reflect the transient filling and draining dynamics within compliant vascular compartments intervening between supplying arteries and draining veins. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using dynamic PC-fMRA to measure vessel-specific hemodynamic responses across the human neurovascular complex. By providing quantitative measurements of macrovascular responses that serve as inputs to and outputs from intervening vascular compartments, this approach offers a framework for probing the hemodynamics within these compartments and studying vascular network behavior during neuronal activation, which may also help improve the physiological interpretation of fMRI signals in humans.

Article.Title: Localising the Seizure Onset Zone from Routine Interictal and Ictal Scalp EEG Via a Factorised Spatiotemporal Ensemble Deep Learning Framework
Article.Authors: Shi, S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy requires precise localisation of the epileptogenic zone (EZ) for surgical resection. Current practice depends on invasive recordings or spontaneous seizure capture, a costly and risky bottleneck. Interictal scalp EEG can exhibit localising features like spikes, but scalp EEG suffers from volume conduction (the smearing of brain signals across multiple electrodes) and low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which obscure subtle spatial dynamics. Neurophysiologist review of long, often multi-day recordings is time-consuming and expertise-dependent, and while computational methods exist, they tend to rely heavily on human-designed features. Deep learning for EEG localisation could therefore help to improve clinical efficiency and sensitivity. Objectives: To develop and validate a non-invasive deep learning approach for lobar-level localisation of the seizure onset zone (SOZ), the primary electrophysiological proxy for the epileptogenic zone (EZ), using interictal and ictal segments from routine scalp EEG. The model is trained on expert-annotated clinical labels and is intended to augment, not supplant, clinical judgement in EZ delineation. Methods: We curated 262 sessions (6,000+ hours) from 100 patients with unilateral focal epilepsy, tested with an extra 28-patient internal and a 9-patient external dataset. The framework integrates: (1) an online augmentation pipeline (Gaussian noise, amplitude scaling, temporal cropping, and hemispheric channel swap) to mitigate overfitting. (2) a multi-scale temporal block for 20-200 ms discharge morphologies; (3) a factorised spatiotemporal Transformer decoupling temporal and spatial attention to counter volume conduction; and (4) a hemispheric mutual exclusivity penalty encoding unilateral priors. A five-model heterogeneous ensemble, fused via model soup, was evaluated on held-out, seizure-free, and cross-institutional cohorts. Results: The ensemble achieved 88.46% session-level exact match on internal test data, outperforming EEGNet (50.00%). Performance generalised to the seizure-free holdout set (82.76%) and to cross-institutional data (84.62%). Rare occipital class (RO) recall rose from 0.500 to 1.000, with zero false positives on healthy controls (n=108). On unlabelled random segments, accuracy was 66.67% (vs. 14% chance). A full 24-hour recording was processed in 4.26 minutes, with inference under 8 seconds, highlighting localising windows for targeted expert clinical review Conclusion: Clinically actionable SOZ spatial information is encoded in routine interictal scalp EEG. Our factorised ensemble provides a safe, interpretable, and efficient tool to expedite presurgical evaluation, potentially reducing reliance on prolonged monitoring and invasive implantation.

Article.Title: Frequency-Resolved Connectivity Graphs for EEG-Based Classification of Alzheimer and Frontotemporal Dementia
Article.Authors: Radwan, M.; yazidi, A.; lind, P. G.
Article.Abstract: In this study, we build EEG based graph model that uses frequency-resolved connectivity features, with Coherence, phase locking value (PLV) and phase lag index (PLI) in five frequency bands as multi-dimensional edge features. The model is used to classify Alzheimer disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) against healthy controls (CN). This paper extends our earlier work on FTD with AD vs CN as the main new task, a feature ablation for it, and a joint analysis of both tasks. With leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation, the model reaches an accuracy of 81.13\% for AD vs CN and 76.06\% for FTD vs CN, which is competitive with the baselines reported with the dataset with far fewer parameters (159 and 282 thousand versus 170.5 million). Under the random cross-validation setting used for the DICE-net model, our model has a comparable accuracy for FTD and a lower accuracy for AD. Node and edge saliency maps highlight occipital and temporal electrodes, the Alpha band for node features and the Theta band for edge features, which is consistent with earlier EEG studies. In an ablation on the AD task, using all 15 edge features performed better than using a single connectivity measure or edge features averaged over the bands.

Article.Title: Learning to Pursue Goals that Conflict with Prior Experience Relies on Fast Revaluation and Slow Value Updating
Article.Authors: Pan, T.-F.; Molinaro, G.; Collins, A. G. E.
Article.Abstract: Humans can flexibly pursue novel goals, learning to reach them from goal-dependent teaching signals. However, the breadth of this flexibility and its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. For example, can humans flexibly learn to reach a typically avoided outcome (e.g., +0) while avoiding a typically sought one (+1)? We hypothesized that humans are sufficiently flexible to learn from counterintuitive goals, but at a cost, and this ability is supported by complementary temporal dynamics of rapid cognitive control and slower, iterative outcome value updating. In two experiments, we confirmed that participants learned when pursuing counterintuitive goals, but less effectively than standard goals. Furthermore, extended practice reduced performance gaps. To characterize the underlying mechanisms, we developed a novel computational model incorporating fast goal switching and slow outcome value updating. This model best captured group-level behavior; individuals differed in the efficiency of these processes, capturing differences in the cost initially incurred by counterintuitive goals. Crucially, a stronger initial cost did not permanently limit performance: slower value updating compensated for early inefficiencies in rapid adaptation. Furthermore, comparing early and late goal-switch learning revealed that greater goal alignment was associated with faster outcome processing, suggesting a transition from effortful control to efficient outcome evaluation. Thus, despite individual differences in initial flexibility, repeated attempts to reach counterintuitive goals decreased initial biases. More broadly, our findings show that goal-dependent outcome valuation leverages complementary fast and slow processes to enable flexible and efficient goal pursuit over time.

Article.Title: MR-Guided Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation of Nucleus Accumbens to Attenuate Oral Fentanyl Motivation in A Self-Administration Rat Model
Article.Authors: Martin, D. A.; Eldirdiri, A.; Ernst, T.; Cunningham, E.; Bernard, S.; Kamdi, S.; Calu, D. J.; Chang, L.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Transcranial low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is being explored as a non-invasive approach for neuromodulation to treat opioid use disorder (OUD). Methods: We evaluated MR-guided focused ultrasound, with LIFU, targeting nucleus accumbens (MRgLIFU-NAc) bilaterally, using MR-acoustic radiation force-imaging (MR-ARFI) to ensure accurate targeting and adjust for FUS intensity delivered at the target. Male and female rats were trained to self-administer fentanyl/sucrose (70ug/ml fentanyl citrate in 5% sucrose) or 5% sucrose alone. Three cohorts of rats (total n=76) were evaluated on progressive ratio (PR) responding for oral fentanyl/sucrose at either 4 or 24 hours post-MRgLIFU-NAc. Animals in the first two cohorts received repeated rounds of LIFU or sham (anesthesia-duration matched). In cohort 3, we used a counterbalanced within-subjects design in which rats received both LIFU and sham one week apart. Results: Reducing sucrose concentrations decreased responding for sucrose alone more than for fentanyl/sucrose, demonstrating a role for fentanyl in the reinforcing properties of fentanyl/sucrose. Across three sonication schemes, MRgLIFU-NAc did not attenuate PR performance for oral fentanyl/sucrose at 4 or 24-hours post-LIFU relative to controls. Adjusting LIFU intensity with MR-ARFI did not correlate with changes in PR from baseline. We confirmed that NAc is the correct target by bilateral inactivation of NAc with muscimol/baclofen mixture (50 + 50 ng/side), which reduced PR responding for fentanyl/sucrose. Conclusion: The three sets of LIFU parameters, with repeated MRgLIFU-NAc sessions, did not produce detectable changes in oral fentanyl/sucrose motivation. Further studies are required to determine effective LIFU parameters needed to reduce NAc-dependent fentanyl motivation.

Article.Title: Opposing plasticity mechanisms enhance visual inputs that violate their context
Article.Authors: Seignette, K.; de Kraker, L.; Halak, M.; Papale, P.; Dorlandt, O.; Petro, L. S.; Montijn, J. S.; Self, M. W.; Wilmes, K. A.; Larkum, M. E.; Roelfsema, P. R.; Muckli, L.; Levelt, C. N.
Article.Abstract: To navigate complex environments, the mammalian visual system prioritizes informative inputs by comparing incoming sensory signals with learned contextual information. While this process is often conceptualized as a difference computation, cortical circuitry poses fundamental challenges: visual contextual feedback is predominantly amplifying, and whether inhibitory circuits support selective subtraction is unknown. Here, we show how layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in mouse primary visual cortex can implement this comparison through plasticity that acts in opposite directions on responses to direct visual stimulation and contextual signals. To dissociate these components, we presented full images to mice or images where one quadrant was occluded, removing direct visual stimulation while preserving surrounding contextual information, and measured pyramidal cell responses to these stimuli before and after visual familiarization. After familiarization to non-occluded images, responses to direct visual inputs were selectively reduced, whereas contextual responses to occluded images strengthened. This strengthening generalized across natural scenes, allowing contextual inputs to also drive responses to novel occluded images and amplify responses to novel non-occluded images. A computational model reproduced these changes by weakening feedforward inputs and strengthening both feedforward-driven inhibition and contextual feedback in response to repeated pyramidal cell activity. This context-contrasting mechanism produced a conserved structure of responses to occluded and non-occluded images across mice and previously acquired monkey and human data. Together, these results suggest a mechanism for saliency assignment that exploits the compartmental organization of cortical pyramidal neurons: they learn the generalized statistical structure of familiar contexts, allowing selective amplification of improbable inputs or omissions.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: visual saliency; layer 2/3; pyramidal neurons
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Visual perception and processing mechanisms; Computer Science > Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition > Visual Attention and Saliency Detection; Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Neural dynamics and brain function

Article.Title: Neocortical Feedback Biases Hippocampal Reactivation Toward Unconsolidated Memories in a Predictive-Coding Model of Systems Consolidation
Article.Authors: Paul, S.
Article.Abstract: During sleep and quiet wakefulness, the brain spontaneously revisits neural activity patterns associated with previous experience, a phenomenon known as reactivation, or replay. Reactivation is thought to support systems consolidation, the process by which memory retrieval becomes progressively more dependent on neocortical circuits and less dependent on the hippocampus. Importantly, reactivation is not indiscriminate: some memory traces, such as newly acquired or weakly learned ones, are preferentially reactivated. These observations have motivated the development of computational models accounting for the spontaneous reactivation of memory traces, their prioritisation for replay, and their transfer between the hippocampus and neocortex. In parallel, predictive-coding (PC) models have shown how computations attributed to hippocampal and neocortical circuits can arise from local prediction-error dynamics. Here, we connect these two lines of work by showing how autonomous intrinsic dynamics in coupled PC networks can transfer stored memory content between neural systems. The hippocampus and neocortex are modelled as two coupled PC associative memory networks, with asymmetric coupling motivated by reported interactions between hippocampal area CA1 and the prefrontal cortex. This coupling establishes a closed-loop hippocampal-neocortical dialogue in which hippocampal activity drives neocortical learning, while neocortical feedback biases subsequent hippocampal activity toward content for which neocortical support remains weak. We prove that this feedback steers hippocampal activity toward states of higher neocortical free energy, so that prioritisation emerges from the dialogue itself rather than from an explicit scheduler. In our model, neocortical learning relies exclusively on spontaneous hippocampal activity, without access to the initial training corpus. Nevertheless, we show that the neocortical network acquires correlated memory content faster than direct training on randomly sampled memory patterns. This advantage appeared for sufficiently correlated patterns, grew with their correlation, and persisted when new patterns were incrementally added during transfer. Together, these results provide a PC account in which neocortical feedback organises hippocampal reactivation to support efficient transfer of memory content during systems consolidation.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: predictive coding; hippocampal reactivation; systems consolidation; associative memory networks; memory replay; prediction error

Article.Title: Stress, Heartbeats, and Biases: Cardiac phase and acute stress modulate affective and spatial response bias.
Article.Authors: von Haugwitz, L.; Sadr, R.; Wascher, E.; Larra, M. F.
Article.Abstract: Threatening situations often require rapid decisions which are particularly susceptible to response bias. The perception of threat also elicits an acute stress reaction, assumed to promote automatic action tendencies via several mechanisms. Cardioafferent signals during systole, for example, increase racially biased misidentifications of tools as weapons. Acute stress, linked to threat-biased decisions may both bias such decisions directly and alter cardiac effects on them. Here, we investigated the effects of cardiac phase and acute stress in a combined Weapon Identification and Simon Task. Thirty-one participants classified laterally or vertically presented weapons and tools with lateralized responses, such that target location and prime emotion provided task-irrelevant spatial and affective information. Target onsets were timed to systole or diastole, and in separate sessions participants were exposed to repeated feet cold pressor tests (CPT) and a warm-water control condition. The CPT reliably increased subjective, cardiovascular, and endocrine stress measures. Both systolic target onsets and CPT exposure strengthened the influence of emotional primes on weapon and tool classification, without evidence for general threat prioritization. For spatial compatibility, acute stress enlarged the Simon effect in sensitivity among fast responses, consistent with stronger initial automatic activation, and cardiac phase modulated the advantage of spatial correspondence over locations without dimensional overlap. Midfrontal theta showed prime-dependent target modulations with distinct patterns for cardiac phase and stress. Cardiac phase and stress did not interact, consistent with independent contributions rather than amplification or attenuation. Together, the findings indicate that acute stress and phasic cardioafferent signals both increase the influence of task-irrelevant affective and spatial information on action through partly distinct processes.

Article.Title: Bandpass corticospinal transmission during repetitive TMS revealed by motor unit recordings
Article.Authors: Cabral, H. V.; Aguiar dos Santos, M.; Rizzardi, A.; Inglis, J. G.; Rizzetti, M. C.; Pilotto, A.; Padovani, A.; Negro, F.
Article.Abstract: We employed a noninvasive high-density surface electromyography (HDsEMG) framework to track spinal motor neuron responses during repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and characterize the transmission of rhythmic corticospinal inputs to the alpha motor neuron pool. Eleven healthy individuals performed isometric thumb flexion while rTMS was delivered over the motor cortex at five frequencies (5, 10, 20, 30, and 50 Hz) and three subthreshold intensities (50%, 60%, and 70% of resting motor threshold). Motor units were decomposed from HDsEMG before stimulation and tracked during rTMS, allowing input-output coupling between the stimulation train and individual motor unit and cumulative spike train activity to be quantified. rTMS inputs were significantly transmitted at all frequencies except 5 Hz, indicating widespread corticospinal coupling. At the motor neuron population level, corticospinal transmission preserved the spectral components of the rTMS input and exhibited intensity-dependent increases in coupling strength, consistent with approximately linear transmission. The estimated corticospinal transmission exhibited a bandpass-like profile, with transmission between 20 and 50 Hz significantly greater than at lower and higher frequency ranges. Transmitted rTMS inputs induced frequency-specific increases in the common synaptic input to motor neurons, with oscillations at the stimulation frequency significantly enhanced during rTMS compared with before stimulation. Computational simulations reproduced this frequency selectivity only when excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic inputs were combined. These findings reveal frequency-selective, approximately linear corticospinal transmission during rTMS and establish a noninvasive framework for assessing corticospinal function, with potential application as a tool for tracking changes associated with neurological disease and response to neurorehabilitation.

Article.Title: Cortico-Hippocampal phase-amplitude coupling is a signature of learned audiovisual associations in humans
Article.Authors: Borderie, A.; Martineau, L.; Lessard Bonaventure, P.; Labelle, C.; Albouy, P.
Article.Abstract: Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been proposed as a neural mechanism for representing sequential information in memory, binding memories, coordinating activity across distributed brain regions, and parsing complex sensory inputs. Importantly, the frequencies contributing to PAC can vary flexibly across brain regions and cognitive states. Here, we asked whether the pattern of coupling across these dynamically varying frequencies can carry information about learned representations. To address this question, we used human intracranial recordings acquired before, during, and after an audiovisual associative learning task. We first identified the emergence of task-related theta- and gamma-band activity within cortico-hippocampal networks during learning and showed that theta-gamma PAC strength within these networks increased following learning. Importantly, PAC comodulograms contained association-specific information: learned associations could be decoded across hippocampal, temporal, and frontal networks during and after learning, with significantly greater decoding accuracy than that obtained from cue-only PAC before learning and from models trained on theta and gamma magnitude alone. This dissociation suggests that the associative information encoded in PAC comodulograms was not reducible to cue-evoked activity or to either of its constituent frequency bands taken independently. Finally, decoding accuracy of models trained on PAC post-learning was positively correlated with behavioral performance. Together, these findings suggest that PAC contains content-specific information in the human brain and identify it as an endogenous neural signature of audiovisual associative learning.

Article.Title: A new neural code for position: generalizable spatial maps in mouse medial frontal cortex
Article.Authors: Sen, R.; Posani, L.; Medoff, A.; Zhang, B.; Abbott, L.; Axel, R.; Fusi, S.
Article.Abstract: Navigation requires the brain to encode spatial relationships that support extrapolation from explored to unexplored regions of space. We identified a novel neural code for space in the mouse medial frontal cortex (mFC) that is well suited for this form of spatial generalization. Using calcium imaging of excitatory neurons in mFC, hippocampus (dorsal CA1), and lateroventral orbitofrontal cortex (lvOFC) as mice explored a square arena with landmarks, we found that mFC activity supports extrapolation. Linear regression of the animal's x or y coordinates trained in one region of the arena generalized to a completely different region. This property was observed in mFC but not in dCA1 or lvOFC. A model in which neurons encode the squared distance from the animal to multiple landmarks explains several properties of the geometry of the mFC representation, including extrapolation. The neural map that we observed in the frontal cortex may provide a basis for vector computation in navigation and complex route planning.

Article.Title: Connexins are essential for the contribution of latent progenitors to healing after spinal cord injury
Article.Authors: Falco, M. V.; Fabbiani, G.; Prieto, D.; Vidal, M.; Benitez, M.; Rehermann, M. I.; Silvera, C.; Simeone, R.; Trigo, F. F.; Russo, R. E.
Article.Abstract: Gap junctions are important regulators of the biology of neural stem cells. Both in vertebrates with regenerative abilities and neonatal rodents, ependymal cells communicate via connexin (Cx) 43 and Cx26. Gap junction coupling and Cx26 are down-regulated as the ependyma becomes quiescent in adulthood, but injury overrules this developmental down-regulation suggesting a role for Cx signaling in the reactivation of ependymal cells. However, direct evidence of the involvement of these Cxs in the reactivation of the ependymal stem cell niche is lacking. Here, we aim to explore the role of Cx26 and Cx43 in the response of ependymal cells to injury by means of specific genetic deletion. We find that Cx26 is critical for the proliferative response of ependymal cells to injury. The reduced response of ependymal cells by Cx26 deletion increased the extension of the lesion because of impaired healing resulting from a weak contribution of the ependymal stem cell niche. On the other hand, Cx43 -via gap junction coupling and hemichannels- plays a key role in the communication of Ca2+ signals between ependymal cells induced by activation of P2X7 receptors. Our data show that Cxs are relevant targets to manipulate the ependymal stem cell niche to achieve better healing after spinal cord injury.

Article.Title: Sequential coupling of sleep oscillations enables concept-neuron reactivation and supports information flow across the human hippocampal-cortical circuit
Article.Authors: Schwimmbeck, F.; Niediek, J.; Borger, V.; Surges, R.; Trinka, E.; Schreiner, T.; Mormann, F.
Article.Abstract: Effective memory consolidation during sleep is thought to rely on the transfer of reactivated memory traces from the hippocampus to the cortex. However, the mechanisms supporting this essential dialogue across brain areas remain poorly understood. Here, we recorded single-neuron activity (n = 1097) in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) of 10 epilepsy patients across 21 nights of sleep. Before sleep, patients engaged in a memory task with stimuli eliciting concept-neuron responses. During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, neuronal firing locked to sharp wave-ripples (SWR) revealed a directed flow of information from the hippocampus to cortical targets. Notably, within SWR-driven activity, experience-dependent concept neurons exhibited elevated co-activation both within and across MTL regions, indicating selective reactivation of behaviorally relevant information. Cross-regional co-activation of concept cells was markedly enhanced when hippocampal SWRs coincided with cortical slow oscillation-spindle complexes, suggesting an active role of the cortex in shaping interregional communication. These findings provide evidence that SWRs in humans selectively reactivate experience-related neural ensembles across the hippocampal-cortical network, while synergistic interactions with cortical slow oscillation-spindle events might facilitate effective memory consolidation.

Article.Title: From Arm to Leg: A Shared Primitive Framework for Solving Inverse Kinematics in Human Movement
Article.Authors: Koren, Y.; Flash, T.
Article.Abstract: In motor control, the idea of a modular control architecture has been repeatedly discussed. This framework has been widely applied to kinematic and kinetic data, primarily to examine how the central nervous system (CNS) controls multiple elements simultaneously and how it handles redundant or excessive degrees of freedom. However, the inverse kinematics problem, traditionally defined as the mapping from a desired task-space outcome to the corresponding joint-space solution, has usually been treated separately from this framework. Recent work from our laboratory suggests that modular control may directly address all these problems by relying on a shared low-dimensional primitive space common to internal and external movement representations, as supported by recent studies of human hand-drawing kinematics. In the present study, we extended this framework from upper-limb drawing to lower-limb gait kinematics. We also used it to explore how different CNS pathologies may alter the organization of movement within this shared space. Overall, this study investigates whether walking, like other forms of movement, can be understood as arising from a small number of underlying primitives that are flexibly combined across coordinate systems.

Article.Title: Rapid experience-dependent tuning of spinal and transcortical stretch reflexes supports goal-directed movement
Article.Authors: Akter, T.; Rohlen, R.; Petersson, P.; Dimitriou, M.
Article.Abstract: The short-latency stretch reflex (SLR) is the fastest sensorimotor response in human limbs. The spinal SLR scales with background muscle activity and is affected by recent movement history. But adaptive plasticity of spinal reflexes has classically been studied through operant conditioning, which induces an arbitrary change in reflex size over days to weeks. In contrast, rapid, experience-dependent feedback adaptation is often attributed to transcortical mechanisms underlying the long-latency reflex (LLR). Whether task constraints can progressively shape the SLR within a single session remains unclear. Here, naive human adults (n = 16; 9 females, 7 males) performed an instructed-delay reaching task while holding a robotic manipulandum which delivered brief haptic perturbations during action preparation. We recorded high-density surface electromyography (64-channel arrays) from the pectoralis major and posterior deltoid to investigate reflex gains. Pre-perturbation muscle activity showed no systematic goal-directed change. With a long-enough preparatory delay (750 ms), SLR gains decreased progressively with experience when the planned movement was expected to stretch the homonymous muscle, rather than shorten it. This tuning occurred in both muscles, was evident within individual participants, and was accompanied by a corresponding decrease in reflexively generated force opposing perturbations toward the cued target. No such tuning was detected with a short preparatory delay (250 ms). LLR responses were goal-directed from the first trial blocks and progressed in a comparable manner across the session, at both preparatory delays. Our study shows that spinal feedback circuits can progressively adapt within a single session to support the performance of goal-directed movements.

Article.Title: Physiological learning involves intrasynaptic reorganization of GluA1-containing AMPA receptors
Article.Authors: Jevtic, M.; Hollergschwandtner, E.; Kartono, B.; Sugiyama, Y.; Strnadova, L.; Ramesh, R.; Fukazawa, Y.; Itakura, M.; Shigemoto, R.
Article.Abstract: Learning and memory formation depend on persistent modifications of excitatory synaptic transmission in the hippocampus through changes in AMPA receptor (AMPAR) content and properties at potentiated synapses. However, directly demonstrating such changes after physiological, behavior-driven learning in the intact brain has remained technically difficult. Using SDS-digested freeze-fracture replica labeling (SDS-FRL), we examined the density and nanoscale localization of AMPAR subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3 in the mouse hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells. GluA2 density was higher than GluA1 and GluA3 densities at both synaptic and extrasynaptic sites, consistent with previous studies showing that AMPARs in CA1 pyramidal cells mostly contain GluA2. The extrasynaptic density of GluA3 was substantially lower than those of GluA1 and GluA2, pointing to distinct trafficking mechanisms. GluA1- and GluA2-containing receptors were enriched at synaptic peripheries, whereas GluA3 was more centrally localized and clustered, a subunit-specific intrasynaptic organization consistent with differential roles in plasticity. To investigate learning-induced reorganization, we combined the inhibitory avoidance, hippocampus-dependent contextual learning paradigm with SDS-FRL in the CA1 stratum radiatum. Learning induced a selective increase in synaptic GluA1 density accompanied by a concurrent decrease in GluA2 density, consistent with a compositional shift toward higher-conductance GluA1-containing receptors, specifically in the proximal CA1 area. Strikingly, we found a redistribution of GluA1 from the synaptic periphery toward the center, accompanied by increased clustering. These findings reveal intrasynaptic receptor redistribution alongside subunit composition change, a nanoscale molecular signature at CA3-CA1 synapses, which may constitute a mechanism of hippocampal memory formation in physiological learning.
