Article.Title: An Oryza orphan gene confers trans-species drought tolerance
Article.Authors: Tu H.; Liu Q.; Ye T.; Ye Y.; Feng X.; Shen L.; Li S.; Bai S.; Liu X.; Liu X.; Wang H.; Li X.; Lin J.; Wang H.; Chen Y.; Feng Z.; Ji B.; Ding J.; Li W.; Zhang J.; Dai M.; Dong F.; Hu H.; Tang N.; Lai X.
Article.Abstract: Drought threatens crop productivity, yet enhancing tolerance often compromises yield. Abscisic acid (ABA) signaling is central to drought response, but its deep conservation can constrain adaptive flexibility. Here, we identify ROAD1 (rice orphan gene adapted for drought 1), an Oryza-specific orphan gene that confers robust drought tolerance without obvious growth defects under normal conditions. ROAD1 originated from Oryza meridionalis, and its functional allele, ROAD1C, was selected during japonica domestication. In field trials, elite rice lines carrying ROAD1C exhibited up to 34.75% higher grain yield than corresponding controls under drought. Mechanistically, ROAD1 bypasses the canonical ABA receptor-ligand complex by binding the phosphatase OsPP2C68, preventing sucrose non-fermenting 1-related protein kinases 2 (SnRK2) dephosphorylation and activating downstream responses. ROAD1 also interacts with protein phosphatase 2C (PP2C) orthologs from maize, wheat, and Arabidopsis, and heterologous expression of ROAD1C enhances drought tolerance in Arabidopsis, rapeseed, maize, wheat, and poplar. These findings reveal that an Oryza-specific orphan gene can co-opt conserved signaling for potential trans-species drought tolerance.

Article.Title: Gasdermin E couples viral pyroptosis to lethal hepatic lipid accumulation
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Zheng X.; Zhang Y.; Shang X.; Qu Q.; Li C.; Zhang X.; Jin N.; Liu W.; Li H.
Article.Abstract: Tick-borne orthonairoviruses, including the emerging wetland virus (WELV), pose a growing public health concern as cases increase, yet their pathogenesis remains unclear. Here, we show that WELV infection causes fatal liver dysfunction in patients, characterized by elevated hepatic enzymes, triacylglycerol accumulation, and hyperinflammation. WELV induces gasdermin E (GSDME)-dependent pyroptosis in hepatocytes through mitochondrial and Fas-mediated apoptotic pathways. Viral RNA activates RIG-I/CASP3-mediated GSDME cleavage, while viral nucleoprotein undergoes CASP3-dependent processing, forming a negative regulatory feedback loop. GSDME directly interacts with fatty acid synthase (FASN) and blocks K48-linked ubiquitination to inhibit FASN degradation, driving lipid metabolic reprogramming and lethal hepatic steatosis. GSDME knockout abolishes pyroptosis and metabolic dysregulation, conferring complete protection against WELV infection. Clinically approved caspase and FASN inhibitors mitigate liver pathology and improve survival in WELV-infected mice. These findings establish a pyroptosis-metabolism axis driving orthonairovirus pathogenesis, highlighting GSDME as a critical determinant of liver injury and a promising target for antiviral therapy.

Article.Title: CRISPR screens identify targets to rescue age-related T cell dysfunction in cancer
Article.Authors: Chen A.; Ji K.; Yerinde C.; Knudsen N.; Bi K.; Hao S.; Zhabotynsky V.; Martinez D.; Carmona-LaSalle T.; Taguchi K.; Xu K.; Seider E.; Schwartz M.; Zschummel M.; Nieman L.; Yates K.; Gazzaniga F.; Miller B.; Mempel T.; Manguso R.; Hacohen N.; Sen D.
Article.Abstract: Immune aging impairs T cell-mediated tumor control as well as cancer immunotherapy outcomes. The most important drivers of T cell dysfunction in aged tumors remain unknown. We performed single-cell CRISPR screens to identify Dusp5 and Zfp219 as key regulators of CD8+ T cell persistence and effector differentiation within aged tumors. Loss of Dusp5 increased extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation and globally enhanced T cell proliferation. Conversely, Zfp219 deletion induced epigenetic reprogramming and increased expression of cytotoxic molecules, enhancing antitumor immunity specifically in aging. Levels of the human ortholog ZNF219 were higher within intratumoral CD8+ T cells from older cancer patients, which correlates with worse survival following immunotherapy. Zfp219 ablation synergized with immune checkpoint inhibitors to expand effector-like CD8+ T cells, leading to tumor clearance in aged mice. Our findings highlight Dusp5 and Zfp219 as critical drivers of age-related T cell dysfunction that can be targeted to rejuvenate antitumor immunity in older cancer patients.

Article.Title: Milk osteopontin alters the infant microbiome to drive DC hematopoiesis and disease tolerance
Article.Authors: Howard D.; Rashid R.; Ahmed T.; Namubiru P.; Sohel Rana M.; Wilkins T.; Morrow J.; Creek D.; Franco R.; Allenby M.; Turner D.; Werder R.; Manna S.; Satzke C.; Lim Y.; Sun J.; Dennis P.; Yadav A.; Kueh A.; Chung C.; Forbes-Blom E.; Noti M.; O’Regan J.; Coelho L.; Brown C.
Article.Abstract: Breastfeeding reduces the risk of severe lower respiratory infections (sLRIs), a leading cause of infant mortality; however, the protective mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we demonstrated that the absence of milk-derived osteopontin (OPN), highly expressed in colostrum, predisposes neonatal mice to viral and bacterial sLRI, consequent to disrupted dendritic cell (DC) hematopoiesis in the developing liver and lung. Amelioration of disease severity by oral OPN supplementation was associated with increased enteric abundance of Lactobacillaceae and elevated levels of serum 3-phenyllactic acid (PLA), a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) agonist. Supplementation with PLA or the PPARγ agonist rosiglitazone restored lung DC hematopoiesis via airway epithelium-derived chemokine ligand 25 (CCL25)-mediated recruitment of lymphoid-myeloid primed progenitors and induction of a supportive lung niche. PLA-induced DC hematopoiesis and disease tolerance were attenuated by plasmacytoid DC depletion, immunoneutralization of stem cell factor, or genetic deletion of airway epithelial Flt3L. Our findings elucidate a microbiome-host interaction by which milk OPN confers protection against sLRI.

Article.Title: Ultrarapid deep 3D histology enables intraoperative mapping of glioma infiltration
Article.Authors: Liu Z.; Li Y.; Chen L.; Wei M.; Wei M.; Sun Y.; Wang T.; Cheng H.; Liu X.; Ji M.; Shi L.
Article.Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) histology provides volumetric insights into tissue microarchitectures across entire specimens, holding great promise for more accurate prognostication. Through the synergistic development of a one-step tissue-clearing protocol and unsupervised learning algorithms, ULTRA delivers high-resolution, formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE)-grade deep 3D virtual histology within 30 min, covering orders of magnitude more tissue than slide-based methods. In human surgical glioma samples, ULTRA accurately resolves key histological features in 3D and delineates depth-dependent tumor infiltration margins at single-cell resolution. By compressing 3D histology from days or hours to an intraoperative timescale, ULTRA addresses a critical clinical gap and enables more informed surgical decision-making in the operating room.

Article.Abstract: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) accomplishes somatic hypermutation (SHM) of VH(D)JH genes in germinal center B cells for antibody diversification and affinity maturation. Article.Authors: Giuliano C.; Kalluraya C.; Kloehn J.; Sloan M.; Bunkofske M.; Hunter C.; Soldati-Favre D.; Harding C.; Lourido S.

Article.Title: Toward autonomous science with agentic artificial intelligence
Article.Authors: Guo L.; Ting D.; Su X.; Aliper A.; Zhavoronkov A.; Ting D.
Article.Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in biomedicine has evolved from pattern-recognition for medical image analysis to generative models like AlphaFold that predict protein structures. Three recent systems (Co-Scientist, Robin, and Biomni) demonstrated agentic AI capable of generating hypotheses, designing experiments, computational analysis, and refining reasoning through experimental feedback. Article.Title: Comprehensive lineage tracing maps the landscape of cell fate decisions in mouse embryogenesis
Article.Authors: Colgan W.; Koblan L.; Villagrana J.; Hou T.; Wang M.; Gowri G.; Chandler W.; Sepúlveda L.; Ciftci D.; Smolyar K.; Yost K.; Young A.; Wittler L.; Markoulaki S.; Loh K.; Zhuang X.; Yosef N.; Smith Z.; Weissman J.
Article.Abstract: A comprehensive cell fate map of mammalian embryogenesis has remained out of reach given the scale, cellular diversity, and non-deterministic nature of development in utero. Here, we use PEtracer to continuously install heritable genetic marks as development progresses, reconstructing lineage trees that resolve ∼75% of cell divisions across >1.4 million cells from 16 replicate embryos. We pair these trees with deep transcriptional profiling to resolve cell fate biases, restriction timing, progenitor pool sizes, and lineage relationships throughout embryogenesis. Using this quantitative reference, we uncover strikingly reproducible lineage architecture between replicate embryos and chart the lineage dynamics driving fate specification across diverse tissues. Specific biological insights include the progressive restriction of neural crest fate, the relative contributions of distinct mesodermal origins to endothelium, and the dynamics of axial elongation. This work provides a foundation for a quantitative and predictive understanding of mammalian development.

Article.Title: Mapping transcriptional responses to cellular perturbations with RNA fingerprinting
Article.Authors: Grabski I.; Lee J.; Blair J.; Dalgarno C.; Mascio I.; Bradu A.; Knowles D.; Satija R.
Article.Abstract: Single-cell perturbation dictionaries measure how cells respond to genetic and chemical perturbations, creating the opportunity to assign causal interpretations to observational data. We introduce RNA fingerprinting, a statistical framework that maps transcriptional responses from new experiments onto reference perturbation dictionaries. RNA fingerprinting learns perturbation representations, or "fingerprints," from single-cell data, then probabilistically assigns query cells to one or more candidate perturbations. We benchmark on ground-truth datasets, demonstrating accurate assignments at single-cell resolution, scalability to genome-wide screens, and the ability to resolve combinatorial perturbations. We demonstrate broad utility across diverse biological settings: identifying context-specific regulators of p53 under ribosomal stress, characterizing dose-dependent drug mechanisms of action, and uncovering cytokine-driven B cell heterogeneity during secondary influenza infection in vivo. Together, these results establish RNA fingerprinting as a versatile framework for interpreting single-cell datasets by linking cellular states to their underlying perturbations.

Article.Title: Rare k-mers reveal centromere haplogroups underlying human diversity and cancer translocations
Article.Authors: Shiraishi Y.; Ochi Y.; Sugawa M.; Sakamoto Y.; Kimura K.; Tsujimura T.; Okada A.; Okuda R.; Namba S.; Hori T.; Kobayashi Y.; Miyauchi T.; Mateos R.; Suzuki H.; Chiba K.; Ito Y.; Nakamura W.; Ohka F.; Motomura K.; Yamamoto T.; Kawai Y.; Okada Y.; Suzuki H.; Fukagawa T.; Kato M.
Article.Abstract: Human centromeres are highly variable but remain among the least characterized regions of the genome because their repetitive structure has hindered conventional analysis of population diversity and disease relevance. Here, we show that rare k-mers in centromeric regions capture lineage-specific variation, defining discrete haplogroups with distinct structural features. We developed ascairn to infer these haplogroups from short-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data. Applying this framework to >3,300 genomes reveals extensive global diversity in centromere haplogroups and signatures of population history. Analyzing short-read WGS data from 142 oligodendroglioma cases with 1p/19q co-deletion, we mapped breakpoints to the centromere regions of chromosomes 1 and 19, revealing a clear positional relationship to kinetochore attachment sites and a link between centromere haplotype structure and rearrangement susceptibility. Rare k-mers thus open centromeres to population-scale analysis, linking centromere structural diversity to human evolutionary history and disease-associated genomic instability.

Article.Title: A high-dimensional population code in the bat motor cortex during natural dexterous flight
Article.Authors: Styr B.; Qi K.; Chen X.; Liberti W.; Yartsev M.
Article.Abstract: Elucidating the neural computations underlying natural, complex movement remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. Bat flight presents a formidable motor control challenge, requiring hand-like wings whose many degrees of freedom must be precisely coordinated to enable rapid three-dimensional (3D) maneuvers. Here, we performed large-scale wireless recordings from the wing motor cortex of freely flying bats, combined with 3D tracking of wing kinematics. Despite the complexity of flight control, bats repeatedly executed accurate flights through precise adjustments of individual wingbeats. Surprisingly, motor cortical activity was not dominated by the wingbeat cycle. Instead, neurons were sparsely active, exhibiting mixed selectivity for flight kinematics and variable entrainment to the wingbeat phase reaching millisecond-scale precision. This yielded a high-dimensional population code driven by successive wingbeats occupying distinct neural states. These findings reveal a mode of motor cortical population dynamics expressed during natural dexterous movement that is not well captured by prevailing views derived from constrained paradigms.

Article.Title: Mechanisms of transcription control by distal enhancers from single-gene nanoscopy
Article.Authors: Cheng L.; De C.; Li J.; Korff R.; Pertsinidis A.
Article.Abstract: Distal enhancers activate genes over vast genomic distances, but how this communication occurs and what signals are transmitted are poorly understood. Using real-time single-gene nanoscopy and targeted perturbations, we define physical parameters and mechanisms of enhancer-promoter communication. We find that productive interactions are dynamic, occur at a proximity of ≲100 nm, and are coordinated with transcriptional bursts. Enhancers and promoters find one another not only through passive diffusion; we often directly observe them being actively brought together by cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, which is a key determinant of transcriptional burst frequency. We also discover that specific general transcription factors (GTFs) of RNA polymerase II machinery are key to initiating transcriptional bursts, and enhancer-promoter interactions activate bursting by embedding the promoter within GTF clusters that form at the enhancers. Our results resolve the molecular and biochemical signals involved in long-range gene activation and elucidate the biophysical mechanisms for their transmission from the enhancer to the promoter.

Article.Title: PTPRS mediates invasion of tetanus neurotoxin into the central nervous system
Article.Authors: Chen P.; Wang H.; Manion J.; Zähringer J.; Liang J.; Mohammed A.; Zhao L.; Zhang J.; Wang Y.; Wang K.; Lee P.; Masuyer G.; Satchell K.; Brunzelle J.; Ha T.; Stenmark P.; Dong M.
Article.Abstract: Tetanus neurotoxin (TeNT) invades the central nervous system (CNS) via retrograde transport through motoneurons. Whether a host factor is needed to mediate TeNT trafficking has remained unknown. Here, using pull-down and mass spectrometry analysis, and by developing a luciferase-based in vivo transport assay, we identify receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPRS; PTPσ) as the retrograde transport receptor for TeNT. Global or motoneuron-specific PTPRS knockout (KO) abolishes TeNT entry into the CNS in mouse models. PTPRS-TeNT interactions occur in endosomes, prevent toxin translocation, and direct TeNT trafficking in neurons. Structural studies establish that the TeNT light chain and belt region bind to the immunoglobulin domain of PTPRS. Disrupting TeNT-PTPRS interactions blocks TeNT trafficking into the spinal cord; consistently, a PTPRS-binding-deficient TeNT mutant induces botulism-like flaccid paralysis. Thus, PTPRS is the host factor mediating TeNT trafficking into the CNS, revealing a targetable pathway for post-entry intervention and drug delivery into the CNS.

Article.Title: A pseudoenzyme sensor of trehalose-6-phosphate directly represses the metabolic integrator SnRK1 in plants
Article.Authors: Sun T.; Li W.; Liu X.; Li K.; Zhang X.; Xiang S.; Chen M.; Liu S.; Lin H.; Nian Y.; Wang L.; Mai Y.; Wang R.; Zhu L.; Wang X.; Li Y.; Li X.; Chen B.; Wang S.; Gao Y.; Xu X.; Ye M.; Geng Y.; Zhang J.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: Trehalose-6-phosphate (T6P) is a central metabolic signal linking sugar availability to plant growth, carbon utilization, and productivity, yet its sensing and signaling mechanisms remain elusive. Using chemical biology and functional approaches, we identify the noncatalytic pseudoenzyme Class-II T6P synthase (TPS-II) as a T6P sensor in Arabidopsis. In the apo state, TPS-II dimerizes to form an autoinhibitory inter-subunit interaction. T6P binding to the N-terminal TPS-like domain triggers a conformational change that releases the C-terminal domain, enabling interaction with the central metabolic integrator SNF1-related protein kinase 1 (SnRK1) to repress its kinase activity. Loss of TPS-II genes activates catabolic and stress-responsive programs while suppressing anabolic gene expression, consistent with constitutive SnRK1 activity. Conservation of this T6P-TPS-II-SnRK1 signaling axis throughout the plant kingdom highlights its fundamental role in coupling carbon availability to metabolic homeostasis. These findings resolve a long-standing question in sugar signaling and provide a framework for improving crop carbon-use efficiency.

Article.Title: Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise
Article.Authors: Maier G.; Hariharan M.; Ramasamy R.; Glina A.; van Rosmalen L.; Pathak S.; Deota S.; Patel S.; Lin T.; Lam M.; Le H.; Powale K.; Shimomura T.; Otobe Y.; Rothenberg V.; Sun M.; Sakurai T.; Chin T.; Wu Y.; Castanon R.; Bartlett A.; Chen H.; Nery J.; Barragan C.; Devulapalli S.
Article.Abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.

Article.Title: Cellular self-organization orchestrates ferroptosis propagation
Article.Authors: Cheng J.; Co H.; Lin H.; Wu C.; Chen S.
Article.Abstract: Self-organization generates cellular patterns that guide morphogenesis, but how it regulates collective cell fate remains underexplored. We show that cellular self-organization constrains the propagation of ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of oxidative cell death that can otherwise spread as unbounded trigger waves. The spatial patterning of cell density and alignment encodes transcriptional programs, priming cells toward ferroptosis-sensitive or -resistant fates. Low-density, misaligned regions with elevated YAP/TEAD1 activity are sensitive, whereas high-density, aligned regions with increased NRF2 expression form propagation-resistant boundaries. Cell elongation establishes a polarized distribution of oxidizable lipids, creating peroxidation hotspots at the cell poles that promote propagation along cell alignment. In silico and pharmacological perturbations reveal that pattern-dependent susceptibility and polarized lipid organization act together to constrain isotropic waves into spatially confined, anisotropic propagation. These findings identify self-organization as a systems-level mechanism governing collective homeostasis, providing a paradigm to explore how tissue-scale organization regulates cell death in development and disease.

Article.Title: An opioid efficacy switch for reversible optical control of analgesia
Article.Authors: Posa L.; Romano G.; Ji X.; Khan S.; Nazarova A.; Sharghi Moshtaghin S.; Paz B.; Han G.; Arefin A.; Gonzalez-Hernandez A.; Srivastava I.; Zaidi S.; Calderon-Godinez K.; Zhang Z.; Tyson A.; Ranjbar M.; Pleil K.; Pande K.; Katritch V.; Gati C.; Trauner D.; Levitz J.
Article.Abstract: The mu-opioid receptor (MOR) is a major target for pain treatment, but its effectiveness is limited by dangerous side effects. However, the systemic administration of opioids makes it difficult both to decipher their underlying mechanisms of action and to limit drug action to specific receptor subpopulations to isolate therapeutic effects from adverse effects. Here, we develop a reversibly photoswitchable morphinan agonist termed "azo-morphine-3" (AM-3) that interconverts from low to high efficacy in response to light to enable optical control of MOR signaling. Structural analysis of the low ("trans") and high ("cis") efficacy states of AM-3 bound to the MOR reveals distinct binding modes, with each state driving unique ligand, receptor, and G protein dynamics. In mice, AM-3 drives reversible and repeatable optical control of antinociception across pain models with a reduced side effect profile owing to its limited brain accumulation and its ability to be locally activated.

Article.Title: Functional diversification of the cephalopod proteome by RNA editing
Article.Authors: Moen J.; Richards A.; Krogsaeter E.; Polacco B.; Gordon M.; Stevenson E.; Boyles R.; Burq M.; Stepec D.; Crampton B.; Sin N.; Gale-Day Z.; Gestwicki J.; Cimermancic P.; Rosenthal J.; Krogan N.; Swaney D.
Article.Abstract: Coleoid cephalopods exhibit the highest levels of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR)-mediated RNA editing of any known taxon, yet the functional consequences of most recoding events remain unclear. Here, we integrated proteomics with biochemical and cellular assays to characterize recoding across the Doryteuthis pealeii proteome. This confirmed the translation of 7,997 recoded sites at the protein level and revealed how recoding reshapes the proteome by altering protein stability, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, and enzymatic activity. We find that recoding also creates or ablates post-translational modification sites, with direct effects on protein function and protein-protein interactions. Recoding the E3 ligase MARCHF5 drives widespread changes in substrate ubiquitylation and perturbs mitochondrial homeostasis, illustrating how RNA editing can influence organelle function. Together, these data give a proteome-scale view of how extensive RNA recoding diversifies protein function in coleoid cephalopods and offer a framework for understanding how RNA-level plasticity shapes protein function and cellular physiology.

Article.Title: A phenome-wide structural variant map from 467,152 UK Biobank genomes
Article.Authors: Atanur S.; Hu F.; Lou H.; Li X.; Zou X.; O’Dell S.; Deevi S.; Sawczuk P.; Megy K.; Fairhurst-Hunter Z.; O’Neill A.; Tian L.; Carss K.; Mitchell J.; MacArthur S.; Wasilewski S.; Dhindsa R.; Wang Q.; Smith K.; Burren O.; Petrovski S.
Article.Abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are large (>50 base pairs) genomic rearrangements that can significantly influence human phenotypes, yet their contribution to health and disease remains undercharacterized. We conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) of 1.6 million SVs identified in whole-genome sequencing data from 467,152 UK Biobank participants, across 13,322 binary, 2,018 quantitative, and 2,923 plasma protein traits. Of these, 82.25% of SVs were outside the detectable range of prior copy-number variant studies. Protein quantitative trait loci analysis linked 3,241 SVs to 1,608 proteins, with effects dependent on SV type and location. In SV-PheWAS, we detected 28,184 associations with human health outcomes. Notably, we uncovered rare SVs with strong phenotypic effects. Furthermore, we show that at known genome-wide association study loci, 32.21% of associated SVs overlapped functional genomic regions. This study underscores the underestimated role of SVs in human genetics and their potential to advance understanding of human biology and drug discovery.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal co-transcriptomics uncovers coordinated rhizobia-legume stress programs supporting nitrogen fixation in Medicago
Article.Authors: Shao W.; Shi X.; Guo X.; Xiang S.; Xiao Y.; Guang X.; Fang D.; Lian X.; Luo L.; Sun Y.; Xu P.; Zhuang Y.; Chen L.; Chen X.; Wen J.; Yan M.; Wang Y.; Xie P.; Mao Y.; Tang C.; Wu J.; Tian C.; Wang Y.; Zhong L.; Zhao C.
Article.Abstract: Rhizobial nitrogen fixation in legume nodules requires precise spatial and temporal coordination between host and bacterial gene expression. Here, we applied spatial enhanced resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) to profile Medicago nodules across five developmental stages, generating a co-transcriptomic atlas of nodule development. Using a mixed-probe capture strategy, we simultaneously detected host and rhizobial transcripts within the same tissue sections, enabling analysis of host-microbe transcriptional coordination during symbiosis. We identified dynamic changes in host cell composition and developmental trajectories and uncovered two transcription factors, MtERF82 and MtDOF53, required for maintenance of the indeterminate nodule meristem. Rhizobial and host genes exhibited stage- and zone-specific expression patterns along the nodule apex-to-base axis. Notably, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated stress responses in both host cells and rhizobia were linked to symbiotic nitrogen fixation. Functional analyses further showed that MtERF71 and MtCBF1 promote nitrogen fixation by regulating ROS homeostasis and activating key symbiotic genes, highlighting stress signaling as an integral component of mutualistic symbiosis.

Article.Title: Cellular scaling laws in the mammalian brain
Article.Authors: Chen F.; Macosko E.
Article.Abstract: Recent whole-brain cell atlases have uncovered a consistent cytoarchitectural feature: the greatest diversity of discrete neuronal cell types resides not in the regions with the most neurons (e.g., the cortex and cerebellum) but rather in deep subcortical structures like the hypothalamus and brain stem. We propose that this discrepancy reflects a fundamental algorithmic division in the vertebrate brain between a "learning subsystem" and a "steering subsystem." The learning subsystem (cortex, striatum, and cerebellum) scales via the replication of repetitive modules to maximize computational capacity, analogous to scaling up parameters in machine learning models. By contrast, the steering subsystem (hypothalamus, pallidum, and brainstem) scales via diversification of bespoke cell types to encode innate drives and reflexes, functioning as a high-dimensional biological "reward function." This framework explains the divergence in how evolution has influenced these subsystems and offers a unified lens for understanding brain architecture and the etiology of brain disease; furthermore, it may inform model designs for artificial intelligence.

Article.Title: A telomere-to-telomere map of somatic mutation burden and functional impact in a cancer
Article.Authors: Sohn M.; Dubocanin D.; Vollger M.; Kwon Y.; Minkina A.; Munson K.; Hart S.; Ranchalis J.; Parmalee N.; Sedeño-Cortés A.; Ou J.; Neph S.; Au N.; Bohaczuk S.; Carroll B.; Frazar C.; Harvey W.; Hoekzema K.; Huang M.; Jacques C.; Jensen D.; Kolar J.; Lee R.; Lin J.; Loy K.
Article.Abstract: Cancer genomes harbor extensive somatic genetic and epigenetic variation, yet large portions of the genome remain inaccessible to conventional reference-based analyses. Here, we demonstrate that pairing a near-telomere-to-telomere (near-T2T) diploid assembly of a donor with deep short- and long-read sequencing of their melanoma reveals that 16% of somatic variants localize to sequences absent from GRCh38, with satellite repeats acting as hotspots for UV-associated mutagenesis. Centromere kinetochore binding domains emerge as focal sites of chromosome arm aneuploidy breakpoints and somatic genetic variation, features we further demonstrate are also present in non-cancerous tissues. By contrast, extensive epigenetic remodeling of kinetochore binding domains appears specific to oncogenesis. Single-molecule telomere analyses reconstruct the cycle of telomere erosion and telomerase-mediated extension during tumor evolution, while haplotype-resolved chromatin maps reveal widespread somatic epimutations impacting regulatory elements. Together, these findings define previously inaccessible dimensions of somatic variation and establish a framework for telomere-to-telomere studies of human mosaicism.

Article.Title: Somatic epimutations cap genetic determinism in the human diploid chromatin epigenome
Article.Authors: Vollger M.; Swanson E.; Neph S.; Mallory B.; Dubocanin D.; Ho C.; Cheng Y.; Ranchalis J.; Munson K.; Sedeno-Cortes A.; Mudeppa D.; Fondrie W.; Bohaczuk S.; Dippel M.; Mao Y.; Parmalee N.; Harvey W.; Kwon Y.; Garcia G.; Hoekzema K.; Meyer J.; Cicek M.; Eichler E.; Noble W.; Witten D.
Article.Abstract: Diploid human cells contain two non-identical genomes, and differences in their regulation underlie human development and disease. We present Fiber-seq inferred regulatory elements (FIRE) and show that FIRE provides a more comprehensive and quantitative snapshot of the accessible chromatin landscape across the 6 Gbp diploid human genome, overcoming previously unrecognized biases in existing regulatory element catalogs. FIRE enables comprehensive detection of haplotype-selective chromatin accessibility (HSCA), exposing imprinted elements lacking underlying parent-of-origin differences in DNA methylation and gene regulatory modules that permit genes to escape X chromosome inactivation. We uncover that the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus harbors the most HSCA in immune cells, where we resolve specific transcription factor (TF) binding events disrupted by disease-associated variants. Finally, we demonstrate that the regulatory landscape of a cell is littered with autosomal somatic chromatin epimutations that are propagated by clonal expansions to create mitotically stable and non-genetically deterministic chromatin alterations.

Article.Title: Comprehensive benchmarking of somatic mutation detection by the SMaHT Network
Article.Authors: Abyzov A.; Natu A.; Voshall A.; Sedeño-Cortés A.; Burn A.; Boyle A.; Veit A.; Urban A.; Cheng A.; Runnels A.; Mo A.; Srinivasa A.; Leonardson A.; Kriz A.; Stergachis A.; Russell A.; Schroeder A.; D’Avino A.; Ruttenberg A.; Caplin A.; Minkina A.; Cho A.; Panda A.; Tsirigos A.; Tariq A.
Article.Abstract: Somatic mosaicism is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of human biology, yet the detection of somatic mutations remains challenging. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network conducted large-scale benchmarking experiments involving cell lines and donor tissues to evaluate sequencing technologies, experimental approaches, and computational methods for detecting different types of somatic mutations, generating community resources with >1,000× short-read and 100-400× long-read data for nine analyzed samples. We determined effective strategies for utilizing short- and long-read sequencing for mutation detection and demonstrated that using donor-specific and pangenome-inferred diploid assemblies improved calling, extending mutation catalogs to challenging genomic regions. We benchmarked six duplex technologies and showed that single-cell sequencing resolves cell-type-specific mutational patterns and heterogeneity. Our results indicate that bulk, single-cell, and duplex analyses are complementary and that leveraging all three provides comprehensive characterization of mosaicism within tissues. Together, these findings provide the scientific and clinical communities with a roadmap for accurate genome-wide somatic mutation analysis.

Article.Title: Mitochondria-targeted tetraoxanes initiate lipid peroxidation to drive ferroptosis and tumor suppression
Article.Authors: Pan Z.; Wong M.; Lu Y.; Mao J.; Wang F.; Gu X.; Huang K.; Shi T.; Wu T.; Zhu Y.; Zhang Y.; Chen E.; Han J.; Qiu Y.; Zhou L.; Li Y.; Lin P.; Li Z.; Deng S.; Fang Y.; Xie Q.; Cao J.; Naowarojna N.; Yang D.; Zou Y.
Article.Abstract: Ferroptosis is implicated as a vulnerability in multiple cancers, yet approaches for effectively inducing ferroptosis in vivo are limited. Bypassing conventional strategies targeting the antiferroptotic glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) proteins, we designed metabolic initiators of lipid peroxidation (MILPOs) and developed the compounds WMK-1/2, which contain tetraoxane radical-generating and mitochondria-targeting groups, as de novo ferroptosis inducers. WMK-1 localizes primarily to mitochondria, induces local lipid peroxidation, and impairs oxidative phosphorylation. WMK-1 induces a "mito-ferroptosis" sub-pathway that skips GPX4 inhibition as a prerequisite, can be rescued by lipophilic radical-trapping antioxidants, yet is minimally sensitive to acyl-coenzyme A synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) perturbation and long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation, and evades retinol-mediated protection. Instead, WMK-1-induced cell death requires labile Fe2+ and can be selectively suppressed by ɑ-lipoic acid, an endogenous, mitochondria-resident antioxidant. WMK-1/2 are bioavailable and exhibit significant efficacy in tumor suppression by eliciting ferroptosis in multiple cancer models and augmenting the antitumor effects of immune-checkpoint blockers. Our work provides a protein-targeting-independent metabolic ferroptosis induction strategy for potential cancer therapy.

Article.Title: A microbiome-bile acid axis mediates protection from chronic liver disease in females
Article.Authors: Li M.; Kuang J.; Chen T.; Ding K.; Chen Y.; Jiao F.; Li Y.; Luo P.; Xia L.; Zhang H.; Wang J.; Zheng D.; Zhao M.; Sun T.; Chao X.; Guo Y.; Zhu M.; Sun Y.; Xia X.; Ge K.; Qu C.; Yao C.; Xie G.; Zhou K.; Louca P.
Article.Abstract: Sex-based differences in chronic liver disease (CLD) incidence and progression are well documented, yet the mechanistic basis of this sexual disparity remains elusive. Here, leveraging a large-scale metabolomics database comprising 9,254 individuals, we identify the endogenous bile acid, isoursodeoxycholic acid (isoUDCA), as a candidate mediator of female-associated hepatoprotection. We trace the origin of isoUDCA to a bacterial consortium, which is selectively enriched by estrogen through shaping a specialized intestinal microenvironment. This upregulates the intracellular transporter STARD4 and its functionally coupled downstream enzyme CYP7B1, thereby facilitating intracellular cholesterol handling and metabolic conversion. Article.Title: The pyrin inflammasome senses OCTN2-mediated uptake of extracellular ʟ-carnitine from muscle injury or ingestion
Article.Authors: Elliott E.; Yoshida T.; Nakandakari S.; Pope S.; Zhang C.; Nottoli T.; Chae J.; Kastner D.; Flavell R.; Dixit V.; Rathinam V.; Sutterwala F.; Wang A.
Article.Abstract: Red-meat-containing diets are epidemiologically associated with diseases of chronic inflammation, while diets that restrict red meat improve health. Yet, it is uncertain how red meat incites inflammation. Here, we discover that ʟ-carnitine, an amino acid highly concentrated in skeletal muscle myocytes, drives inflammasome activation in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-challenged mice and LPS-primed murine and human macrophages. We find that extracellular ʟ-carnitine represses mevalonate synthesis, thereby triggering activation of the pyrin inflammasome, downstream of cellular import by the high-affinity ʟ-carnitine transporter OCTN2. We find that the inflammatory response to skeletal muscle injury also requires pyrin and OCTN2. Thus, in summary, we identify macrophages as sentinels of exogenous and endogenous extracellular ʟ-carnitine that serve as a proxy for skeletal myocyte damage, and we open the field to examine the mechanistic basis for how excess dietary intake of carnitine-rich food drives inflammatory disease.

Article.Title: Contrasting demographic impacts of Roman colonization and early medieval migrations in the Iberian Peninsula
Article.Authors: Carrión P.; Olalde I.; McCormick M.; Harper K.; Garcia-Collado M.; Villalba-Mouco V.; Jiménez-Arenas J.; Coromina N.; Vivó D.; Vergès J.; Costa A.; Botella Ortega D.; Bustamante-Álvarez M.; Heras-Mora J.; Ortega-Ruiz R.; Chaves C.; Quirós-Castillo J.; Roig J.; Suárez-Padilla J.; Navarro-Luengo I.; Cuadrado-Prieto M.; Aguilera I.; Morera J.; Catalán R.; Cerdeño M.
Article.Abstract: It has been unclear how Roman and later Germanic political control shaped the demography of Iberia and how it differed from other parts of Europe. We report genetic data from 243 ancient individuals dating to 100-800 CE, analyzed alongside 58 previously published individuals. In Roman times, we document an influx of people with ancestry from the Eastern Mediterranean and an influx of North Africans, especially in the center and south. Beginning in the 5th century, Germanic and Alan (Sarmatian) groups assumed political control. Although we identify individuals with Central-Northern European-associated ancestry, including siblings buried ∼725 km apart, the Hispano-Roman population remained continuous in Iberia. These demographic patterns contrast sharply with those in Britain, where major demographic change followed Rome's collapse, and with those in the central Mediterranean, where both periods were associated with profound transformations. Together, these findings highlight regional variation in admixture and continuity across post-Roman Europe.

Article.Abstract: Efficient integration of gene-length cargos in vivo remains challenging. Extensive engineering generated elements capable of the efficient and stable insertion of reporter genes in human cells using RNA templates introduced in trans, which we term Gene Writers. Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNA delivery enabled in vivo CAR-T cell generation and stable B cell depletion in a humanized mouse model. Article.Title: Proteomic atlas of T cell exhaustion defines proteostatic collapse
Article.Authors: Shuttleworth S.; Bauer M.; Province D.; Kelliher J.; Scharping N.; Monell A.; Rogers L.; Williams T.; Dawson G.; Wallis K.; Alkam D.; Edmondson J.; Fil D.; Storey A.; Bolding A.; Edmondson R.; Byrum S.; Beenken K.; Mackintosh S.; Goldrath A.; Tackett A.; Koss B.
Article.Abstract: T cell exhaustion limits the success of cancer immunotherapies, yet the proteomic changes underlying this dysfunctional state remain poorly understood. These studies identified pathways regulated through transcriptional and post-translational mechanisms, including degradative and nondegradative ubiquitin modifications, and uncovered widespread changes in proteostasis, metabolism, and DNA repair. These findings position the collapse of proteostasis as a central, underappreciated feature of T cell exhaustion and reveal opportunities to restore T cell function. We demonstrate that overexpression of the E3 ligase RNF166 enhances T cell persistence in vitro and in vivo. This work defines proteome-turnover dynamics as a critical regulatory layer in progressive T cell dysfunction, with broad implications for advancing cancer immunotherapy through manipulation of E3 ligases.

Article.Authors: Naowarojna N.; Gu X.; Pan Z.; Yu J.; Huang K.; Zeng Y.; Xie Y.; Zhang Y.; Wang F.; Mao J.; Yu Y.; Wu T.; Yu J.; Liu S.; Xiao S.; Bai L.; Li D.; Wu Z.; Wei C.; Li Q.; Yao H.; Zhang X.; Li Y.; Xie G.; Gao L.
Article.Abstract: Ferroptosis is implicated in multiple human diseases, but the lack of bioavailable inducers has limited its physiological study and therapeutic translation. Here, we report KY0418, a selective covalent inhibitor of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) featuring an isourea warhead, with high plasma stability and broad tissue distribution after oral dosing in mice. KY0418 specifically targets GPX4SeCys46 to induce ferroptosis hallmarks in human and mouse cancer cell lines, with greater selectivity than existing inhibitors. In a standardizable acute-liver-injury mouse model, KY0418 triggers ferroptotic ultrastructural changes matching those of established inducers, and systemic administration remodels tissue metabolism and generates hydroxyl radicals detectable by a chemiluminescent probe. Subcutaneous tumors from different cancers exhibited variable responses to KY0418 treatment, from no effect to about 70% growth inhibition, but KY0418 consistently eradicated circulating tumor cells and suppressed metastasis across multiple cancer models. These findings position KY0418 as a tool for advancing in vivo ferroptosis research and its clinical translation.

Article.Title: Metazoan lagging-strand DNA synthesis is distributive
Article.Authors: Lynch L.; Park J.; Chistol G.
Article.Abstract: DNA's anti-parallel structure presents a topological challenge to the replisome, as leading and lagging strands must be synthesized in opposite directions. How lagging-strand synthesis is coordinated with leading-strand synthesis remains unresolved in eukaryotes. To address this question, we directly visualized the dynamics of lagging-strand polymerases Pol α and Pol δ at active replication forks using single-molecule imaging in Xenopus nuclear extracts. Surprisingly, we find that neither Pol α nor Pol δ is stably tethered to the replisome. Instead, lagging-strand synthesis occurs distributively and entails the rapid recruitment of new molecules of Pol α and Pol δ for each Okazaki fragment. Consequently, leading- and lagging-strand synthesis are not intrinsically coupled. We propose that metazoans solve the problem of anti-parallel replication not by actively coordinating leading- and lagging-strand synthesis, but instead simply by recruiting new polymerases to synthesize each Okazaki fragment.

Article.Authors: Bell H.; Nair K.; Tison K.; Liao P.; Lei H.; El-Derany M.; Yisimayi A.; Zhang H.; Rebernick R.; Wang W.; Adachi Y.; Castillo C.; Das N.; An J.; Sutton V.; Lin X.; Lin H.; Wang X.; Li Y.; Vatan L.; Aboud A.; Wei S.; Gijon M.; Goodwin S.; Shah Y.

Article.Title: Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance
Article.Authors: Singh A.; Martin L.; Sršen M.; Guttesen F.; Hu B.; Ito Y.; Pedersen S.; Kamounah F.; Pauly F.; Pittelkow M.; Lü J.; Hedegård P.; Tal O.
Article.Abstract: For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage's polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4-6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.

Article.Title: Cave stalagmites document global patterns in monsoon rainfall over the past 450,000 years
Article.Abstract: A 450,000-year stalagmite record of rainfall in the Amazon Basin , combined with existing Asian records, shows that the global monsoon system has oscillated regularly, strengthening in one hemisphere while weakening in the other. However, during intervals of warmth and warming climate, monsoons in both hemispheres failed for millennia. The South American and Asian monsoons have both weakened during past periods of rapid warming.

Article.Title: The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology
Article.Authors: Xing S.; Wu Z.; Shao Q.; Ge J.; Bennett E.; Rao H.; Lin S.; Zhao Y.; Liu F.; Liu Y.; Zhou K.; Feng X.; Jiangzuo Q.; Fu Q.
Article.Abstract: The taxonomy and phylogeny of late Middle Pleistocene hominins in East Asia remain highly debated1. Xujiayao, a key representative assemblage with many fossils and a clear stratigraphy dating to around 199-138 thousand years ago, has been extensively studied, but its evolutionary position remains uncertain. Here, to clarify this, we analysed Xujiayao material through both palaeoproteomic analysis and morphological comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo. Proteomic analysis of two specimens identified 18 endogenous proteins, and the Denisova-specific COL1A2-996 R>K mutation strongly supported their affiliation with the Denisovan lineage. Extended analysis identifies a set of shared morphological traits between Denisovan fossils (Xujiayao and Harbin) and other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong), indicating that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage. This analysis provides a comprehensive view of Denisovan features, showing both traits reminiscent of Homo erectus (such as a thick cranial vault) and those characteristic of modern humans (for example, a strongly arched temporal squama). They also share features with late Neanderthals, such as the structure of the temporal labyrinth and the presence of a suprainiac fossa. Notably, Denisovans are distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.

Article.Title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes
Article.Authors: Kim K.; Gardner C.; Cullen A.; Stelzer J.; Cho K.; Sharma A.; Nemera M.; Law T.; Naz H.; Zhao G.; Gabel H.; Patti G.; Musiek E.; Ahn T.; Yi J.
Article.Abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.

Article.Title: Functional architecture of the human insula
Article.Authors: Quabs J.; Pantis S.; Chen G.; Huang W.; Ma E.; del Vecchio M.; Lyu D.; Wang C.; Avanzini P.; Buch V.; Ramayya A.; Caspers S.; Vogel H.; Parvizi J.
Article.Abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7-10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal-posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral-posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior-polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

Article.Title: Additive manufacturing of ultralong and architected single crystals
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Cui Y.; Wang J.; Han X.; Ji Z.; Liang Z.; Zhang C.; Marian J.; Li Z.; Lu T.; Xu T.; Zhang J.; Cui W.; Liu W.; Fang D.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Single-crystal materials are indispensable for high-performance applications, yet their deployment remains constrained by conventional manufacturing techniques that depend on strict quasi-steady thermal conditions1. This requirement fundamentally conflicts with the intense cyclic thermal fluctuations inherent to additive manufacturing2, historically preventing the 3D printing of large or architected single crystals. Here we present a free-form additive manufacturing approach that resolves this contradiction by using delicately controlled alternating and pulsed heat inputs to govern and direct single-crystal growth. Using this method, we demonstrate the fabrication of metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V alongside, to our knowledge, the first single-crystal lattice structures containing complex zigzag ligaments, effectively eliminating theoretical size constraints for single-crystal components. The resulting bulk single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V exhibits an order-of-magnitude increase in creep resistance over standard grain-size scaling predictions, driven by the synergistic elimination of grain boundaries and an additive manufacturing-induced hierarchical α/β-architecture that regulates dislocation density, mobility and void evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broad applicability of this technique by printing single crystals of hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys. Our work introduces a large-scale method for single-crystal additive manufacturing, expanding the accessible materials library and enabling high-performance, complex geometries previously unattainable by classical methods.

Article.Title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root
Article.Authors: Oliva M.; Stuart T.; Tang D.; Khan A.; Clement O.; Makosa D.; Poppe D.; Pflueger J.; Jabbari J.; Gigante S.; Dragwidge J.; Petterson M.; Whelan J.; Lewsey M.; Lister R.
Article.Abstract: Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1. Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types.

Article.Title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
Article.Authors: Battini L.; Slough M.; Kaur R.; Guo L.; Florez C.; Serris A.; Meola A.; Lasso G.; Tischler N.; Alvarez R.; Lambe U.; Khera L.; Wang J.; Scott R.; Garrido J.; Barria M.; Josleyn N.; Rey F.; Herbert A.; McLellan J.; Jangra R.; Chandran K.; Guardado-Calvo P.
Article.Abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms-occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus-receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.

Article.Title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation
Article.Authors: Meier R.; Morgand E.; Mezine F.; Mengel M.; Mangiola M.; Mohiuddin M.; Montgomery R.; Loupy A.
Article.Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

Article.Title: Octupole-driven spin torque switching of antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions
Article.Authors: Kang J.; Hamdi M.; Cheung S.; Yuan L.; Elekhtiar M.; Matt E.; Rogers W.; Meo A.; Lim P.; Tey M.; D’Addario A.; Konakanchi S.; Athas J.; Arpaci S.; Devincenti A.; Wan L.; Mehta S.; Zogbi N.; Sangwan V.; Incorvia J.; Fowlie J.; Upadhyaya P.; Carpentieri M.; Dravid V.; Hersam M.
Article.Abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions based on ferromagnets are canonical devices in spintronics, with wide-ranging applications in data storage, computing and sensing. They simultaneously exhibit mechanisms for electrical detection and control of magnetic order through the tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR)1-5 and spin-transfer torque6-9 effects, respectively. It was long assumed that neither of these effects could be sizeable in all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions (AATJs), considering that they have no net magnetization. However, it was recently shown that AATJs based on chiral antiferromagnets do exhibit TMR due to their non-relativistic momentum-dependent spin polarization and cluster magnetic octupole moment, which are manifestations of their spin-split band structure10-13. However, the reciprocal effect, that is, the antiferromagnetic counterpart of spin-transfer torque, has been assumed non-existent due to the total electric current being spin-neutral. Here we report nanoscale AATJs that display this reciprocal effect, which we term octupole-driven spin-transfer torque (OTT). We demonstrate current-induced OTT switching of PtMn3|MgO|PtMn3 AATJs, with a TMR value of 363% at room temperature and switching current densities of the order of 10 MA cm-2. Our theoretical modelling explains the origin of OTT in terms of the imbalance between intra- and inter-sublattice spin currents across the AATJ, and, equivalently, in terms of the non-zero net cluster octupole polarization of each PtMn3 layer. This work establishes a new materials platform for antiferromagnetic spintronics and provides a pathway towards deeply scaled magnetic memory and room-temperature terahertz technologies.

Article.Title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
Article.Authors: Woo J.; Williamson M.; Choi D.; Akdemir E.; Zlatkov T.; Yu K.; Kwon W.; Maleki E.; Ko Y.; Sanchez K.; Maleki H.; Choi J.; Serin-Harmanci A.; Deneen B.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51- astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51- astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.

Article.Title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
Article.Authors: Gatti L.; Cunha C.; Blas J.; Denning A.; Reis M.; Marani L.; Arai E.; Messias C.; Conciani D.; Miller J.; Schumacher V.; Naccarato K.; Marengo J.; Alencar A.; Soler L.; Almeida C.; Domingues L.; Correia C.; Neves R.; Nobre C.; Corrêa S.; Campbell E.; Johnson J.; Berry J.; Sanchez A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation 1–5 , rising tree mortality 6–8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest 9–11 . Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions 1–4,11,12 . Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable 1,9,13 . Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts 9,14–17 . Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO 2 measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 , with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 ) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr −1 ) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.

Article.Title: WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry
Article.Authors: Vuillemenot L.; Morales L.; Dragoi C.; Pennycook B.; Harris E.; Lin L.; Weston W.; Brown J.; Graham E.; Moulin L.; Andrew I.; Roumelioti G.; Montoya A.; Game L.; Young G.; Datta K.; Shliaha P.; Novák B.; Yamano H.; Barr A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint 1–3 . Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53- mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in TP53- wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex–cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/C CDH1 ). WEE1 phosphorylates CDH1 ( FZR1 ) at key residues that mediate the interaction between CDH1 and APC/C. Cells with loss of function of WEE1 during G0/G1 have delayed S phase entry, impaired G1/S transition, abnormal S phase accumulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21 Cip1/Kip1 and a p21-dependent G2 arrest. Reduced expression of APC/C CDH1 or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.

Article.Title: Touch-sensing digital pixel fibre enables interactive garment GUI
Article.Authors: Fu H.; Li Z.; Chaturvedi S.; Zhang X.; Li X.; Li Q.; Khudiyev T.
Article.Abstract: Wearable computing promises to transform human interaction with information, yet conventional graphical user interfaces (GUIs) rely on planar, rigid displays incompatible with textiles, which are composed of one-dimensional fibres. Despite recent progress1,2 in flexible and fibre-based displays, bridging this fundamental dimensional mismatch remains challenging because existing approaches do not naturally provide the digitally addressable, high-throughput, information-rich interfaces required for interactive GUIs. Here we present a digital pixel fibre integrating addressable pixels, a common propagation-axis interconnection for scalable in-fibre circuitry and a coaxial sensing layer for fibre-level touch localization. Microelectronic components and a touch-gated resistive path system form a linear circuit that acts as both an interactive display backbone and a computational bus, while peripheral multimodal fibre sensors and actuators enable physiological, inertial, optical, and acoustic input and output. We integrate these fibres into the forearm portion of a garment sleeve to realize a GUI with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30-frame-per-second refresh rate and 8-bit colour depth. It supports dynamic graphics, integrated audio-video playback, wireless data exchange and interactive computing functions, while maintaining the flexibility, washability, breathability and mechanical robustness of everyday textiles. By merging display, sensing and computation within a single fibre, this work establishes a scalable platform for intrinsically interactive textiles, opening pathways toward garments that operate as fully integrated computational systems.

Article.Title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
Article.Authors: Huang Q.; Iida N.; Isobe N.; Kabe T.; Omura T.; Ilangovan M.; Kimura S.; Seok J.; Nomaki H.; Kasuya K.; Iwata T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The accumulation of persistent plastics in the ocean is causing wide-ranging environmental problems 1–3 . Some commercially available compostable plastics 4–7 , developed to address these issues, degrade efficiently under industrial composting conditions; however, their degradation in marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains limited 8–10 . Here we demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate- co -adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate- co -terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m. Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months. Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m. In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation. The mechanical properties of enzyme-embedded polyesters were similar to those of enzyme-free polyesters. Chemical analysis confirmed the formation of low-molecular-mass degradation products and biochemical oxygen demand measurements supported the mineralization of the enzyme-embedded polyesters. The enzyme-embedding strategy enables enhanced marine degradation of compostable polyesters and represents a potential solution to marine plastic pollution.

Article.Title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement
Article.Authors: Qi L.; Sheng Y.; Zhang W.; Ni Y.; He L.; Li B.; Wang A.; Zhu W.; Bell A.; Liu Z.
Article.Abstract: Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1-5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6-12. Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13. Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14-18. Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation. We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h. The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively. Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation. Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes.

Article.Title: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
Article.Authors: Sergio F.; Natsukawa H.; Tanferna A.; Chicano J.; Carro F.; Soriguer R.; Hiraldo F.; Blas J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Interactions among species are increasingly recognized as key determinants of climate change impacts on ecosystems 1–5 . However, we know little about how climatic perturbations affect interactions among top vertebrate predators. Here we show that, when an emergent disease caused the decline of shared prey (rabbits), after decades of neutral co-existence a mammalian carnivore (lynx) started to prey heavily on a top predatory raptor (kites). These predation bouts occurred exclusively under drought conditions and when lynx found rabbit remains under the raptor nests, consistent with the removal of a potential competitor. Drought-induced lynx predation depressed lifetime reproductive success and triggered territory abandonment and dispersal by the raptor, suggestive of a new arms race among predators. A reduction in raptor abundance was associated with an increase in an insectivorous bird (a small owl), showing that the new interaction had the potential to reach lower trophic levels. These results underline the importance of diet flexibility and mobility as important mediators of resilience to stressors. In the future, synergistic effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors may reshape the interactions and ecological roles of many apex predators, with potential cascading consequences for whole ecosystems. A key to forecasting the future impact of global change may reside in understanding how behavioural flexibility and interacting keystone species respond to interacting shocks.

Article.Title: The anatomy of a personal health agent
Article.Authors: Heydari A.; Gu K.; Srinivas V.; Yu H.; Paruchuri A.; Zhang Z.; Zhang Y.; He Q.; Palangi H.; Hammerquist N.; Metwally A.; Winslow B.; Kim Y.; Ayush K.; Yang Y.; Narayanswamy G.; Xu M.; Garrison J.; Schmidgall S.; Armento Lee A.; Vafeiadou J.; Graef B.; Galatzer-Levy I.; Schenck E.; Barakat A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored 1,2 . Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

Article.Title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis
Article.Authors: Yi Y.; Cao Z.; Wu K.; Ding H.; Fu L.; Gao W.; Li L.; Zhou L.; Zhou Z.; Dai L.; Lu Y.; Cheng L.
Article.Abstract: Anaerobic degradation of complex organic compounds to methane and carbon dioxide is common in the deep subsurface biosphere and has long been considered to require syntrophic cooperation, with methanogens confined to the terminal use of simple C1 and C2 substrates. Thermodynamic considerations, multi-omics analyses and microcosm experiments suggest that archaeal lineages are capable of methanogenic degradation of complex substrates1-6. However, experimental validation in pure culture was lacking. Here we report the isolation of a thermophilic archaeon, Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75, affiliated with Archaeoglobi, from a Chinese petroleum reservoir. Strain AA-75 not only converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, but also uses saturated fatty acids varying from C7:0 to C18:0 and unsaturated fatty acids including C16:1, C18:1 and C18:2 to produce methane. We term the latter lipotrophic methanogenesis, which integrates β-oxidation of fatty acids with the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway and the canonical methyl-tetrahydromethanopterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase complexes, together with an intracellular electron transfer system. A formaldehyde-methanol branch probably functions as an auxiliary route for C1 metabolism during methanogenesis. Methane produced from stearate is moderately 13C-enriched (δ13C-CH4 = -40.0‰ to -36.3‰), distinct from the strong 13C depletion characteristic of canonical methanogenic pathways. These findings demonstrate that methanogens can function as primary degraders of complex organic matter, challenging the classical syntrophic paradigm and calling for refinement of current models of carbon cycling in the deep subsurface biosphere.

Article.Title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
Article.Authors: Willemsen P.; Mason V.; Zelst V.; van Bergeijk V.; Breteler M.; Muller J.; Dermentzoglou D.; Vouziouris A.; van Veelen T.; Dzimballa S.; Wijnberg K.; Hoitink A.; Buring P.; Paul M.; Antonini A.; Bouma T.; Borsje B.
Article.Abstract: Salt marshes protect coastlines by attenuating wind waves with their elevated marsh platform and above-ground vegetation1. Confidence in the persistence of this service under a changing climate requires knowledge on how extreme storms damage the platform and vegetation; however, a comprehensive, quantified understanding of salt marsh-wave interactions under extreme events is lacking. A unique experiment was conducted by transferring intact salt marsh to one of the world's largest wave flumes, and subsequently exposing it to increasingly higher waves that reach up to 2 m significant wave height. We show that marsh substrates can persist with negligible erosion, despite cumulative wave exposure. By contrast, the vegetation was progressively damaged during continued wave exposure, gradually reducing vegetation-related wave attenuation. Results emphasize that vegetation was most effective in attenuating waves at low-energy marsh coasts (up to 1 m), where attenuation exceeded 10% (up to 50%), whereas attenuation at high-energy marsh coasts (wave height > 1 m) does not exceed 10%. Our global assessment supports the differentiation between low- and high-energetic conditions resulting from the flume experiment. Our results suggest that the marsh platform remains stable under extreme wave events and that substantial wave attenuation by marsh vegetation is limited to low-energy marsh coasts.
