Article.Title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
Article.Authors: Lee H.; Doğan C.; Koyuncu S.; Wehrmann M.; Artan M.; Petrovic D.; Loureiro R.; Sahu A.; Schnubel J.; Grobushkin P.; Prymidis D.; Georgomanolis T.; Sokol A.; Yang M.; Hoppe T.; Frezza C.; Vilchez D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species 1–3 , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans . Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2–BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

Article.Title: GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control
Article.Authors: Yu F.; Jiang L.; Liu H.; Yang S.; Yuan Y.; Jin H.; Liu J.; Liu X.; Dong Y.; Ren D.; Kang J.; Huang Y.; Meng Q.; Bai F.; Li Y.; Li S.; Liu H.; Zhao W.; Xiao J.; Chen Q.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondria are bound by a double membrane and are semiautonomous organelles, rendering them highly vulnerable to global and internal proteostatic stress1. Multiple surveillance mechanisms at proteostatic and inter-organellar levels have evolved to maintain mitochondrial integrity and cellular health2-7. However, the precise mechanisms by which proteostatic damage relays stress signals across organelles and how the quality surveillance machinery coordinates these functions remain unknown. Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network. Quantitative proteomic and correlative light-electron microscopy analysis revealed that SIMPA mediates inter-organellar communication via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes. Mechanistically, GRP75 coordinates SIMPA biogenesis and focally activates endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response pathways via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes for the targeted clearance of SIMPAs. Functionally, in both cellular and liver disease models, we found that a GRP75-dependent SIMPA signalling cascade attenuates mitochondrial stress and preserves mitochondrial integrity under proteotoxic stress. Overall, we show that SIMPAs, functioning as protein condensates, serve as a central cross-compartment communication hub for mitochondrial quality control, supporting cellular and organismal fitness.

Article.Title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language
Article.Authors: Dai F.; You S.; Zhu Y.; Gao Y.; Fu L.; Zhou X.; Su J.; Wang C.; Fan Y.; Tan Q.; Ma X.; Deng X.; Yu L.; Qian H.; He Y.; Ke Y.; Zhang Z.; Han C.; Chang X.; Zheng L.; Wang S.; Ji Y.; Hao K.; Cao L.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Programming biological function-designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks-is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1-3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein-text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.

Article.Title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
Article.Authors: Mishra S.; Payal N/A.; Evans D.; Bortey K.; Bootwala H.; Gonzalez-Gutierrez G.; Vázquez R.; Baker D.; Lewis J.
Article.Abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1-5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6-8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

Article.Title: Cortex-wide imaging in naturally behaving mice with 1-gram wireless mesoscopes
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Li A.; Yuan L.; Wang M.; Zhao W.; Wang Z.; Zang B.; Zhou Y.; Yu T.; Gao L.; Wu Y.; Zhu R.; Tian M.; Li K.; Wu J.; Dai P.; Dai Q.
Article.Abstract: Revealing how distributed cortical circuits coordinate behavior in freely moving animals remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience, constrained by limited fields of view, low throughput, and the tethering required by current miniaturized microscopes1-4. Here, we present Airscope, a wireless mesoscope delivering 4 μm lateral resolution across a 6 mm field of view at 12.5 Hz, weighing 1.0 gram. An aspheric-lens design achieves a 2.84× shorter total track length than previous miniaturized microscopes1,2,5,6 while matching the neuron yield of benchtop one-photon mesoscopes; a tailored wireless link supports cable-free calcium imaging from >8,500 neurons per animal (25‑fold increase). Paired with a zero-shot behavior analyzer, Airscope enables cortical imaging across rich behavioral conditions, including room-scale enriched arenas, swimming assays, and multi-organ implantation, with concurrent recording from multiple animals. Using Airscope, we demonstrate versatile applications of untethered cortical imaging across diverse behavioral paradigms. We identify cortical activity patterns across multiple dorsal regions that correlate with behavioral signatures of social dominance, and show dorsal-cortical population activity prospectively decodes competition outcomes across paired animals. We observe reward-location-associated cortical activity patterns during maze exploration, and characterize Granger-causal influence from spinal cord to cortex during fear conditioning, enabled by simultaneous brain-spinal recordings. By uniting large-scale, cellular-resolution recording with unconstrained behavior, Airscope makes naturalistic, multi-animal cortical recording experimentally practical, and provides a broadly accessible technology for systems neuroscience.

Article.Title: Nearly half of reef-building corals face elevated relative risk of extinction
Article.Authors: Obura D.; Polidoro B.; Cabada-Blanco F.; Linardich C.; Carpenter N.; Gutierrez L.; Kemppinen K.; Pettersson E.; Strongin K.; Aeby G.; Alliji K.; Alvarado J.; Alvarez-Filip L.; Casado de Amezua P.; Banaszak A.; Bayley D.; Bluemel J.; Cortés J.; Couce E.; Cowburn B.; Crabbe M.; Croquer A.; Dellisanti W.; DeVantier L.; Edwards A.
Article.Abstract: Coral reefs are diverse marine ecosystems that provide ecological functions and economic and social benefits across over 100 tropical countries. Warming driven by climate change is a primary threat to coral reefs and is increasing the frequency of global coral bleaching events. Here we reassessed the IUCN Red List status of 892 reef-building coral species, first assessed in 2008 1. Because species-level population trends are unavailable for most reef-building corals, population reductions were inferred using proxies based on global coral cover trends and projected annual severe bleaching under SSP2-4.5, both over three decades, adjusted using trait-based estimates of species vulnerability. Of the 774 species with sufficient data to be assessed, 340 (44%) were classified as threatened under IUCN Red List criteria. Thirty-three species were assessed as Critically Endangered, 251 as Endangered, and 56 as Vulnerable, most due to risk of population reduction associated with projected thermal stress. These findings predate the three hottest years on record and the fourth global coral bleaching event (2023-2025), and the first exceedance for an annual mean of the 1.5oC global warming threshold. The findings reinforce the importance of limiting further warming to maintain coral biodiversity and reef ecosystem function. The Red List assesses the relative extinction risk of species, whereby species are placed in categories of increasing risk by comparing their population size, decline and geographic range against standardised thresholds. The Red List does not predict whether or when a species may go extinct. As the ranges of coral species remain under-surveyed, future assessments would be strengthened by species-level population data and thermal-stress and recovery metrics that better capture range-representative dynamics.

Article.Title: Evaluating space-based methane detection through a one-year blind test
Article.Authors: Reuland F.; Adams T.; Sherwin E.; El Abbadi S.; Kort E.; Brandt A.
Article.Abstract: Space-based remote sensing allows detection and monitoring of large, concentrated methane sources worldwide1. However, independent evaluation of instruments and algorithms is limited, and new satellites and artificial intelligence techniques have not been tested under controlled, single-blind conditions2. Here we conduct a year-long, single-blind test involving 746 events: 481 methane releases of 9.5-1,183.7 kg h-1 and 265 blank controls. We released metered methane quantities in Arizona, USA, coinciding with overpasses from 12 government, commercial and non-profit satellites. Fifteen analysis teams from nine countries generated more than 2,250 estimates, making this, to our knowledge, the largest controlled test so far and one of the first evaluations of the instruments EMIT, Tanager-1 (Carbon Mapper) and GHOSt. Performance is heterogeneous: 'built-for-purpose' instruments designed to target methane demonstrate excellent detection performance (92-100% true positive rate, 0-11% false positive rate) and quantification accuracy (slope 0.83-1.00, 44% mean absolute percentage error). Instruments repurposed for methane sensing perform more variably (detection rates 62-88%, 46% mean absolute percentage error); still, many demonstrate significant skill. Broad land scanners detect poorly at tested rates but have consistent global coverage and historical archives, motivating additional work. Artificial intelligence-based methods show promise, but caution is warranted; 79% of false positives emerge from these methods. Ground-measured cloud cover >20% degraded performance across systems, raising concerns for use in some locations. Our findings show that satellite-based measurements can achieve accurate detection and quantification of methane point sources when the source location is approximately known.

Article.Title: Intrinsic physicochemical activity at microplastic–water interfaces
Article.Authors: Qian N.; Zhao R.; Chan K.; Vuong V.; Gao X.; Zhao Z.; LaCour R.; Dai Y.; Stapleton P.; Yan B.; Head-Gordon T.; Min W.
Article.Abstract: Plastics have become an integral part of our modern society, largely because they are generally regarded as chemically inert under normal circumstances. However, plastics fragmented into microplastics (less than 5 mm in size) have recently raised significant public concerns, and have been detected widely across ecosystems and human tissues with increasing environmental and health risks1-5. Here we show that commodity microplastics exhibit intrinsic physicochemical activity in water, manifested by the spontaneous generation of reactive oxygen species that increases with interfacial hydrophobicity and strongly correlates with interfacial electrostatics. Ab initio calculations support these observations and reveal that hydroxide oxidation becomes energetically more favourable at increasingly hydrophobic microplastic-water interfaces through the combined effects of partial solvation and electrostatics. These interfacial properties and the resulting oxidative chemistry have direct implications for biomolecular adsorption, protein aggregation, and even cellular damage. Together, our findings challenge the prevailing paradigm of plastic inertness, identify a possibly overlooked mechanism for the detrimental effects of microplastics on health and the environment, and contribute to a fundamental understanding of the structure-activity relationship of interfacial water, which may inform the design of safer and more sustainable plastic materials.

Article.Title: Hidden reaction pathways inform additive engineering for perovskite LEDs
Article.Authors: Baek S.; Yang Y.; Wu P.; Yang H.; Ali M.; Kok H.; Luo X.; Shao W.; Choi H.; Kim J.; Guo L.; Huang L.; Rand B.; Dou L.
Article.Abstract: Perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) have emerged as a promising class of solution-processed light-emitting devices, combining high efficiency with facile fabrication1-5. Amino-acid-based molecular additives are widely used to regulate crystallization and suppress defects in perovskite thin films6-8, yet these molecules are chemically reactive in precursor solutions, in which their transformations and products remain poorly understood. Here we resolve and control the hidden solution-phase chemistry of a ubiquitous additive, 5-aminovaleric acid (5AVA), whose solution-phase reactivity has remained unclear6,9-15. We show that 5AVA undergoes competing in situ reactions during precursor preconditioning, yielding two chemically and functionally distinct products: a beneficial organoamidinium zwitterion and a detrimental Lewis-base lactam. By explaining this reaction dichotomy and establishing targeted reaction-pathway control, we selectively use the beneficial species. Direct synthesis and incorporation of the purified zwitterion decouple its intrinsic passivation function from confounding by-products, yielding perovskite films with a near-unity mean peak photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of 97.2% and PeLEDs with a champion external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 37.1%, alongside a mean peak EQE of 32.8%. Finally, we demonstrate that this reaction-pathway control concept can be extended to further additive chemistries and emission colours, highlighting its potential as a chemistry-driven strategy for rational additive design in PeLEDs.

Article.Title: Evidence for multi-Li+ clustering in lithium-ion battery electrolytes
Article.Authors: Stevenson J.; Agarwal G.; Debnath S.; Goldsmith Z.; Mondal M.; Svirinovsky-Arbeli A.; Yeu I.; Metlay A.; Kwon Y.; Bhai L.; Guha R.; Keeler E.; Weber J.; Steingart D.; Marbella L.; Urban A.; Jacobson L.; Halls M.; Friesner R.
Article.Abstract: In lithium-ion batteries, the bulk solvation structure of the electrolyte is a major determinant of the physical and electrochemical properties of the cell, for example, conductivity, viscosity, salt dissociation and subsequent reactivity, the electrochemical stability window (and thus solid electrolyte interphase formation), and the composition of the electrochemical double layer1-3. However, elucidation of this structure at an atomic level of detail has been challenging to accomplish via a purely experimental approach. Here we combine machine-learning-enabled atomistic simulations4-16, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, electrochemical data3,17-20 and quantum-chemical calculations to reveal previously unstudied multi-Li+ complexes without bound anions that are uniquely facile for reduction. This insight explains the success of empirically chosen ethylene-carbonate-containing solvent mixtures and provides a foundation for the rational design of improved electrolytes. Furthermore, our machine-learning force-field-based lithium-ion-battery electrolyte simulations accurately reproduce a wide range of condensed-phase experiments3,21-24, despite being parameterized to only quantum-chemical gas-phase cluster calculations, and hence provide a compelling demonstration that machine-learning force-field-based models developed from first principles can robustly represent a complex chemical system to atomic resolution.

Article.Title: Clasping folds enable superior elastic strength of graphene films
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Liao Y.; Huang J.; Shen C.; Chen L.; Li X.; Ding D.; Zhang M.; Peng L.; Li K.; Li P.; Liu Y.; Xu Z.; Pang K.; Xu Z.; Gao C.
Article.Abstract: Two-dimensional graphene sheets show strong potential for use in fabrication of macroscopic films, as they have exceptional mechanical properties owing to their in-plane strength1-6. Improvements in the stacking order of flat two-dimensional sheets have led to corresponding improvements in the strength and toughness of such films7-11. In addition, modulation of the spatial conformation of individual units has enabled the development of benchmark materials with superior properties12,13; however, this has remained elusive in the case of two-dimensional sheets. Here we report a strategy for preparation of graphene films with a combination of high strength (2.9 GPa), toughness (84.5 MJ m-3) and elastic strain (5%). We attribute these performance gains to a fold-clasping lamellar structure achieved by modular assembly of surface-folded multilayer graphene oxide flakes. We identify a pull-to-push transition of force chain topology and propose a shear-lock stress transfer strategy in the fold-clasping lamellar graphene film that enables advances in mechanical properties. This work demonstrates the modular design of spatial conformation of two-dimensional flakes on a large scale and further improves the performance of macroscopic films for potential applications in lightweight structural components.

Article.Title: Large blind test of methane-detecting satellites lends credibility to emissions data
Article.Abstract: Twelve methane-sensing satellites were tested for their accuracy in measuring controlled-release events in the Arizona desert over a year-long blind test. Many were found to detect and quantify releases accurately, with instruments purpose-built for methane sensing performing best. Teams that used various methods to analyse satellite data in a methane controlled-release test achieved mostly accurate results.

Article.Title: Alveolar stem cells go beyond making gas-exchange cells to repair damaged airways
Article.Abstract: Alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells are the stem cells of the lung’s air sacs and are responsible for maintaining alveolar structure and gas exchange. A study that tracked AT2 cells shows that, after injury to the airway, they can also migrate between lung compartments and become bronchiolar cells to help repair damaged airways. Alveolar type 2 cells can migrate from the lung’s air sacs into the airways to repair damage there.

Article.Title: Lay of the land: terrestrial conservation efforts cover a wider area than thought
Article.Abstract: Governments around the world have pledged to conserve 30% of the terrestrial realm by 2030, but official data suggest that the target is barely halfway to being met. A combined global and national-level data set now shows that up to 27% of land area is conserved, but gaps in ecological representation remain. Coverage of protected and conserved areas is higher than expected, but ecological representativeness could be improved.

Article.Title: Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K
Article.Authors: Cook D.; Chen X.; O’Leary M.; Rao S.; Wang W.; Belcher C.; Payne M.; Borges P.; Lee T.; Devaraj A.; Asta M.; Lavernia E.; Apelian D.; Minor A.; Liu D.; Kumar P.; Ritchie R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Plastic deformation in body-centred cubic (bcc) metals and alloys is conventionally mediated by screw dislocations. Their temperature-sensitive motion is attributed to a steep rise in strength with decreasing temperature that constricts plastic zones at crack tips, leading to a ductile-to-brittle transition 1 . Here we evaluated the mechanical properties of group IV–V bcc refractory alloys with similar electronic structures at 20 K and found that these materials instead exhibit a plateau in tensile yield strength and fracture toughness as a function of temperature, with no apparent ductile-to-brittle transition. This behaviour arises from the global activation of twinning and an ω-phase transformation, which nucleate dislocations at interfaces before global dislocation motion. The initial mechanism is temperature insensitive and controls yielding, thereby preventing a crack-tip plastic zone from constricting with decreasing temperature.

Article.Title: Parity-dependent coupling of molecular spin chains to a superconductor
Article.Authors: Vaxevani K.; Ortuzar J.; Trivini S.; Monninger G.; Wang D.; Vilas-Varela M.; Gómez-Rodrigo L.; Peña D.; Pascual J.
Article.Abstract: Collective behaviour in quantum materials can produce excitations carrying only a fraction of the quantum numbers of their constituents. A notable case occurs in chains of spin-1 units1, in which a topological gap protects the interior of the chain, whereas spin-1/2 states, half the spin of the units that form it, emerge at the ends2. In short chains, these fractional edge spins couple to each other and their topological protection makes them attractive for hybrid spin-superconductor devices. Whether such fractionalization survives the proximity of a superconducting condensate, however, remains an open question. Here we grow molecular Haldane chains of antiferromagnetically coupled spin-1 triangulene units on a proximitized Au(111)/Nb(110) surface and resolve a parity-dependent coupling of their spin-1/2 edge states to the superconductor by scanning tunnelling spectroscopy. Odd-length chains host Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) bound states inside the superconducting gap, originating from a global S = 1 ground state, whereas even-length chains form an S = 0 ground state decoupled from the superconductor. A two-site model attributes this alternation to the sign and strength of inter-edge interactions, independently confirmed by extra-gap spin excitations in tunnelling spectra. Many-body spin excitations of the S = 1 chain are also detected, decoupled from the superconductor by the much larger Haldane gap. The length-tunable coupling of the edge spins to superconductors opens a route towards molecular spin qubits based on π-conjugated carbon architectures.

Article.Title: Interhemispheric monsoon dynamics over the past 450,000 years
Article.Authors: Olson E.; Gillikin D.; Parmenter D.; Burns S.; Verheyden A.; Miyawaki O.; Vuille M.; Piccirillo L.; Castro R.; Yurivilca G.; Edwards R.; Rodbell D.
Article.Abstract: The global monsoon system provides freshwater to much of Earth's biota, including its human population1. The Milankovitch theory predicts changes in Earth's solar insolation over geologic time, and these variations are expected to result in changes to the global monsoon2. Internal climate forcings, such as ice cover and sea surface temperatures, may also affect the system. However, few records of monsoon variability in the Southern Hemisphere over glacial-interglacial cycles exist to test our understanding of the factors that drive variations in the global monsoon. Here we show that monsoons in both the Southern and Northern Hemispheres vary with Milankovitch forcing, and with internal boundary conditions over the past 450,000 years. We present a record of South American Summer Monsoon (SASM) variability, based on speleothem oxygen-isotope data from the Amazon Basin. South American Summer Monsoon variability and that of a major Northern Hemisphere monsoon-that is, the Asian monsoon3,4-have been strikingly out of phase. However, we observe occasional synchronous behaviour in regions impacted by both monsoons. We identify a synchronicity threshold that is exceeded during ten events, including during glacial terminations. Comparison with palaeoclimatic forcing factors during these intervals indicates that greenhouse gas concentrations, cross-equatorial thermal gradients and sea surface temperatures in both the Atlantic and Pacific probably influence these events. This record demonstrates that the global monsoon can reorganize itself, especially during intervals of rapidly changing planetary boundary conditions.

Article.Title: Targeted stimulation of motor cortex ensembles drives learned movements
Article.Authors: Chen Q.; Wu A.; Yu B.; Chae S.; Tan Z.; Ramot A.; Aljadeff J.; Komiyama T.
Article.Abstract: During the execution of learned motor skills, the neural population in layer 2/3 (L2/3) of primary motor cortex (M1) expresses a reproducible spatiotemporal activity pattern1. It is debated whether M1 actively participates in generating this learned pattern and whether this pattern causally drives the learned movement2-5. Here we combined in vivo two-photon calcium imaging and holographic optogenetic stimulation of functionally defined M1 L2/3 ensembles in mice performing a skilled lever-pressing task. Brief synchronous stimulation of about 20 neurons whose activity onset precedes voluntary movement onset induced movements resembling the learned movement, while producing activity patterns in other M1 neurons resembling the learned activity. Moreover, trial-by-trial variability of optogenetically triggered population activity correlated with variability in the induced movements. These variabilities were predicted by the initial state of M1 activity preceding stimulation. In some trials, stimulation induced the learned activity without inducing movements, indicating that the learned activity is not simply a reflection of movements but can arise internally. Stimulation failed to generate movements or learned activity in task-disengaged mice. Stimulation of neurons whose activity followed movement onsets failed to induce the learned movement in task-engaged mice. Together, the learned activity in M1 L2/3 can be generated when M1 is prepared at the optimal initial state and receives precise triggering inputs, supporting the active role of M1 in generating learned activity and learned movements.

Article.Title: Divergent genomic evolution in astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas
Article.Authors: Chowdhury T.; Tesileanu C.; Kocakavuk E.; Johnson K.; Lee J.; Erson-Omay Z.; Heo C.; Aldape K.; Amin S.; Anderson K.; Ashley D.; Barthel F.; Barnholtz-Sloan J.; Brat D.; Brodbelt A.; Castro A.; Claus E.; Connelly J.; Costello J.; Datta I.; Elliott C.; Finocchiaro G.; French P.; Gan H.; Garofano L.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas are isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas that most commonly arise in adults under the age of 50 and exhibit variable responses to treatment1-3. To understand the genetic drivers of disease progression, here we used whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing to characterize longitudinally collected tumour specimens from 183 patients with IDH-mutant glioma. Samples were collected through the Glioma Longitudinal Analysis (GLASS) Consortium4. Most primary surgery samples were classified as grade 2 on the basis of histology (73% for astrocytomas and 93% for oligodendrogliomas). We validated known genomic markers of tumour progression, including hypermutation and homozygous deletion of CDKN2A or CDKN2B (hereafter, CDKN2A/B)5, and discovered genetic alterations that distinguish between the evolutionary trajectories of astrocytomas and those of oligodendrogliomas. Mutations in phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and NOTCH1 were newly acquired in recurrent oligodendrogliomas, regardless of treatment, and were associated with an increased tumour mutational burden. In recurrent astrocytomas, however, again irrespective of treatment, acquired focal oncogene amplifications and CDKN2A/B homozygous deletions were associated with an increase in chromosomal imbalances, which converged with markers of chromosomal instability such as chromothripsis and whole-genome doubling. In both types of IDH-mutant glioma, we observed a convergence of acquired alterations, genome-wide changes and worse patient outcomes, suggesting that treatment-refractory clones were being selected. Treatment with temozolomide was associated with the mutational signatures SBS11 and SBS119 in both tumour types, whereas the radiotherapy-associated ID8 signature increased in astrocytomas specifically. We show that the genomes of oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas adapt to the selective pressures of tumour progression and treatment in distinct ways, suggesting that oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas differ in their responses to treatment-induced DNA damage.

Article.Title: Modelling mouse embryogenesis from chemically induced totipotent stem cells
Article.Authors: Wu H.; Hu Y.; Yu H.; Huang N.; Shi L.; Gao M.; Du X.; Lu X.; Zhang Y.; Sun X.; Xu X.; Liu Z.; Yuan J.; Zhou W.; Shao Q.; Wang D.; Zhao Y.; Ma T.; Ding S.
Article.Abstract: The ability to faithfully initiate embryogenesis from a single, induced non-germline cell type, akin to the totipotent blastomeres, remains a considerable challenge in developmental and synthetic biology1-14. Here we established conditions that enable the continuous ex utero development of mouse embryo models (EMs), starting solely from the chemically induced totipotent-like stem cells (ciTotiSCs)15 and spanning the pre-implantation morula, blastocysts and post-gastrulation stages with both embryonic and extraembryonic compartments. These ciTotiSCs self-organized into blastocyst-like structures that closely resembled natural blastocysts in both morphology and lineage segregation. The resulting ciTotiSC-derived EMs (ciToti-EMs) successfully progressed through key developmental milestones, including gastrulation, embryonic axis formation, haematopoiesis and early organogenesis, closely resembling embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) natural embryos (NEs). Furthermore, extended culture led to the development of functional cardiac tissues in ciToti-EMs, highly comparable to those of E10.5 NEs. These findings demonstrate an extraordinary ability of a single induced cell type, ciTotiSCs, to autonomously recapitulate the complete spectrum of early mouse embryogenesis. Our ciToti-EM system provides a powerful model for investigating mammalian embryonic development and opens new avenues for creating multicellular organisms from non-germline cells.

Article.Title: Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning
Article.Authors: Guan H.; Mouatadid S.; Orenstein P.; Cohen J.; Dong H.; Ni Z.; Berman J.; Flaspohler G.; Lu A.; Schloer J.; Talib J.; Weyn J.; Mackey L.
Article.Abstract: Decision-makers rely on weather forecasts to plant crops, manage wildfires, allocate water and energy and prepare for weather extremes1-3. Today, such forecasts enjoy unprecedented accuracy as far as 2 weeks thanks to steady advances in physics-based dynamical models and data-driven artificial intelligence models4-10. However, model skill drops precipitously at subseasonal timescales (2-6 weeks ahead) due to compounding errors, systemic model biases and the chaotic nature of the atmosphere11-15. To counter this degradation, we introduce probabilistic bias correction, a machine learning framework that substantially reduces systematic error by learning to correct historical probabilistic forecasts. When applied to the leading dynamical and artificial intelligence models from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), probabilistic bias correction doubles the modest subseasonal skill of the AI Forecasting System16 and improves the skill of the operationally debiased dynamical model17 for 91% of pressure, 92% of temperature and 98% of precipitation targets. We designed probabilistic bias correction for operational deployment, and, in the 2025 real-time forecasting competition of ECMWF18, its global forecasts were the best for all weather variables and lead times, outperforming the dynamical models from six operational forecasting centres, an international dynamical multimodel ensemble, the AI Forecasting System of ECMWF and the forecasting systems of 34 teams worldwide. These probabilistic skill gains translate into more accurate prediction of extreme events and have the potential to improve agricultural planning, energy management and disaster preparedness in vulnerable communities19.

Article.Title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation
Article.Authors: Parada G.; Bretschneider H.; Li J.; Fine J.; Dupas S.; Ellis J.; Braunschweig U.; Bonnal S.; Dalal T.; Engchuan W.; Zarrei M.; Wei W.; Zafar N.; Hemberg M.; Attisano L.; Ellis J.; Irimia M.; Wainberg M.; Trost B.; Scherer S.; Morris Q.; Blencowe B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neuronal microexons are a highly conserved class of alternative splicing events enriched in genes with critical functions in nervous system biology 1,2 . Microexon splicing is often disrupted in the brains of autistic individuals, and mice with microexon deficiencies display autism-like phenotypes 1,3,4 . However, the full landscape of microexons is not known, and the impact of genetic variation on these exons has not been systematically investigated. Here, through extensive transcriptome profiling, we detect hundreds of new microexons, including many with neuronal subtype-specific splicing patterns, and others that activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Using machine learning, we define a sequence code predictive of neuronally spliced microexons and use this to identify critical regulatory elements surrounding the expanded microexon repertoire. This code further reveals genomic variants predicted to alter microexon splicing in individuals affected by autism, with rare variants having the strongest estimated impact. These variants are mostly detected in idiopathic individuals and are associated with autism status. They also converge on synaptic and other autism-linked genes, as well as genes not previously linked to autism. Our results collectively define an expanded repertoire of microexons, delineate their regulatory code, and pinpoint variants predicted to affect their splicing, with implications for the disruption of functions central to neuronal biology and brain disorders.

Article.Title: Wave coarsening drives time crystallization in mechatronic metamaterials
Article.Authors: Veenstra J.; Binysh J.; Seinen V.; Solé Borràs R.; Naber R.; Robledo-Poisson D.; Hunt A.; van Saarloos W.; Souslov A.; Coulais C.
Article.Abstract: When metals are magnetized1, emulsions phase separate2, or galaxies cluster3, domain walls and patterns form and irremediably coarsen over time. This coarsening is universally driven by diffusive relaxation towards equilibrium. Here we discover a vibrational counterpart-wave coarsening-in active elastic media4-13: vibrations emerge and spontaneously grow in wavelength, period and amplitude, before a globally synchronized state called a time crystal14-17 forms. We observe wave coarsening in one- and two-dimensional mechatronic metamaterials and capture its dynamical scaling. We further arrest the process by breaking momentum conservation and reveal a far-from-equilibrium nonlinear analogue to chiral topological edge modes18-24. Our results open new questions about the transient physics of systems with non-potential interactions15,25-28 and suggest an organizing principle for nonlinear waves in acoustics29,30, optomechanics31,32, living matter6,33 and soft robotics9.

Article.Title: Capillary-selective vasodilation through myosin inhibition halts ischaemic cascades
Article.Authors: Pénzes M.; Winternitz M.; Horváth Á.; Mastitskaya S.; Awan U.; Szimler T.; Glaser C.; Kikuti C.; Juillé M.; Heidsieck L.; Rauscher A.; Bálint T.; Nagy D.; Radovits T.; Sayour A.; Gibson C.; Houdusse A.; Gyimesi M.; Málnási-Csizmadia A.
Article.Abstract: In acute myocardial infarction and acute kidney injury, capillary no-reflow denotes that capillary blood flow is still blocked despite successful arterial reperfusion. This is associated with substantially increased mortality and reinfarction risk; nevertheless, no targeted therapy exists so far1,2. Because capillary no-reflow is driven by smooth muscle myosin-mediated hypercontraction of capillary pericytes, we developed R(+)2501, a myosin-specific and capillary-selective vasodilator. In reperfused animal models of acute myocardial infarction and acute kidney injury, direct in vivo imaging showed that R(+)2501 rapidly restored capillary flow, an effect sustained even after rapid drug clearance. Ex vivo experiments confirmed reversal of pericyte constriction directly. Restoration of capillary blood flow, together with clearance of trapped neutrophils, linked resolution of capillary no-reflow to attenuation of an early driver of reperfusion injury. R(+)2501 enhanced capillary perfusion while preserving coronary autoregulation and systemic haemodynamics, and markedly improved survival during acute reperfusion. We further found that acute myocardial infarction induced renal capillary no-reflow, which was reversed by R(+)2501, suggesting that capillary no-reflow contributes to the pathophysiology of cardiorenal syndrome type I. These findings establish pericyte-targeted smooth muscle myosin inhibition as a therapeutic strategy to restore microvascular perfusion and halt the ischaemic cascade across organs, while defining a specific physiological role for capillaries and pericytes in circulatory regulation.

Article.Title: Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat
Article.Authors: Gómez-Banoy N.; Barrero J.; Pinheiro de Carvalho L.; Jiang C.; Lama T.; Karandikar N.; Koenen M.; Lam T.; Plucińska K.; Morozova K.; Chahwan S.; Barraza G.; Agridag Ucpinar B.; Liu J.; Sharma R.; Lafontaine D.; Schöder H.; Cohen P.
Article.Abstract: Adipose tissue has a central role in systemic energy balance and the pathogenesis of obesity and its sequelae1,2. In contrast to white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue (BAT) uses energy to produce heat3. Detectable BAT in humans is associated with decreased prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases4. However, the complete spectrum of health conditions associated with BAT remains unknown, and high-throughput methods to quantify BAT activity in humans are lacking5,6. Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre. Our unbiased analyses revealed that, across all diagnoses, cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases were less prevalent in people with BAT. Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution. People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices. Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence. As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure. Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans.

Article.Title: Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates
Article.Authors: O’Neill H.; Beeken J.; Bingham H.; Golden Kroner R.; He Y.; Stewart J.; Ali A.; Beltran J.; Bull J.; Canney S.; Dharmaratne N.; Eghenter C.; Fitzsimons J.; Hill S.; Jenkins C.; Julianty C.; Leon Y.; MacKinnon J.; Mallya A.; Marnewick D.; Maurer G.; Milkovic M.; Mohammed A.; Pantaleo Y.; Parsons B.
Article.Abstract: Conservation areas are critical for tackling the global environmental crisis1. These sites are reported as covering 18.5% of the terrestrial realm2 and governments have committed through Global Biodiversity Framework Target 3 to increase this to at least 30% by 2030 (ref. 3). There are concerns that this potential near-doubling of conservation area coverage will negatively affect vulnerable people and over-stretch conservation resources4. However, nationally available datasets indicate that more conservation areas exist than are reflected in global figures5-7. We evaluated progress towards the area component of Target 3 using a globally representative sample across 25 countries and territories that incorporated these national datasets8. Extrapolating from this sample, we show that conservation areas likely already cover 26.81% of the terrestrial realm. We may be much closer to achieving 30% terrestrial coverage than previously thought. However, we also show that the extra land does not substantially address gaps in ecological representativeness, indicating that solely meeting the area component of Target 3 will do little to solve continuing global biodiversity loss. More focus and resources are needed to achieve the other components of the target, using a more strategic and inclusive approach to fill present gaps and produce equitable and effective conservation area networks.

Article.Title: De novo design of cysteine proteases
Article.Authors: Choi H.; Bauer M.; Coventry B.; Venkatesh P.; Chen A.; Kim D.; Bera A.; Kang A.; Nguyen H.; Sadre S.; Decarreau J.; Joyce E.; Shankaran B.; Thompson T.; Greenstein G.; Didi K.; Schaaf L.; Gershon J.; Shida A.; Lee G.; Hilvert D.; Pellock S.; Baker D.
Article.Abstract: Despite advances in de novo enzyme design, success has been largely limited to low-energy-barrier model reactions. Amide bonds such as those linking amino acids along the peptide backbone are stable for hundreds of years in neutral aqueous solution because of the high energy barrier to hydrolysis1. Here we describe the de novo design of enzymes that use an activated cysteine nucleophile to hydrolyse the polypeptide backbone in a sequence-dependent manner, with a success rate of 13/69 = 19% and rate enhancements over the background reaction (kcat/kuncat) of up to 3 × 107. The designed proteases have folds that are very different from proteases in nature (TM score < 0.50), and six crystal structures are very close to the design models (Cα root mean squared deviation of <1.2 Å), highlighting the capacity for generalization and the accuracy of the design methodology. Experimental and computational analyses suggest that the remaining gap in activity to the most active native cysteine proteases arises from imperfections in active-site preorganization and substrate positioning. The designed proteases efficiently cleave their targets in mammalian cells, opening the door to a wide range of synthetic biology applications.

Article.Title: Sexual dimorphism in epidermal stem cell dynamics
Article.Authors: Engelman D.; Hochstetter J.; Bauduin A.; Patil S.; Valenti M.; Song Y.; Lian Q.; Toniolo A.; Ghiasloo M.; Bansaccal N.; Delaunois A.; Liagre M.; De Luca M.; Hoste E.; De Rosa L.; Shwartz Y.; Simons B.; Blanpain C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The epidermis is a stratified epithelium comprising proliferative basal cells and differentiated suprabasal cells that are continuously renewed throughout life. Conflicting theories have been proposed regarding the heterogeneity of the basal cell layer, with some studies proposing that all proliferative cells have self-renewal potential during homeostasis 1–5 . Meanwhile, others posit a model in which stem cell differentiation occurs through an intermediate transit-amplifying-like progenitor state with strictly limited proliferative potential 6–10 . Here, to determine the heterogeneity and pattern of cell fate, we performed intravital time-lapse imaging to track the fate of lineage-labelled cells in the skin interfollicular epidermis. Results from quantitative analyses of clonal dynamics support a two-compartment model of epidermal homeostasis, whereby basal cells are organized in a stem cell–transit-amplifying cell hierarchy. Critical to these conclusions was the discovery of sexual dimorphism in epidermal fate, with female mice showing a highly synchronized pattern of cell division, differentiation and delamination that contributes to accelerated wound healing. Single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptional profiling and clonal analyses of castrated mice revealed that male sex hormones promote stem cell differentiation and delamination. In summary, our study provides insight into the functional identity of the stem cell population and identifies sex-specific differences in the regulation of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cell fate.

Article.Title: Jurassic flightless bird reveals early ecological diversity of avialans
Article.Authors: Xu L.; Wang M.; Lin G.; Dong L.; Deng K.; Xu X.; Du H.; Lin M.; Chen R.; Zhou Z.
Article.Abstract: The origin and early diversification of birds remain highly debated in vertebrate evolution. Although estimates of the evolutionary timescales suggest a Jurassic period radiation1,2, a profound scarcity of fossils from this period has hampered how the distinctive bird bauplan was assembled3-5. Selection for powered flight has been viewed as the primary driver of early avialan skeletal modifications3,6,7, attesting to the independent occurrences of aerodynamic features among paravian lineages8. Here we report on the discovery of a Late Jurassic avialan, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, gen. et sp. nov., from the Zhenghe Fauna of southeastern China9. As one of the earliest diverging avialans, Y. yangyuanensis exhibits a striking mosaic of features, combining a mixture of avialan- and troodontid-like cranial characters, paired with derived postcranial traits and a deinonychosaur-like hyperextensible second pedal digit. Phylogenetically informed analyses show that Y. yangyuanensis possesses markedly short forelimbs-a condition present widely among non-avialan theropods. These findings provide strong evidence for a terrestrial, flightless lifestyle of Y. yangyuanensis. Our study demonstrates that evolution works intensively as exemplified by the occurrence of several, divergent ecological pathways being exploited in the initial diversification of birds.

Here we use RFdiffusion methods3,4 to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket. The best design accelerates peptide-bond hydrolysis by more than 108-fold relative to the uncatalysed reaction; four substitutions increase this acceleration to more than 1010-fold by improving active-site preorganization5. We further design caged cytokines and receptor antagonists that are selectively activated by the designed proteases, enabling bioorthogonal control of cell state. Article.Authors: Zhao M.; Millán R.; Skorynina A.; Simonelli L.; Haro M.; Calvino J.; Concepción P.; Corma A.
Article.Abstract: Hydroformylation has been a cornerstone of industrial organometallic catalysis, with regioselectivity being a critical aspect in this process1,2. Present industrial systems use homogeneous Rh-based catalysts with expensive and toxic phosphine-containing ligands, underscoring the need to develop alternative heterogeneous catalysts that could compete with the actual homogeneous ones3. In this direction, atomically dispersed Rh catalysts have been proposed as promising candidates for hydroformylation4,5. However, achieving high regioselectivity at high conversion is still a big challenge. Here subnanometre Rh2O3 clusters are confined inside the channels of the MFI zeolite, which under reaction conditions disrupt into isolated Rh3+ and Rh+ species. Density functional theory (DFT) investigations combined with spectroscopic and catalytic studies demonstrate that Rh3+-mediated hydroformylation is energetically plausibly similar to Rh+, with Rh3+ being intrinsically more selective for hydroformylation and less selective for double-bond isomerization than Rh+. In the coexistence of both Rh3+ and Rh+ species, we demonstrate the possibility to selectively inhibit Rh+ sites through the addition of N-containing molecules such as N-methylpyrrolidine (MP) or 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), which preferentially coordinate to Rh+ inside MFI zeolite channel, thereby suppressing its isomerization function while leaving Rh3+ sites catalytically accessible. This strategy results in a notable enhancement of regioselectivity, with a state-of-the-art reported highest linear to branched aldehydes (l/b) ratio of 817 with 96% undecanal selectivity at 99.8% 1-decene conversion, using NMP as additive.

Article.Title: Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
Article.Authors: Canaria D.; Nguyen T.; Huang H.; Xu H.; Yue L.; Fu Y.; Truong H.; Patel K.; Xing W.; Ravichandar J.; Xing C.; Martin A.; Delidakis G.; Wong S.; Pae A.; Yu Y.; Macdonald R.; Huang Z.; Main M.; Rodriguez A.; Lin X.; Mouchess M.; Hung M.; McGlinchey E.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is a central anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses immune responses in myeloid cells but can also activate T cells, limiting its therapeutic use in chronic inflammatory diseases owing to narrow efficacy windows and dose-limiting toxicities 1–5 . Cryo-electron microscopy structural analysis reveals a distinct receptor cross-linking geometry of the msIL-10R agonist compared with native IL-10 family cytokines. This tetravalent architecture renders signalling strictly TYK2-dependent and highly sensitive to IL-10Rα and IL-10Rβ receptor abundance, thereby conferring selective activity in myeloid cells. This msIL-10R agonist reduces inflammation in humanized mouse models of lipopolysaccharide challenge, delayed-type hypersensitivity and colitis. A humanized version exhibits IgG-like pharmacokinetics, sustained receptor occupancy and durable myeloid suppression up to 30 days without T cell activation or haematological toxicities in non-human primates. These findings establish a geometry-based strategy for achieving cell-type-selective cytokine signalling and identify the msIL-10R agonist as a therapeutic candidate for myeloid-driven inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel diseases.

Article.Authors: Mader M.; Li W.; Scavetti A.; Yoo Y.; Neumayer G.; Han K.; Shibuya Y.; Haney M.; Wyss-Coray T.; George L.; Lefcort F.; Bassik M.; Nakauchi H.; Wilkinson A.; Wernig M.
Article.Abstract: Haematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) transplantation-mediated replacement of microglia-the reconstitution of the central nervous system microglial niche with donor-derived myeloid cells-represents a promising strategy for brain cell therapies1-7. However, the cell-intrinsic molecular regulators of HSPC-derived myeloid lineage commitment in the brain have remained largely uncharacterized. This is partially because the scarcity of primary HSPCs has rendered large-scale genetic interrogation intractable. Here we explored whether ex vivo expansion of primary cultured HSPCs (cHSPCs) enables unbiased genetic interrogation of haematopoietic differentiation. We established that cHSPCs can be genetically manipulated and readily differentiate into myeloid cells and repopulate microglia niches of the brain after transplantation. Moreover, primary neonatal astrocytes contained strong signals to induce myeloid specification of cHSPCs in vitro. To identify genes that regulate glia-induced myeloid differentiation, we successfully screened around 20,000 individual genetic perturbations and characterized genes involved in the regulation of cell signalling, cell cycle, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Among these genes was elongator acetyltransferase complex subunit 1 (Elp1), which suppressed the unfolded protein response during myeloid specification and was essential for the generation but not maintenance of myeloid cells. Article.Title: Early tetrapod neck mobility modelled using an extant analogue
Article.Authors: Korneisel D.; Donatelli C.; Han L.; Stewart T.; Traynor A.; Otoo B.; Martinez M.; Miyashita T.; Standen E.; Maddin H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Tetrapods arose from lobe-finned fishes with a notochord-dominated axial column 1–3 . During this transition, the skull became separated from the shoulder girdle 4–6 , giving rise to a neck region. This head–shoulder separation has generated hypotheses suggesting that neck mobility increased during the origin of tetrapods, facilitating the ecological transition towards more terrestrial habitats 4,5,7–9 . However, incompletely co-ossified vertebral components 10 have posed a challenge to modelling the mobility of these early tetrapod necks. Here we used material tests on the similarly configured axial columns of sturgeon to predict the capacities of the tetrapod neck region for lateral flexion, extension and rotation across the tetrapod stem. Our model indicates that the soft tissue-dominated axial column was surprisingly rigid, despite lacking co-ossified vertebral components. We estimate that most stem tetrapods could move their heads less than 6° laterally and less than 3° dorsally but could not rotate them. Notably, mobility did not shift in conjunction with the head–shoulder separation that occurred between the origin of tristichopterids (represented by Eusthenopteron ) and that of more crownward stem tetrapods. Therefore, mobility in the tetrapod neck did not serve as a functional driver of head–shoulder separation. Instead, forelimb-driven locomotion, implicated in early tetrapods 11–14 , provides a better functional explanation for the head–shoulder separation.

Article.Title: Educational intervention can rewire village social networks
Article.Authors: Papamichalis M.; Forastiere L.; Airoldi E.; Christakis N.
Article.Abstract: Social networks shape behaviour, affect information dissemination and undergird collective action. And they can be exploited in the design of interventions in these domains1-7. Although social networks obey fundamental principles, such as the degree distribution8,9, they can nevertheless evolve as ties form and break. Here, through a randomized controlled trial involving a total of 8,331 people in 110 remote Honduran villages, we evaluate the secondary effects of a 22-month public-health intervention1 on pre-existing social-network structure. We used a design in which a varying fraction of village households received the intervention, and villages in which no one received the intervention were used as the primary reference group. In 'low-dosage' villages (in which 5-30% of households received the intervention), people who received the intervention tended to sever ties with untreated individuals to whom they previously went for health advice. Conversely, in high-dosage villages (50-100%), treated individuals increased their ties. These average changes are explained mainly by tie dynamics; that is, treated-treated pairs persist and form new links, whereas treated-untreated ties dissolve. A mediation analysis indicates that absorption of health information increases the likelihood of tie formation and persistence. The rewiring patterns generally lasted for three years after the intervention ceased. Moreover, although the intervention delivered health information, it reshaped friendship and financial ties, not just health-advice connections. In aggregate, the introduction of a new information regime acted as a kind of social institution, rewiring individuals' connections even though the overall degree distribution of village-wide networks remained relatively stable.

Article.Title: Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs
Article.Authors: Xu L.; Wang X.; Quan X.; Ferguson S.; Liu D.; Chen J.; Wang S.; Liang S.; Huang G.; Huang K.; Liu F.; Pan X.
Article.Abstract: Ionotropic receptors (IRs) are essential for insect olfaction, enabling the detection of carboxylic acids, amines, moisture, and temperature cues that mediate critical behaviors, including mosquito host-seeking 1,2. However, the structural mechanisms underlying ligand specificity and channel activation in these receptors remain unclear. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures and functional validation of the IR8a-IR75k complex from the malaria mosquito Anopheles stephensi, a carboxylic acid detector, captured in four states: the ligand-free full-length closed form (apo state), the ligand induced full-length open state, and the nonanoic acid (NA)- and octanoic acid (OA)-bound extracellular domains. These structures reveal a dynamic ligand-binding pocket in IR75k, in which specificity is determined by alkyl chain length and carboxylate geometry. Ligand binding triggers closure of IR75k's bilobed ligand binding domain (LBD), and this conformational change propagates through conserved mechanical linkers to the transmembrane domain (TMD), functioning as a molecular lever that dilates the pore via outward displacement of transmembrane helices. This gating mechanism was further corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations and electrophysiology. These insights provide an atomic resolution view of IR mediated host detection in mosquitoes and establish a foundation for the rational design of next generation mosquito control strategies targeting host-seeking behavior.

Article.Title: Catalytic transfer of carbon atoms enables spirofusion of C–C σ-bonds
Article.Authors: Fujimoto H.; Mizutani M.; Imachi K.; Nishioka T.; Ikeda R.; Tobisu M.
Article.Abstract: Spirocyclic frameworks, polycyclic structures in which two rings share a single carbon atom, constitute key structural motifs across diverse areas, including optoelectronic and hole-transporting materials1-3, ligand design for coordination complexes4-6, and numerous natural products7. In a spiro skeleton, the two molecular units adopt an orthogonal arrangement, generating a rigid three-dimensional (3D) architecture. Introducing a single carbon atom to join two components to form the spiro centre therefore represents a direct strategy for constructing such frameworks. Previous carbon-atom-transfer approaches have largely relied on π-bond reactivity, whereas controlled insertion of a carbon atom into C-C σ-bonds remains challenging8-11. Here we report a rhodium-catalysed spiro-carbon-atom insertion reaction that converts biphenylene substrates into spirocyclic structures through sequential C-C bond activation. Using N-isocyanoiminophosphorane (PINC)12-14 as an atomic carbon equivalent, the reaction forms four new C-C bonds at a spiro centre. The transformation enables both homo- and cross-spirofusion of biphenylenes and can be extended to reactions combining σ- and π-bond activation. These results establish a catalytic strategy for constructing structurally complex spirocyclic frameworks through C-C σ-bond activation, with a single carbon atom serving as a central linchpin.

Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Yu S.; Cheng X.; Xiao X.; Ma W.; Ma Y.; Quan F.; Song H.; Zhang K.; Zhang Y.; Liu W.; Yadav P.; Sheng H.; Wang A.; Shi X.; Wang Z.; Niu Q.; Gao Y.; Xiang B.; Liu J.; Wang Z.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Altermagnets simultaneously possess momentum-dependent nonrelativistic spin splitting and zero net magnetization (1-6). Their defining crystalline symmetry connects opposite-spin sublattices in real space and imposes alternating spin polarization on the symmetry-related electronic states in momentum space (1-3). Identifying such an order and its associated spin response therefore calls for atomic-scale spin-sensitive measurements in both real and momentum space, an experimental milestone yet to be achieved. Here we show that the helical edge modes of the higher-order topological insulator α-Bi4Br4 can serve as a spin-selective scanning tunnelling microscopy probe of the two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetic order in the surface layer of KV2Se2O. Atomically registered mapping reveals the spatial relationship between the two V sublattices and a density-wave lattice modulation, as well as real-space patterns consistent with the checkerboard antiferromagnetic order. Field-dependent spectroscopy further finds opposite energy shifts of the unidirectional quasiparticle excitations extending along two orthogonal crystal axes and a predominantly out-of-plane magnetic response. In momentum space, spin-sensitive quasiparticle interference imaging reveals a bias-reversing d-wave anisotropy between the symmetry-paired X and Y valleys. These results provide converging evidence for two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetism on the surface of KV2Se2O and demonstrate helical-edge-mode tunnelling as a route for atomic-scale spin sensing in quantum materials.

Article.Title: Selective, Catalytic Oxidation of Polyethylene Surfaces
Article.Authors: Woroch C.; Klivansky L.; McCarthy D.; Miao H.; Fink Z.; Zuo X.; Guthrie C.; Wang C.; Helms B.; Hartwig J.
Article.Abstract: Polyethylene (PE) accounts for more than a quarter of all plastic produced, owing to its exceptional material properties and scalable production.1 However, pristine PE lacks critical properties, such as adhesion, that are needed for many additional commercial applications.2 Selective post-polymerization functionalization of PE can impart properties that are absent in the pristine polymer, but global functionalization in a uniform medium perturbs bulk properties.3-5 Here, we demonstrate catalytic functionalization of solid PE at a solid-liquid interface. The resulting materials possess enhanced surface properties while maintaining bulk properties, such as melting temperature or tensile strength. The method selectively converts methylene units to ketones with just 0.001 mol% iron catalyst below 80 °C with inexpensive oxidants. PE functionalized at the solid-liquid interface adheres to polar surfaces up to 90-fold more strongly than does pristine PE and up to 4-fold more strongly than does PE functionalized in a uniform medium at a comparable level. We demonstrate that the surface ketones can be modified to enhance adhesive strength further and that the augmented surface properties persist for longer than they do after other unselective functionalizations. Thus, selective C-H bond functionalization at the solid-liquid interface produces materials inaccessible by bulk functionalization methods or by traditional surface oxidations.

Article.Title: Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria
Article.Authors: Tang S.; Ramirez J.; He Q.; Rodríguez Mestre M.; Wiegand T.; Zhang D.; Wang M.; Lampe G.; Wang J.; Ma Y.; Jovanovic M.; Pinilla-Redondo R.; Fernández I.; Sternberg S.
Article.Abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) employ diverse and distinctive mechanisms of cDNA synthesis to protect bacteria against viral infection1. However, the functions and mechanisms of many DRTs remain unknown2. Here we identify a new antiviral defense system, DRT10, that associates with a noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to catalyze processive, protein-primed synthesis of tandem-repeat DNA. Reverse transcription is templated by a defined ncRNA region with a characteristic sequence pattern and template boundary elements, both of which are conserved and essential for DNA repeat addition. Cryo-EM reconstructions reveal an unanticipated 2:1 architecture, wherein two RT monomers bind opposite sides of a pseudo-symmetric ncRNA. Biochemical experiments further demonstrate that each RT monomer reverse transcribes the template encoded on its respective side of the ncRNA, but only one generates the long repetitive product, whose template is defined by the distance between two flanking stem-loop anchors. This mode of iterative, boundary-delimited cDNA synthesis exhibits direct parallels to the mechanism of telomeric repeat addition by eukaryotic telomerase, and phylogenetic analyses of RTs across domains of life place telomerase in a monophyletic clade with the DRT family, suggesting a common origin for their DNA polymerization activities. Together with earlier studies of DRT2, DRT3, and DRT93-5, our findings identify a conserved mechanistic logic underlying RNA-templated DNA repeat addition across diverse DRTs, despite vastly different architectural solutions, and expand the repertoire of reverse transcription-based strategies for antiviral immunity in bacteria.

Article.Title: How to control where semiconductor crystals start growing
Article.Abstract: Semiconductor crystals grow from tiny nuclei, but the position of these nuclei is difficult to control precisely and can affect the crystal’s properties. An approach using ‘etching flux’ has now been developed that constrains the position at which a nucleus forms, enabling spatially programmable growth of large single crystals of semiconducting material. Article.Title: Structural basis for regulating lipopolysaccharide transmembrane transport
Article.Authors: Taylor R.; Pahil K.; Caruso A.; Plaman B.; Early S.; Rowe S.; Baidin V.; Wilson A.; Ruiz N.; Walsh R.; Harrison S.; Kahne D.
Article.Abstract: Gram-negative bacteria are surrounded by a multilayered cell envelope with a mostly impermeable outer membrane that provides intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics1-5. The outer membrane is an asymmetrical bilayer with phospholipids in the inner leaflet and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet6,7. An LPS transport (Lpt) machine called LptB2FGCADE moves LPS across a protein bridge from the inner membrane to the outer membrane8,9. LPS biosynthesis is regulated to prevent toxic accumulation of LPS molecules in the inner membrane during growth10-12. Whether LPS transport across the Lpt bridge is also regulated has been unclear. Here we present three structures of the trans-envelope Lpt complex in LPS-free, LPS-bound and ATP-bound states, along with a structure of a partial bridge. These structures, combined with biochemical experiments, show that Lpt bridge assembly triggers movement of the transmembrane helix of LptC (TM-LptC) in an LPS-dependent manner, resulting in increased ATP binding and hydrolysis. We also show that LPS transport in vivo requires bridge formation and movement of the TM-LptC. Our data support a model in which assembled Lpt bridges respond to the presence of LPS in the inner membrane to turn on transport by moving the TM-LptC, thus coordinating LPS transport activity with bridge assembly and the presence of LPS at the inner membrane.

Article.Title: Mechanism of spliceosome termination
Article.Authors: Boreikaite V.; Faraway R.; Vorländer M.; Phillips A.; Opitz L.; Wanke M.; Yakoub G.; Raffl G.; Fin L.; González-Prieto R.; Luijsterburg M.; Ameres S.; Plaschka C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract After excising an intron from pre-mRNA, the spliceosome remains trapped in a non-productive complex bound to the intron 1–5 . Termination of this complex is critical for spliceosome recycling and intron decay 6 , but the mechanism remains unknown. Here we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of human spliceosomes at two sequential stages of termination. First, the RNA helicases DHX15 and Aquarius unwind the RNA active site of the spliceosome, releasing bound components including U2 snRNA and extracting the buried intron–lariat branch point. The branch point is then debranched by the spliceosome-tethered enzyme DBR1, generating the previously unknown debranched intron spliceosome. This state recruits the RNA helicase DHX35 with its co-factors GPATCH1–WDR83, assisted by YJU2B. DHX35 ejects the debranched intron from the U6 snRNA–5′ splice site duplex, driving spliceosome disassembly and intron turnover. In defective spliceosomes stalled on aberrant introns, YJU2B partners with LENG1 to guide DHX35–GPATCH1–WDR83 for termination through spliceosome quality control. Together, we reveal the mechanism of regular spliceosome termination and its parallels with spliceosome quality control, ensuring accurate and efficient pre-mRNA splicing.

Article.Title: Prehistoric global migration of vanishing gut microbes with humans
Article.Authors: Carter M.; Liu Z.; Olm M.; Martin M.; Sprockett D.; Ghadermazi P.; Trumble B.; Kaplan H.; Stieglitz J.; Rodriguez D.; Relman D.; Sonnenburg E.; Gurven M.; Good B.; Sonnenburg J.
Article.Abstract: The gut microbiome is crucial for health and is affected strongly by lifestyle1. Many microorganisms commonly found in non-industrialized populations are disappearing or have become extinct in industrialized populations2-6. Studying which microorganisms have been long-term residents of the human gut and may have co-evolved with humans2,7,8 could provide insights into how microbial biodiversity loss affects human health. However, the genetic complexities of microbial evolution and the plasticity of gut microbiome composition have made it challenging to resolve the evolutionary history of these long-term associations. Here we performed deep metagenomic sequencing of the Tsimane horticulturalists of Bolivia and compared their gut microbiomes with those of the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania3. These two populations, whose ancestors have been separated for tens of thousands of years, share 1,231 microbial species, most of which are rare in or absent from industrialized populations. Population genetic analyses of 636 of the shared species revealed patterns of microbial divergence and gene flow consistent with prehistoric human co-migration, with estimated split times that approximately align with human migration out of Africa and into the Americas. Our findings indicate that a diverse gut microbiome co-migrated with humans worldwide and has persisted over millennia. However, many of these species are now vanishing from industrialized populations and the consequences for human health remain uncertain.

Article.Title: Dynamics of human cardiogenesis and its disruption in trisomy 21
Article.Authors: Cranley J.; Kanemaru K.; Bayraktar S.; Knight-Schrijver V.; Hulbert R.; Lana-Elola E.; Aoidi R.; Pett J.; Wilbrey-Clark A.; Polanski K.; Dabrowska M.; Mulas I.; Johnson H.; Combemorel N.; Yu Y.; Palmer J.; Lee W.; Van Wauwe J.; Ng-Blichfeldt J.; Richardson L.; Semprich C.; Kapuge R.; Perera S.; He X.; Ho S.

Here we combine single-cell and spatial multiomics to define 21 distinct tissue niches in the developing heart, which we use to develop a context-aware, resolution-agnostic niche classification tool (TissueTypist). Applying high-resolution spatial profiling to the developing sinoatrial node, we resolve three pacemaker cell subtypes arrayed along a linear axis. First trimester subpopulations, such as pacemaker cells in the sinus horn and sinoatrial node head region, display neuroattractant programs and interact with parasympathetic neurons via interactions that include Eph–ephrin and semaphorin–plexin signalling. Temporal trajectories map the maturation of atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes and uncover a lipid–metabolic switch and potential key regulators of cell-type identity. In the ventricle, we identify cellular and transcriptional gradients along both pseudotime and transmural axes, which provide molecular insights into myocardial compaction and maturation. Comparative profiling revealed that hearts with trisomy 21 are depleted in compact cardiomyocytes and exhibit increased apoptosis relative to euploid hearts. This finding was validated in isogenic-matched trisomy 21 and euploid cardiomyocytes derived from induced pluripotent stem cells. These early developmental perturbations may contribute to the increased risk of congenital heart disease associated with Down’s syndrome. Article.Title: A split attractor design for rapidly writing a navigational goal
Article.Authors: Lanz A.; Kathman N.; Hao E.; Ermentrout B.; Nagel K.
Article.Abstract: Recurrent attractor networks are widely thought to form the basis of working memory1-3, but how they can be rapidly switched on and off is unclear4-7. Here we investigate stability and switching in a recurrent circuit of the fly navigation centre8. h∆K and PFG neurons are recurrently connected in a ring structure and exhibit shared persistent bump activity that turns on with odour and terminates at the end of a goal-directed run. Using whole-cell recordings, we show that persistence in h∆K depends on recurrence, and that h∆K receives slow recurrent excitation and fast inhibition from its synaptic partners. Computational modelling reveals that these synaptic dynamics yield persistent attractor dynamics over a range of synaptic strengths. Next we examine the mechanisms of rapid switching. We find that whereas both populations show similar activity during runs, they become decoupled during turns and rest. We can reproduce these differential dynamics in our model by using inhibition to dynamically uncouple activity in h∆K from PFG. When h∆K is inhibited, PFG neurons follow their inputs from the compass system; when h∆K is disinhibited, recurrent interactions lock this input into place, forming a heading memory. Consistent with this model, we find that inhibitory inputs onto h∆K increase during turns and are suppressed during odour and goal-directed runs. Our work reveals how disinhibition can serve as a gate to rapidly write an ongoing measurement to a recurrent circuit.

Article.Title: Observation of critical topological phase transition
Article.Authors: Cheng Z.; Zhang X.; Yu X.; Zhou L.; Gong J.; Zhang B.
Article.Abstract: Phase transitions are traditionally understood within two seemingly incompatible theoretical paradigms. Landau-Ginzburg phase transitions1,2 are continuous, occurring at critical points where microscopic details become irrelevant and universal behaviour emerges, driven by gapless fluctuations with scale-invariant correlations3. By contrast, topological phase transitions connect gapped phases characterized by quantized topological invariants4,5 and, in doing so, necessarily pass through gapless phase boundaries where such invariants become ill-defined6-9. Here using an acoustic metamaterial platform, we experimentally demonstrate a unifying scenario-a critical topological phase transition-in which topology becomes well-defined at criticality10-13, overcoming this conventional incompatibility, and reorganizes critical behaviour by driving a phase transition along critical phase boundaries14. This transition gives rise to a topology-enforced multicritical point at an isolated intersection of critical boundaries with distinct topology. Along these boundaries, we observe topological edge states and diagnose criticality by means of logarithmic entanglement-entropy scaling15-17. At the multicritical point, the entanglement entropy shows additive logarithmic scaling given by the sum of contributions from adjacent boundaries, directly evidencing topology-enforced multicriticality. These findings establish a hierarchical organization of phase transitions, in which topology shapes criticality beyond the conventional Landau-Ginzburg paradigm and standard topological phase transitions.

Article.Title: A 7-eV bandgap semiconductor based on silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1−x)2O3
Article.Authors: Steele J.; Bhattacharya D.; Nomoto K.; Pieczulewski N.; Sorensen P.; Ha V.; Pant N.; Shukla I.; Das S.; Kilic U.; Ramesh M.; Giustino F.; Mazumder B.; Senevirathna M.; Williams M.; Schubert M.; Muller D.; Xing H.; Jena D.; Schlom D.
Article.Abstract: In rectifying power electronics, wider-bandgap (Eg) semiconductors allow higher efficiency and power density with the Baliga figure of merit proportional to Eg5.5 (refs. 1,2). Unfortunately, the unique ability of semiconductors to have their conductivities controllably modulated over orders of magnitude by equilibrium doping methods becomes increasingly elusive as the bandgap increases. Increasing demand for wider-bandgap semiconductors has led to many materials previously considered insulators-including GaN, SiC, AlN, Ga2O3 and GeO2-to emerge as useful semiconductors after decreasing defect densities and finding appropriate dopants. Here we report silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1-x)2O3 films with bandgaps exceeding 7.0 eV grown by suboxide molecular-beam epitaxy, surpassing that of cubic boron nitride, the next-widest-bandgap semiconductor known3-5. In the colossal-bandgap regime, >6 eV, our silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1-x)2O3 films have room-temperature conductivities over 100 million times higher than all previous reports6. We fabricate a Schottky diode and a field-effect transistor (the AlphaFET) with colossal-bandgap channels. These α-(AlxGa1-x)2O3 films and devices use sapphire, an abundant, inexpensive substrate with excellent quality that is produced at massive scale, facilitating the development and adoption of colossal-bandgap electronics. Our achievement breaks the trend of increasing synthesis difficulty, cost and small size of ever-wider-bandgap semiconductors, for example, diamond and cubic boron nitride.
