Article.Title: Quadrupolar sea level fluctuations reveal episodes of rapid polar wander
Article.Authors: Domeier M.; Gallo L.; Marcilly C.; Torsvik T.
Article.Abstract: True polar wander (TPW) is presently occurring at a rate of ~10 centimeters per year, exceeding the mean rate of differential plate motion. Whether this rate is transient and negligible on geological timescales or whether Earth has experienced rapid TPW lasting millions of years is unclear. Paleomagnetic evidence has been used to propose fast episodes of TPW, but limitations of the paleomagnetic record have precluded definitive results. Rapid TPW will induce global sea level fluctuations associated with relative changes in centrifugal potential, offering an independent test. We evaluated this prediction using continental flooding reconstructions and identified multiple robust quadrupolar patterns since 320 million years ago, confirming that protracted rapid TPW has occurred on Earth and that couplings among Earth’s rotational dynamics, mantle processes, and surface environments can be strongly episodic.

Article.Abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease, the progression of which is accelerated by systemic metabolic stress. Article.Title: Incorporation of atmospheric components in planetary magma oceans through bubble–metal compounds
Article.Authors: Gaillard F.; Pereira L.; Arbaret L.; Iacono-Marziano G.; Le Trong E.; Bernadou F.; Marrocchi Y.
Article.Abstract: Atmophile elements (carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen) were thought to accrete late during planetary formation, yet cosmochemical and astrophysical evidence suggests that they were already present while small bodies, such as Vesta, were forming. High-temperature magmatic events on small bodies, however, should have outgassed these ultravolatile elements because gravity would have been insufficient to retain them. In this study, experiments reveal that gas bubbles strongly attach to metal droplets in magma ocean–like mixtures, forming compounds that resist segregation. Early flotation of such compounds would have enhanced mantle siderophile endowment, eliminating the need for late accretion. On small bodies, low gravity would have enabled millimeter- to centimeter-sized compounds to sink, trapping atmophiles in their interiors. This mechanism links core formation to the early entrapment of atmophile elements and provides a framework for reconciling volatile delivery across planetary bodies and planetary accretion models.

Article.Authors: Chen H.; Yan H.; Zhao C.; Yang G.; Peng C.; Huang J.; Zhao T.; Li X.; Zhao L.; Jiang L.; Liu M.

Article.Title: Ultrahigh piezoelectricity by polaron-defect complexes
Article.Authors: Shu L.; Peng G.; Shi X.; Zhang Y.; Wang S.; Wu H.; Li Q.; Li H.; Zhang X.; Wang Z.; Wang H.; Fan Y.; Deng C.; Ma Y.; Li J.; Guo L.; Bi K.; Cheng Y.; Yang Z.; Dai Y.; Wei L.; Zhao L.; Liu L.; Liu Y.; Xu K.
Article.Abstract: Materials capable of delivering giant and rapid piezoelectric responses at kilohertz frequencies are pivotal for advanced electromechanical technologies. However, their development has been constrained by a long-standing magnitude–speed trade-off: Ferroelectrics with intrinsic electric dipoles offer fast response but limited polarization, whereas ionic defect motion generates highly polarizable defect dipoles but responds slowly, limiting kilohertz-rate applications. We overcame this fundamental limitation by devising 8 mole % K-doped AgNbO 3 (Ag 0.92 K 0.08 NbO 3 ) thin films engineered to host dynamically reconfigurable polaron-defect complexes through electro-elastic interactions between small electron polarons and lattice defects. This synergy leads to an unprecedented field-induced effective piezoelectric coefficient of ~7170 picometers per volt with ~6.2% strain at kilohertz frequencies in engineered silver niobate–based films.

Article.Title: Reframing menopause and menopause hormone therapy as opportunities for healthy aging
Article.Authors: Gravelsins L.; Perović M.; Alexander M.; Splinter T.; McGovern A.; Rabin J.; Galea L.
Article.Abstract: Menopause is an important biological transition with up to 72 symptoms that shapes aging trajectories across organs and encompasses ~40% of the female lifespan. Although menopause awareness is increasing, research on strategies for menopause symptom management and optimizing health in the postmenopausal period is lacking. This Review highlights that menopause characteristics, such as type, timing, and symptom burden, influence health outcomes and later-life disease risk. Similarly, menopause hormone therapy comes in >200 varieties that differ by dose, formulation of estrogens and progestogens, and timing, each with their own distinct risk-benefit profiles. These distinctions are often missed in the literature but have considerable repercussions for outcomes. Optimized menopause care necessitates a precision medicine approach that considers menopause symptoms, genetics, and previous hormone exposures.

Article.Abstract: Supramolecular polymers with precise micrometer-scale segments of opposite charge are challenging to synthesize as discrete assemblies in water. Article.Title: X and Y chromosomes as determinants of aging and disease
Article.Authors: Dubal D.; Ambrosio F.; Stout M.; Theodorescu D.
Article.Abstract: Sex differences have traditionally been attributed to gonadal hormones, but accumulating evidence shows that sex chromosomes exert distinct, cell-autonomous effects on health, aging, and disease. XX and XY complements alter gene dosage, epigenetic programming, immune signaling, metabolism, and cellular stress responses, which shape aging and disease trajectories in women and men. Article.Title: Stationary entanglement of a levitated oscillator with an optical field
Article.Authors: Deplano Q.; Pontin A.; Marino F.; Marin F.
Article.Abstract: Stationary entanglement between the motion of macroscopic objects and light is a long-standing goal of quantum optomechanics, with implications for both fundamental tests of quantum physics and emerging quantum technologies. Our results establish levitated optomechanical systems as a platform for continuous-variable quantum communication and for tests of macroscopic quantum physics.

Article.Title: Shaping maternal physiology: Immune control of reproductive adaptation
Article.Authors: Corral D.; Belkaid Y.
Article.Abstract: Pregnancy is one of the most extensive physiological transitions of adult life, requiring coordinated adaptation across virtually every maternal organ to support fetal growth while preserving maternal health. Although these changes have traditionally been viewed as endocrine driven, emerging evidence identifies the immune system as an active regulator of maternal physiology. The immune system is increasingly recognized as a broad regulator of host physiology, positioning it as a key driver of maternal adaptation. In this work, we discuss how pregnancy reprograms maternal immunity to orchestrate physiological reprograming of tissues. This framework shifts the view of maternal immunity from one centered on immune homeostasis and fetal tolerance to one in which immune cells actively instruct physiological short- and long-term adaptation across maternal organs to shape health beyond reproduction.

Article.Title: Sex-specific mechanisms of chronic pain

Article.Abstract: For decades, we have known that women, especially younger women, are disproportionately affected by pain disorders, including irritable bowel syndrome, endometriosis, menstrual migraines, fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis, and neuropathic pain, all of which degrade quality of life. Article.Title: Keep AI-augmented science contestable
Article.Authors: Trattner C.
Article.Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving upstream in science. Systems such as AlphaFold have already transformed protein-structure prediction, while newer agentic systems can search literatures, generate hypotheses, write and execute code, interpret results, and automate much of the path from idea to paper. Recent debates have asked how such systems may change scientific progress, surprise, and human understanding. Yet they also change something more fundamental: who—or what—participates in deciding which questions are asked, which evidence is surfaced, and which alternatives survive. As machine intelligence becomes part of science’s epistemic infrastructure, steps must be taken to ensure that researchers who did not build, own, or operate the system can still contest how ideas and evidence became a claim.

Article.Title: Snowball refrigeration of Earth’s crust mimics glacial erosion
Article.Authors: Flowers R.; Macdonald F.; Anderson R.
Article.Abstract: Glaciation cools the crust by setting its surface temperature to 0°C or well below. During the Cryogenian Snowball Earth glaciations, these conditions were in place long enough to cool the entire crustal column. Although crustal thermal history can be deciphered by thermochronology, these data are typically interpreted to record depth changes due to burial or erosion. Thermal models of the crust under Cryogenian boundary conditions predict that thermochronometers were substantially altered in the upper quarter to half of the crust. This Snowball Earth refrigeration, with little to no coeval erosion, may have imparted a cooling signal mimicking up to 3‒5 km of glacial erosion. Rock cooling previously attributed to massive Snowball erosion and linked to the Great Unconformity may instead reflect a great refrigeration of Earth’s crust, with implications for thermochronology across other climate events.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: Snowball Earth; thermochronology; Cryogenian glaciation; glacial erosion; Great Unconformity; crustal cooling

Article.Title: Interneurons and network activity in the cerebral cortex: a developmental dialogue
Article.Authors: Moissidis M.; Marín O.
Article.Abstract: The mammalian cerebral cortex undergoes profound functional changes during early postnatal development. During this period, neurons generate spontaneous electrical activity long before sensory experience, coordinating into distinct patterns of synchronous activity. Traditionally, neuronal activity has been viewed as instructing interneuron development by modulating transcriptional programmes, morphology and connectivity. However, accumulating evidence in rodents reveals that this relationship is bidirectional: cortical interneurons are not merely passive recipients of activity-dependent signals but also active architects of developing network dynamics. They regulate spontaneous activity transitions from gap-junction-mediated synchronous events to large, synaptically driven bursts, and later to sparse firing characteristic of mature circuits. Critically, different interneuron subtypes mature at distinct timelines and orchestrate transitions in network activity. Activity-dependent mechanisms, in turn, regulate interneuron wiring, programmed cell death, diversification and terminal differentiation. This reciprocal dialogue between interneurons and network activity is essential for establishing functional cortical circuits.

Article.Title: The endocannabinoid system and the ageing brain
Article.Authors: Zimmer A.
Article.Abstract: Ageing is accompanied by a progressive decline in homeostatic resilience that increases vulnerability to chronic disease, disability and cognitive impairment. Although unhealthy brain ageing can often be prevented by managing the underlying risk factors, the molecular, cellular and physiological mechanisms that connect risk factors to late-life brain dysfunction remain incompletely understood. This review examines the role of the endocannabinoid system in brain ageing. The endocannabinoid system is a short-range lipid signalling network that helps to maintain neuronal, glial, metabolic and inflammatory homeostasis. Endocannabinoid signalling follows a dynamic lifespan trajectory, with relatively high activity during early adulthood and functional decline during ageing. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of endocannabinoid system activity impairs several processes linked to hallmarks of brain ageing, including neuroinflammatory control, adult neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, cognitive performance, metabolic regulation and epigenetic stability. Conversely, low-dose Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) treatment can ameliorate several ageing-related brain phenotypes in old animals. However, clinical evidence in older humans remains limited, and the therapeutic potential of cannabinoid-based interventions requires further evaluation.

Article.Title: Sensing the skeleton: sensorineural regulation in bone
Article.Authors: Li Z.; Zhu M.; Thottappillil N.; Ramesh S.; James A.
Article.Abstract: The traditional view of bone tissue as an inert mechanical scaffold has been fundamentally revised over time. Perhaps nowhere is this more clear than in the emerging field of 'skeletal neuroscience', which has revealed the skeleton to be a densely innervated organ that senses and integrates mechanical, immune and metabolic stimuli. Here, we review recent evidence for bidirectional crosstalk between somatosensory neurons and the bone microenvironment, and highlight how techniques such as whole-tissue clearing, genetic tracing and single-cell transcriptomics have mapped osteo-neural interactions with molecular precision. Nerve growth factor (NGF)-TrkA signalling coordinates somatosensory nerve growth and survival during skeletal development and repair, yet the same pathways can drive pathological nerve sprouting, skeletal pain and disease progression in skeletal pathologies ranging from osteoarthritis to heterotopic ossification and bone malignancies. We further discuss neuro-immune-bone interactions, conserved neuroregulatory mechanisms in the skeleton, and emerging neuromodulatory strategies. Finally, we identify topics for future investigation, including the effects of age-related neural decline on the skeleton, sex differences in skeletal innervation and bone pain, and translational gaps between rodent and human biology, that may guide the design of precision medicine interventions.

Article.Title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics
Article.Authors: Martínez-de-Morentin X.; Khan S.; Maillo A.; Lehmann R.; Kiani N.; Lagani V.; Gomez-Cabrero D.; Tegner J.
Article.Abstract: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Benchmarking reveals substantial variation in performance across datasets, technologies and evaluation criteria, highlighting trade-offs among segmentation completeness, transcriptomic fidelity and biological interpretability. Cross-technology analyses further demonstrate that segmentation choice critically shapes downstream analyses, including cell-type specificity, transcript contamination and ligand-receptor inference. Together, our unified Nextflow pipeline provides a scalable foundation for standardized evaluation of segmentation and method selection in spatial transcriptomics.

Article.Title: CauTrigger: deciphering biological system state transitions by hierarchical causal decomposition
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Cai D.; Aihara K.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Biological systems exhibit complex hierarchical regulation, with interactions across multiple layers governing transitions between states. Identifying the causal architecture underlying these state transitions remains challenging because confounding can produce spurious associations in observational data. Here we present CauTrigger, a hierarchical deep latent variable model that integrates do-calculus to identify potential causal triggers and predict perturbation outcomes across multiple regulatory layers. By disentangling causal and spurious latent factors, CauTrigger recursively reconstructs the underlying regulatory hierarchy and enables interpretable reasoning from observational data. Across synthetic and real-world datasets with multilayer regulatory structures, CauTrigger outperforms existing methods in identifying causal triggers and forecasting system-level responses. Applied to single-cell multi-omics and gut microbiome datasets, CauTrigger prioritizes candidate causal triggers and uses in silico perturbations to generate testable hypotheses about biological state transitions and inform potential strategies for state navigation. Together, these results establish CauTrigger as a general-purpose framework for causal discovery in complex biological systems.

Article.Title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics
Article.Authors: Nimo J.; Fritzsche S.; Valdes D.; Trinh M.; Pentimalli T.; Klingeberg M.; Schallenberg S.; Klauschen F.; Herse F.; Florian S.; Rajewsky N.; Coscia F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

Article.Title: Multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM): a reconfigurable platform for high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy
Article.Authors: Chen B.; Millett-Sikking A.; Chang B.; Gałecki S.; Daetwyler S.; Jiou J.; Monistrol J.; Shen Q.; Zhou F.; Lin H.; Jenkins E.; Stein M.; Marlar-Pavey M.; Sturm G.; Li A.; Tang Q.; Feng B.; Diaz U.; Chen Y.; Shalizi A.; Gillich A.; Friedman J.; Tomer R.; Marshall W.; Shahmoradian S.
Article.Abstract: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) enables gentle, rapid and efficient volumetric imaging of biological specimens. Despite its potential, LSFM has fragmented into multiple variants, each narrowly optimized for specific samples or imaging regimes, limiting its broad applicability. Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains diffraction-limited performance across a refractive index range of 1.33 to 1.51. It is compatible with standard sample mounting, current clearing protocols and high-throughput 3D imaging. We leverage miOPM to image diverse biological specimens at multiple spatial scales. By expanding the adaptability and ease of use of LSFM, miOPM is poised to democratize advanced 3D imaging.

Validation across 175 metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization-probed genes in 72 models demonstrated accurate predictions. Article.Title: Recent developments of fluorescent proteins and biosensors driven by cross-disciplinary insights
Article.Authors: Gest A.; Mehta S.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Since the discovery and application of green fluorescent protein for use as an optical tag, fluorescent proteins (FPs) have changed the way we observe biological signals and processes. FP and fluorescent biosensor design has continued to advance, facilitated by new technologies and developments in chemistry, physics, engineering and screening technologies. We summarize some of the recent developments in FP engineering, focusing on insights that have led to improved photostability or longer wavelengths, among other improvements, highlighting mScarlet as a case study. We also discuss the engineering of new fluorescent biosensors, focusing on the ways in which screening, quantitative imaging, spatial resolution and multiplexing have been improved in recent years. Finally, we conclude with a perspective on what the future holds for the next generation of FPs and biosensors.

Article.Title: LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment
Article.Authors: Reifenrath L.; van Kempen M.; Kim G.; Kim S.; Radnezhad M.; Gilchrist C.; Mirdita M.; Steinegger M.; Söding J.

Article.Title: Times are changing but order matters: transferable prediction of small-molecule liquid chromatography retention times
Article.Authors: Kretschmer F.; Harrieder E.; Witting M.; Böcker S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Liquid chromatography is a predominant technology for the separation of small molecules. Hundreds of retention time prediction models have been published over the past decades, yet truly transferable prediction (requiring no training data from the target chromatographic system) remains an open challenge. Unfortunately, retention times may change massively, even for nominally identical chromatographic conditions. Retention order is considerably more conserved; but even retention order may change if chromatographic conditions vary. Here we present 2-step, a two-step method for the prediction of retention times in reversed-phase chromatography. In the first step, a machine-learning model predicts a retention order index, taking into account chromatographic conditions. In the second step, we map predicted indices to absolute retention times. Disentangling these two tasks finally enables transferable retention time prediction across chromatographic conditions and compound classes, without requiring any target-system training data. Our 2-step method outperforms existing methods that were trained on the target dataset. Finally, we systematically study what chromatographic conditions result in notable changes of retention order.

Article.Authors: He L.; Tang L.; Cao D.; Duan W.; Yu J.; Zhang P.; Li H.; Wang Y.; Meng B.; Wang H.; Zhou Y.; Li W.; Li X.; Liu Z.; Zhang L.; Cheng J.; Wang S.

Article.Abstract: Cognitive reserve theory posits that compensatory mechanisms during aging stave off cognitive decline and lower risk for Alzheimer's disease. Here, in a screen for hippocampal dentate granule cell (DGC) synapse loss-induced factors in mice, we identified a secreted phospholipase, Pla2g2f, whose expression increases in DGCs during aging and is associated with cognitive resilience in humans. Pla2g2f deletion in DGCs exacerbates aging-associated pathophysiological changes, including synapse loss, inflammatory microglia, reactive astrogliosis, impaired neurogenesis, lipid dysregulation, lipid droplet accumulation and hippocampal-dependent memory loss. Conversely, boosting Pla2g2f in DGCs during aging is sufficient to prevent these pathophysiological alterations in hippocampal-cortical circuits, protect memory and prophylactically modify trajectory of cognitive decline. Mutagenesis of the catalytic site of PLA2G2F prevented lipid droplet mobilization and reduction of reactive gliosis and inflammatory microglia. Neuronal PLA2G2F mediates intercellular signaling to decrease lipid droplet and cholesterol ester load in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Our findings implicate PLA2G2F as a compensatory neuroprotective broadcast signal that maintains lipid homeostasis to counteract aging-associated cognitive decline.

Article.Title: Periventricular gradient pathology is linked to ependymal reactivity and cell adhesion disruption in multiple sclerosis
Article.Authors: Groh A.; Afanasiev E.; Thevakumaran R.; Creeggan F.; Callahan-Martin L.; Bigotte M.; Yaqubi M.; Gertsvolf J.; Pei J.; Wu H.; de Vos J.; Aalders M.; Zandee S.; Prat A.; Rudko D.; Stratton J.
Article.Abstract: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-adjacent brain areas are especially vulnerable to diffuse degeneration in multiple sclerosis (MS). Surface-in gradients arising from CSF-borne cytotoxic factors have been proposed to predict disease relapses independent of white matter lesions. Yet, whether such factors disrupt ependymal cells to penetrate the ventricular border in MS remains unknown. Here, using ultra-high-field magnetic resonance imaging-guided histology, electron microscopy and single-nucleus multiomics, we found that ependymal pathology correlates with periventricular gradients and involves an immune-reactive state marked by transporter and junctional protein dysregulation. We further defined the gene regulatory networks underpinning the MS ependymal state and predicted ligands known to be enriched in MS CSF that could drive the emergence of this state. One of the candidates, IFNγ, increased murine ependymal permeability in vivo, indicating that CSF ligands can modulate ependymal function and regional inflammation. These findings identify CSF-driven ependymal dysfunction as a contributor to periventricular pathology in MS.

Article.Title: A half-center oscillator regulates sleep pressure
Article.Authors: Hasenhuetl P.; Sarnataro R.; Vrontou E.; Rorsman H.; Talbot C.; Brain R.; Miesenböck G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Changes in oscillatory neural dynamics reflect—but may not necessarily determine—transitions between sleep stages and variations in sleep pressure. Here we show that sleep-control neurons innervating the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila (dFBNs) produce slow-wave activity (SWA) that is causally linked to sleep. The dFBN ensemble contains bistable cells whose membrane voltages oscillate between hyperpolarized DOWN and depolarized UP states. The oscillations rely on interhemispheric competition of two half-centers connected by inhibitory glutamatergic synapses. dFBN-restricted interference with glutamate release disrupts SWA and baseline as well as rebound sleep, whereas the optogenetic replay of SWA induces sleep. dFBNs generate SWA throughout the sleep–wake cycle (despite mutual antagonism with arousing dopaminergic neurons) and adjust its power to sleep need via sleep history-dependent increases in excitability and homeostatic synaptic depression. The oscillatory format permits a continuous encoding of sleep pressure but requires mechanisms that convert the amplitude-modulated signal into binary sleep–wake states.

Article.Title: 5-HT2A receptors in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediate the neuroplastic but not the hallucinogenic effects of psilocybin
Article.Authors: Baker J.; Kogan E.; Ma S.; Lu J.; Zuo Y.
Article.Abstract: It is unclear how serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2ARs) in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons differentially contribute to psilocybin-induced hallucinations versus neuroplasticity. Here we show that psilocybin promotes synapse formation and maturation while accelerating the elimination of pre-existing synapses. Cell type-specific manipulation further demonstrated that 5-HT2AR signaling in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for psilocybin-induced synaptic remodeling but dispensable for the head-twitch response, a rodent proxy of hallucination.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal AI-based modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain using Seal
Article.Authors: Hao Y.; Park C.; Theesfeld C.; Troyanskaya O.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 regions, 30 cell types and 7 developmental stages. Seal predictions provide mechanistic interpretation by linking variants to transcriptional regulators in a spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole-genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing cell-type-specific and stage-specific effects. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.

Article.Title: Symmetries and continuous attractors in disordered neural circuits
Article.Authors: Clark D.; Abbott L.; Sompolinsky H.
Article.Abstract: A core challenge in neuroscience is reconciling idealized models with experimental data. Classical continuous-attractor models describe neural representations of continuous variables such as head direction. Symmetry in the weights generates a manifold of stable states, with tuning curves identical up to shifts. Rodent head-direction cells, by contrast, are markedly heterogeneous. Such heterogeneity, we show, is nevertheless compatible with these models. Here we build, directly from head-direction cell data, recurrent networks that behave as quasicontinuous attractors. A generative process then reproduces the heterogeneous tuning of these cells while making connectivity and dynamics tractable at large N. Although the weights appear disordered, they carry a circular symmetry whose eigenvalue degeneracies could signify continuous-attractor organization in connectome data. Dynamical mean-field theory recovers the ingredients of classical ring attractors, namely, Mexican hat interactions and a spontaneously broken symmetry producing bump states. Continuous-attractor mechanisms may thus operate in complex mammalian circuits.

Article.Title: Investigating molecular and hemodynamic effects of LSD in the human brain
Article.Authors: McCulloch D.; Larsen K.; Johansen A.; Reveles Jensen K.; Nykjær C.; Holze F.; Falck N.; Neufeld V.; Steenstrup E.; Skov-Andersen P.; Spanggård A.; Geisler M.; Randrup P.; Jensen P.; Shalgunov V.; Johansen S.; Nielsen M.; Andersen T.; Stenbæk D.; Svarer C.; Fisher P.; Knudsen G.
Article.Abstract: Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) is a potent psychedelic with increasing therapeutic interest, yet qualification of target engagement using in vivo neuroimaging has not yet been performed. Using simultaneous positron emission tomography-magnetic resonance imaging technology, we describe multiple brain actions of LSD in seven healthy volunteers blinded to LSD dose received. Here we show that LSD occupies 5-HT2AR with a high affinity and increases both global cerebral blood flow (CBF) and internal carotid artery flow. LSD also decreases global connectivity, which was negatively associated with changes in CBF. We observe an anticlockwise hysteresis loop between plasma drug levels and subjective effects, suggesting atypical pharmacodynamic mechanisms. We contrast our CBF and global connectivity findings and their relation in a separate cohort of 25 participants administered psilocybin, highlighting key consistencies and differences. By establishing the dose-occupancy relation of LSD in humans, our findings provide insights for the clinical development of psychedelic compounds and demonstrate unique neurophysiological effects that distinguish LSD from psilocybin.

Article.Title: Genome-wide analysis of common structural variants in Alzheimer’s disease identifies a risk-associated regulatory CCG repeat in FAM193B
Article.Authors: Cao H.; Fu Y.; Zhou X.; Duan Y.; Ip F.; Chen Y.; Hu S.; Liu S.; Kwok T.; Mok K.; Cheung T.; Hardy J.; Fu A.; Ip N.
Article.Abstract: Although Alzheimer's disease (AD) has a polygenic architecture, with numerous associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) identified, the contribution of structural variants (SVs) is unclear. In this study, using long-read (n = 11) and short-read (n = 3,190) sequencing data from the Chinese population, we show that common SVs contribute to AD heritability beyond common SNPs. We identify an expanded CCG repeat in the FAM193B promoter that shows a genome-wide significant association with increased AD risk (odds ratio = 2.20 per 10-repeat increase, P = 5.5 × 10-13). The expanded FAM193B-CCG repeat increases FAM193B expression and mediates the pleiotropic association between brain FAM193B expression and AD risk. Analyses of postmortem human brains and cultured neuronal cells show that elevated neuronal FAM193B expression is associated with DNA damage and cell death-related pathways. These findings establish the common FAM193B-CCG repeat as an AD risk genetic factor and highlight the contribution of common SVs to AD heritability.

Article.Title: Alzheimer’s disease target and drug discovery by leveraging multiomics and electronic health data
Article.Authors: Hou Y.; Li Y.; Zhang P.; Lorincz-Comi N.; Gohel D.; Fan F.; Qiu Y.; Yang J.; Chen X.; Song W.; Yang X.; Tan Z.; Liu Z.; Fang X.; Rivera Paz I.; Martin W.; Feng Y.; Zhou Y.; Xu J.; Dou L.; Border J.; Zhang H.; Mazique J.; Hwang S.; Roman R.
Article.Abstract: Despite prolific genomic data from individuals with Alzheimer's disease (AD), translation into treatments has lagged. Here we applied Mendelian randomization to multiple AD genome-wide association studies and functional multiomics datasets to nominate druggable targets, identifying 19 targets for individuals of European ancestry and 7 for African ancestry. This included epoxide hydrolase 2 (EPHX2), for which we identified a protective missense variant (p.Arg287Gln). Experiments in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons and cerebral organoids from patients with AD validated the protective role of p.Arg287Gln via reduced levels of EPHX2 and phosphorylated tau (pTau-181). Pharmacological inhibition of EPHX2 improved cognitive performance in the 5xFAD mouse model of AD. Finally, by leveraging electronic health data from 111,680 patients with mild cognitive impairment, we identified 12 drugs associated with reduced AD incidence, including trazodone (targeting ADRA1A) and baclofen (targeting GABBR1). Thus, integrating multiomics data, functional validation and electronic health data identifies new approaches for treating AD.

Article.Title: Modality-specific reactive and predictive responses in the human superior colliculus
Article.Authors: Chen D.; Barton-Zuckerman M.; Kross Z.; Kragel P.; Savoca P.; Wald L.; Bianciardi M.; Wager T.; Choi J.; Zhang J.; Quigley K.; Satpute A.; Barrett L.; Theriault-Brown J.
Article.Abstract: Inspired by recent theoretical work emphasizing predictive neural processing, we tested whether a midbrain structure for multimodal sensory integration-the superior colliculus-would show predictive responses to both visual and somatosensory stimulation. A multi-stage experimental design allowed us to test predictive activity in the human superior colliculus while 7-Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) allowed us to map its sensory response across superior colliculus layers (N = 80). As expected from non-human animal work, visual and somatosensory stimulation elicited distinct depth-dependent responses. We also observed a predictive response: these same modality-specific and depth-dependent effects occurred during task periods preceding direct stimulation, when sensorimotor input was identical between visual and somatosensory conditions. Further analyses rule out cross-trial carryover and show corresponding effects in the thalamic sensory nuclei. Here our results confirm that, in humans, the superior colliculus is sensitive to both visual and somatosensory input, and they demonstrate that it carries predictive signals for upcoming sensory events.

Article.Title: Astrocytes regulate axonal mitochondrial transport deficits in C9ORF72 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis motor neurons
Article.Authors: Stavrou M.; Heffernan Á.; Carter R.; Dando O.; Jiwaji Z.; Burr K.; Nanda J.; Villarroel-Campos D.; Masoud Abdelhafid A.; Cholewa-Waclaw J.; Soong D.; Story D.; Schiavo G.; Hardingham G.; Chandran S.; Selvaraj B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Disrupted axonal transport and astrocyte dysfunction are implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here we show these processes are linked—human-induced pluripotent stem-cell-derived astrocytes carrying the C9ORF72 mutation disrupt mitochondrial axonal transport and mitochondrial function in cocultured motor neurons (MNs). Conversely, isogenic gene-corrected astrocytes or boosting astrocytic mitochondrial bioenergetics rescue axonal mitochondrial transport deficits in C9ORF72 MNs. Article.Title: Human claustrum neurons encode uncertainty and prediction errors during aversive learning
Article.Authors: Hu M.; Dalvit R.; Medina-Pizarro M.; Dougherty M.; Zhou Y.; Barreto-Nieves J.; Obaid S.; Afrasiyabi A.; Krishnaswamy S.; Kaye A.; Günel M.; Krystal J.; Sheth K.; Gu X.; Pittenger C.; Wise T.; Damisah E.
Article.Abstract: Flexible behavior depends on continuous updating of internal models, yet the neural circuits coordinating this process remain poorly understood. The claustrum, which is reciprocally connected to nearly the entire neocortex, is uniquely positioned to influence cortical processing. Here we report single-neuron recordings from the human claustrum during aversive learning, with anterior cingulate cortex and amygdala recordings for comparison. Claustrum and anterior cingulate neurons displayed structured, task-related responses. Distinct subpopulations encoded stimulus onset and action-contingent outcomes, with outcome representations diverging between regions. Critically, both regions encoded model-derived latent variables, including uncertainty and prediction error, but with different temporal profiles; only the anterior cingulate carried uncertainty signals during the intertrial period, whereas both regions encoded uncertainty and prediction error during the active-avoidance period. By contrast, the amygdala showed minimal latent-variable modulation. These findings provide evidence that human claustrum neurons track higher-order cognitive variables not directly observable from sensory input and reveal dissociable roles for the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex in tracking latent task states.

Article.Title: A human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived spheroid model to investigate myelin injury and repair
Article.Authors: Ramesan S.; Mason J.; Kumar S.; Swanson M.; Korneev D.; Mills S.; Mathangasinghe Y.; Andres A.; Loh L.; Fraser T.; Lewis K.; Beau F.; Chua S.; Kapoor-Kaushik N.; Williams L.; Mrkela M.; Turner B.; Ramm G.; Rutar M.; Shim H.; Gonsalvez D.; Barton S.
Article.Abstract: There are no currently approved therapies that promote new myelin formation after myelin damage, which can, in part, be attributed to a lack of reliable systems that can reproducibly model these processes. Here we engineered a human iPSC-derived spheroid model enriched with mature, myelinating oligodendrocytes and functionally reactive microglia. This model enables the study of human central nervous system remyelination after a demyelinating insult by recapitulating processes of myelin damage and repair. These include myelin fragmentation, microglial reactivity and phagocytosis of myelin debris, oligodendrocyte generation and differentiation, and axonal ensheathment with newly formed myelin. We show that newly generated oligodendrocytes contribute to remyelination, and use ultrastructural quantification to demonstrate that remyelinated axons are ensheathed by thinner myelin after injury. Altogether, we provide a model to interrogate otherwise inaccessible aspects of human myelin biology relevant to multiple sclerosis, providing mechanistic insights into disease pathways and a platform for drug screening.

Article.Title: Different functional connectivity gradients reflect aging and Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Rittmo J.; Franzmeier N.; Strandberg O.; Chauveau L.; Satterthwaite T.; Wisse L.; Spotorno N.; Behjat H.; Dehsarvi A.; van Westen D.; Anijärv T.; N/A N/A.; Landau S.; Palmqvist S.; Janelidze S.; Stomrud E.; Ossenkoppele R.; Mattsson-Carlgren N.; Hansson O.; Vogel J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aging and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) are accompanied by alterations to large-scale communication patterns in the brain, which can be tracked in vivo using functional connectivity. The location, direction and relevance of these changes remain widely debated, although they are rarely studied in the context of whole-cortex communication dynamics. Here, in two independent cohorts (BioFINDER-2, N = 973; Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, N = 129), we show that functional connectivity changes associated with aging and AD are strongly aligned with separate fundamental axes of hierarchical brain communication. Early accumulation of AD pathology and subsequent cognitive decline are both linked to functional change along the sensory–association axis. Meanwhile, age-related functional changes occur along the representation–executive axis consistently throughout the adult lifespan. These findings together suggest that both AD and aging alter major but orthogonal functional pathways in the brain. More broadly, our findings position whole-brain connectivity dynamics as a unifying framework for interpreting functional changes across the adult lifespan.

Article.Title: CLOK: a chemigenetic multicolor labeling system to visualize neuronal birthdate and circuit integration
Article.Authors: Faini G.; Tuffery M.; Saleem A.; Zhang L.; Du F.; Le Bourdelles G.; Duroure K.; Schreiter E.; Tanese D.; Emiliani V.; Del Bene F.; Koyama M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Understanding how neurons integrate into developing circuits and contribute to functional activity is essential for decoding brain development and plasticity. However, current methods to study neuronal integration often suffer from low throughput, limited spatiotemporal resolution or invasive procedures. To overcome these challenges, here we present CLOK, an in vivo birthdate-labeling strategy based on HaloTag technology and its broad palette of fluorescent ligands. We show that CLOK enables precise color-coding of neurons and their subcellular structures by birthdate and allows tracking of functional maturation of newborn neurons in the developing zebrafish visual and motor systems, revealing distinct maturation trajectories of early- and late-born neurons. We further demonstrate the versatility of this approach by coupling it to optical tools enabling age-specific multicolor calcium and voltage imaging, as well as optogenetic manipulation. Altogether, CLOK provides a powerful and flexible tool for optical interrogation of neuronal circuit maturation in a growing and behaving vertebrate.

Article.Title: A population code for semantics in human hippocampus
Article.Authors: Franch M.; Mickiewicz E.; Belanger J.; Joiner B.; Katlowitz K.; Zhu H.; Chavez A.; Chericoni A.; Goldman A.; Krishnan V.; Maheshwari A.; Paulo D.; Bartoli E.; Kemmer S.; Piantadosi S.; Provenza N.; Hennig J.; Sheth S.; Hayden B.
Article.Abstract: Motivated by the successes of large language models (LLMs), we hypothesized that semantic information in the brain may be expressed in distributed patterns of neural activity. We recorded responses of hippocampal neurons while individuals listened to narrative speech. Here, using an encoding model approach, we find robust encoding of semantics, even after controlling for phonemics and grammar. Individual words had complex selectivities that included multiple words in multiple semantic categories. Similar to embedding vectors in LLMs, distance between neural population responses correlated with semantic distance. For semantically similar words, even contextual embedders showed an inverse correlation between semantic and neural distances; we attribute this pattern to the noise-mitigating benefits of contrastive coding. Finally, neural population activity aligned most closely with GPT-2 embeddings, and variation in response patterns correlated with LLM-derived polysemy measures, indicating that semantic encoding is largely contextualized. Ultimately, these results provide a neurocomputational account for understanding how hippocampal neurons encode word meaning during language listening.

Article.Title: Comprehensive profiling of brain dynamics during anesthesia across phylogeny
Article.Authors: Luppi A.; Uhrig L.; Tasserie J.; Shafiei G.; Légaré A.; Muta K.; Hata J.; Okano H.; Golkowski D.; Ranft A.; Ilg R.; Jordan D.; Gini S.; Liu Z.; Yee Y.; Castro P.; Signorelli C.; Cofre R.; Destexhe A.; Menon D.; Stamatakis E.; Desrosiers P.; De Koninck P.; Connor C.; Gozzi A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The behavioral effects of anesthetics are highly conserved across species, hinting at shared and fundamental underlying mechanisms. Here we compile a dataset of multiscale neural activity during wakefulness and anesthesia, encompassing human, macaque, marmoset, mouse, zebrafish and nematode. Applying massive feature extraction, we characterize local neural dynamics across >6,000 time-series features. This reveals a conserved dynamical profile of anesthesia across species, characterized by shorter intrinsic timescales of neural activity and dampened inter-regional synchrony. Deep-brain stimulation of the macaque centromedian thalamus reverses this profile and restores behavioral responsiveness. This conserved dynamical phenotype covaries with conserved transcriptional profiles of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. Biophysical modeling provides a potential mechanistic link between the macroscale dynamical phenotype of anesthesia and microscale effects of key molecular targets on the timescales of synaptic excitation and inhibition. These analyses reveal a shared neural endpoint of anesthesia: across species and scales, anesthetics induce spatiotemporal isolation of local neural activity.

Article.Title: A neural architecture for imagined and overt speech motor dynamics
Article.Authors: Zhao Z.; Wang Z.; Liu Y.; Qian Y.; Yin Y.; Gao X.; Yuan B.; Tong S.; Tian X.; Chen G.; Li Y.; Lu J.; Wu J.
Article.Abstract: Mental imagery is a hallmark of human cognition, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. Speech imagery (the internal simulation of speech without overt articulation) has been proposed to partially share substrates with speech production, but its spatiotemporal dynamics remain controversial. Here, we leveraged high-resolution electrocorticography to investigate shared and modality-specific coding of articulatory kinematic trajectories during speech imagery and articulation. Linear modeling revealed robust articulatory kinematic trajectories encoding in frontoparietal cortex across modalities. Supramodal populations across middle premotor, subcentral and postcentral-supramarginal regions exhibited spatiotemporal stability during integrative planning. In contrast, modality-specific populations for speech imagery and articulation were somatotopically interleaved in primary sensorimotor cortex, revealing a distinct spatiotemporal organization. We further developed a generalized decoding framework that achieved high prediction accuracy for speech imagery (median 80.4%; chance 16.7%), comparable to speech articulation (78.3%). These findings uncover a somato-cognitive organization linking supramodal planning with modality-specific representations, informing imagery-based brain-computer interfaces.

Article.Title: Keratin 9 regulates mechanosensitive YAP1 signalling in palmoplantar epidermis
Article.Authors: Steiner S.; Horst E.; Chiu E.; Athaiya M.; Johnson C.; Shen J.; Kerns M.; Kirma J.; McCarthy R.; Shah S.; Sarig O.; Samuelov L.; Sprecher E.; O’Toole E.; Gudjonsson J.; Mehta G.; Iglesias-Bartolome R.; Coulombe P.
Article.Abstract: The palmoplantar epidermis, in adapting to the exceptional mechanical strain it bears during locomotion, is histologically and molecularly distinct from other skin body sites. The mechanisms specifying and maintaining its unique identity remain incompletely defined. Here we identify the type I keratin 9 (KRT9/K9), a protein uniquely expressed in palmoplantar epidermis, as a key modulator of mechanosensitive YAP1 signalling in response to postnatal mechanical compression. K9 loss-of-function variants driving KRT9-pEDD, a palmoplantar epidermal differentiation disorder, result in aberrant YAP1 subcellular partitioning and elevated levels of the stress-induced keratin 16 (KRT16/K16). Krt9 null mice recapitulate these molecular phenotypes as early as postnatal day 3. We further identify dynamic, YAP1-dependent regulation of Krt16/K16, upstream of and necessary for Krt9/K9 expression, during early postnatal development in situ and in response to mechanical compression of keratinocytes ex vivo, highlighting the role of mechanical stress in epidermal specification. Mechanistically, K9 interacts with the YAP1 binding protein 14-3-3σ and sequesters YAP1 in the cytoplasm, inhibiting its transcriptional activity; these functions are disrupted by KRT9-pEDD-causing variants in K9. Finally, we show that genetic or pharmacological inhibition of YAP1 ameliorates palmoplantar keratoderma in Krt9 null mice. These findings reveal a role for mechanical cues in specification and maintenance of palmoplantar skin and suggest new therapeutic interventions for inherited palmoplantar epidermal differentiation disorders.

Article.Title: The rise of reducing reagent-resistant TfR1 dimer marks ferroptosis
Article.Authors: He J.; Kelleher M.; Veeckmans G.; Zhang Y.; Reynolds L.; Tanczos H.; Huang Z.; McLaughlin B.; Martinez Molina M.; Lightburn A.; Zamarro M.; Huang W.; Owusu S.; Walravens M.; Willemart C.; Hassannia B.; Pope L.; Gager C.; Vaughan A.; Wang Z.; Weaver S.; Boggess W.; Lu X.; Papagiannakopoulos T.; Flores-Mireles A.
Article.Abstract: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent type of cell death caused by excessive membrane lipid peroxidation. It remains a challenge to detect ferroptotic cells, especially in in vivo settings, hindering translational studies. Here we discover that a reducing reagent-resistant (3R) dimer of the transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) is a highly specific indicator for lipid peroxidation. The 3R dimer is elevated in cells when ferroptosis is induced, either by pharmacological agents or by genetic perturbations. Furthermore, the 3R dimer can be used to detect disease-associated ferroptosis in tissue and in extracellular vesicles isolated from mouse or patient plasma. Given the near-ubiquitous expression of TfR1, we posit that the 3R dimer may function as a ferroptosis marker with widespread potential utility for basic and translational studies.

Article.Title: Spatial multi-omic atlas profiles early organogenesis of a Carnegie stage 12 human embryo
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Yang H.; Song J.; Zhao R.; Liu S.; Hou H.; Zhang C.; Tian H.; Gao J.; Chen J.; Chen Z.; Zhao H.; Liu B.; Wu K.
Article.Abstract: Organogenesis marks one of the most dynamic periods of early human embryonic development. Although the morphological features of this period have been described, the underlying transcriptional and metabolic landscapes remain poorly understood owing to the lack of an integrated spatial strategy. We present spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic maps of a Carnegie stage 12 (CS12) human embryo, co-registered with embryonic anatomy to generate a unified spatial multi-omic framework. Unsupervised clustering of the spatial transcriptomic data identified 17 cell populations covering the major organ primordia. Notably, we observed spatially separable hepatocyte- and cholangiocyte-lineage primed transcriptional programmes within the liver primordium, and detected cardiac outflow tract and sinoatrial node progenitors at CS12. Furthermore, integration of gene and metabolite abundance highlighted regional associations between transcription factors and metabolic pathways underpinning lineage specification. Our work presents a spatially resolved multi-omic atlas of a human embryo at the onset of organogenesis.

Article.Title: Monocyte surface Y RNAs potentiate innate immunity
Article.Authors: Jiang X.; He W.; Xu C.; Zheng W.; Li C.; Xu D.; Shao Q.; Li Y.; Liu Z.; Li W.; He S.; Wang Z.; Liu R.; Chu Y.; Luo Z.; Huang X.; Liu J.; Yang E.; Hu L.
Article.Abstract: RNAs can associate with the surface of diverse cell types, yet the functions of specific RNA species on primary immune cells remain unclear. Here, utilizing methods developed to profile, image and quantify surface RNAs in rare primary cell populations, we found that Y RNAs, a family of small noncoding RNAs, preferentially localize to human monocyte surface. In an exploratory pooled inflammatory bowel disease cohort, the proportion of cell-surface-Y-RNA-positive peripheral monocytes was markedly higher in patients with inflammatory bowel disease than in healthy donors or individuals with irritable bowel syndrome. In vivo depletion of cell-surface Y RNAs ameliorates disease activity in mice with colitis. Mechanistically, cell-surface Y RNAs co-cluster with Toll-like receptors TLR2 and TLR4, bind extracellular histones and promote receptor-mediated histone recognition, thereby activating NF-κB and AP-1 signalling and increasing IL6 expression and IL-6 secretion. These findings identify cell-surface Y RNAs as previously unrecognized amplifiers of inflammatory activation.

Article.Title: Global and specific mechanisms stimulate mistranslation in cancer
Article.Authors: Wernaart D.; Fumagalli A.; Adhikary M.; Feng X.; Geintzer O.; Kyei-Baffour E.; Bleijerveld O.; Hoekman L.; Zwart C.; Fish A.; Giebel L.; Burylo A.; Proost N.; Körner P.; Alkan F.; Yang C.; Brouwer J.; Henriksen C.; Westhof E.; Champagne J.; van Tellingen O.; Rodnina M.; Agami R.
Article.Abstract: Tryptophan codon-specific mistranslation, in the form of ribosomal frameshifting and tryptophan-to-phenylalanine (W > F) codon reassignments (substitutants), is induced in cancer cells by the limiting level of tryptophan imposed by anti-tumour immunity. While the oncogenic mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway drives frameshifting, whether substitutants are genetically regulated remains unknown. Here we screened for genes that control W > F substitutants following interferon-γ-mediated tryptophan shortage. This screen identified ADAR1, an enzyme that converts adenosine to inosine in double-stranded RNA molecules, and FTSJ1, an enzyme that 2'-O-methylates the anticodon region of several tRNAs. We demonstrate that ADAR1 sustains expression of key players in the ribosome quality control pathway, which in turn is essential for mistranslation events. FTSJ1, in contrast, specifically drives W > F mistranslation by methylation of tRNATrp to promote its binding to WARS1 loaded with phenylalanine instead of tryptophan. As ADAR1 and FTSJ1 levels are elevated in many cancer types, we propose that cancer cells deploy global and specific mechanisms to promote mistranslation in response to anti-tumour immunity.

Article.Title: Power-law scaling of mitotic spindles with genome sizes across eukaryotes is driven by chromosome crowding
Article.Authors: Gudlin L.; Vukušić K.; Novak M.; Trupinić M.; Ljulj M.; Dundović I.; Petelinec A.; Petrušić L.; Hertel A.; van Ravesteyn T.; Trakala M.; Kops G.; Storchová Z.; Tambača J.; Pavin N.; Tolić I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Genome size varies more than 10,000-fold across eukaryotes, yet how the mitotic spindle adapts to this range remains unknown. Here we show that metaphase plate width scales with genome size following a power law with an exponent of ~1/3 across eukaryotes. Comparative analysis and a physical model reveal that this scaling arises from the linear relationship between total chromosome volume and genome size, with chromosome number playing a secondary role. The same scaling holds across ploidy levels in cell lines, patient-derived cancer organoids and meiotic systems. Physical model and acute spindle compression demonstrate that chromosome crowding generates interchromosome pushing forces that set metaphase plate width. By contrast, spindle length is regulated by microtubule dynamics, cytoplasmic forces and cell size, indicating that spindle dimensions are independently controlled. The revealed scaling law provides a robust mechanism for accommodating large genomic variation and offers insight into the evolution of open mitosis and mitotic cell rounding, as well as polyploidy tolerance in tumours and during speciation.

Article.Title: In vivo DNA damage protection during cell migration across confining embryonic tissue environments
Article.Authors: Häkkinen H.; Villaseca S.; Alhashem Z.; Hamidzadeh A.; Chomiczewski S.; Desevedavy M.; Leleux S.; Liu Y.; Becker J.; Htun M.; Gallo F.; El-Zohiry D.; Petre V.; Stefanowski K.; Franze K.; Renkawitz J.; Scarpa E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cells migrating through confined spaces can experience nuclear deformation, nuclear envelope damage and DNA lesions, but the physiological consequences of confinement in vivo remain unclear. Using the zebrafish neural crest as a model of developmental migration, we show that tissue confinement increases along the antero–posterior axis and scales with the extent of nuclear deformation. Genetic and mechanical disruption of surrounding tissues relieves confinement and restores nuclear morphology in vivo. Surprisingly, even under extreme deformation, neural crest cells exhibit nucleo-cytoplasmic leakage without nuclear envelope rupture or increased DNA damage. Instead, confinement is associated with reduced LaminB2 at the nuclear envelope. Functional perturbation of LaminB2 reveals that its depletion accelerates recovery from deformation, whereas sustained expression causes persistent nuclear distortion, identifying LaminB2 as a regulator of nuclear deformability. RNA-seq of confined trunk neural crest cells reveals broad upregulation of DNA repair pathways, suggesting that these embryonic stem-like cells are intrinsically resistant to confinement-induced mechanical stress.

Article.Title: Quantification of lipid sorting during clathrin-mediated endocytosis
Article.Authors: Lennartz H.; da Costa Nunes S.; Böhlig K.; Chhatre A.; Šachl R.; Kuhn S.; Moneta L.; Barahtjan P.; Yee Yau W.; Iglesias-Artola J.; Hof M.; Opálka L.; Modes C.; Honigmann A.; Nadler A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is a major transport route for proteins from the plasma membrane to the interior of the cell. While the recruitment of cargo proteins to clathrin-coated pits is well understood, it remains an open question whether lipids are also sorted by this process. Here, to address this question, we combined super-resolution stimulated emission depletion imaging of bifunctional lipid probes with mathematical modelling. Quantification of ten different lipid species revealed significant differences in pit partitioning, ranging from slight enrichment to moderate exclusion. We find that the lipid asymmetry in the plasma membrane is sufficient to explain the observed trend. Taken together, our findings imply that clathrin-mediated endocytosis has a minor selectivity for cytoplasmic leaflet lipids, but overall does not substantially contribute to lipid sorting compared with non-vesicular trafficking.

Article.Authors: To K.; Pett J.; Dufva O.; Chipampe N.; Polanski K.; Cujba A.; Roberts K.; Predeus A.; Yayon N.; Kanemaru K.; Patel M.; Horsfall D.; Li T.; Mazin P.; Cakir B.; Kapuge R.; Wilk A.; Memi F.; He X.; Solanky N.; Kayhanian S.; Mair R.; Rademaker K.; Bayraktar O.; Haniffa M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The meninges are increasingly recognized as key stromal and immune niches supporting cranial development. Here we constructed a paired single-nuclei RNA and Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin atlas of human meningeal development from 6 to 21 postconception weeks across cranial regions. By integrating spatial transcriptomics, we resolved cell types across meningeal layers. Our multiomic atlas defines gene regulatory networks underlying blood–brain barrier endothelial identity during development. Within immune compartments, the data support a yolk sac origin for meningeal myeloid lineages, including perivascular macrophages primed for barrier immunity. We present two analytical tools: Nichefinder, for spatial label transfer and proximity analysis, and cell2home, for inferring chemotactic signalling. Using cell2home, we identify interactions potentially driving B cell migration from cranial marrow into prenatal meninges. We studied trisomy 21, and observed reduced fibroblast chemokine expression with enhanced JAK–STAT signalling. Together, this work provides a developmental atlas of the human meninges and defines cellular and regulatory programs shaping early barrier immunity.

Article.Title: Cell atlas of the developing human meninges reveals a dura-like nature of meningiomas
Article.Authors: Vinsland E.; Marco Salas S.; Kapustová I.; Hu L.; Webb S.; Li X.; He X.; Nilsson M.; Haniffa M.; Barker R.; Persson O.; Raleigh D.; Sundström E.; Lönnerberg P.; Linnarsson S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The vertebrate central nervous system is enveloped by the meninges, consisting of the pia, arachnoid and dura layers. The arachnoid is hypothesized to give rise to the most common primary intracranial tumours, meningiomas. However, supporting molecular evidence is lacking. There are no effective medical therapies to treat meningiomas that are resistant to local interventions, encumbered by our limited understanding of their cellular origin. Here, to advance our understanding of meningioma biology, we generated a comprehensive reference single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlas of human fetal meninges at postconceptional weeks 5–13. We found that the meningeal layers develop concurrently, and identified an inner CDH1 -positive dura layer expressing tight-junction genes consistent with barrier function. Comparing meningiomas with fetal meninges, we show that, transcriptionally, meningioma cells resemble dura-lineage cells, and that common meningioma driver genes were expressed in the dura lineage. This raises the hypothesis that meningiomas could originate from dura-lineage cells.

Article.Title: Amygdala excitability across development: mechanisms, environmental influences, and behavioral outcomes
Article.Authors: Ehrlich I.; Lauri S.
Article.Abstract: Recent work in rodent models provides mechanistic insights into how the excitability of principal neurons is dynamically regulated to facilitate the encoding and retrieval of emotionally salient memories in the basolateral amygdala (BLA). In this review, we discuss the physiological mechanisms governing BLA excitability, emphasizing their impact on the recruitment of defined BLA ensembles encoding distinct behavioral states. In addition, we summarize the current understanding of how these mechanisms are established during development and suggest that this may follow distinct developmental phases. Lastly, we outline recent findings on how early-life adversity or genetic risk factors can acutely perturb developmental trajectories and may lead to enduring changes in BLA circuit function, with implications for neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: The nervous system as a systemic organizer of cancer-associated cachexia
Article.Authors: Weng Z.; Cai S.; Zhu H.; Jiang L.; Zhang S.; Zhang Z.; Jiang S.
Article.Abstract: Cancer-associated cachexia (CAC) is a progressive, multiorgan wasting syndrome that critically limits treatment response and survival. In CAC, the nervous system senses, amplifies, and coordinates responses to a broad range of tumor-induced perturbations, including both direct tumor-derived factors and the resulting systemic disturbances in inflammation, metabolism, and immunity. By dysregulating central neural circuits and remodeling peripheral innervation, tumor-hijacked neural coordination drives both anorexia and multiorgan wasting, forming a self-reinforcing cachexia loop. Additionally, treatment-associated neurotoxicity further augments dysfunction across the central and peripheral nervous systems. In this review, we synthesize evidence from patient studies and animal models to examine how tumors co-opt the nervous system to systemically organize cachexia, thereby providing a pathophysiological framework for studying early disease detection, biomarker development, and mechanism-based intervention for CAC.

Article.Title: Spatial navigation and the basal forebrain in Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative diseases
Article.Authors: Laczó M.; Lerch O.; Nedelska Z.; Laczó J.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Lewy body disease (LBD) are frequently associated with spatial navigation impairments. However, these impairments are less pronounced in frontotemporal dementia and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy. While basal forebrain degeneration occurs in all of these diseases, disruption of cholinergic pathways and related cholinergic deficits has been primarily observed in AD and LBD, and in both of these conditions, basal forebrain degeneration appears to be associated with spatial navigation deficits. In this review, we discuss current understanding of spatial navigation impairments in neurodegenerative diseases, with a particular focus on disease-related changes in the basal forebrain and their associations with impaired spatial navigation abilities in humans.

Article.Title: Beyond breathing: multimodal pathways connecting olfaction to autonomic nervous system modulation
Article.Authors: Walter M.; Puech A.; Aliyari F.; Courtiol E.; Buonviso N.
Article.Abstract: The interaction between olfaction and respiration has recently emerged as a central aspect of brain-body interactions. To date, most studies in this context, both in rodents and humans, have focused on how respiratory airflow rhythmically drives brain activity. In this review, we shift the focus to the modulatory effects of odorant molecules, which engage chemical, affective, and trigeminal pathways to elicit integrated sensory experiences and robust autonomic responses. We synthesize recent findings showing that the olfactory system, through its unique connectivity with limbic and autonomic networks, operates at the interface between exteroception and interoception. By modulating respiratory dynamics, and more generally autonomic nervous system activity, odors emerge as a multimodal signal capable of influencing brain-body interactions and supporting well-being.

Article.Title: Temporal astrocytic metabolic reprogramming gates pain chronification
Article.Authors: Park J.; Lee S.
Article.Abstract: Most experimental models of chronic pain emphasize the gradual emergence of sensory hypersensitivity, yet pain chronification can also be conceptualized as a metabolically regulated state transition. In this review, we synthesize evidence mainly from mouse and rat spinal cord and anterior cingulate cortex studies indicating that astrocytes temporally coordinate neuronal excitability, inflammatory signaling, and metabolic coupling. We propose that chronification proceeds through temporally organized astrocytic metabolic remodeling: GPCR-linked lactate-coupled signaling during acute induction, sustained glycolytic gene expression and glycogen remodeling during consolidation, and stabilization of pain-permissive astrocyte states through lactylation-linked inflammatory and chromatin regulation. By integrating these mechanisms along a temporal axis, this framework distinguishes processes that initiate chronicity from those that maintain established pain and suggests stage-specific logic for future interventions.

Article.Title: The dynamics of functional connectivity-based language lateralization across timescales
Article.Authors: Cao W.; Wang N.; Zhou K.; Xu M.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: In most individuals, language is predominantly left-lateralized, a prominent feature of human brain organization. Recent research increasingly views language lateralization as a property of distributed and interacting functional networks. In this article, we review evidence that the lateralization of functional connectivity within the language system varies in both degree and direction across multiple timescales. We propose that this connectivity-based lateralization undergoes long-term developmental, experience-dependent, and perturbation-induced reorganization, while also exhibiting short-term context-driven and spontaneous fluctuations within apparently stable patterns. Furthermore, we discuss neurobiological mechanisms that may support and constrain these dynamics. Together, these findings provide a multiscale framework for understanding how the human brain balances functional flexibility with relative stability in shaping the lateralized organization of language.

Article.Title: The mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome in aging and brain diseases
Article.Authors: Shawky A.; Huang H.; Parikh D.; Morris-Blanco K.
Article.Abstract: The mitochondrial genome is a dynamic regulatory platform that extends far beyond its protein-coding capacity. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) harbors epigenetic modifications and produces diverse noncoding RNAs that influence mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis. Evidence from animal models and human studies indicates that mtDNA methylation, mitochondrial-encoded noncoding RNAs, and cytosolic release of mitochondrial nucleic acids regulate transcription, metabolism, and stress signaling. Article.Title: Resilience and vulnerability in the midbrain dopamine system during aging
Article.Authors: McMurtrie G.; Mabry S.; Glausier J.; Rocha E.; Freyberg Z.
Article.Abstract: The midbrain dopamine system is integral to movement, reward, and motivation, and its dysfunction underlies a range of brain disorders. Age is a primary risk factor for many of these disorders, yet systematic analysis of how the dopamine system changes during healthy aging remains relatively understudied. In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. Elucidating these neuroadaptive mechanisms could offer a path toward preserving dopamine neuron function across the lifespan and potentially preventing age-related neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Apolipoprotein E4 and immune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease: mechanisms and therapeutic implications
Article.Authors: Shi H.; Zhao Y.; Zhu W.; Wang Y.; Bu X.
Article.Abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) functions as an organizer of brain-periphery immune crosstalk, coupling maladaptive microglial states with peripheral immune remodeling to establish a self-reinforcing neuroimmune loop that may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer's disease. In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. In addition, APOE4 erodes the separation between central and peripheral immune compartments, enabling bidirectional immune crosstalk that amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. In this review, we synthesize evidence for APOE4-driven central and peripheral immune dysregulation; discuss therapeutic opportunities for targeting the APOE4 immune axis; and highlight the need for human-derived, longitudinal, cross-tissue studies to identify causal, stage-specific, and targetable immune nodes for precision intervention.

Article.Title: Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and phenotypic plasticity
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Ye Z.; Wang Y.; Tang S.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for therapeutic translation.

Article.Title: Active locomotion predictively rescues head direction attractor dynamics in head-fixed mice
Article.Authors: Pak A.; Aarse J.; Zhu H.; Noel J.; Carrillo Segura S.; Fenton A.; Angelaki D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Head direction (HD) cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus form the brain’s internal compass, and are often modeled as a ring attractor maintaining azimuth coding by leveraging continuous visual and inertial sensory input. Here, we test how the common experimental preparation of head-fixed animals alters this code. Complete head-fixation that creates vestibular conflict disrupts both unit and population encoding of head direction, while selectively constraining head-on-body movements either in real or virtual reality uniquely impairs HD population activity. More specifically, attractor dynamics are altered in head-restrained male mice during periods of immobility, and a computational model recapitulates this effect by perturbing lateral connectivity among HD neurons. These dynamics recover several hundred milliseconds prior to locomotion onset, suggesting that an efference copy or prediction of a re-afferent signal is necessary to maintain HD network activity during head restraint. More generally, the results indicate that the HD network is a context- and state-dependent predictive estimator, stabilized by forthcoming self-motion signals. The classic ring-attractor models should be revised to integrate context-dependent dynamics with prospective motor signals, offering a more complete account of how the brain’s compass remains stable across both naturalistic and constrained conditions.

Article.Title: Structural dynamics of substrate processing by the p97-Ufd1-Npl4-FAF1 machinery
Article.Authors: Drakonaki A.; van den Boom J.; Kröning A.; Meyer H.; Gatsogiannis C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The AAA-ATPase VCP/p97 unfolds ubiquitylated proteins in key signaling and cellular homeostasis pathways, yet the mechanisms by which Ufd1-Npl4 and FAF1 adapters handle ubiquitin chains to coordinate substrate loading and processing remain unclear. Our cryo-EM study of p97-Ufd1-Npl4 and FAF1 engaging a substrate reveal interactions that drive substrate processing. While Npl4 is capped by distal ubiquitins, and the initiator ubiquitin can be traced from the Npl4 groove to the ATPase channel at near-atomic resolution, we find that the Npl4 tower adaptively responds to the configurational changes in the ATPase motor’s spiral staircase. A helix in FAF1 together with the Ufd1-UT3 domain engage proximal ubiquitins while providing the necessary structural plasticity to accommodate this motion and deliver ubiquitins to Npl4’s groove. Our study reveals the intricate, dynamic interplay between p97, Ufd1-Npl4, and FAF1 in efficient processing of ubiquitylated substrates.

Article.Title: Programmable roll-to-roll laser processing for high value application of low-grade carbon fiber materials
Article.Authors: Chen G.; Yu W.; Jiang Y.; Jia L.; Hu Z.; Zhao W.; Yi X.; Liu X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Growing production of carbon fibers generates substantial short-chopped fibers that are difficult for high-value use due to their structural discontinuity. Carbon fiber felts offer potential, yet weak inter-fiber bonding and poor conductivity limit the performance. We report a roll‑to‑roll laser processing strategy that uses a liquid precursor to form laser‑induced graphene at fiber‑fiber interfaces, creating conductive pathways and mechanical interconnections. This approach increases tensile strength from 4.1 to 32.2 MPa and electrical conductivity from 1224.0 to 15151.5 S/m. The resulting films demonstrate efficient electrothermal de‑icing and, after copper deposition, lightning strike protection with a damage area of 9657 mm² and depth of 0.4 mm, comparable to aluminum mesh but with 15% lower weight. A custom‑built laser platform enables scalable production. Here, we show the conversion of low‑grade carbon fibers into lightweight, functional films for aerospace applications via scalable laser processing.
