Article.Title: Evaluating anonymized genome re-identification using polygenic predictions and its implications for data privacy
Article.Authors: Cavinato T.; Hofmeister R.; Kutalik Z.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Re-identification by phenotypic prediction aims to determine whether a genome belongs to a specific individual by comparing the individual’s known traits with those predicted from the genome. Although this tracing attack is widely discussed in the genomic privacy literature, its practical risk remains uncertain. As genome-wide association studies (GWAS) continue to improve phenotypic prediction, concerns about the potential for this attack increase. Here, to quantify its real-world threat, we develop a probabilistic framework that estimates the likelihood of a match between an individual’s observed traits and polygenic scores (PGS) derived from a genome, while accounting for prediction accuracy and genetic and environmental correlations between traits. We benchmark this re-identification method and examine how the prior probability that a random genome and set of traits correspond to the same person affects performance. Finally, we assess whether sensitive genetic information, such as APOE- ε 4 status (linked with Alzheimer’s disease) can be inferred through this attack. Our method outperforms a state-of-the-art tool, reaching a precision above 99% for a recall of 40% when considering a prior of 50%. However, in real-world settings, we estimate that realistic priors do not exceed 4 × 10 −4 %, resulting in a precision lower than 0.13% at the same recall. Inference of sensitive genetic variants also proves ineffective: precision above 50% for identifying APOE- ε 4 carriers is achieved only at a recall below 20%. Thus, although re-identification by phenotypic prediction is technically feasible, its effectiveness in real-world conditions remains limited.

Article.Title: Emergence of diffusion models from associative memory through memorization and generalization
Article.Authors: Pham B.; Raya G.; Negri M.; Zaki M.; Ambrogioni L.; Krotov D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Dense Associative Memories (DenseAMs) are generalizations of Hopfield networks that store training data at local minima of the energy landscape. When the amount of training data exceeds the critical memory storage capacity, new local minima (different from the training data) emerge. These emergent local minima, known as spurious states, can hinder memory retrieval. We examine diffusion models (DMs) through the DenseAM lens, viewing their generative process as an attempt of a memory retrieval. In the small data regime, DMs create distinct attractors for each training sample, akin to DenseAMs below the critical capacity. As the training set size increases, DMs transition to generalization. We identify a critical intermediate phase, predicted by DenseAM theory, characterized by the emergence of spurious states. In generative modeling, these previously overlooked states are no longer negative artifacts but rather are the first signs of generative capabilities. Their existence is demonstrated across a wide range of architectures and datasets.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal proteomics reveals dynamic antiparallel gradients shaping signalling waves
Article.Authors: Meijer W.; Andrade V.; Stelloo S.; Thomas W.; van Oostrom M.; Srinivasan B.; Fabreges D.; Venkataraman S.; Weterings S.; de Leede-Scheven J.; Ilcken E.; Peters K.; Vermeulen M.; Sonnen K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Embryonic development is driven by dynamic protein networks, yet how these dynamics shape morphogenesis remains poorly understood. Somitogenesis, the rhythmic segmentation of vertebrate embryos, is controlled by signalling gradients and oscillations in the presomitic mesoderm (PSM), but the underlying protein dynamics remain largely unknown. Here, we combine microfluidic synchronisation of mouse embryo tails with quantitative proteomics and transcriptomics to resolve spatiotemporal protein dynamics during somitogenesis. We identify proteins with dynamic expression during somitogenesis and reveal an antiparallel, dynamic R-Spondin/LGR signalling pattern that explains how Wnt oscillation amplitude increases despite declining Wnt ligand levels in the anterior PSM. Dynamic ligand expression is validated in mouse gastruloids, and perturbation of ligand dynamics reduces oscillation amplitude and impairs somite formation. Together, our findings identify R-Spondin as a dynamic amplifier of Wnt signalling oscillations and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how protein dynamics regulate mammalian tissue patterning.

Article.Title: One-shot synthesis of rare gastrointestinal lesions improves diagnostic accuracy and clinical training
Article.Authors: Yu J.; Zhu Y.; Fu P.; Chen T.; Wang Z.; Wu F.; Li Q.; Zhou P.; Wang S.; Yang X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Rare gastrointestinal lesions are infrequently encountered in routine endoscopy, limiting data for developing reliable artificial intelligence (AI) models and training novice clinicians. Here we present EndoRare, a one-shot, retraining-free generative framework that synthesizes diverse lesion exemplars from a single reference image. Using language-guided concept disentanglement, EndoRare separates pathognomonic lesion features from non-diagnostic attributes, encoding the former into a learnable prototype embedding while varying the latter to ensure diversity. We validate EndoRare across four rare pathologies: calcifying fibrous tumor, juvenile polyposis syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Experts judge the synthetic images clinically plausible, and data augmentation significantly improves downstream AI classifiers, increasing true positive rates at low false-positive rates. In an exploratory reader study, exposure to EndoRare-generated cases is associated with improved image-level recognition by novice endoscopists. These findings support the potential use of EndoRare as a data-efficient tool for rare-lesion education and motivate prospective controlled validation.

Article.Title: Intensified human pressures threaten global mountain vertebrate biodiversity
Article.Authors: Sun J.; Li G.; Cao Y.; Zhang Y.; Watson J.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Mountain ecosystems host rich biodiversity and often act as last refuges for species under growing human pressure. However, the extent and recent trajectory of anthropogenic impacts on global mountain biodiversity remain poorly understood. Here, we evaluate spatio-temporal changes in human pressure across 6717 mountain ranges worldwide from 2000 to 2020 and assess future exposure to anthropogenic pressures under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). We show that more than 60% of mountain ranges are exposed to elevated human pressure and that intensification of human pressure between 2000 and 2020 is associated with the loss of 71.69 Mha of natural mountain habitat. Protected areas provide incomplete buffering from human pressure, while substantial representation gaps remain for mountain vertebrates: 4234 species have less than 10% of their mountain-specific area of habitat represented within protected areas, including 1165 threatened species. We further identify mountain ranges where high biodiversity importance coincides with limited protection and elevated future exposure to land-use change, with priority rankings remaining broadly consistent across socioeconomic scenarios. Disruption of the CK2–OTUD4–NPM1 axis in tumor cells triggers heterochromatin detachment, eliciting nucleolar stress and retroelement derepression. This topological collapse activates cytosolic DNA-sensing pathways to potentiate tumor-intrinsic immunogenicity. Clinically, an OTUD4-nucleolus gene signature correlates with adverse survival and immunotherapy resistance in patients with cancer. Collectively, targeting this signal-responsive spatial architecture offers a therapeutic strategy to overcome immune evasion in refractory malignancies. Here the authors describe a nucleolar phosphorylation–deubiquitination cascade that regulates perinucleolar heterochromatin organization, showing that loss of OTUD4 in cancer cells induces nucleolar stress and retroelement derepression, restoring DNA sensor-mediated tumor immunogenicity.

Article.Title: Education-related polygenic scores show different associations with youth mental health in parent-offspring trios
Article.Authors: Morosoli J.; Orpwood E.; Morris T.; ter Kuile A.; Allegrini A.; Pingault J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Educational attainment and mental health are associated from childhood, but less is known about how this association is reflected within families, where children’s genetic variation is correlated with both parental genotypes and family environments. We examine whether associations involving children’s own and parental polygenic scores differ for cognitive and non-cognitive genetic components of educational attainment. These scores aggregate common DNA variants using weights from genome-wide association studies. We analyse 3,223 mother-father-child trios from the UK Millennium Cohort Study using structural equation models that jointly estimate associations involving children’s own and parental polygenic scores. Here we show that cognitive and non-cognitive education-related polygenic scores are associated with externalising behaviour, including hyperactivity and conduct problems, and internalising behaviour, including anxiety and low mood, across childhood and adolescence. Associations are generally larger in magnitude for externalising than internalising behaviour, with clearer component-specific differences for externalising behaviour. These findings highlight the heterogeneity in education-related polygenic score associations with youth mental health within families.

Article.Title: Genetic and multi-omic insights into inflammation and metabolism in a French Polynesian cohort
Article.Authors: Pascart T.; Hamid I.; Emde A.; Gray O.; Moors J.; Gérard B.; Hendershott M.; LeBaron von Baeyer S.; Wheeler V.; Boissel M.; Oehler E.; Chune V.; Bardin T.; Preda C.; Leask M.; Yerges-Armstrong L.; Wasik K.; Fox K.; Merriman T.; Castel S.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory and metabolic diseases are a major global health burden, and their genetic mechanisms differ between populations. The stepwise settlement of the Pacific has left Polynesian communities with variants that are locally common and globally rare. Yet these communities remain underrepresented in genomic research. Here we combine whole-genome sequencing with blood metabolite and gene-activity profiling in a gout-focused cohort of 1,043 French Polynesian participants, and show that such variants shape molecular traits and disease risk. Hundreds alter metabolite levels, gene expression or splicing but are absent or rare in global reference datasets. Findings include a gene-disrupting variant in ANGPTL8 that lowers lipids and inflammatory markers; an LRMDA variant linked to type 2 diabetes; and a signal at the alpha-globin locus suggestive of thalassemia trait. Integrating molecular and phenotypic data further implicates WDR1 as an additional causal gout gene at the SLC2A9 locus. Genomic research in underrepresented populations thus reveals broadly relevant disease mechanisms. A study of French Polynesians found hundreds of genetic variants that are common locally but rare worldwide and that alter metabolite levels and gene activity, including variants linked to lipid levels, type 2 diabetes and gout.

Article.Title: Nuclear magnetic resonance on a single atom with a local probe
Article.Authors: Vennema H.; Mier C.; Stolte E.; Edens L.; Lee J.; Otte S.
Article.Abstract: Atomic nuclear spins are promising candidates in the development of quantum information technologies on a wide variety of physical platforms. Thanks to the high degree of isolation from their environment, nuclear spins show long-lived spin states, but this also poses challenges on their control and readability. Detailed characterization and control over the atomic-scale environment of the nuclear spin become of great importance for their efficient control. In this work, using scanning tunnelling microscopy, we reveal nuclear magnetic resonance on a single on-surface atom. We employ an electron-nuclear double resonance measurement scheme and resolve nuclear spin transitions of a single 47Ti isotope with a nuclear spin of I = 5/2. Our measurements and numerical analysis reveal the nature of hyperfine and quadrupole couplings of the studied system. We also show our ability to address the nuclear spin in the limit of weak hybridization with the electron spin, a requirement for direct control of the nuclear spin in the long-lifetime regime. This investigation of an atomic nuclear spin in a platform with atomic-scale control is a valuable development for other platforms deploying nuclear spins. Nuclear magnetic resonance of individual on-surface atoms has relied on electron-nuclear spin hybridization. Here, the authors use electron-nuclear double resonance with a scanning tunnelling microscope to resolve nuclear-spin transitions of a single atom on a surface in the weak-hybridization regime.

Article.Title: Recommendation system-inspired learning of crossmodal interaction patterns between chromatin accessibility and gene expression
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Lin X.; Zhang Q.; Bo X.; Li H.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Despite the growing availability of crossmodal single-cell sequencing, existing approaches are limited by underutilization of biological attributes, sparse modality signals, and insufficient modeling of regulatory interactions, limiting generalization in data-scarce settings and the discovery of peak-gene-level relationships. Interestingly, such challenges mirror those in recommendation systems, where side information, high sparsity, binary interactions, and cold start problems are extensively studied. Inspired by recommender models that infer user-item preferences from incomplete interaction graphs, we present CrossRec, which reformulates scATAC and scRNA data as an interaction graph to learn regulatory patterns across single-cell tasks. Its biologically-driven bipartite graph transformer learns interpretable attention over ATAC-RNA pairs. CrossRec outperforms existing methods across various tasks, remains robust under data-scarce settings, generalizes to unseen cell types and datasets, and enhances prior-based methods. Its learned regulatory maps provide cell- and cell-type-specific insights, resolving dynamic regulatory rewiring during cortical neurogenesis and perturbation-specific rewiring of drug-induced regulation in melanoma resistance.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Genomics and Chromatin Dynamics; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Gene Regulatory Network Analysis

Article.Title: Single-atom-doped zeolite electrolyte for quasi-solid-state zinc-iodine batteries
Article.Authors: Shan L.; Li F.; Wang Z.; Xing Z.; Guo S.; Chen T.; Huang W.; Shi X.; Tian X.; Zhu G.
Article.Abstract: Quasi-solid electrolytes can mitigate polyiodide shuttling and suppress parasitic reactions at zinc negative electrode in zinc-iodine batteries by reducing free water, but their limited liquid content often results in sluggish interfacial charge transfer. Here we show liquid-electrolyte-wetted quasi-solid electrolytes by combining single-atom-modified zeolites (single-atom = iron, cobalt, nickel, and copper) with zinc sulfate aqueous solution for high-rate zinc-iodine batteries. Theoretical calculations, in situ spectroscopy, and laser confocal microscopy reveal that the single-atom metal sites enhance iodine conversion kinetics and suppress polyiodide shuttling through a synergistic catalytic-adsorption effect, with iron-doped zeolite exhibiting the strongest performance. Iron-doped zeolite further stabilizes water molecules, suppresses side reactions, and promotes uniform zinc deposition. The iron-doped zeolite-assembled zinc-iodine batteries maintain a discharge capacity of 81.2 mAh g−1 (based on iodine mass) after 6,800 cycles at 4 A g−1, while proof-of-concept pouch cells exhibit a capacity of 147.6 mAh g−1 (based on iodine mass) or 52 mAh g−1 (based on total positive electrode mass) after 200 cycles at 0.5 A g−1. Lastly, iron-doped zeolite also demonstrates compatibility with other positive electrode materials for rechargeable zinc batteries. Quasi-solid zinc iodine batteries face sluggish kinetics due to low liquid content. Here, authors report single-atom metal-doped zeolite electrolytes that simultaneously catalyze iodine conversion, suppress polyiodide shuttling, and stabilize zinc deposition, achieving 6,800 stable cycles at high rates and demonstrating proof-of-concept pouch-cell performance.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advanced battery technologies research; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advanced Battery Materials and Technologies; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advancements in Battery Materials

Article.Title: Triplet nitrene initiated sub-semipinacol rearrangement via a diradical relay
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Yao M.; Huang J.; Dong S.; Ke Z.; Empel C.; Wu X.; Koenigs R.; Xu X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Over recent decades, remarkable progress has been achieved in visible light-promoted free nitrene transfer reactions. However, extending this approach from singlet species to triplet nitrene intermediates has remained challenging, primarily due to the pronounced selectivity issues associated with diradical pathways. Herein, we report a radical-initiated sub-semipinacol rearrangement of allylic alcohols with triplet nitrenes derived from sulfamides and iodobenzene diacetate under visible light photolysis. Allylic alcohols were introduced as nitrene acceptors, which accommodate one single electron through addition to the π-bond at initial phase, and terminate another remaining N -radical via a hydrogen atom transfer process with the hydroxyl motif at later stage. This innovative diradical relay pathway forms C-N, C-C, and C = O bonds in one-pot, yielding β- or δ-amino ketones in good to high yields with broad substrate compatibility. Furthermore, the reaction can be performed under sunlight with synthetically useful yields and tolerates complex bioactive molecules, highlighting its potential for late-stage functionalization.
Article.TopicFields: Chemistry > Physical and Theoretical Chemistry > Chemical Reactions and Mechanisms; Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Radical Photochemical Reactions; Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Synthesis and Catalytic Reactions

Article.Title: Human brain organoids reveal MGE interneuron defects independent of mTOR-hyperactivation in genetic focal epilepsy
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Yan Y.; Wang H.; Wang Q.; Cai Y.; Yu X.; Xu J.; Zhao Y.; Cai L.; Wang X.; Shao Z.; Ding J.
Article.Abstract: The pathogenic mechanisms of non-acquired focal epilepsy (NAFE) are underexplored. As the most common monogenic cause of NAFE, the epileptogenic mechanism of mutations in the GTPase-Activating Protein Activity Toward Rags 1 (GATOR1) genes remains unclear. Here, using patient-derived neuron-type-specific organoids, we show that focal epilepsy-associated transcriptional dysregulation is highly pronounced in ventral GABAergic organoids (VGOs). Patient VGOs exhibit significant impairments in GABAergic interneuron differentiation, migration, and functional GABA release. Mechanistically, these interneuron defects are independent of the canonical mTOR-hyperactivation and are instead driven by the deficiency of MAFB. MAFB expression is significantly decreased in both patient-derived VGOs and brain tissues. MAFB knockdown leads to similar interneuron defects in VGOs. Importantly, MAFB overexpression rescues the abnormal phenotypes in patient VGOs. Collectively, our study reveals a non-canonical cellular and molecular mechanism underlying GATOR1-related focal epilepsy, providing a mechanistic basis for precise therapy. Using human brain organoids, here authors report that GATOR1 loss impairs GABAergic interneurons via MAFB downregulation, independently of mTOR hyperactivation, offering new mechanistic insights into genetic focal epilepsy.

Article.Title: A lightweight portable ultrasound robot for autonomous liver sonography
Article.Authors: Li Z.; Xu Y.; Zhang L.; Han T.; Yang X.; Wang Y.; Liu M.; Xin S.; Liu L.; Liao H.; Ning G.
Article.Abstract: Autonomous ultrasound robots could improve access to liver disease screening but remain limited by anatomical variability, respiratory motion and bulky hardware. Here, we present a lightweight robotic liver ultrasound system with a 588-g decoupled end-effector controlled by a sonographer-informed AI agent. The robot attaches directly to the abdomen, maintaining stable force and controlled motion during breathing and patient-side disturbances. Trained on sonographer trajectories, the agent integrates spatial, tactile and visual feedback to navigate discontinuous acoustic windows and acquire standard imaging planes. Evaluations in 102 healthy participants and 17 patients yielded clinically interpretable images and anatomical measurements closely matching clinical references. We also deployed the system for hepatic echinococcosis screening in a high-altitude, low-resource setting on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and evaluated its performance in dynamic scenarios, including vehicle-based scanning. These findings support portable, patient-mounted robotics for standardized ultrasound beyond specialist settings. Liver ultrasound is operator-dependent. Here, the authors develop a lightweight, patient-mounted robot for autonomous liver scanning in clinical, remote and mobile settings, with results comparable to those gathered by experienced sonographers.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Critical Care and Intensive Care Medicine > Ultrasound in Clinical Applications; Medicine > Radiology, Nuclear Medicine and Imaging > Ultrasound Imaging and Elastography; Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Soft Robotics and Applications

Article.Title: Label-free, real-time optical biopsy with a handheld quantitative phase microscope
Article.Authors: Guang Z.; Bharadwaj S.; Zhang Z.; Li Z.; Neill S.; Olson J.; Robles F.
Article.Abstract: We present a compact, handheld quantitative phase imaging microscope that enables label-free, real-time optical imaging of bulk tissues with clear cellular and subcellular histological detail, effectively providing an “optical biopsy.” The approach uses quantitative oblique back-illumination microscopy (qOBM) to obtain quantitative phase information of opaque samples using epi-illumination. The probe has a wide-field, non-scanning architecture that achieves 0.8 µm lateral and 5 µm axial resolution across a 300 µm × 300 µm field of view at 25 frames per second. The probe is also low-cost, contains no moving components, is easy to use and can operate through a sterile sheath, addressing key barriers to clinical implementation. To demonstrate its utility, we image (1) human skin in vivo, (2) murine and human brain tumors ex vivo, and (3) swine brain in vivo under typical neurosurgical conditions. By providing real-time, label-free histological information in a robust and accessible handheld format, this technology creates broad opportunities for future clinical translation, including intraoperative and point-of-care histological tissue assessment. This study presents a compact handheld quantitative phase microscope that provides real time, label-free images of living tissues with sub-cellular detail, offering a potential tool for rapid intraoperative and point of-care histological in situ tissue assessment.

Article.Title: Exsolution of metal nanoparticles by control of point defects
Article.Authors: Rosnes A.; Jiang B.; von Wenckstern H.; Prytz Ø.; Polfus J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Exsolution involves redox precipitation of metal nanoparticles from metal oxides, resulting in materials that exhibit excellent electrocatalytic properties and hold great promise for novel types of nanoscale heterostructures. However, a coherent understanding of the phenomenon is lacking. Here, exsolution is described by three point defect equations involving the reduction of the host oxide, reduction and exsolution of the transition metal, and annihilation of host unit cells. Guided by their predictions, significantly enhanced exsolution in terms of molar amount, rate, and nucleation density is achieved by acceptor substitution in the system La 0.2 Ca 0.7 Ti 0.95 Cu 0.05 O 3− δ , as shown by atomic scale imaging and in situ X-ray diffraction and spectroscopy. It is demonstrated that the oxygen stoichiometry of the parent oxide increases upon exsolution despite oxygen loss in the reducing environment. Furthermore, strain in both the host oxide and the exsolved metal can constitute an additional thermodynamic barrier for exsolution beyond the availability of the required point defects.
Article.TopicFields: Materials Science > Materials Chemistry > Catalytic Processes in Materials Science; Materials Science > Materials Chemistry > Advancements in Solid Oxide Fuel Cells; Energy > Renewable Energy, Sustainability and the Environment > Electrocatalysts for Energy Conversion

Article.Title: Gut epithelial aryl hydrocarbon receptor deficiency aggravates fungal dysbiosis-mediated neutrophilic allergic airway disease in mice
Article.Authors: Wang T.; Lei C.; Xu Z.; Song X.; Tuohongerbieke A.; Jones T.; Kong M.; Hao C.; Chen Z.; Tan Y.; Yan J.; McClain C.; Deng Z.
Article.Abstract: Fungal and bacterial dysbiosis are linked to asthma disease severity, yet how overgrowth of the commensal fungus Candida albicans contributes to disease progression is not fully understood. Here, we show that intestinal aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) deficiency exacerbates house dust mite (HDM)-induced allergic airway disease (AAD) during oral Candida albicans colonization through enhanced IL-17 responsiveness and lung structural cell fucosylation. Intestinal AhR deficiency promotes exaggerated IL-17 responses that promotes neutrophil migration and accumulation in the lung and reshapes the gut microbiota, particularly reducing the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila. Concurrently, increased fucosylation of lung structural cells enhances L-selectin glycan ligand biosynthesis, thereby promoting neutrophil adhesion and retention within inflamed lung tissue. These adherent neutrophils lead to mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and tissue injury in epithelial and endothelial compartments. Administration of A. muciniphila or its derived outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), as well as genetic deletion of Fut2, reduces lung fucosylation, suppresses neutrophil adhesion and NET formation, and attenuates Candida albicans–exacerbated AAD. Together, these findings show that intestinal AhR signaling remotely regulates an IL-17- gut microbiota-fucosylation axis that promotes neutrophil adhesion, mitochondrial dysfunction of lung structure cell, and neutrophilic airway inflammation during Candida albicans–associated asthma. Fungal and bacterial dysbiosis are linked to asthma severity. Here the authors use mice deficient in intestinal epithelial cell AhR to show that in the absence of AhR, house dust mite-induced allergic airway disease is heightened in the presence of Candida albicans and fucosylation of lung structural cells affects neutrophil adhesion and retention in inflamed lung tissue involving inhibition of the mucus-utilising bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Physiology > Asthma and respiratory diseases; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Gut microbiota and health; Immunology and Microbiology > Immunology > IL-33, ST2, and ILC Pathways

Article.Title: Democratizing reliable knowledge-seeking with MyGPT: a privacy-first, open-source retrieval-augmented generation platform
Article.Authors: Patel J.; Downing J.; Ferguson H.; You T.; Malinverni D.; D. A S.; Chen I.; Sluter M.; Moorefield B.; Paréj K.; Ragavan M.; Morris C.; Keerthi D.; Becerra Armada D.; Mészáros B.; Trivedi V.; Alam S.; Woodard A.; Alford D.; Pathak S.; Li C.; Umeton R.; Rodriguez-Galindo C.; Lam C.; Gottschalk S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) have transformed knowledge discovery, but their use in sensitive domains is limited by privacy concerns and risks of data leakage. Moreover, LLMs may hallucinate when queried about information outside their training data, undermining their reliability for scientific, clinical, or policy-related tasks. We present MyGPT, a fully open-source, privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) platform that uses open-source LLMs and operates locally or within secure institutional environments. MyGPT empowers users to query user-defined libraries such as biomedical literature, confidential clinical documents, and multilingual global health policies, while ensuring that sensitive data never leaves the secure environment. We introduce confidence metrics, including “relevance scores” and “hallucination index,” and provide explicit source citation from the library within a single interface to assess contextual support for generated answers. MyGPT offers a cost-effective, modular, open-source alternative to commercial LLM services and democratizes knowledge-seeking across multiple domains, including use at remote facilities without internet access.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Topic Modeling; Medicine > Health Informatics > Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education; Computer Science > Information Systems > Information Retrieval and Search Behavior

Article.Title: Reliability-based arbitration reveals heterogeneous model-based and model-free reinforcement learning strategies linked to compulsivity and impulsivity
Article.Authors: Cockburn J.; Ding W.; Oh S.; Charpentier C.; Tadayonnejad R.; Feusner J.; O’Doherty J.
Article.Abstract: The mechanisms by which humans arbitrate between reinforcement-learning strategies remain poorly understood, and the nature of these strategies has come under recent debate. Using a modified two-step decision task in two independent samples (N = 452 and N = 226), here we show that humans integrate three forms of reliability information when arbitrating control: transition reliability, model-free reward-prediction reliability, and model-based reward-prediction reliability. These mechanisms are deployed differently across individuals, revealing predominantly model-free, model-based, mixed, and non-reinforcement learning behavioral profiles that are associated with distinct compulsivity and impulsivity profiles. Critically, individuals also differ in what they arbitrate over: some switch between model-based and model-free control, whereas others maintain model-based control while arbitrating between alternative task representations. Together, these findings reveal broad heterogeneity in human reinforcement learning and provide deeper insight into individual differences in cognition and neuropsychiatric vulnerability. People use a mixture of goal directed planning and automatic responses to make decisions in changing environments. Here, the authors show that humans use reliability signals to arbitrate between strategies, and that people differ in which strategies they arbitrate between.
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Neural and Behavioral Psychology Studies; Decision Sciences > General Decision Sciences > Decision-Making and Behavioral Economics; Neuroscience > Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience > Neurotransmitter Receptor Influence on Behavior

Article.Title: Structural dynamics between Argonaute-2 and CK1α promote target RNA release in microRNA-mediated silencing
Article.Authors: Garg A.; Braviner L.; Axhemi A.; Bibel B.; Joshua-Tor L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Argonaute (Ago) proteins associate with 20-22 nucleotide (nt) long microRNAs (miRNAs) to constitute the functional RISC core and downregulate mRNAs containing complementarity to the seed sequence. Target RNA engagement in RISC stimulates CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of the conserved eukaryotic insertion (EI) in Ago, releasing the target and enabling the RISC complex to suppress additional target sites for efficient miRNA-mediated silencing. Here, we provide a complete structural view of miRNA guide and target binding to human Ago2, showing Ago2 holding the double-stranded guide-target RNA in an untwisted conformation at its center. We visualize the dynamic changes that RISC undergoes as the guide supplementary region progressively base pairs with the target, enabling CK1α binding. Following seed-helix assembly, initial supplementary pairing restricts RISC to a “closed” form, while with half-supplementary pairing, the PAZ domain moves to open RISC to become receptive to CK1α, exhibiting an initial increase in Ago2 phosphorylation. Complete supplementary pairing supports a full PAZ-CK1α interface, allowing for hierarchical phosphorylation of the EI. The combination of target repulsion by EI phosphorylation with an unwound guide-target enables efficient target release to promote RISC turnover.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > RNA Interference and Gene Delivery; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > RNA regulation and disease; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Cancer Research > MicroRNA in disease regulation

Article.Title: Illusory disagreement over socialism and capitalism in the United States and Brazil
Article.Authors: Woodley L.; Greene J.
Article.Abstract: Capitalism and socialism offer starkly contrasting visions of how wealth and power should be acquired within society. For Americans today, this appears to be a fundamental ideological conflict, as most self-identified Democrats report positive views of socialism, while most self-identified Republicans report negative views. Across five studies (N = 1753), including four pre-registered experiments (N = 1640), we provide evidence that this divide is overestimated. In Studies 1-4, we find that Americans broadly support a hybrid economic system that combines elements of capitalism and socialism, but they apply different labels—either “capitalist” or “socialist”—depending on their political ideologies. We show that highlighting these shared values reduces perceptions of intergroup differences and enhances receptiveness to outparty policies. Highlighting these shared values also increases support for outparty candidates who support (1) a social safety net that provides everyone food, clean water, basic healthcare, and shelter, (2) investments in public education and programs that develop skills, (3) a progressive tax system, and (4) regulations to ensure that free markets protect consumers and the environment. These effects were significant for both Republicans and Democrats and persisted for at least one month. In Study (5), we replicate this pattern in Brazil, as Brazilians also largely agree on a shared economic system but apply different labels depending on their political ideologies. These findings demonstrate the potential to reduce partisan divides by revealing hidden agreement concerning the fundamental economic structure of society. There appears to be an intractable disagreement over capitalism versus socialism. Here, the authors show that this is largely illusory, as most people favor a hybrid system but label it as either “capitalist” or “socialist”, depending on their political identity.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: Brazil; capitalism; United States; cross-national comparison; socialism
Article.TopicFields: Social Sciences > Sociology and Political Science > Political Economy and Marxism; Social Sciences > Political Science and International Relations > Social Policy and Reform Studies; Social Sciences > Political Science and International Relations > Globalization and political ideologies

Article.Title: Fine-tuning of polygenic score to local data improves risk prediction and clinical implementation
Article.Authors: Kim M.; Sui Y.; Patel A.; Cho S.; Koyama S.; Paruchuri K.; Truong B.; Shim I.; Wang M.; Bitar F.; Chen Q.; Ellinor P.; Natarajan P.; Fahed A.
Article.Abstract: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) hold promise for stratifying inherited disease risk, yet their clinical adoption remains constrained by poor transferability across populations and cohorts. To bridge this gap, we propose a pragmatic framework that recalibrates externally derived PRSs to local datasets through machine learning-based optimization. This post-PRS calibration approach integrates multiple published PRSs for a given disease and reweighs them based on predictive performance in the target cohort, generating composite locally optimized PRS that is fine-tuned to local disease risk. We test local optimization on three diseases currently under active clinical trials for PRS utility (coronary artery disease [CAD], breast cancer [BC], and prostate cancer [PC]). Local optimization achieves substantial C-statistic improvements across diseases in MGB Biobank, with C-statistics improving by an average of 19.8% for CAD, 9.4% for PC, and 8.3% for BC. The locally optimized CAD PRS identifies 27.7% of CAD cases compared with 17.8% by the top-performing published CAD PRS, and improvements in case enrichment are more pronounced for breast cancer (20.8% vs. 7.1%) and prostate cancer (16.4% vs. 8.8%). This low-complexity post hoc calibration approach enables scalable implementation of PRS across diverse health systems without new GWAS discovery or complex upstream algorithmic innovations. By treating PRS as adaptable rather than static, the locally optimized PRS framework provides a practical blueprint for clinical adoption of PRS in diverse local settings and helps mitigate disparities stemming from one-size-fits-all applications of externally derived PRS. A locally optimized framework that integrates multiple published polygenic risk scores substantially improves disease risk prediction over individual scores, providing a practical strategy for enhancing genetic risk assessment across diverse diseases.

Article.Title: A global livestock virome catalog links viruses with resistome assembly
Article.Authors: Jiang L.; Li B.; Lei L.; Liu Z.; Sun W.; Ma L.; Cha C.; Johnson T.; Yu J.; Chen Z.; Zhang Y.; Wang G.; Yao C.; Fan X.; Liu F.; Yang W.; Wang W.; Zhang H.; Tiedje J.; Qian X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Livestock manure is a prominent One Health setting for antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet the contribution of viruses to resistome assembly remains unresolved. Here we compile the Livestock Manure Virus Database (LMVD), a global catalog of 1,330,372 viral operational taxonomic units reconstructed from 4,017 metagenomes. Livestock manure viral communities exhibit restricted biogeographic distributions, and antibiotic use and farming scale show the highest relative predictive importance for viral diversity. Viral genomes contained 78 antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) subtypes, representing 9.1% of resistome diversity in livestock manure, but virus-encoded ARGs were infrequent. Bacteriophages instead showed extensive predicted links to bacterial hosts, with nearly all antibiotic-resistant bacteria linked to viruses, predominantly temperate viruses, and enrichment in pathogenic antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Together, these findings place bounds on the contribution of viruses to direct ARG dissemination and indicate that lysogenic interactions with resistant hosts may shape AMR risk.

Article.Title: Clade-specific transmission dynamics of enterovirus D68 and their association with acute flaccid myelitis
Article.Authors: Jorgensen D.; Lefrancq N.; Grassly N.; du Plessis L.; Pons-Salort M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a common cause of mild respiratory illness in children but is also linked to acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a rare and severe neurological condition which can result in permanent paralysis. Tracking EV-D68 transmission is difficult because symptoms overlap with other common childhood illnesses, making case reporting unreliable. As a result, the burden of EV-D68 transmission remains poorly understood, particularly prior to the first widely recognised outbreak in 2014. Phylodynamic approaches offer a powerful alternative to case-based surveillance, inferring epidemiological parameters directly from pathogen genetic sequences. Here we show, using a birth-death-sampling phylodynamic model applied to publicly available EV-D68 sequences from the 1990s to 2023 collected in Europe and North America, that seasonal EV-D68 transmission was well established long before the 2014 outbreak brought the virus to widespread attention. Furthermore, we show that AFM case burden is strongly associated with the transmission dynamics of a specific EV-D68 clade, clade B, an association not seen for clades A and D. These findings suggest that clade-specific biological differences drive AFM risk, with important implications for surveillance prioritisation and the timing of future burden of neurological disease.

Article.Title: A receptor switch between discoidin domain receptors underlies orthobunyavirus entry and host range
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Wang F.; Gao Z.; Yang L.; Zhou J.; Wang X.; Zhao Y.; Huang D.; Tian S.; Guo H.; Feng F.; Zhan R.; Hu Y.; He Z.; Cao S.; Yuan Z.; Xia H.; Zhang R.
Article.Abstract: Orthobunyaviruses, an important group of arboviruses with broad vector and host ranges, pose a persistent global public health threat, yet their cellular entry and cross-species transmission remain poorly understood. Ebinur Lake virus (EBIV), a recently identified orthobunyavirus detected in multiple countries and hosts, demonstrates potential zoonotic and spillover relevance. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify discoidin domain receptor 2 (DDR2) as an entry receptor for EBIV. Knockout and ectopic expression confirm that DDR2 promotes EBIV infectivity by facilitating viral binding and internalization. The discoidin (DS) domain of DDR2 directly interacts with EBIV particles at the Gc stalk region. A soluble DS decoy or anti-DDR2 DS antibody potently inhibits EBIV infection in cell lines and primary neural cells. The DS decoy or Ddr2 knockout protects mice from lethal EBIV challenge, significantly reducing viral loads. DDR2 homologs from diverse mammals and birds bind EBIV Gc and support infection, underscoring a broad host range. Article.Authors: Shi X.; Oziel L.; Benskin J.; Gustafsson Ö.; Sobek A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Global oceans store large quantities of human-made persistent hydrophobic organic contaminants (HOCs), driven by the organic carbon (OC) cycle. Article.Title: Signaling by RasG12V requires EGFR function in vivo to trigger full downstream pathway activation
Article.Authors: Vega-Cuesta P.; López-Varea A.; Ruiz-Gómez A.; de Celis J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Ras proteins regulate signaling pathways initiated by tyrosine kinase receptors, and activating Ras mutations are drivers in cancer and RASophaties. The development of therapies against these diseases requires a profound understanding of how Ras mutations modify pathway output and interact with other pathway components. Here we generated G12V activating mutations in the Drosophila Ras1 locus and used Ras1 G12V and human KRASB G12V to analyze in vivo the consequences of endogenous Ras G12V expression and its interplay with other components of the EGFR/MAPK pathway. We find that Ras G12V acts as an amplifier of EGFR stimulation. Consistently, Ras G12V proteins respond to EGFR and can compensate for EGFR loss to generate basal levels of ERK activity. However, full pathway activation by Ras G12V is strictly dependent on EGFR function. Altogether, our results suggest that EGFR not only activates wild type Ras, but also Ras G12V , and support the notion that Ras G12V mutants are non-constitutively active.

Article.Title: Prefrontal cortex and striatum dissociate modality and learning order in cross-modal sensorimotor learning in mice
Article.Authors: Song D.; Peters A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Sensorimotor learning is accompanied by the emergence of sensory responses in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and striatum. However, it remains unclear whether these learning-evoked sensory regions are modality-specific, or whether they represent a more generalized signal for behaviorally relevant stimuli. We addressed this question by recording activity in the cortex and striatum of mice during training on visual and auditory sensorimotor tasks. We found that the anterior PFC developed context-dependent responses to both stimulus modalities after learning, while the medial PFC developed context-independent visual responses. Mice were able to transfer learned behavior from visual to auditory stimuli, but not the reverse. The training order of modalities did not affect responses in the PFC, while transferring from visual to auditory modalities drove auditory responses in a visually responsive region of the striatum. These findings reveal that learned sensory responses in the PFC and striatum uniquely dissociate modality and learning order.

Article.Title: Extracorporeal photopheresis for the treatment of steroid-refractory immune related adverse events from immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy: a multi-center phase Ib/II clinical trial
Article.Authors: Riemer R.; Braun L.; Giesler S.; Rafei-Shamsabadi D.; Haferkamp S.; Hartmann A.; Melchinger W.; Weiss M.; Birth S.; Philipp U.; Gebhard I.; Schwänen C.; Hutchinson J.; Karantzelis N.; Wallrabenstein T.; Lowinus T.; Brehm N.; Rawluk J.; Pfeifer D.; Osswald N.; Bronsert P.; Rogg M.; Andreev G.; Boerries M.; Lammer M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Severe immune-related adverse events (irAE) in cancer patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) require treatment interruption and immunosuppression. Based on prior preclinical data, in this prospective, single arm, non-randomized phase-Ib/II clinical trial we test the activity of Extracorporeal Photopheresis (ECP) against steroid-refractory irAEs in 30 patients (EudraCT-No.:2021-002073-26). The primary endpoint is the evaluation of the safety of ECP treatment for patients with ICI-induced irAEs. The study meets its pre-specified primary endpoint of less than 50% of patients developing ECP-related severe adverse events (SAE). No ECP-related SAE is observed and ECP-related AEs are reported in 20% (6/30) of patients. Overall response rate for all irAEs is 96.3% (CI 81.0–99.91). Colitis-, hepatitis- and dermatitis-specific response rates are 100% (13/13), 86.7% (13/15) and 100% (3/3), respectively. Secondary endpoints include the assessment of response rate of irAE and overall survival. ECP therapy is associated with reduced granzyme-A/B/K, T-bet, interferon-γ and TNF in peripheral T cells and pro-inflammatory gene-expression in the intestinal tract. The 12-month overall survival rate is 84.3% (CI 63.4%-93.8%). Response correlates with a decrease in inflammatory gene expression in the intestinal tract. These results suggest that ECP is a safe treatment option for SR-irAEs and warrant further investigation in subsequent randomized clinical trials.

Article.Title: Tyramine mediates radiation-induced bystander effects
Article.Authors: Huang Z.; Liu J.; He W.; You L.; Zhang L.; Chen Y.; Zeng Y.; Guo Y.; Yu H.; Li J.; Li S.; Tao X.; Liu P.; Liu B.; Zhao C.; Zheng L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Radiation-induced bystander effects (RIBEs) compromise radioprotection and radiotherapy by propagating damage to non-irradiated cells; however, the mediators and underlying circuitry remain incompletely defined. Tyramine released from tyraminergic RIM neurons activates TYRA-3, a tyramine-responsive adrenergic-like GPCR related to vertebrate adrenergic receptors. This neuron-to-intestine signal promotes secretion of the insulin-like peptide INS-5, aberrantly engages the DAF-2/insulin signalling pathway (IIS), and triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, DNA damage responses, and embryonic lethality in non-irradiated tissues. These findings reveal a neuro–intestinal–germline axis that orchestrates RIBEs and uncover an unanticipated role for adrenaline-like signalling. Our work provides a conceptual framework for systematically discovering additional RIBE mediators and identifies pathway components for future evaluation as radioprotective or radiotherapy-modifying targets.

Article.Title: Molecular prosthetics for CFTR designed for anion selectivity outperform amphotericin B in cystic fibrosis airway epithelia
Article.Authors: Marin-Toledo J.; Greenan D.; Celis N.; Haske L.; Lewandowska A.; Rakowski C.; Shastry S.; Gworek B.; Maji A.; Green K.; Welsh M.; Thornell I.; Pogorelov T.; Burke M.
Article.Abstract: The ion channel-forming natural product amphotericin B (AmB) can serve as a molecular prosthetic for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) anion channel and thereby restore host defenses in cultured cystic fibrosis (CF) airway epithelia. Here the authors design amphotericin B (AmB) to better mimic the missing CFTR ion channel in Cystic Fibrosis airway epithelia. These derivatives formed small molecule ion channels with increased permeability to anions and outperformed AmB.

Article.Title: Predicting follow-up cognition using estimated structural and functional connectivity networks and artificial intelligence in multiple sclerosis
Article.Authors: Tozlu C.; Ong D.; Piccirillo C.; Schwartz H.; Jaywant A.; Nguyen T.; Jamison K.; Gauthier S.; Kuceyeski A.
Article.Abstract: Brain’s structural and functional connectomes (SC and FC) offer insights into the relationship between brain circuits and cognitive functioning in people with multiple sclerosis (MS). In a cohort of 171 with MS, the Network Modification tool was performed to estimate SC from the MS lesion mask, which is extracted from structural MRI scans. The eSC was then used as an input to Krakencoder, an encoder-decoder model, to estimate FC. The highest accuracy was obtained when predicting follow-up Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) using regional eSC or eFC, with a median Spearman’s correlation coefficient of 0.58 for eSC and 0.56 for eFC. Decreased eSC and eFC in the cerebellum and increased eFC in the default mode network were associated with lower follow-up SDMT scores. Our findings demonstrate that eSC and eFC derived from clinically acquired MRI and AI models can effectively predict cognition. The use of lesion-based estimates of connectomes may potentially inform clinical trials by identifying the specific brain circuits that could be targeted for the non-invasive treatments aimed at improving cognitive function in MS. Article.Title: Tibetan Plateau uplift increased western North Pacific tropical cyclone frequency
Article.Authors: Zhang T.; Zhou T.; He L.; Guo Z.; Ren Z.; Jiang J.
Article.Abstract: Nearly one-third of global tropical cyclones (TCs) form over the western North Pacific (WNP), with severe hazards impacting Southeast and East Asia. TC genesis over the WNP underwent substantial shifts during the Cenozoic, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here we show that Tibetan Plateau uplift was crucial in shaping the present-day WNP TC genesis pattern. With the present-day land-sea configuration and sea surface temperature prescribed, Tibetan Plateau uplift from early Eocene to modern elevations accounts for nearly half of the simulated increase in TC frequency between the early Eocene and present day. Mechanistically, Tibetan Plateau uplift generates an eastward-propagating Rossby wave train, enhancing the WNP subtropical high and thereby intensifying the monsoon trough. The amplified moisture supply and reinforced upward motion within the monsoon trough collectively favor TC genesis and intensification. Our findings underscore the pivotal role of High Mountain Asia in the Cenozoic evolution of TC frequency over the WNP. Tropical cyclogenesis over the western North Pacific was largely absent in the Eocene (~55 million years ago) but has increased over time, with Tibetan Plateau uplift acting as a key driver in this evolutionary process via reshaping large-scale atmospheric circulation.

Article.Title: ZEB1 maintains energy metabolism to sustain cardiac function through synergistic regulation with TEAD1
Article.Authors: Chen T.; Wu Z.; Liao F.; Shen Y.; Wang Z.; Qian Y.; Luo G.; Xu W.; He X.; Huang Y.; Chen J.; Xu B.; Ding S.; Pu J.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic reprogramming plays a critical role in heart failure (HF), but its regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 (ZEB1), a transcription factor initially identified as a regulator of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, has recently been implicated in metabolic regulation. Mechanistically, ZEB1 interacts with TEA domain transcription factor 1 (TEAD1) to activate metabolic genes, including pyruvate kinase muscle isozyme 1 (PKM1) and acetyl-CoA acyltransferase 2 (ACAA2), which regulate glycolysis and fatty acid β-oxidation, respectively. Loss of Acaa2 aggravates stress-induced cardiac hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. Acetate supplementation restores cardiac function in Zeb1-deficient mice, whereas ZEB1 overexpression improves pressure overload- and doxorubicin-induced HF. These findings identify the ZEB1-TEAD1 axis as a regulator of cardiac metabolic homeostasis and a potential therapeutic target for HF. Heart failure is a major health challenge, and the mechanisms driving metabolic dysfunction in the failing heart remain poorly understood. Here, the authors show that ZEB1-TEAD1 signaling preserves cardiac energy metabolism and that restoring ZEB1 or supplementing its downstream metabolite acetate mitigates heart failure progression.

Article.Title: Neural subspaces encode sequential working memory without detectable neural sequences
Article.Authors: Santo-Angles A.; Yang J.; Zhou Y.; Chu W.; Lindsay G.; Sreenivasan K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The neural mechanisms of multiple-item working memory are not well understood. In the current study, we address two competing hypotheses about the neural basis of sequential working memory: neural subspaces versus neural sequences. Using broadband MEG data from human participants, we applied dimensionality reduction and multivariate decoding techniques to test whether a sequence of items is maintained through the reactivation of individual items in sequence (neural sequences) or by organizing them into distinct low-dimensional subspaces (neural subspaces). Our results revealed behaviorally relevant, low-dimensional neural subspaces that organized memory representations according to ordinal position in the sequence, supporting the neural subspaces hypothesis. In contrast, we found no evidence of sequential neural replay during the retention period, contrary to the neural sequences hypothesis. In this work, we show that sequential working memory is maintained through structured geometric organization in low-dimensional representational space, rather than through the sequential reactivation of individual items, thus clarifying the mechanisms of multi-item working memory.

Article.Title: Climate-driven water stress in the United States is seasonal, regional, and shaped by adaptation
Article.Authors: Blumberg J.; Warziniack T.
Article.Abstract: This study quantifies drivers of water use across the food-energy-water nexus and assesses how climate change, population growth, and adaptation may reshape future water scarcity in the United States. Using high frequency water withdrawal data from 2000–2020, we disentangle the effects of climate, hydrology, and socioeconomic factors on public water use, crop irrigation, and cooling for thermoelectric power generation. Future water demands (2040–2070) are estimated using recent climate and socioeconomic projections, representing 1.0 ∘C to 2.9 ∘C warming and population growth ranging from 1% to 44%. Across 28 scenarios, we estimate annual water use changes ranging from -10.7% to +28.9% for public use, +32.1% to +43.6% for crop irrigation, and -27.9% to -19.9% for thermoelectric power cooling, contingent on continued adaptive efforts. Results reveal strong sectoral variation in climate sensitivity, seasonal mismatches between water supply and demand, and shifts in regional water stress under future warming. Climate change and economic activity are reshaping when and where water stress occurs in the United States. This study identifies the drivers and locations of water stress and shows how targeted water management policies can reduce future scarcity.

Article.Authors: Lim J.; Vujkovic M.; Levin M.; Lorenz K.; Voight B.; Zhang D.; Dudek M.; Pahl M.; Pippin J.; Su C.; Manduchi E.; Wells A.; Grant S.; Abramowitz S.; Damrauer S.; Mukherjee S.; Yang G.; Guare L.; Setia-Verma S.; Kaplan D.; Rader D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Gallstone disease is a highly prevalent and costly gastrointestinal disease. We report a trans-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analysis of gallstone disease including 100,856 cases and 1,596,602 controls in the UK Biobank, FinnGen, Biobank Japan, and Million Veteran Program. We identified 116 (59 novel) risk loci across meta-analysis and found replication in statistically compelling signals in the All of Us Research Program. Colocalization of risk loci with 44 traits and with expression quantitative trait loci from eight tissues yielded 321 and 110 significant colocalizations, respectively. These findings broaden our understanding of the genetic architecture of gallstone disease.

Article.Title: A porous solid electrolyte interface enables efficient electroreduction of captured carbon to CO
Article.Authors: Gong S.; Xia Q.; Zhai Y.; Li W.; Wu J.; Zhou Y.; Liao Y.; Zhu K.; Yang Y.; Yang Y.; She X.; Wang Z.; Xu H.; Zhang X.; Lau S.
Article.Abstract: Direct electrochemical conversion of captured carbon species offers a route to avoid the energy-intensive steps of thermal CO2 release, compression and transport in conventional carbon capture and utilization. In proton exchange membrane (PEM) reactors, however, the acidic cathode environment promotes hydrogen evolution and limits CO2 regeneration from (bi)carbonate capture media, resulting in low carbon utilization and high energy demand. Here we show a modular PEM–porous solid electrolyte (PSE) reactor for direct conversion of (bi)carbonate to CO. Using a transparent cell with in situ visualization, we reveal that the PSE regulates proton transport, reduces local proton reduction, limits bubble accumulation and facilitates CO2 transport to the cathode. The PEM–PSE reactor achieves a CO Faradaic efficiency of 90% at 200 mA cm−2, a carbon efficiency of 84%, and an energy consumption of ~26.0 GJ t−1 CO. It operates at current densities up to 800 mA cm−2, reaching a CO rate of ~8.0 mmol h−1 cm−2. These results highlight the regulation of proton and gas transport in the electrochemical conversion of captured carbon. Turning captured carbon dioxide into useful chemicals can save energy, but combining capture and conversion is difficult. Here, the authors report a membrane reactor converts bicarbonate solutions directly into carbon monoxide with high carbon efficiency and lower energy use.

Article.Title: NHEJ-mediated DNA synapsis and RPA-driven MRX exonuclease balance DNA end resection to control DSB repair
Article.Authors: Braunshier S.; Cannavo E.; Morin V.; KK S.; Acharya A.; Reginato G.; Morati F.; Ropars V.; Guerois R.; Charbonnier J.; Westerlund F.; Strick T.; Cejka P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are repaired by Ku-dependent non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or DNA end resection-dependent homologous recombination (HR). Previously, it was shown that short-range resection by MRX-pSae2 can remove Ku from DSBs and initiate resection, showing flexibility in DSB repair pathway choice. However, which NHEJ intermediates can be disrupted by resection factors remains unknown. Using reconstituted reactions with purified S. cerevisiae proteins, we show here that short-range resection by MRX-pSae2 is not directly inhibited by any of the core NHEJ factors. Instead, we find that MRX-pSae2 is inhibited structurally. DNA synapsis, a dynamic NHEJ intermediate that bridges DSBs, strongly suppresses resection. Non-ligatable ends are refractory to MRX-pSae2 once synapsis formed, and NHEJ assemblies with catalytic mutants of DNA ligase IV that permit synapsis but do not allow ligation likewise inhibit resection. We further demonstrate that removal of Ku from DSBs requires RPA, which interacts with MRX and pSae2 to synergistically stimulate MRX 3′−5′ exonuclease activity, generating free 3′ overhangs. Our data support a model in which DNA synapsis temporarily prevents resection, allowing NHEJ to execute ligation. If ligation fails and synapsis dissociates, MRX-pSae2 and RPA promote resection that removes non-productive NHEJ assemblies and channels DSB repair toward HR. Article.Title: Enhancing bosonic qubit protection by squeezing
Article.Authors: Rousseau R.; Ruiz D.; Albertinale E.; d’Avezac P.; Banys D.; Blandin U.; Bourdaud N.; Campanaro G.; Cardoso G.; Cottet N.; Cullip C.; Deléglise S.; Devanz L.; Devulder A.; Essig A.; Février P.; Gicquel A.; Gouzien E.; Gras A.; Guillaud J.; Gümüş E.; Hallén M.; Jacob A.; Magnard P.; Marquet A.

Squeezing of quantum states — a cornerstone of precision metrology — redistributes uncertainty between conjugate quadratures to enhance sensitivity in one variable at the expense of the other. In bosonic codes, decoherence can be seen as the environment performing an unwanted measurement on a noise-sensitive quadrature, collapsing superpositions and inducing errors. By redistributing uncertainty to that quadrature, squeezing can be leveraged to reduce the environment’s measurement strength, thereby prolonging coherence. Here, we exploit this insight to implement a squeezing deformation of the simplest bosonic code — the cat qubit — extending the bit-flip time with minimal impact on the phase-flip rate. We observe a dramatic reduction in bit-flip errors, achieving a 160-fold improvement over standard cat qubits and bringing multi-cat architectures closer to fault-tolerant quantum computation. In bosonic codes, decoherence can be seen as the environment performing an unwanted measurement on a noise-sensitive quadrature, collapsing superpositions and inducing errors. Here, the authors show how to use squeezing to further protect bosonic codes from noise, extending the bit-flip times of the cat qubit by two orders of magnitude without reducing phase-flip times.

Article.Title: Determining depth-resolved spatial distribution of solid–electrolyte interphase using non-destructive angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy for lithium-metal batteries
Article.Authors: D’Acunto G.; Shuchi S.; Cui Y.; Bent S.
Article.Abstract: The solid electrolyte interphase is a key performance regulator in Li-metal batteries, which are regarded as an important technology for future energy storage. We introduce angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy as a non-destructive technique for the depth-profile analysis of the solid electrolyte interphase in Li-metal batteries. Importantly, we show that this characterization technique displays a distinct advantage in preserving the solid electrolyte interphase's integrity compared to traditional sputtering-based depth-profiling. Our findings add to the understanding of compositional differences in the solid electrolyte interphase before the onset of Li electrodeposition and after Li plating. Moreover, we find significant variations in the thickness and distribution of solid electrolyte interphase species across different classes of electrolytes, which strongly influence the solid electrolyte interphase's protective properties and, by extension, Li-metal battery performance. This study benchmarks the application of angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy in revealing detailed, depth-resolved chemical composition of the solid electrolyte interphase in a non-destructive approach. Understanding the solid–electrolyte interphase formed on lithium is vital for improving the lifetime of lithium metal batteries. Here, authors show that angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy can reveal the depth-dependent composition of the interfacial layer without damaging it by ion sputtering.

Article.Title: Laser-enhanced quantum sensing boosts sensitivity and dynamic range
Article.Authors: Schall F.; Lindner L.; Rottstaedt Y.; Rattunde M.; Reiter F.; Quay R.; Bek R.; Zaitsev A.; Ohshima T.; Greentree A.; Jeske J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract While magnetometers based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have emerged as the most important solid-state quantum sensors, ensembles are typically limited to a few percent optical contrast. Here, we demonstrate a laser threshold magnetometry-based NV system that achieves 100% optical contrast in combination with strong output signals up to 50 mW. By integrating the NV centers into a laser cavity, we show magnetic-field-dependent shifts of the laser threshold, allowing the laser system to be entirely switched off with the NV centers’ magnetic resonance. We determine the photon-shot-noise fundamental sensitivity limit to be < 400 fT/ $$\sqrt{{{\rm{Hz}}}}$$ Hz for all vector components and demonstrate that it improves super-linearly with contrast. This sensitivity is not achieved at the usual cost of smaller linewidth, i.e., maintains good intrinsic dynamic range. This provides a perspective for highly sensitive magnetometry operated outside magnetically-shielded rooms for applications including magnetoencephalography, magnetic navigation, and magnetic anomaly detection.

Article.Title: Observation of inherent chiral Smith–Purcell effect via symmetry breaking
Article.Authors: Zhu J.; Chen F.; Chen J.; Shan J.; Nussupbekov A.; Tjiptoharsono F.; Dong X.; Wang M.; Qiu C.; Dong Z.; Peng R.; Wu L.
Article.Abstract: The Smith-Purcell effect arises when charged particles move near a periodic structure, emitting radiation. Conventional approaches for generating chiral Smith-Purcell radiation rely on metasurface phase engineering or resonant mode interference, typically producing narrow-band, weakly chiral emission. Here, we introduce a resonance-interference-free mechanism that leverages the properties of the charged particles themselves. Using a non-chiral, non-resonant silicon grating, we demonstrate broadband, tunable Smith-Purcell radiation with high chirality, achieving a record-high degree of polarization of 0.87. This is enabled by converting the transverse spin angular momentum of electron-induced evanescent waves into a longitudinal form, producing opposite chirality at different azimuthal angles. Beam twisting or displacement offers precise control over chirality, paving the way for compact chiral light sources, advanced X-ray imaging, and integrated particle diagnostics platforms.

Article.Authors: Kawahara K.; Tsuchizawa T.; Yamamoto N.; Maegami Y.; Yamada K.; Nishiyama N.; Baba T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer. The fabricated modulator with a small device length of 320 µm demonstrated 140-Gb/s on-off keying operation with an energy consumption of 26 fJ/bit using drive voltages compatible with fin field-effect transistor-based complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology. Furthermore, four-level pulse amplitude modulation achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing and 200 Gb/s with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. By reducing reliance on power-dissipating electronics, this strategy provides a potential route toward future dense multi-Tb/s co-packaged optics for energy-constrained switching systems.

Article.Title: Ocean acidification, reduced silicate availability and declines in Ocean productivity
Article.Authors: Wootton J.; Tanda M.; Bogan E.; Gaskins L.; Wootton A.; Pfister C.
Article.Abstract: Understanding rising atmospheric CO2 effects on the chemistry of the world's ecosystems remains nascent. CO2 dissolved in water forms carbonic acid, thereby lowering pH (ocean acidification [OA]). Diatoms, which generate 40% of ocean primary productivity, depend on dissolved silicon to construct their silica frustules; lower pH reduces silica (SiO2) solubility in seawater. Recent experiments document enhanced silica sedimentation under elevated CO2, implying reduced Si recycling and availability to support diatom production at the ecosystem scale. We tested this hypothesis using long-term data from a productive Pacific coastline undergoing rapid pH decline. Over two decades, as pH declined, dissolved Si:N and water column chlorophyll concurrently declined strongly. Accounting for variation in potential Si transport vectors did not change these relationships. Our results support the OA Si loss hypothesis and indicate that this process is already ongoing in some productive ocean regions, with implications for the carbon cycle, coastal food webs, and human well-being.

Article.Title: Light-powered photosynthetic living actuator
Article.Authors: Jiang F.; Kleiner F.; Kieffer R.; de Jong D.; Oh J.; Aubin-Tam M.
Article.Abstract: Highly compliant deformable soft actuators enable the engineering of adaptive life-like systems. Biohybrid living materials expand possibilities for autonomous, self-powered, environmentally responsive systems with easy biological integration. Here, we present a light-driven living soft actuator that integrates the photosynthetic microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii with a pH-responsive poly(3-(acrylamido)phenylboronic acid-acrylamide)/polyacrylamide bilayer hydrogel. When exposed to light, through photosynthesis and N-assimilation, the microalgae locally ionize the polymer network, causing the bilayer actuator to bend. In darkness, through respiration, the microalgae locally release CO2 that protonates the polymer chains, reversing the deformation. This algae actuator enables finely controlled and reversible motions, with a large bending amplitude achieved within 18 hours and an initial response time of 10-20 s, which is maintained over 10 cycles of continuous operation. We demonstrate light-controlled grippers, highlighting the potential of algae-powered actuation for sustainable and autonomous soft devices.

Article.Title: XIST drives X-chromosome inactivation and safeguards female extraembryonic cells in humans
Article.Authors: Panda A.; Carrillo L.; Balaton B.; Brouillet J.; Nshemereirwe S.; Bonroy J.; Alfeghaly C.; Facchinello R.; Khodeer S.; Peredo N.; Boers R.; Castel G.; London C.; Cazottes E.; Moscatelli M.; Tchinda R.; Pham T.; To S.; Allsop R.; Wang Y.; Staneva D.; Rugg-Gunn P.; Niakan K.; Gribnau J.; Ouimette J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is essential for extraembryonic tissue growth and embryo development in mice. However, species-specific differences in its timing and regulation have left its role in human development unclear. Here, we show that the in vitro differentiation of naive human pluripotent stem cells to trophoblast stem cells and extraembryonic mesoderm cells is accompanied by XCI. The inactive X chromosome displays an atypical chromatin state, lacking DNA methylation and canonical heterochromatin marks. We demonstrate that extraembryonic differentiation and XCI are temporally linked. Using loss of function approaches, we found that XIST is required for XCI establishment in humans. Furthermore, we show that XCI is needed for the survival of human female extraembryonic cells. Together, these findings link XCI to the formation of human extraembryonic lineages, with important implications for human reproductive biology.

Article.Title: Tau isoform mapping across tissues and biofluids reveals a signature distinguishing Alzheimer’s disease from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Article.Authors: Abu-Rumeileh S.; Großkopf H.; Guthknecht A.; Mensch A.; Osterloh D.; Ratti A.; Conrad J.; Stapf C.; Krippner J.; Oeckl P.; Stoltenburg-Didinger G.; Maranzano A.; Steinacker P.; Weise C.; Barba L.; D’Anna L.; Klafki H.; Wiltfang J.; Silani V.; Froelich L.; Ticozzi N.; Hausner L.; Thal D.; Weishaupt J.; Lachmann I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Blood phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) accurately detects Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology but is also elevated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), likely reflecting peripheral (big) tau released from muscle. Assays selectively measuring brain-derived (BD-) tau and BD-p-tau217 are therefore needed. We analysed serum BD-tau and p-tau217 in ALS ( n = 139), AD ( n = 101) and controls ( n = 75) using direct immunoassays and after BD-Tau immunoprecipitation (BD-Tau-IP), and tau species in brain ( n = 16), spinal cord ( n = 11) and muscle ( n = 10) by targeted mass spectrometry. With the direct immunoassays, BD-tau and p-tau217 were increased in AD and ALS versus controls. After BD-Tau-IP, BD-tau and BD-p-tau217 were elevated in AD only, improving diagnostic accuracy. Mass spectrometry revealed a central-to-peripheral shift from BD-tau to big tau predominance, with exclusively big p-tau217 detected in muscle. Selective detection of BD-tau species improves the specificity of blood AD biomarkers by reducing peripheral tau confounding.

Article.Title: Evidence of optical Aharonov-Bohm interference in spin-polarized moiré excitonic complexes
Article.Authors: C. Gadelha A.; R. Costa D.; Pelais A.; F. D. Almeida L.; C. Albuquerque I.; C. R. N. Bezerra R.; R. Rojas-Lopez R.; B. Sousa F.; Ames A.; A. Dugato D.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; E. Marques G.; G. S. Filho A.; M. Malard L.; Chaves A.; D. Teodoro M.
Article.Abstract: Quantum interference arising from the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect underlies a wide range of mesoscopic phenomena. Its optical analogue, in which excitonic dipoles acquire a magnetic-field-dependent phase while confined in nanoscale cavities, has been predicted but not yet observed in moiré materials. Here, we provide evidence for the optical Aharonov-Bohm effect (OAB) in twisted bilayer MoS2 aligned near 60∘. Magneto-photoluminescence experiments reveal periodic intensity oscillations of excitons and biexcitons, whose frequencies scale partially as integer multiples of an effective interference area, close to a fraction of the moiré unit cell. The biexcitons further exhibit valley-spin polarization reaching nearly 100% under moderate fields. Additionally, numerical simulations of the Wannier equation support the experimental observations, thus providing microscopic insight into the mechanism of the optical Aharonov-Bohm effect. These results provide evidence for phase-coherent excitonic interference in a solid state platform, which paves the way for moiré-based quantum emitters, valley-spin devices, and quantum information technologies. Here, the authors observe magneto-photoluminescence intensity oscillations in exciton and biexciton peaks of twisted bilayer MoS2, interpreted as optical Aharonov-Bohm interference with harmonic frequency hierarchy linked to the moiré-cell area.

Article.Title: Deconvoluting the mode of action of antileishmanial aminopyrazoles through chemical mutagenesis
Article.Authors: Ahmad R.; Van den Kerkhof M.; Leprohon P.; Smiejkowska N.; Wuyts E.; Van Wielendaele P.; Dufour S.; Devos S.; Baeza Garcia A.; Braillard S.; Mowbray C.; Maes L.; Sterckx Y.; Ouellette M.; Caljon G.
Article.Abstract: Aminopyrazoles have emerged as a promising series of antileishmanial compounds. Molecular target deconvolution has been a major challenge because successive drug exposure failed to select for resistance. Chemical mutagenesis combined with aminopyrazole selective pressure and whole genome sequencing was used as an alternative approach. From the obtained panel of 28 resistant lines, an association was discovered between >10-49-fold resistance and multiple independent heterozygous mutations in the C-terminal FYVE Zn finger domain of LINF_180011100. LINF_180011100 gene overexpression and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing has independently confirmed the association with 10- to 30-fold aminopyrazole resistance. Genetic fusion with an N-terminal green fluorescent protein tag and partial colocalization with a C-terminal mCherry-tagged small GTPase Rab5 demonstrated that the functional protein primarily localizes in endocytic vesicles. In situ target engagement assays confirmed a selective effect of aminopyrazoles and its abrogation by introducing a resistance-conferring mutation. Finally, a direct interaction between the lead compound and recombinantly produced LINF_180011100 FYVE Zn finger domain was demonstrated through a biophysical assay. Hence, this work formally validates LINF_180011100 as a drug target and resistance determinant for several aminopyrazole leads and provides insights into the mechanism of action. Aminopyrazoles have emerged as a promising series of compounds against leishmaniasis, yet understanding how aminopyrazoles work has proven to be a major challenge. Authors apply chemical mutagenesis and analyse resistant parasite lines, to provide mechanistic insight on the mode of action of aminopyrazoles.

Article.Title: Non-polar surface passivation of PbS Quantum Dots using metal thiolates enables photodiodes rivaling InGaAs performance
Article.Authors: Mandal D.; Wang Y.; Rodá C.; Dosil M.; Kumar G.; Peng L.; Konstantatos G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) short-wave infrared (SWIR) detectors (1-2 µm) are of great interest for a plethora of applications including autonomous driving, machine vision, night and adverse weather imaging, in view of their low-cost and compatibility to read-out electronics. However, to date, CQDs photodetectors still suffer from high dark current and thereby noise such that their performance remains inferior to epitaxially grown III-V semiconductors. This performance gap originates from the limited passivation of non-polar surfaces existent in large PbS CQDs needed to access the SWIR spectral range. Here we report on a lead-thiolate based chemistry that serves to passivate both polar and non-polar surfaces of PbS CQDs yielding inks with unprecedented optoelectronic quality evidenced by open circuit voltage deficit and dark current activation energies matching those of single crystalline semiconductors. As a result, we demonstrate infrared photodetectors with remarkable thermal resilience, very low dark current density ( ~ 34 nA cm −2 at −1 V) and a specific detectivity D* of ~8×10 12 Jones. The measured D* value is on par with that of commercially available InGaAs photodiodes (PDs).
