Article.Title: Regulation of PDH via cysteine oxidation on DLAT
Article.Authors: Garcia-Cortizo F.; Weber T.; Nůsková H.; Pfaff D.; Büttner M.; Wirth A.; Kliemank E.; Poschet G.; Freichel M.; Fleming T.; Sulaj A.; Nawroth P.; Szendroedi J.; Teleman A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex is a key regulator of metabolism, controlling flux from glycolysis into the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. PDH is often dysregulated in metabolic diseases and cancer. We discover here that in addition to its well characterized regulation by phosphorylation, PDH activity is also regulated via inhibitory oxidation of three cysteines of the DLAT subunit - Cys488, Cys586 and Cys618. Oxidation of these cysteines increases under oxidative stress, and is highly prevalent in mouse and human tissues. This mechanism enables cells to efficiently fight oxidative stress. Under oxidative stress, cells execute a metabolic shift, blocking glycolytic flux into the TCA cycle to shunt glycolytic carbons toward the pentose phosphate pathway. This generates NADPH which cells use to detoxify H 2 O 2 and to reduce oxidized cysteines. We find that DLAT oxidation is required for cells to mount an effective antioxidant response. Mutations preventing DLAT oxidation render PDH resistant to oxidative inhibition, impair NADPH generation, reduce peroxide detoxification, and sensitize cells to oxidative damage and death. DLAT oxidation also drives a Warburg-like metabolic phenotype of increased glucose uptake, elevated lactate secretion, and reduced TCA cycle activity. Thus DLAT oxidation is a redox-sensing mechanism that regulates PDH activity and central carbon metabolism.

Article.Title: Spontaneous ferromagnetic Fe–La geminal atoms with spin and coordination modulation for acidic oxygen reduction
Article.Authors: Kong F.; Gong Q.; Mei B.; Kang C.; Ye J.; Du C.; Yin G.; Dong J.; Zhao S.

Moreover, La enables dynamic self-adaptive stabilization of Fe sites, which mitigates the conventional activity–stability trade-off. This finding provides an avenue to rationally design efficient and selective electrocatalysts. Here, the authors report spontaneous ferromagnetic Fe–La geminal atoms that create high-spin Fe sites and a spin pinning effect for fuel-cell catalysis.

Article.Authors: Wang S.; Gainey L.; Liu L.; Zeng Z.; Xiao S.; Zhu R.; Couperthwaite S.; Gu Y.; Xi Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Clay minerals are the most crucial constituents in brickmaking clays, yet the specific role of different clay minerals remain poorly understood due to their natural coexistence and formidable challenges of separation. Article.Title: Luminal geometry and coiled coil length determine submembrane localization of type II transmembrane Golgi proteins
Article.Authors: Wong J.; Hübner B.; Mahajan D.; Tie H.; Surya W.; Torres J.; Ludwig A.; Lu L.

These findings identify intraluminal width as a mechanism governing the lateral partitioning of type II transmembrane proteins with long luminal coiled coils. Article.Title: Multiplexed live imaging deciphers nuclear force-driven chromatin dynamics and embryo development
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Qiu J.; Zhao Y.; Yang M.; Lu S.; Ding S.; Xie Y.; Xu F.; Luo Y.; Sun K.; Chien S.; Zhou J.; Peng Q.
Article.Abstract: Mechanical forces transmitted to the nucleus regulate chromatin organization and gene expression to guide cell fate transitions. Our study establishes a mechanochemical framework linking nuclear forces to chromatin organization and function. Here, they develop a nuclear tension sensor (NuTS) to quantify SUN2 force for perinuclear chromatin anchoring at ~6 pN. They further demonstrate that LINC-complex force transmission is critical for cell migration and zebrafish notochord development.

Article.Title: Orientation tomography of lanthanide-doped nanoprobes by polarization-resolved micro-spectroscopy
Article.Authors: Magermans L.; Bonetti M.; Gacoin T.; Kim J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Quantifying three-dimensional (3D) orientation is critical for understanding self-assembly and collective behavior in soft matter and biological systems. We develop a confocal imaging setup optimized for lanthanide luminescence and a theoretical framework to extract both the local director and order parameter in nanorod assemblies. The technique achieves 0.5 μm lateral and 1 μm axial spatial resolution and is demonstrated in dense nematic liquid-crystal assemblies, resolving complex 3D topological structures, and in microfluidic flows, mapping alignment under hydrodynamic shear. This approach provides a versatile platform for quantitative studies of collective orientation, self-assembly mechanics, and alignment induced by external forces, and can be extended to other lanthanide-labeled particles and molecular probes.

Article.Title: Signatures of bi-altermagnetism revealed by sublattice-specific circular dichroism in resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
Article.Authors: Channagowdra G.; Singh A.; Huang H.; Furo M.; Gao B.; Dai P.; Chen C.; Kuneš J.; Fujimori A.; Cheong S.; Hariki A.; Huang D.
Article.Abstract: An altermagnet is a recently identified class of magnets that exhibit a zero net magnetic moment but break symmetry under the combined operations of parity and time reversal. It typically consists of two magnetic sites of opposite spins related by rotation within the unit cell. Here, we use circular dichroism (CD) in resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to reveal symmetry signatures of a distinct form of altermagnetism, namely bi-altermagnetism, in the correlated insulator Fe2Mo3O8, which comprises two altermagnetic sublattices: one with alternating quasi-octahedral Fe environments and the other with alternating tetrahedral Fe environments. We experimentally revealed the emergence of CD in an achiral, zero-magnetization system, thereby probing mirror-symmetry breaking associated with altermagnetic order. Notably, the CD appeared at sublattice-specific excitations of the octahedral and tetrahedral sites, indicating symmetry breaking in both altermagnetic sublattices. Calculations based on a model with the bi-altermagnetic order along the c axis successfully reproduce the observed CD. Our findings support the realization of bi-altermagnetism in Fe2Mo3O8, and showcase the use of RIXS-CD as a probe of magnetic sublattices in systems with zero net magnetization. The standard definition of altermagnetism is of two magnetic sites of opposite spin related by rotation within the unit of a material. Here, using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, Channagowdra et al. unveil a ’bi-altermagnetic’ state in Fe2Mo3O8, where the two inequivalent Fe sites each form an opposite-spin sublattice pair that independently satisfies the conventional criteria for altermagnetism.

Article.Title: Shifting balance between habitat and climate in boreal biodiversity patterns across space, time and taxa
Article.Authors: Guilbault E.; Antão L.; Santangeli A.; Jones M.; Heliölä J.; Henttonen H.; Huikkonen I.; Huitu O.; Korpimäki E.; Kuussaari M.; Lehikoinen A.; Lindén A.; Pietiäinen H.; Pöyry J.; Sihvonen P.; Laine A.; Roslin T.; Saastamoinen M.; Vanhatalo J.
Article.Abstract: Climate and habitat are key drivers of biodiversity patterns. However, how they independently and jointly affect species distribution across space, time, and taxa remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluate the relative importance of habitat and climate variables underpinning occurrence and abundance patterns of 503 terrestrial animal species over 20 years and a ~ 1100 km latitudinal gradient in Finland. Habitat composition is the main explanatory variable of biodiversity patterns, with varying importance and uncertainty across taxa, regions, and years, and with effects being partially correlated for many species. Specifically, habitat dominate in importance for butterflies, birds, and small mammals, while both habitat and climate explain the patterns of large mammals and moths. Additionally, patterns between biogeographical regions and years are mainly explained by climate, while habitat explains most variation within regions and years. Further differences emerge among functional groups, as body size, pace of life and specialization modulate the relative importance of habitat and climate. Our findings emphasize that land use is a major force in shaping terrestrial biodiversity, while highlighting its tight connection with climate. Considering functional, spatial, and temporal contexts is thus essential for building effective conservation strategies for biodiversity under global change. Climate and habitat jointly shape species distributions and biodiversity. The authors show that habitat is the main driver of boreal terrestrial biodiversity, while the relative roles of climate and habitat vary by region, year and species traits.

Article.Title: Bioinspired nanozyme-exoskeletonized yeast-derived polysaccharides for treating comorbid anxiety and depression in inflammatory bowel disease
Article.Authors: Zhang F.; Chen L.; Wang S.; Chen X.; Du K.; Song F.; Jiang L.; Feng Y.; Du S.; Jiang T.; Liu Y.; Xiao J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic condition frequently accompanied by psychological comorbidities, such as anxiety and depression. Although current treatments may alleviate some of these symptoms, the intricate pathogenesis of these comorbidities highlights an urgent need for therapeutic strategies with combined anti-inflammatory, barrier-reparative, and microbiota-modulating effects. Herein, we develop a series of nanozyme-exoskeletonized yeast-derived polysaccharides (NZEP) by integrating nanozymes with yeast-derived polysaccharides using an insect sclerotization-inspired strategy. Among them, NZEP TA-Ce , with the highest degree of nanozyme-exoskeletonization, is capable of disrupting the inflammatory vicious cycle by inhibiting MAPK and NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling pathways. Oral administration of NZEP TA-Ce in mice enables effective retention and accumulation in inflamed colonic regions, reverses the homeostasis imbalance of intestinal inflammation and promotes intestinal barrier repair. Furthermore, NZEP TA-Ce treatment reverses gut microbiota dysbiosis and optimizes the composition of microbial metabolites, thereby alleviating anxiety and depressive symptoms associated with IBD. This study provides a safe and promising therapeutic strategy for the management of IBD patients and their associated psychological comorbidities.

Article.Title: Hemispheric asymmetry in predicted range shifts of anti-tropical fish under future climate change
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Yuan S.; García Molinos J.; Mammola S.; Huang H.; Bede-Fazekas Á.; Liu Y.; Xing W.; Zhang L.; Qin G.; Lin Q.
Article.Abstract: Anti-tropically distributed species have long intrigued biogeographers. However, how they will respond to future climate change remains a key unresolved question, particularly for marine species given an expected hemispheric asymmetry in ocean warming. Here, using species distribution models for 172 anti-tropical marine fishes, we predict that northern hemispheric lineages will experience significantly higher range contractions, in agreement with the hemispheric asymmetry in ocean warming. Our predictions show that suitable habitat will be reduced at a similar rate both within and outside marine protected areas, leading protection efficacy (the proportion of the total suitable habitat protected) to remain at current levels, irrespective of the scenario and period considered, and the level of protection efficacy to remain significantly higher in the Southern Hemisphere. These results highlight the need for accounting for hemispheric asymmetry in ocean warming when designing future conservation strategies. As oceans warm unevenly between hemispheres, the future of anti-tropical fishes is unclear. Despite larger future range contractions for northern lineages, protected area efficacy remains unchanged and significantly higher for southern lineages.

Article.Title: Enhancing ω-transaminase catalysis of bulky substrates guided by binding mechanism
Article.Authors: Teng H.; Yu H.; Xu Z.; Xiao L.; Yuan X.; Yang L.; Wu J.; Xu G.
Article.Abstract: Chiral amines are indispensable building blocks in pharmaceutical synthesis. (R)-3-([1,1′-biphenyl]-4-yl)-2-aminopropan-1-ol (ABP), a key chiral amine intermediate of the drug Entresto, has remained difficult to access via enzymatic asymmetric synthesis due to the inability of ω-transaminases to accommodate its bulky ketone precursor. Here, we engineer an ω-transaminase from Bacillus megaterium by integrating Funnel metadynamics, PathDetect-SOM, and path collective variables to reconstruct the free energy surface of substrate binding, pinpointing high-energy barrier regions of the binding process and the trade-off between tunnel accessibility and productive binding. Dynamic cross-correlation network analysis further identifies distal regulatory sites governing these bottleneck regions. Iterative experimental optimization yields the 13M variant, exhibiting catalytic activity 106 times that of the wild type with >99% enantiomeric excess, enabling the efficient enzymatic asymmetric synthesis of ABP. This integrated computational-experimental framework for resolving the tunnel-pocket binding trade-off offers a generalizable strategy for engineering ω-transaminases toward bulky substrates in green pharmaceutical synthesis. This study combines enhanced sampling with experiments to reveal how bulky substrates enter and bind to ω-transaminases. Distal-site engineering balanced tunnel access and binding stability, yielding 106-fold activity and >99% selectivity.

Article.Title: On predictability of slip, rupture geometry, and speed of the 2025 M7.8 Mandalay, Myanmar, earthquake
Article.Authors: Ulrich T.; Zou X.; Marchandon M.; Schliwa N.; Tan F.; Gabriel A.; Fan W.; Shearer P.; Thant M.; Tin T.; Lindsey E.; Fialko Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The 2025 M 7.8 Mandalay earthquake ruptured ~480 km of the Sagaing Fault, producing one of the longest strike-slip events documented and impacting a vulnerable region. Here we combine remote sensing observations and numerical modeling to show that the subsurface fault geometry and slip distribution could be anticipated from pre-event observations. Along-strike variations in coseismic and interseismic deformation reveal a helix-shaped fault geometry. The average coseismic slip equals or exceeds the interseismic slip deficit, consistent with a minimally slip-predictable model. We generate an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models, constrained by the best-fit static slip model, then discriminate among them using independent space-geodetic, seismic, and near-field video observations. The preferred scenario begins bilaterally, then transitions to unilateral southward supershear propagation at depth, while shallow rupture remains subshear. These dynamics are shaped by localized stress heterogeneity and low fracture energy, characteristic of a structurally mature fault zone. Our approach can inform rupture scenarios in understudied regions.

Article.Title: Small viruses reveal bidirectional evolution between HK97-fold viruses and encapsulins via procapsids
Article.Authors: Aguilar A.; Miranda Perez I.; Nadel O.; Nayfach S.; Ruiz Pestana L.; Segall A.; Rohwer F.; Roux S.; White S.; Luque A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The HK97-fold is an ancient, conserved protein structure that assembles protein shells, forming the capsids of Duplodnaviria viruses and prokaryotic biochemical compartments called encapsulsins. It has been proposed that encapsulins evolved from HK97-fold viruses. But the higher complexity of viral capsids represents a biophysical paradox in the evolution of HK97-fold protein shells. To resolve this problem, we hypothesize the existence of simpler HK97-fold viral capsids associated with smaller genomes than those of known HK97-fold viruses. Such small viral genomes are searched in environmental metagenomes across public databases, including IMG/M and MGnify. Using hidden Markov models and protein language models, we identify and characterize small viral genomes encoding HK97-fold proteins that exhibit molecular similarities to encapsulins yet lack portal and tail genes. The phylogenetic analyses of HK97-fold proteins reveal independent mixed groups of viruses and encapsulins, and structural analyses identify similarities between encapsulins and procapsids, the immature state of viral capsids. The observations support a bidirectional evolution between encapsulins and HK97-fold viruses enabled by the viral procapsid state. Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions.

Article.Title: Vacancy-mediated ultrafast oxide-ion conduction in excess-oxygen Sillén oxybromides
Article.Authors: Kanenori Y.; Udagawa H.; Saito K.; Sakuda Y.; Fujii K.; Kluczny M.; Yatoo M.; Mori K.; Ishihara T.; Skinner S.; Yashima M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) require electrolytes with high oxide-ion conductivity at low temperatures (200–400 °C) to reduce costs. Here, we report that Bi 1.9 Te 0.1 LaO 4.05 Br exhibits oxide-ion conductivity of 0.01 S cm⁻¹ at 233 °C within the “Norby gap” in dry atmospheres. This performance exceeds that of leading proton conductors, such as BaZr 0.8 Y 0.2 O 2.9 and BaZr 0.4 Ce 0.4 Y 0.1 Yb 0.1 O 2.9 , as well as representative oxide-ion conductors, including yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ), LaGaO 3 -based phases (LSGM), and Bi 2 V 0.7 Sb 0.3 O 5.5 . Bi 1.9 Te 0.1 LaO 4.05 Br also exhibits negligible chemical expansion and high chemical stability under oxidizing, reducing, and CO 2 -containing atmospheres. The high conductivity is associated with a layered Sillén structure composed of Bi-containing triple fluorite-like slabs and Br layers, together with oxygen vacancies that enable vacancy-mediated oxide-ion migration. Despite the presence of excess oxide ions, oxide-ion transport predominantly occurs via a vacancy mechanism, as revealed by ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, static density functional theory calculations, and neutron diffraction analyses. These findings establish a design principle for high-performance oxide-ion conductors based on vacancy-mediated oxide-ion transport in excess-oxygen Bi-containing Sillén oxyhalides.

Article.Title: EphrinA4/EphA4 controls blood pressure via arterial sympathetic innervation in male mice
Article.Authors: Simonnet E.; Martin S.; Vilar J.; Monceau V.; Vessieres E.; Pallot G.; Rio M.; Taib S.; do Rego J.; do Rego J.; Salaün C.; Raynaud F.; Pardanaud L.; Laude D.; Bouby N.; Vion A.; Eichmann A.; Silvestre J.; Henrion D.; Brunet I.
Article.Abstract: The autonomic sympathetic nervous system innervates peripheral resistance arteries, thereby controlling arterial diameter and modulating blood supply to organs and arterial tone. Despite its fundamental role in blood flow regulation and cardiovascular adaptation to challenging situations, how sympathetic arterial innervation develops remains poorly understood. We here show that sympathetic arterial innervation is regulated by the axonal guidance molecule EphrinA4 in arterial Smooth Muscle Cells (SMCs), which repels sympathetic axons via the EphA4 receptor. Using the EphA4flox-THCRE mouse, we specifically inactivated EphA4 in sympathetic axons, inducing a loss of repulsion and increased sympathetic innervation of peripheral arteries throughout life. Functional consequences included a significant increase in arterial tone, including resistivity and vasoconstriction, associated with elevated systemic arterial blood pressure at rest and a marked increase during acute stress. These findings identify a pathway that negatively regulates sympathetic arterial innervation and could contribute to elevated systemic blood pressure in male mice. The sympathetic nervous system regulates blood pressure, but how arterial sympathetic innervation is established remains unclear. Here, the authors show that EphrinA4/EphA4 signalling limits sympathetic arterial innervation, thereby controlling vascular resistance and systemic blood pressure.

Article.Title: Mapping cell-type-specific spatial gene programs uncovers tissue architecture and microenvironment organization
Article.Authors: Zeng Y.; Wang Z.; Liu Y.; Chen Y.; Wang J.; Chen H.; Yang C.
Article.Abstract: The complex organization of tissues is shaped by the spatial arrangement of diverse cell types executing specialized gene programs. Cell-type-specific spatial gene programs (SGPs) are transcriptional modules that capture spatial expression co-variation within cell types. However, identifying these SGPs remains challenging in spatial transcriptomics. Here we present MacSGP, a scalable framework that integrates deep graph neural networks with probabilistic modeling to identify cell-type-specific SGPs through low-rank structures while accounting for cell type mixtures. Through comprehensive simulations and real data analyses spanning diverse tissues and technologies, we demonstrate that MacSGP effectively distinguishes cell-type-specific SGPs from cell-type marker gene expression patterns while uncovering tissue architecture and cellular microenvironments. In a mouse brain dataset, we identify replicable SGPs reflecting subregional neuronal specializations, with these genes significantly enriched for heritabilities associated with brain-related phenotypes. Across colorectal cancer datasets from various platforms, MacSGP identifies consistent SGPs that define distinct cellular niches within the tumor microenvironment. MacSGP identifies cell-type-specific spatial gene programs, capturing coordinated gene activity that varies across locations within cell types. This study dissects gene programs that reveal patterns of tissue organisation and cellular environments within brain and tumour contexts.

Article.Title: Effects of time-restricted eating and supervised exercise on intrahepatic fat and cardiometabolic health in adults with obesity: the TEMPUS randomized controlled trial
Article.Authors: Clavero-Jimeno A.; Camacho-Cardenosa A.; Martin-Olmedo J.; Molina-Fernandez M.; Boira-Nacher B.; Cortés-Martín A.; López-Vázquez A.; Hernández-Martínez C.; Amaro-Gahete F.; Jurado-Fasoli L.; Cupeiro R.; De-la-O A.; Gatti A.; de Teresa Galván C.; Carlén A.; Corpas-Pérez S.; Carneiro-Barrera A.; Suárez-Catalina A.; Martín-Márquez R.; Concepción M.; Morillo Moreno-Torres P.; García Pérez P.; Cabeza R.; Martín-Rodríguez J.; de Cabo R.
Article.Abstract: Lifestyle interventions targeting intrahepatic fat remain limited. We investigated whether 8-hour time-restricted eating (TRE), supervised exercise, or their combination reduced intrahepatic fat fraction (IHFF) more than usual care (UC; Mediterranean diet and physical activity education) and each other. This investigator-initiated, parallel-group randomized controlled trial was conducted in Granada, Spain. Participants were recruited from May 2023 to April 2024, and the trial was completed on 5 September 2025. Primary outcome assessors and statisticians were blinded to group allocation, whereas intervention personnel were not. All 187 randomized adults with obesity (50% women) were included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis: UC (n = 48), TRE (n = 46), Exercise (n = 47), and TRE+Exercise (n = 46). The primary outcome was change in IHFF measured by magnetic resonance imaging after 12 weeks. IHFF change did not differ with TRE (−0.4%; 95% CI, −2.0 to 1.2; P = 0.93), Exercise (−0.8%; −2.4 to 0.8; P = 0.54), or TRE+Exercise (−1.1%; −2.7 to 0.5; P = 0.28) compared with UC, nor among intervention groups. These findings do not support greater short-term IHFF reductions with TRE, exercise, or their combination than with UC or between intervention groups. Trial registration: NCT05897073. Time-restricted eating and structured exercise training have both been reported to reduce hepatic steatosis and improve cardiometabolic profile. Here the authors report a randomized controlled trial showing that in adults with obesity, time-restricted eating, supervised exercise, or their combination did not reduce intrahepatic fat more than usual care that consisted of Mediterranean diet and physical activity education.

Article.Title: Observation of dark magnons in a van der Waals antiferromagnet/ferromagnet interface
Article.Authors: Yu K.; Wang H.; Hu C.; He Y.; Zhuang H.; Song H.; Yang T.; Sheng L.; Shen D.; Yang G.; Yu R.; Han X.; Liu S.; Yu D.; Ansermet J.; Ziman T.; Yu H.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Magnons, the quanta of spin waves, offer a promising platform for low-power information processing owing to their charge-free propagation. Dark magnon modes, which are intrinsically decoupled from electromagnetic fields, exhibit high robustness against environmental perturbations and enable stealth-like propagation, making them highly attractive for magnonic applications. However, the excitation and detection of dark magnons in antiferromagnets remain highly challenging. Here, we report the direct observation of a magnon dark mode in a van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr interfaced with a ferromagnetic insulator YIG. In CrSBr, the canted (spin-flop) phase is nearly bypassed and the spin-flip phase has two magnon branches, one of which, the dark mode, has nearly zero net dynamic magnetization. We demonstrate that the interfacial exchange interaction enables the experimental detection of the magnon dark mode, while its presence is confirmed by the observation of coherent magnon-magnon coupling between YIG and CrSBr magnons. Micromagnetic simulations and a theoretical model reveal that the dark mode in CrSBr at the heterostructure interface hybridizes with YIG magnons via interfacial exchange interaction. Our results provide a new route for detecting dark magnon modes in antiferromagnets and open up opportunities for stealth-like magnon transport and hybrid magnonic devices based on van der Waals heterostructures. Dark magnons refer to magnons that are decoupled from electromagnetic fields, making them robust against external perturbations. This feature also makes dark magnons challenging to detect, but here, Yu, Wang, Hu, He, and coauthors succeed in directly observing the dark magnon mode in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr, by interfacing a thin flake of CrSBr with ferrimagnetic YIG.

Article.Title: Lesion penetration predicts tuberculosis treatment shortening through a validated translational tool to de-risk development
Article.Authors: Ernest J.; Bustion A.; Patel A.; Sarathy J.; Kaya F.; Rodriguez S.; Zimmerman M.; Strydom N.; Silva C.; Flori L.; Vu H.; Westergren V.; Via L.; Dartois V.; Savic R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Anti-tuberculosis (TB) drugs must reach the disease site to be effective, but complex TB pathology limits drug distribution and efficacy, as bacteria in the necrotic center of lung cavities are difficult to access and kill. Our study generates the most comprehensive database of site-of-disease distribution for 24 drugs and drug candidates in a rabbit model of cavitary TB. We validate a lung lesion penetration model with clinical data and develop an integrated approach that combines microenvironment-specific pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Next, we simulate site-of-disease coverage of shortened regimens tested in major Phase 3 trials over the past decade, allowing direct comparisons with trial outcomes. We propose that regimens including at least two drugs achieving bactericidal concentrations in pulmonary cavities are more likely to meet primary clinical endpoints in patients with cavitary disease. Our translational platform constitutes a validated tool to support drug evaluation, smart regimen design, and de-risking of late-stage trials.

This cell type-specific regulatory landscape provides genomic and epigenomic insights into the pathological role of the cerebellum in AD/ADRD. Here, the authors use single‑nucleus multiomics to map disease‑associated regulatory alterations in cerebellar cell types and identify functional risk variants linked to neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: A South Atlantic atmospheric river dipole as a key precursor of Amazon wildfires
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Dong W.; Chen D.
Article.Abstract: Wildfires in the Amazon have far-reaching climatic and ecological impacts, yet their predictability remains limited. Here we identify a large-scale atmospheric precursor of August–September Amazon wildfires: a June–July dipole mode of South Atlantic atmospheric rivers (ARs), characterized by suppressed AR activity in the north and enhanced activity in the south. This dipole is strongly linked to interannual variability in Amazon wildfire activity through land–atmosphere feedbacks associated with reduced precipitation and humidity, enhanced surface warming and solar radiation, and increased vegetation stress. We estimate that wildfire-related forest loss associated with this AR dipole mode accounts for approximately 26% of the observed interannual variability in total forest loss. Adding the South Atlantic AR dipole to predictors based on May–June sea surface temperature anomalies and June–July wildfire activity yields substantial predictive skill for August–September burned area (R² = 0.67). Climate model projections further indicate a future intensification of the South Atlantic AR dipole mode, implying increased wildfire-driven ecological degradation in the Amazon under continued warming. This study identifies a South Atlantic atmospheric river dipole as an early warning signal for Amazon wildfires, linking shifts in moisture transport to hotter, drier conditions and increased fire activity in the region.

Article.Title: Whole-genome sequencing reveals inter-household networks of gut-colonising ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in two rural Malawian districts
Article.Authors: O’Ferrall A.; Lally D.; Makaula P.; Namacha G.; Lewis J.; Musicha P.; Goodman R.; Allman E.; Moyo S.; Waddington C.; Kayuni S.; Feasey N.; Musaya J.; Stothard J.; Roberts A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Infection with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-Ec) is a global health concern that disproportionately affects sub-Saharan Africa. Gut mucosal colonisation is thought to precede invasive infection. Understanding ESBL-Ec colonisation and transmission across communities is therefore essential. Here, we investigate the genomic epidemiology and spatial structure of 159 gut-colonising ESBL-Ec isolates from the faeces of 211 people in two rural Malawian villages using longitudinal sampling (2023–24), whole-genome sequencing and household mapping. Isolates belonged to 33 sequence types (STs), most commonly ST38 and ST131, harbouring 46 distinct antimicrobial resistance gene types. Fifteen strains were identified in ≥3 households that were typically separated by short geographic distances ( < 400 m). Of 190 pairwise comparisons between same-strain isolates from different households sampled concurrently within villages, 88.9% differed by ≤10 single nucleotide polymorphisms, consistent with multi-household involvement in community transmission networks. Lineage-specific ST38 and ST131 network analyses linked rural isolates to urban Malawian isolates collected within the last decade. Our findings provide a transferable framework for inferring ESBL-Ec flow in community settings and highlight the need for One Health surveillance and improved sanitation infrastructure to limit transmission.

Article.Title: Universal crystallization kinetics of solution-processed semiconductors
Article.Authors: Ling Z.; Brzezinski M.; Wang S.; Bidinakis K.; Gao L.; Li C.; Zhou X.; Wang H.; Weber S.; Blom P.; Pisula W.; Marszalek T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous crystallization kinetics critically govern the morphology and performance of solution-processed semiconductors, yet morphology control is often achieved through trial-and-error optimization. Quantitative understanding of crystallization is essential for precise morphology control but is limited by the simultaneous occurrence of heterogeneous nucleation and crystal growth. Here, a time-defined induced nucleation strategy has been developed to initiate crystallization at specific stages of solution processing. Systematic variation of nucleation timing reveals three distinct morphological regimes, whose emergence is explained by the concentration-dependent critical cluster radius in bulk, interfacial, and cusp environments. Leveraging these curated SAGs, we identified 6,474 host–mobilome linkages across 2,378 SAGs; these linkages not only showed high concordance with host-association data within the Integrated Microbial Genomes (IMG) system but also significantly expanded species-level host assignments. Furthermore, we detected frequent inter-species sharing patterns of diverse cryptic plasmids within the order Bacteroidales. Together, this work demonstrates that high-throughput single-cell genomics, empowered by the robust framework, resolves fine-scale heterogeneity and host–mobilome dynamics, advancing culture-independent microbiome research. In this study, the authors develop a computational framework, Scellmate, that curates and analyzes large-scale microbial single-cell datasets from complex environments, and show that this helps to reveal microbial diversity and infer microbe–plasmid and microbe–phage associations in sewage.

Article.Title: Soil proteogenomics uncover microbial strategies for soil depth-specific carbon cycling under whole-soil warming conditions
Article.Authors: Karaoz U.; Alves R.; Tolic N.; Chu R.; Nicora C.; Toyoda J.; Eloe-Fadrosh E.; Torn M.; Brodie E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Soils are Earth’s largest carbon reservoir, yet microbial mechanisms controlling decomposition, and their warming response, remain poorly resolved, especially in subsoils. Using genome-resolved proteogenomics within a replicated whole-soil warming experiment (0–90 cm, +4 °C, 7.5 years) we map microbial traits, their depth stratification, and warming responses. Depth is the dominant driver of microbial community and trait structure. Depth-wise, metabolism converge on low-molecular-weight and C1 compounds, challenging glucose-centric models, with surface soils enriched in methanol oxidation and deep soils in alcohol fermentation, CO oxidation and N₂ fixation. Abundant sialidases in deep soils implicate glycoproteins as a key carbon source. Warming effects are smaller and decrease over time but are depth-specific: surface soils show enhanced amino sugar and sugar alcohol transport, phosphorus mobilization, and stress tolerance, whereas mid- and deep soils exhibit stimulated C1 metabolism, CO oxidation, and altered nitrogen turnover. These depth-specific microbial trait shifts may critically influence soil carbon–climate feedbacks.

Article.Title: Unmet care needs at the end-of-life among older adults with activity limitations
Article.Authors: Long C.; Lin Z.; Swearinger H.; Ailshire J.; Qian Y.; Ming W.; Zhao H.; Hou X.; Wu B.; Yang W.; Chen X.; Chen S.
Article.Abstract: Despite the growing global demand for end-of-life care resulting from rapid social transformations, significant gaps exist in cross-national research examining unmet end-of-life care needs. Using harmonized end-of-life survey data (2010-2021) from the United States, 28 European countries, South Korea, China, and Mexico, here we show that the United States, Europe, and South Korea exhibit higher overall unmet end-of-life care needs than China and Mexico, where limited formal care provision is compensated with high levels of informal care. Death at institutions is associated with lower overall unmet end-of-life care needs in the United States and South Korea, with Mexico presenting an exception. Similarly, urban areas in Europe and South Korea exhibit lower unmet formal end-of-life care needs compared to rural areas. Among married individuals, only Mexico exhibits significantly lower unmet overall end-of-life care needs compared to unmarried individuals. Having children is consistently linked to lower unmet informal end-of-life care needs across the United States, Europe, and South Korea. Our findings highlight the complex interplay between care systems and family demographic structures in shaping end-of-life care access, and underscore the need for tailored policy approaches that strengthen both formal and informal care systems while addressing sociodemographic disparities in care access. Formal end-of-life care expansion in the US, Europe, and South Korea has not fully compensated for declining informal care, resulting in care gaps. Demographic transitions interact with development contexts to create distinct care landscapes.

Article.Title: NiCLIP: neuroimaging contrastive language-image pretraining model for predicting text from brain activation images
Article.Authors: Peraza J.; Kent J.; Nichols T.; Poline J.; de la Vega A.; Laird A.
Article.Abstract: Predicting cognitive processes from brain activation maps remains a key challenge in neuroscience. Meta-analytic functional decoding provides an estimation of behavioral profiles associated with specific brain regions; however, existing methods fail to capture the full semantic content of the neuroimaging literature. To address this, we present NiCLIP, a contrastive language-image model trained on over 23,000 articles to predict cognitive tasks, concepts, and domains from brain activation patterns. NiCLIP achieves optimal performance when using full-text articles and a curated cognitive ontology with precise task-concept-domain mappings. Our results show that NiCLIP accurately predicts cognitive tasks from Human Connectome Project group-level maps across multiple domains (e.g., emotion, language, motor) and precisely characterizes the functional roles of specific brain regions, including the amygdala, hippocampus, and temporoparietal junction. However, NiCLIP showed limitations with noisy subject-level activation maps. NiCLIP represents a significant advancement in functional decoding, offering a powerful tool for hypothesis generation and scientific discovery. Researchers developed NiCLIP, an AI model that decodes cognitive tasks, concepts, and domains from brain activation patterns. Trained on over 23,000 papers, NiCLIP excels at group-level decoding, outperforming traditional decoders.

Article.Title: Mitochondria-localized circRNA BRAKE restrains adipogenesis under nutrient overload by disrupting ATP synthase assembly in mice
Article.Authors: Huang Y.; Zhu T.; Hong X.; Yang Y.; Liao J.; Liu J.; Li C.; Wang W.; Chen S.; Saw P.; Li Y.; Xiao H.; Ren M.; Su S.; Huang Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Impaired adipogenesis contributes to obesity-associated metabolic disorders, in which mitochondrial dysfunction plays an important role. Emerging evidence suggests that mitochondria-localized circular RNAs (circRNAs) influence mitochondrial function; however, whether they regulate adipogenesis and systemic metabolism is unclear. By profiling circRNAs in mitochondria isolated from the white adipose tissue (WAT) of obese male mice, we observe an upregulation of Birc6 -circRNA Repressing Adipogenesis and Krebs-cycle Energy (BRAKE) in mitochondria. In vivo, adipocyte-specific circRNA BRAKE knockdown in male mice reduces body weight, restricts fat expansion, and improves insulin sensitivity. In vitro studies show that circRNA BRAKE inhibits adipogenesis. Mechanistically, circRNA BRAKE binds ATP5A and disrupts ATP synthase assembly, thereby reducing ATP production and mTORC1 signaling and suppressing adipogenesis. In omental WAT (oWAT) of patients with obesity, mitochondrial circRNA BRAKE levels are elevated and inversely correlated with mitochondrial bioenergetic function. Collectively, our data identify a mitochondria-localized circRNA that regulates energy metabolism and adipogenesis, suggesting that circRNA BRAKE may represent a potential therapeutic target for obesity-related metabolic diseases.

Article.Title: Current aviation roadmaps are not within planetary boundaries
Article.Authors: Païs B.; Gondran A.; Hamelin L.; Simatos F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aviation decarbonization roadmaps predominantly rely on replacing fossil kerosene with alternative jet fuels, yet the systemic impact of these alternatives on planetary boundaries other than climate change has not been quantified. Here we integrate prospective life-cycle inventories with the planetary boundaries framework to evaluate the absolute impacts of aviation roadmaps as time-dependent trajectories, rather than endpoint snapshots. Across scenarios to 2050, we find that fuel-switch-centered roadmaps do not achieve sustainability, persistently transgress the climate change and biosphere integrity core boundaries, and exert large demands for energy, land, freshwater and CO 2 capture that challenge their feasibility. Slower traffic growth brings aviation closer to its share of the safe operating space in terms of lowering energy demand, but respecting additional planetary boundaries requires air traffic to decline by at least 7.2% yr −1 . Our results show that aligning aviation with Earth’s safe operating space cannot be achieved through fuel substitution alone and requires governance strategies that combine supply-side solutions with explicit demand-side measures.

Article.Title: Multi-day recalibration-free electrophysiology interface based on carbon nanotube thin film dry electrodes
Article.Authors: Wen Y.; Schlegel H.; Fox D.; Wang C.; Harutyunyan A.; Gao R.; Gao W.; Zhang Q.; Khanna P.; Arias A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Electrophysiological signals provide crucial and reliable information for decoding behavioral and cognitive human states. However, existing electrode interfaces are susceptible to artifacts or drift over time, thereby requiring frequent machine-learning model retraining. Here we present an end-to-end design of dry electrodes based on carbon nanotube (CNT) thin films, synthesized by a roll-to-roll floating catalyst chemical vapor deposition process. By balancing structural and electrical properties, we achieved low electrode-skin impedance, high signal fidelity, minimal motion artifacts, high breathability, and biocompatibility, outperforming the gold standard wet electrodes. In a multichannel myoelectric interface demonstration, these CNT electrodes maintained stable signals and consistent task performance across 14 days using only minutes of training data and no further model retraining. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a multi-day recalibration-free dry electrode system under naturalistic conditions, achieved by stable electrode–skin interface, rather than ongoing algorithmic adaptation.

Article.Title: Reinforcement learning guided robotic platform that investigates and discovers asymmetric reactions
Article.Authors: Klochowicz P.; Kassir A.; Parida C.; Granda J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Autonomous robotic platforms accelerate chemical discovery by coupling automated experimentation with algorithmic decision-making, but most lack integrated support for chirality and the sequential decision-making required to explore asymmetric reaction spaces with unknown reactivity and stereochemical outcomes. Here, we report a bespoke robotic platform guided by deep reinforcement learning that autonomously navigates a defined asymmetric reaction space by scouting reaction conditions, discovering chiral products, screening catalysts and mapping substrate scope. The structure-agnostic workflow is enabled by a digital twin of asymmetric catalysis, in which control policies are trained before transfer to the laboratory. We validate the approach in chiral phosphoric acid catalysis: over 30 days, the system made more than 3,000 decisions and uncovered four highly enantioselective transformations, including an axially chiral molecule and three allene syntheses, one involving the enantioselective functionalization of a pyrrolopyrrole moiety. These results highlight deep reinforcement learning-guided autonomy as a strategy for discovery in complex catalytic systems.

Article.Authors: Wei J.; He W.; Liu Q.; Lu X.; Wang P.; Song W.; Takeda O.; Liu G.; Matsubae K.; Yang Y.; Zhu H.; Jiao S.
Article.Abstract: Recycling end-of-life (EoL) NdFeB magnets is critical for securing supply of rare-earth element neodymium in the low-carbon transition. Life-cycle assessment shows that the proposed process lowers climate change impacts to 17.36–18.18 kg CO2 eq. kg⁻¹ Nd, approximately 15% of that of primary production. Techno-economic analysis shows that neodymium metal production costs fall to 90.0 USD kg⁻¹ Nd at the 3000 A scale scenario, which is approximately one-third lower than the sales price of Nd metal. Such approach demonstrates significant potential for industrial-scale application and facilitates the integration of neodymium recycling into circular economy strategies. Molten-salt electrolysis with a consumable magnesium cathode recovers neodymium from end-of-life NdFeB magnets at high current efficiency, while life-cycle and economic analyses indicate potential for industrial-scale recycling.

Article.Title: Epitaxial-strain engineering of supported tensile noble metallene oxides for enhanced oxidation catalysis
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Lin D.; Yu A.; Qi H.; Jiang Z.; Zheng X.; Feng X.; Yang Y.; Fu Z.; Dai S.; Li L.; Wang A.; Guo Y.; Zhan W.; Wang L.; Guo Y.; Tang X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Supported two-dimensional noble metal oxides (metallene oxides) hold great promise for heterogeneous catalysis owing to their maximized surface exposure and tunable electronic structures. However, their high surface energy and low oxidation potentials make them intrinsically unstable under reaction conditions. Here, we report an epitaxial strain strategy to stabilize and modulate the electronic structure of supported PtO 2 metallene oxide. By employing rutile TiO 2 and rutile SnO 2 supports with distinct lattice parameters, we achieve epitaxial growth of PtO 2 metallene oxide layers with controlled strain states, where the larger-lattice SnO 2 substrate imposes biaxial tensile strain on PtO 2 . The tensile-strained PtO 2 /SnO 2 exhibits a reconfigured Pt–O electronic environment that simultaneously improves structural resilience and enhances the intrinsic reactivity of PtO 2 , delivering markedly improved methane oxidation performance with a T 90 of 370 °C (versus 434 °C for PtO 2 /TiO 2 and 469 °C for PtO x /Al 2 O 3 ) and <1% conversion loss over 38 h under both dry and wet conditions. Moreover, this epitaxial strain strategy is generalizable to other environmentally relevant oxidation reactions and rutile-type noble metal oxides, establishing tensile strain imposed by epitaxial lattice matching as a general principle for stabilizing atomically thin noble metal oxides while tuning their electronic structure.

Article.Authors: Horowitz J.; Tye O.; Nix O.; Tan S.; Chang H.; Min J.; Chung H.; Kim T.; Bawendi M.
Article.Abstract: The heterogeneity in optically active nanomaterials often hinders efforts to understand their basic photophysics and can limit their use in practical applications. This work demonstrates SPICEE to be an efficient and powerful tool for analyzing nanoscale systems. Traditional methods struggle to quantify the optical heterogeneity in nanomaterials. Article.Title: A multi-stage engineering framework for feasible scheduling of large-scale energy batch transport systems
Article.Authors: Tu R.; Liao Q.; Zhang H.; Li Z.; Qiu R.; Fu G.; Zio E.; Liang Y.
Article.Abstract: The energy transition is driving batch transport systems toward multi-product, high-frequency operations, with more batches and smaller batch volumes. However, strong couplings among material flows, operational decisions and temporal constraints make large-scale scheduling increasingly difficult, often rendering direct optimization computationally infeasible within practical engineering timeframes. This challenge is particularly pronounced in large-scale multi-product pipeline systems. To address this, this study proposes a multi-stage engineering framework that enables feasible and scalable scheduling of large-scale, batch-centric transport systems. The framework integrates two complementary mechanisms: a coarse-to-fine feasibility identification strategy that progressively narrows the admissible operational space, and a divide-and-conquer temporal decomposition strategy that partitions long scheduling horizons into tractable sub-horizons. The proposed framework is validated using two distinct industrial-scale pipeline systems. In a six-product benchmark, the framework achieves zero or negligible optimality gaps. For a complex branching network, it obtains feasible, high-quality schedules within the engineering time limit, whereas direct optimization fails to achieve a gap below 3%. Temporal decomposition reduces active binary variables and improves solution quality by over 50%. The framework provides a generalizable approach for large-scale batch transport and emerging multi-carrier energy infrastructures. A multi-stage framework enables feasible, high-quality scheduling of large-scale energy transport systems that challenge conventional optimization, supporting more efficient operation of emerging multi-carrier energy infrastructure.

Article.Authors: Kang B.; Shin J.; Kang M.; Choi U.; Seo U.; Kim H.; Chung K.; Ok J.; Jin H.; Sohn C.

These results establish CuAlO2 as a natural oxide platform that bridges broadband low-loss birefringence and ultraviolet hyperbolic photonics. Article.Authors: Zhao L.; Cai J.; Qian Q.; Zhang S.; Wang C.; Chen T.; Xiao C.; Ren C.; Zeng Q.; Bao B.; Lin Q.; Liao H.; Zhu L.; Zhang B.
Article.Abstract: Soft robots operate safely in delicate, confined environments and require materials that combine softness and large deformation in complex architectures. Article.Authors: Shen C.; Wang Y.; Yao J.; Gao P.; Peng B.; Guo X.; Peng L.; Zhu Y.; Hou G.; Xu Y.; Ding W.; Chen Y.
Article.Abstract: Gamma alumina is a well-known solid Lewis acid catalyst. The heterolytic activation of hydrogen is thus boosted with lower kinetic barriers for carbonyl hydrogenation. Such discovery is pivotal to uncover secrets of other classic and important catalytic materials. Gamma alumina is a well-known solid Lewis acid catalyst with a wide range of applications. Here, the authors demonstrate that γ-alumina can be deciphered by molecular nitrogen as a highly active solid frustrated Lewis-pair hydrogenation catalyst.

Article.Title: Wireless, optoelectronic, multimodal skin sensor for simultaneous monitoring of mechanical stress and vascular responses
Article.Authors: Cho S.; Moon J.; Han H.; Ahn J.; Lee K.; Adi G.; Lee D.; Oh Y.; Gao W.; Park I.
Article.Abstract: Prolonged mechanical loading and subsequent vascular ischemia drive the development of severe pressure injuries. Effective prevention of irreversible tissue damage requires monitoring both multiaxial mechanical forces and physiological erythema. However, conventional diagnostic tools remain limited by rigid architectures, single parameter detection, and subjective visual assessments. Here, a wireless, battery free optoelectronic multimodal sensor platform provides an integrated framework for tracking posture dependent mechanical loading and localized erythema. The soft, skin conformable device uses geometric light modulation within an isolated optical cavity to quantify normal pressure and biaxial shear stresses. To resolve complex mechanical environments, a deep neural network regression model decouples simultaneous tri-axial forces, Fx, Fy, and Fz, at the skin interface. Concurrently, a dual wavelength optical reflectance mechanism quantifies skin erythema by capturing subtle variations in hemoglobin absorption. Opaque elastomeric encapsulation shields the internal optics, supporting stable optical measurements under varying ambient illumination and skin conditions. System level integration via near field communication enables untethered operation across a multiplexed sensor network. On-body evaluations in a simulated clinical bed setting demonstrate the ability of the platform to dynamically map posture-dependent biomechanical loading and localized vascular responses, providing a technological basis for future studies on data-driven monitoring of the mechanical and vascular factors associated with pressure-injury risk. Pressure injuries arise from sustained mechanical loading and reduced blood flow, but current tools cannot objectively track both together. Cho et al. built a soft, wireless, battery-free, optoelectronic sensor that simultaneously maps three-axis stress and redness on the body.

Article.Title: CD200+ fibroblasts prime the immunoregulatory function of granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells in inflammatory arthritis
Article.Authors: Angeli M.; Schütz C.; Schmidt H.; Demmler R.; Chang J.; Labinsky H.; Raimondo M.; Lalazi B.; Stergioula K.; Huang K.; Fedorchenko V.; Li M.; Winter Z.; Tsiami S.; Lienert A.; Rütten S.; Weber S.; Luber M.; Bäuerle T.; Bahrami R.; Boehm H.; Schett G.; Rauber S.; Baraliakos X.; Ramming A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (G-MDSCs) are immunoregulatory cells of the neutrophil lineage. Here, we show that immunoregulation by G-MDSCs is imprinted by the joint tissue microenvironment in patients with axial spondyloarthritis and in animal models of inflammatory arthritis. We demonstrate that the suppressive function of G-MDSCs is significantly enhanced in the joint tissue, but not in the circulation. Analysis of public single-cell RNA sequencing datasets was consistent with Cd200r1 high Hmgb2 + precursors differentiating into G-MDSCs following interaction with Cd200 + fibroblasts. In hTNFtg/ Il23mc mice, treatment with a CD200R1 agonist promoted an immunoregulatory signature associated with PD-L1 expression, whereas CD200 blockade reversed the phenotype. Following adoptive transfer of G-MDSC precursor cells into arthritic mice, administration of a CD200-blocking antibody impaired the differentiation of PD-L1 + G-MDSCs and exacerbated disease severity. These findings reveal a tissue-intrinsic program that facilitates resolution of inflammation through fibroblast-myeloid crosstalk that enhances G-MDSC function.

Article.Title: Precise construction of antiparallel-stacked 2D imine covalent organic frameworks for atmospheric water harvesting
Article.Authors: Huang Q.; Huang C.; Qiao J.; Gao Q.; Yuan W.; Wu H.; Li X.; Qian C.; Liao Y.
Article.Abstract: Interlayer stacking modes dictated by noncovalent interactions play a pivotal role in influencing pore structures and emergent properties of 2D covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs), yet precise control over stacking modes remains challenging. Herein, we report a supramolecular strategy based on dipole-dipole interactions originated from 4,7-bis(phenylethynyl)benzo[c][1,2,5]thiadiazole (BT) units, enabling precise construction of antiparallel-stacked 2D imine-linked COFs. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction and density functional theory calculations reveal that BT incorporation directs antiparallel stacking through cooperative hydrogen bonding and multiple π–π interactions between adjacent layers. The resulting COF-BB-R (R = H, 2Me and 4Me) exhibits higher crystallinity and stability than the corresponding eclipsed-stacked COF-PB-R. Notably, COF-BB-H achieves a total water uptake of 0.70 g g−1 at 298 K, 2.2-fold higher than COF-PB-H (0.32 g g−1) and surpassing that of most imine-based COF adsorbents. This work provides an effective approach for precisely fabricating antiparallel-stacked 2D COFs for next-generation functional porous materials. Interlayer stacking modes dictated by noncovalent interactions play a pivotal role in influencing pore structures of 2D covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) but manipulating noncovalent interactions to control stacking modes of 2D COFs remains challenging. Here the authors report a supramolecular strategy based on dipole-dipole interactions originated from thiadiazole units, enabling precise construction of antiparallel-stacked 2D imine-linked COFs.

Article.Title: High average and linear scaling of Ecological Footprint in cities
Article.Authors: Xu B.; Zhang K.; Li L.; Yu Y.; Linden K.; Goldstein B.; Dadashova B.; Newman G.; Ye X.; Lin D.; Jiao W.
Article.Abstract: Cities are often assumed to be environmentally efficient in high-income countries, but their indirect impacts through consumption make this efficiency uncertain. Studies of agglomeration effects and urban scaling have reported contradictory results, with most analyses relying on consumption-based carbon footprints and rarely examining non-carbon impacts. Here we present spatially and sectorally detailed Ecological Footprint estimates covering all 83,603 populated US census tracts and disaggregating consumption into 52 categories in 2021. We found that per-capita Ecological Footprint was highest in cities, followed by suburbs and rural areas, with only small differences in effect size. Total urban Ecological Footprint scaled approximately linearly with population and remained robust across city delineations. These results indicate that cities do not exhibit clear footprint efficiency and that policies targeting settlement type or individual sectors alone are unlikely to deliver meaningful reductions. We suggest treating Ecological Footprint reduction as a wicked problem and reframing it toward actionability. Xu et al. show that US cities have high per-capita Ecological Footprints and that total urban Ecological Footprint scales linearly with population. The findings suggest that cities may not be inherently more footprint-efficient in high-income countries.

Article.Title: Targeting MDA5 induces immunogenic cell death and promotes anti-tumor immunity
Article.Authors: Niu Z.; Cheng B.; Jiang Y.; Weng Y.; Xiao Q.; Long G.; Wei C.; Liu Q.; Chen J.; Wen X.; Chen Y.; Wang P.; Huang Y.; Tan J.; Pan W.; Zhang R.; Yu Q.; Wu X.; Wang W.
Article.Abstract: Identifying targets to enhance tumor immunity is an urgent need. Although nucleic acid sensors play critical roles in promoting tumor immune clearance, their exceptionally low mutation rate in cancers suggests potential unexplored roles in tumor progression. Here, we demonstrate that the RNA sensor melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5) promotes immune evasion, and its high expression is strongly predictive of poor survival and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy in patients. Targeting MDA5 reshapes the tumor microenvironment, strengthening immune memory responses and enhancing effector CD8⁺ T cell activity in preclinical models in female mice. Mechanistically, MDA5 deficiency triggers unfolded protein response driven immunogenic cell death through induction of damage-associated molecular patterns, leading to enhanced dendritic cell-mediated antigen engulfment and T cell activation. Additionally, MDA5 loss primes the ASK1-JNK/P38 signaling pathway, sensitizing tumor cells to TNF-α/IFN-γ, further amplifying this process. Consequently, targeting MDA5 enhances the efficacy of ICB therapy across multiple cancer types, positioning it as a promising therapeutic target. RNA sensors have been linked to antitumor immune responses. Here, based on results of in vivo CRISPR screens, the authors propose the RNA sensor MDA5 as a regulator of immune evasion, showing that its targeting induces immunogenic cell death and anti tumor immunity.

Article.Title: Plant invasions are associated with lower community stability at multiple spatial scales
Article.Authors: Shan R.; Hu M.; Ma Z.
Article.Abstract: Plant invasions are threatening the long-term sustainability of ecosystem functions. Yet, how plant invasions impact the temporal stability of community cover across spatial scales remains poorly understood, hindering effective invasion management. Using the National Ecological Observatory Network dataset, we examine how plant invasions influence multi-scale stability of total community abundance (used total community cover) via altering community functional diversity, as well as growth and dispersal strategies. We find that invasion-associated losses of functional α diversity and functional shifts toward acquisitive strategies, reduce species asynchrony and species stability, respectively. These changes ultimately lead to lower temporal stability at the local scale (α stability). Meanwhile, invasion-associated functional shifts toward acquisitive seed dispersal strategies weaken functional β diversity, which reduces asynchrony community dynamics among local communities (spatial asynchrony). These concurrent declines in α stability and spatial asynchrony collectively destabilize metacommunity-scale stability. Our findings reveal that plant invasions may trigger destabilizing effects across spatial scales, associated with changes in functional diversity as well as growth and dispersal strategies, underscoring the need for a multi-scale invasion management framework focusing on both local diversity and the connectivity among local communities. Plant invasions can threaten ecosystems by making plant communities less stable over time. The study shows that invasions reduce stability from local to metacommunity scales by eroding functional diversity and favoring fast-growing strategies.

Article.Title: Sleep forms flexible context representations in toddlers
Article.Authors: Bastian L.; Kurz E.; Gutjahr L.; Noack H.; Born J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Sleep consolidates episodic memory through a hippocampus-dependent process in adults. Whether and how sleep supports memory consolidation during early life, when hippocampal function is immature, remains unclear. Here, we examined effects of sleep on the consolidation of spatial context, a core component of episodic memory, in toddlers aged 2–3 years. Toddlers were familiarized with two spatial contexts, followed by a ~ 90-min nap or equivalent wake period. Afterwards, using a hide-and-seek game we tested their ability to relocate toys within these contexts. Only after post-familiarization sleep, toddlers showed significant context memory and formed stronger associations between toys and specific contexts compared to wakefulness. Contextual memory was positively correlated with spindle density and slow oscillation–spindle phase-amplitude coupling during non-rapid eye movement sleep. Here, we show that, despite hippocampal immaturity, memory effects in the sleeping toddler’s brain are accompanied by thalamo-cortical oscillatory dynamics that are also implicated in adult memory consolidation.

Article.Title: Sea-level contribution from Thwaites Glacier doubles in an observation-constrained ice-sheet model
Article.Authors: Poinelli M.; Rignot E.; Seroussi H.; Cuzzone J.; Pelle T.; Larour E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Thwaites Glacier is a major contributor to Antarctic mass loss and a key source of uncertainty in future sea-level rise. Ocean-driven melting at its grounding line drives rapid retreat, yet most models treat the transition between grounded and floating ice as a sharp boundary, neglecting kilometer-scale seawater intrusions that develop as the grounding line migrates and forms a grounding zone. Here, we show that actively-melting grounding zones are required to reproduce nearly three decades of observed retreat, thinning, and acceleration of Thwaites Glacier in a calibrated ice-sheet model, with successful reconstruction occurring only when grounding zones are represented as 2-5 km wide regions. Extending this model forward, we show that grounding-zone processes govern glacier’s detachment from stabilizing seafloor ridges, enabling unpinning as early as 2038 and producing up to 30 ± 6 mm of global mean sea-level rise by 2100 - approximately double previous projections even without additional climate warming.

Article.Title: Whole blood transcriptomics atlas across human diseases
Article.Authors: Li M.; Tatar A.; Green E.; Simsek E.; Kahraman C.; Ceylan M.; Laloglu F.; Ceviz N.; Tatar A.; Laloglu E.; Akcay G.; Cadirci K.; Yapca O.; Ozmen H.; Yapanoglu T.; Kudas O.; Simsek F.; Yılmaz E.; Senocak G.; Doneray H.; Ozden A.; Cayir A.; Tasar P.; Kara M.; Aktaş Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract We present a WBT Atlas, comprising 4444 WBT samples across 98 distinct health conditions, enabling systematic exploration of disease-associated transcriptomic signatures. Health condition–specific profiles are characterized across immune, metabolic, and cell-type specific features at the gene, gene module, and pathway levels. By integrating matched plasma proteomics data from 1280 participants across 28 health conditions, we further assess blood RNA–protein relationships and demonstrate their complementary biological roles. By integrating RNA and protein signatures, we develop multi-class classification models that accurately distinguish among a wide range of health conditions, with integrated models consistently outperforming those based on single-omics data alone. The identified RNA and protein signatures are validated across ten independent WBT cohorts and the UK Biobank. Together, the WBT Atlas provides a genome-wide resource that enables translational discovery in precision medicine.

Article.Title: KMT2B facilitates long-range gene regulation through LINE1 elements
Article.Authors: Shahidian L.; Di Filippo L.; Robert S.; Rada-Iglesias A.
Article.Abstract: Transcriptional regulation is tightly linked to chromatin organization, with H3K4me3 marking active and bivalent promoters. In embryonic stem cells, KMT2B deposits H3K4me3 at bivalent promoters, yet loss of H3K4me3 at these sites leaves developmental gene transcription largely unaltered. Here, we show that, in both mouse embryonic stem cells and during differentiation, the primary role of KMT2B is not to counteract Polycomb-mediated repression at bivalent promoters. Instead, we uncover a distinct regulatory function for KMT2B at the CG-rich 5’UTR of young LINE-1 elements. KMT2B binds LINE-1 5’UTRs and maintains their active chromatin state (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H4K16ac) while preventing repressive H3K9me3 accumulation. Using complementary genomic methods and targeted deletions, we show that KMT2B-bound LINE-1 elements act as enhancers modulating neighboring gene expression in embryonic stem cells and, particularly, during differentiation. Our findings define KMT2B regulatory functions at LINE-1 repeats and highlight transposable elements as key components of long-range gene expression control. The authors demonstrate that KMT2B primarily regulates gene expression through LINE-1 elements with enhancer-like function, rather than by counteracting Polycomb repression, revealing an underappreciated link between Trithorax proteins and transposable elements during cell differentiation.

Article.Title: DigiDent: integrated bristle-level sensing and AI for contact-aware toothbrushing assessment
Article.Authors: Ren H.; Chang H.; Yu T.; Yang L.; Zhang T.; Li G.; Tang Y.; Sang T.; Ye Z.; Shen Y.
Article.Abstract: Oral hygiene is fundamental to systemic health, yet toothbrushing, the most common preventive practice, remains largely unguided and unquantified, contributing to the global burden of oral diseases. Current smart toothbrush systems fundamentally fail to capture the critical fine-scale biomechanics at the bristle-tooth interface, which is essential for evaluating clinical adherence and preventing gingival damage. Here we present DigiDent, an AI powered sensing to interpretation system that renders brushing micro-biomechanics computationally interpretable by measuring in-situ contact dynamics at bristle-tooth interface with an embedded E-Bristle sensor. DigiDent fuses bristle-level contact sensing with inertial sensing through a dual-stream neural inference architecture, converting contact-rich brushing behavior into quantitative and interpretable metrics of force, duration, contact-motion pattern, and fine-grained coverage. In validation experiments, DigiDent achieved >99% recognition of motion-contact patterns and 99.84% classification accuracy across 21 brushing subregions. Pilot user-operation verification further demonstrates the feasibility of DigiDent for real-use brushing monitoring and quantitative feedback. These results establish embedded co-deformation sensing and AI-based interpretation as a technical foundation for future personalized toothbrushing assessment and coaching. Oral hygiene is fundamental to systemic health, yet toothbrushing behavior remains largely unquantified because existing monitoring approaches cannot capture the distributed micro-contact dynamics within the bristle field. Here, the authors report DigiDent, a hardware-software co-designed framework combining embedded co-deformation sensing with AI-based analysis to quantify contact-rich brushing behavior. Pilot human studies demonstrate its potential for real-world brushing monitoring, personalized feedback, and habit assessment.

Article.Title: An international multicenter study of MASLD prevalence among children and adolescents assessed by VCTE
Article.Authors: Zhang L.; Fan J.; Zhou X.; Yao X.; Kim S.; Wang H.; Fan Y.; Wang D.; El-Kassas M.; Chen E.; Zhang Y.; Shi J.; Chi X.; Alisi A.; Méndez-Sánchez N.; Liu F.; Yilmaz Y.; Lin S.; Zhou Y.; Garibay-Nieto N.; Xu L.; Sebastiani G.; Gana J.; Kamal N.; Chongsrisawat V.
Article.Abstract: The worldwide prevalence of pediatric metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) remains uncertain. Using vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE), we estimate the prevalence of MASLD among children and adolescents in community and hospital populations and conduct additional analyses of hepatic steatosis and fibrosis severity grades. In this international multicenter study, we include 9352 children and adolescents aged 6–18 years from 38 centers across 17 countries on five continents. In the overall population, the median age is 12.0 years (IQR: 8.5–15.1), and 5471 (58.5%) are male. The prevalence of MASLD is 17.60% (95% CI: 16.63–18.61) in the community population and 58.03% (95% CI: 56.34–59.70) in the hospital population, with corresponding age-standardized prevalences of 20.97% and 52.34%, respectively. The prevalence of MASLD in the community population is highest in South America (47.92%), followed by North America (25.05%) and Asia (13.96%). MASLD prevalence among adolescents is significantly higher in 2021–2024 compared to 2017–2020, except among those with normal weight or below. Older age, obesity, and elevated serum aminotransferase levels are independently associated with hepatic steatosis and fibrosis, whereas steatosis (grades S2 and S3) is independently associated with greater hepatic fibrosis. Our findings provide useful contemporary data for estimating the epidemiology of pediatric MASLD across diverse populations. A multicenter study in 17 countries on pediatric MASLD, a liver disorder, finds a prevalence of 18% in community populations and 58% in hospital populations, differences between regions, associations with obesity and elevated liver enzyme levels.

Article.Title: Genomic bases of short-term evolution in wild barn owls revealed by long-term monitoring and population-scale sequencing
Article.Authors: Cumer T.; Topaloudis A.; Lavanchy E.; Ducrest A.; Sarmiento Cabello S.; Hewett A.; Becciu P.; Simon C.; Marquis J.; Charpagne A.; Almasi B.; Roulin A.; Goudet J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Understanding how wild populations undergo rapid phenotypic evolution requires linking phenotypic change to its underlying genomic architecture over contemporary timescales. Here, we leverage a 30-year study of Swiss barn owls ( Tyto alba ) to examine long-term changes in two melanin-based traits (plumage coloration and spottiness) that have previously been linked to multiple fitness-related traits. We document a consistent temporal shift toward darker and more heavily spotted individuals and show, using whole-genome sequencing of 3,102 individuals, that these traits are controlled by a small number of loci of major effect with partially overlapping architectures. Temporal allele frequency analyses reveal subtle but consistent changes at these loci. By comparing empirical trajectories to simulations, we show that genetic drift alone is insufficient to explain the observed patterns at one major locus, indicating a role for selection. Our results demonstrate how selection acting on a small number of loci can contribute to rapid phenotypic evolution of continuous traits in the wild and highlight the value of long-term genomic and phenotypic monitoring for disentangling evolutionary processes.

Article.Title: Structures and molecular mechanisms of RAD54B in modulating homologous recombination
Article.Authors: Liang P.; Tye S.; Ertl da Costa J.; Maharshi N.; Argunhan B.; Kuhlen L.; Battley M.; McCormack E.; Heyer W.; Löbrich M.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Genome stability is essential for cellular viability yet constantly threatened by DNA-damaging agents. Among these, DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are particularly harmful and in S/G2 phases are faithfully repaired through homologous recombination (HR). The RAD51 recombinase forms nucleoprotein filaments on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) that performs critical functions in HR. The efficiency of HR depends on precise regulation of RAD51 filament dynamics by accessory factors, including RAD54B, a double-strand DNA-dependent ATPase. Here, using cryogenic electron microscopy, mutagenesis, and biochemical assays, we show that RAD54B stabilizes RAD51–DNA filaments, inhibits RAD51 ATPase activity, and promotes D-loop formation and strand exchange. RAD54B contains two main RAD51-interacting sites and a β-domain that bridges RAD51 protomers, is positioned to contact donor dsDNA, and regulates RAD54B’s ATPase activity. Cellular assays reveal that the RAD51-interacting sites are required for repairing DSBs by HR in human cells. Our findings uncover a modular architecture and mechanistic framework for RAD54B’s critical role in genome maintenance.

Article.Title: Hysteresis of extreme precipitation in East Asia under various CO2 removal pathways
Article.Authors: Lee M.; Park J.; Kim H.; Kim M.; Min S.; Park D.; Park H.; Byun Y.; Sung H.; Hong J.; Park J.; Jeon W.
Article.Abstract: Extreme precipitation poses severe societal and economic risks under elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2), yet current understanding of how it will respond to various future CO2 removal scenarios remains limited. Focusing on East Asia, a region highly vulnerable to monsoonal dynamics and anthropogenic influences, here we assess the hysteresis of extreme precipitation responses under four CO2 concentration thresholds and two emission reduction rates using climate model simulations. The extreme precipitation indices based on intensity and frequency exhibit an increase during the CO2 peak, but fail to fully return to their initial states even after CO2 levels decline to their initial levels. This hysteresis behavior is amplified by delayed and slower emission reductions. The hysteresis is linked to increases in mean monsoon precipitation associated with hysteresis in tropical Pacific warming patterns and subsequent atmospheric teleconnections. Moisture budget analysis further indicates that enhanced precipitation is attributed to increased moisture transport into East Asia, driven by early-summer rises in specific humidity (thermodynamic factor) through mean circulation and late-summer intensification of monsoon circulation (dynamic factor). These findings reveal the mechanisms shaping East Asian extreme precipitation under different carbon removal pathways and highlight the critical role of both timing and pace of emission reductions in determining regional climate outcomes. Across carbon removal experiments, East Asian extreme precipitation can remain elevated as CO2 declines, with later and slower CO2 removal producing stronger hysteresis associated with delayed tropical Pacific warming and changes in the monsoon circulation.

Article.Title: Neuronal signatures of successful one-shot memory in mid-level visual cortex
Article.Authors: DiRisio G.; Xue C.; Cohen M.
Article.Abstract: High-capacity, one-shot visual recognition memory challenges theories of learning and neural coding because it requires rapid, robust, and durable representations. Most studies have focused on the hippocampus and other higher areas. However, behavioral evidence demonstrating links between image properties and memorability and revealing image specificity of visual memory suggests an important role for mid-level visual cortex. We tested the hypothesis that area V4 contains signals critical for recognition memory in two male rhesus macaques. Our task increased difficulty, allowing comparisons of neuronal population responses on correct and error trials. We observed signatures of several proposed memory mechanisms including magnitude coding, repetition suppression, sparse coding, and population response consistency, but only sparse coding and population response consistency predicted behavior. Familiar images also evoked faster dynamics, consistent with pattern completion. These findings demonstrate that fast, high-capacity memory is supported by neural codes in mid-level sensory cortex independent of stimulus features per se, highlighting its role in distributed memory networks. Neural mechanisms underlying one-shot memory are not fully understood. In this study, macaque monkeys were trained to perform a continuous image recognition task and simultaneously recorded from groups of neurons in area V4. The authors found that the perceptual building blocks of fast, high-capacity memory are present in mid-level sensory cortex.

Article.Title: The mechanosensitive PIEZO1 channel promotes CD54+/iNOS+ neutrophil expansion in pulmonary fibrosis
Article.Authors: Zhuang L.; Shi J.; Lin Z.; Ruan X.; Qian Y.; Su R.; Zhong X.; Zou H.; Wang Y.; Wang S.; Lai Y.; Guo Y.; Yang N.; Zhang H.
Article.Abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) represents the common end-stage outcome of a broad range of interstitial lung diseases. The shared pathophysiologic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify two phenotypically distinct neutrophil subsets in PF: a pro-inflammatory subset characterized by CD54 (human) or iNOS (mouse) expression, and an alternative subset marked by Arg1 expression. Notably, CD54+ and iNOS+ neutrophils were markedly expanded in PF patients and mice with bleomycin-induced PF, respectively. Adoptive transfer of iNOS+ neutrophils exacerbated fibrosis in bleomycin-induced PF, whereas transfer of Arg1+ neutrophils had no significant effect.
