Article.Title: Receptor and cell-type-specific mechanisms in mesocortical dopamine circuits gate chronic pain and comorbid anxiodepression
Article.Authors: Cai Y.; Hou X.; Wang G.; Chang Y.; Zhang Z.; Shi T.; Liu B.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: The mesocorticolimbic dopamine (DA) circuitry is implicated in chronic pain and comorbid depression, yet the specific receptor and circuit mechanisms distinguishing them remain unclear. Here, we show that orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) D1R- and D2R-expressing neurons serve as a checkpoint, independently mediating anxiodepression and allodynia in a trigeminal neuralgia (TN) mouse model. TN induced a hypodopaminergic state in the ventral tegmental area (VTA)-OFC circuit. Activation of the VTADA-OFC pathway effectively ameliorated TN-induced allodynia and anxiodepressive-like behaviors; these therapeutic effects were abolished by selective blockade of D2Rs and D1Rs, respectively. Activation of OFCD1 excitatory pyramidal neurons and their projections to the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus (LDTg) improved TN-induced anxiodepressive-like behaviors, whereas disinhibition or activation of OFC D2+ excitatory pyramidal neurons and their projections to the basolateral amygdaloid nucleus (BLA) produced analgesia. Thus, selectively targeting VTA-OFCD1 and VTA-OFCD2 or OFC D1Rs and D2Rs may provide new strategies for controlling different symptoms of chronic pain.

Article.Title: Real-time reinforcement for human-machine interface control
Article.Authors: Vassiliadis P.; Pinheiro D.; Fleury L.; Zenon A.; Esparza-Iaizzo M.; Ingster A.; Micera S.; Shokur S.; Hummel F.
Article.Abstract: A major challenge involved in human-machine interfaces is developing feedback strategies that improve control and benefit patients with motor disabilities. Here, we propose, validate, and mechanistically characterize a personalized, closed-loop strategy that delivers reinforcement feedback in real time during human-machine interface control. Across five experiments involving 106 participants and two control interfaces, fewer than 20 reinforcement trials produced immediate improvements in force control and lasting retention gains. These effects were strongest when visual and/or somatosensory feedback was limited, a finding that suggests translational relevance for tasks, technologies, and pathologies with limited sensory feedback. In chronic stroke patients, real-time reinforcement likewise improved online force control under limited visual feedback, although short training did not yield retention gains. Information-theoretic analyses further revealed that reinforcement compensates for reduced feedback control when sensory feedback is sparse and promotes motor exploitation of successful actions. Overall, these findings identify real-time reinforcement as a promising strategy for enhancing human-machine interface control.

Article.Title: Early visual experience elicits cellular and functional plasticity in the retina and alters behavior
Article.Authors: Reynolds P.; Marchi D.; To Ling Y.; Slangewal K.; Capelle M.; Chalakova Z.; Bahl A.; Hindges R.
Article.Abstract: Our interaction with the environment shapes how our brain processes sensory information and drives adaptive behavior. This plasticity allows brain adjustments in response to specific sensory experiences. While plasticity has been consistently detected in visual targets, only limited data exist on its extent in the primary sensory organ, the retina. Here, we show that the zebrafish retina demonstrates plastic transformations in response to visual environment alterations during development. We demonstrate that orientation-selective amacrine cells undergo profound morphological changes in animals previously exposed to distinct visual environments. We further find that the functional orientation-selective retinal output is altered, consistent with the visual environment in which the animals are raised, and that these changes are persistent. Finally, we show that early exposure to different visual environments changes the animals' visuomotor response preference for specifically oriented patterns. Our findings unveil a developmental form of sensory organ plasticity with continuing structural, functional, and behavioral consequences.

Article.Title: From first impressions to bonds: The neural dynamics of social relationships
Article.Authors: Jain P.; Schiller D.
Article.Abstract: Social relationships are best understood not as isolated interactions but as dynamic representations shaped through evaluative processes, interaction-driven learning, motivational value, and memory-based structure. This review synthesizes research across these domains to trace how relationships develop from initial impressions through repeated interactions to stable social bonds and networks. We organize the literature by relationship stage and highlight how overlapping neural systems are differentially engaged as relationships evolve over time. By treating relationships as unfolding processes, we reveal computational principles that become apparent only across time. Building on cognitive map theory, we propose that social relationships are represented as structured relational spaces supporting updating and generalization. We further highlight emerging computational and methodological approaches-including map-based models, naturalistic paradigms, and tools for analyzing dynamic social behavior-that enable the study of relationships across their temporal arc. This framework offers new ways to study the formation, maintenance, and adaptation of social bonds.

Article.Title: Advancing NeuroAI through developmental alignment
Article.Authors: Ayzenberg V.; Bonner M.; Bayet L.
Article.Abstract: The goal of artificial intelligence (AI) modeling in neuroscience, or NeuroAI, is to uncover the factors that give rise to human-level intelligence. However, current models overwhelmingly focus on simulating adulthood, the end state of intelligence, and often do not consider how this state was achieved in the first place. We argue that, to understand adult intelligence, it is important to model the developmental process by which intelligence arose. Here, we describe how developmental changes in children's neural architecture, experiences, and learning objectives are adaptively suited to support rapid learning and illustrate how these principles can be incorporated into the AI engineering process. Finally, we describe the early developing capacities of children and how these capacities provide an ideal set of benchmarks for evaluating AI models. Together, by modeling the developmental process by which humans achieve intelligence, we may build more mechanistically plausible models as well as improve the capabilities of AI.

Article.Title: Tunneling nanotubes in the nervous system: The fourth pillar of brain connectivity
Article.Authors: Budinger D.; Heneka M.
Article.Abstract: Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) are thin, actin-based membranous conduits that enable direct and indirect cytoplasmic exchange between distant cells. Once considered a rare in vitro phenomenon, TNTs are increasingly recognized as dynamic intercellular communication routes in the central nervous system. Here, we discuss emerging evidence supporting the presence and functional relevance of TNTs in the brain, their roles in physiological coordination and pathological spread, and the conceptual shift they demand in how we understand neural connectivity. We argue that TNTs represent a previously underappreciated layer of brain organization-one that may critically shape neurodegeneration, neuroinflammation, and repair-and outline key experimental and theoretical directions to move the field forward.

Article.Title: Tau-induced mitochondrial reverse electron transport drives neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Li W.; Rimal S.; Bhurtel S.; Yeung L.; Lu B.; Grinberg L.; Spina S.; Sillero M.; Seeley W.; Guo S.; Lu B.
Article.Abstract: Hyperphosphorylation and aggregation of tau are pathological hallmarks of tauopathies. Mitochondrial dysfunction is also a common feature of tauopathies. The mechanistic link between tau abnormalities and mitochondrial dysfunction and its relationship to the physiological function of tau, however, is unclear. Here, we demonstrate that tau regulates mitochondrial reverse electron transport (RET), which produces excess reactive oxygen species (ROS), reduces the NAD+/NADH ratio, and is activated by aging or stress. In flies, mice, and human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons, tau depletion eliminates stress-induced RET and confers resilience. Mechanistically, tau enters mitochondria and directly interacts with the complex I subunit NDUFS3 to promote RET in a phosphorylation-dependent manner. Elevated RET further drives tau hyperphosphorylation, establishing a self-perpetuating pathological loop. Inhibition of RET ameliorates tau toxicity across species. RET regulation thus represents a previously unrecognized normal function of tau that becomes pathological in disease, providing a therapeutic target for various conditions characterized by tau abnormalities and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Article.Title: Unifying the structures of language in a neural population code
Article.Authors: Nastase S.; Zada Z.; Goldberg A.; Hasson U.
Article.Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have mastered human language in ways that no previous computational system has. While rule-based, symbolic systems sufficed for constrained, well-defined problems, they were not able to accommodate the context-sensitive expressivity of natural language. LLMs instead use statistical learning to encode the diversity of linguistic structures into a unified high-dimensional embedding space. Strikingly, this context-driven, distributed representation closely parallels neural population codes, suggesting that the human language system may have converged on a similar computational strategy. Drawing on a growing body of work at the intersection of artificial intelligence and cognitive neuroscience, we show that LLMs can serve as cognitively plausible models of the neural computations supporting language in the human brain. We conclude that explaining how language can emerge from neural population codes, in both biological and artificial systems, will not be achieved through the incremental refinement of algebraic-symbolic theories but will demand new theoretical paradigms.

Article.Title: The recipe for intelligence in natural and artificial systems
Article.Authors: Summerfield C.; Stachenfeld K.
Article.Abstract: Ten years ago, two landmark papers discussed open problems in AI research from the standpoint of neuroscience and cognitive science. Today, many of these problems have been solved, mostly without direct inspiration from the study of the human brain. In this paper, we consider what is still shared between the twin endeavors of understanding natural brains and building artificial ones. We argue that, as well as understanding the "ingredients" of intelligence (its component parts), both fields are now coming to grasp the "recipe" for intelligence (how they fit together). Surprisingly, this recipe has many parallels in biological and artificial systems. Despite rapid progress in AI research, there are many computational problems that remain unsolved. We discuss how these problems may be addressed in natural intelligence.

Article.Authors: Gordon A.; Benowitz B.; Barbakh J.; Montequin I.; Campuzano A.; Stevenson H.; Lu P.; Hjort M.; Ancell E.; Critz M.; Witten D.; Stuber G.
Article.Abstract: The lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) contains γ-aminobutyric acid (GABAergic) and glutamatergic neurons that converge on midbrain dopamine circuits, exerting opposing control over feeding and reinforcement. How these neurons behave during consummatory behavior and how they shape dopamine release across the striatum remains unresolved. Here, we show that LHA GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons independently scale their activity as mice consume rewarding and aversive solutions and that their balance sets a spatially organized dopamine landscape along the striatum's anterior-posterior axis: anterior regions track solution value and recent history, posterior regions encode sensorimotor features, and release at each site is controlled locally rather than propagated across subregions. These results position the LHA as a central regulator of a striatum-wide dopamine landscape during consumption, providing a circuit-level framework for how the hypothalamus shapes motivated behavior.

Article.Title: Circuit mechanisms of psychotic symptoms across disorders
Article.Authors: Braun U.; Wolf J.; Hirjak D.; Schwarz E.; Tost H.; Meyer-Lindenberg A.
Article.Abstract: Psychotic symptoms, including hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thought, occur across psychiatric and neurological disorders, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly integrated across scales. Here, we propose a transdiagnostic framework in which disturbances in dopamine, glutamate, GABA, serotonin, and acetylcholine alter neuronal gain and synaptic efficacy, disrupting the precision weighting of sensory evidence, prediction errors, and internally generated representations. These local disturbances propagate through cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits and large-scale functional networks, producing abnormal integration-segregation dynamics and unstable attractor states. This multilevel model links molecular and cellular perturbations to circuit dysfunction, network instability, and symptom expression while allowing distinct biological pathways to converge on shared computational vulnerabilities. Emerging neuroimaging, dynamical systems, and artificial intelligence approaches may enable individualized tests of these mechanisms and support more precise, circuit-informed interventions for psychotic symptoms.

Article.Title: Simultaneous awake replay of multiple spatial representations
Article.Authors: Mou X.; Ji D.
Article.Abstract: How the hippocampus processes multiple spatial memories during awake decision-making remains unclear. Using a rat observational navigation task, we tested whether distinct spatial representations are replayed simultaneously during sharp-wave ripple-associated population bursts. These simultaneous replay events reflected the spatial organization of the maze, preferentially converged on reward sites, distinguished future behavioral choices, and were associated with choice-selective activity in anterior cingulate cortex. Replay of a single trajectory showed weaker relationships to behavior and cortical activity. These findings establish simultaneous awake replay of multiple spatial representations and support a role for parallel hippocampal processing during reward-directed observational navigation.

Article.Authors: Elston T.; Wallis J.
Article.Abstract: A core feature of cognitive control is the ability to interrupt behaviors that conflict with current goals. Disorders impairing this ability involve abnormal interactions between the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and the caudate nucleus (CdN). However, how these regions normally interact to interrupt automatic behaviors remains unknown. To find out, we trained monkeys on a decision task that created a conflict between competing value representations, thus evoking an automatic-then-controlled response pattern that provided a window into how initial responses are interrupted and overridden. Simultaneous OFC-CdN Neuropixels recordings revealed that during corrective responses, OFC population dynamics vacillated between competing value states. These dynamics appeared to be transmitted to the CdN via enhanced local field potential synchronization, which coincided with disruption of structured CdN population activity. Critically, this occurred without changes in striatal firing rate. This suggests that interrupting an automatic response can occur through top-down disruption of striatal population geometry without suppressing firing rates.

Article.Title: Stepwise engagement of cingulate ensembles underlies motivational decline in chronic pain
Article.Authors: Xu W.; Sun J.; Chu C.; Yi X.; Lin S.; Wang S.; Liang J.; Wu Y.; Wang Y.; Li X.; Liu Y.; Lv Y.; Wu J.; Sun B.; Xu T.; Liu Z.; Song L.; Li W.
Article.Abstract: Chronic pain can progress from sensory hypersensitivity to impaired motivation, but the underlying circuit mechanisms remain unclear. ACC neurons projecting to the basolateral amygdala (BLA) are preferentially engaged early, respond to allodynic stimulation, and contribute to mechanical hypersensitivity, whereas neurons projecting to the lateral habenula (LHb) are engaged later and contribute to impaired effortful persistence. Anteromedial thalamic input is biased toward ACC→BLA neurons, while recurrent ACC-BLA-ACC signaling provides a candidate route to later ACC→LHb dysfunction. These findings reveal a temporally organized cingulate circuit framework for the sensory and effort-related consequences of persistent pain.

Article.Title: Tau phosphorylation from neuronal adaptation to Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Trouvé R.; Verstreken P.; Hoekstra M.
Article.Abstract: Tau phosphorylation is classically associated with neurodegeneration, yet similar phosphorylation patterns emerge during physiological states and acute stress responses. How these overlapping patterns of phosphorylated Tau (pTau) relate to neuronal adaptation and Alzheimer's disease pathology remains unresolved. We synthesize findings from human to rodent and fly brains and from neuronal cell models, across neurodevelopment, sleep, hibernation, cellular stress, and disease. Across these contexts, pTau changes are associated with altered Tau localization and functions involving synaptic transmission, mitochondrial activity, RNA metabolism, and genomic integrity. Physiological and acute stress responses are generally transient and reversible, whereas aging, repeated stress, and amyloid-β-associated stress can promote persistent pTau accumulation, impaired clearance, aggregation, and neurodegeneration. We propose that pathological Tau phosphorylation reflects dysregulation of a shared adaptive response rather than activation of an entirely distinct pathway. Article.Title: A cross-species AAV platform for precise microglial interrogation
Article.Authors: Yu F.; Wang R.; Di R.; Xu K.; Gao J.; Shang H.; Yuan Z.; Dai R.; Wu W.; Weng D.; Gao X.; Li H.; Yu T.; Zhang Y.; Wang X.; Luan G.; Zhao F.; Luo M.

Article.Abstract: Adolescent brain development is difficult to study at scale because diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures are sensitive to technical variability across scanning environments. Article.Authors: Ma K.; Park K.; Honma P.; Zhang Y.; Brady E.; Qiu Y.; Opitz-Araya X.; Ting J.; Levi B.; Akassoglou K.; Palop J.

Article.Abstract: Recovery sleep alleviates pain in humans, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. ZI NTS projections to the LH specifically regulate NREM sleep without affecting nociception, whereas projections to the PO selectively mediate analgesia without impacting sleep. Collectively, these findings reveal that ZI sleep ensembles mediate recovery-sleep-induced analgesia, achieving modality specificity through segregated downstream targets.

Article.Title: A brainstem module for backward locomotion reveals direction-selective premotor circuits
Article.Authors: Liu Z.; Lu L.; Di R.; Cui Y.; Liu Y.; Ren Q.; Dai R.; Wu W.; Wang R.; Luo M.
Article.Abstract: Smooth locomotion requires precise directional control, yet the neural circuits governing navigational transitions remain elusive. Article.Title: Raphe nuclei in cognition: A network-level framework for behavioral-state control
Article.Authors: Khalighinejad N.; Rushworth M.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive behavior requires organisms to maintain, update, and switch between behavioral states as environmental conditions change. Article.Title: More than just accuracy: A pathway-level framework for implementing blood and digital biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease care
Article.Authors: Perneczky R.; Schöll M.; Rauchmann B.; Hofmann A.
Article.Abstract: Blood biomarkers are transforming Alzheimer's disease diagnostics by enabling a scalable, minimally invasive assessment of pathology. Food and Drug Administration clearances and European market certifications of different plasma tests mark a shift toward biological diagnosis in routine care. However, clinical implementation is not guided by diagnostic accuracy alone but will depend on improved patient-centered and pathway-level outcomes, including diagnostic confidence, the appropriate use of CSF and PET assessments, time to diagnosis, amyloid-targeting treatment eligibility assessment, and trial recruitment. Digital biomarkers may complement blood tests by providing repeated measures of cognition, speech, and mobility. Yet, their evidence base remains more heterogeneous regarding construct validity, supervision requirements, device dependence, adherence burden, cultural portability, interpretability, and regulatory classification. This review defines how combined blood-digital workflows could be evaluated beyond accuracy, including the context of use, downstream decisions, ethical aspects, governance, and post-market monitoring, ultimately aiming to translate biomarker innovation into meaningful benefits for patients and health systems.

Article.Authors: Grégorio S.; Lauderdale J.; Nadeau L.; Ferrari R.
Article.Abstract: Glacial-interglacial transitions punctuate Earth’s Quaternary climate, accompanied by substantial atmospheric carbon dioxide and ocean carbon storage changes. Here, we show that the combined expansion of Antarctic sea ice and associated changes in the meridional overturning efficiently sequester carbon in the ocean abyss, leading to a decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide. In contrast, changes in sea ice and circulation individually result in ocean carbon dioxide outgassing. When sea ice expansion and circulation changes act together, they enhance biological carbon storage by reducing ocean-atmosphere fluxes in the Southern Ocean, without invoking external drivers of the biological pump. This reduction inhibits the outgassing of upwelled remineralized carbon and promotes its resubduction into the abyss. Together, these results reveal a reinforcing feedback linking atmospheric cooling, Antarctic sea ice expansion, and ocean circulation changes to enhanced biological carbon storage and atmospheric carbon dioxide drawdown.

Article.Authors: Hao J.; Liu C.; Liu F.; Zhang C.; Mondal J.; Glein C.; Cardon H.; Montagnac G.; Cao X.; Daniel I.

Article.Title: DMRT1 is required at two steps of ovarian differentiation in rabbits
Article.Authors: Dujardin E.; Poulat F.; Aura I.; Dewaele A.; André M.; McKey J.; Le Gras S.; Frambourg A.; Jouneau L.; Lupiáñez D.; Mandon-Pépin B.; Pailhoux E.
Article.Abstract: The transcription factor Doublesex and Mab-3 Related Transcription Factor 1 (DMRT1) is essential for testis differentiation and male fertility, but less is known about its potential involvement in ovarian differentiation. In mice, Dmrt1 −/− females are fertile, although they show a reduction of Stra8 expression. Using our DMRT1 mutant rabbit model, we analyzed ovarian differentiation when DMRT1 expression is abolished. First, we observed that during early gonadal development, DMRT1 −/− gonads display a specific transcriptome different from control ovaries and control testes. Second, we assessed the infertility phenotype of mutant females. DMRT1 is highly expressed in germ cells until meiosis initiation, and its disruption leads to a down-regulation of key genes involved in the meiotic process. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing data highlighted that DMRT1 can bind these genes in the rabbit ovary. Our study using the rabbit model shows that in addition to its role in testicular differentiation, DMRT1 has two important functions in ovarian differentiation: an initial involvement in the differentiation of somatic cells and a pivotal role in the differentiation of germ cells. Our data suggested that DMRT1 could be considered in human health as a gene necessary for female fertility.

Article.Title: Vortex-mediated spin current injection into two-dimensional superconductor NbSe <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Yang M.; Yin X.; Liu J.; Chen Y.; Gao Q.; Zhu H.; Huang D.; Chen L.; Yang S.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Injection of pure spin current into superconductors remains a major challenge in superconducting spintronics. Previous studies have primarily focused on spin-polarized quasiparticles and spin-triplet supercurrents, while vortices—ubiquitous topological defects in type-II superconductors—have been theoretically proposed as alternative carriers of spin angular momentum, yet direct experimental evidence is still lacking. Here, we report the vortex-mediated spin current injection in NbSe 2 /LiAl 2 Fe 3 O 8 (LAFO) bilayer, an Ising superconductor/ferrimagnetic insulator heterostructure. Under an out-of-plane temperature gradient and an in-plane magnetic field, the NbSe 2 /LAFO bilayer shows a pronounced thermoelectric peak near the upper critical magnetic field, which has the opposite sign to the conventional vortex Nernst signal observed in a single-layer NbSe 2 . The sign reversal suggests that the vortex flow induced by spin current injection is opposite to the flow driven by the temperature gradient, which is consistent with theoretical mechanisms including spin-vorticity transmutation and the inverse vortex spin Hall effect. By mapping the field–temperature phase diagram, we reveal that the spin current injection occurs exclusively in the vortex liquid phase of NbSe 2 . Absence of the thermoelectric signal above the superconducting transition temperature further rules out the quasiparticle contribution. Our results establish vortices as efficient carriers of spin information in superconductors, opening a new route towards vortex-mediated superconducting spintronic devices.

Article.Title: Multiple allosteric sites allow for synergistic enhancement of GPCR signaling
Article.Authors: Wang K.; Dimova S.; Hanson J.; Thakur A.; Xu Y.; Liu Y.; Moritz A.; Goldberg A.; Xie B.; Rayadurgam J.; Wang F.; Nilson A.; Luderman K.; Free R.; Hu W.; Zhang J.; Xu H.; Frankowski K.; Wang Y.; Shi L.; Sibley D.; Zhuang Y.
Article.Abstract: Allosteric modulation of G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs) offers promising therapeutic opportunities. Although multiple allosteric binding sites have been identified in GPCRs, whether and how these spatially distinct sites cooperate to regulate receptor activation remain poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the molecular mechanism of cooperative multisite allostery in the dopamine D1 receptor (D1R). We developed two novel D1R positive allosteric modulators (PAMs), UNC9815 and UNC10062, and used cryo–electron microscopy to structurally identify two previously uncharacterized D1R allosteric sites occupied by UNC9815/UNC10062 and another D1R PAM, BMS-A1. Both sites localize to the transmembrane helix (TM) 1 to 7 interface as vertically adjacent allosteric pockets organized in a spatially complementary manner. Our structures demonstrate the simultaneous binding of the chemically distinct PAMs (LY3154207, BMS-A1, and UNC9815/UNC10062) in three nonoverlapping pockets. Concurrent engagement of all three allosteric sites produces pronounced functional cooperativity, increasing dopamine potency by >1000-fold, thereby demonstrating that coordinated multisite modulation can achieve substantial pharmacological amplification beyond the limits imposed by single PAM administration. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that multisite PAM engagement restricts intracellular loop 3 dynamics and stabilizes the TM7-NPxxY activation motif, effects not achieved by binding of LY3154207 alone, thereby biasing the receptor toward a more stabilized active conformation, and may also improve agonist potency by stabilizing extracellular loop 2. Together, these findings establish the structural framework for cooperative multisite allostery in a GPCR, revealing how distributed allosteric sites act in concert to amplify receptor activation and providing a conceptual foundation for developing innovative GPCR allosteric therapeutics.

Article.Title: Accessing invasion-competent Plasmodium vivax merozoites reveals antibody-dependent NK cell activation
Article.Authors: Salvador J.; Guselli L.; Yeat R.; Lay S.; Thol T.; Ya N.; Feufack-Donfack L.; Heng S.; Bohaud C.; Orban A.; Baldor L.; Tat B.; Chitnis C.; Cantaert T.; Popovici J.
Article.Abstract: Malaria pathogenesis and clinical symptoms arise from blood-stage replication of Plasmodium parasites, which depends on rapid invasion of red blood cells by merozoites. Despite the central importance of this stage, direct functional studies of Plasmodium vivax ( P. vivax ) merozoites remain limited by the lack of continuous in vitro culture and restricted access to viable, invasion-competent merozoites from clinical isolates. Consequently, key aspects of P. vivax merozoite biology and immune recognition remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a robust platform enabling synchronized release and high-yield isolation of invasion-competent P. vivax merozoites from ex vivo cultures. Reversible inhibition of parasite egress using the PKG inhibitor ML10 enables synchronization at the segmented schizont stage, followed by rapid mechanical release of merozoites using a liposome-based extrusion approach. This workflow yields highly pure merozoites with recovery rates exceeding 75% while preserving structural integrity and invasive capacity. Leveraging this platform, we demonstrate that antibody-opsonized P. vivax merozoites activate human natural killer cells, revealing functional antibody-dependent immune responses.

Article.Title: Voice patches in the marmoset auditory cortex revealed by multimodal optical imaging
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Chen C.; Song X.; Guo Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Species-specific vocalizations (including human voices) are important for the survival and social interactions of both humans and animals. In both humans and nonhuman primates, voice/vocalization–selective regions have been identified on the lateral temporal cortex. Here, we provide evidence of localized and hierarchically organized voice patches in the auditory cortex of the common marmoset, a highly vocal New World primate, using multimodal optical imaging techniques that directly measure activity from the smooth cortical surface in a noise-controlled environment. Both intrinsic imaging and calcium imaging data revealed two discrete voice patches in a region of the auditory cortex. Our results provided precise functional localization of the two voice patches (posterior and anterior) by anchoring their positions to the tonotopic map and core/noncore areas of the auditory cortex. Both patches preferentially respond to marmoset vocalizations, exhibit quantifiable neural selectivity beyond spectral features, and encode call type and caller identity. Distinct response properties reveal functional differentiation between the posterior and anterior voice patches, with latency differences consistent with a hierarchical relationship. These findings provide new evidence for an evolutionarily conserved cortical architecture in primates that supports vocal communication via voice patches, analogous to face processing systems in human and nonhuman primate brains.

Article.Title: The mRNA-based RSV vaccine mRNA-1345 induces robust and durable CD4 <sup>+</sup> T cell responses against RSV in younger and older adults
Article.Authors: DiPiazza A.; Marcisak E.; Yu W.; Makrinos D.; Kuo H.; Landy J.; McGrath S.; Chang X.; Cavallaro M.; Wu C.; Essene A.; Lin H.; Walker L.; Carfi A.; Oostendorp J.; Paris R.; Sun Y.
Article.Abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a health threat, particularly for infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. Although neutralizing antibodies can help limit infection and viral replication, T cells are essential for reducing disease severity. Assessment of age-related declines in T cell function are important for vaccine evaluation. We used intracellular cytokine staining, activation-induced marker, and Meso Scale Discovery assays and single-cell multiomic profiling to evaluate RSV vaccine mRNA-1345 responses in younger and older adults. mRNA-1345 induced comparable CD4 + and CD8 + T cell responses in both cohorts, with CD4 + responses persisting for 24 months. The CD4 + response was strongly T helper 1 (T H 1)–polarized, with increased interferon-γ, interleukin-2, and tumor necrosis factor–α and minimal T H 2 cytokines. Both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells showed increased polyfunctionality that remained elevated at 2 years. Single-cell and T cell receptor repertoire analyses showed similar Pre-F–specific phenotypes, transcriptional profiles, and clonal overlap across age groups, supporting robust, durable cellular immunity after mRNA-1345 vaccination. These findings indicate shared vaccine-elicited T cell immunity in adults.

Article.Title: Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Wei H.; Boutet D.; Dou R.; Ahrens J.; Zeramdini N.; Voppel A.; Gonzales-Aste F.; Abboud F.; Baillet S.; Palaniyappan L.
Article.Abstract: Schizophrenia disrupts both how people perceive the world and how they express and act on their thoughts, yet these symptoms are usually studied separately. Using magnetoencephalography during multisensory and motor tasks, we tested whether reduced event-related beta-band (15 to 30 hertz) modulation, a signal implicated in predictive control, provides a candidate neural marker across these domains. Compared to healthy individuals, patients showed diminished beta changes during sensory processing and movement completion, suggesting reduced flexibility in updating internal models. This neural pattern covaried with audiovisual simultaneity-judgment behavior, disorganized natural speech, and greater clinical severity. These findings suggest that distributed beta modulation may serve as a candidate cross-domain marker associated with perceptual, motor, and language disturbances in schizophrenia, motivating future studies that directly test predictive updating mechanisms.

Article.Title: Physical confinement modulates the rate-limiting transition in the release of phosphate from actin filaments
Article.Authors: Herman K.; Iyer S.; Wang Y.; Pollard T.; Voth G.
Article.Abstract: The nucleotide state and rates of transitions between states regulate the dynamics of ATPases. Slow inorganic phosphate (P i ) release following ATP hydrolysis is often rate limiting and associated with key conformational changes. Actin filaments offer a unique opportunity to understand the fundamentals of P i release because identical subunits at filament ends and the interior release P i at markedly different rates. The molecular origin of this difference is debated, so we used extensive all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize P i release from different subunits within an actin filament. The calculated dissociation rates of P i from ADP-Mg 2+ in the active site correlate with experimentally measured P i release rates and scale inversely with the numbers of water molecules in the cavity surrounding the γ-phosphate. Simulations show that egress of P i through the protein channels, including through the N111-R177 backdoor, is not rate limiting and that subunits at the filament ends use alternative egress pathways.

Article.Title: Prioritizing reducing impacts on species to minimize residual reserves
Article.Authors: Fleury A.; O’Hara C.; Everett J.; Halpern B.; Klein C.; Richardson A.; Dunn D.
Article.Abstract: International conservation goals have driven rapid expansion of protected areas. This growth has favored quantity over quality, and often results in residual reserves (i.e., areas where species already experience minimal anthropogenic impact). Spatial prioritization is commonly used to help design protected area networks that represent species while minimizing costs to stakeholders. This approach can result in the siting of protected areas that do not decrease impacts on species of conservation concern. Here, we show how measures of cumulative impacts on species can be used in a spatial prioritization to site protected areas to reduce impacts on species of conservation concern. We use a trait-based vulnerability framework and anthropogenic stressor maps to quantify cumulative impacts from four human activities, and incorporate those impacts into spatial prioritizations. We demonstrate that the inclusion of cumulative impacts on species in spatial prioritization can more efficiently protect biodiversity, balance socioeconomic objectives, and avoid residual reserve outcomes.

Article.Title: Spatial decoupling of recognition and signaling in aptamer switches via tri-strand intermolecular competition
Article.Authors: Li A.; Stewart S.; Belzberg C.; Hariri A.
Article.Abstract: Despite decades of progress in aptamer engineering, the development of a single, modular signaling architecture capable of transducing target recognition into a measurable output across structurally diverse analytes remains an unmet challenge in biosensing. We report the Competitor Bridge Aptamer (CoBrA) framework: a modular DNA tridomain architecture that functionally isolates target recognition from signal transduction. Unlike conventional sensors where signal output depends on unpredictable aptamer folding, the CoBrA system uses an aptamer switch to trigger a predictable, concerted spatial displacement between signaling end points. By leveraging computational simulations and energetic balancing, we systematically optimized the CoBrA framework to consolidate recognition, displacement, and ratiometric signaling within a single, minimal-component system. Using the dopamine and cortisol aptamers as models, we demonstrate strong thermodynamic and kinetic synchronization between the Cy3 and Cy5 channels across both targets for dopamine (Cy3: K d = 13.3 ± 3.2 μM, τ = 447 ± 31 seconds; Cy5: K d = 24.0 ± 3.3 μM, τ = 537 ± 22 seconds) and cortisol (Cy3: K d = 36.6 ± 3.9 μM, τ = 205 ± 7 seconds; Cy5: K d = 30.7 ± 5.5 μM, τ = 259 ± 4 seconds) in buffer, serum, and artificial cerebrospinal fluid. Because the signaling event is a predictable, geometry-defined change rather than a fluorescence-specific phenomenon, this architecture is in principle adaptable to surface-based transduction modalities, including electrochemical, field-effect transistor, and plasmonic readouts.

Article.Title: In-memory phononic learning toward cognitive mechanical intelligence
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: Mechanical intelligence seeks autonomous materials that embody memory, perception, learning, and decision-making within the mechanical domain. A fundamental challenge is to integrate memory with information processing in an efficient, scalable, and interpretable way that supports cognitive learning and decision-making. Here, we introduce in-memory phononic learning, a framework that unifies non-volatile mechanical memory with wave-based perception in a phononic metastructure. Spatial information is stored as structural states that program elastic-wave responses, allowing probing waves to act as queries that retrieve informative features through parallel, physically transparent localization modes. Learning is achieved by offline optimization of input waveforms to selectively combine these features for multitask memory-pattern recognition without hardware redesign, with decisions inferred directly from output-energy responses. We experimentally and numerically demonstrate high-accuracy classification across tasks from geometric shapes to handwritten digits. Overall, this work elevates “materials that compute” toward “cognitive matter” that can interpret, reason, and learn through wave physics, laying a foundation for scalable and robust autonomous material systems.

Article.Title: All-soft organic electrochemical diodes based on asymmetric active layers for signal isolation in deformable electronics
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Kim M.; Park H.; Sim K.; Jang J.; Kim Y.; Park J.; Shin D.; Na M.; Sim K.
Article.Abstract: All-soft electronics have emerged as a promising platform for deformable and human-centric systems, yet the development of mechanically compliant diodes remains a major challenge due to limitations in material compatibility, device architecture, and stable operation under deformation. Electrochemical approaches offer a viable route to address this challenge by enabling bulk, low-voltage charge modulation in soft materials without relying on rigid junction interfaces. Here, we report, to the best of our knowledge, the first all-soft organic electrochemical diode (OECD) based on an asymmetric active-layer geometry. The device incorporates a transfer-printed ultrathin ion-gel interface that preserves conformal coverage and the active electrochemical architecture under strain. The device achieves high rectification through polarity-dependent electrochemical potential redistribution, with a rectification ratio of up to 2.23 × 10 4 at ±1 V and stable operation under tensile strains of up to 30% and repeated mechanical deformation. This ion-gel-based architecture preserves the electrochemical asymmetry required for diode operation while maintaining structural integrity under strain. Beyond the individual device, the all-soft OECD enables deformable rectifiers and logic gates and functions as a key signal-isolation element that suppresses cross-talk in a deformable pressure-sensing array. These results establish an electrochemical diode platform that combines mechanical deformability, high rectification performance, and circuit-level compatibility, providing a pathway toward fully deformable and integrated human-centric electronic systems.

Article.Title: Observations show increased nitrate in coastal cloud droplet residuals from large-particle activation and N <sub>2</sub> O <sub>5</sub> hydrolysis
Article.Authors: Williams A.; Russell L.; Han S.; Berta V.; Dedrick J.; Campos T.; Robinson L.; Chang R.; Farley R.; Aiken A.; Twohy C.; Wheeler M.; Wentzell J.; Liggio J.
Article.Abstract: Clouds change the chemical composition of aerosols, yet observations characterizing these processes are quite limited. Ground-based in-cloud measurements in coastal Southern California show that the highest nitrate to sulfate ratio (2.5 ± 1.7) in droplet residuals is near cloud base where cloud liquid water content and droplet number concentration are below the observed 20th percentile. The number size distribution of nitrate-rich particles peaks at a larger diameter than sulfate-rich particles, supporting growth to droplets of nitrate-rich particles at lower supersaturations than for sulfate-rich particles. Nitrate mass concentrations are up to three times higher in-cloud compared to pre-cloud and correlated with statistically significant reductions in ozone concentrations, consistent with contributions from in-cloud nitrate formation by N 2 O 5 hydrolysis. This study provides quantitative relationships of cloud properties to nitrate production in droplet residuals and associated ozone reduction, illustrating the impacts of aqueous reactions in clouds.

Article.Title: Submesoscale feedback suppresses marine heatwaves
Article.Authors: Dong J.; Sun W.; Fox-Kemper B.; Jing Z.; Dong C.
Article.Abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are devastating extreme ocean temperature events whose frequency and severity have surged under global warming, threatening marine ecosystems and fisheries. Yet, the fundamental mechanisms that control their intensity and persistence remain incompletely understood. Here, using a submesoscale-permitting global model simulation validated by long-term observational and reanalysis data, this study reveals a previously overlooked submesoscale feedback that exerts a critical control on MHW severity. It is demonstrated that the submesoscale-induced vertical heat flux suppresses the intensity and persistence of atmosphere-driven MHWs in winter via a negative feedback mechanism. Enhanced air-sea net heat flux strengthens stratification and shoals the mixed layer, weakening submesoscale vertical heat transport by 19.4%, reducing MHW intensification by 18.1%, and accelerating decay by 21.7%. This missing regulatory mechanism indicates that models ignoring the submesoscale feedback likely overestimate MHW severity, with critical implications for future climate projections.

Article.Title: Wave vortices around oscillating subwavelength holes: Water-wave observation
Article.Authors: Ye J.; Li Z.; Nikitin A.; Nori F.; Liu W.; Bliokh K.; Shi L.
Article.Abstract: We consider a two-dimensional wave system containing a subwavelength hole, such as an aperture in an interface supporting surface electromagnetic or acoustic waves or an island in a fluid surface sustaining gravity-capillary waves. Recent studies have revealed the emergence of pronounced wave vortices around such structures, termed type II vortices, in contrast to conventional (type I) vortices associated with phase singularities and intensity nulls. A notable natural manifestation of type II vortices occurs in ocean tides around islands such as New Zealand, Madagascar, and Iceland, where the tidal phase increases by ±2π around the island. Although this phenomenon is usually associated with the Coriolis effect from the rotation of the Earth, here, we demonstrate the controlled generation of type II vortices using a minimal and tunable setup: a dipole-oscillating subwavelength hole and a single incident plane wave. Using laboratory gravity-capillary waves and an oscillating subwavelength “island,” we directly measure the resulting phase structure, topological charge, and wave angular momentum. We show that the emergence and handedness of the vortices can be precisely controlled via the relative phase between the dipolar source and the incident wave. Our results offer a simple and versatile mechanism for engineering subwavelength wave vortices, with potential applications in a variety of two-dimensional wave systems.

Article.Title: Differential sex-dependent responses of circulating steroid hormones and cortical gene expression in a traumatic brain injury model
Article.Authors: Simmons A.; Wilferd S.; Campagnuolo S.; Pena V.; Bimonte-Nelson H.; Newbern J.; Sirianni R.; Plaisier C.; Stabenfeldt S.
Article.Abstract: Accumulating evidence supports sex differences in traumatic brain injury (TBI) outcomes. However, the underlying processes that lead to sex differences are not well understood. TBI results in the initiation of molecular and cellular responses that facilitate the progression of neurodegeneration. Little is known about how the circulating hormone profile is altered in response to TBI and whether sex differences in endocrine responses might shape secondary injury pathologies. Using intact male and female mice in a preclinical TBI model, we assessed changes in plasma hormone concentrations and cortical gene expression at 24 and 72 hours after TBI. We demonstrate that males and females exhibit sex-specific alterations in circulating levels of testosterone, androstenedione, estradiol, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) in response to TBI. We also identified sex differences in the expression of genes that are involved in immune responses and tissue remodeling after injury. Moreover, we report divergent circulating hormone and gene expression correlations between sexes.

Article.Title: Enterococcus faecalis biofilm rewires neutrophil metabolism to suppress antimicrobial activity
Article.Authors: Antypas H.; Gonçalves da Silva R.; Wong G.; Liang C.; Muthualagu Natarajan L.; Tan R.; Neo C.; Wong S.; Kline K.
Article.Abstract: Enterococcus faecalis is an opportunistic pathogen that persists in biofilm-associated infections despite robust neutrophil recruitment. How E. faecalis evades neutrophils remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how E. faecalis biofilms alter effector functions in human neutrophils and a murine wound infection model. We found that E. faecalis biofilm suppresses neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, bacterial engulfment, and neutrophil-mediated control of biofilm growth. This suppression is partly driven by production of lactic acid through the lactate dehydrogenases (LDHs) of E. faecalis , which acidifies the extracellular environment, lowers neutrophil intracellular pH, and disrupts glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway. In a murine wound infection model, loss of LDH increased neutrophil recruitment and NETosis . We also found that high bacterial density, a defining feature of biofilms, suppresses NETosis through a lactic acid–independent mechanism. Collectively, these findings identify biofilm immune evasion strategies mediated by bacterial metabolism and the high-density structural organization of biofilm-associated bacteria.

Article.Title: BCG vaccination mitigates tau pathology and restores cognitive function in PS19 mice
Article.Authors: Shee S.; Huang M.; Baghel M.; Zheng Y.; Lun S.; Yadav S.; Yadav N.; Ruiz-Gonzalez C.; Tyagi S.; Nuermberger E.; Jain S.; Bhujwalla Z.; Slusher B.; Wong P.; Bishai W.
Article.Abstract: Retrospective studies in patients with nonmuscle invasive bladder cancer have reported a significant reduction in Alzheimer’s disease incidence (12 to 78%) among Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) recipients versus controls. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we evaluated BCG in the PS19 mouse model of tauopathy. We found that BCG administration reduced hippocampal phospho-tau and microgliosis while preserving neuronal markers. In vivo volumetric T2–magnetic resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated attenuation of brain atrophy accompanied by increased glutamate-weighted chemical exchange saturation transfer–MRI signals. Functionally, BCG-treated mice showed improved performance in the novel object recognition test, as well as improved body-weight maintenance and survival. Transcriptomic profiling of the hippocampus revealed near complete normalization of the PS19 disease-associated gene expression signature toward that of healthy controls. Flow cytometric profiling of brain myeloid populations demonstrated a reduction in activated resident microglia, but total microglia cells remain elevated. Moreover, an increase of trained immunity marker CD80 on the recruited peripheral myeloid cells ensues following BCG treatment. Consistent with this shift in myeloid state, primary brain myeloid cells from BCG-treated mice also exhibited enhanced phagocytosis of fluorescein isothiocyanate-labeled tau fibrils and increased lactate production. Together, these findings indicate that BCG induces systemic and central nervous system myeloid cell reprogramming that limits neuroinflammation, enhances tau clearance, and rescues cognitive and neurodegenerative phenotypes in a tauopathy model. BCG is a safe, readily available therapy that merits consideration as a preventive agent against dementia.

Article.Title: Interpreting the Hall effect of highly doped conducting polymers
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Ren X.; Fan J.; Hoek S.; Sirringhaus H.
Article.Abstract: Accurate determination of carrier density and mobility is fundamental to understanding the transport physics of conducting polymers and optimizing their performance. However, Hall effect measurements, widely used for determining carrier concentrations in other materials, have been of limited use for conducting polymers. Applying the conventional Hall coefficient expression ( R H = [ n H q ] − 1 ) consistently yields unphysically high carrier densities in heavily doped polymers. Here, we resolve this problem using a quasi–one-dimensional (Q1D) tight-binding model of the band structure of uniaxially aligned polymer films to analyze the p-type to n-type transition in the Hall effect observed upon increased doping. Our Q1D framework achieves excellent agreement between Hall-derived carrier densities and other independent measurements over a wide doping range. Our findings indicate that the transport physics of aligned polymers is governed by the topology of a single Q1D band within a simple band-filling framework and establish Hall measurements as a powerful tool for studying their charge transport physics.

Article.Title: A continuous confinement-deconfinement transition in a triangular quantum magnet
Article.Authors: Hosoi S.; Park S.; Hirata M.; Lee M.; Dioguardi A.; Thompson J.; Ronning F.; Scheie A.; Imamura K.; Hashimoto K.; Shibauchi T.; Belbase B.; Unnikrishnan A.; Knolle J.; Banerjee A.; Matsuda Y.
Article.Abstract: A continuous transition between phases hosting distinct excitations—bosonic magnons versus fermionic spinons—is a long-sought phenomenon in quantum magnetism, analogous to the confinement-deconfinement transition in quantum chromodynamics. We report evidence for such a transition in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet thallium ytterbium disulfide. Antiferromagnetic order develops below T N ≈ 0.53 kelvin. A c -axis field suppresses this order, driving the system into a gapless quantum spin liquid with a spinon Fermi surface above μ 0 H c ≈ 3 T , evidenced by a finite residual linear term in thermal conductivity, a Pauli-like susceptibility, and a temperature-independent nuclear magnetic resonance Knight shift. Approaching H c from above, the scattering rate of itinerant excitations is strongly enhanced, while their density of states shows no critical enhancement, atypical of conventional magnetic quantum criticality. These results point to a continuous confinement-deconfinement transition governed by fractionalized excitations beyond the Ginzburg-Landau paradigm.

Article.Title: A phosphorylation-gated GAPDH-MAPK6-LBD1 module controls drought-responsive transcription
Article.Authors: He Z.; Wang Z.; Gao C.; Ji X.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Drought adaptation requires rapid spatial reorganization of signaling proteins to reprogram stress-responsive transcription, yet how phosphorylation coordinates this process remains unclear. Here we aimed to define how phosphorylation-gated protein relocalization regulates a BpLBD1-centered drought pathway in Betula platyphylla (birch). Drought activated two kinase branches: BpAGC phosphorylated BpMAPK6 at Ser318 within a cryptic nuclear localization signal, promoting importin α recognition, whereas BpCKII phosphorylated BpGAPDH at Thr109, Thr270, Ser279 and Thr298, promoting importin β recognition. Dual phosphorylation enabled coordinated nuclear accumulation of BpMAPK6 and BpGAPDH. In the nucleus, phosphorylated BpGAPDH acted as a scaffold-like adaptor coupling BpMAPK6 to BpLBD1, enabling BpMAPK6-mediated phosphorylation of BpLBD1 at Ser29. This weakened BpLBD1 binding to the BpMYB123 promoter, reduced expression of the drought-sensitivity regulator BpMYB123 , and de-repressed drought-responsive genes such as BpRD29B . Disrupting BpGAPDH or BpLBD1 Ser29 phosphorylation compromised drought tolerance. Thus, a phospho-spatial GAPDH-MAPK6-LBD1 switch couples nuclear protein assembly to drought-responsive transcription.

Article.Title: Biophysically constrained learning from healthy neural priors improves motor decoding in pathological cortical networks
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; Chang T.; Chen S.; Quan Y.; Sun Q.; Van Hulle M.; Liu Y.; Jiang N.; Farina D.; Yang Y.; Mao Q.; He J.
Article.Abstract: High-performance brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) rely on stable neural representations, yet brain functional impairments inherently disrupt canonical encoding, creating a fundamental decoding paradox. Conventional data-driven approaches struggle to bridge this gap because of pathological data scarcity and heterogeneity. Here, we propose to leverage healthy neural priors and introduce Pathology-Aware Consensus Training (PACT), a paradigm embedding biophysical constraints into healthy neural recordings to guide neural decoding. In a gesture classification task using high-density electrocorticography from patients with gliomas infiltrating the motor cortex, PACT improved the accuracy by more than 10%, effectively restoring the distorted semantic geometry of motor commands and realigning them with healthy canonical representations (correlation increase: r = 0.66 to r = 0.94). Mechanistically, PACT induced an emergent “inverse weighting” strategy: The model autonomously suppresses high-power pathological noise while reanchoring spatial attention to functional compensatory regions. This study provides a proof of concept for improving decoding in compromised networks by harnessing healthy neural dynamics, laying the theoretical foundation for future BCI deployments in clinical populations.

Article.Title: An in situ forming immunomodulatory hydrogel reinvigorates exhausted CD8 <sup>+</sup> T cells via preserving their mitochondrial fitness
Article.Authors: Qi Y.; Li J.; Chen Z.; Zou C.; Zhu H.; Shen Yi Shan A.; Fu Y.; Hou J.; Zheng C.; Ren Q.; Qiao Y.; Jin Z.; Wang F.; Guo S.
Article.Abstract: CD8 + T cell exhaustion driven by mitochondrial dysfunction remains a major barrier to effective cancer immunotherapy. Here, we report an in situ forming d -α-tocopheryl polyethylene glycol succinate (TPGS)–based hydrogel [multifunctional thermosensitive composite gel (MTC Gel)] that reinvigorates exhausted CD8 + T cells by preserving mitochondrial fitness through a two-pronged strategy. After intratumoral injection, MTC Gel rapidly undergoes gelation at physiological temperature and dissociates to generate a high local concentration of TPGS, which targets cancer cell mitochondria to trigger prodeath mitophagy. This process induces robust immunogenic cell death (ICD) and blocks tunneling nanotube–mediated mitochondrial hijacking. Meanwhile, NLG919-loaded hybrid nanoparticles released from MTC Gel synergistically restore mitochondrial biogenesis in CD8 + T cells suppressed by indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1. Across multiple murine tumor models, MTC Gel reprograms T cell immunity by reducing CD8 + T cells exhaustion while enhancing effector and cytotoxic functions, thereby eliciting potent tumoricidal activity. These findings highlight this rationally designed hydrogel system as a clinically translatable platform for next-generation ICD-based cancer immunotherapies.

Article.Title: NRF2 coordinates cystine import and glutathione use to sustain ferroptosis resistance and formaldehyde tolerance in cancer
Article.Authors: Morellato A.; Alquezar-Artieda N.; Guerrero-Maldonado A.; Singh R.; Beja L.; Umansky C.; Perich-Pallaruelo L.; Pellicer M.; Fernandez-Deu P.; Aira N.; Bourached-Silva N.; Chorostecki U.; Jones D.; Roué G.; Hopkinson R.; Pontel L.

Here, we show that NRF2 promotes formaldehyde tolerance through up-regulation of the cystine transporter SLC7A11, enabling a protective mechanism that is largely independent of GSH, which remains necessary for ferroptosis resistance. Article.Title: An innovative colon inflammation-targeting platform for ulcerative colitis treatment
Article.Authors: Islam W.; Chen H.; Li L.; Salimian K.; Selaru F.
Article.Abstract: The therapeutic options for patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) have recently expanded substantially. Tofacitinib, an oral small-molecule inhibitor of Janus kinase (JAK), recently FDA approved for ulcerative colitis, represented a paradigm shift in a field previously dominated by biologics. Tofacitinib, however, carries a black box warning for major adverse cardiovascular events, an elevated risk of malignancies, risk of blood clots, and pulmonary embolism. In addition, tofacitinib is avoided in pregnancy and used with caution in women of child bearing age due to potential risks to the developing fetus. Notably, these potential complications are all due to the systemic distribution of tofacitinib. To address these issues, we developed Lipo-tm-HA, a liposomal platform incorporating mannitol (m) and hyaluronic acid (HA) for targeting tofacitinib (t) to the inflamed colon. We characterized Lipo-tm-HA and have shown that it (i) remains stable in gastric conditions due to HA coating, (ii) adheres to transferrin in inflamed mucosa due to its negative charge, and (iii) enhances macrophage uptake through mannose receptor–mediated endocytosis. Due to targeting, we show that a single oral administration of Lipo-tm-HA at a dose of 10 milligrams per kilogram is superior in efficacy compared with daily treatment with free tofacitinib in a dextran sodium sulfate–induced colitis model. Collectively, our innovative formulation will enable colonic inflammation targeting, reduce systemic exposure, and allow administration of decreased doses.

Article.Title: Primary tumor–derived lactate primes prostate cancer cells for a dormant fate
Article.Authors: Ippolito L.; Pranzini E.; Gangarossa G.; Iozzo M.; Comito G.; Venditti G.; Roccabianca S.; Pardella E.; Lulli M.; Santi A.; Nesi G.; Giannoni E.; Chiarugi P.
Article.Abstract: The metastatic outcome depends on the state of disseminated cancer cells (DCCs) leading to overt metastasis or undergoing dormancy. Article.Title: CASTOR1 functional inactivation drives KRAS -mutant NSCLC and therapy resistance by a noncanonical mechanism of tumor suppression
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Ding L.; Meng W.; Byrnes E.; Loo S.; Sun S.; Chen L.; Li T.; Wang M.; Pennathur A.; Huang Y.; Gao S.
Article.Abstract: CASTOR1, a cytosolic arginine sensor and regulator of mTORC1 signaling, is identified here as a tumor suppressor in KRAS -driven non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Loss of CASTOR1 results in constitutive mTORC1 hyperactivation, impaired arginine-dependent regulation of mTORC1 signaling, elevated p-4EBP1 and p-S6 levels, increased AKT and ERK activation, genomic instability, and resistance to KRAS G12D inhibitors. These findings identify CASTOR1 as a critical link between nutrient sensing and oncogenic signaling and reveal its functional inactivation as an important mechanism contributing to KRAS -driven NSCLC progression and therapeutic resistance. The results further support rational combination therapies to overcome KRAS inhibitor resistance in CASTOR1-low NSCLC.

Article.Title: Learning by moving: Physical motion accelerates category learning
Article.Authors: Rosedahl L.; Sasaki Y.; Watanabe T.
Article.Abstract: Categorization is crucial for survival, helping animals forage, navigate, and avoid predators—all tasks involving movement. Yet, dominant theories of category learning treat it as a purely cognitive or perceptual process. Here, we challenge this view by demonstrating that physical movement can enhance category learning—but selectively. Using immersive virtual reality, we found that performing large actions, such as swinging a lightsaber, substantially improved learning of categories requiring integration of multiple cues (e.g., distinguishing aggressive from noncancerous lesions), while having minimal impact on categories involving independent evaluation of features (e.g., sorting by color and shape). This selective enhancement reveals a previously unrecognized motor contribution to categorization and may explain why prior studies missed it, opening avenues for optimizing training in critical categorization tasks.

Article.Title: Polycomb factor PHF19 affects AML initiation, patient prognosis, and survival
Article.Authors: Gamarra Figueroa G.; Gutierrez A.; Blanco E.; Vizán P.; Ballaré C.; Sparavier A.; Tosto M.; Minucci S.; Velten L.; Di Croce L.
Article.Abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is marked by unchecked expansion of undifferentiated myeloid cells. Although oncogenic fusions such as MLL-AF9 can initiate disease, the early steps of leukemogenesis and the role of cell-intrinsic regulators remain unclear. Article.Authors: Yi S.; Xiao J.; Wang R.; Wang M.; Le C.; Yang G.; Yi S.; Liu W.; Wang H.; Li X.; Liu X.; Wang K.; Jiang C.; Gao S.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: The human placenta is essential for pregnancy, yet the dynamic regulation of its DNA methylome during development remains poorly understood. Article.Title: PhagoID: Quantitative in situ proximity labeling defines the proteomes of bead- and microbe-containing phagosome lumina across species, maturation, and immune activation
Article.Authors: Allsup B.; Gharpure S.; Gunnarsson C.; Stagg M.; Bryson B.
Article.Abstract: The phagosome is an immune organelle that integrates signals from diverse cargos to drive pathogen killing, tissue homeostasis, and antigen presentation. Applying PhagoID to murine and human macrophages, we define conserved and species-specific phagosomal proteomes that include both canonical lysosomal components and unexpected contributors from nuclear, mitochondrial, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) compartments. Integrating these proteomes with 25 genome-scale CRISPR screens of phagosomal phenotypes, we identify a network of lumenal proteins that regulate cargo uptake, acidification, antigen presentation, and microbial control highlighting previously unrecognized phagosomal effectors. We next adapt PhagoID to profile the microbe-containing phagosome and compare the sterile bead-containing phagosome to the Escherichia coli –containing phagosome, demonstrating a modest E. coli signature of phagosome remodeling. Comparative analyses further reveal that loss of LAMP1 enhances recruitment of ER-derived proteins to the phagosome, whereas loss of TFEB minimally perturbs the lumenal proteome despite its role in lysosomal biogenesis. Last, cytokine stimulation remodels the phagosome lumen to enrich for proteins involved in antigen presentation and antimicrobial activity in response to type I and II interferons. These data demonstrate that PhagoID delivers a high-confidence, quantitative, and integrative map of the phagosome lumen, revealing previously unidentified axes of organellar communication and regulatory control in innate immunity.

Article.Authors: Shi X.; Peng Q.; Guo J.; Wu W.; Wang P.; Zhou X.; Chen Q.
Article.Abstract: PrimPol-mediated fork repriming generates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps during DNA damage tolerance (DDT), which, if not properly repaired, can threaten genomic stability. PrimPol is a highly error-prone polymerase. Thus, PrimPol activity should be tightly regulated to fit into DDT and remain low during unstressed DNA replication. Here, we show that SCML2A is a suppressor of PrimPol. SCML2A directly binds two domains of PrimPol: Its RBR domain binds the C terminus of PrimPol, and its SAM domain binds the amino-terminal AEP domain, thereby inhibiting ssDNA-binding capacity of the AEP domain. SCML2 depletion leads to increased nascent DNA synthesis and accumulation of PrimPol-mediated ssDNA gaps under replication stress. SCML2 depletion also enhances PrimPol engagement during unstressed DNA replication, leading to subsequent accumulation of ssDNA gaps, which are filled by REV1/POLζ-mediated translesion synthesis (TLS) and RAD51-mediated template switching (TS). SCML2 depletion confers cellular hypersensitivity to RAD51 or REV1/POLζ inhibition, which is associated with increased accumulation of ssDNA gaps. Furthermore, CDK2 phosphorylates SCML2A at Ser 267 , which suppresses RBR-mediated PrimPol interaction. Cyclin E1 overexpression leads to CDK2-mediated SCML2A Ser 267 hyperphosphorylation, which releases the inhibitory effect of SCML2A on PrimPol and subsequently induces ssDNA gap accumulation. Article.Title: Scalable architecture for measurement-induced squeezed light interferometers
Article.Authors: Verma A.; Hastrup J.; Neergaard-Nielsen J.; Andersen U.
Article.Abstract: Scalable interferometers lie at the heart of photonic quantum technologies, but their expansion has been fundamentally limited by optical losses that grow with circuit depth. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a measurement-induced architecture for multimode squeezed-light interferometers that overcomes this barrier. By shifting complexity from deep optical networks to programmable homodyne measurements, we realize effective transformations within a shallow, low-loss platform. We validate the principle with a six-mode device and extend it to a 400-mode interferometer, marking a leap in scale beyond conventional designs. Crucially, this strategy not only enables scalable squeezed light interferometry but also provides a powerful route to the generation of large-scale entangled states—a key requirement for quantum computing, simulation, and communication. Our results establish measurement-induced circuits as a practical pathway toward noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) applications and future demonstrations of quantum advantage.

Article.Authors: Chakraborty S.; Jiang J.; Camallonga J.; Gazgalis D.; Gero T.; Tavares M.; Dittemore G.; Tkacik E.; Beyett T.; Jang D.; Ha B.; Gottlieb F.; Levitz T.; Metivier R.; Schmoker A.; Scott D.; Jeon H.; Jänne P.; Eck M.

However, how MEK inhibitor potency varies across the three RAF isoforms remains poorly understood. Our studies highlight the importance of the activating RAF isoform as a determinant of MEK inhibitor sensitivity and provide proof of concept for the development of MEK inhibitors that more effectively block ARAF-driven MEK signaling via covalent targeting of Cys 514 .

Article.Title: TET2-driven activation of AGO2 links epigenetic remodeling to myeloid commitment and leukemia
Article.Authors: Lazarenkov A.; Valcárcel G.; Martinez A.; Berenguer C.; López-Rubio A.; Obiols M.; Fontanet C.; Barba A.; Rodríguez-Sevilla J.; Stik G.; Jeremias I.; Menendez P.; Sardina J.
Article.Abstract: DNA methylation dynamics shape hematopoietic differentiation and leukemogenesis, yet how the dioxygenase TET2—frequently mutated in myeloid malignancies—directs lineage-specific regulatory programs remains unclear. Among these, we identified and functionally validated an AGO2 myeloid-specific intragenic enhancer that is frequently hypermethylated in patients with TET2 -mutant acute myeloid leukemia. AGO2 expression stratifies patient survival, and AGO2 depletion abrogates leukemic engraftment in vivo. These findings uncover a TET2-AGO2 regulatory axis that integrates epigenetic remodeling, 3D genome reorganization, and leukemic fitness, and they highlight AGO2 as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target in myeloid leukemia.

Article.Title: Histone methyltransferase NSD2 shapes CD8 + T cell fates through the H3K36me2- Zbtb20 axis
Article.Authors: Yuan S.; Xu Y.; Liu H.; Xue Y.; Zhu M.; Xie X.; Wu X.; Xia Y.; Li L.; Luo Y.; Huang Z.; Yang X.; Du H.; He R.
Article.Abstract: CD8 + T cells, as the most important cytolytic cells in adaptive immunity, can differentiate into distinct subpopulations with specific functions and fates. During this process, CD8 + T cells exhibit substantial plasticity in their differentiation trajectory. Notably, epigenetic regulation has emerged as a pivotal mechanism to govern T cell fate decisions. In this study, we demonstrate that the histone methyltransferase NSD2 critically regulates CD8 + T cell differentiation during acute viral infection. While NSD2 deficiency enhances the early expansion of activated CD8 + T cells, it severely compromises their survival fitness during the contraction phase, leading to a disproportionate collapse of the antigen-specific pool and limiting the establishment of robust long-lived memory. Mechanistically, this defect is driven by the disruption of the H3K36me2- Zbtb20 regulatory axis. Furthermore, we show that in the absence of NSD2, CD8 + T cells in tumor exhibit an increased proportion but dysfunctional resident memory T cell phenotype. Collectively, our findings highlight a critical role for NSD2 in providing more mechanistic insights into how epigenetic mechanisms fine-tune T cell differentiation.

Article.Title: High-throughput droplet-based enzymatic DNA methylome profiling enables single-cell resolution of epigenetic heterogeneity
Article.Authors: Li G.; Yang Y.; Li Z.; Wang Q.; Wang Y.; Guo B.; Yang K.; Tan M.; Li J.; Sun J.; Zhang G.; Xiong S.; Zhang M.; Zhang Z.; Xie Y.; Shi Y.; Ma X.; Ci W.
Article.Abstract: DNA methylation is a fundamental epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression, cellular identity, and disease-associated regulatory programs. This design substantially reduces DNA loss and enables robust profiling of tens of thousands of single cells per experiment. scEM-seq generates high-quality single-cell methylomes with moderately improved CpG coverage and balanced read utilization compared with other droplet-based microfluidic methods. Article.Title: NAD <sup>+</sup> metabolic restoration resolves the inflammation-immunocompetence trade-off in lung graft-versus-host disease
Article.Authors: Li J.; Zhou Z.; Qi J.; Zhang F.; Zhang Z.; Li X.; Jiang S.; Li X.; Wang L.; Xie X.; Chen J.; Zeng K.; Han Y.; Jiang J.; Ye M.
Article.Abstract: Chronic lung graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) remains difficult to treat, and broad immunosuppression increases infection risk. Because free NAD + is poorly cell-permeable and rapidly consumed, we engineered CaNAD + -PGB-LiP (CNAPL), a high-payload NAD + nanomedicine enabling direct intracellular replenishment. In murine allo-HSCT GVHD, CNAPL improved clinical scores and survival, reduced vascular and epithelial injury, and curtailed hyperinflammation and effector overactivation across GVHD target organs. Unlike immunosuppression, CNAPL preserved phagocytosis, NK/NKT cell (natural killer/natural killer T cell) cytotoxicity, and T cell memory. In posttransplant influenza or Klebsiella infection, CNAPL maintained pathogen control without rekindling GVHD, decoupling inflammation control from infection susceptibility. This metabolism-centered, host-directed strategy restores immune-tissue homeostasis and provides a practical translational path for durable lung GVHD control with preserved antimicrobial defense.

Article.Title: Loss of KAT5-dependent H2A.Z acetylation provokes chromosomal instability in recurrent pregnancy loss
Article.Authors: Bi S.; Chen Y.; Zhang L.; Zhang J.; Wang Y.; Huang B.; Li S.; Huang L.; Wang Y.; Wang H.; Meng R.; Tu Z.; Du L.; Wang H.; Wang Z.; Chen D.; Zhang S.; Wang F.
Article.Abstract: Placenta defects are one of the major causes of miscarriages, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Moreover, mutation of a key lysine acetyltransferase 5 (KAT5) substrate, H2A.Z, via the introduction of H2az1-K5R K8R K12R K14R (which prevents H2A.Z acetylation), phenocopies the effects of KAT5 loss. Integrated RNA sequencing and CUT&Tag in mouse trophoblast stem cells reveal that KAT5, through H2A.Z acetylation, regulates transcription of key mitotic genes ( Aurka , Aurkb , and Cenpa ). We extend our finding to human trophoblast stem cells, demonstrating a conserved role for KAT5 in preventing CIN. Clinical analysis of placental villi from recurrent pregnancy loss patients with copy number variations revealed reduced expression of KAT5 and acetylated H2A.Z. This study demonstrates that the conserved KAT5–H2A.Z acetylation pathway safeguards chromosomal stability in trophoblast cells, supporting placenta development and successful pregnancy.

Article.Title: Direct observations of submesoscale turbulence driving mesoscale eddy leakage
Article.Authors: Cao H.; Jing Z.; Fox-Kemper B.; Qiu B.; Lacasce J.; Yan T.
Article.Abstract: Understanding oceanic transport and material fate has long relied on observations that primarily resolve mesoscale, largely geostrophic flows, leaving the role of submesoscale turbulence comparatively unobserved and poorly understood. Here, using new high-resolution drifter-cluster experiments with closest initial spacings below 1 km, we provide direct Lagrangian observations of how submesoscale turbulence modifies mesoscale eddy coherence and transport pathways. The clustered drifters resolve intense, transient ageostrophic motions that are fundamentally absent from geostrophic descriptions of eddy behavior. Analyzed in an eddy-centered reference frame, the observations reveal pronounced submesoscale-driven radial dispersion that facilitates substantial water-mass exchange between the eddy core and its periphery in both the mixed layer and the subsurface. Quantitative estimates indicate submesoscale horizontal diffusivity of O (10 to 100) m 2 /s and a nonlocal dispersion regime across submesoscales. These results challenge the traditional view of mesoscale eddies as coherent structures containing a persistent water mass, with broad implications for interpreting and predicting the transport and fate of tracers in the ocean.

Article.Title: Morphological intelligence for dynamic aerial interactions
Article.Authors: Jiang Y.; Li J.; Meng S.; Zhou Y.; He B.; Paik J.
Article.Abstract: Biological flyers achieve ecological dominance not through flight alone, but by seamlessly integrating aerial locomotion with forceful physical interactions, including snatching prey, perching on irregular surfaces, and operating across diverse media. Translating this agility into aerial robotics demands reconciling a fundamental conflict: impulsive, high-force actions destabilize the flight platform. Here, we present a bio-inspired unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) equipped with a mechanically intelligent impulsive limb that resolves this tradeoff through physical decoupling. An asymmetric bistable impulse module delivers a 2.3-fold extension within 70 ms, while a soft-linkage architecture reduces the transmission of impulsive interaction forces to the airframe. For the tested seven-segment configuration, intrinsic geometric tolerance corresponds to a passive vertical accommodation range of approximately 70% of the fully deployed arm length, reducing the need for precise altitude regulation within the tested range. We demonstrate the system’s multimodal capacity through dynamic in-flight snatching, energy-efficient perching, high-impact solid fracture, and cross-medium capture in viscous fluids, establishing a new paradigm for UAVs executing physically demanding tasks in complex environments.

Article.Title: Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains
Article.Authors: Gerdes P.; Karlsson O.; Garza R.; Atacho D.; Hsieh P.; Prajapati B.; Yoo D.; Muralidharan C.; Adami A.; Davis-Hansson C.; Johansson E.; Sharma Y.; Castilla-Vallmanya L.; West W.; Vinod M.; Domitrovic L.; Johansson P.; Johansson J.; Douse C.; Kanduri C.; Jern P.; Eichler E.; Jakobsson J.

CRISPR-mediated deletion of this PTERV1 restored LINC00662 expression in chimpanzee induced pluripotent stem cells. Article.Title: Structural basis for start codon selection by eIF5-mimic proteins
Article.Authors: Zottig X.; Huang C.; Seraj Z.; Grigorieff N.; Korostelev A.
Article.Abstract: Start codon selection extensively regulates the cellular proteome and is implicated in cancer and other diseases. Cryo-EM structures of 48 S preinitiation complexes (PICs) reveal 5MP1 bound at the A site of the small ribosomal subunit. 5MPs act as initiation factors that stabilize an open PIC conformation, promoting mRNA scanning and inhibiting initiation at suboptimal start codons. We propose to designate 5MP as eIF1S (eukaryotic initiation factor 1 scanning). These findings reveal the structural basis for proteome modulation by 5MPs and may help correct dysregulated translation in disease.
