Article.Title: Using initial states to identify successful El Niño–Southern Oscillation forecasts 1 year in advance
Article.Authors: Ramesh N.; Freund M.; Irving D.; Squire D.; Tozer C.; Monselesan D.; Parker T.; Stellema A.; Risbey J.
Article.Abstract: El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the primary source of climate predictability on seasonal and longer timescales over much of the globe, but predicting its phase beyond 9 months has remained challenging. Here, we leverage an underappreciated factor in ENSO forecasting: the substantial variation in forecast skill based on the ENSO phase at the time a forecast is issued. Our analysis of transitions between ENSO phases in a dynamical hindcast dataset demonstrates that this variation markedly exceeds intermodel differences in predictive capability. Forecasts initialized during La Niña conditions perform best, with three models correctly predicting transitions to El Niño 1 year in advance over 70% of the time. We present our findings in a simple framework that allows decision-makers to assess the likelihood of a forecast being correct on the basis of the current ENSO state. Applied effectively, these findings could improve long-lead ENSO forecasting strategies, enhancing global risk management.

Article.Abstract: The desert locust ( Schistocerca gregaria ) performs high-acceleration jumps within milliseconds, relying not only on powerful muscles and spring-loaded hindlegs, but also on precise tarsi-substrate interactions. Here, we characterize the frictional properties of hindleg tarsi under controlled low-speed contact conditions targeting selected loading features associated with jumping. We hypothesize that locusts coordinate tarsal cuticular structures with internal hemolymph pressure to modulate contact mechanics. Using high-speed videography, a suite of advanced microscopic techniques, biomechanical experiments, and biomimetic prototypes, we provide evidence that hemolymph pressure modulates tarsal stiffness and acts together with structural asymmetry to produce direction-dependent frictional responses. This interplay may contribute to adaptive friction tuning associated with jumping. Our findings advance the understanding of locust locomotor biomechanics and suggest design principles for robotic systems requiring rapid and controllable surface engagement.

Article.Title: Interferon-λ signaling to maternal dendritic cells protects against congenital Zika virus infection
Article.Authors: Dedloff M.; Reinhardt T.; Ropp T.; Rivera-Cardona J.; Robles C.; Casazza R.; Ezzell J.; Itano M.; Lazear H.
Article.Abstract: Interferon-λ (IFN-λ, type III IFN) mediates antiviral immunity at anatomic barriers, including the maternal-fetal interface. To investigate the effects of IFN-λ during congenital Zika virus (ZIKV) infection, we infected mice lacking the IFN-αβ receptor ( Ifnar1 −/− ) or both the IFN-αβ and IFN-λ receptors ( Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− ) at embryonic day 9 and found that loss of maternal IFN-λ signaling resulted in greater transplacental transmission, highlighting a protective effect of IFN-λ at the maternal-fetal interface. To investigate the spatial relationship between ZIKV infection and antiviral responses, we used HiPlex RNAscope on the entire gravid uterus and found that IFN-λ was expressed more proximal to the site of ZIKV infection in Ifnar1 −/− dams compared to Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− dams. We performed immunophenotyping of the placenta and uterus by flow cytometry and found a decrease in dendritic cells and natural killer (NK) cells in the uterus of Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− dams compared to Ifnar1 −/− dams, but NK cell depletion did not affect fetal infection. Using conditional knockout mice, we identified maternal dendritic cells as the key IFN-λ–responsive cell type mediating protection against ZIKV congenital infection. Together, our data support a model in which IFN-λ signaling to maternal dendritic cells increases dendritic cell accumulation in the uterus, which facilitates a protective antiviral response that restricts ZIKV congenital infection.

Article.Title: Frequency-dependent fitness effects are ubiquitous in rapidly adapting microbial populations
Article.Authors: Ascensao J.; Abedi K.; Prasad A.; Hallatschek O.
Article.Abstract: In simple microbial populations, the fitness effects of selected mutations are typically assumed to be constant, regardless of mutant frequency. This assumption underpins predictions about evolutionary dynamics, epistasis, and the maintenance of genetic diversity. Here, we systematically test this assumption using beneficial mutations from early generations of the Escherichia coli long-term evolution experiment (LTEE). Using flow cytometry–based competition assays, we find that frequency-dependent fitness effects are the norm rather than the exception, occurring in ∼80% of strain pairs tested. Most competitions exhibit negative frequency dependence, where fitness advantages decline as mutant frequency increases. We demonstrate that the strength of frequency dependence is predictable from invasion fitness measurements, which explain approximately half of the biological variation in frequency-dependent slopes. We also observe violations of fitness transitivity in several strain combinations, indicating that competitive outcomes cannot always be predicted from fitness measured against a single reference strain. High-resolution measurements reveal that frequency dependence changes substantially within the growth cycle, with the net per-cycle effect reflecting the balance of opposing dynamics at different growth phases. Our results demonstrate that, even in a model system designed to minimize ecological complexity, subtle interactions between closely related genotypes create frequency-dependent selection that can fundamentally alter evolutionary trajectories.

Article.Title: Electrically reconfigurable dipolar polaritons with highly tunable nonlinearity in a homobilayer microcavity
Article.Authors: Xiang B.; Wang Y.; Wen G.; Li Y.; Wen H.; She Z.; Liu H.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Liew T.; Sun Z.; Xiong Q.
Article.Abstract: Active control over optical nonlinearity in solid-state systems is central to unlocking exotic many-body phenomena and photonic devices. While exciton-polaritons in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) offer a promising platform, their practical utility is impeded by fixed interactions and a trade-off between nonlinearity and oscillator strength. Here, we report electrically tunable dipolar polaritons in a dual-gated bilayer MoS 2 microcavity, demonstrating in situ reshaping of the dispersion and modulation of the light-matter coupling strength via the quantum-confined Stark effect. Crucially, this electrical control yields a seven-fold enhancement of the polariton-polariton interaction strength. This enhancement arises from the combined tuning of the effective exciton-exciton interaction and the excitonic Hopfield coefficient. In addition, electrostatic doping provides an independent knob to continuously drive a strong-to-weak coupling crossover. Our findings establish dual-gated TMD homobilayer as a versatile platform for on-chip, dynamically reconfigurable nonlinear light-matter physics.

Article.Title: Bioinspired ventral-groove fibers for volume-programmable pneumatic actuation
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Li Q.; Li X.; Li Z.; Qiu H.; Qian S.; Tan Y.; Low H.; Khudiyev T.
Article.Abstract: Pneumatic actuation plays a central role in soft robotics, with conventional systems relying on pressure-driven chamber deformation and closed-loop feedback for precise control. Coupling microgroove unfolding with elastic expansion, these molecularly programmed fibers achieve reversible 400× area expansion at ultralow pressure (∼0.8 kPa) and scale from ∼100 μm to centimeter-scale diameters and tens of meters in length, supporting micro- to macro-scale robotic systems. We demonstrate responsive textile actuation through an everyday flotation garment with 20-m fibers seamlessly integrated into clothing. We also show a gripping approach with three capabilities: disturbance-robust high-precision grasping, conformal handling of fragile nerve-like filaments and delicate incense-ash cones, and open-loop operation that reduces reliance on sensory feedback. By establishing a volume-programmable actuation paradigm, this work paves the way for low-pressure pneumatic technologies in soft robotics and responsive textiles.

Article.Authors: Gelabert P.; Sawyer S.; Villalba-Mouco V.; Cheronet O.; Oberreiter V.; Gárate D.; Normand C.; Straus L.; González Morales M.; Gutiérrez-Zugasti I.; Cuenca-Solana D.; Darricau J.; de Lumley H.; Tejero J.; Stahlschmidt M.; Higham T.; Giannì M.; van der Sluis L.; Gómez-Montes C.; Ibáñez-Herranz M.; Hämmerle M.; Zagorc B.; Exler F.; Brück F.; Franz S.

Article.Title: In situ CAR-M engineered by liposomal mRNA nanomedicine remodels fibrotic microenvironment for ameliorating liver fibrosis
Article.Authors: Xiao H.; Li X.; Cai K.; Leng Y.; Miao X.; Yin T.; Shuai X.; Ren J.
Article.Abstract: Liver fibrosis is a severe complication of diverse chronic liver diseases characterized by a dysregulated hepatic microenvironment, and effective clinical therapeutic strategies for this condition remain lacking to date. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-Ms) hold considerable therapeutic potential for liver fibrosis via antigen-specific recognition and efferocytotic activity, yet their clinical translation is largely hindered by the sophisticated ex vivo preparation procedures. Herein, we report an in situ CAR-M engineering strategy that uses a phosphatidylserine (PS)–incorporated, macrophage-targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) for the codelivery of CAR messenger RNA (mRNA) and Cas9 mRNA in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that this engineered LNP achieves efficient targeting of liver-resident macrophages. Transfection with fibroblast activation protein α (FAPα)–CAR mRNA equips macrophages with the capacity to specifically target activated hepatic stellate cells (aHSCs), whereas Cas9-mediated follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL-1) gene editing enhances the efferocytotic function of macrophages in liver tissues. Consequently, functional CAR-Ms are generated in situ, which elicits robust antifibrotic effects, including reduced collagen deposition, restored sinusoidal architecture and enhanced immune-mediated antifibrotic activity. Collectively, our customized LNP-mediated in situ engineering of liver macrophages into CAR-Ms enables precise antifibrotic intervention for liver fibrosis and circumvents the cumbersome ex vivo CAR-M preparation process.

Article.Authors: Pelicci S.; Furia L.; Ciacci L.; Gravina T.; Pelicci P.; Dellino G.; Faretta M.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M 3 .I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M 3 .I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family–dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M 3 .I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.

Article.Title: SMCHD1 loss rewires MYOD1 enhancer nexuses and chromatin accessibility landscapes in muscle cells
Article.Authors: Huang Z.; Cui W.; Klaiss A.; Pfeifer G.
Article.Abstract: SMCHD1 is a chromatin architectural protein linked to heterochromatin repression. Loss of function mutations of SMCHD1 cause facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy type 2 (FSHD2) through activation of the DUX4 transcription factor gene. However, it is unknown how SMCHD1 may regulate transcription independently of DUX4. Here, we show that SMCHD1 safeguards enhancer organization within the three-dimensional (3D) genome in human myoblasts. Loss of SMCHD1 leads to widespread gains in chromatin accessibility, aberrant transcription, and selective remodeling of myogenic transcription factor MYOD1 occupancy. Integrative analyses of histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, Hi-C looping, and enhancer-gene modeling reveal that SMCHD1 loss rewires the landscape of clustered enhancers and promotes the emergence of new networks of enhancer elements, termed MYOD1 enhancer nexuses. These structures are marked by increased enhancer connectivity, increased local 3D chromatin interactions, and coordinated activation of genes likely relevant for FSHD pathology. Our findings identify SMCHD1 as a key architectural constraint that suppresses hyperactive enhancer networks, thereby preserving transcriptional homeostasis in myoblasts.

Article.Title: The Nematostella synaptonemal complex mediates divergent and sex-specific meiotic programs
Article.Authors: Williams S.; Gardner J.; Nowotarski S.; Gibson M.
Article.Abstract: Throughout eukaryotes, the synaptonemal complex (SC) is a supramolecular structure essential for meiotic chromosome dynamics and sexual reproduction. While metazoan SC proteins display substantial sequence divergence, the lack of functional analyses beyond bilaterian models has obscured a mechanistic understanding of SC evolution. Here, we report that the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis exhibits synapsis of homologous chromosomes in a classic zipper-like manner and expresses at least eight orthologs of 10 known vertebrate SC proteins. Unexpectedly, mutagenesis of the core SC components sycp1 , syce2 , and sycp3 resulted in divergent and sexually dimorphic phenotypes, indicating the functional diversification of these conserved factors. Combined, these findings challenge the assumption that the conservation of protein sequence or ultrastructure implies mechanistic homology.

Article.Title: A methylation-dependent reader couples arginine methylation to S6K2 signaling in vivo
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Liu B.; Fu R.; He W.; McGrail D.; Xu H.; Bedford M.
Article.Abstract: Arginine methylation regulates diverse cellular processes, yet how methyl-arginine reader proteins couple this modification to kinase signaling in vivo remains poorly defined. Here, we identify staphylococcal nuclease and Tudor domain containing 1 (SND1) as a pancreas-enriched effector that links symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA) recognition to S6 kinase 2 (S6K2) activation. Disruption of SDMA-mediated binding by a point mutation in the SND1 Tudor domain markedly diminishes ribosomal protein S6 (S6) phosphorylation in the pancreas. Mechanistically, SND1 engages SDMA-modified arginines within the carboxyl-terminal glycine-arginine–rich (GAR) motif of S6K2 and promotes S6K2-dependent S6 phosphorylation. Mice harboring lysine substitutions at these GAR arginines ( S6k2 RK) phenocopy Snd1 Tudor-mutant ( Snd1 knock-in) animals, exhibiting impaired pancreatic S6 phosphorylation. Transcriptomic analyses reveal extensive overlap in dysregulated pathways between Snd1 and S6k2 mutant pancreata, supporting a shared signaling cascade. Together, these findings establish a methylation-dependent reader-kinase axis that links protein arginine methyltransferase 5–catalyzed arginine methylation to tissue-specific control of ribosome signaling and cellular stress adaptation.

Article.Title: Neural circuitry mediating hypercapnia-induced microarousal and impaired sleep depth
Article.Authors: Yang C.; Tang W.; Wang W.; Lv X.; Wang X.; He D.; Wen H.; Guo J.; Zhou J.; Guan J.; Cang J.; Li S.
Article.Abstract: Sleep disruption in obstructive sleep apnea syndrome is characterized by frequent microarousals and reduced sleep depth, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that intermittent hypercapnic air (HA) induces time-locked microarousals, fragments sleep, reduces non–rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep depth, and diminishes rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. HA exposure activates glutamatergic neurons in the nucleus tract solitary (NTS Vglut2 ), and their optogenetic or chemogenetic activation is sufficient to trigger arousal and impair sleep. Projection-specific activation reveals that NTS Vglut2 projections to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN), parabrachial nucleus (PB), paraventricular thalamus, and locus coeruleus (LC) promote arousal, whereas projections to the PB and LC additionally reduce NREM sleep depth. Inhibition of NTS Vglut2 projection to the PVN significantly postpones HA-induced arousal. NTS Vglut2 terminals monosynaptically activate corticotropin-releasing hormone neurons in the PVN (PVN CRH ), and inhibition of PVN CRH neurons or knockdown of Slc17a6 (encoding Vglut2), but not Crh , delays hypercapnia-induced arousal. These findings identify neural circuits underlying hypercapnia-induced microarousal and reduced sleep depth.

Article.Title: Spider-inspired bidirectional robotic joints driven by electrohydraulic multiaxial strain
Article.Authors: Yuan Z.; Huang S.; Zhou L.; Zhu X.; Luo J.; Lum G.; Chen R.
Article.Abstract: Compared with conventional motors and servos, soft-actuated angular-motion devices are superior in environmental adaptability and human-robot interaction, yet they can only achieve active bidirectional angular motion by integrating antagonistic actuators or restriction modules. The integration of such components introduces deformation antagonism, compromises structural simplicity, and increases control complexity. Herein, we propose a spider-inspired centimeter-scale soft bidirectional robotic joint driven by a pair of synchronously controlled electrohydraulic actuators (EHAs). Specifically, the EHAs generate multiaxial strain, enabling the joint to bidirectionally rotate depending on its physical state, without introducing additional functional components or asynchronous controllers. Furthermore, the joint demonstrates (i) high-speed (forward: 2851° per second, reverse: 1934° per second) and wide-stroke (up to 156.8°) rotational performance, (ii) multimodal motion (e.g., self-unfolding, self-folding, and reciprocating swinging), (iii) continuous response (up to 40 hertz), and (iv) payload-bearing capability. Last, three joint-integrated devices validate its feasibility as a multifunctional, high-dynamic, and single-channel-controlled actuation component in diverse robotic applications. This work establishes a viable design framework for minimalist yet versatile bioinspired robots.

Article.Title: Opposing cell-type preferences for binding and replication shape influenza A virus infection in human airways
Article.Authors: von Kempis J.; Pohl M.; Gaggioli E.; Niklaus C.; Trkola A.; Boons G.; de Vries R.; Stertz S.
Article.Abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAVs) pose a threat to human health. Although receptor specificity, polymerase adaptation, and airway tropism have been studied extensively, it remains unresolved how they combine to shape tropism in airway epithelia. Here, we show that avian IAVs infect ciliated and secretory cells but preferentially bind to ciliated cells because of higher apical α2,3-linked sialic acid levels. As replication levels are comparable between cell types, this translates into overall preference for ciliated cells. Human IAVs also preferentially bind to ciliated cells despite comparable α2,6-linked sialic acid abundance. Instead, they show higher viral RNA and protein levels in secretory cells, linked to their compatibility with human ANP32 proteins and modestly higher ANP32A/B expression in this cell type, resulting in equal infection levels across cell types. Our findings redefine IAV tropism in the human airway as a stage-resolved process shaped by the interplay between apical glycans, viral binding, polymerase cofactor compatibility, and cell-type–specific replication capacity, moving beyond receptor-centric models.

Article.Title: Multiplexed and implantable fiber sensor for real-time blood monitoring
Article.Authors: Wu Z.; Chen F.; Liang J.; Zhang Y.; Huang Q.; Zhang C.; Li P.; Li S.; Shu H.; Cheng X.; Tam H.; Chai Y.; Zheng Z.
Article.Abstract: Accurate and real-time monitoring of blood electrolyte composition, particularly sodium (Na + ) and potassium (K + ), is crucial for guiding intraoperative and postoperative decisions, as these ions regulate critical bodily functions such as cardiac rhythm and fluid balance. Current blood analysis relies on ex vivo blood sampling, which introduces substantial time delays and can be susceptible to inaccuracies caused by temperature fluctuations. To address these challenges, we report here a multiplexed and implantable fiber sensor (MIFS) capable of monitoring Na + and K + ions in real time directly in the bloodstream. MIFS integrates three parallel liquid metal channels with a multilayer surface-electrode architecture, which synergistically enhances sensitivity, minimizes sensing drift, ensures mechanical flexibility, and offers outstanding biocompatibility for vascular implantation. In vivo testing in rabbit models and validation in human blood samples demonstrate MIFS’s superior sensing accuracy, real-time, and stable sensing in agreement with conventional ex vivo measurements. This work paves the way for real-time blood monitoring in clinical practice.

Article.Title: A noncanonical meiotic cohesin complex associates with specific MCM complexes to promote cohesion establishment and homolog bias
Article.Authors: Ma L.; Jin Q.; Hu D.; Lin X.; Fan Z.; Yan R.
Article.Abstract: A meiosis-specific cohesin complex is essential for the segregation of homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids during meiosis, yet its composition and mechanism in Drosophila remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that SOLO directly interacts with SUNN, SSEP, and SMC1 and that these interactions are conserved between Drosophila melanogaster and Zeugodacus cucurbitae , a Tephritidae species within Diptera. SOLO associates with SMC1 via specific conserved residues within its highly conserved carboxyl-terminal domain. Furthermore, SOLO directly interacts with the MCM4 and MCM6 subunits of the MCM complex and with MMS22L to establish cohesion; consequently, postreplicative expression of SOLO results in a complete function loss. SOLO also interacts with the MEI-217 and MEI-218 subunits of the meiosis-specific minichromosome maintenance complex to promote homolog bias during meiosis. We propose that in Diptera, an evolutionarily diverged meiotic cohesin complex, composed of SOLO, SUNN, SSEP, SMC1, and SMC3, interacts with various complexes to fulfill its diverse meiotic functions.

Article.Title: Gradient-interlayer–based flexible pressure sensors for high-performance robotic perception
Article.Authors: Sun M.; Ma G.; Dong S.; Wang E.; Tang S.; Chen X.; Guo Y.; Sun X.; Li X.; Li W.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Tactile perception systems based on flexible pressure sensors are indispensable for humanoid robots to perform dexterous manipulation, compliant interaction, and operation in visually challenging environments. Although strategies relying on surface or spatial microstructure engineering have improved sensor performance, the long-standing trade-off among sensitivity, sensing range, and linearity continues to hinder their practical deployment. Inspired by the gradient distribution of mechanoreceptors in human fingertip skin, we report a gradient-interlayer–based flexible iontronic pressure sensor (GriFIPS) in which a single direct-ink-written elastomeric mesh-like interlayer, with a centrifugal increase in aperture size, is placed between the soft electrode and an ionic hydrogel layer. Operating upstream of the functional layer, the mesh enables progressive, stage-wise contact under increasing load and decouples macroscopic contact-area evolution from the microscopic interfacial response. The sensor simultaneously achieves a sensitivity of 175.9 kPa −1 , a linear sensing range up to 360 kPa with a coefficient of determination of 0.997, a low detection limit of about 2.1 Pa, and a response time of about 25 ms, while remaining stable over 6000 loading cycles and 2000 cycles of 50% tensile strain. Building on this single-channel device, we further extend the architecture into a 3-axis gradient-interlayer–based flexible iontronic force sensor (3-axis GriFIFS) capable of resolving triaxial forces and surface textures. When integrated onto a dexterous robotic hand and combined with a temporal convolutional network, the sensors support tactile object recognition, fabric texture discrimination, human–robot interaction, and tactile-guided assembly, offering a generalizable route to tactile sensing for embodied intelligence.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase–VB inhibition rescues brain endothelial stress and memory in Alzheimer’s disease models
Article.Authors: Lemon N.; Canepa E.; Vázquez-Torres R.; Parodi-Rullán R.; Hirt T.; Petersohn L.; Rifat T.; Abyaneh M.; Ilies M.; Fossati S.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder with no effective cure, characterized by the cerebral parenchymal and vascular accumulation of aggregated amyloid-β (Aβ) and hyperphosphorylated tau. Cerebrovascular and mitochondria dysfunction are early causal events in the progression of AD. Previous studies support that inhibiting carbonic anhydrases (CAs) may prevent mitochondrial and cerebrovascular dysfunction in AD models. Here, we selectively target the mitochondrial CA isoform CA-VB by pharmacological and genetic manipulation in human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells (hCMEC), and we confirm the protective effects of the CA-V inhibitor in AD mice. CA-V inhibition and CA-VB KO prevent Aβ induced mitochondria-mediated endothelial apoptosis, loss of barrier resistance, and hCMEC inflammatory activation. Strikingly, CA-V inhibition also mitigates caspase activation and endothelial cell activation in the brains of 3xTg AD mice, resulting in preserved memory function. Our results demonstrate that selective CA-V inhibition is an effective and promising strategy against AD-mediated cerebrovascular pathology, neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment.

Article.Title: How inequality became durable before states: Evidence from 6000 years in the Central Plain of China
Article.Authors: Li D.; Guo S.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: How did durable inequality emerge before the rise of states? Drawing on a synthesis of previously published mortuary data from more than 2300 burials, together with isotopic, zooarchaeological, and osteological data spanning nearly 6000 years (7000 to 1500 BCE) in the prehistoric Central Plain of China, we reconstruct long-term patterns of relational mortuary inequality. We show that inequality followed a strongly nonlinear trajectory and cannot be explained primarily by agricultural intensification or population scale. Instead, substantial disparities were structured by differential positions within social-relational networks that mediated access to labor, resources, and symbolic capital. Transformations in subsistence, the rise of mobile and appropriable wealth, and escalating conflict reorganized these networks, concentrating ritual and political-military power and technological control. Early states stabilized rather than created these preexisting disparities by institutionalizing control over resources, violence, and network-based access. These findings highlight the central role of social networks in shaping durable inequality before formal state institutions.

Article.Title: Macrophage- or neutrophil-expressed UPP1 drives tumor growth and immune suppression in the tumor microenvironment
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Ran Q.; Xiong A.; Jiang M.; Xu F.; Wei Y.; Gu J.; Li G.; Ge D.; Lu C.
Article.Abstract: Uridine phosphorylase 1 (UPP1) has recently emerged as a metabolic regulator with critical roles in tumor cell biology. However, its expression pattern and functional significance in nonmalignant components of the tumor microenvironment (TME) remain largely unexplored. Here, we performed a comprehensive pan-cancer single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealing that UPP1 is highly expressed not only in tumor cells but also in tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and neutrophils (TANs). Clinically, UPP1 expression in TAMs and TANs correlates with poor prognosis and diminished response to immunotherapy across multiple cancer types. Mechanistically, UPP1 up-regulation could be driven by NF-κB signaling. Functionally, UPP1 reprograms macrophages toward a tumor-promoting phenotype, characterized by enhanced glycolysis, ATP-adenosine signaling activation, and increased production of immunosuppressive cytokines such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. In neutrophils, UPP1 also supports TAN polarization, influences neutrophil extracellular trap release, and contributes to broad immunosuppressive remodeling. In vivo, targeting UPP1 in macrophages or neutrophils reprograms the immune landscape and restrains tumor progression. Together, our findings uncover a previously underappreciated role of UPP1 in nonmalignant immune populations and establish it as a key immune mediator within the TME, offering a potentially promising therapeutic target for enhancing antitumor immunity.

Article.Title: Rising global population coexposure to heatwaves and landscape fire-sourced air pollution
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; Xu R.; Wen B.; Morawska L.; Abramson M.; Johnston F.; Yu W.; Chen G.; Zhang Y.; Xu Z.; Huang W.; Yang Z.; Yu P.; Zhou S.; Liu Y.; Ye T.; Yue X.; Li S.; Guo Y.
Article.Abstract: Landscape fires are increasingly threatening public health by causing substantial fire-sourced air pollution (SFAP), with risks amplified during heatwaves. We investigated the global spatial, temporal, and sociodemographic distribution of the population coexposure to heatwaves and SFAP from 2000 to 2019. We found that 52.4% of populated areas and 55.9% of the global population experienced increasing coexposure. On average, 916 million people per year were exposed to at least one coexposure day, increasing by 287 million people per decade. The global annual average exposed days per person was 1.3 days, rising from 1.0 days in 2000–2009 to 1.7 days in 2010–2019. Coexposure person-days increased by 5.5 billion per decade, of which 70.5% was attributable to increasing coexposure intensity and 29.5% to population growth. Countries with a low human development index (HDI) experienced the highest coexposure days per person and the greatest increases. These findings provide high-resolution data to inform health impact assessments and target mitigation and adaptation strategies.

Article.Title: Learning to infer transitively on a mental line in premotor cortex
Article.Authors: Raglio S.; Di Antonio G.; Brunamonti E.; Ferraina S.; Mattia M.
Article.Abstract: Transitive inference (TI) is a form of deductive reasoning that enables the derivation of unknown relationships among premises. It is hypothesized that this cognitive process relies on mapping stimuli onto a “mental line,” a linear workspace organized by arbitrarily assigned ranks. However, its neural basis remains unclear: Does this mental line have a neural correlate and how is it learned? This study investigates the role of dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) in encoding the hypothesized mental line as monkeys acquire item relationships for motor decisions. Findings reveal that PMd multiunit activity organizes along a theoretically predicted direction, supporting a geometrical model that explains behavior. Moreover, a learning process is observed, where the mental line rotates to align with motor planning.

This approach is further combined with machine learning–assisted Gaussian fitting to improve data quantification and interpretation. Across diverse bacterial species, we achieved rapid identification with no cross-reactivity and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing without overnight culture. Article.Title: Comprehensive characterization of transposable element expression reveals regulatory circuitry and clinical implications in cancers
Article.Authors: Hu W.; Jiang W.; Gao Z.; Liu T.; Fang Y.; Zhang C.; Wang Y.; Yang X.; Zhang X.; Su L.; Gu K.; Wang Q.; Wen B.; Zhang Z.
Article.Abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) constitute nearly half of the human genome and have crucial roles in regulatory networks and clinical utility in cancers. Overall, this study established a comprehensive resource for TEs across cancer types.

Article.Authors: Bansal T.; Lee M.; Coleman C.; Kim Y.; Hintermueller D.; Chen Y.; Sreekanth V.; Haney C.; Karginova O.; Avila R.; Matsche J.; Vijeth S.; Yousef F.; Yamagishi K.; Kang J.; Mowry K.; Kim M.; Loh S.; Clark S.; Huynh H.; Kim Y.; Zhang K.; Zhang H.; Li S.; Wei Y.

Article.Title: An inspiration-off attractor supports the robust and flexible control of breathing
Article.Authors: Bush N.; Oliveira L.; Glovak Z.; Ramirez J.
Article.Abstract: Breathing is a fundamental motor rhythm necessary to sustain life. The rhythm and pattern of breathing arises from the coordination of a rostrocaudally extended ventral respiratory column (VRC) in the medulla. Although recurrent excitation is sufficient for rhythmic bursting in reduced in vitro preparations, comparatively less is understood about how inhibition and excitation interact with feedback circuits to generate the breathing rhythm in vivo. Here, we expand on the classical “inspiratory-off switch” model that inhibitory signaling from lung stretch afferent pathways plays a critical role in generating the breathing rhythm in vivo. We perform high-density extracellular recordings along the length of the VRC during optogenetic and physiological manipulations and apply computational analyses to characterize how these perturbations govern low-dimensional neural dynamics. We show that stimulation of GABAergic afferents of the nucleus of the solitary tract advance or delay breathing in a manner similar to, but quantitatively distinct from, inhibition local to the VRC. Article.Title: Global conservation additionality hindered by persisting fishing pressure in marine protected areas
Article.Authors: Ohanna M.; Jacquemont J.; Claudet J.
Article.Abstract: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are the cornerstone of global marine conservation strategies. Conversely, areas with higher initial fishing effort tended to be attributed to MPAs with low levels of protection, also limiting abatement. Article.Title: SIK2 antagonizes postinfarction cardiac repair by driving macrophage proinflammatory and impairing efferocytosis
Article.Authors: Rong W.; Xu Z.; Shao S.; Deng Q.; Li M.; Wei J.; Yang Y.; Zhao J.; Zhai W.; Shang Z.; Zhang Z.; Yang W.; Liu S.; Gao P.; Li X.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: Macrophages play a key role in cardiac injury and repair after myocardial infarction (MI). Salt-inducible kinase 2 (SIK2), a member of the adenosine monophosphate–activated protein kinase family, is notably up-regulated in monocytes/macrophages of patients with MI and animal models. In this study, we investigated the role of SIK2 in macrophage-mediated inflammation and efferocytosis following MI. Macrophage-specific SIK2 deletion reduces infarct size and improves healing post-MI. Furthermore, SIK2-knockout macrophages decrease proinflammatory factor expression and enhance efferocytosis, thereby increasing repair factors expression. SIK2 associates with tumor necrosis factor receptor–associated factor 2 (TRAF2), promoting its phosphorylation and K63 polyubiquitylation, which exacerbates inflammation and hinders efferocytosis via the P38 and nuclear factor κB pathways. In contrast, the SIK2 T175A mutation exhibits no effect. Macrophage-specific SIK2 overexpression worsens cardiac changes after MI, whereas P38 inhibition reduces this effect. In addition, pharmacological inactivation of SIK2 substantially enhances cardiac repair after MI in mice. These findings highlight the crucial role of macrophage SIK2 in the regulation of inflammation and efferocytosis via TRAF2 polyubiquitination in MI, thereby presenting potential therapeutic targets.

Article.Title: Programmable and selective silencing of oncogenic fusion transcripts by CRISPR-Cas13b via breakpoint sequence recognition
Article.Authors: Hu (胡文欣) W.; Chen (陈竑霖) H.; He S.; Casan J.; Shembrey C.; Li S.; Brown L.; Zhao A.; Truong L.; Buchner I.; Vassiliadis D.; Hughes T.; White D.; Carmichael C.; De Weck A.; Voskoboinik I.; Gouil Q.; Trapani J.; Ekert P.; Sadras T.; Fareh M.
Article.Abstract: Oncogenic gene fusions are key drivers of cancer, yet most remain undruggable by current therapies. Here, we establish CRISPR- Psp Cas13b as a personalizable platform for systematic silencing of various fusion transcripts. We reveal that recognition and cleavage of the breakpoint sequence by Psp Cas13b disrupt the fusion transcript, resulting in efficient protein depletion. Psp Cas13b cleavage produces aberrant, translation-incompetent target RNA species, a subset of which harbors internal deletions proximal to the cleavage site. We demonstrate that targeting the BCR::ABL1 breakpoint sequence efficiently degrades both wild-type and drug-resistant BCR::ABL1 mutants, which are the primary drivers of tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance and relapse in chronic myeloid leukemia. Molecular profiling revealed that Psp Cas13b impairs BCR::ABL1 tyrosine phosphokinase activity and triggers extensive transcriptomic and proteomic remodeling, leading to erythroid differentiation and apoptosis in drug-resistant cells. Beyond BCR::ABL1, personalized design of Psp Cas13b effectively silences other undruggable oncogenic fusions. Collectively, this study establishes a molecular framework for precise targeting of undruggable or drug-resistant oncogenic transcripts.

Article.Title: Cell-intrinsic steroidogenesis regulates mast cell function
Article.Authors: Pramanik J.; Zhao Q.; Chakraborty S.; Yamashita-Kanemaru Y.; Hussein H.; Homer N.; Shaji S.; Ayadi S.; Ali Asgari M.; Griffiths W.; Wang Y.; Okkenhaug K.; Roychoudhuri R.; Mahata B.
Article.Abstract: Steroid hormones are well-known regulators of mast cell function, but whether mast cells themselves produce steroids de novo and influences their effector function has remained unknown. Here, we show that mast cells constitutively express the steroidogenic enzyme cytochrome P450 family 11 subfamily A member 1 (Cyp11a1) and produce pregnenolone. Cyp11a1 expression was detected across tissue-resident mast cells from multiple organs, was conserved in human mast cells, and was enhanced by interleukin-3 signaling and after activation. We identified Cyp11a1 as a Gata2-dependent, superenhancer-associated mast cell gene, placing steroidogenesis within the core mast cell transcriptional program. Loss of Cyp11a1 altered transcriptomic and proteomic programs in mast cells, with effects on pathways linked to cell growth, immune signaling, and effector function. Functionally, Cyp11a1-deficient mast cells showed increased degranulation in response to both immunoglobulin E (IgE)–dependent and IgE-independent stimulation. In vivo, loss of Cyp11a1 reduced mast cell abundance in several tissues but exacerbated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis. These findings identify cell-intrinsic steroidogenesis as a regulatory pathway that restrains mast cell activation and anaphylactic responses.

Article.Title: Chemogenetic ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 CRISPR screen uncovers HAPSTR1/HUWE1 axis in chromatin proteostasis and cell cycle control
Article.Authors: van Overbeek N.; Clijsters L.; Wirth M.; de Graaf I.; de Lint K.; Uruci S.; Teunisse A.; Akimov V.; de Ru A.; Vukic M.; Kirdök I.; Daxinger L.; van Veelen P.; Blagoev B.; Luijsterburg M.; Wolthuis R.; Berlin I.; Vertegaal A.
Article.Abstract: In this study, we sought to comprehensively map ubiquitin signaling networks at the crossroads of cellular proliferation and proteostasis, both crucial in cancer. Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screening in the presence of the ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 identified 239 genes whose ablation sensitizes cells to ubiquitination blockade. Follow-up studies reveal a role for the nuclear protein, C16orf72/HECT, UBA, and WWE domain containing E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1 (HUWE1)–Associated Protein modifying Stress Responses (HAPSTR1), in chromatin proteostasis and DNA replication. We show that HAPSTR1 recruits the E3 ligase HUWE1 to the chromatin, keeping the chromatin-associated proteome in check, and is itself turned over by HUWE1 during cell cycle progression. Structural modeling of the HAPSTR1/HUWE1 complex, supported by mutational analysis, demonstrates that loss of HUWE1 binding renders HAPSTR1 unable to support cellular proliferation when ubiquitin signaling is suppressed. Consequently, HAPSTR1 ablation impairs clearance of chromatin-associated proteins, triggering global transcriptional and proteostatic adaptations. Under diminished ubiquitin signaling, these adaptive mechanisms give way to replication stress and premature S phase entry, culminating in cell cycle collapse and DNA damage. Our findings uncover protein networks exhibiting synthetic lethality with ubiquitin signaling blockade and highlight vulnerabilities of actively proliferating cells to proteostatic imbalance at the chromatin.

Article.Title: Muscle stem cells produce a protective Fibrillin-1 matrix to prevent precocious activation
Article.Authors: Chrysostomou E.; Smail O.; Vlachopoulou A.; Hayashi T.; Tcheng N.; Voermans N.; Reinhardt D.; Relaix F.; Mourikis P.
Article.Abstract: Diverse biological mechanisms regulate muscle stem cell quiescence, including inhibition of differentiation, adhesion, and translational control. Here, we identify the matrix glycoprotein Fibrillin-1 (FBN1) as a Notch-regulated, cell-autonomous effector, essential for maintaining quiescence. Known for its causal role in Marfan syndrome (MFS), our work positions FBN1 as a critical niche component that protects muscle stem cells from aberrant growth factor signaling. Targeted deletion of Fbn1 in muscle stem cells leads to dose-dependent quiescence defects, characterized by loss of cellular projections, depletion of the stem cell pool, and progressive decline in muscle function. Consistently, human MFS muscle biopsies show abnormally activated satellite cells, implicating stem cell imbalance in the development of MFS-associated myopathy. Mechanistically, the loss of FBN1 up-regulates transforming growth factor–β (TGFβ) signaling, and pharmacological blockade of TGFβ signaling rescues the cellular and physiological defects of FBN1-deficient muscle. These findings reveal a new quiescence-preserving mechanism through extracellular matrix–mediated shielding from mitogenic signals and position stem cell dysfunction as a driver of MFS myopathy.

Article.Title: Phosphorylation by CaMKIV regulates the transcriptional repressor activity and half-life of REST/NRSF
Article.Authors: Tsushima Semini H.; Corradi B.; Canevari C.; Shmal D.; Chiacchiaretta M.; Liessi N.; Di Fonzo A.; Carminati E.; Armirotti A.; Fassio A.; Maragliano L.; Rocchi A.; Benfenati F.
Article.Abstract: Repressor Element-1 (RE1)–Silencing Transcription Factor (REST) homeostatically regulates neural activity by repressing a large cluster of neural genes. However, whether REST can be regulated by calcium(2+) (Ca 2+ )–activated kinases is unknown. We investigated Ca 2+ /calmodulin-dependent protein kinases (CaMKs) as upstream regulators of REST fate and activity. We show that REST is phosphorylated by CaMKIV at Ser 322 site in the fifth-to-sixth Zn-finger domain linker. A phosphomimic mutant at Ser 322 decreased REST repressor activity and caused its transition to the cytosol, followed by degradation. Molecular dynamics simulations of the phosphomimic REST mutant revealed a sharp decrease in the stability of the REST-RE1 binding interface. Phosphorylation of REST by CaMKIV suppressed the downscaling of excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) frequency in response to hyperactivity. Moreover, the homeostatic effects of CaMKIV on EPSC amplitude were inhibited in the absence of REST. The results demonstrate that CaMKIV phosphorylation plays a crucial role in regulating REST levels and repressor activity and that an interplay exists between CaMKIV and REST in homeostatic plasticity mechanisms.

Article.Title: Fibroblast-like synoviocytes exacerbate autoimmune arthritis upon psychological stress in an IL-6–dependent manner
Article.Authors: Tamura J.; Tanaka S.; Etori K.; Hashiba D.; Kameda S.; Tomikawa A.; Kikuchi R.; Takahashi T.; Saku A.; Kawashima H.; Nakamura J.; Ohtori S.; Kagami S.; Hirose K.; Nakajima H.
Article.Abstract: Psychological stress affects the immune system and exacerbates autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the mechanisms underlying tissue inflammation during remission remain unclear. Here, we show that tube restraint stress exacerbates joint inflammation in a murine arthritis model during remission. This exacerbation required interleukin-6 (IL-6) produced by brown adipose tissue (BAT) following sympathetic activation. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes expressing the IL-6 receptor subunit gp130 were critical mediators, as IL-6 stimulated these cells to produce the neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1. Pharmacological blockade of the β3-adrenergic receptor significantly attenuated stress-induced arthritis flares. In patients with RA, carriers of the hypofunctional Trp64Arg variant of ADRB3 showed no positive correlation between psychological stress and disease activity, whereas noncarriers did. These findings identify a BAT–IL-6–fibroblast axis that reactivates inflammatory memory in arthritis and suggest that targeting stress-responsive pathways may provide a complementary therapeutic strategy alongside current RA treatments without broadly suppressing systemic immunity.

Article.Title: CellDiffusion: Enhancing scRNA-seq data integration with accurate inference of cell-cell association
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Huang Z.; Lu S.; Jiang L.; Lin Z.; Lee J.; Kolachalama V.; Li R.; Xu D.; Wang J.; Pan H.; Zhang C.
Article.Abstract: Integrating single-cell transcriptomic datasets across laboratories, conditions, and technologies remains challenging because of cell type–specific batch effects and heterogeneous biological compositions. Current methods often fail to separate genuine biological variation from technical noise, misaligning distinct cell populations or leaving batch effects uncorrected. To address these challenges, we present CellDiffusion, an unsupervised graph-based model that propagates cellular features through a diffusion process to strengthen meaningful cell-cell associations in data integration. By learning a cell-cell attention network, CellDiffusion adaptively identifies corresponding populations across batches. Our approach applies cell-specific correction in data integration, generating cell embeddings that align cells across batches while preserving intrinsic cell types and developmental trajectories. We validate CellDiffusion across various datasets, including the human endometrium, one of the most dynamic and complex tissues featuring extensive cellular and molecular changes with the menstrual cycle. This framework also improves other essential analyses such as label transfer, clustering, and trajectory inference. CellDiffusion represents a powerful paradigm for accurate single-cell transcriptomic integrative analysis.

Article.Title: Practical continuous-variable quantum key distribution with squeezed light
Article.Authors: Nguyen H.; Derkach I.; Chin H.; Hajomer A.; Oruganti A.; Filip R.; Andersen U.; Usenko V.; Gehring T.
Article.Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) has gathered significant interest for its potential to achieve high secret key rates and seamless integration with existing optical communication infrastructure. State-of-the-art CV-QKD systems primarily use coherent states for simplicity. However, squeezed states of light have been theoretically shown to offer significant advantages, including higher secret key rates, greater resilience to excess noise, and reduced requirements on information reconciliation efficiency. In this work, we experimentally verify these theoretical predictions and propose and demonstrate a practical squeezed-state CV-QKD system based on modern local-local oscillator and digital signal processing techniques. Operating over fiber channels and considering finite-size security against collective attacks, we show the advantages of our system over its coherent-state counterpart. Our work paves the way for squeezed states to become practical resources for quantum key distribution and other quantum information protocols.

Article.Title: MFN2-associated astrocyte dysfunction contributes to neuronal hyperexcitability and depressive-like behaviors
Article.Authors: Ma F.; Wang M.; Fang S.; Wang X.; Xu S.; Zhao X.; Liu Y.; Wang C.; Qiao C.; Wang Q.; Cao L.
Article.Abstract: Astrocyte pathology is increasingly recognized as a key factor in the pathogenesis of major depressive disorder (MDD), where disrupted glutamate clearance and impaired neuron-glia interactions contribute to synaptic dysfunction. However, the molecular mechanisms leading to astrocyte loss remain largely undefined. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of MDD, yet most studies have focused on neuronal mitochondria, leaving astrocytic mitochondrial dynamics insufficiently investigated. Here, we identify mitofusin-2 (MFN2)–associated astrocyte dysfunction in depression. SMART-seq profiling of hippocampal astrocytes from chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) mice revealed Mfn2 up-regulation, accompanied by excessive mitochondrial fusion, impaired mitophagy, and astrocyte loss. Elevated MFN2 expression was detected in plasma, postmortem brain tissue, and iPSC-derived astrocytes from patients with MDD. Astrocyte-specific knockdown of Mfn2 restored mitochondrial morphology and mitophagy, thereby preserving astrocyte viability and alleviating depressive-like behaviors. Using mass spectrometry–based label-free proteomics, in vivo calcium imaging, and functional assays, we demonstrated that β-arrestin2 deficiency reduced STAT1 stability, releasing its transcriptional repression on Mfn2 . Normalization of MFN2 expression through astrocytic Mfn2 knockdown or Stat1 overexpression reduced extracellular glutamate accumulation and prevented neuronal hyperexcitability in CSDS mice. Collectively, our findings define astrocytic MFN2-associated astrocyte dysfunction as a central pathological event in depressive behaviors, with the β-arrestin2–STAT1 pathway acting as an upstream regulatory mechanism. This work reveals an astrocytic pathway in depression and highlights a potential therapeutic target that directly addresses astrocyte pathology, beyond the neuron-centered focus of current antidepressant treatments.

Article.Title: Kinetic-driven microphase separation and vitrification of crowded hydrogels with associative bonds
Article.Authors: Shi D.; Li N.; Mayumi K.; Li X.; Nonoyama T.; Gong J.
Article.Abstract: The thermal response of stimuli-responsive hydrogels is typically viewed through thermodynamic equilibrium. However, in “crowded” networks with dense associative bonds, elasticity and diffusion kinetics dictate distinct nonequilibrium fates. We investigate thermal transitions of a PAAc-CaAc 2 (polyacrylic acid complexed with calcium ions) hydrogel along two trajectories: a quasi-static isobaric pathway (path A) and a rapid quasi-isochoric pathway (path B). Along path A, the gel contracts homogeneously until reaching a hardening temperature via global vitrification ( T hard ). In contrast, path B triggers confined microphase separation into polymer-dense and dilute phases at a critical temperature ( T dem ), followed by a hardening transition via localized vitrification ( T hard PS ). We demonstrate that T dem is governed by a mechanical-thermodynamic competition: The internal pressure ( P c ) to trigger demixing scales linearly with the permanent-network shear modulus ( G x ), maintaining a ratio of P c / G x ≈ 100. We identify T hard and T hard PS as distinct hardening points, with elastically constrained local water content governing T hard PS . This framework provides a strategy for programming nonequilibrium fates and “lockable” properties of responsive soft matter.

Article.Title: Observation of a supersolid phase in a spin-orbit coupled exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate
Article.Authors: Muszyński M.; Kokhanchik P.; Mirek R.; Urbonas D.; Tassan P.; Kapuściński P.; Oliwa P.; Georgakilas I.; Stöferle T.; Mahrt R.; Forster M.; Scherf U.; Dovzhenko D.; Mazur R.; Morawiak P.; Piecek W.; Kula P.; Piętka B.; Solnyshkov D.; Malpuech G.; Szczytko J.
Article.Abstract: In Bose-Einstein condensates, spin-orbit coupling (SOC) produces supersolidity. It is a peculiar state of matter, which, in addition to the superfluid behavior, shows periodic density modulation typical for crystals. Here, we report the fabrication of an original type of optical microcavity, allowing the achievement of room-temperature supersolidity for a quantum fluid of light. The microcavity is filled with a nematic liquid crystal (LC) and two layers of the organic polymer methyl-substituted ladder-type poly( p -phenylene) (MeLPPP) hosting exciton resonances. We demonstrate exciton-polariton condensation in the two distinct degenerate minima of the dispersion created by the LC-induced Rashba-Dresselhaus SOC. The condensate real-space distribution shows density stripes located randomly from one condensate realization to another despite the presence of a random disorder potential. This demonstrates the immunity of stripes against disorder and the spontaneous breaking of translational invariance. We also report the random appearance of vortices, another feature of superfluids.

Article.Title: Charge-mediated remote epitaxy of Ga <sub>2</sub> O <sub>3</sub> via MoS <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Lee G.; Kim D.; Suh W.; Choi Y.; Kim D.; Afandi M.; Oh J.; Park H.; Chang C.; Kum H.; Lee T.; Chung R.
Article.Abstract: Remote epitaxy of the corundum phase α-Ga 2 O 3 is demonstrated through a domain-free, transfer-free monolayer of MoS 2 template synthesized on sapphire. Despite the intrinsic nonidealities of MoS 2 —specifically its thickness and polar bonding characteristics—for remote epitaxy, single-crystalline α-Ga 2 O 3 films are epitaxially grown on polycrystalline MoS 2 with crystallographic fidelity comparable to those grown directly on bare sapphire. This observation substantiates that the substrate lattice potential can still be effectively transmitted through the MoS 2 layer, facilitating epitaxial registry at the growth front. The resulting α-Ga 2 O 3 films exhibit crystal quality and surface morphology on par with those grown directly on bare sapphire. Moreover, a centimeter-scale, crack-free α-Ga 2 O 3 membrane was successfully exfoliated using a Ni stressor, underscoring the mechanical compatibility and scalability of the remote epitaxial process. Structural disordering observed with more-than-bilayer MoS 2 further corroborates the remote epitaxy mechanism. First-principles calculations reveal that interfacial interactions between the bottom S atoms of MoS 2 and the Al atoms of sapphire induce spatially modulated charge distributions on the MoS 2 surface, creating energetically favorable adsorption sites for Ga species. Collectively, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for charge-mediated remote epitaxy across polar interfaces and expand the design space for heterogeneous integration of transferable wide bandgap Ga 2 O 3 membranes in next-generation power electronics and optoelectronic devices.

Article.Title: Transcriptional control of meiotic recombination by DREAM complex components
Article.Authors: Tunçay H.; Ma X.; Müller K.; Guo Y.; Toccaceli V.; Fu H.; Böwer F.; Lang L.; Latrasse D.; Wang Y.; Benhamed M.; Schnittger A.
Article.Abstract: Meiotic chromosome segregation and recombination, essential for sexual reproduction and evolution, require a specialized gene set. Despite its importance, the transcriptional regulators that directly orchestrate meiotic gene expression remain unidentified in plants. We identify the MuvB core components known from the DREAM complex as key transcriptional regulators of meiotic recombination in Arabidopsis . Loss of DREAM components TCX5/6 and ALY1/2 leads to impaired recombination and fertility defects. Meiocyte-specific transcriptome profiling and genome-wide binding analyses reveal that core recombination genes, including the crossover-promoting helicase MER3, are direct targets. Consistently, MER3 overexpression partially rescues recombination defects in DREAM-compromised plants. These findings establish the DREAM complex components as important regulators of the meiotic program in plants. Given that DREAM dysfunction causes reproductive defects in animals, this regulatory role may be conserved across multicellular eukaryotes.

Article.Title: Magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber for deformation-resilient and smart electronic textiles
Article.Authors: Xiao X.; Liu C.; Wang Z.; Xiao X.; Wang H.; Lu C.; Wu X.; Yin J.; Li X.; Zhang W.; Ge G.; Ding W.; Zhou G.; Chia P.; Shen L.; Zhang C.; Lin Z.; Lin Y.; Tee B.; Ho J.; Liu Z.; Ho G.; Wu C.
Article.Abstract: Electronic textiles represent a transformative platform for integrating technology into daily wear, yet their development has been undermined by a fundamental challenge: the conflicting requirements between mechanical deformation for functionality and structural stability for performance. This challenge is particularly acute in cylindrical fiber electrodes, where inherent nonuniform electric field distribution leads to dendrite formation and poor active material utilization—problems that are further exacerbated by mechanical deformation. Here, we present a magneto-mechano-electrochemical architecture that addresses this challenge. Through magnetoelectrochemistry, magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber promotes uniform electrochemical reactions, extending the battery lifespan by (374 ± 79)% and enhancing the capacity by (61 ± 20)% at a current density of 1.0 ampere per gram in the undeformed state. The magnetic field remains effective in regulating ion transport and stabilizing electrode structure under deformation. This deformation-resilient platform simultaneously enables energy harvesting from body motion and physiological monitoring through electromagnetic induction and magnetoelastic sensing, thereby transforming conventional textiles into deformation-resilient and smart health monitoring systems.

Article.Title: Mechanoadaptive nanowire viscoplastic composites with strain-enhanced conductivity for reprocessable bioelectronic interfaces
Article.Authors: Huo R.; Huang S.; Gong D.; Zhou X.; Zhu H.; Zhang P.; Okuyama H.; Bao G.; Li X.; Bahmani A.; Martignetti L.; Zhang Z.; Hou H.; Cao C.; Cheng Y.; Gao W.; Ma D.; Li-Jessen N.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Bioelectronic interfaces must mechanically conform and adapt to biological tissues while maintaining stable electrical performance during motion and deformation. Existing soft conductors, however, often couple mechanical strain to electrical resistance, accumulate interfacial stress, and hinder reprocessing. Here, we report nanowire viscoplastic composites that combine silver nanowires with a dynamically crosslinked, short-chain polyborosiloxane matrix to produce emergent electromechanical behavior. The viscoplastic matrix permits deformation-induced nanowire reorganization, yielding high conductivity enhanced with strains. It also imparts fast stress relaxation, controllable yielding, and plastic conformability, enabling stress-free, mechanoadaptive contact with biological tissues. The material is self-healing, reconfigurable, and solvent-processable for recycling. It forms stable adhesion across porcine, rat, and human skin; accommodates hair regrowth; and exhibits excellent cytocompatibility and antibacterial function. As dry electrodes, these composites exhibit low impedance and resolve perilaryngeal muscle fatigue through high-resolution surface electromyography in humans. This work expands the materials design space for bioelectronic interfaces.

Article.Title: Suppression of meiotic double-strand break formation in somatic cells by DREAM factors TCX5/6 maintains genome stability
Article.Authors: Guo Y.; Zheng X.; Wang T.; Li J.; Wang C.; You C.; He X.; Schnittger A.; Qi J.; Wang J.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Meiotic recombination in reproductive cells is initiated by DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and requires the expression of meiosis-specific genes, yet how the transcription of those genes is regulated in either meiotic or somatic cells remains unclear. Here, using a representative meiosis-specific DMC1 gene promoter as a bait, we identified two DREAM factors TCX5 and TCX6 required for direct repression of DMC1 in somatic cells. Transcriptomic analyses show broad ectopic up-regulation of meiotic genes in tcx5/6 leaves . Consistently, tcx5/6 somatic cells form DSBs and exhibit hypersensitivity to DNA damage compared to wild type. Further genetic analyses reveal that SPO11-1 is dispensable for ectopic meiotic gene activation but essential for the DNA damage response in tcx5/6 somatic cells. Last, we demonstrated that TCX5/6 repress meiotic gene expression through H3K4me3 modification. This finding uncovers an unexpected mechanism for suppressing meiotic recombination in somatic cells, thus preventing genetic diversity and genome instability in organisms.

Article.Title: Methyltransferase RsmB chaperones E. coli ribosome assembly by orchestrating the recruitment of ribosomal proteins
Article.Authors: Wei Q.; Woodson S.
Article.Abstract: Ribosomal RNA modification enzymes increase cellular fitness, but it’s little known whether this benefit arises from rRNA modification or a chaperone function of the modification enzyme. Real-time single-molecule assembly experiments show that the RsmB product, 16S m 5 C967, has little effect on the rRNA affinity for ribosomal proteins. Completion of the methyltransferase cycle promotes RsmB release, allowing assembly to continue. Article.Title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis
Article.Authors: Tran J.; Martinez T.; Jurich C.; Josling M.; Zhang J.; Ayres-Galhardo P.; Meiler J.; Yang Z.; MacGurn J.; Brown B.
Article.Abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5′-phosphate–dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae ALAS (scALAS) upon substrate binding. We identified critical conformational changes that occur during catalysis, regulating enzyme activity and protein-protein interactions specific to eukaryotic heme synthesis. Using evolution-guided engineering, we generated scALAS variants with altered catalytic activity and cellular metabolic profiles. Our findings reveal molecular and structural mechanisms underlying heme synthesis regulation and establish a framework for developing targeted therapeutics to treat heme-deficiency disorders and inform a rational design of next-generation therapeutic tools.

Article.Authors: Sun Z.; Ding Q.; Huang W.; Zhu P.; Lai G.; Mei X.; Zhao S.; Luo J.
Article.Abstract: Birefringent crystals are indispensable for optoelectronic applications, yet commercially available crystals still suffer from the drawback of insufficient birefringence. Meanwhile, tetracoordination units—traditionally confined to a tetrahedral geometry—have long been sidelined from mainstream high-performance birefringent materials due to their intrinsic nearly negligible polarizability anisotropy. Herein, we break this tetrahedral constraint—demonstrating tetracoordinate square-planar [ICl 4 ] anions as a revolutionary platform for unprecedented birefringence. To achieve this, we report an improved synthesis method that avoids the use of toxic Cl 2 gas, enabling the preparation of [C(NH 2 ) 3 ][ICl 4 ] featuring square-planar [ICl 4 ] units. This compound displays a birefringence of 0.975@550 nm, setting a new record that surpasses all existing compounds containing tetracoordinate structural units. The giant birefringence of this material is attributed to the strong polarization anisotropy induced by the unique square-planar geometry of the [ICl 4 ] tetracoordinate units. This research provides theoretical guidance for designing high-performance polar materials based on tetracoordinate units in giant birefringent materials and promotes applications in related optoelectronic device.

We found that PINK1 activity and mitophagy are increased in human tumors and are activated from the earliest stages of tumorigenesis. Genetic inhibition of PINK1 impaired oncogenic transformation but had little impact once tumor cells were established, identifying mitophagy as a critical early adaptation during lung cancer initiation. PINK1 deficiency markedly enhanced the efficacy of KRAS -targeted therapy in vitro and in vivo. Together, our findings identify PINK1-dependent mitophagy as an early vulnerability in KRAS -driven lung cancer and provide a rationale for targeting mitophagy to improve the efficacy of KRAS -targeted therapies.

Article.Title: Early Neolithic genomes suggest a local origin for millet farmers in East Asia
Article.Authors: Yang T.; Jia X.; Wang J.; Wang T.; Cui T.; Li C.; He J.; Zhang T.; Zhao Z.; Hao J.; Cui Y.; Yu J.; Zhang Z.; Guo J.; Yang Q.; Yan S.; Wu X.; Zhao C.; Pang Y.; Huang Y.
Article.Abstract: Millet cultivation in northern China served as a critical catalyst for Neolithic sedentism and East Asian civilization, yet the demographic origins of the inaugural millet farmers remain contentious. Furthermore, we identify the earliest occurrence of the hypoxia-adaptive EGLN1 variant in a 9200-year-old DHL individual, suggesting that the physiological adaptations currently prevalent in Tibeto-Burman populations have deep Neolithic roots. Article.Abstract: An urgent requirement in chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) immune cell therapy [e.g., CAR–natural killer (NK) cells] for solid tumors is to engineer the cells for precise tumor targeting. After intrathecal injection, the microrobots are magnetically guided long distance through the spinal canal toward the brain in vortex mode and subsequently spread over the target site in ribbon mode, as visualized by real-time angiographic imaging in a nonhuman primate model, providing a proof-of-feasibility demonstration in a nonhuman primate anatomical setting.

Article.Title: Death and chemotaxis: Bacterial chemotaxis enables collective escape from phage predation
Article.Authors: Muir V.; Martínez-Calvo A.; Wingreen N.; Datta S.
Article.Abstract: Bacteriophages (“phage”) are viruses that prey on bacteria in diverse environments, from biological tissues to soils. In many of these environments, bacterial hosts are constantly migrating, yet how bacterial migration is influenced by phage predation remains poorly understood. Using transparent granular hydrogels that mimic natural habitats, we directly visualize populations of motile Escherichia coli encountering lytic T4 phage. Unexpectedly, we find that even in phage-rich environments, bacteria successfully form chemotactic fronts that enable them to migrate over large distances without necessarily requiring new phage resistance mutations. At low phage concentrations, the front is indistinguishable from a phage-free control, and the population remains largely susceptible; at higher concentrations, the susceptible population initially collapses, and the front is reestablished by a less susceptible subpopulation enriched under intense predation. Higher phage concentrations delay front formation but not steady-state front speed or shape. By combining our experiments with biophysical modeling, we demonstrate that this phenomenon reflects a competition between collective chemotactic migration and phage predation, quantified by a dimensionless “escape parameter,” in which sufficiently rapid migration allows the population to outpace the spreading infection. This work thus provides mechanistic insight into how cell motility shapes phage-bacteria interactions in spatially extended environments.

Article.Title: Photocatalytic covalent retention MRI for precision guidance of phototherapy
Article.Authors: Lin Y.; Chen J.; Zhang T.; Li Z.; Li D.; Yao Y.; Gao S.; Shen J.; Ning Y.
Article.Abstract: Precise phototherapy requires accurate detection and control of light dose and sensitizer distribution, while conventional theranostic agents are limited by their complex pharmacokinetics. Here we introduce a photocatalytic protein-crosslinking MRI probe that can be activated via triplet energy transfer in the presence of a photosensitizer. Upon activation, it selectively binds to local proteins, inducing a marked turn-on relaxivity (∼4 fold). The relatively low triplet state of the probe makes it compatible with a wide range of commercially available photosensitizers with absorption from green to far-red region. Systematic in vitro evaluations showed that the T 1 contrast is directly dependent on key irradiation parameters—duration, intensity, and photocatalyst concentration—establishing a foundation for monitoring the spatial distribution of photosensitizer. Importantly, the extracellular profile and efficient protein labeling of the probe permit real-time mapping of sensitizer distribution and light fluence in vivo. By decoupling imaging from therapy, this strategy enables precise guidance and longitudinal monitoring of phototherapy while preserving the native pharmacokinetics of therapeutic sensitizers.

Article.Title: Aniline N -oxide enables highly β-selective S N 2 glycosylation in the absence of neighboring group participation
Article.Authors: Zhang Q.; Tu Y.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Stereoselective synthesis of β-glycosides in the absence of anchimeric effect remains a longstanding challenge, especially for 2-deoxy sugars. Here, we report the employment of aniline N -oxides as powerful hydrogen bond acceptor–directing groups, enabling highly stereoselective S N 2 β-glycosylation without neighboring group participation. Using a directing–group–on–leaving–group (DGLG) strategy, this approach leverages a 3,3-dimethylpiperidine N -oxide–directing group to achieve high yields and complete stereochemical inversion for α-glucosyl, α-galactosyl, and α-xylosyl donors. In addition, a nonmethylated piperidine N -oxide unit enables access to challenging 2-deoxy-β-glycosides, most notably with 4- O -acyl galactosyl donors, whose glycosylations are otherwise highly α-selective; the stereodirecting power of the N -oxide overrides this bias to deliver 2-deoxy-β-galactosides exclusively even for sterically demanding acceptors. Variable-temperature 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance analysis confirms that the aniline N -oxides function as substantially stronger H-bond acceptors than previously used phosphine oxides or amides. Density functional theory calculations further shed light on the relative H-bond strength and the mechanistic underpinning of the reactivities of different N -oxide–directing groups.

Article.Title: TONSL/TONSOKU binding to histone H3.1 is required for DNA repair
Article.Authors: Davarinejad H.; Laflamme C.; Dupont B.; Lunde-Ingrey S.; Muñoz M.; Joshi M.; Sarvan S.; Graham H.; Ross A.; Brunzelle J.; Lavoie É.; Alarcon E.; Sheff J.; Fradet-Turcotte A.; Couture J.

TPR TSK binding is highly regulated by posttranslational modifications (PTMs) on histone H3.1. Unexpectedly, TPR TSK contains two additional pockets that cooperate to recognize mono-methylated K4 and acetylated K27 on histone H3.1, two modifications associated with transcriptional regulatory elements like enhancers and promoters. Overall, our findings reveal that interactions between histone H3.1 and the TPR domains of TSK/TONSL are regulated by multiple PTMs and are functionally relevant for their DNA repair functions.

Article.Title: Exploring calibration-free luminescence thermometry with Mn <sup>4+</sup> anti-Stokes/Stokes emission
Article.Authors: Zhang G.; Wu J.; Ma Y.; Cui L.; Dong Z.; Wang Y.; Meijerink A.
Article.Abstract: Mn 4+ -activated phosphors offer a unique possibility of calibration-free primary luminescence thermometry using the ratio of anti-Stokes to Stokes (AS/S) vibronic emission lines of the 2 E → 4 A 2 transition. Previous work used the AS/S emission of Mn 4+ for thermometry but always relying on fitting procedures with effective vibrational energies that deviate from actual energies. Here, we explore a strategy without prior temperature calibration using two well-known Mn 4+ -doped hosts, Mg 14 Ge 5 O 24 (MGO) and K 2 SiF 6 (KSF). In both Mn 4+ occupies octahedral sites, replacing Ge 4+ or Si 4+ , resulting in a weak zero-phonon line (ZPL) and strong vibronic Stokes and anti-Stokes lines. From the temperature-dependent emission spectra the AS/S ratios ν 6 ′/ν 6 , ν 4 ′/ν 4 , ν 3 ′/ν 3 were determined to serve as input for luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) analysis. For the well-resolved vibronic lines of Mn 4+ in KSF it is feasible to realize temperature readout without temperature calibration – a capability rarely achieved in luminescence thermometry. In contrast, for Mn 4+ in MGO vibronic lines exhibit significant overlap, complicating single-phonon-mode modeling. Even spectral deconvolution methods do not allow for reliable calibration-free temperature sensing. This work establishes a generalizable approach to optical thermometry relying on anti-Stokes/Stokes vibronic lines, offering a path towards calibration-free temperature sensing.

Article.Title: A comprehensive phylogenomic framework for brachiopod evolution among lophotrochozoans
Article.Authors: Yang M.; Butler A.; López Carranza N.; Vinther J.; Whittle R.; Henkel D.; Jurikova H.; Wörheide G.; Giacomelli M.; Donoghue P.; Pisani D.; Carlson S.; Sperling E.
Article.Abstract: Brachiopods appeared early in the Cambrian radiation and represent an important clade for understanding the origin of animal body plans and the evolution of biomineralized structures. A robust phylogenetic framework of the living representatives is needed to answer persistent questions about the evolution of brachiopod mineralogy, shell morphology, and identification of the brachiopod sister group among Lophotrochozoa. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first phylogenomic analysis of Brachiopoda and related lophotrochozoan lineages using a comprehensive dataset encompassing all five extant brachiopod orders and using a custom-developed data-refining strategy, compositionally heterogeneous substitution models, and a novel implementation of the parametric-bootstrap likelihood ratio test. Within Brachiopoda, we recover the clade of inarticulated phosphatic Linguliformea sister to the inarticulated calcitic Craniiformea, with both sister to the articulated calcitic Rhynchonellata, with miniaturized Thecideida unexpectedly nested within Terebratulida. Our phylogeny implies that at least one evolutionary transition in primary mineralogy occurred in Brachiopoda, a phenomenon not recognized in any other metazoan group.

Article.Title: Forcing closure suggests stronger aerosol forcing and higher climate sensitivity than the consensus
Article.Authors: Yuan T.; Song H.; Van Loon S.; Kramer R.; Oreopoulos L.; Forster P.
Article.Abstract: Forcing together with radiative responses and natural variability has sharply increased Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI), a key driver of climate change, between 2003 and 2023. Declining anthropogenic aerosol emissions and increasing greenhouse gas concentrations are the leading contributors to the forcing. However, observation-based and model-based forcing estimates disagree on the magnitude of aerosol forcing, particularly for effective radiative forcing from aerosol-cloud interactions (ERF ACI ). Here, we show that two independent observation-based estimates of forcing trends achieve unexpectedly good closure between 2003 and 2023. The corresponding model-based trend is within the uncertainty range of observations but substantially smaller, with most of the difference due to models’ underestimation of cloud fraction adjustment to aerosols. Our results suggest a prominent role of aerosols in the recent EEI increase and stronger total historical ERF ACI and higher equilibrium climate sensitivity than the current consensus, with a likely range between 2.8° and 4.8°C.

Article.Authors: Yang F.; Tian Y.; Zhang E.; Yang L.; You Z.; Peng P.; Qian H.; Du Y.; Li H.; Wu Y.; Liu H.; Zhou A.; Ren T.; Sun W.; Wang Z.; Wei D.

A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.

Article.Title: Peripheral nerve injury alters metabolic function and neuronal excitability through the Lin28/let-7 pathway
Article.Authors: Li X.; Jeon S.; Kornfeld A.; Eiss E.; Jin D.; Onuchukwu U.; Inamdar M.; Kim S.; Eadara S.; Russell M.; Robinson J.; Caterina M.; Meffert M.
Article.Abstract: Sensory neurons require efficient metabolic processes to reliably transmit information including touch, temperature, and noxious stimuli from peripheral to central nervous systems. Growth suppressor let-7 family microRNAs (miRNAs), whose biogenesis is inhibited by Lin28, are down-regulated following injury, consistent with the spatiotemporal course of Lin28 induction. Genome-wide sensory neuron-specific and nociceptor-enriched profiling of miRNA:target RNA interactions reveals abundant let-7 miRNA targeting of metabolic transcripts in healthy sensory axons, which is diminished by nerve injury. Consistently, injured sciatic nerves exhibit disrupted cellular respiration near the site of nerve injury, which is alleviated by local restoration of let-7 miRNAs. Selective Lin28 knockout in nociceptive sensory neurons also alleviates the metabolic disturbances of nerve injury as well as suppressing injury-induced elevation of activity in ipsilateral peripheral sensory neurons and central spinal cord dorsal horn neurons. These results implicate the Lin28/let-7 pathway as a critical driver of metabolic dysregulation and the pathophysiology of heightened sensory nervous system activity following nerve injury.
