Article.Title: Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation at 40 Hz Improves Social Functioning in Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
Article.Authors: Gao B.; Lin L.; Smith R.; Tobe R.; Zamora D.; Wang L.; Li X.; Shi X.; Zhang H.; Shao P.; Davis J.; Wu R.; Shen Y.; Ou J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) lacks rapid and effective interventions for its core social difficulties. The right temporoparietal junction (rTPJ), a critical hub for social cognition, together with gamma band abnormalities implicated in ASD, provides a promising neuromodulation target. Methods: In this randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 47 children with ASD (39 male; mean [SD] age = 8.79 [2.71] years) were assigned to receive either 21 sessions of 40-Hz high-definition transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) targeting the rTPJ (3 sessions/day for 7 days) or sham stimulation, with assessments conducted at baseline, postintervention (week 1), and a 3-week follow-up (week 4). The primary outcome was change in Ohio State University Autism Rating Scale-DSM-5 (OARS-5) total scores. Secondary outcomes included the Aberrant Behavior Checklist-Second Edition, Social Responsiveness Scale-Second Edition, and Short Sensory Profile. Eye-tracking metrics during Frith-Happé animations were exploratory measures of theory of mind (ToM)-related social cognitive processing. Results: The active group demonstrated significant improvements in OARS-5 total scores at week 1 (mean difference = -1.13, 95% CI [-1.78 to -0.47], p < .001) and week 4 (mean difference = -1.47, 95% CI [-2.20 to -0.74], p < .001). Improvements in selected behavioral and sensory domains were observed. Average fixation duration during ToM animations showed a significant group × time interaction. No serious adverse events occurred. Conclusions: These findings suggest that 40-Hz tACS targeting the rTPJ may be associated with rapid improvements in ASD symptom severity, particularly social functioning, in children with ASD, while being well tolerated. Clinical significance requires further evaluation.

Article.Title: Breastfeeding and Development of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Symptoms Across Childhood
Article.Authors: Solberg B.; Brantsæter A.; Kvalvik L.; Hartman C.; Xie T.; Klungsøyr K.; Li L.; Larsson H.; Gjestad R.; Haavik J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Studies suggest that breastfeeding may be associated with a reduced risk of childhood attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, determining causality is challenging because potential confounders, including genetic predisposition, may influence this relationship. We prospectively examined the relationship between full (exclusive or predominant) breastfeeding duration and ADHD symptoms in children, accounting for sociodemographic and perinatal factors and polygenic risk of ADHD. Methods: We obtained data from 37,643 children (49.1% girls) born from 1999 to 2009 and 18,349 mother-father-child units from the MoBa (Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study). We examined the effect of full breastfeeding per month (self-reported when the child was 6 months of age) on parent-rated ADHD symptoms in offspring at 3, 5, and 8 years (multivariate regression models). Measures are expressed as unstandardized regression coefficients (B) with 95% CIs, adjusting for socioeconomic and perinatal factors and ADHD polygenic scores in child, mother, and father. Results: Full breastfeeding per month was significantly associated with lower ADHD symptom scores at all ages (adjusted Bage3 = -0.08 [95% CI, -0.09 to -0.07], Bage5 = -0.07 [95% CI, -0.08 to -0.06], Bage8 = -0.06 [95% CI, -0.07 to -0.05]), indicating that each month of full breastfeeding associated with lower ADHD symptoms. Similar results were observed when we modeled breastfeeding as a categorical variable including both full and partial breastfeeding. Inverse probability weighting, accounting for loss to follow-up, and sibling analyses with discordant breastfeeding exposures, accounting for unmeasured confounding, supported the main results. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that full breastfeeding could partially protect against childhood ADHD symptoms. Further studies are needed to understand the potential mechanisms of the association between breastfeeding and lower ADHD symptoms.

Article.Title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Signaling in Learning and Memory: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Therapeutic Implications
Article.Authors: Bashaw A.; Roman-Ortiz C.; Gao S.; Schier L.; Borner T.; Kanoski S.
Article.Abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is primarily known for its role in glucose homeostasis and food intake control, and GLP-1 analogs (either as monotherapy or dual agonists) are commonly used for type 2 diabetes and obesity treatment in humans. Beyond these functions, the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) is widely expressed throughout the brain, including in the hippocampus (HPC) and interconnected regions that contribute to learning and memory processes. Here we review emerging evidence supporting a role for GLP-1 signaling in promoting learning and memory function, particularly in dementia and other conditions that manifest with HPC dysfunction. Evidence is synthesized from preclinical rodent models revealing that GLP-1 analog treatment improves deficits in memory function and HPC neuronal signaling processes in various models of dementia, aging, and metabolic disruption. While findings from human clinical trials and meta-analyses also show promise for GLP-1 analog-based treatment for memory disorders, results thus far are mixed, with many studies underpowered and/or lacking comprehensive memory evaluation. We describe several distinct yet non-mutually exclusive neurobiological mechanisms by which GLP-1R signaling can enhance memory, including blood-brain barrier penetration and direct action on HPC GLP-1Rs, improved peripheral and central insulin sensitivity, vagus nerve GLP-1R activation, and peripheral metabolic and inflammatory improvements. We conclude by emphasizing important considerations for future clinical trials for GLP-1 analogs in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease and other memory disorders, including focusing on metabolically vulnerable individuals, stratifying results by cardiovascular and metabolic status, and leveraging existing GLP-1 analogs and drug delivery approaches toward maximizing bioavailability and brain penetrance.

Article.Title: Divergent Modulation of Dopaminergic Neurons by Hypocretin/Orexin Receptors 1 and 2 Shapes Dopaminergic Cell Activity and Socioemotional Behavior
Article.Authors: Tzanoulinou S.; Astori S.; Grandi L.; Gullo F.; Kalusivikako R.; Rai S.; Limorenko G.; Tafti M.; Becchetti A.; Vassalli A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Many neuropsychiatric disorders involve dysregulation of the dopaminergic (DA) input to the forebrain. DA afferents from the midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA) are particularly relevant. A key neuromodulatory influence on DAVTA neurons arises from lateral hypothalamic area hypocretin/orexin (OX) neurons. Despite being a major input, the differential actions of OX peptides A and B on their receptors (OX1R and OX2R) in DA neurons are poorly understood. Methods: Using genetically engineered mice whose DA cells selectively lack OX input via Hcrtr1 (DAOx1R-KO) or Hcrtr2 (DAOx2R-KO), we assessed DAVTA neuron intrinsic excitability ex vivo and evaluated behavioral phenotypes across socioemotional and cognitive domains. Results: We discovered previously unrecognized effects of OX peptides on DAVTA cell response. While OXA enhanced DAVTA neuron firing via OX1Rs, OXB diminished firing via OX2Rs. Behaviorally, DA OX1R loss generated anxiety-like responding and context-dependent hyperactivity, while DA OX2R loss decreased sociability and compromised aversion-driven learning. Loss of either OX1Rs or OX2Rs in DA cells elicited impulsivity and compulsivity-like behavioral patterns. Conclusions: We evidenced distinct functions of OX1R versus OX2R signaling in modulating the intrinsic excitability of DAVTA neurons and influencing DA-related behaviors. Our data implicate OX→DA signaling pathways in neuropsychiatric endophenotypes relevant to obsessive-compulsive, attention-deficit/hyperactivity, and autism spectrum disorders and inform therapeutic strategies targeting OX receptors.

Article.Title: From Satiety to Substance Use: Neural Mechanisms of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Signaling in Appetite and Reward
Article.Authors: Baumer-Harrison C.; Graham M.; De Jonghe B.; Hayes M.
Article.Abstract: The central glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) system encompasses homeostatic and hedonic neural circuits. GLP-1-producing neurons within the brainstem project broadly to GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R)-containing brainstem, hypothalamic, limbic, and mesolimbic nuclei. The diverse expression of the GLP-1R throughout metabolic and reward nuclei positions this system to integrate motivated behavior with physiological state. GLP-1 acts as a state-dependent behavior-ending signal that suppresses appetite, promotes satiety, and dampens hedonic and motivational reward value-effects that extend beyond palatable foods. GLP-1R agonists, which can partially cross the blood-brain barrier, engage central GLP-1Rs via circumventricular organs and adjacent nuclei leading to polysynaptic relays that suppress feeding and drug-seeking behaviors. An abundance of preclinical and clinical evidence highlights the efficacy of GLP-1R agonists for the treatment of obesity and other metabolic disorders. Emerging evidence also indicates that the therapeutic application may extend to other disorders characterized by reward-related maladaptive behaviors, including substance use disorders.

Article.Title: GLP-1 and Alcohol-Related Behaviors: Insights From Preclinical Studies
Article.Authors: Jerlhag E.
Article.Abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) has gained attention for its broad physiological effects, and both short-acting (exenatide/exendin-4 [Ex4]) and long-acting (liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide) GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists have been approved for type 2 diabetes and/or obesity. Initial preclinical research has highlighted the role of GLP-1 and its receptor in the pathophysiology of alcohol use disorder (AUD) and their potential use in the treatment of AUD. Specifically, systemic treatment of Ex4 reduces alcohol intake, the motivation to consume alcohol, and relapse-like behavior in male animals. Similarly, alcohol consummatory behaviors are reduced in male or female animals treated with either of the long-acting GLP-1R agonists. Moreover, both short- and long-acting GLP-1R agonists consistently attenuate the rewarding properties of alcohol, as measured by locomotor stimulation, dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, and conditioned place preference in male mice. Because alcohol consumption is largely driven by alcohol-induced reward, it is hypothesized that GLP-1R agonists attenuate the rewarding effects of alcohol, thereby decreasing alcohol intake. However, it should be emphasized that other factors, including altered gastric emptying, nausea, and enhanced stress, may also contribute to these effects. Taken together, these preclinical studies offer insight into the potential use of GLP-1R agonists in the treatment of AUD.

Article.Title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists as a Candidate Treatment for Opioid Use Disorder: From Rats to Humans
Article.Authors: Grigson P.; Bunce S.; Brick T.; Freet C.; Nyland J.; Kawasaki S.; Brandl C.; Shealy E.; Huddleston K.
Article.Abstract: Despite recent progress and at least 3 medications approved for the treatment of opioid use disorder (OUD), the number of deaths due to opioid overdose remains unacceptably high. Therefore, there is a need for new treatments. To this end, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), dual GLP-1RA+glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonists (e.g., tirzepatide), and triple agonists (e.g., GLP-1RA+neuropeptideY1/Y2 receptor agonists) show promise. Here, we review preclinical and clinical data. In the preclinical studies, acute administration of exendin-4 and the longer-acting liraglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, and other dual and triple agonists reduced opioid taking and/or opioid seeking when elicited by exposure to drug-related cues, the drug itself, or by stress. Chronic treatment with GLP-1RAs also reduced responding for opioids, but tolerance occurred with chronic administration of higher doses of GLP-1RAs. In the human studies, 1 small clinical trial found a 40% reduction in opioid craving following treatment with the GLP-1RA liraglutide. Three other clinical trials are ongoing, with 2 testing the efficacy of semaglutide and 1 testing the efficacy of tirzepatide as adjunctive treatments to buprenorphine or methadone. Pending completion of these clinical trials, recent studies used data from electronic health records, the TriNetX database, and Medicare claims and found a 40% reduction in opioid overdose and in hospital admissions for OUD in patients treated with a GLP-1RA or a GLP-1RA/GIP agonist for type 2 diabetes and/or for obesity. Thus, while additional clinical trials are needed, these data suggest that GLP-1RAs hold promise as a novel treatment for OUD in humans.

Article.Title: Therapeutic Potential of Incretin-Based Therapies for Alcohol Use Disorder: A Narrative Review of Available Clinical Evidence
Article.Authors: Klausen M.; Fink-Jensen A.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains a major global health burden, but pharmacological treatment options are limited, and there is an urgent need for novel molecular targets for the treatment of AUD. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have been used for more than 2 decades to treat type 2 diabetes and subsequently overweight and obesity. Unexpected effects, including reduced alcohol intake, have been reported by patients as well as by clinicians, and these (often anecdotal) reports have been supported by a growing body of data from large registry studies; target trial emulation analyses; preclinical experiments with mice, rats, and nonhuman primates; and randomized clinical trials associating the use of GLP-1RAs with reduced alcohol consumption. This convergence has sparked growing interest in GLP-1RAs as a novel therapeutic strategy for AUD. In this narrative review, we synthesize current evidence on the effects of GLP-1RAs in individuals with AUD. To date, only 3 randomized controlled trials have examined GLP-1RAs in AUD, showing reductions in alcohol cue brain reactivity and alcohol consumption, particularly among individuals with overweight or obesity. We also report on observational data, including large registry studies, target trial emulation analyses, and real-world data, which have consistently associated GLP-1RA use with reduced alcohol consumption. Case reports and social media analyses further corroborate reductions in alcohol craving and consumption. Mechanistically, emerging evidence points to modulation of reward circuitry, incentive salience, gastric emptying, and metabolic signaling. Overall, GLP-1RAs represent a promising and mechanistically novel approach to AUD treatment, warranting confirmation in larger, long-term randomized trials.

Article.Title: Connection-Level Multi-Omics Reveals Cerebellar-Cortical Dysconnectivity and Divergent Molecular Signatures Across Major Psychiatric Disorders
Article.Authors: Diao Y.; Huang Y.; Zhu B.; Guo M.; Wang W.; Li Z.; Zhang X.; Li K.; Li W.; Wang H.; Zhou J.; Li X.; Wu F.; Wu K.
Article.Abstract: Background: Understanding how disease-related connectome alterations relate to underlying molecular systems remains a major challenge in psychiatric disorders. Methods: Here we introduce BrainNetAnno (https://brainnetanno.readthedocs.io/en/latest), an open-source framework for molecular annotation of brain network connections that extends multi-omics mapping from regional nodes to inter-regional edges. We applied this framework to resting-state functional connectivity data from a discovery cohort of 2,453 participants and an independent validation cohort of 442, including individuals with major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, generalized anxiety disorder, autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and healthy controls. Results: Our analyses revealed a shared transdiagnostic abnormal connectivity pattern (STACP), characterized by cerebellar-cortical dysconnectivity, alongside distinct disorder-specific connectivity deviations (DSCDs) that exhibited structured inter-disorder relationships, including opposition, partial alignment, and near-orthogonality. These connectivity patterns were differentially associated with molecular systems, with mitochondrial phenotypes linked to the STACP and selected DSCDs, and neurotransmitter receptor/transporter profiles primarily associated with DSCDs. Conclusions: These findings establish a robust, connection-level framework for linking large-scale connectome abnormalities to multi-omics molecular systems in psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Inhibitory control and error processing in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A mega-analysis of task-based fMRI data by the ENIGMA-OCD consortium
Article.Authors: Džinalija N.; van den Heuvel O.; Simpson H.; Ivanov I.; Araújo A.; Balachander S.; Beucke J.; Brandeis D.; Brem S.; Bruin W.; Buitelaar J.; Castelo-Branco M.; Choi S.; Eng G.; Fitzsimmons S.; Fortea L.; Fullana M.; Grützmann R.; Hansen B.; Huijser C.; de Joode N.; Kathmann N.; Kaufmann C.; Kim M.; Koch K.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a chronic condition in which impaired inhibitory control and excessive error monitoring may contribute to maintenance of obsessions and compulsions. This mega-analysis investigates neural activation during response inhibition and error processing using adult (OCD=563; control=348) and child (OCD=83, control=114) data from the ENIGMA-OCD consortium and the ABCD study (probable OCD=343; control=361). Methods: Individual participant data was uniformly processed using HALFpipe to extract statistical maps for response inhibition and error processing contrasts. Bayesian multilevel models were used to assess regional and whole-brain effects of OCD, and to examine the association between the OCD clinical profile and task-related activation. Results: Across inhibitory control tasks, both OCD and control participants showed robust activation in regions implicated in response inhibition and error processing. During response inhibition, compared to controls, adults with OCD showed stronger somatomotor cortex activation, while children with OCD showed stronger occipital cortex activation. Children with probable OCD from the ABCD cohort showed weaker activity in the frontoparietal network in the anterior insula/frontal operculum region. During error processing, relative to controls, adults with OCD showed weaker activation in fronto-striatal regions, while children with OCD showed stronger activation in frontoparietal and attention networks. Greater OCD symptom severity was associated with weaker task-related activation in adults and stronger activation in children during response inhibition. Conclusion: Case-control differences in brain activation during inhibitory control varied by age group and task contrast. Symptom severity emerged as the main clinical correlate of activation during inhibition, suggesting that inhibitory control deficits in OCD may be both state-dependent and developmentally specific.

Article.Title: TMS-Evoked Cortical Reactivity Signatures as a Multidimensional Biomarker of Depression: A TMS-EEG Meta-Analysis from Diagnosis to Prognosis
Article.Authors: Xie J.; Zhao T.; Guo L.; Li D.; Zhao Y.; Wang Z.; Wang P.; Meng L.; Wang G.; Yang Z.
Article.Abstract: Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) enables perturbation-based assessment of cortical reactivity and has emerged as a promising tool for identifying neurophysiological biomarkers in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the literature remains fragmented, and TMS-EEG metrics have yet to be systematically integrated within a unified framework spanning diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Ovid, and Web of Science were systematically searched for studies reporting single-pulse TMS-EEG measures in MDD. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to synthesize evidence across three hierarchical biomarker validation domains: characterization (diagnostic discrimination and state-related symptom tracking), treatment response (intervention monitoring and clinical coupling with remission), and baseline prediction. Results: Across 21 studies comprising 1,025 patients with MDD and 517 healthy controls, negative-polarity components were significantly enhanced in MDD (Hedges' g = 0.36), driven primarily by the N100 (g = 0.35), which was also associated with greater symptom severity (g = 0.67). Treatment attenuated N100 (g = -0.21) while elevating P180 (g = 0.52). Critically, treatment-induced reduction in negative-polarity responses was strongly coupled with clinical remission (g = 0.91), with the N100 showing the most robust component-level effect (g = 0.85). Preliminary evidence further indicated that baseline negative-polarity components predicted treatment response (g = 1.35). Conclusions: TMS-EEG cortical reactivity signatures, particularly negative-polarity components and their N100 subcomponent, demonstrated convergent effects across disease characterization, treatment monitoring, and outcome prediction, supporting their candidacy as multidimensional neurophysiological biomarkers for MDD with potential clinical utility in biomarker-guided precision psychiatry.

Article.Title: Maternal immune activation influences social behavior development in a nonhuman primate model
Article.Authors: Hubbard J.; Chen S.; Iosif A.; Ryan A.; Murai T.; Hogrefe C.; Lesh T.; Smucny J.; Maddock R.; Schumann C.; Hanks T.; Van de Water J.; McAllister A.; Carter C.; Bauman M.
Article.Abstract: Background: Women exposed to infection during pregnancy have an increased risk of giving birth to a child who will later be diagnosed with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) characterized by changes in social development, such as autism and schizophrenia. Preclinical rodent models of maternal immune activation (MIA) have established causal links between elevated maternal cytokines and offspring social deficits indicative of human NDDs. Methods: Here, we use a unique nonhuman primate (NHP) MIA model to explore the longitudinal development of social behavior, given their phylogenetic similarity, social complexity, and translational potential for identifying the emergence of NDDs in humans. We explore social behavior (N=28 males) in pairs, social groups, and a dominance assessment. Results: MIA-exposed and control offspring developed a species-typical repertoire of social behavior and interacted with conspecifics. Yet, consistent with rodent and human studies, we found that MIA-exposed NHP offspring were, overall, less social towards familiar peers. We also found that MIA-exposed offspring were more likely to play with their treatment-matched pair mate during the weaning period, while controls did not exhibit a partner preference. There were also patterns suggesting that MIA exposure led to reduced contact with dams during infancy, greater withdrawals from pair-mates, and reduced positive social interactions with peers. Conclusions: These results confirm that NHP models of MIA are consistent with evidence from rodent and human studies indicating that MIA exposure reduces overall sociality. They also suggest that social deficits may be specific to certain behaviors and more subtle or masked during observations in large social groups.

Article.Title: Sleep and Drug Use: Neuroimaging Evidence for a Multidimensional Brain Framework
Article.Authors: Zhang R.; Volkow N.
Article.Abstract: Sleep plays a critical role in the initiation and maintenance of drug use, as well as recovery among individuals with substance use disorders. Sleep is a multidimensional construct, and a growing body of research has demonstrated the relative independence of various components. Specific sleep characteristics including insomnia (self-reported sleep disturbances), short sleep duration, late sleep timing and sleep irregularity have each been associated with increased risks of drug use. However, it remains unclear whether these sleep components contribute to substance use through shared neurobiological pathways. Conversely, drug use across different drug classes disrupts sleep. The extent to which drug-induced alterations in brain circuits account for shared and drug class-specific sleep disturbances remains poorly understood. In this review, we synthesize evidence from human neuroimaging studies to map sleep components predictive of drug use onto brain regions and large-scale brain networks. The anterior cingulate, insular and orbitofrontal cortices emerge as the brain regions most consistently implicated across sleep dimensions, and these regions play a key role in drug use initiation. We further discuss how chronic use of different drug classes also disrupts these brain regions and broader neural circuits involved in sleep regulation, thereby exacerbating initial sleep disturbances and potentially extending their effects to other sleep dimensions. This review underscores the importance of integrating multimodal sleep and neuroimaging assessments to advance the neurobiological understanding of the bidirectional relationship between sleep, drug use and addiction and highlights directions for future research.

Article.Title: The genetic orchestra of autism and its intersections with epilepsy, intellectual disability, and ADHD
Article.Authors: Korkmaz S.; De Sainte Agathe J.; Cliquet F.; Martin L.; Barthome E.; Fleury M.; Segers J.; Bonnot-Briey S.; Grimaldi de Puget V.; Zhou Y.; Wolke D.; Grove J.; Børglum A.; Delorme R.; Leblond C.; Bourgeron T.
Article.Abstract: Autism is a complex condition with marked phenotypic variability and a multifactorial etiology orchestrated by diverse genetic and environmental influences. In this review, we dissect what we refer to as autism's "genetic orchestra", spanning from the high-impact "soloists", de novo and ultra-rare variants with large effect sizes, to the "polyphonic background" of common variants which individually exert modest effects but collectively have significant impact. We examine how this orchestra wires neural circuits, with convergent biological pathways modulating synaptic function and chromatin remodeling. Although de novo, rare, and common variants are often studied independently, converging evidence supports a model whereby their influences are largely additive. This genetic orchestra is not condition-specific; autism frequently co-occurs with other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, reflecting substantial pleiotropy across both rare and common variant landscapes. Notably, ultra-rare variants tend to associate with co-occurring intellectual disability, ADHD, epilepsy, and psychiatric conditions highlighting their high phenotypic impact. Beyond genetics, layers of environmental and contextual factors further modulate clinical outcomes. In this framework, we also discuss the challenges of identifying genetic variants associated with autism through clinical genetic testing, where yields remain context-dependent, varying by sex and co-occurring conditions. Finally, we address current limitations and future directions in refining our understanding of autism's genetic basis.

Article.Title: Development of a messenger RNA therapy for schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Simons N.; Patel V.; Li H.; Iyer S.; Zhong Y.; Cao D.; Yu C.; Obiajulu D.; Keller K.; Hynes G.; Lee S.; Nadukuru R.; Cheng E.; Chen E.; Hashemi A.; Lund A.; Rogers H.; Jackson R.; Preuss M.; Thibeau H.; Nadkarni G.; Liharska L.; Charney D.; Barbosa M.; Marro S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Few gene-disease associations identified by human genetic studies lead to new drugs that advance to first-in-human trials. Schizophrenia exemplifies this translational gap: thousands of gene-disease associations have been reported, but antipsychotics act via mechanisms introduced in the 1950s. To close the gap, clinical research strategies are needed that generalize across genes and diseases. Methods: Candidate drug targets were defined as genes linked to schizophrenia by population-based studies. Clinical validation of candidate targets was performed through family-based studies. The molecular effects of clinically validated targets were confirmed by correcting mutations in the neurons from affected family members. For one validated target, a messenger RNA (mRNA) drug was developed, and pre-clinical studies of the drug were performed. Results: Carriers of rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in schizophrenia risk genes were identified in 30,813 patients of a US healthcare system. These included two female relatives with a rare PTV in GRIA3, which encodes the GluA3 subunit of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. Further investigation of the family found an X-linked pattern of inheritance between the PTV and severe mental illness. Correction of the PTV in neurons of affected male family members restored GRIA3 expression. A GRIA3 mRNA drug was developed and in mice was well tolerated, resulted in broad brain expression of GluA3, and rescued behavioral abnormalities in a pharmacologically induced psychosis model (MK-801). Conclusions: Further development toward clinical evaluation of a novel GRIA3 mRNA drug to treat schizophrenia is warranted.

Article.Title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression
Article.Authors: Momi D.; Wang Z.; Oveisi M.; Kadak K.; Bastiaens S.; Lissemore J.; Noda Y.; Downar J.; Rodriguez F.; Strafella R.; Daskalakis Z.; Zrenner C.; Zomorrodi R.; Rolle C.; Saggar M.; Williams N.; Keller C.; Blumberger D.; Voineskos D.; Griffiths J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation. Methods: We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Individualized whole-brain models were fitted to pre- and post-iTBS TMS-evoked potentials, yielding subject-specific estimates of synaptic connectivity, excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, and cortical dynamics. Brain states were defined by singular value decomposition of the model's population activity, and partial least squares analysis with nested cross-validation identified the brain-state pattern distinguishing responders from non-responders. Results: We identified two neurophysiological signatures associated with treatment response. First, responders showed greater post-treatment reductions in 3-10 Hz oscillatory power, driven by shifts in E/I balance toward greater inhibitory control through reduced excitatory drive and increased inhibitory-to-pyramidal connectivity. Second, a pre-treatment brain state characterized by opposite-polarity dynamics between subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and left DLPFC distinguished responders from non-responders, consistent with prior fMRI findings on frontolimbic anticorrelation. Neural trajectory analysis further revealed greater dynamical reorganization and increased attractor stability in responders following treatment. Conclusions: These findings provide a neurophysiologically-informed framework linking iTBS treatment efficacy to specific changes in cortical E/I balance and frontolimbic circuit dynamics, pointing toward candidate markers that, with subject-specific structural connectivity and independent validation, may inform personalized neuromodulation approaches in treatment-resistant depression.

Article.Title: Neural Circuits of Social Behavior in Autism Spectrum Disorder: From Mechanism to Intervention
Article.Authors: O’Reilly Sparks K.; Pedapati E.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Difficulties in social communication and interaction are core diagnostic features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet interventions targeting these difficulties have modest and variable effects. Understanding mechanistically distinct contributions to social behaviors may identify new therapeutic opportunities. Methods: This narrative review integrates human neuroimaging studies, supporting rodent circuit neuroscience, clinical intervention research, and developmental studies. We organize the findings into four overlapping functional-computational domains and relate these domains to the Research Domain Criteria Social Processes framework. Results: The four domains are: (1) Social Reward and Social Interest, encompassing the incentive and hedonic value of social contact and motivation to engage; (2) Social Memory and Social-Affective Value, encompassing recognition of familiar individuals and learned affective or motivational associations; (3) Social Cue Perception, Action Representation, and Social Prediction/Timing, encompassing the processing and forecasting of dynamic social information; and (4) Higher-Order Social Cognition and Model Updating, encompassing mental-state inference and the updating of person-specific social models. Because these domains are not independent, interactions among reward, memory, cue processing, prediction, and higher-order inference create multiple possible developmental entry points, such that early differences in one process may alter experience-dependent learning in others. Evidence for specific causal cascades remains preliminary and requires longitudinal testing. Conclusions: A circuit-and-development framework may improve hypothesis generation, domain-specific phenotyping, target-engagement assessment, and mechanism-aligned outcomes. Clinical translation, however, requires caution. Biomarkers should be validated as predictors of treatment response, cascade models should be tested longitudinally, and interventions should combine mechanism-informed targets with behavioral support that promotes generalization to daily life.

Article.Title: Genetic architecture and risk of suicide attempt across neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions
Article.Authors: Starnawska A.; Nielsen T.; Grove J.; Cordero-Solorzano J.; Bybjerg-Grauholm J.; Havdahl A.; Carracedo A.; Hakonarson H.; Dziobek I.; Underwood J.; González-Peñas J.; Duan J.; Buxbaum J.; Weiss L.; Tebartz van Elst L.; Scherer S.; Kuo S.; Thomas T.; Ahlqvist V.; Zhang Y.; Corfield E.; Anney R.; Docherty A.; Børglum A.; Demontis D.
Article.Abstract: Background: Suicide attempt (SA) is prevalent among individuals with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, yet similarities and differences in the genetic architecture of SA across these conditions remain unclear. Methods: In the iPSYCH cohort (N=98,069), SA was identified using ICD-10 codes among individuals diagnosed with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (N=22,962), autism (N=17,670), schizophrenia (N=5,974), bipolar disorder (N=3,028), depression (N=28,844), and controls (N=34,049). We evaluated 21 polygenic scores (PGSs) in individuals with and without SA within each diagnosis, stratified individuals into PGS quantiles, estimated absolute SA risk, and conducted sex-stratified analyses. Results: SA was 1% among controls but ranged from 5% in autism to 31% in schizophrenia. Several PGSs were increased in individuals with SA across diagnoses, including PGS for ADHD, depression, and substance use disorders (SUD). SA-PGS stratification showed marked SA absolute risk differences, e.g., 40% in the top PGS tertile vs 29% in the lowest tertile in schizophrenia. PGS-loads did not differ between females and males with SA across diagnoses. However, absolute SA risk differed substantially. In the highest SA-PGS tertile in ADHD, the absolute SA risk reached 36% for females and 22% for males and was further increased to 48% in those with comorbid SUD. Conclusions: SA genetic architecture is similar across neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions and individuals can be stratified into SA risk groups based on PGSs, and co-occuring SUD. Being a female or having comorbid SUD are strong risk factors for SA, however SA common variants, still affect SA risk in the presence of those factors.

Article.Title: Simultaneous measurement of Midbrain and Striatal Dopamine in Schizophrenia using an agonist radiotracer
Article.Authors: Slifstein M.; Gil R.; Weinstein J.; Van Snellenberg J.; Horga G.; Carson R.; Huang Y.; Nabulsi N.; Abi-Dargham A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Imaging studies showing greater amphetamine-induced dopamine release in patients with schizophrenia (SCZ) compared to matched healthy controls (HC) have been repeatedly replicated, but these studies all used radiotracers that were dopamine D2 receptor antagonists. A more recent study using an agonist radiotracer did not detect this increase, raising a question whether the difference in radiotracer pharmacology affected the result. Another study examining the extrastriatal response to the amphetamine challenge with an antagonist tracer observed a blunted effect in SCZ in the midbrain, suggesting mechanisms local to the striatum might have contributed to the striatal imaging results independent of midbrain dopamine availability. Here, we sought to address both of these questions by performing neuroimaging in SCZ and HC with the agonist tracer [11C]-(+)-PHNO that is quantifiable in striatum and extrastriatal brain regions including midbrain. Methods: 28 SCZ and 29 HC were scanned at baseline and 3 hours after oral administration of 0.5 mg/kg d-amphetamine. Outcome measures were baseline binding (BPND) and the percent change following amphetamine (ΔBPND). Results: There were no significant group differences in any of the outcome measures, but we observed trend level lower BPND and ΔBPND in SCZ compared to HC. Post-hoc analysis showed this was mainly driven by dorsal striatum subregions. Associations between ΔBPND in midbrain and striatal regions were modest in both groups. Conclusions: Our results are consistent with the prior study using an agonist tracer that did not observe greater ΔBPND in SCZ.

Article.Title: Brain NaV1.5 fine-tunes neuronal excitability to facilitate female-directed social behavior in male mice
Article.Authors: Ke W.; Zhang H.; Li L.; Xiao Y.; Lyu S.; He Q.; Zhang X.; Yin L.; Tai Y.; Shu Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: The voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.5, an essential subtype for cardiac action potential generation, is also enriched in limbic regions of the brain, but its function in the central nervous system remains poorly understood. Methods: We performed RNAscope, immunostaining, electrophysiology, fiber photometry, Scn5a knockdown, and behavioral testing to dissect the functional role of NaV1.5 in the brain. Results: NaV1.5 channels are enriched in neurons of posterior bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNSTp) and accumulated at the axon initial segment. Activation of these tetrodotoxin-resistant channels lowers action potential threshold and accelerates spike initiation at relatively hyperpolarized levels of membrane potential (Vm). In vivo fiber photometry showed that BNSTp NaV1.5-expressing neurons in male mice were recruited by salient social stimuli and exhibited hyperpolarizing Vm dynamics during social contacts. Scn5a knockdown selectively attenuated neuronal responses to female chemosensory cues, and disrupted sex preference and female-directed behaviors. Conclusions: These findings identify NaV1.5 as a Vm state-dependent regulator of BNSTp neuronal excitability, and reveal an unexpected role of this channel subtype in female-cue processing and female-directed social behavior in males.

Article.Title: Thalamocortical dysconnectivity shapes cortical hierarchy disruption across illness durations in schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Huang H.; Palaniyappan L.; Li H.; Zhou J.; Tang Y.; Hou C.; Liu Z.; He H.; Jiang S.; Jin L.; Yi Q.; Tang Y.; Wang J.; Cui L.; Rodriguez-Labrada R.; Chang X.; Feng J.; Jiang Y.; Yao D.; Luo C.
Article.Abstract: Background: Schizophrenia is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of circuit-level dysfunction. However, how thalamocortical abnormalities differ across cohorts with varying illness durations and relate to large-scale cortical hierarchical organization remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 1,223 patients with schizophrenia and 1,224 matched healthy controls across 12 datasets. The datasets were grouped as early-, middle-, and late-stage cohorts. Connectivity gradient mapping was applied to characterize thalamocortical organization, and computational modeling evaluated simulated hierarchical changes after modifying thalamic-salience connectivity. Results: We identified a schizophrenia-relevant sensorimotor-salience-association axis that captures systematic differences in thalamocortical abnormality profiles across the stage cohorts. Along this axis, case-control effects in association regions were positive in the early-stage cohort but negative in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, whereas sensorimotor regions showed the converse pattern. This cross-cohort pattern was accompanied by reduced cortical hierarchical separation in cohorts with longer illness duration. In contrast, salience-related thalamic regions showed negative case-control effects in all three stage cohorts, with larger effect sizes in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, and these alterations were associated with clinical symptoms. Computational modification of thalamic-salience connectivity increased simulated cortical hierarchical differentiation, particularly in the middle-stage cohort. Conclusions: These findings indicate that thalamocortical dysconnectivity, centered on disrupted thalamic-salience interactions, is associated with systematic differences in cortical hierarchical organization across cohorts. The cross-cohort pattern of salience-related abnormalities highlights thalamic-salience coupling as a circuit-level link to cortical hierarchical differentiation and a candidate for future mechanistic and interventional investigation.

Article.Title: Positive–affective and negative–cognitive brain–behavior axes in clinical high risk for psychosis
Article.Authors: Vieira S.; Aleman Y.; Bici L.; Meijer J.; Penzel N.; Jacobs G.; Yassin W.; Alameda L.; Bastürk Ö.; Pries L.; Kiakos D.; Armando M.; Klauser P.; Abrahamyan-Empson L.; Conus P.; Wannan C.; Dwyer D.; Cho K.; Knight S.; Cecchi G.; Polosecki P.; Allott K.; Addington J.; Arango C.; Breitborde N.
Article.Abstract: Background: Individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR) present with heterogeneous combinations of positive, negative, and affective symptoms, cognitive difficulties, and functional impairment. However, reproducible multivariate links between this multidomain phenotype and brain morphology remain limited. This study explored the multivariate brain-behavior associations in CHR using a data-driven approach. Methods: Baseline data from 720 CHR participants from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership® Schizophrenia program (AMP® SCZ) were analyzed using sparse canonical correlation analysis to identify associations between 95 regional brain volumes and 28 behavioral variables indexing symptoms, cognition, and functioning. Generalizability was tested using leave-one-network-out cross-validation (PRoNET and PRESCIENT), and stability was assessed using bootstrapping and leave-one-site-out analyses. Associations with demographic, clinical and site-related variables were examined. Results: Two brain-behavior dimensions generalized across networks. A positive-affective axis (r=0.21-0.23), linking higher depression, anxiety/stress, positive symptoms and anhedonia with predominantly frontal-cingulate-insular volume reductions and relatively larger corpus callosum and putamen volumes. This axis was associated with comorbid depression, cannabis use and family history of depression or affective psychosis. A negative-cognitive axis (r=0.17-0.18) linked greater asociality, alogia, emotional withdrawal, blunted affect, and motor retardation, poorer cognition and functioning with reduced cerebellar and parietal volumes, and relatively larger lateral ventricles and corpus callosum. This axis was associated with lower IQ and poorer premorbid adjustment. Conclusions: Two partially dissociable brain-behavior dimensions were identified: a positive-affective axis capturing the co-expression of affective and attenuated positive symptoms, and a negative-cognitive axis suggestive of neurodevelopmental vulnerability.
Article.Keywords: brain morphology; brain-behavior associations; canonical correlation analysis; cognition; high-risk psychosis; symptoms

Article.Title: Clinically unresponsive patients with acute brain injury activate a brain-computer interface
Article.Authors: Shen Q.; Eliseyev A.; Kansara V.; Neves Briard J.; Song Y.; Carmona J.; Gonzales I.; Velazquez A.; Klein A.; Agarwal S.; Park S.; Ghoshal S.; Roh D.; Connolly E.; Claassen J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Brain activation to verbal commands can be detected by EEG in clinically unresponsive patients. These patients with cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) are unable to communicate with the environment despite preserved consciousness. Advanced brain-computer interfaces (BCI) are promising to support motor function in patients with motor neuron disease or spinal cord injury. Our primary objective was to determine if clinically unresponsive patients can control a self-paced, one-way BCI early after acute brain injury. Secondarily, we assessed the association of BCI control with short- and long-term outcomes. We conducted a prospective single-centre cohort study in 41 clinically unresponsive, critically ill and acutely brain injured patients, as well as in a convenience sample of 8 healthy volunteers and 22 conscious critically ill patients. The self-paced BCI analysed EEG in real time and modulated frequency and pitch of a tone that patients controlled by attempting a motor task: patients were provided with instructions ‘to make the beep sound faster, keep opening and closing your right hand’ alternating with ‘to make the beep sound slower, stop opening and closing your right hand’. CMD was detected by applying machine learning to EEG recorded while patients listened to motor commands. Clinical outcomes were recovery of consciousness by hospital discharge, assessed with the Coma Recovery Scale–Revised, and recovery of functional independence at 12 months, defined as a Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended score of 4 or higher (denoting the ability to function independently for 8 h or more). Additionally, we invited conscious patients as well as family members of conscious and clinically unresponsive patients to complete a survey on perceived utility and challenges associated with the BCI. In this study, 13 clinically unresponsive patients (32%) achieved BCI control and 8 of 41 (20%) were CMD-positive. All healthy volunteers and nine conscious patients (41%) were able to control the BCI. Median signal delay for BCI control was 49.8 [interquartile range (IQR) 39.9–75.6] seconds for clinically unresponsive patients, 17.1 (IQR 7.8–19.9) for conscious patients and 15.5 (IQR 12.9–21.2) for healthy volunteers. In the group of 41 clinically unresponsive patients, 4 of 13 patients with (31%) and 1 of 28 without BCI control (4%) recovered clinical consciousness at hospital discharge [odds ratio (OR) 21.2; 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.3–930.7]. At 12 months, 6 of 13 patients with (46%) and 2 of 28 without BCI control (7%) recovered functional independence (OR 9.9; 95% CI 1.8–81.6). None of the patients that were unable to control the BCI and were CMD-negative recovered. Patients with BCI control had shorter times to recovery of functional independence by 12 months than those who did not (hazards ratio 6.0; 95% CI 1.2–30.6). All respondents of the BCI survey (n = 37) expressed strong support for the potential future use of BCI devices. These results suggest that BCI control is a strong predictor of outcomes following acute brain injury and provide initial evidence that a bedside, EEG-based BCI system might permit bidirectional communication in critically ill unresponsive patients.

Article.Title: TMEM106B risk converges on C-terminal fragment homeostasis: genetics, mechanisms and therapy
Article.Authors: Lastra Osua M.; Perneel J.; Vicente C.; Rademakers R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract TMEM106B is a genetic modifier influencing susceptibility to multiple neurodegenerative disorders, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP), Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, as well as contributing to healthy brain aging and neuronal reserve. The gene harbours single nucleotide polymorphisms and structural variants that define risk and protective haplotypes, and despite extensive efforts to identify the functional variant within these haplotypes, consensus remains elusive. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of TMEM106B genetics from human cohorts and mechanistic studies, highlighting how variants may influence its regulatory network and protein levels, with an emphasis on its aggregation-prone C-terminal domain. We further integrate evidence on the roles of TMEM106B within the endo-lysosomal system and beyond, including insights into protein structure, posttranslational modifications, interactors, proteolytic processing, and fibril formation. These findings are contextualized using data from mouse and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, highlighting current gaps in the available models and the advances required to study its functions and cleavage. Finally, we explore therapeutic strategies targeting TMEM106B, focusing on modulation of expression, specific functional pathways, and fibril formation.

Article.Title: Progenitor transcriptional alterations link fetal and adult pathology in Huntington’s disease
Article.Authors: Battistella M.; Damaggio G.; Conforti P.; Scolz A.; Maestri S.; Bocchi V.; Iafolla D.; Galimberti M.; Morrocchi M.; Cordiglieri C.; Vezzoli E.; Lodato S.; Ranzani V.; Viale S.; Thompson L.; Vogt T.; Felsenfeld D.; Chen J.; Besusso D.; Cattaneo E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Huntington’s disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Although the mutant huntingtin protein is expressed from conception, clinical symptoms typically emerge in mid-adulthood. Imaging and molecular studies have raised the possibility that HD may involve neurodevelopmental abnormalities, but direct evidence at the single-cell level in the human fetal brain has been lacking. Here we investigated whether early, cell type–specific transcriptional vulnerabilities arise during neurodevelopment, persist into adult pathology, and might be rescued. To address this, we performed single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the lateral ganglionic eminence (LGE) and cortex from a rare, anatomically intact human HD fetal brain, alongside matched controls. These data were complemented by an allelic series of HD mouse embryos and cross-compared with already published human post-mortem brains and brain organoid models’ datasets. Neural progenitors displayed the highest number of differentially expressed genes in the human fetal brain, and were also impacted in the HD mouse model, where additional cell types displayed transcriptional alterations. Notably, human HD progenitor transcriptional signatures were moderately enriched in the developing mouse LGE. These progenitors exhibited increased expression of synaptic pathways coupled with reduced expression of cell maintenance genes. Cross-comparison with publicly available post-mortem HD datasets revealed that components of this transcriptional signature persist into adulthood. Furthermore, cellular interactions were found to mitigate these alterations, highlighting a potentially rescuable fetal-to-adult transcriptional signature with important implications for HD pathogenesis and therapeutic strategies. Together, these findings reinforce the view of HD as a disorder with developmental origins, in which early transcriptional changes may shape neuronal function while increasing susceptibility to later neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Serum β-synuclein predicts dementia conversion and mortality beyond amyloid-β and phospho-tau
Article.Authors: Oberstein T.; Schwarz J.; Rudtke L.; Jablonowski J.; Marterstock D.; Schmidt M.; Doerfler A.; Kiesel J.; Klement N.; Schulz P.; Lewczuk P.; Maler J.; Kornhuber J.; Oeckl P.; Otto M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Synaptic dysfunction is among the earliest pathological events in Alzheimer's disease and among the strongest neuropathological correlates of cognitive impairment, yet blood-based synaptic biomarkers are lacking. Whether serum β-synuclein provides prognostic information independent of established amyloid-β (A; CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio) and tau (T1; CSF pTau181) biomarkers has not been determined. We studied 259 non-demented individuals with subjective or mild cognitive impairment from a single-centre memory clinic, classified by CSF biomarkers using externally validated cut-offs into A−T1− controls (n = 97), A−T1+ PASSED (‘pTau and Aβ surge with subtle deterioration’, n = 65), and A + T1+ Alzheimer's disease (n = 97), with parallel analyses using Aβ40-normalised pTau181. Endpoints comprised dementia conversion (n = 185, median follow-up 4.1 years), all-cause mortality (n = 258, median 7.0 years), longitudinal MMSE trajectories (n = 185), and regional brain volumes (n = 137). Independence from CSF biomarkers was quantified through systematic effect attenuation analysis. Serum β-synuclein was selectively elevated in the Alzheimer's disease group (Cohen's d = 0.69 vs controls, P < 0.001) but not in PASSED individuals (P = 0.40), and was more strongly associated with CSF pTau181 (r = 0.36) than with the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio (r = −0.20) across the cohort. Each standard deviation increase was associated with higher risk of dementia conversion (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.40; 95% CI: 1.11, 1.77; P = 0.005), faster cognitive decline (−0.11 SD/year, 95% CI: −0.18, −0.04, P = 0.002, corresponding to −0.20 MMSE points/year), and higher mortality (HR = 1.33; 95% CI: 1.07, 1.65; P = 0.010). For dementia conversion and mortality, adjustment for continuous CSF pTau181 and Aβ42/Aβ40 produced minimal attenuation (≤13%). Both associations were preserved under Aβ40-normalised T1 staging but not against continuous pTau181 normalised to CSF Aβ40. For cognitive decline, β-synuclein's effect remained significant after Aβ42/Aβ40 adjustment (25% attenuation; P = 0.007) but was substantially attenuated by pTau181 (58.5%; P = 0.186). Serum β-synuclein was associated with lower bilateral temporal lobe volume—the only lobar regions to survive hierarchical testing—with sub-regional involvement spanning the hippocampi, entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus, and explained 5.0–8.9% of unique variance beyond CSF biomarkers. Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) showed a strong association with β-synuclein, estimated in the PASSED subgroup (β=0.34 per SD, P < 0.001). Serum β-synuclein provided prognostic information largely independent of CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 across all endpoints and of pTau181 for survival outcomes, while sharing substantial prognostic variance with pTau181 for cognitive trajectory, supporting its candidacy as a blood-based synaptic complement to core Alzheimer's disease biomarkers.

Article.Title: Prematurity insults remodel cerebellar development and behaviour
Article.Authors: Sanidas G.; Simonti G.; Ghaemmaghami J.; Woyshner K.; Vidva R.; Bittel D.; Wolff N.; Triantafyllou M.; Polyviou A.; Byrd C.; Lowe C.; Salisbury H.; Goldstein E.; Sathyanesan A.; Koutroulis I.; Stein-O'Brien G.; Sidiropoulos D.; Gallo V.; Kratimenos P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Preterm survivors often develop motor and socio-cognitive impairments that implicate altered cerebellar development, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. A key challenge is that prematurity involves overlapping perinatal insults that converge on the developing brain, making their individual effects difficult to disentangle. Here, we model two major prematurity-associated insults, maternal immune activation (MIA) and neonatal hypoxia (Hx), in mice. By controlling timing and sequence, we define how these insults shape cerebellar assembly during rapid maturation. Comparative analysis with human tissue confirmed that these insults recapitulate key features of the human preterm cerebellum, establishing the translational validity of this model for dissecting insult-specific outcomes. Behavioral and kinematic profiling revealed divergent motor and social phenotypes, which we traced to insult-specific cerebellar remodelling. Hypoxia compromised both granule cell maturation in the internal granule layer and the principal excitatory afferents to Purkinje cells, a circuit state that manifested as impaired motor execution and stereotyped, sensory-disengaged social investigation. Maternal immune activation, by contrast, expanded the granule cell progenitor layer and reduced Purkinje cell dendritic complexity, a phenotype that preserved social preference but reorganized the kinematic structure of social investigation. When hypoxia followed maternal immune activation, it acted on this primed substrate to produce a distinct state in which the features established by prior inflammation were compounded by granule cell proliferative arrest, progressive mitochondrial dysfunction, and aberrant, hyper-interactive social investigation. Together, these findings reframe prematurity-associated insults as cerebellar reprogramming events shaped by both the identity and sequence of insults, linking distinct mechanistic substrates to divergent neurodevelopmental outcomes.

Article.Title: Neuronavigated dual-target transcranial magnetic stimulation for schizophrenia negative symptoms
Article.Authors: Wei Y.; Wang J.; Tang X.; Qian Z.; Xu L.; Cui H.; Song Y.; Zhu H.; Ju M.; Long B.; Zhai W.; Zeng L.; Jiao X.; Lan X.; Wei X.; Tang Y.; Wang J.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Negative symptoms in schizophrenia severely impair function and quality of life, yet respond poorly to current therapies. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial aimed to investigate the efficacy of neuronavigated dual-target repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) and cerebellum for improving negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04853485). Participants with first-episode schizophrenia or clinical high-risk for psychosis were enrolled from Shanghai Mental Health Center and Suzhou Guangji Hospital. Participants were randomly assigned to either a real or sham group under MRI-guided neuronavigation, targeting rDLPFC with 1Hz at 100% motor threshold(MT), cerebellar with intermittent theta burst stimulation(iTBS) at 120% MT for 20 consecutive days. Clinical assessments were conducted at baseline(T0), 10-session(T1), 20-session(T2) and one month after the intervention(T3). Cognition and MRI were evaluated at T0 and T2. The primary outcome was change of negative subscale score of the Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale(PANSS), while secondary outcomes included alterations in other PANSS subscale scores and fronto-cerebellar circuit functional connectivity. In total, 75 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (36 active, 39 sham). The pre-specified primary linear mixed-effects analysis revealed a non-significant group-by-time interaction for PANSS negative subscale scores (F(3,174.6)=1.45, p=0.230). At the 4-week endpoint (T2), the nominal unadjusted between-group p-value was 0.049; after Sidak correction for multiple comparisons, the adjusted mean difference was −2.48 points (95% CI −4.99 to 0.03, adjusted p=0.150, Cohen’s d=−0.51). Descriptive uncorrected t-tests indicated greater negative-symptom reductions in the active group at T1 and T2, and the 4-week negative-symptom response rate (≥50% reduction) was higher under real rTMS (χ2=9.5, p=0.002). A significant group-by-time interaction was observed for PANSS positive subscale scores (F(3,172.0)=3.26, p=0.023). Both groups exhibited substantial within-group symptom improvement. Resting-state fMRI demonstrated group-by-time interactions within cerebello-temporal, parahippocampal, caudate, and parietal networks (FWE-corrected p<0.05), and negative-symptom change correlated with cerebello-caudate connectivity (r=0.33, p=0.026). These findings suggest neuronavigated dual-target rTMS over rDLPFC and cerebellum may be associated with numerical improvements in negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis.

Article.Title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood
Article.Authors: Dutta S.; Atashgaran A.; Sahoo A.; Chatzimichail S.; Kapanidis A.; Tofaris G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Parkinson’s disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34–45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

Article.Title: Biallelic variants in PIKFYVE cause a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with endolysosomal dysfunction
Article.Authors: Averdunk L.; Groß M.; Hamacher A.; Donkervoort S.; Herebian D.; Mohammad S.; Knaus A.; Seibt A.; Schaper J.; Sticht H.; Bryen S.; Bergmann A.; Langener M.; De Simone L.; Markshausen A.; Lenk G.; Ghosh S.; Sandaradura S.; Guthoff T.; Leventer R.; Orbach R.; Rius R.; Morton N.; Gilmour K.; Mayatepek E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The PIKfyve-FIG4-VAC14 lipid kinase complex generates phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2. Pathogenic variants in VAC14 and FIG4 cause neurodevelopmental disorders and PIKFYVE has been linked to autosomal dominant fleck corneal dystrophy. We searched for the underlyging, genetic cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder in five affected individuals from three families using exome- or genome sequencing. Cranial MRI images and clinical phenotypes were analyzed. Size, number and acidity of cellular vacuoles were investigated in patient-derived fibroblasts from family 1 using LysoSensor acidophilic probes. Levels of PI(3,5)P2 were quantified in patient-derived fibroblasts from family 1 using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae were injected with wildtype-mRNA or mutant mRNA harboring the PIKFYVE missense variant identified in family 3. Pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae were treated with metformin, bafilomycin A1, or rapamycin. We identified biallelic PIKFYVE variants in five affected individuals with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, brain hyperintensities of inferior olives, thalami, long tracts, and optic nerves. Clinically, they presented with intellectual disability, spasticity, muscular weakness, and nystagmus. Additional features included feeding difficulties, auditory dysfunction, insulin resistance, microcephaly, peripheral neuropathy, and mild creatine kinase elevations. We detected four distinct PIKFYVE variants: three loss-of-function variants (family 1 & 2), and one p.Arg1156Pro missense variant (family 3). The pathogenicity of the p.Arg1156Pro variant was confirmed by phenotypic rescue of pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae injected with wildtype-mRNA but not with p.Arg1156Pro mRNA. Consistent with the role of PIKfyve in maintaining endolysosomal homeostasis, patient-derived fibroblasts of family 1 accumulated enlarged, hyperacidic vacuoles and showed a reduced PI(3,5)P2 production upon hyperosmotic stimulation. Exposing pikfyve-mutant zebrafisch larvae to the mTORC1 inhibitor and TRPML1 activator rapamycin attenuated cellular vacuolization, highlighting potential therapeutic approaches. Our findings establish PIKFYVE deficiency as a novel cause of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy and endolysosomal dysfunction.

Article.Title: Target engagement and efficacy in disease-modifying trials of synuclein-related disorders
Article.Authors: Artusi C.; Gallo S.; Galli S.; Rinaldi D.; Tinazzi M.; Rascol O.; Espay A.; Fabbri M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Disease-modifying trials in Parkinson’s disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to demonstrate target engagement, de-risk subsequent phases of drug development and provide mechanistic evidence of biological activity. Whether biomarker modulation predicts clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant review of phase II and III disease-modifying trials (2020-2025) that included at least one biomarker intended to assess target engagement. Twenty-six trials met inclusion criteria (PD=19, MSA=4, DLB=3; n=2,195 participants). Target engagement was reported in 14 of 19 PD trials (12 phase II/2 phase III), 1 of 4 MSA trials, and 2 of 3 DLB trials (all phase II). Concordance between target engagement and clinical improvement was uncommon, as only 8/26 studies (7 phase II/1 phase III) demonstrated both target engagement and statistically significant clinical benefit, and just two of these (both phase II, one in PD and one in MSA) were rigorously controlled with low or moderate risk of bias. Nine trials showed target engagement without clinical benefit, whereas two reported clinical improvement without measurable target engagement. Baseline biomarker-guided patient selection was uncommon and rarely aligned with the compound’s mechanism of action. Patient-reported outcomes were widely used but rarely improved. Across recent disease-modifying trials in PD, DLB, and MSA, target engagement was frequently demonstrated, yet clinical benefit rarely followed. These findings question the predictive value of currently used target-engagement biomarkers and highlight the need to biologically align trial populations with the mechanisms targeted by experimental molecular interventions.

Article.Title: The genetic landscape of myotonic dystrophy type 1: insights from nearly one million genomes
Article.Authors: Rahman R.; Futema M.; Behr E.; Matthews E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Myotonic Dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a multisystem disorder caused by CTG repeat expansions in the dystrophia myotonica protein kinase (DMPK) gene. Current prevalence estimates of 1 in 3,000-8,000 have traditionally relied on clinically ascertained and geographically restricted cohorts, underestimating population burden and failing to capture ancestry diversity. Using large-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) datasets, we aimed to identify DMPK repeat expansions across nearly one million participants, define their ancestry-specific distribution, and evaluate associated clinical phenotypes, with particular focus on cardiac manifestations and early-onset cataracts. We analysed WGS participants from three cohorts: Genomics England (n = 80,110), UK Biobank (n = 490,086), and the All of Us Research Program (n = 414,830). DMPK repeat lengths were estimated using ExpansionHunter. Alleles were classified as Normal (≤37 repeats), Intermediate (38-49 repeats), or Pathogenic (≥50 repeats). Genetic ancestry was assigned using cohort-specific methods. Linked health record data assessed cardiac phenotypes in UK Biobank and early-onset cataracts in Genomics England and UK Biobank. Across all cohorts (n = 985,026), pathogenic DMPK repeat expansions were identified in 645 individuals (0.07%; ∼1 in 1,527), a prevalence two-to-five times higher than previous estimates. Most expansions occurred in those of European ancestry, although expansions were detected across all groups, including up to 1 in 6,693 African and Asian ancestry. In UK Biobank, individuals with a pathogenic expansion had increased odds of any cardiac diagnosis (odds ratio [OR]: 2.06, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.58–2.67; p = 5.8×108) and greater cardiac diagnostic burden (risk ratio 2.46, CI: 1.92–3.15; p = 1.6×10−13). Conduction abnormalities—particularly atrioventricular and left bundle-branch block, atrial fibrillation, and flutter—showed the strongest association with expansion status (OR: 4.86, CI: 3.38–6.79; p = 2.7×10−18). No sex differences were observed among those with a DMPK expansion, although male sex was independently associated with conduction disease in the overall population. Approximately one-in-ten individuals with pathogenic expansions had a cataract diagnosis before age 55. Most individuals with an expansion had no prior DM1 diagnosis, highlighting the value of systematic genetic testing in these phenotypes to improve diagnosis, shorten the diagnostic interval, and mitigate harm. By integrating WGS data from nearly one million individuals, this study refines understanding of the population distribution and clinical consequences of DMPK repeat expansions, revealing a reservoir of undiagnosed and potentially untreated multisystemic disease. These findings support routine inclusion of DMPK analysis within specified cardiac and ophthalmic diagnostic pathways to enable earlier detection.

Article.Title: White matter hyperintensity burden in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: motor and survival correlates
Article.Authors: De Lorenzo A.; Maranzano A.; Cocuzza A.; Gentile F.; Passaretti M.; Colombo E.; Torre S.; Aiello E.; Calcagno N.; Gendarini C.; Olivero M.; Scheveger F.; Patisso V.; Spagliardi J.; Di Maio A.; Pierro S.; Treddenti M.; Gagliardi D.; Comi G.; Corti S.; Pereira J.; Agosti P.; Peyvandi F.; Messina S.; Doretti A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor neuron degeneration. Microvascular dysfunction has been implicated by recent research in ALS pathogenesis and motor neuron vulnerability. The aim of this study is to investigate whether MRI markers of white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), reflecting small-vessel disease, are associated with motor and cognitive impairment, disease staging and prognosis in ALS. In this retrospective cohort study MRI scans from 399 ALS patients were evaluated for periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities (pvWMH and dWMH) using visual grading scales together with semi-automated volumetric quantification of relative WMH volume (WMHrv). The primary outcome was survival. Secondary outcomes included disease staging, functional impairment, motor and cognitive outcome measures. WMH burden was associated with more advanced King’s topographic staging [pvWMH (P < 0.001), dWMH (P = 0.002)] and MiToS functional staging [pvWMH (P < 0.001), dWMH (P = 0.017)]. High pvWMH burden was associated with shorter survival [exp(β) = 3.503; 95% CI = 1.131, 10.832; P = 0.030] after adjustment for known prognostic factors. WMH measures correlated with greater functional impairment on ALSFRS-R score [pvWMH (P < 0.001), dWMH (P = 0.003), WMHrv (P = 0.008)]. WMH burden correlated with more severe lower, but not upper, motor neuron impairment, as measured with the MRC sum score [pvWMH (P = 0.002), dWMH (P = 0.024), WMHrv (p=0.030)] and lower motor neuron score [pvWMH (P < 0.001), dWMH (P = 0.001)]. WMH burden was also associated with cognitive deficits on the Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen (ECAS), as indicated by total [pvWMH (P = 0.007), dWMH (P = 0.009), WMHrv (P = 0.037)] and ALS-specific ECAS scores [pvWMH (P = 0.001), dWMH (P = 0.020), WMHrv (P = 0.022)]. This large-scale MRI study links small-vessel disease to clinical staging, survival and ALS-specific motor (distinctively LMN) and cognitive impairments. These results suggest that WMHs may reflect a diffuse neurovascular pathology spanning cortical and spinal regions and may be relevant to ALS progression. Routine MRI assessment of WMHs could aid patient stratification and inform trial designs. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify causal relationships and neurovascular-targeted therapeutic implications.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial DNA damage elicits PINK1 upregulation in pontine cholinergic neurons in Parkinson’s disease
Article.Authors: Lu H.; Pyle A.; Steyn J.; Lawless C.; Hussain R.; Falkenberg M.; Elson J.; Pienaar I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In Parkinson’s disease, cholinergic neurons of the pedunculopontine nucleus, located in the upper pons, undergo extensive degeneration, contributing to severe hypokinetic-motor and non-motor symptoms. We previously demonstrated that loss of these neurons is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, driven by high mitochondrial DNA deletion burden. Increased mitochondrial DNA replication was also observed in these neurons, contrasting with reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number previously reported in Parkinson’s-affected surviving nigral-dopaminergic neurons. Here, ultra-deep whole-genome sequencing combined with stringent quality control was used to characterise mitochondrial DNA alterations within single-cell pedunculopontine-cholinergic neurons isolated from Parkinson’s-affected and neurologically-normal post-mortem specimens. Analyses included mitochondrial DNA deletion spectrum, -size distribution, genomic location, heteroplasmy levels, breakpoint classification, and point-mutation frequency. Thermodynamic modelling was used to investigate whether the stability of mitochondrial DNA secondary structures surrounding deletion breakpoints could provide insight into the mechanisms underlying mitochondrial DNA deletion formation in Parkinson’s disease. In parallel, nuclear-encoded mitochondrial pathway responses were assessed using a customised single-cell multiplexed multi-target gene expression assay, comparing Parkinson’s and control post-mortem neurons. Parkinson’s-affected neurons exhibited substantial mitochondrial DNA damage, characterised by large-scale mitochondrial DNA deletions predominantly locating within mitochondrial DNA’s major arc. Mitochondrial DNA deletions ranged ∼50-5,500 base-pairs, with most exceeding 1,000 base-pairs. Clonal expansion of large-scale mitochondrial DNA deletions, likely arising from replication-associated errors, represented the dominant mutant species. Small mitochondrial DNA deletions (<50bp) were rare, suggesting that free radical–induced strand breakage was not the primary driver of somatic mitochondrial DNA damage. Point-mutation frequency was similar between Parkinson’s and control neurons but showed greater functional impact on electron transport chain complex-I subunits in Parkinsonian neurons. Thermodynamic modelling revealed reduced stability of mitochondrial DNA secondary structures flanking mitochondrial DNA deletion breakpoints in Parkinsonian post-mortem neurons, with an average decrease of ∼2 kJ/mol across two major mitochondrial DNA deletions formation models. The increased mitochondrial DNA damage was accompanied by marked upregulation of the nuclear-encoded mitophagy regulator PINK1, specifically in PD patients with extended survival, suggesting activation of a compensatory cytoprotective response. Together, these findings provide comprehensive single-cell resolution profiling of mitochondrial genomic alterations in pedunculopontine-cholinergic neurons in Parkinson’s, displaying extensive mitochondrial DNA structural disruption dominated by large-scale mitochondrial DNA deletions. Our results further suggest that upregulation of mitophagy-related pathways may represent an adaptive mechanism to mitigate progressive mitochondrial genomic instability and preserve neuronal energy homeostasis.
