Article.Title: Nerve growth factor metabolic dysfunction in Down’s syndrome brains
Article.Authors: Iulita M.; Do Carmo S.; Ower A.; Fortress A.; Flores Aguilar L.; Hanna M.; Wisniewski T.; Granholm A.; Buhusi M.; Busciglio J.; Cuello A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons play a key role in cognition. This neuronal system is highly dependent on nerve growth factor (NGF) for its synaptic integrity and the phenotypic maintenance of its cell bodies. Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons progressively degenerate in Alzheimer’s disease and Down’s syndrome, and their atrophy contributes to the manifestation of dementia. Paradoxically, in Alzheimer’s disease brains, the synthesis of NGF is not affected and there is abundance of the NGF precursor (proNGF). We have shown that this phenomenon is due to a deficit in NGF’s extracellular metabolism which compromises proNGF maturation and exacerbates its subsequent degradation. We hypothesized that a similar imbalance should be present in Down’s syndrome. Using a combination of quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, western blotting and zymography, we have investigated signs of NGF metabolic dysfunction in post-mortem brains from the temporal (n = 14), frontal (n = 34) and parietal (n = 20) cortex obtained from Down’s syndrome subjects and age-matched controls (age range 31–68 years). We further examined primary cultures of human fetal Down’s syndrome cortex (17–21 gestational age weeks). We report a significant increase in proNGF levels in human Down’s syndrome brains, with a concomitant reduction in the levels of plasminogen and tissue plasminogen activator mRNA as well as an increment in neuroserpin expression; enzymes that partake in proNGF maturation. Down’s syndrome brains also exhibited elevated zymogenic activity of MMP9, the major NGF-degrading protease. Our results indicate a failure in proNGF maturation in Down’s syndrome brains and a likely enhanced proteolytic degradation of NGF, changes which can compromise the trophic support of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons. The alterations in proNGF and MMP9 were also present in cultures of Down’s syndrome fetal cortex; suggesting that this trophic compromise may be amenable to rescue, before frank dementia onset. Our study thus provides a novel paradigm for cholinergic neuroprotection in Alzheimer’s disease and Down’s syndrome.

Article.Title: NKCC1 coordinates SPAK–PP1 signalling to regulate KCC2 membrane stability and seizure susceptibility
Article.Authors: Pol E.; Delhaye C.; Cases-Cunillera S.; Boiko E.; Russeau M.; Samba N.; Pillon E.; Blachier S.; Bouchet A.; Piesse C.; Di Scala C.; Pallud J.; Huberfeld G.; Pietrancosta N.; Lévi S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chloride homeostasis, and thereby the efficacy of chloride-permeable GABAA receptor signaling, depends on the dynamic balance between NKCC1 (Na+–K+–2Cl− cotransporter 1) and KCC2 (K+–Cl− cotransporter 2), which respectively mediate chloride influx and extrusion to tightly control intracellular chloride concentration ([Cl−]i). Here, we uncover an unexpected mechanism by which NKCC1 regulates KCC2 membrane stability and function. Co-immunoprecipitation experiments from mouse brain lysates revealed that KCC2 associates with NKCC1 and SPAK (STE20/SPS1-related proline-alanine-rich kinase), indicating that these proteins are within a common molecular interaction network. Furthermore, we show that NKCC1 and KCC2 form co-clusters in the plasma membrane of hippocampal neurons and that freely diffusing KCC2 molecules become trapped within NKCC1 membrane clusters. These observations suggest that NKCC1 coordinates SPAK- and PP1-dependent regulation of KCC2. Guided by molecular modeling, we designed peptides targeting specific interactions within this complex. Peptides that activate SPAK by engaging NKCC1’s PP1-binding motif decrease KCC2 surface expression and impair chloride extrusion, whereas a SPAK-inhibiting peptide that prevents SPAK recruitment to NKCC1, stabilizes KCC2 in membrane clusters, and enhances chloride extrusion. An optimized peptide analog suitable for in vivo use preserves KCC2 clustering under hyperexcitable conditions, reduces seizure frequency and severity in an acute pentylenetetrazol-induced (PTZ) seizure model, and suppresses ictal activity in chronically epileptic human tissue. Together, these findings identify NKCC1 as a key regulator of KCC2 membrane stability, reveal NKCC1-KCC2 coupling as a critical determinant of inhibitory signaling, and establish this complex as a potential therapeutic target for restoring chloride homeostasis in epilepsy and related neurological disorders.

Article.Title: CRISPR screen reveals FTO-mediated m6A modification of ATF3 as protective in ischaemic stroke
Article.Authors: Yu J.; Zhu X.; Lu Q.; Ma H.; Zhang Z.; Yu Q.; Liu Z.; Li Z.; Li G.; Jin X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract RNA modifications, especially N6-methyladenosine (m6A), have emerged as pivotal regulators of gene expression in neurological disorders, yet their roles in ischaemic stroke remain unclear. Here, we performed a CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screen targeting 118 RNA modification-related genes in neuronal cells subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) and validated the findings in a mouse model of middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R). We identified Fto as a top negatively selected gene, with its expression progressively reduced and global m6A levels increased during ischaemic injury. Neuron-specific Fto knockout aggravated infarct size, neurological deficits, cognitive impairment, and neuronal apoptosis, accompanied by activation of multiple signalling pathways revealed by RNA-seq analysis. Integrated m6A-seq and RNA-seq profiling uncovered Atf3 as a hypermethylated and upregulated hub gene downstream of Fto deficiency, linking m6A dysregulation to enhanced neuronal apoptosis. In vitro assays confirmed that FTO knockdown increased ATF3 mRNA methylation and expression under OGD/R conditions, whereas Fto overexpression in vivo alleviated ischaemic brain injury, improved neurological outcomes, reduced Atf3 expression, and lowered global m6A levels. Together, our findings reveal the Fto/m6A/ATF3 axis as a critical mediator of ischaemic injury and highlight Fto restoration as a potential therapeutic strategy for stroke.

Article.Title: Blood–brain barrier opening with focused ultrasound reduces neuromelanin in a non-human primate model
Article.Authors: Esteban-García N.; Martín-Flórez C.; Pineda-Pardo J.; López-Aguirre M.; Carrillo M.; Rodríguez-Rojas R.; Trigo-Damas I.; Lanciego J.; Vila M.; Obeso J.; Blesa J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Age-related accumulation of neuromelanin (NM) has been implicated in the intrinsic vulnerability of catecholaminergic neurons in Parkinson’s disease. Postmortem studies in Parkinson’s disease patients have revealed elevated intracellular and extracellular NM in the substantia nigra pars compacta, whereas experimental enhancement of NM synthesis in animal models disrupts neuronal homeostasis and accelerates neurodegeneration. Low-intensity focused ultrasound combined with microbubbles (LIFU-MB) induces focal opening of the blood–brain barrier. It has been shown to influence protein aggregation and modulate pigment-related processes, thereby raising the possibility that it may also impact NM dynamics in the brain. Here, we investigated the possibility that repeated LIFU-MB–mediated blood–brain barrier opening could modify NM accumulation in a non-human primate model that overexpresses human tyrosinase, leading to elevated NM accumulation in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Comprehensive characterization revealed that these animals exhibit several features compatible with early pathological changes in Parkinson’s disease including extracellular NM release, increased iron accumulation, nigral inflammatory changes, and intracellular inclusion formation. Importantly, these alterations occur in the absence of substantial dopaminergic cell loss and behavioral deficits. LIFU-MB–treated animals showed a marked reduction in both intracellular and extracellular NM, accompanied by a trend toward decreased free ferric iron. These results indicate that early, non-invasive LIFU-MB intervention can counteract mechanisms linked to excessive NM accumulation. Moreover, this approach provides a translational framework to explore the broader feasibility of reducing intracellular pigments and pathological aggregates in the brain. Given its clinical safety, capacity to reach deep brain structures, and non-invasive nature, LIFU-MB warrants further investigation as a possible therapeutic approach in Parkinson´s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders.

Article.Title: Multi-molecular adaptations of long-term opioid use in chronic pain
Article.Authors: Baliki M.; Vigotsky A.; Rached G.; Jabakhanji R.; Huang L.; Branco P.; Barroso J.; Cong O.; Centeno M.; Cermak S.; Griffith J.; Wasan A.; Schnitzer T.; Apkarian A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Millions of chronic pain patients are managed with opioids, yet the neuropsychological implications of stable long-term daily opioid consumption remain unknown. Here, we contrasted the psychosocial profiles and brain structure and function of 70 chronic back pain patients prescribed opioids (CBP+O, average current daily opioid exposure of 7.8 years) with tightly matched 70 opioid-naïve patients (CBP−O) and 30 healthy subjects. Despite CBP+O exhibiting only modestly worse psychosocial profiles and small differences in brain morphology relative to CBP−O, CBP+O showed stark differences in brain activity (ALFF). A large portion (38% of the variance) of this pattern was captured by a model using 19 receptor/transporter distributions. The patients’ (across all 140 CBP) psychosocial profiles were summarized by three principal components (PCs, explaining 70% of variance): functional disability, pain quality, and negative affect. These PCs were respectively associated with serotonergic (5HT1a and 5HT6) and opioidergic (mu-opioid receptor, MOR) receptor-related activities. In additional analyses and new data, 5HT1a- and MOR-related activities tracked opioid dose, abstinence status, and tapering success, while 5HT6-related activity tracked pain intensity. Overall, our findings uncover molecularly defined brain circuits in opioid use and chronic pain.

Article.Title: Endothelial Malat1 promotes post-stroke angiogenesis and neurovascular recovery via the Tek axis
Article.Authors: Xiong T.; Zhang M.; Sun P.; Zhang Y.; Ni A.; Zhang S.; Zhang Y.; Huang X.; Qiu N.; Li S.; Sun D.; Yin K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide, yet current therapeutic strategies, such as thrombolysis and thrombectomy, are constrained by narrow treatment windows and incomplete microvascular repair. While angiogenesis is pivotal for long-term functional recovery, the epigenetic mechanisms governing post-stroke vascular remodeling remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) Malat1 acts as a critical endothelial regulator of angiogenesis and neurological restoration. Using an endothelium-specific Malat1 overexpression mouse model (EC-Malat1 Tg), we demonstrate endothelial Malat1 upregulation enhances angiogenesis, restores cerebral blood flow, and improves sensorimotor and cognitive function following ischemic stroke. Mechanistically, fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-based RNA sequencing of brain endothelial cells identified novel downstream targets of Malat1, including Hapln2, Bcl6, Esr1, Sox17, Tfrc, Hsp90aa1, and Tek. Among these, Tek (Tie2) showed robust endothelial co-localization and direct interaction with Malat1. Notably, while Malat1 overexpression markedly increased Tek protein expression, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated endothelial knockdown of Tek abrogated the pro-angiogenic and neurovascular reparative effects of Malat1. Collectively, our data establishes the Malat1-Tek axis as a novel signaling pathway essential for driving post-ischemic cerebrovascular remodeling and long-term functional recovery. Targeting Malat1 represents a novel restorative therapeutic approach for ischemic stroke.

Article.Title: Next-generation brain organoids: neural complexity from cellular diversity to functional networks
Article.Authors: Duan C.; Wang Y.; Tang T.; Jiao J.; Tang Y.; Teng Z.; Hu B.; Liu C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Brain organoids, as pioneering three-dimensional (3D) in vitro platforms, have profoundly advanced our understanding of human brain development and disease mechanisms. This review summarizes recent progress in enhancing cellular diversity, structural organization, and functional complexity within brain organoids. A key application of these models lies in disease modelling, encompassing neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders as well as brain tumours, which enables personalized drug screening and mechanistic studies. Despite persistent challenges related to neuronal maturation, vascularization, reproducibility, and functional integration, we highlight emerging bioengineering strategies, multi-organ integration approaches, and ethical considerations that provide a roadmap for next-generation organoid platforms. Collectively, brain organoids hold transformative potential for both fundamental neuroscience and translational research, bridging critical gaps between conventional experimental models and human-specific pathophysiology.

Article.Title: Striatal dopamine synthesis in schizophrenia decreases from psychosis to psychotic remission
Article.Authors: Schulz J.; Thalhammer M.; Bonhoeffer M.; Neumaier V.; Knolle F.; Sterner E.; Yan Q.; Hippen R.; Leucht S.; Priller J.; Weber W.; Mayr Y.; Yakushev I.; Sorg C.; Brandl F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Schizophrenia frequently follows a chronic relapsing-remitting course, comprising alternating episodes with and without psychotic symptoms (hereafter: psychosis and psychotic remission). One potential neurobiological correlate of this course is aberrant dopamine synthesis and storage (DSS) in the striatum, which can be estimated by the 18F-DOPA positron emission tomography (PET) outcome kicer. We conducted a longitudinal study of state-related kicer changes in striatal subregions in medicated patients with multiple-episode schizophrenia. We hypothesised that striatal DSS in patients with schizophrenia decreases from psychosis to psychotic remission, with higher striatal DSS during psychosis and lower striatal DSS during psychotic remission, compared to healthy subjects. Additionally, we explored whether striatal DSS is associated with psychotic relapse after remission. 18F-DOPA PET scans and clinical assessments were conducted in 28 patients with schizophrenia at two timepoints, first during psychosis and second during early-to-moderate psychotic remission (6 weeks to 12 months after the first timepoint, 189±80 days between-scan interval), as well as in 21 healthy controls, assessed twice in a comparable time interval. The averaged influx constant kicer of the striatal subregions nucleus accumbens, caudate and putamen was calculated as a proxy for DSS, using voxel-wise Gjedde-Patlak modelling with a cerebellar reference region. Mixed-effects models and post hoc analyses were used to test for longitudinal changes in kicer and cross-sectional group differences. An exploratory clinical follow-up 12 months after the second scan was conducted to assess psychotic relapse, and post hoc ANCOVAs were used to test for differences in kicer at each session between relapsing and non-relapsing patients. Patients’ kicer changes from psychosis to psychotic remission in caudate and nucleus accumbens differed significantly from assessments in healthy controls at comparable time points, with a significant longitudinal decrease of caudate kicer in patients. Furthermore, kicer in both caudate and accumbens was significantly lower in patients during early-to-moderate psychotic remission compared to controls, but no significant group difference was observed during psychosis. At the exploratory clinical follow-up, 32% of patients had experienced a psychotic relapse; they showed higher caudate kicer compared to non-relapsing patients during psychosis, with no difference during psychotic remission. These findings provide evidence for longitudinal changes of striatal, particularly caudate, DSS from psychosis to psychotic remission in medicated, multiple-episode schizophrenia patients, with lower caudate DSS during early-to-moderate psychotic remission but no aberrance during psychosis. The data indicate aberrant, fluctuating striatal dopamine synthesis across disorder states in schizophrenia.

Article.Title: Sub-second and multi-second dopamine dynamics underlie variability in human time perception
Article.Authors: Sadibolova R.; DiMarco E.; Jiang A.; Maas B.; Tatter S.; Laxton A.; Kishida K.; Terhune D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aberrant interval timing in the millisecond-to-second range is a consistent feature of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders involving striatal dysfunction, yet its neurochemical substrates in the human brain remain poorly characterised. Striatal dopamine has long been implicated in temporal processing, but evidence from animal models and human pharmacological studies has proved difficult to reconcile, in part because endogenous dopamine dynamics in humans have been inaccessible at relevant timescales. Patients with Parkinson’s disease (N=5, 62–73 years; two women) completed a temporal bisection task (300 trials), judging whether visual stimulus intervals (500–1100 ms) were closer to a learned short (500 ms) or long (1100 ms) reference. Dopamine and serotonin concentrations were measured in the caudate nucleus during awake deep brain stimulation surgery using fast-scan cyclic voltammetry. Elastic net machine-learning models trained on in vitro voltammetry data were applied to human recordings to derive dopamine and serotonin time series at 10 Hz. We used cluster-based permutation analysis to identify stimulus-aligned time windows in which dopamine or serotonin differed between short and long judgements, and entered mean concentrations from these windows as predictors of temporal performance in trial-level hierarchical mixed-effects models. Slower, steady-state dopaminergic and serotonergic tone, quantified as the mean concentration within successive multi-minute periods, was also assessed as a predictor of temporal behaviour. Finally, behavioural performance was compared with a healthy control cohort (N=17, 50–66 years; seven women). Elevated phasic dopamine (625–670 ms after stimulus onset) increased the likelihood of short judgements and was associated with reduced temporal overestimation bias. This association was independent of objective clock time, with the identical analysis yielding non-significant results for the short versus the long stimulus intervals. By contrast, tonic dopamine levels covaried with sensitivity in discriminating stimulus intervals (temporal precision). Lower tonic dopamine was associated with poorer temporal precision both within patients over the experimental session and in patients relative to healthy controls. No corresponding effects were observed for serotonin, indicating dopamine specificity across phasic and tonic timescales. By resolving endogenous striatal dopamine with sub-second precision during conscious human behaviour, this study links temporally distinct dopaminergic dynamics to dissociable aspects of timing behaviour in Parkinson’s disease. This challenges accounts of dopamine as a single modulatory influence and situates these findings within the literature on dissociable effects of phasic and tonic dopaminergic signalling, reconciling discrepancies between human and animal evidence and advancing understanding of the neurochemical basis of human time perception.

Article.Title: Unlocking the complex interplay between epigenetics and epitranscriptomics in neuropsychiatric disorders
Article.Authors: Dwivedi Y.; Roy B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Epigenetic and epitranscriptomic mechanisms work together to control gene expression, which is essential for brain development, synaptic plasticity, and the risk of neuropsychiatric disorders. Traditional epigenetic processes, such as DNA methylation and histone modifications, alter chromatin structure to regulate gene accessibility. On the other hand, epitranscriptomic marks such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A) affect RNA metabolism after transcription. Studies in both neural and non-neural systems show that these layers of regulation interact in both directions and together shape gene expression. This review looks at how m6A-modified non-coding RNAs, including chromosome-associated regulatory RNAs (carRNAs), enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), microRNAs, and circular RNAs, work with chromatin to influence genome function, including chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and the overall structure of the genome. It also covers recent discoveries about how eRNAs form R-loops, how m6A affects RNA stability, and how these processes are involved in neuronal signaling and plasticity. Many of these findings come from studies outside the nervous system and need more research in neuropsychiatric disease models. By bringing together established knowledge and new ideas, this review suggests that the interaction between epigenetic and epitranscriptomic mechanisms is a key factor in determining risk and resilience for neuropsychiatric disorders, and offers new directions for future research and therapy development.

Article.Title: LRSAM1, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, modulates TDP-43 proteostasis in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Article.Authors: Shirakawa T.; Mikuriya S.; Inoue Y.; Murasaki K.; Salinas F.; Takegawa-Araki T.; Tamura M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by the cytoplasmic mislocalization, aberrant phosphorylation and pathological aggregation of TDP-43, a nuclear RNA-binding protein essential for RNA metabolism. Despite its central involvement in ALS pathogenesis, the molecular mechanisms that govern TDP-43 proteostasis remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of LRSAM1, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, in regulating TDP-43 localization and degradation. Postmortem spinal cord tissues from five patients with sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and five healthy controls were examined. Immunohistochemical analyses revealed that LRSAM1 preferentially colocalized with diffusely mislocalized cytoplasmic TDP-43 but not with dense cytoplasmic aggregates, suggesting a potential role in early-stage pathological processing. To model these effects in vitro, induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons from three patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and four healthy control participants were used. Knockdown of LRSAM1 in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons from patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis significantly increased cytoplasmic TDP-43 accumulation and phosphorylation, as measured by immunofluorescence imaging. Moreover, STMN2 mRNA splicing, a well-established TDP-43 functional readout, was disrupted upon LRSAM1 depletion. Conversely, overexpression of LRSAM1 ameliorated stress-induced TDP-43 mislocalization and phosphorylation in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons from patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis but had minimal impact in control cells, indicating disease-specific vulnerability. Mechanistically, LRSAM1 interacted directly with the aggregation-prone C-terminal fragments of TDP-43 via the RRM2 domain of TDP-43 and promoted their proteasomal degradation. This selective interaction reduced the accumulation of toxic TDP-43 species and supported cytoplasmic proteostasis, particularly under conditions of cellular stress. In summary, our study identifies LRSAM1 as a novel modulator of cytoplasmic TDP-43 dynamics in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. By facilitating degradation of pathogenic TDP-43 fragments, LRSAM1 preserves neuronal RNA processing and mitigates molecular hallmarks of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. These findings enhance our understanding of post-translational control of TDP-43 and highlight LRSAM1 as a promising therapeutic target for modifying disease progression in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Article.Title: Education reduces dementia incidence and mitigates genetic risk
Article.Authors: Barcellos S.; Carvalho L.; Langa K.; Nimmagadda S.; Turley P.
Article.Abstract: There is little causal evidence on factors that can protect individuals against Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) risk. We study the causal effect of education on ADRD, exploiting a regression discontinuity generated by a compulsory schooling reform. ADRD was ascertained based on medical history, hospital records, and death registries, addressing concerns about selective sample attrition. We find that education reduces incidence of ADRD. Using molecular genetic data, we show that the reform weakened the relationship between genetics and ADRD incidence, implying genetic risk of dementia is not immutable and can be modified by social policy.

Article.Title: Capillary physics links HIV capsid geometry to nuclear pore translocation
Article.Authors: Brown A.; Al-Izzi S.; Parker J.; Hertel S.; Jacques D.; Kusumaatmaja H.; Morris R.
Article.Abstract: The protective capsid encasing the genetic material of HIV can traverse the nuclear pore complex (NPC) intact, despite being far larger than conventional passive cargo. This is attributed to the properties of the capsid surface, which promote partitioning into cohesive assemblies of the disordered proteins that form the NPC’s permeability barrier: phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins (FG-Nups). The implication, at the mesoscale, is that capsid–NPC interactions are characterized by the interfacial physics of wetting and capillarity. To capture this, we develop a minimal theory that reduces to an interplay between capsid geometry, effective cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic contact angles, and a ratio of interfacial tensions. By combining analytical calculations, sharp- and diffuse-interface numerics, we make several predictions: A geometry-dependent trade-off between penetration depth and the wetting transition; asymmetric capillary forces that generate torques and lead to metastable “stalled” states that are tilted; a topological classification of the possible mechanisms underlying the largest energetic barrier; and spontaneous symmetry breaking of displaced FG-Nups. These behaviors connect capsid shape and orientation to the topology and symmetry of FG-Nup displacement, and to the molecular compositions on each side of the pore. They are consistent with published cryoelectron tomography orientations, which provide an initial estimate of the cytoplasmic contact angle. Crucially, our results identify a capillary advantage for the HIV capsid’s characteristic broken-symmetry geometry.

Article.Title: High-resolution measurements of thermal conductivity matrix and search for thermal Hall effect in La <sub>2</sub> CuO <sub>4</sub>
Article.Authors: Hu J.; Xu H.; Gu G.; Li Q.; Ong N.
Article.Abstract: We investigated the longitudinal thermal conductivity κ xx and thermal Hall conductivity κ xy in La 2 CuO 4 at temperatures T between 2 and 20 K in magnetic fields H up to 10 T. Within the temperature and field intervals studied, we do not resolve any thermal Hall signal with a conservative upper bound of | κ xy / T | < 1 × 10 − 4 Wm − 1 K − 2 . The longitudinal thermal conductivity κ xx / T agrees well with previous reports, in both its magnitude and T dependence. Both κ xx and κ xy were measured using the field-swept protocol. To achieve high resolution, we carefully took into account relaxation effects after each step-increase in H . At low T , we find a weak linear decrease in κ xx / T vs. H , as well as weak hystereses near the metamagnetic transitions of the spins.

Article.Title: Local growth laws determine global shape of molluscan shells
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Bhattacharya K.
Article.Abstract: Molluscan shells come in various shapes and sizes. Despite this diversity, each species produces a shell with a characteristic shape that is independent of environmental conditions. We seek to understand this robust complexity. We are guided by two principles in the spirit of D’Arcy Thompson. First, the growth is governed by the repeated and continuous application of a fixed growth law, even as the shell evolves in overall shape, without any complex biological machinery to monitor and control the growth. Second, the growth law depends solely on local geometry at the shell’s growing edge. The first principle naturally leads to the mathematical statement that the shape of the shell is generated by the action of a Lie group on a protoconch. The second naturally leads to a particular representation of the Lie group. We use this representation to show that the shapes of nearly all known molluscan shells can be described by essentially three parameters: a scalar (scaling), a vector (orientation), and a curve (edge of the protoconch). We relate these parameters to the phylogenetic tree. In addition to the morphogenetic insight, our results potentially point to a alternative growth-based approach to engineering complex structures.

Article.Title: The revised diploid genome sequence of an individual human: A workflow for near telomere-to-telomere assemblies using only Oxford Nanopore Technologies Simplex-reads
Article.Authors: Lok S.; Lau T.; Tong A.; Trost B.; Reuter M.; Thiruvahindrapuram B.; Paton T.; MacDonald J.; Lau L.; Marshall C.; Craig Venter J.; Scherer S.
Article.Abstract: The first draft diploid genome assembly (HuRef) of an individual in 2007 was a milestone in genomics. Here, we report HuRef2.0, a revision of HuRef assembled using only Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) Simplex-reads and the hifiasm assembler. Results are close in continuity to the telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assemblies but were assembled from standard DNA samples without using multiple sequencing and mapping technologies, including ultra-long-reads and/or proximity-ligation. Three ONT flowcells (~103× coverage) from fresh blood DNA produced an assembly comprising 26 contigs, with gapless assembly of 23 chromosomes (Chr). Two gaps on ChrY were locally assembled to yield the final T2T-assembly, HuRef2.0, with base accuracy >Q60.34 and 2,393 phase blocks with an NG50 value of 2.36 Mb. Assembly from a single ONT flowcell (~35× coverage) consistently produced an assembly more contiguous than GRCh38.p14, providing a foundation for further optimization and scaling. Assembly quality was assessed by direct chromosome-level alignments to a reference genome, variant calling, and annotation of gene-rich regions at Chr22q11, the extended MHC locus, and at several difficult to assemble regions, including the rRNA gene clusters, the subtelomeric region on Chr4q35, ChrY, and the centromeres. More accurate but shorter Pacific Biosciences HiFi-reads produced less contiguous assemblies than from equivalent coverage of error-corrected ONT reads, indicating the importance of read-length. We compared HuRef2.0 to an assembly of a low-passage EBV-transformed lymphoblastoid cell line derived from the same donor. At least at a 400 kb resolution, we did not observe notable structural differences in the two assemblies.

Article.Title: Si-scRNA-seq: Enabling ambient-stable single-cell transcriptomics through spatially confined biosilicification
Article.Authors: Zhou L.; Ruan T.; He Y.; Xie G.; Qi J.; Cao X.; Brinker C.; Liu Y.; Zhu W.
Article.Abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is constrained by rapid RNA degradation during sample storage, necessitating cold-chain logistics. Here we present spatially confined biosilicification (SCB), wherein RNA is encapsulated within a nanoscopic layer of amorphous silicon dioxide, as a highly effective methodology enabling ambient-temperature preservation of single-cell transcriptomes. By judiciously incorporating a silicification inhibitor, SCB achieves spatiotemporal control over both intra- and extracellular silica deposition, preventing excessive crosslinking and cell aggregation while preserving RNA biointegrity and accessibility. scRNA-seq performed with biosilicified cells (Si-scRNA-seq) maintained high transcriptomic fidelity with fresh samples (R 2 = 0.95 after 7 d) extending RNA half-life to 54.8 d at 25 °C, a 685-fold improvement compared to unprotected samples. Furthermore, Si-scRNA-seq confers robust resistance against oxidative and UV degradation. Compatible with mainstream platforms at ~0.1 RMB per sample, Si-scRNA-seq successfully resolves cellular heterogeneity in clinical lung, liver, and ovarian cancer specimens after extended room-temperature storage. Si-scRNA-seq provides a scalable and cold-chain–free solution for single-cell transcriptomics in research and clinical settings.

Article.Title: Deconfined criticality between an antiferromagnetic insulator and a nodal d -wave superconductor: A quantum Monte Carlo study
Article.Authors: Chen C.; Sachdev S.; Meng Z.
Article.Abstract: We present a quantum Monte Carlo study of the transition between the insulating Néel state and the nodal d -wave superconductor on the square lattice at half-filling. We access a regime of frustrated magnetic order without a sign problem using a parton representation of the electron in terms of fermionic spinons and bosonic chargons. Both partons move in a background π -flux (so the electron experiences no net flux) and are coupled to a quantum fluctuating SU(2) lattice gauge field. In contrast to earlier studies directly on the electronic degrees of freedom, we find evidence for a second-order deconfined quantum phase transition at which both the Néel and d -wave superconductivity orders vanish continuously. We compute correlators of the spinon-chargon composite with the same quantum numbers as the electron: we find a gapless Dirac dispersion inside the d -wave superconductor, turning into a gapped dispersion in the antiferromagnet.

Article.Title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision
Article.Authors: Jung H.; Jain H.; Han X.; Feilong M.; Han J.; Shokeen D.; Van Uden C.; Hanson I.; Connolly A.; Wager T.; Haxby J.; Nastase S.
Article.Abstract: Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. A variance partitioning analysis revealed that the action features captured the most unique variance in neural activity across a much larger extent of cortex than the agent or scene features. Our findings suggest that cortical activity during dynamic, natural vision is dominated by features for understanding the actions of others.

Article.Title: A functional two-pore-domain K <sup>+</sup> channel from a large DNA virus
Article.Authors: Rauh O.; Mach S.; Clarke O.; Toews J.; Van Etten J.; Althaus M.; Moroni A.; Thiel G.
Article.Abstract: The evolutionary history of proteins helps to understand their structure/function correlates and suggests on how functional complexity evolved from primitive precursors. In the superfamily of K + channels, functional features of complex eukaryotic inward rectifier (Kir) channels and voltage-dependent (Kv) channels could be understood in terms of an increase in structural complexity of their prokaryotic precursors. K2P channels, which are made from tandem repeats of two pore domains, are not found in prokaryotes and their evolutionary origin is still unknown. In searching for primitive K2P channel precursors, we screened the genomes of nucleocytoplasmic large DNA viruses (NCLDVs) for genes coding for K2P channels. This was motivated by two reasons: NCLDVs are already known for coding primitive Kir type channels, and they play important roles in the evolution of eukaryotes. Here, we report that the NCLDV Pyramimonas orientalis virus codes for K2P-like K + channels. With only 178 amino acids and no cytosolic domains, this Kpov protein is much smaller than any eukaryotic K2P channel, but still functional as K + selective channel in lipid bilayers. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that Kpov is not the product of molecular piracy from the host but may result from fusion of primitive viral K + channel pore domains.

Article.Title: Integrating ecology with genetics to explain gene reuse during repeated evolution
Article.Authors: Nosil P.; Gompert Z.; Montoya J.; Feder J.; Oakley T.; Peichel C.
Article.Abstract: The role of determinism and chance in the evolutionary history of life is often analyzed through the lens of the repeatability of evolution. Although it is now clear that evolution often repeats itself, we are only beginning to understand why this varies in degree. For example, the probability of gene reuse during repeated bouts of adaptation often declines with time since divergence, but the causes of this pattern remain unclear. Here, we explore two core hypotheses for time-dependent variation in the repeatability of gene reuse during adaptation. Specifically, gene reuse depends on the extent to which lineages have 1) similar genomes such that they have similar genetic architectures, mutations, and mutational effects (i.e., a fairly well-appreciated “shared genetics” hypothesis), and 2) similar ecologies such that they have similar environments and patterns of natural selection (i.e., a mostly unexplored “shared ecology” hypothesis). The latter hypothesis emphasizes ecology’s role in gene reuse and has received little explicit attention. In particular, testing the shared ecology hypothesis requires moving beyond a simple dichotomous characterization of ecology to embracing ecological divergence as a multivariate and continuous phenomenon. Although such tests are only beginning to emerge, they already illustrate how integration of ecological factors can help explain variation in gene reuse. Here, we advocate a framework that integrates the influence of both genetic and ecological factors in the repeatability of evolution and can be applied to a range of organisms to better understand the role of determinism and chance in biological diversification.

Article.Title: Contactless continuous guidance of matter in its main states using curved elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields
Article.Authors: Nikolaev D.; Iablonskyi D.; Martinez-Marchese A.; Sirkka M.; Aldea M.; Okwudire C.; Hæggström E.; Marzo A.; Salmi A.
Article.Abstract: Acoustic manipulation uses sound waves to exert force on matter, enabling contactless movement, trapping, and the structuring of particles in bulk media. It offers a contamination-free approach for handling matter in applications spanning across chemistry, biology, and advanced manufacturing. However, state-of-the-art techniques, including acoustic holograms or phased arrays of transducers (PATs) are limited to transporting individual particles or small clusters one by one, and are not suitable for dispersed matter such as gases or aerosols. Here, we introduce a method for guiding a continuous flow of matter along reconfigurable three-dimensional trajectories using elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields (EBAFs). These fields generate converging radial acoustic forces along a programmable path, forming stable mid-air conduits that continuously transport matter. Compared to existing methods such as near-field acoustic levitation, acoustofluidic separation, particle manipulation with vortex and Airy beams, the proposed method offers enhanced versatility, scalability, and real-time control of transport trajectories in mid-air without requiring physical guiding structures. We developed methods to generate EBAFs with PATs tailored to different particle sizes and material properties, and experimentally demonstrated guidance of solids, liquids, aerosols, and gases along programmable trajectories. This technique enables containerless laboratory operations, precise and contamination-free reagent or energy delivery, and integration into advanced additive manufacturing processes that require controlled distribution of matter in different states to target zones.

Article.Title: Susumu Tonegawa (1939–2026): A molecular biologist who transformed immunology and neuroscience
Article.Authors: Lafaille J.; McHugh T.
Article.Abstract: Susumu Tonegawa transformed two fields of biology. His discovery of the genetic mechanism generating antibody diversity established the foundations of modern immunology and earned him the 1987 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Remarkably, he then began a second scientific career in neuroscience, pioneering genetic approaches to dissect the molecular and circuit mechanisms of learning and memory and, ultimately, the neuronal ensembles that store specific memories. He was also an ambitious institution builder whose leadership shaped neuroscience at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and RIKEN. As former trainees from his immunology and neuroscience labs, we remember a scientist of extraordinary curiosity, intensity, and intellectual courage, who was never afraid to leave familiar territory in pursuit of a fundamental question.

Article.Title: c-FLIP loss links arrest of gene expression to TNFα-dependent antiviral guard immunity
Article.Authors: Sonnett M.; Boersma S.; Ward M.; Van Eyndhoven L.; Centofanti E.; Brambach M.; Zhou C.; Knipe D.; Raj A.; Oyler-Yaniv A.; Oyler-Yaniv J.
Article.Abstract: Cells sense infection through dedicated receptors, yet these surveillance pathways are often subverted by pathogen-encoded virulence factors. Guard immunity provides complementary defense by rapidly killing infected cells in response to infection induced stress. However, the symptoms of infection frequently resemble noninfectious stress, raising the question of how they are distinguished. Using quantitative transcriptomics, proteomics, and global translation measurements during viral infections in vitro and in vivo, we show that infection globally suppresses host gene expression and prevents direct antiviral responses. However, the resulting proteostatic stress does not activate guard immunity unless tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) is present. We identify the anti-apoptotic protein c-FLIP as a guard for gene expression integrity: its loss sensitizes cells to TNFα, triggering cell death and limiting viral spread. Modeling demonstrates that TNFα and c-FLIP loss function as a biological AND-gate, providing specificity and speed. These findings show how cells integrate internal stress signals with external inflammatory cues to improve the fidelity of death decisions, and how this circuitry may misfire during noninfectious inflammation.

Article.Authors: Lin W.; Qian S.; Sun Q.; Zhu L.; Liao W.; Li T.; Li F.; Shi X.; Wang T.; Zhao E.; Zhang H.; Li P.
Article.Abstract: Close-in planets orbiting core-helium-burning red-clump giants directly challenge tidal-engulfment theory, which predicts that planets within about 1 au of Sun-like stars should be engulfed during red-giant-branch (RGB) expansion. The existence of such survivors would imply missing physical processes in the late stages of stellar and planetary evolution. Yet only one such “forbidden” planet had been identified to date. Here we report three systems—24 Boo b, HD 12648 b, and TYC 4282-605-1 b—whose host stars are confirmed red-clump giants through asteroseismology, showing that each has already undergone dramatic expansion and contraction following helium ignition. Their planets now reside at orbital separations smaller than the maximum stellar radii attained during the RGB phase, implying that they should not have survived. Among them, 24 Boo b orbits at only 0.183 au with a 30-d period, making it the closest planet known around a red-clump giant. These findings demonstrate that this paradox is not an isolated anomaly but signals the emergence of a class of evolved planetary systems. Their survival defies current models of stellar–planetary coevolution and points to unexplored physics shaping planetary architectures around post-RGB stars.

Article.Title: Neuropharmacology of language: ERP evidence for catecholaminergic modulation of syntactic processing
Article.Authors: Tan Y.; Lewis A.; Schmits I.; Verkes R.; Cools R.; Hagoort P.
Article.Abstract: A few studies have shown that brain catecholamines are implicated in language comprehension. However, the specific cognitive processes they modulate remain underexplored. We hypothesized that catecholamines enhance the unification of syntactic roles and word meanings into coherent multiword structures. This study combined electroencephalography and psychopharmacology to examine the effects of a catecholaminergic stimulant (methylphenidate) on processing sentences containing local syntactic ambiguities. Methylphenidate amplified the P600 event-related potential effect, which has been linked to the recruitment of cognitive resources for processing sentences with increased syntactic load. The drug’s impact on semantic processing was subtler, showing a suggestive attenuation of the N400 effect to ambiguous sentences. Furthermore, the increase in the P600 effect under methylphenidate was most pronounced in participants with lower working memory capacity. This study provides evidence for linking catecholamine activity to syntactic unification in healthy individuals. Elevated catecholamine levels appear to increase the cognitive effort invested in syntactic unification, and to support the dynamic prioritization of syntactic information when contextual demands require it.

Article.Title: Molecular drivers of cotranslational protein assembly in bacteria
Article.Authors: Schmitt J.; Auburger J.; Wruck F.; Koubek J.; Tans S.; Bukau B.; Kramer G.
Article.Abstract: Protein complexes are pivotal to all major cellular processes. Translation-coupled complex assembly is ubiquitous in eukaryotes, but its molecular basis and prevalence in bacteria remain poorly understood. Here, we combine ribosome profiling and single-molecule optical tweezers to establish principles governing cotranslational assembly of four structurally diverse complexes in Escherichia coli . We reveal how heterotetramers form cotranslationally via hierarchical assembly pathways, with initial heterodimer formation priming the assembly of higher-order oligomers through a topology-dependent organization of homomeric and heteromeric interfaces. Co-post assembly, defined as interaction between nascent and fully synthesized subunits, initiates when dimerization domains are completely exposed at the ribosome. The assembly order is predominantly unidirectional and matches the operon gene order, with upstream-encoded subunits being synthesized first, and then engaging downstream nascent partner subunits. The co-post assembly efficiency depends both on the native operon structure and the ribosome-associated chaperone trigger factor, which binds emerging oligomerization domains and whose dissociation marks the onset of partner subunit engagement. The handover from chaperone engagement to cotranslational assembly is mediated by nascent chain folding. Finally, we show that co-post assembly provides a fitness advantage. Together, these findings reveal how genome organization and chaperone-assisted folding coordinate cotranslational assembly to promote efficient complex biogenesis and cellular fitness in bacteria.

Article.Title: HAP40 functions as a proteostasis regulator by controlling huntingtin interactions and its release into the extracellular space
Article.Authors: Silva Ramos E.; Boeddrich A.; Haenig C.; Trepte P.; Ammar O.; Secker C.; Popp O.; Ivanov A.; Beetz S.; Roth L.; Papawassiliou R.; Hernandez Jeppesen L.; Wallenfang T.; Keith B.; Harding R.; Schindler F.; Koudelka T.; Scharek N.; Zenkner M.; Neuendorf N.; Golusik S.; Mertins P.; Piazza I.; Schnoegl S.; Wanker E.
Article.Abstract: Huntingtin-associated protein 40 (HAP40) forms a stable protein complex with huntingtin (HTT). Its cellular function and how HAP40 loss influences mutant HTT (mHTT) abundance and pathobiology are currently unclear. Here, using diverse cellular models and omics methods, we demonstrate that HAP40 is an obligate interaction partner of HTT and through its binding controls HTT interactions and the abundance of HTT-associated proteins, indicating that it functions as a HTT interaction regulatory unit. Also, loss of HAP40 in mHTT-expressing striatal cells impairs autophagic protein degradation and triggers transcriptional activation of the CLEAR network, demonstrating that it functions as a proteostasis regulator that acts on quality control pathways. Finally, mHTT-expressing cells lacking HAP40 showed increased secretion of a ~205 kDa mHTT fragment through an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)/Golgi-associated route, indicating that striatal cells reduce intracellular mHTT-induced proteotoxicity through activation of secretory pathways. Together, these results establish HAP40 as a critical proteostasis regulator that through controlling HTT interactions maintains cellular homeostasis.

Article.Title: Mechanistic insight into conflicting valence fluctuation of Cu(I) photocorrosion pathways: The role of charge behaviors
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Xu C.; Sui P.; Feng R.; Liu Y.; Zhang H.; Zeng H.; Wang X.; Luo J.
Article.Abstract: Photocorrosion remains a major challenge that hinders the development of photoelectrochemical (PEC) solar fuel production. Although Cu 2 O is a promising photocathode material due to its suitable band structure and visible light absorption, both oxidative and reductive photocorrosion pathways have been reported, with no consensus established in the research community in the PEC system. In this work, we fabricate three Cu 2 O photocathodes with distinct charge transport properties to investigate the correlation between charge accumulation and photocorrosion behavior. Both oxidative and reductive photocorrosion were observed depending on the type and location of charge accumulation. Notably, we propose a refined oxidative photocorrosion mechanism in which photogenerated holes induce surface Cu 2 O dissolution to Cu 2+ , followed by coordination with adsorbed *OH to form Cu(OH) 2 /CuO under illumination, which is contrary to the widely assumed direct oxidation from Cu 2 O to CuO. This work not only provides a unified understanding of the dual photocorrosion pathways in Cu 2 O, but also offers a generalizable framework for understanding photo-induced degradation in metal oxide photocathodes and for guiding the design of more robust PEC systems through charge transport engineering.

Article.Title: m <sup>7</sup> G modification in mRNA cooperates with QKI to promote homologous recombination repair
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Li M.; Liu Z.; Di L.; Meng Q.; Feng T.; Zhang J.; Zhu Q.; Lu X.; Shu Y.; Huang J.; Gullerova M.; Tian Y.; Zhu W.
Article.Abstract: DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) are repaired through distinct pathways, with homologous recombination (HR) favored when DNA ends undergo extensive resection. Although cytoplasmic N7-methylguanosine (m7G)-modified RNA increases after UV-induced single-strand breaks, its role in DSB repair (including HR) remains unclear. Here, we show that m7G-modified RNA accumulates at DSB sites, where it recruits the m7G reader protein Quaking (QKI)5, to selectively promote HR. Mechanistically, QKI5 directly interacts with MRE11 and enhances its DNA binding affinity, thereby facilitating DNA end resection. Depletion of QKI5 impairs recruitment of the MRE11–RAD50–NBS1 complex to DSBs and reduces HR repair efficiency. Moreover, elevated QKI5 expression is associated with resistance to radiotherapy in both mouse models and clinical cohorts. Together, these findings identify the m7G RNA–QKI5–MRE11 axis as a regulator of HR pathway choice and suggest QKI5 as a promising therapeutic target in cancer treatment.

Article.Title: Superlubricity by glycerosome boundary layers
Article.Authors: Dong Y.; Cao W.; Kamyshinsky R.; Kampf N.; Zhao P.; Schilt Y.; Raviv U.; Klein J.
Article.Abstract: The search for high-performance lubricants is of broad relevance to biomedical applications, including artificial joints, regenerative scaffolds, and osteoarthritis therapies. Here we introduce glycerosomes—phosphatidylcholine (PC)-based vesicles containing glycerol—as a promising boundary lubricant. Using a surface force balance, we show that glycerosomes achieve a friction coefficient as low as 10 − 5 under a high compression pressure of 15.6 MPa, representing a 20-fold reduction compared to conventional PC liposomes. This level of lubrication surpasses any previously reported boundary lubricant system at such pressures in aqueous media. Mechanistically, glycerosomes exhibit substantially lower adhesion energy than PC liposomes, and theoretical simulations reveal enhanced vesicle stability and flexibility. Our findings establish glycerosomes as a superior hydration lubrication platform, with promising implications for both biomedical implants and industrial applications requiring robust lubricity.

Article.Title: Virus transmission required for maintenance and host adaptation mirrors neurophysiological differences in rabies-derived peptides
Article.Authors: Remal A.; Acheson E.; Leighton P.; Rees E.; Rhodes J.; O’Brien B.; Weltzin M.; Hueffer K.
Article.Abstract: Pathogen adaptations to new hosts are central to the disease ecology of cross-species transmission and host switching of viruses. The rabies virus is a model for adaptations to different hosts as it induces behavioral changes that facilitate transmission, while being maintained in distinct species-specific cycles of infection. Here, we demonstrate that the rabies virus requires distinct transmission dynamics in two hosts with different ecologies to establish maintenance, using agent-based modeling, analyses of virus glycoprotein-mediated manipulation of neuroreceptor function, and phylogenetic analysis. Epidemiological models suggest that rabies virus variants adapted to arctic foxes, which sustain rabies virus at very low host densities, require a higher probability of transmission than viruses adapted to raccoons. Using in vitro electrophysiology, we demonstrate that the rabies glycoprotein-derived peptides from arctic fox rabies variants are more potent antagonists of alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. These findings suggest a possible functional basis for the behavioral modifications that drive enzootic rabies transmission in the context of host ecology. In addition, a large proportion of residues that may drive rabies virus adaptation to raccoons and arctic foxes are found within this neurotoxin-like region. Furthermore, a residue in the neurotoxin-like region of the mature rabies virus glycoprotein (residue 183) has been associated with pathogenicity, host switching, and disease ecology in previous studies. We propose the hypothesis that rabies virus transmission dynamics adapt to the ecology and physiology of novel hosts through the selection of glycoproteins that elicit specific degrees of behavioral modification and transmission probability.

Article.Title: Reduction of aflatoxin contamination in maize kernels mediated by host-induced gene silencing
Article.Authors: Ahmed A.; Cavanaugh K.; Baldrich P.; Stergiopoulos I.; Michelmore R.
Article.Abstract: Aflatoxins produced by some species of Aspergillus pose a significant threat to global food safety, because they contaminate a variety of crops including maize. In this study, we used host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) to reduce aflatoxin accumulation in maize upon infection with Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus . Two RNAi constructs were designed and introduced into maize, one targeting two essential fungal genes involved in ergosterol biosynthesis ( CYP51A and CYP51B ) and the other targeting three aflatoxin biosynthesis genes ( AflC , AflD , and AflR ). The presence of RNAi transgenes was confirmed in 17 and 14 independent lines possessing the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi construct and the AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi construct, respectively. Most transgenic lines had single-locus integrations and one or two copies of the transgene. Transgene expression varied considerably among the lines. Small RNA sequencing confirmed the production of siRNAs from the HIGS trigger sequences. Levels of CYP51A , AflC , AflD, and AflR transcripts in Aspergillus spp. were successfully decreased upon infection of transgenic maize. However, significant reduction in the level of CYP51B transcripts was not achieved and the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi transgene had no discernible effect on fungal growth in infected maize. In contrast, we observed significant reductions in aflatoxin accumulation in four AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi transgenic lines infected with A. flavus and in two transgenic lines infected with A. parasiticus . Notably, one AflC/AflD/AflR transgenic line exhibited minimal aflatoxin contamination upon kernel infection with A. parasiticus . These results demonstrate the potential of HIGS to reduce aflatoxin production in mature corn kernels.

Article.Title: System-level reorganization of gene networks underlies the nurse-to-forager transition in honeybees
Article.Authors: Page R.; Bonabeau E.
Article.Abstract: Division of labor in social insects is enabled by coordinated changes in physiology, neural signaling, and gene regulation, yet it remains unclear to what extent behavioral maturation reflects incremental changes in individual genes and/or a reorganization of transcriptomic regulation at the system level. Here, we analyze the nurse-to-forager transition in worker honeybees ( Apis mellifera ) from a network perspective, treating the transcriptome as a gene–gene correlation system whose global organization reflects collective regulatory states. Using fat body gene expression data across five developmental time points that span an interval of behavioral transition, we construct signed gene–gene correlation networks and quantify their macro- and mesostate properties. We then descend to the level of the gene and construct microstate gene lists of interacting genes. Behavioral maturation of worker honeybees is accompanied by coordinated, nonmonotonic changes in global network structure rather than simple global shifts in interaction strength across the network. Early stages exhibit broadly positive, globally synchronized correlations, whereas later stages show increased modular segregation and the emergence of antagonistic gene–gene relationships. Despite this differentiation, networks remain fully connected with high global efficiency, consistent with a flexible small-world–like organization. Positive correlations primarily support global integration, while negative correlations act as localized, boundary-enforcing constraints. Negative correlations form a structured pattern of antagonism that is sparse and module-specific, occurring primarily between functional gene modules rather than within them. Network layouts and module analyses reveal two polarized, attractor-like regulatory states, a structure recapitulated in a vitellogenin-centered subnetwork and consistent with prior experimental perturbation studies.

Article.Title: Blinks are strategically coupled with head movements in unconstrained natural gaze behavior
Article.Authors: Goettker A.; Hayhoe M.
Article.Abstract: Blinks are a ubiquitous yet largely unnoticed aspect of human vision, despite causing frequent interruptions of visual input that can amount to up to 10% of waking time. By leveraging a large dataset of unconstrained gaze behavior during two natural tasks, we found a behavioral strategy to limit the impact of blinks: blinks were strategically coupled with head movements, which minimizes information loss due to unreliable visual input during head movements. Specifically, blink probability increased with higher head velocities and showed strong temporal modulation relative to head movement onset: Blink probability was reduced before head movement initiation and then peaked during the head movement. The strength of this coupling was tailored to the individual needs of participants, with participants with higher baseline blink rates showing stronger synchronization. This indicates that blinks are a part of an individually coordinated strategy when orchestrating eye and head movements during unconstrained natural behavior.

Article.Title: Linguistic intervention unlocks the economic gains of diversity
Article.Authors: Levine S.; Siegenthaler S.; Wilson B.
Article.Abstract: Gains from trade generate prosperity, yet interpersonal exchange can falter along racial lines. We study incentivized experimental economies where participants must spontaneously initiate and sustain trading relationships with others whose race is visible. When the highest gains from trade require cross-race exchange, diverse economies underperform: welfare and specialization suffer as many retreat to autarky. This underperformance reflects not segregation into racial trading blocs, but a collapse in exchange. Opportunities for contact alone do not close the performance gap, which persists and even widens over time. To understand why, we turn to communication itself. Lower welfare is associated with less communication, fewer expressions of affiliation and achievement, and less explicit signaling of needs, deficits, and surpluses. We call this communicative misalignment: differences in shared-language use that raise search, bargaining, and coordination costs. A brief linguistic intervention equips participants with a communicative toolkit. It increases communication volume and the frequency of motivational and state-signaling language. Crucially, when gains depend on cross-race exchange, the intervention restores specialization and cross-race trade, closing the performance gap. Its effects are minimal when efficient trade need not cross race, indicating specificity rather than generic skill training. Language thus operates bidirectionally, both revealing the state of cooperation and causally shaping it. Although we examine racial boundaries, the mechanism may operate along other fault lines where interactional norms diverge, including hierarchy, geography, or culture. Language, a primary conduit of culture, can impede exchange when misaligned and facilitate it when aligned. This suggests a scalable micro-governance tool for reducing transaction costs.

Article.Title: C1ql2 gates stress vulnerability by regulating microglia-mediated synaptic pruning in the BLA-vHPC circuit
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Liu W.; Liao S.; Niu J.; Pan H.; You W.; Zhao K.; Ma B.; Lu M.; Zou J.; Hu P.; Zhang W.; Pan B.

Article.Title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands
Article.Authors: Gacetta E.; Laws M.; Aulet L.; Ozaydin T.; Tsay J.; Zapanta C.; Cantlon J.
Article.Abstract: Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners’ spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

Article.Title: Random, fragile, or correlated: Mechanisms of synteny decay in mammals
Article.Authors: Moffett A.; Di Pierro M.
Article.Abstract: We formalize three models of genome evolution, yielding analytical distributions of synteny block sizes between pairs of genomes. To evaluate each model, we fit theoretical synteny block size distributions to empirical distributions from a comparative analysis of nearly 200 mammalian genomes. Between the random breakage model (RBM), with uniformly distributed breakpoints, the fragile breakage model (FBM) with breakpoint hotspots, and what we term the correlated breakage model (CBM) with pairs of nearby breakpoints, we find that the FBM and CBM are far more consistent with mammalian genome evolution than the RBM. Inferred parameters of each model qualitatively agree with previously calculated rates of mammalian genome evolution. The FBM and CBM perform comparably with each other, suggesting that either model could serve as an improved null model of genome evolution to use in statistical tests for syntenic regions that are unlikely to exist due to random chance.

Article.Title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models
Article.Authors: Cullen M.; Biancaniello C.; Taškova K.; Miletić V.; De Simone A.; Mercadante D.
Article.Abstract: With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from C α -only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to explore phenomena such as secondary structure propensity and nucleation in condensates, conformationally selected binding motifs across disordered ensembles or conformational preferences of sequence-specific short-linear motifs.

Article.Title: Gene conversion is a key driver of diversity hotspots in Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens and virulence-associated loci
Article.Authors: Marin M.; Quinones-Olvera N.; Jin H.; Harris M.; Jeffrey B.; Rosenthal A.; Murphy K.; Sassetti C.; Li H.; Farhat M.
Article.Abstract: Despite the long-held view of Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) as a genetically conserved pathogen, many genomic regions remain poorly resolved due to high sequence homology and repetitive content. Using complete genome assemblies generated from long-read sequencing of 151 globally representative clinical isolates, we comprehensively analyzed genome-wide patterns of genetic diversity and evolution across the Mtb genome. Our analysis uncovers pronounced diversity hotspots within paralogous regions (PRs) generated by recurrent gene conversion between homologous genes. In many cases, these hotspots exhibit more than an order of magnitude greater genetic diversity than the rest of the Mtb genome, which is otherwise characterized by remarkably low variation. Mutations within these regions display clustered substitution patterns, excess paralog-matching variants, and distinct mutational spectra consistent with ongoing gene conversion. Our analysis identifies over 300 individual gene conversion events (GCEs) distributed throughout the Mtb phylogeny. These GCEs occur predominantly within gene families associated with virulence and host–pathogen interactions, including the PE, PPE, and ESX families. Several of the most pronounced diversity hotspots occur in antigens encoded within PRs. Among these, the vaccine candidate PPE18 harbors mutations in validated epitope sequences and predicted alterations in HLA-II binding. Together, these findings demonstrate that gene conversion actively shapes antigenic and virulence-associated diversity in Mtb .

Article.Title: In-cloud motions shape warm-rain production in marine clouds: Evidence from multiyear observations
Article.Authors: Lamer K.; Kollias P.; Kim J.; Zhu Z.; Yang F.; Battaglia A.; Luke E.
Article.Abstract: Despite years of research, the processes controlling warm-rain formation remain uncertain. Leveraging multiple years of observations collected across four oceanic regions, we systematically reassess the properties of precipitation just beneath cloud base. The observations show that warm-rain characteristics are remarkably consistent within cloud regimes yet differ substantially between stratocumulus and cumulus, indicating that cloud-regime properties exert a stronger influence on warm precipitation than regional environmental variability. Precipitation is observed beneath marine stratocumulus in over 56% of cloudy columns with liquid water path (LWP) <130 g m −2 , rising to more than 84% in columns with LWP beyond 130 g m −2 . This indicates that marine stratocumulus routinely support warm-rain formation and suggests that barriers to precipitation onset in this regime are weaker than commonly assumed. For the same LWP, oceanic cumulus precipitate less frequently than stratocumulus but on average produce two times larger and one to two orders of magnitude fewer precipitation drops. This contrast is consistent with cumulus presenting two times stronger updrafts and lower adiabaticity than stratocumulus, both of which can affect drop growth histories. Whereas the precipitation characteristics of stratocumulus are generally consistent with growth by collision–coalescence during gravitational free fall in low LWP clouds, those of cumulus cannot be explained without invoking additional processes. Together, these findings suggest that warm-precipitation parameterizations should more explicitly account for the influence of small-scale dynamical processes on precipitation growth. The apparent importance of drop growth histories further motivates continued exploration of Lagrangian particle-tracking approaches in both models and observations.

Article.Title: Anomalous narrow-band correlation in a natural superconducting heterostructure
Article.Authors: Sun X.; Wei Z.; Shan M.; Peng S.; Wang Z.; Wu P.; Luo Y.; Shen J.; Huai L.; Miao Y.; Ou Z.; Onbasli M.; Wang Z.; Wu T.; He J.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: A new frontier in condensed matter physics is to stack atomically thin layered materials with different properties and create intriguing phenomena which do not exist in any of the constituent layers. Transition metal dichalcogenide 4Hb-TaS 2, with an alternating stacking of a spin liquid candidate 1T-TaS 2 and a superconductor 1H-TaS 2 , is a natural heterostructure for such a purpose. Recently, rare phenomena were indeed observed, including chiral superconductivity, two-component nematic superconductivity, topological surface superconductivity, and enigmatic magnetic memory. A widely proposed starting point to understand such a mysterious heterostructure requires strong electronic correlation, presumably provided by 1T-TaS 2 layers with a narrow flat band near the Fermi level (E F ). Here, by using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we reveal the theoretically expected flat band near E F in the energy-momentum space. However, this flat band only exists on the 1T-TaS 2 terminated surface layer with broken translational symmetry, but not on the 1T-TaS 2 subsurface layers buried in the bulk. These results directly challenge the foundation of the current theoretical paradigm. On the 1T-TaS 2 terminated surface layer, we further revealed a pseudogap and an anomalous doping effect. These phenomena and the dichotomy between surface and bulk layers also shed light on the unusual coexistence of distinct electronic orders in this mysterious heterostructure.
Article.Keywords: angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy; charge density waves; electronic structure; flat bands

Article.Title: Translational control of microglial metabolism, inflammatory responses, and survival by the eIF4E-binding proteins
Article.Authors: Bermudez S.; Choi J.; Mahmood N.; Vogel J.; Almousa H.; Huang Z.; Kim S.; Zhu V.; Zhou L.; Casas-Antillon D.; Yaqubi M.; Cozachenco D.; Stratton J.; Hansson O.; Healy L.; Aguilar-Valles A.; Sonenberg N.
Article.Abstract: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes microglial neuroprotective functions by engaging multiple cell receptors. However, the relevant downstream effectors are not fully understood. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) promotes mRNA translation by phosphorylating and inactivating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 and 2 (4E-BP1/2), which are expressed in microglia. 4E-BP1 levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in AD and correlate with markers of microglial reactivity and disease progression. Using linear regression analysis, we found that elevated CSF 4E-BP1 levels strengthen the association between soluble TREM2 levels and neurodegeneration in amyloid-positive individuals. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we performed in vitro experiments demonstrating that amyloid-β inactivated 4E-BP1 in murine microglia. The mTOR-mediated inactivation is highly dependent on Spleen Tyrosine Kinase (SYK) signaling and repeated exposure to amyloid-β impaired this process, whereas prolonged exposure increased 4E-BP1 levels in microglia. Deletion of 4E-BP1/2 resulted in increased mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation, reduced pro-inflammatory signaling, and protected microglia from amyloid-induced apoptosis. Thus, impaired 4E-BP1 inactivation—due to reduced mTOR signaling or excess 4E-BP1—disrupts immune resolution, leading to metabolic exhaustion and microglial cell death. We identify the SYK–mTORC1–4E-BP1 signaling axis as a key regulator of microglial mitochondrial biogenesis and immune resolution in AD.

Article.Title: Mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation driven by energetic-particle irradiation of icy solids
Article.Authors: Dominguez G.; Caplan C.; Tafla L.; Lucas J.; Liu M.; McKeegan K.; Gillis J.
Article.Abstract: Mass-independent isotope fractionation (MIF) of oxygen provides key insights into atmospheric chemistry and the origin of isotopic anomalies in planetary materials. To date, MIF has been primarily associated with gas-phase processes involving symmetry-dependent reaction pathways, most notably ozone formation. Whether analogous effects can arise in condensed phases or at interfaces remains an open question. Here we report laboratory experiments demonstrating that energetic particle irradiation of icy oxide surfaces produces mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation at temperatures as low as 10 K. Electron irradiation of SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 substrates in the presence of H 2 O ice results in measurable shifts in Δ 17 O in the underlying solids. The resulting three-isotope relationships include slope-1-like behavior in SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 and distinct, substrate-dependent trends in Al 2 O 3 , indicating that irradiation-induced defect formation and interfacial chemistry govern the isotope effects. The magnitude of the observed anomalies demonstrates that irradiation-driven processes can generate substantial oxygen isotope heterogeneity in condensed phases. These results identify a previously unrecognized class of MIF and provide a quantitative framework for interpreting oxygen isotope signatures in radiation-processed environments, including interstellar grains and early solar system materials.
