Article.Title: A promoter G-quadruplex recruits Hrb27C to regulate NEMO and immune defense against Lyme disease pathogens in the deer tick
Article.Authors: Lyu B.; Gao X.; Anderson D.; Stanley D.; Song Q.
Article.Abstract: Genomic DNA can adopt noncanonical secondary structures, such as G-quadruplexes (G4s), which serve as critical regulatory elements beyond the traditional double helix. Whether promoter G4s also participate in controlling innate immune signaling and host–pathogen interactions, however, remains unknown in arthropods. In this study, we identify a G4 structure within the promoter of the NEMO (NF-κB essential modulator) gene in the deer tick Ixodes scapularis . Using a combination of circular dichroism, isothermal difference spectra, and fluorescence-based assays, we demonstrate that this sequence forms a stable, parallel G4 topology in vitro and in vivo. Functional characterization via luciferase reporter assays reveals that this G4 scaffold is essential for proper NEMO transcriptional output. Importantly, disruption of the G4 structure significantly reduces NEMO expression and increases the burden of the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi . Genome-wide expression profiling further reveals that perturbation of the NEMO G4 produces transcriptional changes that overlap with those observed following NEMO silencing. These shared transcriptional responses are enriched for immune-associated genes and ribonucleoprotein-related pathways. We further identify the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein Hrb27C as a structural binding protein that specifically recognizes the NEMO G4 through its RNA recognition motif domains and facilitates NEMO expression. Collectively, our findings establish promoter G4 architecture as an important regulatory layer in tick immunity, linking DNA topology to pathogen proliferation and providing a structural framework for understanding host–pathogen dynamics in disease vectors.

Article.Title: Modulation of avian iridescence via melanogenesis
Article.Authors: Barbosa S.; Bittner C.; Arbore R.; Araújo P.; Pereira P.; Andrade P.; Fekete C.; Afonso R.; Afonso S.; Amorim M.; Marques C.; Nicolaï M.; Carita J.; Brejcha J.; Lopes R.; Alves J.; Cruz F.; Gómez-Garrido J.; Zamarreño C.; Gut M.; Alioto T.; Ali M.; Hilpert A.; Hecht A.; Spiecker E.

Previous work provides evidence that poly(phenolic) deposition precedes, and is necessary for, poly(aliphatic) deposition. To test this further, we generated RNAi knockdown lines of three wound-induced peroxidase genes, PRX19, PRX55, and PRX105 , in potato ( Solanum tuberosum ), the tubers of which produce an abundance of suberin upon wounding. The wound-induced suberin of PRX19-RNAi tubers had severely reduced poly(phenolics), reduced poly(aliphatics), and no apparent lamella. Functionally, wound-induced PRX19-RNAi tubers were more permeable to water loss and susceptible to bacterial soft rot. Article.Title: Physical origins of speed control in swimming fishes
Article.Authors: Seo J.; Zhou J.; Peterson A.; McHenry M.; Di Santo V.; Mittal R.
Article.Abstract: The linear relationship between tail-beat frequency and swimming speed in fish, first described by Bainbridge in 1958, has since been confirmed in species as disparate as eels and tuna. Dimensional scaling has explained why linearity should emerge at high Reynolds numbers, but the frequency–speed relationship itself has remained empirical, with no physical framework describing its behavior across swimming regimes, and no account of what sets the two quantities that define it: the distance covered per tail beat and the frequency below which forward motion supposedly ceases. Here, we derive a relationship from a balance of fin thrust, generated by a leading-edge vortex, and drag due to the boundary layer on the body. This framework yields an explicit expression for speed in terms of midline kinematics and body morphology. This formulation shows that the maximum stride length is set by the undulatory wavelength and the tail-beat phase offset, rather than by the conventional scaling metric of body length, and that no minimum frequency is required for forward motion. The model reproduces kinematic measurements from freely swimming glass catfish, published simulations, and Bainbridge’s original data. Without recalibration, it predicts the results of independent simulations spanning wide variations in wavelength, phase offset, and morphology to within ten percent. Linear scaling is thus one asymptotic limit of a more general propulsive relationship linking morphology and body-wave kinematics to swimming speed in fishes and bioinspired vehicles, where the body waveform, rather than the actuation frequency, emerges as the variable that sets performance.

Article.Title: Omega-3 fatty acids reprogram tumor-associated macrophage cytokine signaling and suppress pancreatic cancer growth
Article.Authors: Sakuma S.; Zhao S.; Hildreth A.; Liu G.; Shah V.; Sun M.; Tan S.; Jacobs E.; LaPorta M.; Furguiele J.; Avina-Ochoa N.; Globig A.; Tripple V.; N/A N/A.; Maier G.; Panda S.; Reyzer M.; Kang J.; Ma D.; Rodeheffer M.; Shaikh S.; Kaech S.; Liu A.; Chervonsky A.; Cassano A.

Article.Title: A muscle-enriched mitochondrial protein regulates postnatal heart growth through mitonuclear ubiquinone–PPAR signaling
Article.Authors: Hirose K.; Chen X.; Kalyanaraman C.; Waddingham M.; Nakamura M.; Zhang F.; Chen C.; Yao S.; Chang S.; Yu H.; Wang J.; Barca E.; Nakano H.; Hsu A.; Khyeam S.; Gonzalez Ortega S.; Tajima K.; Yoneshiro T.; Zhang H.; Padmanabhan A.; Kajimura S.; Haldar S.; Nakano A.; Murai M.; Fujihara Y.
Article.Abstract: Increased mitochondrial biogenesis and aerobic respiration in postnatal mammalian organs are essential for adaptation to extrauterine life, yet the functions of many tissue-enriched, developmentally regulated mitochondrial proteins remain poorly defined. By integrating mitochondrial proteome annotations with mouse and human transcriptomic datasets, we identified Coenzyme Q10a (Coq10a), a striated muscle-enriched mitochondrial protein, as a regulator of postnatal cardiac growth. Coq10a, the mammalian homolog of the yeast ubiquinone-binding protein Coq10p, is highly induced in the heart after birth through thyroid hormone-, Nkx2.5-, and Tbx5-dependent regulation. To define its physiological function, we generated three independent Coq10a -deficient mouse models. Both global and cardiomyocyte-specific loss of Coq10a promoted postnatal cardiac hypertrophy without impairing basal cardiac function or mitochondrial respiration. Instead, Coq10a deficiency altered intracellular ubiquinone partitioning, resulting in increased ubiquinone accumulation in a microsomal membrane fraction. Transcriptomic analyses revealed enrichment of PPAR-associated metabolic gene sets and induction of established PPAR-responsive genes in Coq10a -deficient hearts. Pharmacological inhibition of PPARα and PPARγ, but not PPARδ, attenuated the hypertrophic phenotype. Molecular dynamics simulations, docking analyses, and mutagenesis identified PPARα residues that contribute to differential responsiveness to ubiquinone. Although Coq10a -deficient hearts maintained near-normal function under basal conditions, they exhibited increased susceptibility to pressure-overload stress. Together, these findings establish Coq10a as a regulator of intracellular ubiquinone partitioning and support a model linking altered mitochondrial lipid distribution and PPAR-associated signaling to postnatal cardiac growth. More broadly, they demonstrate how tissue-enriched mitochondrial proteins can mediate organ-specific physiological functions beyond energy production.

Article.Title: Nuclear BbAtg8 interacts with BbMac1 as a transcriptional modulator to sustain nuclear copper homeostasis during conidial germination
Article.Authors: Ding J.; Qi G.; Ye D.; Li B.; Lu M.; Feng M.; Cai Q.; Ying S.
Article.Abstract: Pathogenic fungi endure host impose copper starvation by tightly coordinating trace metal homeostasis. However, how pathogens synchronize endogenous metal recycling with exogenous copper uptake to promote infection remains enigmatic. Using the entomopathogenic fungus Beauveria bassiana , we uncovered a synergistic regulatory network that prioritizes nuclear copper enrichment during conidial germination. Under copper deprivation, the fungus deploys a highly coordinated dual-track survival strategy. In the cytoplasm, the core autophagy protein BbAtg8 drives autophagic flux, specifically triggering mitophagy to degrade mitochondria, thereby promoting the turnover and mobilization of endogenous copper stores. Concurrently, a nonlipidated pool of BbAtg8 translocates to the nucleus to coordinate exogenous uptake. Within the nucleus, BbAtg8 directly interacts with the copper-fist transcription factor BbMac1 via a functional Atg8-interacting motif (AIM). This physical interaction serves as a potent transcriptional modulator, significantly enhancing BbMac1’s DNA-binding affinity. Consequently, the Atg8-Mac1 complex hyper-activates the expression of three functionally redundant copper transporters (BbCtr1, BbCtr2, and BbCtr4) to aggressively absorb extracellular copper. Strikingly, severe copper deprivation triggers a dynamic spatial enrichment of these classical copper transporters at the nuclear envelope, which correlates with the sustained maintenance of nuclear copper homeostasis required for essential genomic functions and full fungal virulence. Together, these findings reveal how pathogens synchronize mitophagy-mediated endogenous turnover with Mac1-driven exogenous uptake, fundamentally expanding the role of autophagy proteins BbAtg8 into direct transcriptional coordinators of metal homeostasis. This dual-track regulatory model not only deepens our understanding of fungal adaptation to nutritional immunity but also provides potential targets for disrupting copper homeostasis to control fungal pathogens.

Article.Title: S -adenosyl-L-homocysteine triggers an adaptive response that extends lifespan through the YBT1 ABC transporter
Article.Authors: Masumura K.; Kawasaki S.; Tsutsumi M.; Yamashita H.; Kanai M.; Nakajo H.; Yagi W.; Katsunoi S.; Yoneyama K.; Kawano-Kawada M.; Sekito T.; Ogawa T.; Soga T.; Mizunuma M.
Article.Abstract: S -adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) is a fundamental methyl donor; however, the physiological role of its byproduct and competitive inhibitor, S -adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH), remains unclear. Here, we show that transient reactive oxygen species (ROS) production triggered by SAH during the early logarithmic phase mimics partial SAH hydrolase inhibition, extending the yeast chronological lifespan (CLS) through a hormetic mechanism. This study reveals that the dual nature of ROS in aging is determined by the specific degree of SAH hydrolase activity. We identified the adenosine 5’-triphosphate-binding cassette (ABC) transporter Ybt1 as a key downstream effector of SAH. Ybt1 localizes to the vacuolar membrane and facilitates the sequestration of SAM from the cytosol into the vacuole. Notably, YBT1 overexpression extends CLS, mimicking SAH effects through an integrated pathway involving target of rapamycin complex 1 downregulation, autophagy, and adenosine 5’-monophosphate-activated protein kinase activation. Our findings establish that SAH acts as a metabolic signal coupling nutrient and energy availability to longevity via Ybt1, defining an adaptive/hormetic response for lifespan regulation in yeast.

Article.Title: A conserved Hox9–10 code underlies the early establishment of hind appendage progenitors in zebrafish and the Iberian ribbed newt
Article.Authors: Nakazawa H.; Urakawa K.; Maeno A.; Fujibayashi T.; Ishizaka M.; Ishizu A.; Asano T.; Matsubara H.; Takeuchi T.; Watakabe I.; Higashijima S.; Abe G.; Kawamura A.
Article.Abstract: The acquisition of paired appendages was a key innovation in vertebrate evolution. Although HoxA/D paralog groups (PGs) 9–13 play central roles in patterning paired fins and limbs, the evolutionary origin of this paired appendage-patterning system remains unknown. Here, we show that HoxA/D PG9–10 genes are essential for the early establishment of pelvic fin progenitors in zebrafish, and that Hox9–10 function is similarly required for hindlimb progenitor formation in the Iberian ribbed newt. In zebrafish, combined disruption of five HoxA/D PG9–10 genes abolishes the detectable pelvic fin progenitor population, resulting in complete loss of pelvic fins. Importantly, simultaneous CRISPR-mediated disruption of all seven Hox9–10 paralogs in the Iberian ribbed newt similarly impaired the establishment of hindlimb progenitors, suggesting that an early requirement for Hox9–10 function in hind appendage development predates the divergence of ray-finned and lobe-finned vertebrates. Together, these findings identify an evolutionarily conserved role for posterior Hox9–10 genes in the initial establishment of hind appendage progenitors. Because overlapping posterior Hox paralog groups are subsequently deployed during paired appendage patterning, this early Hox9–10 requirement provides a developmental link between the posterior axial Hox code and the paired appendage-patterning system. Article.Title: Dynamic partitioning shapes the in vivo organization of the Escherichia coli RNA degradosome
Article.Authors: Troyer L.; Wang Y.; Wu K.; Kim S.; Kim S.
Article.Abstract: The bacterial RNA degradosome is a central mediator of RNA turnover, yet how its components are organized and regulated in living cells remains unclear. Using live-cell single-molecule imaging, we quantified the spatial distribution and dynamics of the four major Escherichia coli degradosome components: RNase E, RhlB, PNPase, and enolase. These proteins occupied distinct membrane-associated and cytoplasmic pools whose relative abundance varied among proteins and changed with physiological state. In particular, PNPase underwent pronounced redistribution between membrane-associated and cytoplasmic states in response to altered RNA availability and growth conditions, whereas RNase E and RhlB remained largely membrane associated. To determine the functional consequences of this organization, we examined the degradation of lacZ reporter transcripts with different translation initiation strengths. PNPase and RhlB preferentially promoted degradation of weakly translated transcripts, whereas strongly translated transcripts were largely insensitive to their loss. Together, these results reveal that the bacterial RNA degradosome is not a static, uniformly assembled molecular machine. Instead, RNA decay is organized through dynamic intracellular partitioning of degradosome components, linking physiological state and translation status to transcript degradation.

Article.Title: A “knob-in-hole” gate in the antibody C <sub>H</sub> 1 domain underlies subclass-independent IgA hinge cleavage by the commensal metallopeptidase IgAse
Article.Authors: Sebastián Ramírez-Larrota J.; Estivill G.; López-Martín M.; Effantin G.; Gragera M.; Sorzano C.; Marcos E.; Eckhard U.; Gomis-Rüth F.
Article.Abstract: Human immunoglobulin (Ig) A (IgA) protects ≈400 m 2 of mucosae from microbes. Bacterial IgA-peptidases subvert this defense by cleaving the F ab –F c hinge of subclass IgA1 while sparing the hinge-divergent, colon-dominant IgA2 subclass. The exception is IgAse, a ≈140-kDa, seven-domain, membrane-bound metallopeptidase from the colonic commensal Thomasclavelia ramosa that targets both subclasses but no other protein. We previously narrowed the minimal functional assembly down to the IgAse catalytic and wrapping domains (CD and WD) plus the IgA1/2 F ab ′, i.e., the hinge and a F ab of light and heavy chains (LC, HC), each with a variable and a constant Ig domain (V L + C L , V H + C H 1). The transient interaction culminates in cleavage of a proline–valine bond within the first two hinge residues, downstream of a conserved C-terminal C H 1 disulfide (SS2). Here, single-particle cryoelectron microscopy of a disulfide-stabilized minimal IgAse:IgA2 F ab ′ complex yielded high-quality density strongly supporting two states along the cleavage reaction coordinate, a “recognition complex” and a subsequent “precatalytic complex,” in which F ab ′ binds frontally to the IgAse CD via a C H 1 β-sheet and overhang loop LβEβF. This loop binds like a knob to a preformed hole in the active-site cleft. Binding rearranges the knob and rotates SS2 ≈ 180°, enabling access of the hinge into the cleft of the otherwise unaffected precatalytic complex. Together, this work defines a unique, C H 1-mediated hinge-delivering “gate” mechanism, validated by a crystal structure of unbound IgA2 F ab , point mutations disrupting the C H 1:CD interface, and molecular dynamics calculations, which provide the structural framework for subclass-independent IgA cleavage.

Article.Title: Controlled functionalization of cellulose nanocrystals directs polymer-specific protein coronas and immune cell interactions
Article.Authors: Fuku R.; Giuliana P.; Liu Y.; Kumar B.; Malhotra K.; Jiang V.; Sedighi A.; Gunning P.; Edgar L.; Winnik M.
Article.Abstract: Polymer coatings are widely used to suppress nonspecific protein adsorption and modulate nanoparticle–cell interactions. However, the biological outcomes of polymer-functionalized nanoparticles remain difficult to predict in complex biological environments because protein corona formation rapidly alters nanoparticle identity. This challenge is particularly pronounced when hydrophobic moieties are incorporated for imaging or therapeutic applications, as they can promote nonspecific interactions at the nano–bio interface. Herein, we establish a modular grafting-to platform based on cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) that enables systematic comparison of polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based, zwitterionic, and acrylamide-based polymers with controlled grafting density and chain conformation on a common porphyrin-modified surface. We demonstrate that dense polymer brushes reduce nonspecific protein adsorption in single-protein assays. By contrast, all CNC surfaces form dynamic coronas upon exposure to serum proteins, while specific polymer coatings selectively enrich or suppress distinct protein populations. We further demonstrate that polymer-dependent immune cell interactions are substantially reduced following protein corona formation, although differences among polymer chemistries persist. Zwitterionic coatings broadly suppress immune cell interactions, whereas PEG-based coatings preferentially promote interactions with antigen-presenting cells. These findings establish design principles for polymer-functionalized nanoparticles with specific immune cell interaction profiles.

Article.Title: Nitrogen deposition does not alter the temperate forest soil carbon pool: A 14-y experiment on varied nitrogen fertilization
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Hobbie S.; Schlesinger W.; Sun T.
Article.Abstract: Soil carbon (C) pools in nitrogen-limited temperate forests are critical to the global C cycle, but there are no long-term experiments examining soil C, with various nitrogen (N) forms. Here, a 14-y experiment (100 kg N ha −1 y −1 ), with added N simulating atmospheric deposition proportions (~70% inorganic, ~30% organic) did not affect soil C pools, whereas organic N (ON) and inorganic N (IN) individually significantly increased values by 2.7-fold and 1.8-fold, respectively. Although no treatment significantly affected soil pH, treatment effects on pH were negatively associated with soil C pools. In addition, treatments containing ON forms increased mineral-associated organic C fractions, indicating enhanced C stability vs. IN. These findings enhance our understanding of N deposition-soil C pool interactions.

Article.Title: Membrane contact activation of Piezo2 drives lysosome–mitochondrion Ca 2+ transfer and signaling in Trypanosoma cruzi
Article.Authors: Huang G.; Docampo R.
Article.Abstract: Calcium ion (Ca 2+ ) transfer from other organelles is central to mitochondrial metabolism and cell survival, yet how mechanical forces regulate interorganelle communication remains unclear. Here we report a lysosome-to-mitochondrion pathway in Trypanosoma cruzi , the etiologic agent of Chagas disease, mediated by the mechano/osmosensitive channel TcPiezo2. Using ultrastructural, biochemical, and live-cell superresolution imaging, we define lysosome–mitochondrion contact sites (LMCs) that enable direct Ca 2+ transfer. TcPiezo2 triggers Ca 2+ release, which generates perilysosomal nanodomains that drives mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake via the voltage-dependent anion channel and the mitochondrial Ca 2+ uniporter complex. Disruption of TcPiezo2-dependent Ca 2+ transfer impairs mitochondrial metabolism, perturbs redox homeostasis, induces autophagy, and eventually leads to parasite death. These findings establish LMCs as a signaling platform that directly regulates interorganelle Ca 2+ transfer and mitochondrial bioenergetics.

Article.Title: Thermal imbalance drives avian performance and responses to climate warming
Article.Authors: Porter C.; Adams D.; Levy O.; Urinovsky N.; Riddell E.
Article.Abstract: Thermal performance curves are widely used to predict ectothermic responses to climate warming but are less effective for predicting endotherm performance across environmental conditions because thermoregulation often decouples body temperature from ambient temperature. We develop theory and provide empirical evidence for performance curves in endotherms structured by net sensible heat flux (Q), an integrative index of thermoregulatory imbalance. Using biophysical simulations in tree swallows, we show that performance varies predictably with Q (which we term “QPCs”), thereby explaining variation in nestling provisioning performance, reproductive fitness, and geographic limits, while also forecasting responses to climate change. We also demonstrate that thermal imbalance helps shape breeding ranges of birds across North America. Our findings introduce Q as a broadly relevant ecophysiological dimension that constrains performance in endotherms and provides a framework for predicting endotherm responses to climate warming.

Article.Title: Global origins of tuna and billfish fisheries reveal the transition from coastal access to oceanic exploitation
Article.Authors: Rick T.; Andrews A.; Béarez P.; Festa M.; Fossile T.; Hudson M.; Janßen-Kim M.; Juan-Jordá M.; Lambrides A.; LeFebvre M.; Luthra A.; Newsom B.; O’Connor S.; Quintana Morales E.; Spiess A.; Zancan C.; Zimmer C.; Smith E.
Article.Abstract: Ocean ecosystems have played a crucial role in people’s lives around the world for millennia. However, questions persist about when, why, and how people first began removing biomass from offshore habitats and established fisheries in distant, oceanic environments. We explore the antiquity and evolution of tuna (Thunnini) and billfish (Istiophoridae/Xiphiidae) fisheries, two groups of fishes that occur around the world, are economically significant, and are ecologically important open ocean apex predators. The earliest archaeological evidence of fishing for tuna occurs ~44,000 years ago and billfish at ~10,000 years ago, with early fisheries for some tuna species appearing around the world by 3,000 to 1,000 years ago. Most early fisheries are in areas where tunas and billfishes could be accessed relatively close to shore (e.g., submarine canyons) and/or where these fishes may come inshore seasonally or during warm ocean events. Early tuna and billfish fisheries were often linked to ceremony/ritual, alongside advances in maritime technologies. With few exceptions, sustained and intensive commercial exploitation of pelagic predators in offshore and oceanic habitats is a late development in the human past, occurring primarily during the last 200 y. Our findings document a long-term continuum of human interactions with global marine ecosystems spanning thousands of years, including significant differences between the timing and pathways by which people became dominant ecological drivers in nearshore compared to offshore/oceanic ecosystems.

Article.Title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
Article.Authors: Lu Y.; Lu T.; Zhang D.; Ye L.; Li H.
Article.Abstract: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.

Article.Title: Tipping point forecasting in nonstationary dynamics on function spaces
Article.Authors: Liu-Schiaffini M.; Singer C.; Kovachki N.; Leung S.; Bae H.; Azizzadenesheli K.; Anandkumar A.
Article.Abstract: Tipping points are abrupt, drastic, and often irreversible changes in the evolution of nonstationary and chaotic dynamical systems. For instance, increased greenhouse gas concentrations are predicted to lead to drastic decreases in low cloud cover, referred to as a climatological tipping point. In this paper, we learn the evolution of such nonstationary dynamical systems using a recurrent neural operator (RNO), which learns mappings between function spaces. After training RNO on only the pre-tipping dynamics, we employ it to detect future tipping points using an uncertainty-based approach. In particular, we propose a conformal prediction framework to forecast tipping points by monitoring deviations from physics constraints (such as conserved quantities and partial differential equations), enabling forecasting of these abrupt changes along with a rigorous measure of uncertainty. We illustrate our proposed methodology on nonstationary ordinary and partial differential equations, such as the Lorenz-63 and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equations. We also apply our methods to forecast a climate tipping point in stratocumulus cloud cover and airfoil wake and stall transitions using only limited knowledge of the governing equations. For the latter, we show that our proposed method zero-shot generalizes to forecasting multiple future tipping points under varying Reynolds numbers. In our experiments, we demonstrate that even partial or approximate physics constraints can be used to accurately forecast future tipping points.

Article.Title: The historical domestication of a Clostridium botulinum strain used for the industrial production of botulinum neurotoxin
Article.Authors: Keim P.; Nottingham R.; Guevara M.; Miller E.; Vogler A.; Williamson C.; Smith T.; Posner R.; Pellett S.; Lenski R.; Sahl J.
Article.Abstract: Laboratory production of botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) began more than 90 y ago for medical, military, and later pharmaceutical applications, creating one of the longest-running examples of microbial cultivation under sustained human control. A single Clostridium botulinum Group I lineage, Army Hall A (AHA), was established by the US military in 1942 and later gave rise to Hall A-hyper (HAH), the strain widely used for pharmaceutical BoNT production. We analyzed more than 1,000 C. botulinum genomes to identify AHA’s closest relatives and to infer the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) shared with its nearest lineage. Relative to this MRCA, AHA accumulated nearly 100 genetic changes, including 46 single-nucleotide substitutions, 44 small insertions or deletions, and several large deletions and structural variants that led to the loss of more than 80 genes. A nonsense mutation in mutS generated a hypermutator phenotype that accelerated mutation rates and increased genetic diversity. This event is inferred to have occurred early in the lineage’s domestication and appears to have facilitated laboratory-adaptive traits, including the lack of sporulation and increased BoNT yield. Competition experiments under standard growth conditions confirmed substantial laboratory adaptation, with AHA exhibiting a strong fitness advantage over a close relative. Together, these results reconstruct the genomic trajectory of a bacterium evolving under prolonged human-mediated selection and provide a genome-resolved example of microbial domestication. The findings show how laboratory conditions, industrial selection, and changing mutation rates can shape bacterial evolution, and they offer a general framework for understanding domestication and laboratory adaptation across microbial systems.

Article.Title: Mechanistic versus descriptive interpretation of brain activity pattern reconstruction
Article.Authors: Jung K.; Eickhoff S.; Patil K.
Article.Abstract: The geometric eigenmodes, derived from the shape of the cortical surface, have been suggested as a better model for explaining brain function due to their high accuracy in reconstructing patterns of both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked brain activity patterns captured by functional MRI, when contrasted with alternative models including structural connectome derived bases. While a descriptive representation offers valuable utility for neuroimaging studies, it is necessary to examine the extent to which it supports a mechanistic explanation for human brain function. Although the observation that geometric eigenmodes accurately fit brain activity is intriguing, we argue that accepting them as a model of brain function risks conflating descriptive and mechanistic interpretations. While a representation that effectively describes the underlying geometry is inherently adept at fitting patterns within that geometric space; it does not necessarily shed light on mechanisms that give rise to the brain’s functional attributes. To this end, we provide two lines of empirical results: a) geometric eigenmodes demonstrate a high flexibility when fit to a range of manipulated patterns, and b) localized parcel-based representations can reconstruct activity patterns as well. Based on those results, theoretical considerations, and previous data, we argue that more consideration is needed regarding the complementary roles of descriptive representation and mechanistic explanation in neuroimaging research. As O 2 increases in the oxycline, competition with aerobic metabolisms and intensified grazing gradually exclude denitrifiers. However, because they draw on more abundant substrates, N 2 O-producing denitrifiers persist to higher O 2 than N 2 O consumers, reflecting the vulnerability of populations dependent on intermediate metabolites. This ecological decoupling drives N 2 O accumulation and captures the characteristic double-peaked vertical structure without imposing physiological O 2 intolerance thresholds. More broadly, by revealing how niche partitioning and producer–consumer coupling shape other features of OMZ biogeochemistry, these results provide a basis for projecting future shifts in marine nitrogen loss and N 2 O emissions.

Such associations varied only modestly across societies. Notably, the associations between infection-risky contact and societal-level factors depended on target interpersonal value and were concentrated among high-value targets—contact was lower where historical pathogen prevalence and tightness were greater and higher where individualism and relational mobility were greater. These findings suggest that infection-risky contact is primarily guided by the value of social targets, with ecological and cultural factors playing a lesser role.

Article.Title: Changing contributions of emotion and reward information to learning through adolescence
Article.Authors: Phaneuf-Hadd C.; Phelps E.; Somerville L.
Article.Abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8 to 22 y completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hampered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially hindered by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

Article.Title: Abiotic conversion of nitrate to ammonium enhances nitrogen use efficiency in paddy soils
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Wang M.; Li H.; Li J.; Xu J.; Zhang N.; Zhu C.; Shan J.; Zhu G.; Zhu Y.
Article.Abstract: Nitrogen (N) use efficiency is critical in ensuring food production while reducing nitrate (NO 3 − -N) to ammonium (NH 4 + -N) is widely recognized as a key for reducing N loss from paddy fields. Microbial involvement has long been regarded as the indispensable step for NO 3 − -N reduction to NH 4 + -N in nature; it remains largely unknown whether abiotic processes can drive this. Here, using laser confocal fluorescence microscopy and thermodynamic laws, we find that Fe(II) ions in the rice rhizosphere exist on iron plaque in a specific manner with strong reducing capability. These specifically adsorbed Fe(II) ions (Fe(II) SA ) could mediate the abiotic reduction of NO 3 − -N to NH 4 + -N, accounting for 57% of the total NO 3 − -N reduction. When cultured in a sterile nutrient solution containing only 15 NO 3 − -N and Fe(II) ions, over 90% of N in the xylem of rice plants exists as 15 NH 4 + -N, directly proving the occurrence of NO 3 − -N reduction to NH 4 + -N and taken up by rice. Theoretical calculations elucidate the Fe(II) SA -induced local electron depolarization enhances interfacial charge transfer which drives this reaction with the conversion of *NO to *NOH/*NHO identified as the rate-limiting step. We then propose a regulatory strategy to establish a stable Fe(II) SA /Fe(III) SA cycle utilizing FeC for controlled-release of Fe(II) ions. Two-year field experiments confirmed this strategy can increase rice yield by 16.1% while cutting half of the N input. Our work enables the design of novel pathways in improving N use efficiency for sustainable rice production.

Article.Title: Two clusters of brain regions with distinct age-related profiles of functional connectivity in autism spectrum disorder
Article.Authors: Li X.; Zuo F.; Cheng Y.; Perkins K.; Cao F.
Article.Abstract: Brain functional connectivity changes throughout development, and individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may follow trajectories that differ from those of typically developing controls. Using large multisite resting-state fMRI cross-sectional datasets, we examined how functional connectivity differences between ASD and typically developing controls change across a broad age range of 5 to 64 y. A data-driven analysis identified two spatially distributed clusters of cortical regions showing distinct age-related profiles of ASD–TD connectivity differences. Cluster 1 was marked by consistent hypoconnectivity across ages, suggesting a stable neural signature of ASD. Cluster 2 was characterized by hypoconnectivity in childhood that gradually diminished with age, suggesting a temporary delay profile. These clusters were systematically organized along the sensory–association axis. Cluster 1 mainly involved lower-rank sensory and sensorimotor cortices, while Cluster 2 mainly involved higher-rank association cortices. Brain–behavior analyses revealed greater and broader ASD symptom associations across ages in the consistent hypoconnectivity profile than the delay profile. Further subtype analyses suggested that social-affect symptoms were associated with greater hypoconnectivity than repetitive behavior symptoms in both clusters. Spatial correlation analyses with neurotransmitter maps revealed associations of Cluster 1 with mGluR5 and of Cluster 2 with GABA A α5, providing insight into the neurobiological basis of the two clusters. In a cross-disorder validation analysis, applying the same analytic framework to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder did not reveal comparable results. Together, these findings suggest that ASD-related functional connectivity alterations are developmentally heterogeneous and organized along the cortical hierarchy, providing a developmental perspective for understanding the neurobiology of ASD.

Article.Title: Suspected distortion of citations in high-impact cancer journals
Article.Authors: Scancar B.; Byrne J.; Causeur D.; Barnett A.
Article.Abstract: Research and scholarship are shaped by article citations, which underpin the communication of ideas, assignment of credit, journal impact factors, and author career progression. Given their key influence on author and journal metrics, citations can be intentionally manipulated to inflate the reputation of journals and researchers. Paper mills, unethical organizations that produce and sell manuscripts and publishing services, may also be manipulating citations, but the extent of this manipulation is unknown. Here, we show that molecular cancer articles sharing features with retracted papers from paper mills display citation patterns that suggest systematic inflation. These articles were published in journals in the top decile of journal rankings. Suspected paper mill articles received 50 to 100% more citations than other papers 1 to 3 y after publication, while paradoxically attracting fewer readers and online accesses. Suspected paper mill articles also cited—and were cited by—other suspected paper mill articles, which frequently appeared in journals previously reported as paper mill targets. Citations from suspected paper mill articles measurably inflated journal citation metrics. These findings suggest that paper mills inflate the citation metrics of supported publications and affected journals at scale. This widespread manipulation of citation metrics may amplify unreliable findings, slowing scientific progress and spurring unreasonable citation benchmarks for research articles, journals, and authors. Our findings point to measurable signatures of citation manipulation that could support article- and journal-level screening.

Article.Title: Superconductivity in the high-pressure tetragonal phase of UTe <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Deng Y.; Mee G.; Wannamaker T.; Feng K.; Xu M.; Xie W.; Maple M.
Article.Abstract: Electrical transport and magnetic measurements have been made on UTe 2 under pressure P up to ~16 GPa to determine the superconducting transition temperature T c vs. P phase diagram in the high-pressure tetragonal phase. Superconductivity emerges near ~5 GPa, coincident with the orthorhombic—tetragonal phase transition; in the tetragonal phase, T c reaches a maximum value of ~4 K at 6 GPa and then decreases with P and appears to vanish near 18 GPa. Tetragonal UTe 2 has a relatively small upper critical field H c2 (0) ≈ 1.2 T at 5.3 GPa, smaller than the Pauli paramagnetic limit, and is orbitally limited with a coherence length ξ tetra ≈ 16.5 nm. This small value of H c2 (0) favors more conventional superconductivity; in contrast, the large values of H c2 ( T ) for orthorhombic UTe 2 exceed the Pauli paramagnetic limit in all three crystallographic directions and have been attributed to unconventional superconductivity, widely believed to involve spin-triplet pairing. The temperature–pressure phase diagram of UTe 2 shows a striking dichotomy: a narrow, fragile, unconventional superconducting region in the orthorhombic phase vs. a broad, robust, and more conventional superconducting dome in the tetragonal phase. This dichotomy is consistent with the proposal that U-dimers, present (absent) in the orthorhombic (tetragonal) phase, may play a role in spin-triplet superconductivity of orthorhombic UTe 2 . In the tetragonal phase, the normal-state electrical resistivity ρ( T ) exhibits metallic behavior with a “knee” at 200 to 240 K that depends weakly on P and most likely marks the onset of a transition to a magnetically ordered phase that coexists with superconductivity.

Article.Title: The impact of modulator therapy on the Pseudomonas aeruginosa cystic fibrosis lung transcriptome
Article.Authors: Letizia M.; Whiteley L.; Diggle F.; Davis A.; Morgan S.; Grogan B.; Baugh J.; McKone E.; Singh P.; Whiteley M.
Article.Abstract: Chronic lung infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major complication of cystic fibrosis (CF), contributing to lung function decline and increased morbidity and mortality. Laboratory models are used to study CF infections, but their relevance depends on how accurately they reproduce microbial physiology during human infection. We previously developed a framework that uses bacterial gene expression in human infections to quantify model accuracy. Here, we applied this framework to determine how a major therapeutic intervention impacts P. aeruginosa physiology in the lungs of people with CF (pwCF) and to develop and evaluate refined preclinical models. We focused on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), a highly effective CFTR modulator therapy that has improved outcomes for pwCF. However, evidence indicates that P. aeruginosa lung infections persist despite ETI therapy. Analysis of P. aeruginosa transcriptomes from human sputum collected before and after ETI initiation revealed minimal changes in gene expression, indicating that the CF airway continues to support a similar bacterial transcriptional state despite therapy. We then evaluated how strain selection, zinc limitation, and polymicrobial coculture influence the ability of laboratory models to recapitulate P. aeruginosa gene expression in human CF sputum. Growth of CF clinical isolates in zinc-limited synthetic CF sputum medium produced the most accurate model, whereas population-based cultures and coculture with Staphylococcus aureus had limited effects. Article.Title: Structure-based targeting of Atg8 uncovers its essential role in autophagy-mediated detoxification
Article.Authors: Yan J.; Zhu X.; Li L.; Shen Z.; Bao J.; Liang S.; Wu H.; Asif N.; Luo X.; Lv H.; Daskalov A.; Cai Y.; Wei Y.; Lu J.; Liu X.; Naqvi N.; Wilson R.; Lin F.
Article.Abstract: Autophagy degrades and recycles intracellular material, allowing cells to maintain homeostasis and adapt to environmental stress. Article.Title: Ice-ray pentagonal packing of pseudo-fivefold helices
Article.Authors: Aeindartehran L.; Kwan L.; Tahir I.; Unruh D.; Petrov M.; Stoll W.; Alvarez A.; Hu J.; Ahmed E.; Seal N.; Taton N.; Milenkova A.; Dinnebier R.; Martins M.; Cheng Y.; Ramirez-Cuesta A.; Zhang J.; Ruggiero M.; Naumov P.; Runčevski T.
Article.Abstract: While fivefold point symmetry is common in nature, fivefold spatial symmetry is seldom observed. Regular pentagons cannot tile a plane without leaving voids, and even the densest “ice-ray” packing is exceptionally rare. Fivefold helices are equally elusive. We report a small molecule that self-assembles into hydrogen-bonded pseudo-fivefold helices and adopts an ice-ray pentagonal packing motif over crystallographic length scales using peripheral disorder that partially occupies regions that would otherwise be void in an ideal pentagonal tessellation. This structural anisotropy gives rise to single crystals with large aspect ratios and distinct mechanical behavior. This realization of two rare structural motifs within a single crystal shows the capability of simple organic molecules to form complex structures and highlights an untapped potential for symmetry engineering in molecular solids through the interplay of intermolecular interactions with pronounced differences in strength and directionality.

Article.Title: Convergent genome streamlining accompanies independent miniaturization in the world’s smallest fishes
Article.Authors: Sudasinghe H.; Matschiner M.; Britz R.; Conway K.; Tan H.; Salzburger W.; Peichel C.; Rüber L.
Article.Abstract: Miniaturization, the reduction of adult body size to an extreme degree, has evolved repeatedly across vertebrates. Yet its genomic underpinnings remain poorly understood. Cypriniformes, the most species-rich order of freshwater fishes, contains multiple miniaturized lineages that have evolved via contrasting developmental processes. Proportioned dwarfs are tiny-bodied but otherwise morphologically similar to larger relatives, while progenetic miniatures exhibit developmental truncation and retain larval-like anatomical features into adulthood. Using a new time-calibrated phylogeny of 309 cypriniform species and comparative genomic analyses of 33 high-quality genome assemblies, we investigated the evolutionary history and genomic correlates of miniaturization across this order. Ancestral state reconstruction revealed multiple independent origins of both miniature types, with reversals to the nonminiature state rarely recovered and miniature origins nonrandomly distributed across the phylogeny. The origins of the two types of miniatures differed in their timing. Progenetic miniatures arose predominantly in the Eocene whereas proportioned dwarfs arose mainly within the Miocene period. Genome size variation across Cypriniformes has been overwhelmingly driven by polyploidy. However, progenetic miniatures showed a directionally consistent, though nonsignificant, trend toward genome size reduction. Comparative genomic analyses revealed that all three independently evolved progenetic miniature lineages share convergent signatures of repeat loss alongside genome-wide intron shortening, patterns absent in proportioned dwarfs. Our study provides the broadest evidence to date that progenetic miniaturization, despite independent origins, is underpinned by predictable structural genomic changes, revealing a fundamental link between developmental truncation and genome architecture in vertebrates.

Here, we have shown that MBD3 deficiency in the T cell compartment resulted in spontaneous development of T cell–mediated multiorgan autoimmune diseases including fatal autoimmune myocarditis. The MBD3-deficient mice notably showed a significant reduction of CD25 + Foxp3 + regulatory T (Treg) cells in both the thymus and periphery without much affecting the development and function of conventional T (Tconv) cells. Mixed bone marrow (BM) chimeras reconstituted with wild-type and MBD3-deficient BM revealed a cell-intrinsic defect in thymic Treg cell lineage differentiation in MBD3-deficient cells. The impairment markedly limited thymic Treg precursor cell generation and substantially reduced overall thymic Treg cell output. By contrast, MBD3 deficiency scarcely impacted the TGF-β/IL-2-dependent in vitro Treg cell generation from Tconv cells. Thus, Treg-specific developmental properties such as high IL-2/CD25 dependency of their thymic differentiation may render them more sensitive than Tconv cells to epigenetic changes of the whole T cell compartment. The results provide a mechanistic basis by which general epigenomic alterations in the T cell compartment can be causative of autoimmune and other immunological diseases through selectively affecting thymic Treg cell development.

Article.Title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South
Article.Authors: Chen M.; Song W.; Lu D.; Deng Y.; Wang C.; Jiang H.; Zhou Y.; Scown M.; Chen L.; Ma J.; Zheng H.; Bai X.
Article.Abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between “low” and “high” vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

Article.Title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
Article.Authors: Pagan N.; Törnberg P.; Bail C.; Barrie C.
Article.Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

Article.Abstract: Modern slavery remains pervasive across many economic sectors. Progress toward eradicating it has been partially hindered by a lack of tested, comprehensive policy responses. Using data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, we evaluated how ranchers changed their selling behavior after being added to the “Dirty List,” a public registry that names and shames employers found to use modern slavery. Dirty Listed ranchers significantly reduced direct sales to slaughterhouses that signed sustainable supply chain commitments but evaded sanctions by laundering cattle through compliant intermediaries or selling to nonsignatory slaughterhouses. Article.Title: Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees
Article.Authors: Tang S.; Sapsis T.; Azizan N.
Article.Abstract: Chaotic dynamics, commonly seen in weather systems and fluid turbulence, are characterized by their sensitivity to initial conditions, which makes accurate prediction challenging. Recent approaches have focused on developing data-driven models that attempt to preserve invariant statistics over long horizons since many chaotic systems exhibit dissipative behaviors and ergodicity. Despite the recent progress in such models, they are still often prone to generating unbounded trajectories, leading to invalid statistics evaluation. To address this fundamental challenge, we introduce a modular framework that provides formal guarantees of trajectory boundedness for neural network chaotic dynamics models. Our core contribution is a dissipative projection layer that leverages control-theoretic principles to ensure the learned system is dissipative. Specifically, our framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator and an energy-like function, where the latter is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint within the projection layer. Furthermore, the learned invariant level set provides an outer estimate for the system’s strange attractor, which is known to be difficult to characterize due to its complex geometry. We demonstrate our model’s ability to produce bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserve invariant statistics for chaotic dynamical systems, including Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.

Article.Title: In mice, a population of male germ cells shows characteristics of nonapoptotic cell death during G0 arrest
Article.Authors: Stark K.; Hatkevich T.; Miao E.; Souma T.; Capel B.
Article.Abstract: In mammals, a small population of spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) is established shortly after birth. These cells self-renew and produce sperm for the male’s reproductive lifespan, passing the genome on to the next generation. Establishment of a population of SSCs with high genomic integrity is essential. SSCs are derived from a much larger precursor population of male germ cells (MGCs) that differentiate during fetal life. During the last third of gestation, MGCs undergo a prolonged period of G0 cell cycle arrest during which they sustain high levels of transcription and acquire epigenetic programming for SSC fate. Although these differentiation steps can cause cellular and genomic damage, it has been unclear whether selection for germ cell quality occurs during G0 arrest since no classic markers of cell death have been detected. In this study, we used a mouse model to characterize a population of MGCs that begin to accumulate markers of cell death, such as AnnexinV (AnV) and propidium iodide (PI), at E16.5. The AnV- and PI-positive MGC population is characterized by low expression of the RNA-binding protein, Dead End 1, and exhibits dsDNA breaks and mitochondrial dysfunction. Interestingly, we do not see evidence of an active cell death cascade until the time of birth, when phosphorylation of MLKL, a hallmark of necroptotic cell death, occurs. Based on these findings, we propose that variable cellular health is an important basis for selection of SSC precursors.

Article.Title: Shedding light on left hippocampal mGlu5 in Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Zussy C.; Mathias M.; Vitalis M.; Moujellil-Legagneur T.; Malhaire F.; Canet G.; Desrumaux C.; Claeysen S.; Gómez-Santacana X.; Goudet C.; Llebaria A.; Givalois L.
Article.Abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5) is essential for synaptic plasticity and memory, making it a potential therapeutic target in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). While hemispheric asymmetries in hippocampal function have been observed in AD patients, the lateralized contribution of mGlu5 signaling to cognitive decline remains unclear. Here, we show a physiological left-right asymmetry in hippocampal mGlu5 expression in wild-type mice, with higher levels in the left hemisphere, consistent with previous reports. This physiological asymmetry is lost in two distinct mouse models of AD, the J20 and 5xFAD mice, revealing a hemisphere-specific disruption of hippocampal mGlu5 regulation. Using the light-controllable negative allosteric modulator Alloswitch-1, we show that selective inhibition of left, but not right, hippocampal mGlu5 restores working and short-term memory in AD mice. This finding indicates that altered mGlu5 expression does not simply reflect receptor loss, but rather a dysregulated signaling state that remains functionally relevant and pharmacologically targetable. Left-specific modulation also normalizes pathological downstream signaling, including aberrant Pyk2 and GSK-3β activation and tau hyperphosphorylation, across both hemispheres, indicating a widespread impact of hemisphere-selective intervention. These findings establish a functional lateralization of hippocampal mGlu5 signaling and identify the left hippocampus as a critical site for mGlu5-dependent memory dysfunction in AD. They also highlight the therapeutic potential of region-specific photopharmacology for precise intervention in early AD pathology, providing a strategy for spatially targeted modulation of pathological synaptic signaling in neurodegenerative disease.

Article.Title: Evolution shapes ecosystem resilience through spatial self-organization
Article.Authors: Dong X.; Richardson A.; Muneepeerakul R.
Article.Abstract: Drylands are globally widespread and ecologically important but vulnerable to climate change. Many exhibit spatially self-organized vegetation patterns that enhance resilience by enabling vegetation to reorganize their patterns under drying, thereby optimizing water use and maintaining productivity. Plants can also undergo evolution in response to environmental change. Although both spatial self-organization and rapid evolution are fundamental mechanisms of resilience, their interaction remains largely unknown. Using a theoretical model, we examine how these mechanisms interact to shape vegetation transitions—abrupt or gradual—and ecosystem resilience under climatic drying. We find that pattern formation can suppress adaptation by maintaining soil moisture beneath vegetation patches despite rainfall decline, thereby limiting selection for increased drought tolerance. However, this suppression is largely alleviated under the variable rainfall typical of drylands. In turn, evolution feeds back on self-organization by increasing the spatial plasticity of vegetation patterns and their ability to reorganize under changing climate, although this positive effect weakens as evolutionary rate increases. Considering direct (adaptation) and indirect (pattern-mediated) effects, evolution enhances resilience, with indirect effects via pattern plasticity dominating. Within model scenarios spanning plausible rainfall variability and relative evolutionary-to-ecological rates, more than half of vegetation transitions are abrupt involving biomass losses exceeding 50%, highlighting a potential mechanism underlying recent global observations of widespread abrupt vegetation losses in drylands. These results demonstrate that evolution and spatial self-organization jointly determine dryland resilience under environmental change and highlight the unexpected role of evolution in patterned landscapes, calling for integrative approaches to predict ecosystem responses in a changing world.

Article.Title: Competing presynaptic protein assemblies coordinate basal neurotransmission with homeostatic plasticity
Article.Authors: Hsieh W.; Han T.; Vicidomini R.; Nguyen P.; Serpe M.
Article.Abstract: Neural circuits establish a stable basal level of synaptic transmission that is maintained throughout life. When synaptic activity is perturbed, homeostatic mechanisms restore this set point, but how neurons reconcile long-term stability and rapid compensatory plasticity remains unclear. Here, we identify two competing presynaptic multimolecular complexes that control steady-state transmission and homeostatic potentiation and define the molecular switch that enables transitions between these functional states. At Drosophila neuromuscular junction, the transmembrane protein PlexinB (PlexB) and the auxiliary subunit Neto-α regulate both basal synaptic function and homeostatic plasticity. PlexB association with presynaptic KaiR1D/Neto-α receptor complexes modulates channel properties and fine-tunes neurotransmitter release, whereas PlexB signaling with Semaphorin2b (Sema2b) and Neto-α drives homeostatic potentiation. KaiR1D and Sema2b/PlexB compete for a limited pool of presynaptic Neto-α. Motor neurons switch from steady-state transmission to homeostatic potentiation by exchanging KaiR1D/Neto-α/PlexB complexes for Neto-α/PlexB/Sema2b. Critically, Neto-α must dissociate from KaiR1D-containing complexes to initiate the homeostatic response. Variants of Neto-α or KaiR1D that fail to dissociate support normal basal neurotransmission but abolish homeostatic plasticity. These findings demonstrate that dynamic reorganization of competing presynaptic protein assemblies enables neurons to preserve stable baseline transmission while mounting robust compensatory responses to perturbations. Given the widespread roles of presynaptic receptors and Semaphorin/Plexin signaling in synaptic regulation, this mechanism may represent a conserved strategy for balancing stability and plasticity in neural circuits.

Article.Title: Multiyear dual-isotope fingerprinting at South Asian receptor sites constrains carbon monoxide sources and enhanced oxidation
Article.Authors: Yao P.; Holmstrand H.; van der Veen C.; Elena Popa M.; A. Brashear C.; Budhavant K.; Remani Manoj M.; Romson J.; Salam A.; Röckmann T.; Gustafsson Ö.
Article.Abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) is an indirect short-lived climate forcer with uncertainties both in sources and its role in atmospheric oxidation. Based on nine winter-long dual-isotope campaigns at two South Asian receptor sites intercepting the continental outflow, we quantified CO source contributions and emission–sink dynamics. Combustion accounts for 68 to 74% of South Asia regional CO (including 34 to 37% from biomass burning) with secondary atmospheric oxidation contributing 26 to 32% (dominated by oxidation of nonmethane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) at 21 to 26%, with methane oxidation contributing 5.5 to 6.4%). These isotope-observational constraints suggest a twice higher role for atmospheric oxidation than in model estimates. Spatially, the absolute contributions of both primary and secondary CO decrease from the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the northern Indian Ocean, while the relative contribution of oxidation-derived CO increases, indicating enhanced secondary CO production near source regions. Observation-model comparison suggests that transport from the continental areas dominates CO over adjacent oceanic regions, with minor local production. During the COVID-19 emission perturbation, combustion-derived CO fell sharply in absolute terms, NMVOC-derived CO rose, and CH 4 -derived CO remained stable, providing an observational constraint on the sensitivity of atmospheric oxidation to emission changes. Our results reveal a significant contribution of CO from atmospheric oxidation in South Asia, calling for a reassessment of regional emission–oxidation coupling in models and of mitigation strategies.

Article.Title: Antiferromagnetism and tightly bound Cooper pairs induced by kinetic frustration
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Batista C.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Antiferromagnetism and superconductivity are often viewed as competing orders in correlated electron systems. Here, we demonstrate that kinetic frustration in hole motion facilitates their coexistence within the square-lattice repulsive Hubbard model. Combining exact analytical solutions on tailored geometries with large-scale numerical simulations, we reveal a robust pairing mechanism: Holes on opposite sublattices behave as if they carry opposite effective charges due to spin singlet formation from kinetic frustration. This emergent property suppresses phase separation and fosters a coherent d -wave superconducting channel embedded within a long-range antiferromagnetic background. Our findings establish a minimal yet broadly applicable framework for stabilizing strong-coupling superconductivity in doped Mott insulators.

Article.Abstract: Labile zinc ions (Zn 2+ ) are stored in glutamatergic vesicles at specific excitatory synapses in the central nervous system and released into synaptic clefts in an activity-dependent manner. Using a chemical knock-in strategy, we introduced activity-based Zn 2+ probes with distinct affinities into endogenous α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole-propionic acid or γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptors. These in-brain-constructed Zn 2+ sensors enabled region-specific mapping of Zn 2+ in synaptic clefts in the living mouse brain. Imaging-based analyses revealed differences in apparent Zn 2+ levels at excitatory and inhibitory synapses across hippocampal regions during kainate-induced seizures, providing insights into the physiological and pathological functions of synaptic Zn 2+ .

Article.Title: Astrocytic facilitation of somatic NMDARs underpins hippocampal E-S potentiation
Article.Authors: Dong X.; Chen Z.; Fu Y.; Wang Z.; Lu W.
Article.Abstract: EPSP–spike (E-S) potentiation is a form of plasticity defined by a persistent increase in neuronal spike output for a given synaptic input, reflecting enhanced E-S coupling independent of synaptic strength. However, its cellular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that brief induction of E-S potentiation triggers a sustained calcium activity increase in astrocytes adjacent to the hippocampal CA1 pyramidal layer. Mechanistically, E-S potentiation critically requires GluN2B-containing N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) localized to the neuronal soma. Sustained astrocytic activity promotes E-S potentiation through vesicular release of D-serine, which enhances tonic activation of somatic NMDARs, suppresses A-type potassium currents, and produces a lasting increase in neuronal excitability. Functionally, this astrocyte-dependent E-S potentiation lowers the threshold for subsequent long-term potentiation, conferring a metaplastic influence on hippocampal circuits. These findings identify an astrocyte-neuron signaling mechanism that drives intrinsic plasticity and establish somatic NMDARs as a key site of astrocytic regulation of hippocampal output.

Article.Title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT
Article.Authors: Rajan A.; Piacentino M.; Bronner M.; Hutchins E.
Article.Abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin , which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3′ untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.

Article.Title: Heterochronicity shapes brain network formation
Article.Authors: Poli F.; Oldham S.; Mousley A.; Bullmore E.; Vértes P.; Astle D.
Article.Abstract: Brain network formation unfolds on a nonuniform developmental timetable, with different cortical regions generating connections at different developmental phases. Generative network models (GNMs) aim to uncover the principles underpinning the organization of connectomes by creating synthetic networks according to simple computational rules. These models capture the connectome’s topology, operationalized here as the cumulative distributions of network metrics (e.g., modularity, small-worldness, rich-club structure). However, GNMs typically ignore the differential timing of connectivity formation, and by omitting this temporal programme they often misplace topological features in physical space. Here, we add a heterochronous growth term to GNMs and use a model fitness function that weighs topology and topography equally. Topography refers to the spatial embedding of the network—the actual anatomical positions of the axonal tracts. With these advances, we can generate synthetic networks that more faithfully reproduce the spatial layout of diffusion-MRI connectomes from two independent adult cohorts. Compared with classical, temporally agnostic models, heterochronous simulations improve model fit, accurately locate cortical hubs and modules across individuals, and converge on a single caudal-to-rostral gradient of brain maturation. Overall, integrating heterochronicity makes GNMs more faithful to brain development, and allows for better identification of individual differences in network formation.

Article.Title: A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation
Article.Authors: Han C.; Tsay K.; Lobo S.; Najafi S.; Monahan K.; Hong E.; Shell M.; Shea J.; Han S.
Article.Abstract: Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation water has been proposed to be a signature of such hot spots at both the tau fibril-end surface and soluble tau monomers. Although jR2R3-P301L tau exhibits a heterogeneous hydration landscape in its intrinsically disordered state, with enhanced water structuring near the P301L mutation site, it is unclear whether a localized hotspot exists at the fibril end surface and surface water facilitates the initial contacts in templated aggregation. Using rapid 1 H- 15 N SOFAST-HMQC NMR to track seed-induced aggregation of jR2R3-P301L in real time, complemented by molecular dynamics simulation of fibril surface hydration, we identify a residue-specific pinning hotspot that is prone to dewetting followed by sequential folding and incorporation of the remaining segment in a two-step dock-and-lock process. Site-specific spin labeling further demonstrates that blocking this pinning hotspot disrupts templated aggregation, leading to shorter fibrils. The identification of a dominant pinning site will facilitate the rational design of binders to effectively disrupt fibril extension or serve as diagnostic or therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Coordinated transformations of the labyrinth and occiput during the dinosaur–bird transition
Article.Authors: Navalón G.; Evers S.; Hughes E.; Bjarnason A.; Chiappe L.; Walsh S.; Neenan J.; Panciroli E.; Field D.; Benson R.
Article.Abstract: Evolutionary shape changes of the vertebrate semicircular canals (SCCs) are often ascribed to evolutionary transitions in locomotion, including the origin of flight during the dinosaur–bird transition. Notably, rotation of the occiput toward a ventral orientation is associated with important changes to SCC shape that match those observed during the dinosaur–bird transition. This suggests that evolutionary transformations of SCC shape during the Mesozoic origin of avian flight resulted from evolutionary changes in the orientation of the craniocervical joint, and not from tuning of SCC sensory function. These findings illuminate the importance of integrated morphological changes to the head-neck system during bird origins and challenge the long-standing assumption that SCC morphology enables confident inferences of the locomotor capabilities of extinct vertebrates.

Zhuang, Science 339 , 452–456 (2013); K. L. Hedstrom, Y. Ogawa, M. N. Rasband, J. Cell Biol. 183 , 635–640 (2008)]. By contrast, the AnkG-associated cell-adhesion protein neurofascin-186 appears in clusters of varying sizes that are consistent with the periodic organization of AnkG pairs, yet suggesting a more complex molecular arrangement between the two molecules. Article.Title: Improved assessment of Alaskan Arctic coastal wave exposure accounting for landfast ice
Article.Authors: Henke M.; Yang Z.; Branch R.
Article.Abstract: Simulations of the ocean wave climate are critical for assessment of coastal processes and hazards in observation sparse regions such as the Arctic. While the multidecade wind and ice datasets necessary for driving long-term wave simulations have proven reliable for such efforts, the presence of landfast ice along shorelines at scales not represented by these data has been a persistent uncertainty impeding accurate analysis of impacts to Arctic coasts. Here, we explore this uncertainty by producing a historical high-resolution wave simulation and combining simulation outputs with landfast ice data for the Alaskan Arctic. The resulting dataset yields an improved assessment of coastal waves and identifies stark contrasts in the seasonal wave exposure of the Chukchi and Beaufort regions. Notably, analysis shows that absent supplemented landfast ice, coastal ice cover is broadly underestimated by 10 to 25 d, resulting in wave energy being overestimated by 5 to 10% in shallow depths nearshore. Notably, these figures can reach up to 70 d of underestimation for ice cover and 48% overestimation of wave energy in certain locations. The persistent overestimation and potential for extreme positive biases in coastal wave assessment highlight the need for representation of landfast ice in Arctic coastal analysis efforts and our analysis reveals the spatial and temporal biases for related research.

Article.Authors: Du S.; Wang Y.; Zhang F.; Engel M.; Zheng X.; Gong D.; Zhou C.; Cai C.

Article.Title: Thermodynamic origin of atmospheric new particle formation: Theory for stable nucleating pairs
Article.Authors: Halonen R.
Article.Abstract: Atmospheric new particle formation (NPF) has been observed across virtually all tropospheric environments, yet the meteorological conditions that favor or suppress it have resisted clear theoretical resolution. Article.Title: Cell identity competes with surface tension to determine stromal organization in tumor spheroids beyond the CAF shell paradigm
Article.Authors: Wilhelm C.
Article.Abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often found forming a peripheral stromal barrier around tumors. Besides, CAFs consistently occupy the highest end of the surface tension hierarchy, predicting core rather than peripheral localization and directly challenging the shell paradigm. Yet confocal imaging reveals not only central accumulation but also complete CAF-tumor mixing, including in spheroids where cancer cells exhibit surface tensions nearly two orders of magnitude lower than CAFs. Together, these results identify surface tension, EMT state, and assembly chronology as joint determinants of tumor–stroma architecture, revealing a context-dependent organization landscape rather than a universal CAF shell.

Article.Authors: Liu Q.; Zhao X.; Lee J.; Zare R.
Article.Abstract: The abiotic emergence of ribonucleosides remains a central challenge in origin-of-life research because ribonucleosides form inefficiently and are often unstable under prebiotically plausible conditions. Article.Title: The honey bee stinger: An unusual pump with collapsible double pistons
Article.Authors: Ramirez-Esquivel F.; Klose C.; Lee H.; Graco Q.; Narendra A.; Ravi S.
Article.Abstract: Most stinging animals deliver venom by contracting muscles around a venom reservoir, but honey bees employ a fundamentally different strategy. Article.Authors: Reed C.; Lemoine N.; Budny M.; Clarke V.; du Toit J.; Helcoski R.; Knoetze H.; Lucas J.; Schimel J.; Smit I.; Strydom T.; Tallian A.; Thompson D.; Burkepile D.

These results demonstrate that elephant megacarcasses generate coldspots of biodiversity but hotspots of ecosystem processes, unveiling a cryptic ecological function of megaherbivores that is extreme in both magnitude and duration relative to carcasses of smaller animals. Prior studies have implicated SETDB1 and the Human Silencing Hub (HUSH) complex in heterochromatin formation-based TE repression, but precise characterization of repeat subclass and locus-specific effects for SETDB1 and related mechanisms has been limited by short-read transcriptome mapping. Knockdown of SETDB1 or core HUSH factors reveals robust and reproducible derepression of a restricted subset of long terminal repeat (LTR) retroelements distinct from those of global DNA demethylation. This derepression is heterogeneous within TE subclasses and is confined to discrete genomic loci, highlighting regulatory diversity that is obscured by aggregate, family-level analyses. Time-resolved SETDB1 depletion followed by histone 3 lysine 9 (H3K9)me3, H3K9me2, and Pol II ChIP-seq reveals a stratified derepression response: ERVK and ERV1 elements show concordant H3K9 methylation loss, Pol II gain, and RNA expression induction, consistent with direct H3K9me3-mediated silencing, whereas LINE/L1 elements show transcriptional activation without corresponding H3K9me3 loss, implicating parallel repressive mechanisms. These data support a model in which SETDB1-dependent H3K9 methylation maintains silencing of evolutionarily young LTRs, while long interspersed nuclear element (LINE) repression engages broader heterochromatic pathways not fully captured by any single chromatin readout. Collectively, our findings refine current models of heterochromatin-mediated TE control and provide a framework for dissecting how chromatin-based mechanisms cooperate to maintain subclass-selective TE repression.
