Article.Title: The deep-time history of soils and plants
Article.Authors: Strullu-Derrien C.; Rillig M.
Article.Abstract: For a large community of ecosystem ecologists, plant-soil interactions have moved center stage in the understanding of both plant and soil ecology. Frequently, plants are deemed to be the main drivers of these interactions. However, soils existed before the evolution of land plants (i.e., embryophytes), and terrestrial communities were already highly diverse around 400 million years ago (Ma), reflecting an earlier origin of the organisms that populated them. But which organisms were contemporaneous at the origin of soil and in what type of environment they lived is not well established. Here, we trace the development of soil and its biotic components from the beginnings, about one billion years ago (Ga), by using the fossil record and geochemical data. We show that the first terrestrial ecosystems were probably situated near the ocean, where organisms were already adapted to high oxygen pressures and where plants were not yet present. Drawing on this, we discuss the need to rethink the primacy of plants in modern terrestrial ecosystems, considering that persistence of the soil system over deep time could help explain the enormous current biodiversity found in soil. We advocate for a shift in perspective by embracing a vision of terrestrial ecosystems with interdependent and equally important above- and below-ground system compartments. Finally, we highlight the importance of 'bending the curve' on the increasing rate of soil degradation and loss of soil health, and we discuss the outlook for the future of soils and their interactions with plants.

Article.Title: Deep microbial biosphere
Article.Authors: Beaver R.; Neufeld J.
Article.Abstract: The deep microbial biosphere is a vast ecosystem extending kilometers beneath Earth's surface in terrestrial rocks, aquifers, marine sediments, and oceanic crust. Blocked from sunlight, and often severely limited in organic carbon and oxygen, these environments host microorganisms sustained by energy sources such as hydrogen gas, reduced metals, and sulfur compounds. Over the past few decades, advances in sampling, cultivation-independent methods, and deep-sea drilling have revealed diverse bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic life in the subsurface, including still poorly understood lineages with unusual metabolic strategies. Despite extreme energy limitation and often harsh conditions, subsurface microorganisms persist through adaptations and strategies such as metabolic versatility, streamlined genomes, efficient carbon fixation pathways, and slow growth. Collectively, microbial communities exert an important yet poorly constrained influence on Earth's long-term carbon, sulfur, and nitrogen cycles. Although uncertainties remain related to rates of metabolic activity, generation times, and global contributions to biogeochemical cycles, the deep biosphere has emerged as a central component of Earth's biosphere and is growing in relevance as human activities increasingly intersect with the deep subsurface.

Article.Title: Birds shape biogeochemistry and ecosystem function globally
Article.Authors: Duvall E.; Abraham A.; Bellvé A.; Doughty C.; Rodewald A.; Subalusky A.; Flecker A.
Article.Abstract: Birds inhabit nearly every environment on Earth, shaping ecosystems through diverse functions that include contributions to biogeochemical cycles. By transporting and recycling nutrients, birds influence the availability and distribution of chemical elements that regulate key ecological processes. Yet, as bird populations decline, their biogeochemical roles remain poorly synthesized, limiting our understanding of the broader consequences of biodiversity loss. Here, we systematically review the role of birds in biogeochemistry, with consequences for ecosystem function, structure, and connectivity globally. We highlight key mechanisms, ecological impacts, and future research and management priorities. We find that birds - by virtue of their broad distribution and abundance, flight-enabled mobility, nutrient-rich diets, and high metabolic demands - play distinct roles in nutrient transport. Although research has focused largely on waterbirds, growing evidence reveals birds' substantial chemical impacts on diverse environments, locally restructuring plant, microbial, and animal communities. Delivery of key limiting elements, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, can boost primary productivity and increase autotroph nutrient content, with bottom-up effects on higher trophic levels. However, bird subsidies can also promote soil acidification, contaminant accumulation, plant damage, and eutrophication. Because birds vary in their diet, size, life history, and behavior, declines in diversity can trigger uneven and cascading ecosystem effects. Human-driven changes in bird abundance, distribution, movement, and nutrition are modifying and diminishing avian-mediated biogeochemical processes across the biosphere, with potential consequences for ecosystem fertility, productivity, functional connectivity, and carbon storage. Nevertheless, opportunities remain to harness bird biogeochemistry in ecological restoration to revitalize Earth's natural nutrient networks.

Article.Title: Navigation map has to be learned by migration-naïve Eurasian reed warblers
Article.Authors: Utvenko G.; Gorvat P.; Akhapkina A.; Pakhomov A.; Chernetsov N.
Article.Abstract: It used to be thought that young migrating birds perform their first migration using an innate 'clock-and-compass' programme that specifies the timing of onset of movement and its direction and duration, but did not require information about the bird's current position1. In classic displacement experiments, young birds continued to fly in their normal migratory direction, whereas adults were able to adjust their course after displacement2. More recent evidence, however, suggests that young birds may estimate their position and adjust their behaviour when delayed or displaced, even during their maiden flight3,4. Evidence for innate magnetic map responses in hatchling sea turtles and juvenile salmonids5 suggests that birds may also inherit magnetic positional information. We have investigated this hypothesis in the Eurasian reed warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus), a species in which compensation for physical and virtual magnetic displacement has been demonstrated in experienced migrants6,7. We used migration-naïve birds trapped in early autumn as juveniles and kept in captivity over winter. In spring, the birds were tested first in the natural magnetic field at Rybachy in Russia, and then under a virtual magnetic displacement to Keele, UK. Under the virtual magnetic displacement, the birds did not change their orientation as expected if they possessed a magnetic map. We found no evidence that migration-naïve Eurasian reed warblers use a functional innate magnetic map under the conditions of our experiment. In this species, the first migration is guided primarily by an inherited compass programme, whereas a functional magnetic map develops through migratory experience.

Article.Title: Ecosystem engineering, regime shifts and the rise of animals
Article.Authors: Darroch S.; Casey M.; Clapham M.; Contreras D.; Cover Z.; Craffey M.; Cribb A.; Duijnstee I.; Gearty W.; Gibson B.; Gotelli N.; Hayes R.; Hull P.; Ibarra D.; Lee J.; Looy C.; Muddiman B.; Shupinski A.; Sjosten S.; Smith F.; Stigall A.; Tingle K.; Tomé C.; Turk K.; Villaseñor A.
Article.Abstract: The term 'ecosystem engineering' refers to biotic processes that modulate the availability of resources to other species. These processes thus modify, maintain or create habitats and impact the abundance and diversity of species within ecosystems. In turn, the study of ecosystem engineering in the fossil record is leading to a re-evaluation of the influence of organisms on the deep-time evolution of Earth-system structure and function. With this comes a growing recognition that biological forces may be key drivers of major transitions in Earth history. There are two crucial questions: first, have new ecosystem engineering processes emerged randomly throughout geologic time, or are they clustered? Second, to what extent has their emergence driven episodes of evolutionary radiation or extinction? Here, we address these questions through the lens of the Ediacaran-Cambrian transition (∼575-530 million years ago) - an interval that witnessed the rapid rise of animals, following nearly four billion years of microbial dominance. We propose that an engineering regime shift occurred in the late Ediacaran that gave rise to new rules of community assembly, new ecological niches, and altered macroevolutionary trajectories. We argue that the recognition of ecosystem engineering regime shifts may help us not only to understand other key intervals in the Phanerozoic, but also to project the future of ecosystems under human influence.

Article.Title: Locomotor kinematics and head stabilization in rolling snakes
Article.Authors: Kojima Y.; Fukuyama I.; Hossman M.; Kaliang C.; Nishikawa K.
Article.Abstract: Morphology constrains the strategies available to organisms and their functional capacities. A striking example is the absence of wheels and the rarity of rolling locomotion across the animal kingdom1,2. Although rolling can confer high speed, it poses a fundamental mechanical challenge, as body rotation destabilizes the head and disrupts sensory-guided adjustment, particularly at high speeds. Here we report a behavioral solution to this problem: our video analyses show that dwarf reed snakes (Pseudorabdion) stabilize their head during dynamic rotational motion of the posterior body by using precisely coordinated body movements. This acrobatic behavior enables fast and controlled rolling locomotion that would otherwise be impossible, illustrating how behavioral innovation can circumvent deep morphological constraints and expand the capacities of animals.

Article.Title: Plant evolution: How duckweeds became so small
Article.Authors: Mateo-Elizalde C.; Ernst E.; Martienssen R.
Article.Abstract: Duckweeds are highly reduced flowering plants with a simplified body plan. A new study reveals that the duckweed frond retains ancestral organ identities despite compression and fusion. Together with previous evidence of root loss, these findings highlight distinct evolutionary routes to plant miniaturization.

Article.Title: Crop engineering: Plant genes tied to the weather

Article.Abstract: Coupling of a late blight disease resistance gene to a humidity-responsive cis-element in potato achieves resistance under high-humidity conditions that favor disease. This strategy sidesteps the yield penalties associated with constitutive resistance gene expression.

Article.Title: Tectonics, geomorphology and biodiversity
Article.Authors: Pellissier L.; Willett S.
Article.Abstract: The global distribution of biodiversity broadly follows latitude and climate with regions of high species richness in the tropics and environments rich in energy, water and other factors conducive to life. However, superimposed on the correlation with climate is a correspondence between biodiversity and physical geography. High biodiversity is also associated with mountain systems. The inference is that topographic relief generates ecological heterogeneity through the creation of complex topography, landforms and the interaction of that topography with climate, creating temperature and rainfall gradients, geographic barriers and habitat patchiness. All of these factors create new niches for species, driving formation of new species and thus biodiversity. Mountain ranges are the product of tectonic activity where mantle convection and tectonic plate motion have deformed the surface of the Earth, uplifting crustal rock and creating rugged topography and high relief. Tectonics creates topography, but surface processes, such as mineral weathering, physical erosion by wind, water and ice, as well as sediment transport and deposition, modify that topography. The result is the complex patchwork of landscapes of the Earth's surface whose description is at the core of the field of geomorphology. There is a vast complexity to the processes within tectonics, geomorphology, ecology and evolutionary biology, and the links between the physical and biological processes are only beginning to be understood. To complicate matters, these processes are time dependent, coupled and include multiple feedbacks. Mountain ranges rise and fall. Ocean basins open and close. Moving plates and active faults displace terrains or entire continents across climatic gradients or relative to each other. Rivers and valleys may connect regions, but rivers can be redirected, providing new connections bringing species into a common competitive arena, or closing connections, leaving populations isolated and free to evolve without competitive constraints. Biodiversity emerges from this continual interplay of tectonics, geomorphology, and ecology, with Earth's surface persistently creating and erasing opportunities for life to diversify.

Article.Title: Large animal restoration and carbon storage across climate-relevant timescales
Article.Authors: Abraham A.; Roman J.; Pearson H.; le Roux E.; Kristensen J.; Malhi Y.; Duvall E.
Article.Abstract: By virtue of their size and mobility, large animals can play important roles in Earth's carbon cycle. This has led to suggestions that restoring their populations can contribute to mitigating the climate crisis through removal and storage of atmospheric carbon. However, as animals can affect both release and sequestration of carbon, understanding when, where and how much they impact climate-relevant carbon is critical for evaluating their potential to become a trustworthy climate nature-based solution. Here, we review scientific evidence for the carbon impacts of elephants and great whales - two well-studied animal groups commonly cited for climate mitigation and suggested for carbon monetization. We identify six lessons to guide future research, policy and practice: first, large animal carbon impacts vary considerably by individual, species, ecosystem and biospheric conditions, making predictions of future impacts hard and wildlife-based carbon investments high-risk; second, meaningful carbon impacts will likely take longer to manifest than the Paris Agreement's mid-century net-zero target, but wildlife restoration should nonetheless begin now to realize immediate co-benefits and potentially support longer-term climate recovery; third, current conservation remains highest priority, as loss of animals may exacerbate climate breakdown; fourth, caution is needed when incorporating wildlife into climate policy to prevent false confidence in mitigation potential or perverse outcomes; fifth, potential wildlife carbon benefits should be communicated transparently and cautiously to manage expectations; sixth, robust monitoring and validation are essential to ensure carbon sequestration is real and durable. With these lessons in mind, conservation and restoration of large animals may realize their potential to aid long-term climate recovery as well as ecological resilience and adaptation under ongoing global change.

Article.Title: The evolution of oxygen, temperature, and marine aerobic habitat for animals over the last billion years of Earth history
Article.Authors: Ashing-Giwa K.; Payne J.; Bergmann K.; Monarrez P.; Gaskell D.; Stockey R.; Sperling E.
Article.Abstract: Atmospheric and ocean oxygen levels and temperature have changed considerably over Earth history, and many of these changes coincided with similarly dramatic changes in marine life. The synergistic interaction between oxygen availability and temperature sets aerobic capacities for marine animals, determining whether a given environment is habitable. Here, we explore the relationship between oxygen, temperature and aerobic habitability across the last billion years of Earth history using a metric known as the 'metabolic index' (Φ). Idealized scenarios for oxygen-temperature trajectories indicate several distinct avenues for a concurrent transition from 'non-permissive' to 'permissive' aerobic environments at the onset of the Cambrian Period. Thereafter, the continued presence of fossils in shallow, tropical habitats sets clear constraints on oxygen-temperature combinations, suggesting that the most extreme published estimates for each are improbable. We then draw on published oxygen and temperature estimates to illustrate how these variables have controlled aerobic habitability for marine animals over the Phanerozoic. The dominance of hypoxia-tolerant faunas during the Paleozoic is explained in part by low oxygen oceans, while increasing oxygen levels in the Devonian likely led to lower extinction rates. Sharp spikes in temperature, such as during the end-Permian, led to the contraction of aerobic habitat and mass extinction, but probably also to a more temperature-tolerant modern fauna. We emphasize the need for more robust environmental records of early animal evolution and a better understanding of trade-offs in animal physiology. Finally, exciting future applications of the metabolic index to astrobiology have arisen as knowledge of extraterrestrial environmental conditions increases.

Article.Title: Astrobiology
Article.Authors: McMahon S.
Article.Abstract: Astrobiology aims not only to determine whether life exists beyond Earth but to understand how biology 'fits' into a physicochemical universe of stars and planets, including Earth itself. The field coalesced in the late twentieth century around a core of much older questions about the origin, evolution, distribution and future of life in the universe. Today, it is a rapidly advancing interdisciplinary collaboration that draws on many sources of data - from planetary missions and exoplanet surveys to field-based, experimental, computational and analytical methods in biology, geology, chemistry, physics and astronomy. A recurrent concern across many branches of astrobiology is the fuzziness of the boundaries between life and non-life as well as the difficulty of discriminating biological signals from an 'abiotic baseline'.

Article.Title: Chunking: What working memory gains and loses
Article.Authors: Xie Y.; Zhang H.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: Chunking compresses information into fewer meaningful units, reducing working memory demands. During chunking, neural representations in the prefrontal cortex exhibit reduced dimensionality and are biased toward chunk centers, suggesting lossy compression that improves overall retention while reducing precision within chunks.

Article.Title: Trace fossils
Article.Authors: Benton M.
Article.Abstract: Ichnology (from the ancient Greek ichnos, a footprint or track) is the study of ichnofossils, or trace fossils. These are all the fossils that cannot be called 'body fossils' (skeletons, shells, preserved bodies and body parts). Trace fossils are typically tracks, trails or burrows, and they provide information on ancient environments and ancient behaviour. Ichnologists and palaeobiologists can identify whether a suite of trace fossils was produced in an ancient desert or on the deep abyssal ocean floor. Even more startling is that a trackway of dinosaur footprints can reveal the animal's speed, or even a behavioural shift like walking to the edge of a lake and then leaping in and swimming away.

Article.Title: Jiayang Li
Article.Authors: Li J.
Article.Abstract: Jiayang Li received his master's degree from the Institute of Genetics (now the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology, IGDB), Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) in 1984 and his PhD from Brandeis University in 1991. He subsequently undertook postdoctoral research on plant molecular genetics at the Boyce Thompson Institute for Plant Research at Cornell University. He has been a Professor at IGDB since 1994, served as Vice President of CAS (2003-2011) and President of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (2011-2016), and has been Director General of the Yazhouwan National Laboratory since 2022. His research focuses on the molecular basis of complex traits regulating high yield, superior quality, and strong resilience, and breeding elite rice varieties by rational design. He has been elected as a member or associate member of CAS (2001), the World Academy of Sciences (TWAS; 2004), the US National Academy of Sciences (NAS; 2011), the German Academy of Sciences (2012), and the UK Royal Society (2015).

Article.Title: Gaia with a thousand faces
Article.Authors: Maderspacher F.
Article.Abstract: Life and Earth are intimately connected — a connection we have long overlooked at our peril. It is the core of the ‘ Gaia hypothesis' — the notion that Life and Earth act as a unit to self-regulate planetary conditions so they remain favorable for life's persistence. A shape-shifting, amorphous entity, straddling scientific disciplines and audiences, the Gaia hypothesis has a complex history: disdained in some scientific disciplines, foundational in others and enthusiastically endorsed further afield. Lately, renewed scientific interest and a more consilient view of Gaia is emerging, precipitated not least by the planetary polycrisis. Florian Maderspacher on Gaia 's many guises.

Article.Title: Interbacterial competition triggers stress-induced CRISPR immunity against bacteriophages
Article.Authors: Custodio R.; Martignoni M.; Zhu W.; Kuske R.; Alseth E.; Moura-Alves P.; Brown S.; Westra E.
Article.Abstract: Bacteria-phage interactions are often studied in relatively simple experimental systems involving a single bacterial strain infected by a single phage.1 In natural environments, however, bacteria typically inhabit complex multispecies communities where species compete for limited resources and ecological niches.2,3,4 Recent studies show that the microbial community context can have profound effects on the evolution of phage resistance.5 For example, Pseudomonas aeruginosa evolves phage resistance primarily through receptor loss when grown in isolation but switches to CRISPR-based immunity in the presence of bacterial competitors.6,7 Previous work showed that interspecies competition can favor CRISPR-immune bacteria over surface mutants after phage resistance has evolved.6 However, it remains unknown whether competition also alters the initial generation of CRISPR immunity by changing CRISPR-Cas expression and spacer acquisition before selection among resistance phenotypes occurs. Here, we show that interbacterial competition can trigger CRISPR-Cas activation and adaptation in P. aeruginosa. When co-cultured with Acinetobacter baumannii, P. aeruginosa exhibited markedly increased expression of CRISPR-Cas genes and a higher frequency of new spacer acquisition, whereas no such induction occurred in monoculture or mixed communities lacking A. baumannii. This upregulation was associated with markers of DNA damage and stress signaling, indicating that competition-induced stress primes the bacterial adaptive immune response. These findings identify interbacterial antagonism as an ecological and physiological trigger for CRISPR activation, linking competitive interactions to enhanced antiphage defense. More broadly, our results suggest that bacteria sense and respond to competitive stress in complex microbial communities by increasing the generation of more adapted genotypes.

Article.Title: Dynamic roles of embryonic glial cells in octopus brain development
Article.Authors: Lassnig M.; Geslain E.; Nguyen B.; Abaffyová D.; Styfhals R.; Spanier K.; Patel A.; Gattamraju A.; Poovathingal S.; Wojno M.; Van Dijck M.; Almansa E.; Rogers T.; Simakov O.; Accorsi A.; Seuntjens E.
Article.Abstract: Coleoid cephalopods, such as octopus, squid, and cuttlefish, have evolved remarkably large nervous systems with neuron numbers comparable to those of small mammals. Despite this, little is known about how these nervous systems develop, which genetic programs drive the formation and diversification of their neural cells, and what factors contribute to evolutionary brain expansion. This study combined single-cell multi-omics with spatial expression analysis to uncover the cell types and the regulatory mechanisms underlying nervous system development and evolution in Octopus vulgaris. We discovered an early embryonic glial cell population that is distinct from neurogenic progenitors and defined by orphan nuclear receptor 4a (nr4a), distal-less homeobox (dlx), and prospero homeobox (pros) regulons. Their spatial distribution and dynamic transcriptional profile during embryogenesis indicated that these cells might orchestrate cell migration, axon guidance, and brain patterning before expressing neuronal markers or differentiating into mature glia. Comparison of embryonic glial transcriptional signatures across two cephalopods, a gastropod, and Drosophila revealed shared expression of nr4a, dlx, and pros in mollusks, while embryonic glia in Drosophila expressed pros, dlx, repo, ttk, and gcm but not nr4a. Intriguingly, the overall gene expression profile of cephalopod embryonic glia has diverged from that of Pomacea canaliculata (golden apple snail), whose glia do not express guidance or patterning genes. Together, these findings identified a conserved embryonic glial cell type in mollusks that might have acquired new functions in coleoid cephalopods to organize neuronal migration and wiring in their expanded brain.

Article.Title: Integration of hydrogen peroxide sensing and detoxification by the C. elegans nervous system
Article.Authors: Xu Y.; Gangadharan S.; Seyedolmohadesin M.; Gebeyaw E.; Flack M.; Fulton A.; Ashih C.; Duncan M.; Zelich M.; Liu J.; Torkashvand M.; Shaw D.; Gusarova K.; Macwan M.; Kelly A.; Beslic I.; Sood A.; Liu O.; Scholz M.; Venkatachalam V.; Apfeld J.
Article.Abstract: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is the most common reactive chemical threat organisms face. Here, we map the neural circuit that drives chemotactic escape from environmental H2O2 in the nematode C. elegans. Twenty-four neuron classes with sensory endings at the mouth and nose respond to H2O2, with dynamics encoding stimulus intensity and exposure history. Sensing begins when H2O2 oxidizes the peroxidatic and resolving cysteines of the cytosolic peroxiredoxin PRDX-2, which relays this oxidative signal to cysteines on the LITE-1 and GUR-3 ion channels, triggering calcium influx in sensory neurons that drive escape. Most of these neurons release glutamate to drive H2O2-dependent excitation of AIA interneurons, whereas others signal through non-glutamatergic routes. Thus, the C. elegans nervous system monitors H2O2-induced changes in the intracellular H2O2-detoxification machinery and relays them to interneurons driving organism-wide escape. This raises the possibility that changes in neuronal activity in aging and neurodegenerative diseases arise from altered peroxiredoxin-mediated H2O2 signaling rather than primarily from direct macromolecular damage by H2O2.

Article.Title: Selective control of course correction over long timescales in the Drosophila central complex
Article.Authors: Crown A.; Wu A.; Hofflander L.; Barnea G.
Article.Abstract: The insect central complex governs intricate navigational behaviors. One key region of the central complex, the fan-shaped body (FB), is where movement decisions are computed during goal-directed behaviors. However, our knowledge of when FB circuits are deployed is limited, and the FB has only been directly implicated in a few, narrowly defined behaviors. Here, we demonstrate that FB circuits affect course-correcting movements that, over long timescales, align the fly's heading with the perceived direction of optic flow. Silencing a major input neuronal population to the FB, the PFNd neurons, abolishes this behavior while leaving certain reflexive turning behaviors intact. Further, introduction of a fictive error signal in either the PFNd or PFNa neurons via optogenetic activation reveals that they are sufficient to affect the forward movement of the fly while slightly biasing its heading direction. We propose a model whereby the fly recruits the circuitry of the central complex to selectively influence features of movement that emerge over long timescales.

Article.Title: Top-down inferior colliculus signals engage unipolar brush cell circuits in the dorsal cochlear nucleus of the mouse auditory system
Article.Authors: Candler C.; Peña G.; Witteveen I.; Murphy S.; Whittaker K.; Poole O.; Balmer T.
Article.Abstract: Sensory systems comprise ascending pathways that convey information from the sense organs and descending pathways that provide feedback and contextual signals to guide sensory processing. How top-down signals are integrated at early stages to improve sensory function remains poorly understood. The dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) is a cerebellum-like circuit proposed to perform adaptive filtering, including suppression of self-generated sounds. A major question is how sound-frequency-specific top-down information is processed by the DCN, since many top-down inputs target granule cells whose axons span the tonotopic axis and are unlikely to maintain frequency-specific signals. Here, we characterize neurons in the inferior colliculus that provide descending input to DCN. We show that among their targets are unipolar brush cells (UBCs) that distribute and transform descending signals directly to principal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in a circuit that bypasses granule cells. In vivo activation of UBCs attenuated auditory responses in awake mice. Together, these findings identify a circuit through which top-down signals from IC could influence early auditory processing and potentially guide adaptive filtering in the DCN.

Article.Title: Females shape hunting of vertebrates in wild bonobos
Article.Authors: Hohmann G.; Bessone M.; Balduccio N.; Decina F.; Deville T.; Pashchevskaya S.; Soliday V.; Stewart K.; Fruth B.
Article.Abstract: Hunting and meat consumption are widely considered key drivers of human evolution, and hypotheses about their origins draw on comparisons with our closest living relatives, chimpanzees and bonobos. These comparisons typically set up a behavioral dichotomy in which chimpanzees are characterized by cooperative hunting of arboreal primates by male-dominated parties, whereas bonobo hunts are thought to involve the opportunistic targeting of terrestrial ungulates, primarily by individual females.1,2,3 Observations from two habituated bonobo communities at LuiKotale covering 10 years challenge this dichotomy. LuiKotale bonobos hunted both terrestrial ungulates (42%) and arboreal primates (43% of vertebrate prey), with red colobus monkeys comprising the majority of primate prey (77%). Males and females hunted arboreal primates at similar rates, and females accounted for most non-primate captures. Female age affected the hunting frequency of primates and ungulates, with the former being biased to younger and the latter to older females. The prominent role of female bonobos in hunting supports predictions that relate hunting activity to intersexual dominance relations rather than risk aversion, with the dominant sex being more active. Comparing data from neighboring communities revealed differences and suggests that social and environmental parameters affect prey choice by each community in different ways. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that chimpanzee-like, male-biased hunting represents the ancestral condition. They highlight the contribution of females to obtaining vertebrate prey, call for a reassessment of the role of females in hunting and meat sharing, and by extension, the framing of models of early hominin subsistence and social organization.

Article.Title: A language-model approach to species distribution reveals alternative stable states
Article.Authors: Coulon N.; Servajean M.; Thomazo J.; Flandrin U.; Hautecoeur C.; Stuart-Smith R.; Joly A.; Mouillot D.
Article.Abstract: Ecological communities are reorganizing rapidly under accelerating global change, yet predicting how species assemble, persist, or collapse remains a major challenge.1,2,3,4 Most species distribution models treat species as independent entities, overlooking the dependencies that structure ecological communities. Here, we introduce a language-model-inspired approach5,6 to species distribution that generates ecological communities sequentially, predicting each species and its biomass conditional on previously assembled species. Trained on ∼27,000 reef fish surveys,7 the generative framework reveals multiple coherent community configurations emerging under identical environmental conditions.8,9 For instance, the model can generate both coral-associated and macroalgal-associated fish communities, consistent with alternative ecological regimes described in these ecosystems. The model also uncovers a hierarchy of emergent species positions within the learned dependency structure, including core species strongly associated with particular environmental conditions, bridging species linking alternative configurations, and satellite species occupying more peripheral positions. Despite this richer representation of ecological communities, the model also improves predictions of species occurrence and biomass relative to a species-by-species machine-learning baseline (XGBoost10) and a multispecies deep-learning baseline (MLP11). Together, these results show that ecological communities can be learned and generated as a structured syntax, from which multistability, directional assembly patterns, and hierarchical species positions naturally emerge.

Article.Title: Plant synergid embryonic potential is unlocked following egg cell collapse
Article.Authors: Xiong H.; Wang W.; Sun M.
Article.Abstract: Cell-cell communication is indispensable for cell specification and differentiation throughout plant reproduction. The egg cell and its sister synergid cell have long been considered closely coordinated partners during fertilization, yet the nature of this interplay and their specific roles remain unclear. Here, we show that synergid cells could acquire the competence to initiate cell division for embryogenesis following egg cell collapse. Unlike the traditional view, synergid cells appear to take over the egg cell role without undergoing fate conversion to adopt the egg cell identity. These findings suggest that synergid cells possess an intrinsic embryogenic potential, which is specifically unlocked upon egg cell collapse, thus enabling embryogenic initiation in the absence of a functional egg cell. Building on this discovery, we established an in planta haploid-induction system independent of conventional haploid-inducing genes. Importantly, this system also functions in tomato, a distantly related dicotyledonous crop, thus offering a broad conceptual framework for engineering haploid production across diverse plant species.

Article.Title: Dorsal forerunner cells couple epiboly movements to zebrafish notochord extension
Article.Authors: Small C.; Williams M.
Article.Abstract: Convergence and extension (C&E) cell movements promote anteroposterior axis extension and narrow both neuroectodermal and mesodermal tissues during gastrulation. Mediolateral cell intercalation is largely responsible for this morphogenetic process in vertebrates, but evidence suggests that additional cell-extrinsic forces generated by surrounding tissues contribute to the shaping of many structures. In zebrafish, for example, mechanical forces generated by the anteriorly migrating prechordal plate cooperate with tissue-autonomous cell intercalations to promote extension of the notochord. Here, we propose a novel model for notochord morphogenesis by which epiboly forces within the enveloping layer are transmitted to the posterior end of the notochord via a cluster of dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs) that physically links the two. We found that scattering or absence of DFCs caused by loss of crb2a or sox32, respectively, reduces notochord C&E and exacerbates axis extension defects in planar cell polarity signaling-deficient embryos. Using an automated image segmentation and cell shape analysis pipeline, we show that cells within the posterior notochord fail to properly elongate when DFCs are scattered or absent. Finally, we demonstrate that the loss of crb2a and sox32 fails to disrupt C&E of zebrafish embryonic explants in which no epiboly occurs and all extension is driven by cell-intrinsic behaviors. Together, these findings support a model in which DFCs facilitate mechanical coupling of the enveloping layer to the posterior notochord during epiboly to ensure its robust morphogenesis during gastrulation.

Article.Title: Alerting acoustic stimuli enhance the internal representation of head direction
Article.Authors: Hofmann F.; Blanco-Hernández E.; Balsamo G.; Hage S.; Burgalossi A.; Preston-Ferrer P.
Article.Abstract: Animals rapidly execute goal-directed spatial behaviors in response to threats, yet how alerting cues engage spatial representations remains unknown. Here, we tested whether head direction (HD) neurons-key components of the brain's navigation system-are recruited by alerting stimuli. We recorded thalamic and cortical HD cells in head-fixed mice during alerting acoustic stimuli while monitoring arousal via pupillometry and facial motion. Identified HD cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus exhibited ectopic axons and projections to the thalamic reticular nucleus. These cells responded to artificial and natural alerting sounds, with frequency tuning closely matching facial motion patterns. Thalamic responses comprised fast and slow components, whereas cortical responses in the dorsal presubiculum were sparser and dominated by the slow component. In the thalamus, the fast component was independent of HD tuning, whereas the slow component was selectively amplified by alerting stimuli. This gain modulation enhanced HD coding, with decoding accuracy scaling with facial motion. Together, these findings identify the thalamocortical HD system as a non-canonical auditory pathway relaying alerting signals to spatial navigation circuits, providing a mechanism by which alerting stimuli sharpen the internal compass for goal-directed behaviors.

Article.Title: A kleptomyiophilous orchid exploits milichiid flies through mimicry of common pentatomoid bugs with high levels of toxicity
Article.Authors: Liu M.; Hu A.; Li T.; Chen J.; Mochizuki K.; Siu T.; Hau B.; Johnson S.; Gale S.
Article.Abstract: To attract pollinators, mimetic flowers imitate the visual and olfactory cues that their pollinators use when responding to models.1,2 However, it is unclear which processes influence the mimicry of particular models. One possibility is that selection favors mimicry of models that act as "magnet species" by attracting large numbers of potential pollinators.1,3,4,5 According to this hypothesis, models should be highly common, even if they are not the most attractive resources. This may apply to kleptomyiophilous flowers that exploit kleptoparasitic flies by imitating injured insects.6,7,8,9,10 In this form of mimicry, the injured insect models would be highly common, even if they emit toxic defensive volatiles that could impede pollinator activities.11,12 We report that the eastern ecotype of Bulbophyllum claviforme attracts a specific kleptoparasitic milichiid pollinator Phyllomyza sp. 1. Orchid floral scent is similar to (E)-2-decenal-dominated emissions of multiple pentatomoid bugs in the families Pentatomidae, Scutelleridae, Plataspidae, and Acanthosomatidae. Bioassays suggest that undecane, (E)-2-decenal and (E)-2-decenyl acetate are critical for attraction. Three (E)-2-alkenals, namely (E)-2-hexenal, (E)-2-octenal, and (E)-2-decenal, are both toxic and attractive to Phyllomyza sp. 1, with the toxicity of dominant (E)-2-alkenals negatively correlated to attractiveness. The orchid paradoxically appears to mimic pentatomoids that are less attractive due to higher toxicity. Selection may have favored mimicry of these bugs because (E)-2-decenal is emitted by a wide range of species, representing 68% of the pentatomoid species sampled. Our findings are congruent with the hypothesis that magnet species effects on pollinator abundance are important for the evolution of floral mimicry.

Article.Title: Allelic variation in OsATG3 enhances nitrogen-responsive tillering to sustain rice productivity
Article.Authors: Hu Z.; Li C.; Shen H.; Guo Y.; Xing R.; Gao X.; Yuan Y.; Li H.; Liu H.; Han X.; Cheng M.; Wang Y.; Shen Z.; Xue Y.; Zhong C.; Guo M.; Li Y.; Chen R.; Yang Y.; Sun S.; Zhou Y.; Liang G.; Gu M.; Fu X.; Yan C.
Article.Abstract: Nitrogen (N) deficiency constrains crop productivity by limiting shoot growth, yet the adaptive mechanisms that reprogram shoot development under low N conditions remain largely elusive. OsATG3 functions as an essential autophagy component and promotes selective degradation of IDEAL PLANT ARCHITECTURE1 (IPA1) via OsATG8d-mediated autophagy in shoot apices, thereby enhancing N-responsive tillering. Natural variation in the promoter of OsATG3 modulates its transcriptional activity and underlies the adaptive range of tiller number under low N conditions. The elite haplotype OsATG3-H enhances both tillering and grain yield under N-limited supply and appears to contribute to geographical adaptation both in O. sativa and O. glaberrima. Our findings uncover a genetic and molecular mechanism that couples N deficiency to shoot developmental plasticity, providing a promising target for sustainable rice breeding with reduced fertilizer input.

Article.Title: Testing neurobiological models of reward/incentive sensitization in the continuation of alcohol use disorder (AUD) symptoms in young adults with AUD: A four-year longitudinal study
Article.Authors: King A.; Nordgren R.; Cao D.; Wellendorf C.; Fridberg D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains an urgent public health problem. Alcohol response phenotype may be an important factor underlying vulnerability to and progression of AUD. This study examined the prospective association between acute alcohol responses and continued or remitted AUD over time in young adults with AUD. This sample was N = 101 AUD participants (M age =27.1 ± 4.0 SD yrs) comprising the third cohort of the Chicago Social Drinking Project. They completed two beverage challenge laboratory sessions (0.8 g/kg fixed-dose alcohol vs . placebo) and four years of follow-up to ascertain future AUD symptoms, drinking behaviors, and consequences. Retention was high with an overall 99.2% follow-up rate. Analyses identified three AUD trajectory subgroups over follow-up including a high AUD trajectory subgroup ( n = 37), a medium AUD trajectory subgroup ( n = 48), and a low AUD trajectory subgroup ( n = 16). Generalized estimating equations showed that greater sensitivity to alcohol’s pleasurable effects, including stimulation and hedonic and motivational reward (liking and wanting, respectively) predicted more AUD symptoms over follow-up ( p s<0.001) and were positively associated with AUD trajectory subgroups. However, sedation, heart rate, and cortisol response to alcohol were not significantly associated with AUD trajectory subgroups. In sum, greater alcohol stimulation, liking, and wanting prospectively predicted the continuation and increasing severity of AUD over a four-year period. The findings challenge theoretical models emphasizing reward deficit and global tolerance in addiction and support the role of positive reinforcement, indexed by sensitivity to alcohol’s pleasurable effects, as an important factor in AUD persistence. Article.Title: A living systematic review, meta-analysis, and open data resource of trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD
Article.Authors: Sevchik B.; Singleton S.; Lahey A.; Cuijpers P.; Harrer M.; Jones M.; Nayak S.; Strain E.; Vandekar S.; Yaden D.; Dworkin R.; Scott J.; Satterthwaite T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) has emerged as a potential treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, rapidly changing evidence in a fast-moving field can be challenging to integrate. Here, we present a living systematic review and open-data meta-analytic resource on MDMA treatment for PTSD. In this initial release, 6 randomized controlled trials comprising 286 participants are included in the database. All six studies included in the review to date are sponsored by the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS). Our primary model uses inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis of standardized mean differences on primary outcomes of PTSD. Compared to control conditions, MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) showed a greater reduction in PTSD symptoms (Hedges’ g = −0.71). Meta-regressions on dosing variables were explored. Treatment with MDMA-AT as compared to placebo also resulted in higher response (risk ratio [ RR ] = 1.35) and remission ( RR = 2.25) rates. Most studies included in the database had a low risk of bias according to Cochrane guidelines, though these fail to capture pertinent challenges in the field such as expectancy, functional unblinding, potential issues with study conduct, and safety. The current findings were assigned an overall low certainty rating using the GRADE approach. Together, this systematic review and meta-analysis suggests that MDMA-AT results in short-term decreases in PTSD symptoms across studies to date. This living systematic review, meta-analysis, database, and online dashboard ( sypres.io ) will continue to be updated as evidence emerges, providing a valuable, open, and transparent resource for researchers in a rapidly evolving field.

Article.Title: Modulation of the noradrenergic system using transcranial ultrasonic stimulation targeted to the brainstem locus coeruleus in awake mice
Article.Authors: Lescrauwaet E.; Raedt R.; Plovie T.; Caestecker S.; Stieve B.; Neyt S.; Tarnaud T.; Tanghe E.; Murphy K.; Carrette E.; Boon P.; Vonck K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a novel neuromodulation technique that can be used to non-invasively target the locus coeruleus (LC). The LC provides the majority of noradrenergic input to the brain and has been implicated in several neurological and psychiatric disorders. Before translation to human studies, establishing a dose-response relationship requires systematic characterization of two distinct effects: (1) the influence of stimulation protocol variations on norepinephrine (NE) release in LC target structures, and (2) the broader brain and bodily effects of LC-targeted TUS. We used fiber photometry to measure TUS-induced activation of LC neurons and release of NE in one of its major projection areas, the hippocampus. To evaluate widespread functional effects, we investigated changes in [ 18 F]FDG uptake in the brain and body in response to LC-targeted TUS using small-animal PET imaging. Five-second trains of TUS resulted in intracellular calcium level increases in the LC, accompanied by a biphasic change in NE levels in the hippocampus and LC, i.e., an initial rise followed by a transient decrease. The same TUS protocol showed a decrease in [ 18 F]FDG uptake across the brain and a strong increase in [ 18 F]FDG uptake in brown adipose tissue. If TUS was prolonged to 30 s the initial biphasic change in hippocampal NE levels was followed by a secondary increase that persisted throughout the remainder of the stimulation period. This study provides the first demonstration that TUS can modulate the LC–NE system in awake mice. Adjusting the stimulation protocol resulted in distinct patterns of hippocampal NE release, highlighting the therapeutic potential of LC-targeted TUS as distinct stimulation protocols may differentially restore disrupted NE levels across disorders. PET imaging further revealed engagement of both central and peripheral systems, emphasizing the broad physiological reach of this approach.

Article.Title: BLA kappa opioid receptor inputs to the BNST mediate social stress-induced increases in alcohol drinking
Article.Authors: Paliarin F.; Doré E.; Mirza S.; Finlay L.; Weiser E.; Panthagani P.; Nguyen T.; Duplantis C.; Basavanhalli S.; Guillory S.; Messing R.; Pomrenze M.; Maiya R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aversive social experiences can increase alcohol consumption and precipitate relapse during abstinence. Individuals who drink to alleviate social stress are at a heightened risk for developing an alcohol use disorder (AUD). In rodents, repeated social defeat stress (SDS) enhances motivation to consume alcohol, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of dynorphin/kappa opioid receptor (Dyn/KOR) signaling in regulating stress-induced increases in alcohol consumption. We show that repeated SDS increased alcohol intake and preference in both sexes, effects that were attenuated by systemic administration of the KOR antagonist norBNI or local administration of norBNI into the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST). Chemogenetic activation of basolateral amygdala (BLA) KOR-expressing neurons and their projections to the BNST, as well as knockdown of KORs in the BLA, attenuated increased alcohol consumption following SDS. At the molecular level, SDS increased Pdyn mRNA expression and selectively activated BNST-projecting dynorphin neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus. Together, these findings support a working model where Dyn/KOR modulation of the BLA–BNST pathway is critical for increased alcohol drinking induced by social stress, while pointing to the DRN as a candidate upstream source of Dyn. Our results highlight Dyn/KOR systems as a promising therapeutic target for comorbid stress-related pathology and AUD.

Article.Title: ICER-Controlled inhibitory plasticity of amygdala engram neurons regulates fear memory precision
Article.Authors: Lee H.; Lee S.; Yoo T.; Nghi T.; Truong L.; Ryu G.; Park J.; Park S.; Kim J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Fear discrimination—the ability to distinguish threatening stimuli from non-threatening ones—is an essential adaptive behavior, yet the neural mechanisms underlying individual differences in discrimination precision remain unclear. Here, we show that parvalbumin-positive interneuron (PV-IN)-mediated feedforward inhibition to fear engram neurons (ENs) in the lateral amygdala is selectively enhanced following auditory fear conditioning, driven by increased postsynaptic expression of α1 subunit (Gabra1)-containing GABA A receptors. Disruption of PV-IN activity during fear retrieval—via optogenetic or chemogenetic inhibition—or selective induction of inhibitory long-term depression at PV → EN synapses impaired fear discrimination, increasing freezing to novel tones while sparing responses to the conditioned stimulus. Mechanistically, we identify inducible cAMP early repressor (ICER) as a transcriptional regulator that limits inhibitory plasticity by downregulating Gabra1 expression, thereby promoting fear generalization. These findings establish a previously unrecognized form of inhibitory synaptic plasticity that governs the precision of fear memory and suggest potential therapeutic targets for maladaptive fear overgeneralization in disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder.

Article.Title: Multiple-context extinction strengthens fear suppression through hippocampal dopamine D2R-dependent memory updating
Article.Authors: Hammerman E.; Penna S.; Gonzalez S.; Patel S.; Roebuck C.; Lock E.; Desmond C.; Fukunaga Y.; Maloy G.; Cazares V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Extinction learning, which underlies exposure therapy, generates safety memories that are often context-dependent, limiting their persistence and generalization. Although varying contextual cues during extinction has been proposed to strengthen safety learning, the neural mechanisms remain unknown. Dual Fos-TRAP activity mapping revealed differential recruitment of the fear conditioning-tagged cells following MCFE and identified the hippocampus as a key node supporting MCFE. Consistent with this, chemogenetic silencing of dorsal, but not ventral, hippocampus selectively impaired extinction acquisition during MCFE and abolished its behavioral advantage. Likewise, local blockade of dopamine D2-, but not D1-like, receptors in the dorsal hippocampus eliminated the enhancement in extinction acquisition produced by MCFE. Together, these findings demonstrate that contextual variation strengthens and generalizes extinction learning through dorsal hippocampal dopamine D2-like receptor-dependent memory updating, identifying a neural mechanism through which behavioral modifications of exposure therapy can improve fear suppression.

Article.Title: Reduced prefrontal total choline MRS levels characterize the neurodevelopmental phenotype of bipolar disorder
Article.Authors: Petitgas L.; Belzeaux R.; Sein J.; Anton J.; Neilson S.; Havard D.; Samalin L.; Chassain C.; Auzias G.; Deruelle C.; Lefrere A.
Article.Abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity, motivating efforts to identify biologically grounded subtypes such as the recently defined neurodevelopmental phenotype (NDP). These associations were not accounted by traditional diagnostic subtypes (BD-I vs BD-II). Moreover, sensitivity analyses performed using an independent quantification pipeline (Osprey) confirmed the association between higher NDP load and lower tCho concentrations in the left PFC, whereas associations involving glutamatergic metabolites and tNAA were not replicated after adjustment for covariates. These findings provide the first neurochemical evidence linking NDP load to prefrontal metabolites and highlight choline pathways as a biologically coherent marker of the developmental dimension of BD.

Article.Title: High-resolution paleobiome reconstructions highlight ecological and historical dynamics underpinning global terrestrial vertebrate diversity
Article.Authors: Skeels A.; Rogger J.; Cardillo M.; Farnsworth A.; Lunt D.; Karger D.
Article.Abstract: Past climate change has repeatedly reshaped Earth’s biomes, yet how their expansion and contraction influence biodiversity patterns through time remains unclear. Competing hypotheses propose that either historical biome area has a strong influence on diversity, or that biodiversity responds rapidly to environmental change, such that present-day biome area and energy are sufficient to explain diversity patterns. Progress in testing these ideas has been limited by sparse and inconsistent proxy data and the coarse resolution of existing paleoclimate models. Here, we reconstructed global biome histories for the Cenozoic (66–0 Ma) by downscaling five different paleoclimate simulations. Estimates of change in biome area through time were generally consistent among alternative climate models and with the empirical proxy record. Accounting for variation among models, we found that present-day area and energy were consistently better predictors of vertebrate diversity than historical measures. These findings suggest biodiversity tracks the ecological limits set by shifting biomes, leaving sparse legacy of past dynamics. Our results highlight the importance of integrating multiple paleoclimate reconstructions when assessing the historical drivers of biodiversity.

Article.Title: A cortical semantic map integrates fractions and integers in the human brain
Article.Authors: Valério D.; Debray S.; Karami A.; Cauté M.; Gravel N.; Dehaene S.
Article.Abstract: How does the human brain represent the meaning of abstract symbols? Some theories postulate the existence of semantic spaces where concepts occupy positions that reflect their conceptual relationships. In the number domain, psychological evidence suggests that integers are represented along a mental number line which, with education, integrates higher-level number concepts such as fractions. To test this hypothesis, we recorded whole-brain 7T fMRI responses to integer and fraction symbols during an active magnitude comparison task designed to engage magnitude processing. Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.

Article.Title: Host–virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation
Article.Authors: Belyi A.; Du Y.; Wilson A.; Longdon B.; Jiggins F.
Article.Abstract: Host–parasite coevolution is expected to generate strong selection for resistance and infectivity that has the potential to erode genetic variation. Despite this, natural populations often retain extensive genetic variation in these traits. Genotype-by-genotype interactions on fitness can generate negative frequency-dependent selection, which helps maintain this variation by preventing any host or pathogen genotype from retaining a permanent advantage. Because these interactions place genetic variance in the interaction term rather than in additive differences among hosts or pathogens, that variance is masked from directional selection and can remain ‘cryptic’. Here we combine coevolutionary modelling with large‑scale experimental infection assays to quantify how host-pathogen interactions structure fitness variance in a vertically transmitted virus system, Drosophila melanogaster and sigma virus. Simulations show that coevolution typically erodes additive genetic variance in host and pathogen fitness, concentrating variance in host-virus interaction terms. Consistent with these predictions, experiments spanning 90 host-virus genotype combinations reveal that transmission, viral load, and virulence are overwhelmingly governed by host-virus genetic interactions rather than host or virus main effects. As a result, neither host resistance alleles nor viral genotypes confer consistently higher fitness across genetic backgrounds. Interactions tend to be sex‑specific, further limiting heritable fitness variation. Our results demonstrate that coevolution can substantially mask heritable genetic variation from directional selection by rendering fitness context-dependent. This extensive cryptic genetic variation may be revealed either when ecological or evolutionary conditions shift, or when the process of coevolution itself alters the direction of selection. This demonstrates the need to account for genotype-specific interactions when forecasting evolutionary responses.

Article.Title: A macrophage-targeted TIMD4 Peptide-Nanoparticle attenuates colitis symptoms and monocyte recruitment in a mouse model
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Wang Y.; Yu R.; Liu K.; Zheng D.; Wang B.; Chang Y.; Liu B.; Yue X.; Wu Z.; Li C.; Liang X.; Ma C.; Liu G.; Li J.; Xu L.; Gao L.
Article.Abstract: Macrophages play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing molecule 4 (TIMD4) is involved in the regulation of tissue-resident macrophages. TIMD4 expression is elevated in colonic tissues from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, but its role in IBD pathogenesis remains unclear. In this study, we found that Timd4 deficiency aggravated DSS-induced colitis, accompanied by increased infiltration of monocytes into the colonic tissues. Treatment with a CCR2 antagonist attenuated colonic inflammation and reduced monocyte infiltration into colonic tissues in Timd4 KO mice. Mechanistically, in vitro studies revealed that TIMD4 stabilized the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex via its intracellular domain, thereby activating the AMPK pathway and suppressing NF-κB-dependent chemokine production in macrophages. Based on these findings, we designed a TIMD4-derived peptide and developed a macrophage-targeted nanoparticle system (T4 (365–378) ‑NPs). Treatment with T4 (365–378) -NPs reduced P65 phosphorylation and attenuated DSS-induced colitis in mice. Treatment with either T4 (365–378) -NPs or the CCR2 antagonist attenuated DSS-induced colitis, and no statistically significant differences in the assessed outcomes were detected between the two groups. Administration of T4 (365–378) -NPs before DSS exposure also attenuated subsequent colitis. Furthermore, combining the T4 (365–378) ‑NPs with anti-α4β7 or anti-TNF-α antibodies produced greater improvements than either monotherapy in the DSS-induced colitis model. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of TIMD4-derived peptide delivery as a potential therapeutic approach for intestinal inflammation.

Article.Title: Non-adaptive evolutionary forces predominantly shape nucleotide composition near human transcription start sites
Article.Authors: Qiu Y.; Hebraud E.; Pouyet F.; Palazzo A.
Article.Abstract: In the human genome, mutation rates vary along genes, yet how their fine-scale structure contributes to gene evolution has remained largely unexplored. Here, we map inherited mutations at single-nucleotide resolution and uncover a striking hypermutation peak at transcription start sites (TSSs) of human protein-coding genes. This pattern is observed both in population polymorphisms and in de novo mutations from parent-offspring trios, and is dependent on transcriptional activity in testes. We also find similar hypermutation peaks at TSSs used to produce long noncoding RNAs and at intergenic RNA Polymerase II pause sites. In addition, we identify distinct mutational signatures at exon-intron boundaries and in introns. By comparing the current nucleotide content to predicted equilibrium levels, inferred from mutation and fixation rates, and by analyzing derived ancestral frequency spectrums, we detect signals that are compatible with a low level of ongoing background GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) throughout the region and ancestral elevated gBGC activity that is centered right downstream from the TSS. Using a forward-in-time simulation algorithm, we show that the current nucleotide composition surrounding the TSS of protein-coding genes is best explained by local mutation biases coupled to ongoing and ancestral patterns of gene conversions. Our simulations allow us to infer several features of these gBGC events. Overall, these findings indicate that the nucleotide composition around TSSs is largely shaped by non-adaptive forces, particularly mutation bias and gBGC.

Article.Title: Oxidative signaling thresholds shape vulnerability in the central and peripheral nervous systems
Article.Authors: Wakatsuki S.; Araki T.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegeneration is frequently associated with oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms that convert reactive oxygen species (ROS) into irreversible degenerative signals remain incompletely understood. Neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems often differ in their responses to injury, but these differences cannot be reduced to a simple contrast between weak and strong antioxidant capacity. This Essay proposes that neuronal vulnerability is shaped by multilayered signaling thresholds comprising ROS production, antioxidant and thiol buffering, redox-sensitive signal detection, molecular gating, and commitment to degeneration, survival, or repair. This framework may help explain selective neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases and identify intervention points downstream of global ROS suppression.

Article.Title: The mechanosensitive channel TMEM63B contributes to noxious heat sensation in the dorsal root ganglia
Article.Authors: Ye C.; Zang Y.; Duan G.; Chen J.; Wu D.; Wang D.; Li C.; Xu Y.; Xia T.; Gu X.; Shi Y.
Article.Abstract: In mammals, heat sensation is primarily mediated by thermosensitive channels, particularly transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. However, whether additional channels contribute to noxious heat detection remains unclear. Here, we investigated the role of the mechanosensitive cation channel TMEM63B in DRG neurons and unexpectedly discovered its involvement in noxious thermosensation rather than mechanosensation. TMEM63B was broadly expressed in DRG neurons, and its global knockout or DRG-specific conditional knockout markedly reduced heat sensitivity. Deletion of TMEM63B significantly attenuated heat-induced calcium responses and currents in DRG neurons and elevated the temperature threshold for action potential initiation. Recombinant TMEM63B exhibited moderate heat response in calcium imaging assays. Notably, in the presence of arachidonic acid, TMEM63B was strongly activated by heat, suggesting that its thermosensitivity is modulated by the membrane lipid environment. Together, these findings identify TMEM63B as a novel channel contributing to heat sensation and reveal a lipid-dependent modulation of its channel activity.

Article.Title: A broad-host-range Rhizobium rhizogenes strain enables transient expression across diverse crop species
Article.Authors: King F.; Lopez-Agudelo J.; Stephens C.; Aung M.; Ibrahim T.; Yuen E.; Chen A.; Eilmann N.; Jenkins S.; Vuolo C.; Swee Y.; Liu W.; Bruty S.; Toghani A.; Kuo C.; Lai E.; Kourelis J.; Derevnina L.; Wu C.; Bozkurt T.
Article.Abstract: Agrobacterium -mediated transient expression has revolutionised plant research, enabling numerous landmark discoveries across diverse areas of plant biology. Yet this powerful approach remains largely confined to solanaceous species, leaving most economically important crop families without a comparable rapid assay platform. Here, we show that an engineered Rhizobium rhizogenes strain, AS109, mediates efficient transient expression across diverse dicot species spanning multiple taxonomic families, consistently outperforming commonly used laboratory agrobacterial strains. Leveraging the broad host range of AS109, we establish a suite of functional assays in faba bean ( Vicia faba ), including protein localisation, RNA interference-mediated gene silencing, cell-surface elicitor recognition screens, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor (NLR) activation, and infection cell biology at the host-pathogen interface. We further demonstrate that both singleton NLRs and sensor-helper NLR pairs from Solanaceae retain effector recognition and cell death activity when transferred into faba bean, establishing a rapid platform for evaluating cross-family transferability of disease-resistance genes. AS109 thus provides an accessible and versatile chassis for functional genomics in non-model crops, bridging the widening gap between hypothesis generation and experimental validation across diverse plant species.

Article.Title: Oxytocin receptor signaling in the dorsal lateral septum is essential for social transmission of food preference in mice
Article.Authors: Fu H.; Liu Z.; Zhou J.; Zhang L.; Liu C.; Tang D.; Zhang S.; Li A.; Wang D.
Article.Abstract: Social learning is a fundamental adaptive strategy that critically shapes decision-making and feeding behaviors. Through the social transmission of food preference (STFP), animals acquire information about food safety via social interactions, forming a food-odor memory that overrides innate preferences and guides subsequent food preferences. However, the neural mechanisms through which social cues durably influence feeding preferences remain unclear. Here, we identify the lateral septum (LS) as a key node in STFP. We show that LS neuronal activity increases following social learning and reliably distinguishes between socially cued and uncued foods. Chemogenetic inhibition of the dorsal LS (dLS), but not the ventral LS (vLS), abolishes STFP-driven food preference, revealing subregional specificity within the LS. Furthermore, oxytocin receptor (OXTR) signaling within the dLS is required for STFP in mice, where it enhances neuronal excitability through PLC pathway activation. Together, our results reveal a subregion-specific circuit mechanism through which the dLS integrates social information with feeding motivation, and highlight oxytocinergic modulation as a key mediator of socially guided food preferences.

Article.Title: Deficiency of placental GDF15 causes fetal growth restriction by inhibiting fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 axis
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Zhang X.; Cai C.; Qin M.; Leng X.; Chen J.; Han Y.; Xiao J.; Huang J.; Wu J.
Article.Abstract: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Here, we show that growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) levels are significantly reduced in the placenta and fetal circulation in mouse and pig FGR models and correlate positively with fetal weight. Placenta-specific GDF15 deficiency causes FGR, while placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA delivery through targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) effectively alleviates FGR. Mechanistically, placental GDF15 is a major contributor to the fetal circulating GDF15 pool and enters the fetal compartment, where it activates the hepatic STAT3 signaling pathway to stimulate IGF2 production during pregnancy. Placental GDF15 deficiency decreases hepatic STAT3 phosphorylation and IGF2 levels in fetuses. Inhibition of STAT3 in primary mouse fetal hepatocytes blocks GDF15-induced IGF2 upregulation. Placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA-LNP administration rescues the decreased hepatic p-STAT3 and IGF2 levels in FGR fetuses. Collectively, our findings identify a placenta-fetal liver metabolic axis where placental GDF15 promotes fetal growth by activating the fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 pathway, revealing a potential therapeutic target for FGR.

Article.Title: A systematic fluorescently tagged protein toolkit for dissecting apical extracellular matrix patterning in C. elegans
Article.Authors: Ragle J.; Pooranachithra M.; Ashley G.; Cadena E.; Blank B.; Kang K.; Chen C.; Bhowmick A.; Mercado S.; Wells T.; Clancy J.; Chisholm A.; Ward J.
Article.Abstract: Barrier epithelia are shielded from the external environment by their apical extracellular matrices (aECMs). The molecular complexity of aECMs has challenged understanding of their organization in vivo. To define the molecular architecture of a model aECM we generated a toolkit of 105 fluorescently tagged aECM components using gene editing in C. elegans , focusing on proteins secreted by the epidermis to form the collagen-rich cuticle. We developed efficient pipelines for modular protein tagging and rapid fluorophore swapping. Most tagged collagens were functional and exhibited exquisitely specific patterning across stages, cell types, and matrix substructures. We define multiple reference markers for key substructures including the little-understood cortical layer, as well as the helical crossed fiber arrays that function as a hydrostatic skeleton to maintain organismal shape. We further tagged 30 members of key aECM protein classes including proteases, protease inhibitors, and lipid transporters. Our standardized markers will allow dissection of the mechanistic basis of aECM spatiotemporal patterning in vivo.

Article.Title: Interindividual vocal tract diversity influences the phonetic diversification of spoken languages
Article.Authors: Moran S.; Danner T.; Ponce de León M.; Zollikofer C.
Article.Abstract: Human vocal tracts, like other physical traits, exhibit extensive interindividual variation. However, little is known about how this variation translates into phonetic diversity between speakers, and ultimately, across languages. Here we develop a biocultural model of phonetic evolution, analogous to Russell Lande’s model of multivariate phenotypic evolution. We show that individual vocal tract morphologies and associated articulatory strategies leave consistent acoustic signatures, resulting in a characteristic pattern of phonetic variation within speaker groups that correlates with the pattern observed between groups. Recalling a central tenet of evolutionary biology—that within-group variation feeds between-group diversification—our findings suggest that phonologically similar vowel systems can attain phonetically diverse realizations according to a neutral-like evolutionary process. Our model serves as a null hypothesis for disentangling the biological versus cultural mechanisms underlying phonetic diversification, where deviations from the neutral expectation may indicate culturally mediated language change.

Article.Title: Bridging energy and proteome allocation models allows prediction of the resource cost of traits across environments
Article.Authors: Meghrazi M.; Otto S.
Article.Abstract: Many traits divert resources from reproduction and are costly due to the physiological trade-offs organisms face. These traits might require the allocation of different resources, e.g., energy expenditure or production of macromolecules, and it is unclear how their costs can be compared given their different units. Moreover, the effect of environmental conditions and genetic background on the cost of traits is not well understood. Two different frameworks have been proposed to quantify the resource costs of traits, focusing on either energy allocation or proteome allocation. These frameworks implicitly assume energy provisioning or protein production limits growth, respectively, but the connection between the two limitations has been underexplored. To better connect these frameworks, we develop a framework that considers limitations in energy provisioning and macromolecule biosynthesis simultaneously to quantify and compare the cost of traits that require different resources. Using this model, we explore how environmental quality and genetic background affect the cost of traits. Notably, our model predicts that increasing food quality increases the cost of traits that require the production of new structures, while decreasing the cost of traits requiring energy expenditure. Moreover, our model makes novel predictions about the effect of degradation, recycling, and energetic demands for maintenance on the relationship between the macromolecular composition of the cells and growth rate (also known as bacterial growth laws).

Article.Title: Eye movements reflect capacity-dependent organization of working memory
Article.Authors: Huang Q.; Doeller C.
Article.Abstract: Human cognition is capacity-limited, requiring strategies to actively structure information. Eye movements offer a natural mechanism for sequential sampling, but whether such sequences reflect memory organization is unknown. We developed a working-memory task where color-frequency pairings created a latent ordinal structure to optimally reduce memory load. Across two experiments, gaze patterns spontaneously aligned with this structure. Participants sampled items following this sequence during encoding and revisited them during maintenance. Critically, the expression of this structure depended on cognitive demand. In a 3-item task, high performers showed robust sequential sampling during encoding, whereas lower performers compensated with replay-like revisitation during maintenance. Under higher demand (4 items), encoding-based organization was disrupted, and structured revisitation emerged primarily during maintenance. These findings suggest that eye movements provide an overt expression of an internally generated organizational process that flexibly adapts to cognitive demands, revealing a behavioral analogue to neural replay when encoding resources are strained.

Article.Title: PrimeStack editors enable efficient and site-specific integration of large multigene cargos in plants
Article.Authors: Sánchez E.; Sedeek K.; Butt H.; Mahfouz M.
Article.Abstract: Precise, site-specific integration of large DNA sequences into plant genomes is a long-standing goal of crop biotechnology and synthetic biology, yet remains constrained by random insertion, inefficient homologous recombination, and gene targeting. Here, we present PrimeStack, a DSB-independent platform that integrates PE with the unidirectional large serine integrase Bxb1, leveraging evolved variants for enhanced activity, to achieve the programmable insertion of multigene, multikilobase cargos at predefined genomic safe harbors (GSH) in rice ( Oryza sativa ). Optimized prime editors first install attP landing sites with high fidelity and heritability followed by Bxb1-mediated recombination that generates irreversible integration of genetic information. PrimeStack enabled targeted large-cargo integration in regenerated rice plants with efficiencies of up to 45%, as determined by junction-specific PCR analyses. No obvious morphological differences from WT plants were observed at 5 weeks after transfer to soil under the evaluated conditions. We validate its utility by achieving targeted insertion of a carotenoid cassette at an experimentally confirmed genomic safe harbor. PrimeStack delivers a modular, site-specific gene stacking platform that enables predictable, multigene trait pyramiding and pathway construction at GSH, thereby accelerating the development of improved and resilient crop varieties, as well as scalable plant-based biomanufacturing and a powerful chassis for synthetic biology.

Article.Title: An inositol receptor Itr4 coordinates carbon catabolite regulation and virulence in Cryptococcus neoformans
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Tancer R.; Wear M.; Jackson K.; Zhang Y.; Li K.; Wang J.; Gao Y.; Nielsen K.; Casadevall A.; Xue C.
Article.Abstract: Nutrient sensing and utilization are critical for microbes to adapt to their environment and evade predators. The encapsuled yeast Cryptococcus neoformans has a unique ability to sense and utilize the sugar inositol as both a signaling molecule and as a carbon source. This trait is advantageous not only in the natural environment but also to promote its pathogenesis, including invasion of the central nervous system. In this study, we have identified a novel inositol transporter-like receptor (transceptor) Itr4 that coordinates inositol and glucose metabolism by regulating inositol transporters ( ITR s) and glucose sensor Hxs1. Itr4 binds inositol and regulates the function of other ITR s and its loss leads to a significant decrease in inositol uptake activity, resulting in a lack of mating, reduced capsule size, reduced blood–brain barrier (BBB) penetration, and virulence attenuation. Mutagenesis analysis of Itr4 protein identified an essential N-terminal tail and two amino acids, Q388 and Q389, as sites of functional importance. The ITR4 Q388A, Q389A allele showed a dominant phenotype with increased inositol uptake, enlarged capsule and significantly attenuated virulence. In summary, we identify a new C. neoformans inositol transceptor, Itr4, the first such example in eukaryotes, with novel regulatory roles in both inositol and glucose metabolism and fungal virulence.
