Here, we employed a human embryonic stem cell (ESC) line carrying an inducible RUNX1-ETO transgene to determine whether endothelial signaling pathway activation depends on disease progression or is directly induced by RUNX1-ETO. Single-cell analyses demonstrate that RUNX1-ETO reprograms ESC-derived myeloid progenitors towards endothelial cells. We show (1) that endothelial reprogramming is RUNX1-ETO concentration-dependent and irreversible, (2) at similar RUNX1-ETO and RUNX1 expression levels, a sub-population of blood progenitors can escape reprogramming, and (3) keeps proliferating when co-cultured with endothelial cells. Our experiments highlight the role of cellular interactions in the maintenance of pre-leukemic cells and provide important insights into the earliest stages of genomic reprogramming by oncogenic transcription factors.

Article.Title: The lysis mechanism of the haloarchaeal virus HFTV1
Article.Authors: Kuiper B.; van Tilburg M.; Bäcker L.; Maity S.; Ariyanto Y.; Petters J.; Aguirre-Sourrouille Z.; Nijland J.; Karsens H.; Berrelkamp-Lahpor G.; Tittes C.; Wiechert J.; Frunzke J.; Daum B.; Roos W.; Marrink S.; Quax T.
Article.Abstract: Tailed bacteriophages can lyse their host with help of the holin-endolysin system. However, for archaeal tailed viruses (arTVs), whose archaeal hosts have a fundamentally different cell envelope, lysis mechanisms are unknown. In this study, we use the model archaeal virus-host system: Haloferax tailed virus 1 (HFTV1), which infects the methanobacteriote Haloferax gibbonsii LR2-5. We identified and characterized the lysis protein GP33, a small membrane protein that has no sequence homology with bacterial holins. Overexpression resulted in cell lysis, and the protein forms foci near the cell envelope. Molecular dynamics simulation suggests that it forms pores from which the lipids are repelled, which might result in cell lysis. Indeed, atomic force microscopy (AFM) showed that GP33 forms pores in membranes, which lead to complete membrane disruption at higher concentrations. With this work, we gain insight into a lysis mechanism from a tailed archaeal virus at the molecular level.

Article.Title: Dopamine signaling in the medial accumbens shell constrains the duration of reinforced actions
Article.Authors: Valyear M.; M-L. Eustachon N.; Morris M.; Alymova I.; Tremblay B.; Mitrikeski N.; Britt J.
Article.Abstract: Dopamine regulates the frequency of motor actions, but it is unclear whether it similarly regulates the duration of discrete behaviors. Here, we show that dopamine signaling within the medial accumbens shell reinforces actions while simultaneously constraining their duration. When mice hold down a lever to continuously self-stimulate dopamine axons in the medial accumbens shell, hold-downs are rarely longer than 5 s, and higher stimulation frequencies elicit shorter, but more numerous, lever hold-downs. This disengaging property of medial accumbens shell dopamine also applies to consummatory behavior, as mice are quicker to both terminate and reinitiate bouts of licking paired with high-frequency dopamine axon stimulation. Dopamine D1 receptors underpin this disengaging property of dopamine signaling, as we demonstrate a D1 agonist shortens both self-stimulation hold-downs and bouts of consummatory behavior. Altogether, we uncover an anatomically defined role of dopamine, which is to disengage its own reinforcing properties through D1 receptor signaling.

Article.Title: RAD54L counteracts topoisomerase I cleavage complexes by stabilizing E3 ligase TRIM21 to maintain genome stability
Article.Authors: Li C.; Wang S.; Xu W.; Kong Z.; Wen C.; Zhao S.; Cao L.; Chen Z.; Zhao S.; Qin Y.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: Preserving a high degree of genome stability through potent DNA damage response (DDR) mechanisms is of utmost importance for gametogenesis, ensuring the faithful transmission of genetic information. Rapidly dividing primordial germ cells (PGCs) lay the foundation of reproductive reserve in both sexes, but the regulatory mechanisms of DDR in maintaining their genome stability remain largely unknown. This study reveals that mouse PGCs deficient in the DDR factor RAD54 like (RAD54L) exhibit proliferation defects, resulting in insufficient reproductive reserve and impaired fertility. RAD54L deficiency exacerbates DNA damage derived from the accumulation of topoisomerase I cleavage complexes (TOP1ccs). Mechanistically, RAD54L promotes TOP1cc degradation via ubiquitin-proteasome pathway by interacting with and stabilizing tripartite motif-containing protein 21 (TRIM21), a newly identified E3 ligase for TOP1cc clearance. These results uncover a novel function of RAD54L in preventing TOP1cc-induced DNA damage, extending our understanding of regulatory mechanisms in safeguarding genome integrity during the mitotic process of gametogenesis.

Article.Title: Targeting GPR183 to reduce peripheral sensitization: evidence from rodent and human tissue analyses
Article.Authors: Oberkrom K.; Braden K.; Li E.; Shah S.; Maric D.; Mannes A.; Pacifico P.; Jayaraj N.; Arnatt C.; Menichella D.; Sapio M.; Salvemini D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Peripheral sensitization is a key process in the development of painful inflammatory conditions, driven in part by immune-cell mediator release following tissue injury. The G protein–coupled receptor, GPR183, predominantly expressed on immune cells, regulates their migration, positioning, and mediator production. However, its role in peripheral sensitization and the specific immune cells involved remains insufficiently understood. In rats, intraplantar injection of 7α,25-dihydroxycholesterol (7α,25-OHC), the most potent endogenous GPR183 ligand, produced long-lasting nociception that was prevented by the selective GPR183 antagonist SAE-14. As GPR183 activates extracellular signal-regulated kinase signaling, which influences pain pathways including nitric oxide synthase (NOS) activity and NO formation, we used NOS inhibitors and knockout animals to test the contribution of inducible and neuronal NOS isoforms to 7α,25-OHC-induced sensitization. We found that both isoforms influence this response, independent of cyclooxygenases. In a well-characterized rat incisional injury model, GPR183 protein expression increased in injured paw tissue, and SAE-14 reversed hypersensitivity. Meta-analysis of human postsurgical skin samples similarly showed elevated GPR183 expression and transcriptional changes favoring 7α,25-OHC production after injury. We identified macrophages, Langerhans cells (LCs), and T cells as the principal GPR183 -expressing cell types in human skin. Ablation of LCs and removal of mature B and T cells revealed that 7α,25-OHC-evoked hypersensitivity does not depend on these cell types, leaving GPR183 + macrophages as the most likely drivers of GPR183-induced hypersensitivity. Overall, our findings define the cellular and molecular pathways linking GPR183 to peripheral sensitization and highlight GPR183 antagonism as a promising strategy for pain management.

Article.Title: Pain education in Brazilian medical schools: a national curriculum analysis
Article.Authors: Silva T.; Domingues F.; Medeiros D.; Gandolfi A.; Reis F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide, yet undergraduate medical education remains insufficient to prepare future physicians for its assessment and management. The International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) has proposed a competency-based curriculum framework; however, its implementation in Brazilian medical education is unclear. The aim of this study was to evaluate the availability of pain education in Brazilian medical schools and assess its alignment with the IASP Curriculum Outline on Pain for Medicine. We conducted a national cross-sectional documentary analysis of all medical schools registered in the Brazilian Ministry of Education database between May 2024 and December 2025. Institutional websites were systematically screened for publicly available curricular documentation, and data were independently extracted by 2 reviewers. Variables included the presence of pain-related content, existence of a dedicated pain course, course workload, timing within the curriculum, and type of offering. Among 447 identified schools, 277 (62.0%) provided accessible curricular information. Only 47 institutions (16.9%) offered a stand-alone pain course, and 29 had detailed syllabi for item-level analysis. Most analyzed courses were mandatory and delivered in the early years of training. Alignment with IASP competencies was incomplete across all domains, with greater coverage of neurobiological and pharmacological content and limited inclusion of pain assessment and measurement, psychosocial and behavioral management, public health, ethics, and care for special populations. Pain education in Brazil is inconsistently structured and only partially aligned with international recommendations, indicating the need of comprehensive, competency-based curricular reform.

Article.Title: The analgesic efficacy of opioids in different application modalities for the treatment of breakthrough cancer pain—a systematic review with network meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Dinges H.; Thiedmann S.; Weyland J.; Volberg C.; Schmitt F.; Wulf H.; Schubert A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Breakthrough cancer pain episodes often require oral immediate release opioids or parenteral opioid treatment. Different formulations and application modalities have been approved for this condition. This study aimed to identify the most effective of the available substances and applications to treat breakthrough cancer pain. We conducted a comprehensive systematic review with network meta-analysis. The database search included MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible were randomized controlled trials comparing opioids and application modalities for the treatment of breakthrough cancer pain episodes. Primary end points were the pain intensity difference (PID) at 15 and 30 minutes. Secondary end points were side effects and adverse events, as well as dichotomous outcomes of treatment success. Frequentist network meta-analysis was conducted using the package netmeta in R. From 5133 records initially identified by the literature review, 23 studies were eligible for quantitative analysis. Compared with placebo, the most effective interventions at 15 minutes (PID) were intravenous or subcutaneous applications of morphine, and intranasal fentanyl or sublingual fentanyl tablets. After 30 minutes (PID), the most effective interventions were still subcutaneous and intravenous morphine, but also sublingual fentanyl tablets. Intranasal fentanyl spray was equally effective as buccal and other transmucosal applications by 30 minutes. The quality of evidence on the topic is poor as most studies are phase III trials for drug approval. The risk of publication bias is therefore high. Sublingual fentanyl tablets were as effective as intravenous or subcutaneous morphine and are a practical modality for self-administration.

Article.Title: Evoked alpha oscillatory activity is suppressed by prolonged elbow pain and modulated by repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
Article.Authors: Chowdhury N.; Hoddinott J.; Chang W.; Cheng D.; Manivasagan N.; Schabrun S.; Seminowicz D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Alpha-band oscillatory activity, assessed using electroencephalography (EEG), is among the most widely studied neurophysiological markers of pain. However, the literature has focused predominantly on resting-state measures, leaving unclear whether pain also alters evoked alpha-band dynamics, measured via cortical perturbation using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Here, we examined whether prolonged pain alters TMS-evoked alpha event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) and intertrial coherence (ITC), reflecting cortical reactivity and phase consistency, and whether 10-Hz repetitive TMS (rTMS) modulates these responses. We performed a secondary analysis on 2 previous experiments, which used nerve growth factor (NGF) injection to induce prolonged elbow muscle pain. In experiment 1, participants underwent primary motor cortex (M1) TMS-EEG at baseline (day 0) pre-NGF injection and day 2 (peak pain) and day 7 (pain resolution) post-injection. In experiment 2, M1-TMS-EEG was assessed on day 0 before NGF injection and again on day 4 after injection, with active or sham 10-Hz rTMS delivered to M1 between these assessments. In experiment 1, M1 TMS-EEG showed reductions in alpha ERSP ( P = 0.014) and alpha ITC ( P = 0.041) from day 0 to day 2. In experiment 2, active rTMS produced a more positive pre-to-post change in alpha ERSP ( P = 0.006) relative to sham but did not alter alpha ITC ( P = 0.804). Our findings suggest that prolonged experimental pain is associated with diminished evoked alpha oscillatory activity, whereas high-frequency rTMS modulates this activity in the positive direction. These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked alpha metrics warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of pain state and response to neuromodulation.

Article.Title: Beyond intensity: pain distribution shapes healthcare- and treatment-seeking beliefs in individuals with and without clinical pain
Article.Authors: Frankenstein T.; Intert S.; Szikszay T.; Katra M.; Elsner B.; Coghill R.; Luedtke K.; Adamczyk W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain is commonly described in sensory terms, yet its spatial characteristics are rarely quantified. We investigated whether lay beliefs about pain distribution influence theoretical decisions to seek care and treatment preferences. In a cross-sectional survey (N = 503; 49% reporting pain), participants completed thought experiments in which both visually presented pain distribution patterns (small, moderate, or large) and pain intensity (Numerical Rating Scale scores: 2, 5, 8/10) were systematically varied. For each scenario, they rated the likelihood of (1) seeking professional help (LoSH) and (2) taking analgesic medication (LoTM) on 0 to 100 scale. Participants also completed a spatial–intensity trade-off task, in which they chose between a fixed 20% reduction in intensity and variable reductions in pain distribution (20%-80%). A reversed version contrasted a fixed 80% reduction in pain distribution with variable reductions in pain intensity. LoSH and LoTM increased significantly with greater pain distribution ( P < 0.001), mirroring the gradient observed for pain intensity. In the spatial–intensity trade-off task, participants' choice followed a sigmoid-like function ( P < 0.001): 1% reduction in intensity was treated as equivalent to approximately a 3% reduction in distribution, indicating a systematic valuation of pain distribution. This ratio was lower in individuals experiencing pain compared with pain-free individuals. Moreover, 61% reported that pain distribution should be routinely considered in pain management alongside intensity. Results suggest that pain distribution is not merely a trivial descriptor, but a meaningful determinant of healthcare-related decision-making beliefs. Incorporating spatial metrics into clinical assessment and research may better capture how individuals implicitly evaluate pain severity.

Article.Title: Brain gray matter changes across chronic pain trajectories: MRI evidence from 35,000 individuals
Article.Authors: Zorina-Lichtenwalter K.; Bango C.; Petre B.; Rader L.; Čeko M.; Lindquist M.; Friedman N.; Wager T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic pain affects brain gray matter structure, but the magnitude, pattern, and reversibility of brain changes upon pain recovery remain unclear because of inconsistent findings from small-scale studies. We analyzed data from 35,052 UK Biobank participants who completed chronic pain assessments at 2 time points, approximately 9 years apart, evaluating pain lasting 3 months or more, across 8 body sites. Brain magnetic resonance imaging data were available from the second time point. Participants were grouped into 4 categories: Pain-free controls, New chronic pain, Persistent chronic pain, and Resolved chronic pain. We examined relationships between these categories and 313 brain-wide measures across cortical surface area, cortical thickness, and subcortical volume. New chronic pain was associated with surface area reductions in sensorimotor, temporo-parietal, and medial and lateral prefrontal cortices. Persistent chronic pain showed larger and more widespread area reductions and mixed changes in cortical thickness and subcortical volumes, including cerebellar atrophy and hypertrophy in the thalamus and basal ganglia. Resolved pain demonstrated reversibility of most brain changes, except sustained surface area reductions in the primary somatosensory cortex. No areas showed effects consistent with a predisposition to pain. Brain structural changes in chronic pain reflect adaptive neuroplasticity rather than irreversible damage or preexisting vulnerability. Most changes appear reversible with pain resolution, underscoring the importance of effective pain treatment to alleviate symptoms and support recovery of brain structure and function.

Article.Title: Pain as a predictive process in the brain: how the Bayesian brain generates, amplifies, and relieves pain
Article.Authors: Lyndon S.; Nedeljkovic S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain is not a passive readout of nociceptor traffic; it reflects the brain's inference about bodily threat under uncertainty. Building on predictive processing, active inference, and the free energy principle, we frame acute, chronic, and phantom pain as regimes of hierarchical inference in which memory, affect, and context shift the relative influence of prior beliefs vs incoming nociceptive evidence. Prior work links expectations to pain, but translating these ideas into a clinically usable account that links expectation mechanisms to measurable proxies of belief updating and to principled routes for personalized intervention remains challenging. We propose a generative model that links inferred threat to action policies, so that pain intensity and pain behavior can be studied within the same inferential loop. Within this framework, chronic pain can persist when threat beliefs remain overly influential despite corrective evidence. Placebo/nocebo effects illustrate how shifting expectations can amplify or relieve pain. Phantom pain illustrates how stable body-related beliefs can sustain pain-like perception even with minimal or absent afferent input. We outline candidate measurements and falsifiable predictions by linking expectation- and precision-related effects to a cingulate–insula-centered hub and associated descending control circuitry (periaqueductal gray to spinal dorsal horn). This account suggests principles for selecting and sequencing treatments to target belief content (expectations), evidence (corrective sampling), and gain control (context and neuromodulation), for matching mechanisms to patient-specific phenotypes, and for stratifying patients by dominant mechanism (overly threat-biased beliefs, reduced corrective sampling, or biased precision/gain control) to enable more testable trials and clearer interpretation of treatment response.

Article.Title: A role for the BBSome in restricting the entry of non-ciliary proteins into cilia
Article.Authors: Cevik S.; Yenisert F.; Kantarci H.; Pucak D.; Gallrein C.; Stöckl S.; Dünninger X.; Cakici O.; Stigloher C.; Kirstein J.; Kaplan O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cilia possess the inherent ability to restrict the entry of non-ciliary components through the ciliary gate. Mutations in genes encoding components of the ciliary gate result in various cilia-related diseases known as ciliopathies. Yet, how non-ciliary residents are prevented from accumulating in cilia remains unclear. Here, we observe ciliary accumulation of non-ciliary proteins in BBSome-deficient mutants (Bardet-Biedl syndrome), a phenotype reminiscent of ciliary gate-defective mutants such as mks-5 and nphp-4 . Time-lapse imaging shows that these non-ciliary proteins move bidirectionally along cilia at IFT velocities, and bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) reveals that the non-ciliary protein ELMD-1 associates with the IFT component IFT-43 in BBSome-deficient mutants, indicating that they are mis-loaded onto IFT trains. This misloading allows them to bypass the ciliary gate. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) suggests the gate remains largely functional, supporting a potential two-step model of ciliary composition control: cargo selection/loading and ciliary gating. We propose that defects in cargo selection/loading (and potentially export) alter ciliary composition, allowing unintended protein entry.

Article.Title: Inhibition of spinal astrocytic GPR177 attenuates neuropathic pain by modulating C3/C3aR signaling in male rats
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Yang M.; Li A.; Liu Y.; Guo K.; Yang Y.; Yao Y.
Article.Abstract: Neuropathic pain (NP) remains refractory to conventional therapy partly because its pathogenesis is incompletely understood. G protein-coupled receptor 177 (GPR177), a multi-pass transmembrane protein, regulates Wnt trafficking and secretion. Here, we use a chronic constriction injury model in male rats and find GPR177 predominantly expresses in spinal astrocytes and co-localizes with complement component 3 (C3). During NP development, astrocytic GPR177 expression increases, accompanied by activation of C3/C3a receptor (C3aR) signaling in the spinal dorsal horn. Gpr177 silencing with siRNA alleviates nerve injury-associated hypersensitivity and reduces the increases in GPR177, glial fibrillary acidic protein, C3, and C3aR. Intrathecal administration of the C3 inhibitor compstatin and the C3aR antagonist SB290157 reduces hypersensitivity and suppresses C3/C3aR activation, supporting the involvement of C3/C3aR signaling in NP development. These findings demonstrate that spinal GPR177 contributes to NP by activating astrocytes and regulating the C3/C3aR signaling pathway, suggesting the GPR177/C3/C3aR axis as a potential therapeutic target for NP.

Article.Title: Anatomical differences in the brain organization between Australopithecus and early Homo based on computational neuroanatomy
Article.Authors: Amano H.; Tanabe H.; Bruner E.; Ogihara N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Encephalization is a hallmark of human evolution, but how regional brain morphology changed during early hominin evolution remains unclear. Here, we show regional brain morphological differences between sampled Australopithecus and early Homo specimens. Using computed tomography and endocranial casts, we generated brain models for Australopithecus africanus , Homo habilis , and Homo ergaster using an anatomically homogeneous cross-species interpolation technique. Our reconstructions suggest that the posterior cerebellum was enlarged in early Homo compared with the sampled A. africanus specimens. In contrast, relative frontal lobe volume remains largely unchanged among the sampled fossils. We also identify enlargement of temporoparietal regions that, in modern humans, are associated with functions including social communication and tool use. By integrating fossil endocranial morphology with comparative neuroanatomical information from extant primates, the present approach provides a quantitative framework for generating and testing hypotheses about regional brain evolution in extinct hominins.

Article.Title: Serum albumin maintains Wnt3a water solubility and activity
Article.Authors: Yeo J.; Chae J.; Kwon S.; Han J.; Kusen I.; Lim J.; Lee H.; Kim H.; Haam S.; Cheong J.; Kim T.; Moon S.; Jung Y.; Lee J.; Kim C.
Article.Abstract: Wnt proteins regulate adult tissue homeostasis and repair by driving stem cell self-renewal and differentiation. High-performance Wnt preparations have enormous therapeutic potential, especially alongside various stem cell technologies. Currently, a major limitation of most Wnt preparations is that they inevitably require fetal bovine serum (FBS) or detergents to maintain Wnt solubility and activity. Recently, afamin (AFM) was identified as a serum factor that solubilizes Wnt3a in conditioned media (CM), obviating the requirement for animal sera. Here, we show that serum albumin (SA) helps maintain the activity and stability of AFM-solubilized Wnt3a in CM, likely through a stabilizing effect. We further demonstrate, using test-tube assays, that SA alone efficiently solubilizes purified Wnt3a (pWnt3a) independently of AFM. This approach enables the conversion of conventional detergent-solubilized pWnt3a (CHAPS–pWnt3a) into SA–pWnt3a through dialysis-mediated detergent removal. Together, these findings define a simple and robust SA-based strategy for preserving Wnt3a activity, addressing a long-standing challenge in both experimental and therapeutic settings.

Article.Title: Dysregulation of the Hippo pathway enhances PD-L2 transcription to promote immune evasion in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
Article.Authors: Ando T.; Okamoto K.; Sato K.; Goto Y.; Izumi H.; Kataoka N.; Ueda Y.; Kobayashi Y.; Omachi K.; Maeda Y.; Furusho H.; Iglesias-Bartolome R.; Yoshimoto T.; Shintani T.; Yanamoto S.; Miyauchi M.; Gutkind J.; Kajiya M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Hippo pathway and its downstream effectors, YAP/TAZ, exhibit aberrant regulation in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, facilitating cancer cell growth. However, the influence of YAP/TAZ on cancer immune evasion remains poorly understood. Herein, we show that cancer patients harboring mutations regulating the Hippo pathway and YAP/TAZ hyperactivation may be sensitized to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy owing to genome instability and PD-L2 expression. LATS1/2 deletion, accompanied by YAP/TAZ hyperactivation, was associated with loss of squamous differentiation and genome instability, which may contribute to elevated DNA damage. Our data suggest that YAP/TAZ may recruit TEAD, BRD4, and RNA polymerase Ⅱ to the super-enhancer and promoter regions of PD-L1 and PD-L2 . YAP/TAZ predominantly contribute to PD-L2 expression, which is associated with Stat3 activation, partially enhancing PD-L1 transcription. YAP/TAZ-activated cells can be targeted by antigen-specific T cells but evade them through PD-L2. These findings suggest that Hippo pathway alterations and associated YAP/TAZ hyperactivation may serve as potential prognostic factors for stratifying patients undergoing ICI therapy. Targeting YAP/TAZ/TEAD could offer a promising treatment avenue for cancers harboring YAP/TAZ hyperactivation.

Article.Title: Hdac3 shapes adipocyte size, death susceptibility, macrophage turnover, and vascular remodeling in a mouse model of obesity
Article.Authors: Coppi L.; Severi I.; Bonacina F.; Villa S.; Peri C.; Longo R.; Senzacqua M.; Perugini J.; Galli C.; Pedretti S.; Mitro N.; Catapano A.; Norata G.; Giordano A.; De Fabiani E.; Crestani M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The crosstalk between adipocytes and macrophages is crucial in adipose tissue biology. The aim of this study was to investigate the role of adipocyte-expressed histone deacetylase 3 (Hdac3) on adipose tissue plasticity and immune cell composition in response to high-fat feeding. Here we show that adipocyte-specific deletion of Hdac3 gene in mice affects the response to high-fat overload, by reducing fat mass and adipocyte size in visceral fat of knockout mice. In the absence of adipocyte Hdac3, visceral fat shows vascular remodeling and increased macrophage content. Colocalization of F4/80 with Ki-67 indicates proliferation of resident macrophages. This is coupled with increased crown-like structures and adipocyte death in visceral fat of knockout mice, exacerbated by high-fat feeding. Hdac3 silencing in cultured adipocytes and inactivation in mice promotes a pro-apoptotic microenvironment, as assessed by positivity to Annexin V and cleaved Caspase 3. In conclusion, we propose that Hdac3 acts as a rheostat in visceral fat, differentially affecting lipid accumulation and adipocyte size during the progress of high fat diet (HFD) feeding, and limiting cell death, vascularization, and macrophage proliferation, in a mouse model of obesity.

Article.Title: Relationship between X chromosome mosaicism, neuroanatomy and cognitive performance in females
Article.Authors: Karipidis I.; Klabunde M.; Jordan T.; Chromik L.; Hosseini S.; Reiss A.; Hong D.
Article.Abstract: Females have two X chromosomes, one of which is inactivated early in development with specific regions and genes ‘escaping’ inactivation. Thus, X chromosome loss putatively results in decreased ‘dosage’ of X chromosome escapee and pseudoautosomal genes, impacting downstream pathways. Evidence from Turner syndrome (TS) indicates that X chromosome monosomy results in consistent neuroanatomical and cognitive phenotypes. However, it remains unclear whether mosaic karyotypes, with mixed proportions of 45X and 46XX cells, attenuate these phenotypes. Using support vector regression, we examined whether X chromosome mosaicism is predicted by features derived from structural brain MRI and neurocognitive assessments of 48 pre- and early pubertal girls with monosomic TS, with mosaic TS, and without TS. Higher proportion of 46XX cells was significantly predicted by structural properties in somatosensory, motor, visual, and language brain areas, and by performance in visuospatial, fine-motor, and language tasks. Thus, mosaicism partially ‘rescues’ phenotypes linked to full 45X monosomy and may explain the role of the X chromosome not only across heterogeneous phenotypic expression in females, but also in sex differences observed in neuropsychiatric conditions. X chromosome mosaicism in Turner syndrome partly mitigates the brain and cognitive effects of X monosomy. Higher proportions of 46XX cells predict more typical brain structure and better visuospatial, motor, language, and cognitive performance.

Article.Title: FLASHS reveals multiscale spatial gene programs at atlas scale
Article.Authors: Yang C.; Zhang X.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics links gene expression to tissue architecture, but detecting spatially variable genes at atlas scale remains difficult because biologically relevant patterns are multiscale, sparse, and often non-parametric. Here we show that FLASHS, a frequency-domain kernel test using random Fourier features, sparse sketching, and a kurtosis-corrected null, retains Gaussian-kernel flexibility at near-linear per-gene cost without permutation. Across 50 benchmark datasets spanning 9 spatial transcriptomics platforms, FLASHS achieves the highest ranking accuracy among 14 compared methods while maintaining calibrated inference under simulation and full-atlas permutation. In human heart tissue, it recovers a mitochondrial biogenesis program that co-localizes with ventricular cardiomyocytes. On the Allen Brain MERFISH atlas containing 3.94 million cells, FLASHS completes in minutes on a single workstation and separates biological signal from negative-control barcodes even when p -values saturate.

Article.Title: A review of self-supervised imaging phenotypes for genome-wide association studies
Article.Authors: Patel K.; Zhao X.; Xie Z.; Zhi D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Biobank-scale imaging-genomic cohorts enable genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of organ structure and function. Traditional approaches rely on expert-defined image-derived phenotypes (IDPs), which capture only a fraction of the biological variation in high-content images. Powered by artificial intelligence, self-supervised learning (SSL) learns representations directly from intrinsic image structures, creating scalable, data-driven traits. Here, we review the technical frameworks and challenges of SSL-based imaging genetics and their applications in brain MRI, cardiac MRI, and retinal imaging. Early studies suggest that these data-driven approaches can complement traditional IDPs and may expand the phenotypic space available for discovery of heritable imaging traits, although broader validation across cohorts, ancestries, scanners, and imaging protocols remains needed.

Article.Title: Single-cell and spatial mapping reveals GCLC+ mesenchymal tumor cells linked with favorable outcomes in TNBC
Article.Authors: Girnius N.; Vallius T.; Chen W.; Launonen I.; Palomino-Echeverria S.; Lin J.; Mills C.; Kauppila S.; Kronqvist P.; Ellonen A.; Perala M.; Withnell E.; Chen Y.; Secrier M.; Santagata S.; Sorger P.; Färkkilä A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Oxidative stress response (OSR) is suggested as a therapeutic target in triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). We generated a multiplex immunofluorescence dataset of 345 TNBC samples that showed OSR proteins GCLC and NQO1 are differentially expressed across tumor, immune, and stromal cells, and elevated in inflamed regions. We identified a mesenchymal-like tumor cell state characterized by co-expression of GCLC and vimentin (GCLC⁺VIM⁺), with increased proliferation and reduced anastasis-associated signatures, suggesting a vulnerability to chemotherapy. Consistently, TNBC cell lines with higher GCLC expression showed increased sensitivity to cisplatin. Moreover, patients with higher proportions of GCLC⁺VIM⁺ tumor cells had longer overall survival. Our findings indicate that OSR proteins are expressed in spatially and phenotypically distinct tumor microenvironments, and that the GCLC⁺VIM⁺ tumor cell state is associated with favorable outcomes in TNBC.

Article.Title: Anatid herpesvirus 1 US10 recruits TRIM13 to ubiquitinate STING for autophagic degradation and immune suppression
Article.Authors: Tian Y.; Tian B.; Xiao Z.; Ran R.; Cai D.; Wang M.; Wu Y.; Yang Q.; Zhang S.; Zhu D.; Liu M.; Zhao X.; Sun D.; Huang J.; Ou X.; Wu Z.; He Y.; Pan Y.; Jia R.; Chen S.; Cheng A.
Article.Abstract: The innate immune response is central to antiviral defense, and viruses have evolved sophisticated evasion strategies. Anatid Herpesvirus 1 (AnHV-1) is a pathogenic alphaherpesvirus causing immunosuppression with economic and biosecurity impacts, yet its evasion of immune signaling pathways remains poorly understood. Here we show that AnHV-1 tegument protein US10 suppresses innate immunity by targeting stimulator of interferon genes (STING) for autophagosome-lysosome degradation. US10 associates with STING and binds the autophagy-related protein microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta (LC3B), enhancing delivery to lysosomes. Mechanistically, US10 recruits E3 ligase tripartite motif-containing protein 13 (TRIM13) and induces stress in the endoplasmic reticulum through the Protein kinase R-like Reticulum Kinase (PERK). These synergistic actions inhibit type I interferon (IFN-I) production and IFN-stimulated gene expression. Deletion of US10 reduces viral replication and pathogenicity while enhancing immune activation in cells and animals. Our findings uncover a dual autophagy-based mechanism of immune evasion and highlight potential therapeutic targets against AnHV-1 and related alphaherpesviruses.

Article.Title: Individualized morphometric-similarity deviations in autism linked to cortical hierarchy and microarchitecture
Article.Authors: Mamat M.; Chen Y.; Li L.
Article.Abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) shows marked interindividual variation that complicates efforts to identify coherent neuroanatomical signatures. Here we combine subject-wise morphometric-similarity networks with hierarchical Bayesian normative regression to map per-region, per-subject departures from expected cortical organization across 308 parcels in a large multisite cohort. Normative z-maps reveal that ASD individuals have a higher prevalence of extreme, spatially focal deviations than controls, yet fewer than 12% of cases show extreme deviation in any single region. These deviations are not random: they preferentially redistribute morphometric similarity from association and heteromodal cortex toward sensory and visual territories and align with canonical cortical gradients. Network-level analyses identify a spatially localized subnetwork of altered similarity (dominant in occipito-temporal/visual nodes). Semi-supervised clustering of individual z-maps resolves a reproducible continuous axis of deviation whose opposite ends carry opposite global polarity and distinct cortical-molecular couplings revealed by transcriptomic and neurotransmitter-receptor density maps, as well as divergent cognitive meta-analytic associations. Together, these findings reframe ASD neuroanatomy as gradient-constrained and molecularly tethered at the individual level and support normative, subject-wise approaches for mechanism-informed stratification. Normative models of morphometric similarity across 1,344 brains map where each autistic individual’s cortex departs from expectation. Deviations are focal and largely idiosyncratic, yet shift similarity from association toward sensory cortex.

Article.Title: Maltreatment predicts centiles of individual variation from normative brain growth in children
Article.Authors: Mohn J.; Bauer M.; Hoffmann F.; Rasmussen J.; Tietze A.; Entringer S.; Winter S.; Buss C.; Heim C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Exposure to maltreatment in childhood is posited to profoundly disrupt brain development with adverse consequences for cognitive development and health across the lifespan. Here we use “brain charts” from the largest available neuroimaging database to quantify individual brain volumes relative to normative brain growth distributions in 299 children, aged 3 to 13 years, including 123 children with clinically verified maltreatment exposure. Using magnetic resonance imaging, we obtain volumes of cortical grey, total white, and subcortical grey matter and derive chart-based centiles for each child and tissue type. In our sample, children with maltreatment exposure exhibit lower mean brain centiles across tissues than unexposed children. Associations of greater maltreatment severity with lower brain centiles do not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Lower brain centiles are associated with lower intellectual ability and more behavioural problems. These findings provide evidence for widespread differences in brain structure associated with childhood maltreatment and their relevance to intellectual ability and behavioural functioning.

Article.Title: Emerging links between gut dysbiosis, aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation, and Parkinson’s disease
Article.Authors: Aziz N.; Kortagere S.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common progressive neurodegenerative disorder, is classically defined as a motor disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuron loss in the substantia nigra and motor dysfunction. Increasing evidence, however, identifies PD as a multisystem disorder with early non-motor features, including sleep, psychiatric, and gastrointestinal disturbances, implicating the gut-brain axis. Tryptophan metabolism through serotonin, kynurenine, and indole pathways generates bioactive metabolites, many of which regulate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). AhR is a ligand-activated transcription factor involved in xenobiotic metabolism through canonical signaling pathways; however, growing evidence supports its role in immune balance, glial responses, and barrier integrity. Altered AhR signaling may therefore connect gut dysbiosis and disrupted tryptophan metabolism to sustained, systemic and central inflammation in PD. This review examines gut dysbiosis, tryptophan metabolism, and AhR signaling as potential mechanisms underlying idiopathic PD and highlights their relevance to early diagnosis and disease-modifying therapies.

Article.Title: Predicting transcriptional burst kinetics from histone modifications with deep learning
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Zhang Z.; Huang Z.; Yu X.; Wang Z.; Qiu H.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Transcription is inherently bursty, and burst frequency and burst size provide mechanistically informative phenotypes that are not uniquely determined by mean expression alone. Yet it remains difficult to quantify, at genome scale, how histone-modification landscapes encode these burst kinetics. Here we show that DeepBurst, a deep learning model, predicts gene-specific burst-frequency and burst-size regimes from histone-modification profiles around transcription start sites. DeepBurst uses self-attention to learn combinatorial, position-dependent predictive patterns, with training labels inferred from single-cell transcriptome data using mechanistic bursting models. Across three human cell lines and two label-inference procedures, DeepBurst achieves consistent performance under chromosome-based splits and shows strong cross-cell type generalization. Model interpretation shows that burst frequency benefits from broader chromatin context, whereas burst size depends more strongly on promoter-proximal signals. Model-constrained in silico perturbations further identify histone-profile changes predicted to shift bursting regimes. DeepBurst therefore enables genome-wide mapping from readily measurable histone-modification landscapes to hard-to-assay transcriptional bursting dynamics, while generating testable hypotheses for future perturbation studies.

Article.Title: Hepatitis E virus genome plasticity: a marker of chronicity and therapy failure?
Article.Authors: Janshoff S.; Sirkinti L.; Nocke M.; Bechtel T.; Gömer A.; Brüggemann Y.; Steinmann E.; Brown R.; Todt D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a globally distributed zoonotic pathogen, spread by contaminated food and blood products, and a leading cause of acute viral hepatitis. Recent data indicate that the HEV genome contains a highly heterogeneous hypervariable region (HVR) that can tolerate extensive genomic rearrangements, especially among immunocompromised patients. These rearrangements can increase HEV replication in tissue-culture and have further been observed in HEV-infected patients. Insertions comprise either duplications of virus-derived sequences, or alternatively, host-derived sequence fragments and exhibit enrichment of specific amino acids and functional motifs. However, the molecular mechanisms driving these insertions, as well as their functional significance, remain largely unexplored. Given that sequences not required for infectivity or replication are typically rapidly eliminated in small RNA viruses such as HEV, the persistence of HVR insertions suggests a potential biological role in HEV replication and/or pathogenesis. This review summarizes our current understanding of the role of HVR insertions during HEV infection, as well as the potential mechanisms underlying these insertions. We further discuss the factors driving the selection of genomic insertions and speculate on their functional role by analyzing over 650 publicly available HEV genotype 3 genome sequences and systematically cataloging identified insertions.

Article.Title: Identification of candidate key genes involved in natural rubber biosynthesis in Periploca sepium
Article.Authors: Lu G.; Yong J.; An Y.; Lang S.; Zhang H.; Chen R.
Article.Abstract: Natural rubber is a critical industrial material facing supply shortages. Periploca sepium has emerged as a promising alternative for producing the rubber component cis-polyisoprene. To investigate its biosynthesis, we performed genome and transcriptome sequencing. Our results indicate that this plant possesses complete mevalonic acid (MVA), 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate/2-C-methyl-D-erythritol-4-phosphate (DXP/MEP), and polyisoprene pathways, as well as contains corresponding rubber particle membrane proteins. Using weighted gene co-expression network analysis, we identified 11 key genes positively correlated with levels of cis-polyisoprene and precursor allylic diphosphates (IPP/DMAPP, GPP, FPP, GGPP). Overexpressing acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase, and 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate reductoisomerase genes from the MVA and DXP/MEP pathways in P. sepium increased IPP/DMAPP levels. Molecular docking and enzyme assays indicated that cis-prenyltransferase exhibits the highest affinity for FPP, suggesting it is the dominant initiator of IPP condensation in cis-polyisoprene biosynthesis. Overexpressing the FPP synthase gene enhanced FPP levels, leading to increased cis-poly7isoprene content. Overexpressing cis-prenyltransferase, small rubber particle protein, and rubber elongation factor genes, especially in combination, significantly raised cis-polyisoprene content and high-molecular-weight proportions. These findings demonstrate that targeted gene up-regulation can improve both rubber yield and quality in P. sepium. The candidate key genes involved in rubber biosynthesis in P. sepium were identified via genome and transcriptome sequencing combined with WGCNA. Up-regulation of the key genes by overexpression, especially in combination, can improve both rubber yield and quality in P. sepium.

Article.Title: In vivo replication of a fully functional nerve net in a clonally reproducing animal
Article.Authors: Sakib E.; Hofacker L.; Noack C.; Ströbel F.; Giez C.; Wittlieb J.; Klimovich A.; Bosch T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nerve nets are considered the evolutionarily oldest form of nervous system. How such networks develop and how complex nervous systems become fully functional is largely unknown. In a phylogenetically ancient animal, the freshwater polyp Hydra , we demonstrate how a nerve net consisting of distinct neuronal populations is precisely replicated over the course of asexual proliferation by budding. During this process, precursor cells first accumulate at the site of the emerging neural network, followed by a stepwise formation of functional neural circuits composed of distinct neuronal populations. These circuits become arranged according to an accurately controlled spatiotemporal pattern and take control of behaviors independently of the existing parental network. Since similar processes also govern the formation of more complex nervous systems in other invertebrates and vertebrates, we suggest that the basic requirements for a neuronal network to replicate were already in place at the beginning of the evolution of the nervous system.

Article.Title: Evolution towards higher unitary conductance in mammals makes BK channels more efficient and precise
Article.Authors: Hepburn I.; Hellemans S.; Taniguchi T.; Bourguignon T.; De Schutter E.
Article.Abstract: The large-conductance calcium-activated potassium (BK) channel plays a critical role in neuronal excitability and spike timing precision. Mammalian BK channels are distinguished by an exceptionally high unitary conductance (~250 pS), while invertebrates exhibit a significantly lower unitary conductance. We confirmed the evolutionary trend to high unitary conductance and used computational models to examine how differences in unitary conductance affect calcium activation of BK channels and influence neuronal dynamics. We show that mammalian BK channels are activated more efficiently by calcium and generate stronger repolarizing currents than lower unitary conductance channels. Channels with lower unitary conductance require greater channel density in the cell membrane, leading to stronger competition for calcium and reduced activation. In contrast, high unitary conductance channels minimize competition, enabling more effective activation and repolarization. Incorporating these channel properties into a neuronal model revealed that mammalian-type BK channels enhance spike-timing precision, consistent with the evolution of fine motor control and advanced neuronal processing in mammals.

Article.Authors: Brosseau N.; Pincez T.; Lo K.; Lo C.; Beaudoin M.; Lettre G.

Article.Authors: Klaourakis K.; Kulkarni S.; Zvonickova K.; Kalisch-Smith J.; Smart N.; Sparrow D.; Jackson D.; Riley P.; Vieira J.

Article.Authors: Wang H.; Kroeschell G.; Zhu Y.; Mumm J.; Yi J.
Article.Abstract: Accurate detection of swim bouts is essential for decoding motor behavior in larval zebrafish, yet conventional threshold-based methods rely on subjective cutoffs and per-experiment tuning. Both improved precision over threshold-based methods, particularly for low-amplitude bouts. Using the offline model, we show that a head-fixed, closed-loop preparation largely preserves naturalistic swimming kinematics. Repeated trials reduced bout frequency and increased interbout interval, whereas genetic background primarily affects bout duration and maximum amplitude; notably, casper larvae lacked the late-trial decline observed in wildtype and nacre. We further show that detector choice can alter inferred behavioral outcomes. Together, these results establish a high-throughput framework for robust and reproducible analysis of zebrafish swimming behavior across experimental conditions.

Article.Title: Extragonadal role of FSH in regulating corneal homeostasis in Keratoconus
Article.Authors: Chatterjee A.; Kanu L.; Ross A.; Yeung V.; Boychev N.; Venkateswaran N.; Saeed H.; Yang M.; Hutcheon A.; Ciolino J.
Article.Abstract: Keratoconus (KC) is a multifactorial, progressive, ectatic disease of the cornea, which often manifests during puberty. The clinical phenotype includes progressive loss of stromal collagen, with emerging evidence indicating inflammation contributes to the disease pathology. Using a 3D collagen hydrogel system, co-culture models, and patient-derived tears, we found the following: FSH levels were low in KC patients; FSH supplementation inhibited MAP kinase signaling, leading to decreased MMP2 activity and increased collagen accumulation; FSH increased pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, driving macrophage polarization, migration, and tunneling nanotube formation; FSH regulated the HDAC1-miR-29b feedback loop in chromatin immunoprecipitation and overexpression studies; Gene ontology linked FSH to leukocyte adhesion and extravasation; and Motif analysis identified NF-Y as a possible HDAC1-interacting partner. Collectively, FSH plays a dual role in keratoconus by regulating collagen accumulation through the MAP Kinase-MMP2 axis and inflammation through the HDAC1-miR-29b pathway. Human patient tears, 3D corneal hydrogel model, and co-culture model were used to identify the role of FSH in the cornea. We found that the FSH played a dual role in the regulation of corneal extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammation.

Article.Abstract: Adult central nervous system neurons fail to regenerate after injury, in part due to epigenetic constraints that maintain a growth-restrictive chromatin state. We previously showed that the transcription factor PATZ1 reprograms chromatin accessibility in injured corticospinal neurons and primes the regeneration associated gene loci, but the underlying mechanism remained unclear. Here we use nucleosome-resolution profiling to reveal that PATZ1 induces widespread nucleosome eviction at regeneration-associated gene loci. PATZ1 overexpression (PATZ1 OE) dramatically reduces both nucleosome occupancy and fuzziness, indicating active chromatin reorganization rather than passive destabilization. This reorganization occurs preferentially at distal regulatory elements, where PATZ1 drives a greater than 3-fold expansion of H3K27ac-marked active enhancers. Nucleosome eviction at these sites likely helps in enhancer activation, establishing a mechanistic link between chromatin reorganization and transcriptional reprogramming. Our findings demonstrate that targeted nucleosome eviction at enhancers underlies PATZ1-mediated chromatin reorganization, providing mechanistic insight into the epigenetic barriers that constrain regenerative gene expression in the central nervous system (CNS).

Article.Title: Inhibition of DCLK1 promotes spinal cord injury recovery: implications for KATNA1 phosphorylation in microtubule-dependent neurite outgrowth
Article.Authors: Li S.; Ma A.; Lei C.; Meng Z.; Zhu J.; Zhang G.; Tan W.; Tan M.
Article.Abstract: Functional recovery after spinal cord injury (SCI) remains challenging, requiring therapeutic targets. Here, we show that doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) is upregulated after SCI in mice. Pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 with DCLK1-IN-1 improved motor recovery, reduced glial scar formation and fibrosis, and preserved neurons at the lesion site. Mechanistically, we identified the microtubule-severing protein KATNA1 as a downstream target of DCLK1. DCLK1 directly phosphorylated KATNA1 at threonine 118 (T118), suppressing its microtubule-severing activity. DCLK1 overexpression inhibited, whereas DCLK1 knockdown or inhibition enhanced KATNA1 function. The T118D mutation reduced KATNA1 activity, while T118A resisted DCLK1-mediated suppression. In neurons, DCLK1 inhibited KATNA1-induced neurite outgrowth, whereas DCLK1 inhibition restored this effect. Together, these results identify DCLK1 as a promising therapeutic target for SCI and reveal a mechanism by which DCLK1 regulates KATNA1 phosphorylation to modulate microtubule severing and neurite outgrowth.

Article.Title: Standardizing deoxygenation studies in coral biology
Article.Authors: Million W.; Alderdice R.; Dilernia N.; Kühl M.; Pacherres C.; Pernice M.; Randall C.; Skeer A.; Suggett D.; Voolstra C.; Camp E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deoxygenation, the global loss of biologically available oxygen (O 2 ) from the world’s oceans, presents a pervasive and intensifying threat for reef-building corals that will require coordinated efforts to understand and manage. However, recent expansion of coral deoxygenation experimentation has produced methodological gaps, limiting collective knowledge generation. Here, we show that growing divergence in this field arises primarily from differences in focal phenotypes, deoxygenation exposures, and experimental execution that together prevent biological from technical variation from being disentangled between studies. To address this, we propose a series of recommendations to establish the foundation for a future standardized framework for coral deoxygenation methodology. Such efforts are critical to establish a robust consensus of scientific data to support effective management of reef deoxygenation. Waiting decades for diverging methodologies to prompt a call for standardization may be imprudent given the urgent threat of deoxygenation and the abundant methodological divergence present in coral deoxygenation experimentation.

Article.Title: SGLT2 inhibitors attenuate diabetic kidney disease by suppressing YAP dependent ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Feng L.; Feng C.; Li H.; Wang T.; Zhang H.; Zhao Y.; Liu H.
Article.Abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors provide renal protection in diabetic kidney disease (DKD) through mechanisms beyond glucose lowering, but these remain incompletely understood. In human DKD kidney tissues, nuclear YAP accumulation correlates positively with ferroptosis markers acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) and 4-hydroxynonenal, and negatively with renal function. In a diabetic rat model, dapagliflozin attenuates renal dysfunction, tubular injury, and fibrosis alongside reduced YAP activation and ferroptosis. In high-glucose-treated renal tubular epithelial cells, YAP promotes nuclear translocation, upregulates ACSL4 and transferrin receptor expression, induces iron accumulation and mitochondrial damage, and drives ferroptotic cell death. YAP knockdown and pharmacological inhibition both confirm an upstream regulatory role for YAP in ferroptosis. Mechanistically, YAP and TEAD4 enhance ACSL4 promoter activity through a conserved TEAD-binding motif, an effect suppressed by dapagliflozin. These findings identify the YAP/TEAD4-ACSL4 axis as a therapeutic target underlying glucose-independent renoprotection by SGLT2 inhibition.

Article.Title: Integrating corneal endophenotypes with classic GWAS approaches identifies novel keratoconus loci
Article.Authors: Shabani H.; Buch G.; Lee S.; van Camp G.; van den Biggelaar F.; Haudum C.; Smoor M.; Geerards A.; Ghanbari M.; Habeeb M.; Pfeiffer N.; Marx-Groß S.; N/A N/A.; Wesselius A.; van der Kallen C.; van Asten F.; A. Article.Abstract: Keratoconus is a chronic progressive disorder characterized by corneal deformation. Gene-set analysis implicates pathways involved in extracellular matrix integrity, glucosylceramidase regulation and cellular differentiation. These findings expand the genetic landscape of keratoconus, provide insight into the biological mechanisms underlying disease development, and support future efforts in genetic risk profiling and therapeutic target discovery.

Article.Title: Chronic XBP1s signaling promotes B cell dysfunction and anergy
Article.Authors: Deng B.; Zaleski O.; Hill M.; Seeto S.; Benson D.; Woyach J.; Hu C.; Liu B.
Article.Abstract: B cells are central mediators of humoral immunity, and their development is tightly regulated to prevent autoreactivity. The unfolded protein response (UPR) plays a crucial role in supporting the high biosynthetic demands of B cells. Here we demonstrate that sustained activation of XBP1s shapes anergic B cell development and peripheral tolerance. We generated a B cell-specific XBP1s knock-in mouse model that induces chronic XBP1s expression. We find that chronic XBP1s overexpression drives the accumulation of anergic transitional 3 B cells, which exhibits attenuated activation responses to both BCR and TLR stimulation. Mechanistically, XBP1s overexpression upregulates the anergy-associated factor Egr2 and suppresses Irf4 expression. Our study provides insights into how dysregulated XBP1s expression may contribute to immune tolerance and dysfunction.

Article.Title: Molecular mechanisms of NLR proteins in inflammasome activation
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Ji K.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Nucleotide-binding domain and leucine-rich repeat-containing proteins (NLRs) are central mediators of inflammasome signaling, activating caspase-1 to drive pyroptotic cell death and pro-inflammatory responses. Article.Title: Organelle associations and metabolic rewiring of size-defined hepatic lipid droplets
Article.Authors: Liao Q.; Fu X.; Wang Y.; Xu Y.; Cao Z.; Wang Y.; Pan B.; Wang J.; Liu P.; Yang Z.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Lipid droplet (LD) size is a key determinant of hepatic lipid metabolism, yet the molecular programming routing size-defined subpopulations to distinct fates remains unclear. Moreover, comparative proteomics of fasted livers reveals a clear ‘division of labor’: Large LDs (L-LDs) function as specialized mitochondrion-coupled ‘putative fueling hubs’, whereas small LDs (S-LDs) serve as lysosome-coupled ‘putative trafficking and turnover hubs’. This interaction map is highly plastic; metabolic stress (fasting or steatosis) triggers a programmatic remodeling where lysosomal machinery is inducibly recruited to S-LDs. Crucially, in vivo stress recruits mitochondria to both pools, supporting a ‘parallel programs’ model where S-LD-associated mitochondria are hypothesized to power the energy-intensive degradative machinery. These findings establish that metabolic state leverages LD size to direct organelle partnerships, nominating the small-LD lysosomal axis as a critical regulatory node in metabolic-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD).

Article.Title: Vascular tree structure-based perfusion phantom fabrication using modified Hele-Shaw cell method
Article.Authors: Das S.; Rakshe M.; Sarkar S.; Paul R.; Marathe S.; Abraham N.; Gandhi P.; Varma H.
Article.Abstract: Tissue phantoms mimicking microvasculature and perfusion are essential for vasculature modelling and calibrating imaging systems, which require faithful replication of vascular geometry and flow. Conventional fabrication methods, including lithographic micromachining and additive manufacturing remain constrained by predefined designs, rectangular channel cross-sections, limited scalability, and high production costs. Here we present a lithography-free approach based on a modified lifted Hele-Shaw cell method where, unlike above-mentioned methods, random fractal-like vascular structures emerge naturally. This results in channels of widths 100-1000 μ m with smooth Gaussian cross-section and natural diameter tapering. We demonstrate this with four phantom designs: a planar vascular tree, a cerebral vasculature-mimicking guided tree network, a conformable curved substrate and a retinal vasculature-mimicking network. Flow visualisation with laser speckle contrast imaging shows close agreement with in vivo observations and consistency with the generalized Murray’s law. This approach uniquely combines fractal-like network formation leading towards realistic vascular geometry and flow characteristics, offering an in vitro alternative to small animal vascular models.

Article.Title: FOXO3 induces chromatin changes in a model of DNA damage-induced senescence
Article.Authors: Brown A.; Arevalo J.; Holcom A.; Finch A.; Maybury-Lewis S.; McNamara A.; Webb A.
Article.Abstract: FOXO transcription factors are critical for cellular homeostasis and the stress response and have been implicated in longevity in several species. Yet, how these factors function at the chromatin level in differing conditions in human cells is poorly understood. Here, we take an integrated multi-omics approach to identify the chromatin-level mechanisms by which FOXO3 coordinates transcriptional programs in replicating cells and in a model of cellular senescence. Increased FOXO3 expression induces expression of chromatin remodeling factors, and impacts chromatin accessibility across the genome together with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers. As cells enter DNA-damage induced senescence, FOXO3 is essential for chromatin remodeling and reprogramming of a genomic network that functions to modulate cell stress and lineage-specific cellular functions. Altogether, we identify a FOXO3-SWI/SNF network that regulates key cellular processes including metabolism, proteostasis, epigenetics, and cell lineage, and is dynamically controlled under DNA damaging conditions.

Article.Title: Large-scale functional overlap between dorsal and ventral object-responsive networks
Article.Authors: Simmons C.; Behrmann M.; Ayzenberg V.
Article.Abstract: The processes of acting on and recognizing objects have traditionally been attributed to dorsal and ventral visual pathways, respectively. Although extensive evidence suggests that the two pathways interact, the extent and the strength of these interactions across whole-brain networks remain unclear. In two experiments, we characterized the whole-brain network connections of object-selective regions in each pathway using functional magnetic resonance imaging data acquired while participants viewed objects. Here, we show substantial spatial overlap in connectivity networks generated from the dorsal and the ventral seed region—with greater similarity between object networks within an individual than each network shows across individuals. This overlap persists across viewing of tools and non-tools and even after controlling for the shared variance between pathways. Together, these findings reveal that dorsal and ventral pathways form highly overlapping and distributed networks in the service of object perception.

Article.Title: Estradiol deficiency aggravates AngII-induced vascular remodeling by failing to inhibit GRK2 through ERα-mediated autophagy
Article.Authors: Ji M.; Song N.; Adu-Amankwaah J.; Liu C.; Wang G.; Zhou W.; Hao Y.; Shi Y.; Wu J.; Li K.

Article.Authors: Bujo S.; Fujiwara T.; Kubota M.; Toko H.; Kawana H.; Kano K.; Ito M.; Ishizuka M.; Umei M.; Kadowaki H.; Zhai B.; Kishikawa R.; Takeda N.; Harada M.; Takeda N.; Aoki J.; Komuro I.

Article.Title: A Colletotrichum orbiculare-based fungal model recapitulates conserved cellular defects of Niemann–Pick type C disease and enables therapeutic evaluation
Article.Authors: Sano H.; Takezawa S.; Saomoto N.; Chiba A.; Tanaka C.; Kato N.; Nishiuchi T.; Nishisaka H.; Kitatani K.; Kodama S.; Kubo Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Niemann–Pick type C disease is a fatal lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in NPC1 or NPC2 , leading to lipid accumulation and progressive neurodegeneration. Current mammalian models recapitulate major pathological features but are limited by long disease courses and low throughput. Here, we establish the plant-pathogenic fungus Colletotrichum orbiculare as a scalable eukaryotic model of Niemann–Pick type C disease. Introduction of disease-associated mutations into fungal NPC1 or NPC2 homologs abolishes pathogenicity, showing that NPC dysfunction compromises lipid-dependent morphogenesis required for host penetration. Conversely, human NPC1 partially restores fungal infection. Together, these findings support functional conservation of NPC-dependent cellular processes across kingdoms. Miglustat and 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin restore pathogenicity through distinct lipid pathways. These complementary modes of rescue indicate that NPC1 and NPC2 dysfunction converges on lipid-dependent morphogenesis closely linked to actin organization. Article.Title: Flippability of Escherichia coli membrane proteins under lipid stress reveals a new job for old genes
Article.Authors: Sawasato K.; Bogdanov M.
Article.Abstract: Normally, the “flip-flop” motion is reserved for small lipid molecules which move from one leaflet of the membrane to the other, and even that process is very slow without the aid of specific enzymes. Unexpectedly, we recently found that despite a prohibitively high energy barrier, Escherichia coli cardiolipin (CL) synthase A (ClsA) flips its large catalytic domain across the inner (cytoplasmic) membrane (IM) when cells were fully or partially depleted of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and that this was necessary to support cell viability. Here, we demonstrated that production of the non-native phospholipid phosphatidylcholine (PC) in PE-depleted cells prevents ClsA flipping and halts cell growth, a phenotype rescued by constitutively inverted ClsA. Surprisingly, properly oriented lactose permease (LacY) acts as a multicopy suppressor, rescuing the growth defect in the -PE+PC cells. These data indicate that neutral PC regulates the membrane topology of ClsA and LacY, and subsequently the appearance of CL to the periplasmic leaflet required for viability. Therefore, ClsA and potentially LacY may achieve varied roles from the same amino acid sequence through an unusual flip-flopping mechanism. This fruitful “repurposing” of genetic material highlights the remarkable adaptability of living organisms and their membranes. Altering E. coli lipids disrupts growth, but controlled membrane protein flipping simulates natural selection and resemonstrates that membrane proteins can re-evolve under the selective pressure of an altered lipid bilayer.

Article.Title: The representation of order and randomness in the auditory cortex
Article.Authors: Bashari S.; Jankowski M.; Nelken I.
Article.Abstract: Perception fundamentally relies on the brain’s ability to extract structure from its sensory environment. The auditory cortex possesses significant sensitivity to statistical regularities in tone sequences. To examine this phenomenon at the single-neuron level, we used multitone sequences and recorded responses from the auditory cortex of awake adult female Sprague Dawley rats. Tones were presented in periodic sequences with a fixed, repeated cycle; in a fully random condition; or in an intermediate condition in which cycles were maintained, but tones were randomly permuted within each cycle (random cycle condition). Units showed a continuum of preferences between order-preferring neurons and randomness-preferring neurons. Unexpectedly, we found sensitivity to the position of sounds in the cycle (‘phase modulation’). The strongest and most consistent phase modulations were in the responses to the random cycle condition. Finally, we show how such phase sensitivity may emerge from a simple, biologically plausible computation. Neurons in the auditory cortex exhibit a continuum of preferences from order to randomness, and show sensitivity to the position of tones in abstract repeating patterns.

Article.Title: VASP cooperates with zyxin to organize mechanically competent adhesions
Article.Authors: Chung W.; Boujemaa-Paterski R.; Winograd-Katz S.; Eibauer M.; Geiger B.; Medalia O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Focal adhesions (FAs) are dynamic macromolecular assemblies that anchor the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix via integrin receptors, thereby regulating cell morphology and migration. Article.Title: BUB signaling in cancer and molecular insights into targeted therapies
Article.Authors: Baweja B.; Saini C.; Vats P.; Soni R.; Jangir K.; Patidar P.; Kumar A.; Nema R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) is vital for proper chromosome segregation during cell division and for maintaining genomic integrity; its disruption can cause aneuploidy and tumors. Dysregulation leads to chromosomal instability (CIN), contributing to cancer progression, heterogeneity, metastasis, and therapy resistance. Beyond mitosis, BUB proteins influence DNA repair, chromatin remodeling, transcription, and immune responses. They interact with cell cycle and genome stability pathways, impacting cancer prognosis and therapy response. Research is ongoing to validate BUB proteins as biomarkers and develop inhibitors, possibly combined with immunotherapies or DNA-damaging agents for resistant tumors. This review summarizes their functions, highlighting their potential in personalized cancer treatment.

Article.Title: A circRNA-microRNA-Pdcd1 axis drives microglial activation and retinal ganglion cell degeneration
Article.Authors: Sun L.; Ke X.; Yu J.; Wei J.; Gu J.; Zhou W.; Cen Y.; Huang J.; Zhang X.; Zhang J.; Zhang S.; Liu X.; Ji Y.; Yan W.; Pan S.; Zhou M.; Wu W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration is the primary cause of vision loss, driven by the complicated effects of intrinsic neuronal damage and neuroinflammation. However, current single-target therapies fail to address these dual pathological challenges. Here we show that, using whole‑transcriptome sequencing of optic nerve crush (ONC), we bioinformatically predicted nine candidate ceRNA networks. Article.Title: Towards a comprehensive landscape and mechanism understanding of virus-disease associations
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; You R.; Feng Y.; Lu S.; Chen S.; Fu P.; Zhu Z.; Lu C.; Zhang Z.; Xu L.; Li H.; Wang X.; Wang X.; Huang Q.; Liu X.; Xu Z.; Dong G.; Li S.; Hu X.; Xiang Z.; Hu Y.; Mao L.; Miao Z.; Meng X.; Peng Y.
Article.Abstract: Viruses are linked to human diseases through complex molecular mechanisms, yet a comprehensive investigation of virus-disease associations and their molecular basis remains lacking. We curated 3,555 high-confidence virus-disease associations involving 267 viruses and 954 diseases through text-mining over 28 million PubMed abstracts followed by rigorous manual verification, establishing the most comprehensive resource in this field to date. We then developed AVD, a user-friendly online database to store, visualize, and analyze these associations and their molecular mechanisms. Our analysis revealed that virus-disease association patterns are significantly influenced by viral taxonomy, phenotype, and key biological traits such as transmissibility, transmission routes, and tissue tropism. Molecular analysis identified a core set of bridging genes involved in the majority of virus-disease associations. Notably, these bridging genes were extensively involved in viral infections and diseases, and exhibit distinct characteristics, including a high proportion of secreted proteins, elevated expression across human tissues, and high centrality in the human protein-protein interaction network. Furthermore, we developed a machine-learning model capable of accurately predicting virus-disease associations. Collectively, this study provides a valuable data resource and analytical framework for studying virus-disease relationships and offers novel insights into their molecular mechanisms. In this manuscript the authors analyze viral-disease associations and identified that virus-disease associations are significantly influenced by viral taxonomic, phenotype, and their biological traits. Genes that may mediate the viral-disease associations are also discovered. A database called AVD (Association of Virus and human Diseases) is also constructed to facilitate the storage and convenient analysis of the associations.

Article.Title: Metabolic characteristics and evolutionary history of the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts of pennate diatoms
Article.Authors: Cheung S.; Cornejo-Castillo F.; Bianchini G.; Coale T.; Vieyra-Mexicano C.; Sánchez-Baracaldo P.; Zehr J.; Turk-Kubo K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are important sources of bioavailable nitrogen on Earth. Some nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are endosymbionts of algae, and recently one of them, UCYN-A2, was shown to be an early-stage organelle (nitroplast) of haptophytes. These biological associations are important models for studying co-evolution and organellogenesis. Endosymbioses between Rhopalodiaceae diatoms and nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria (spheroid bodies, SBs) are widespread in marine and freshwater ecosystems, but their adaptation and evolution remain unclear. We found that the genomes and metabolic characteristics of marine and freshwater SBs are remarkably similar. Purifying selection pressures dominated SB diversification both within marine and freshwater habitats and across habitat boundaries. The metabolic characteristics and genome reduction of SBs are substantially different from UCYN-A, suggesting different evolutionary journeys for the endosymbionts influenced by different hosts. We estimated that the marine SBs diversified ~185 Mya (95% highest posterior density (HPD): 340-88 Mya), which was within a prolonged oligotrophic period in the ocean, during which UCYN-A also diversified. The freshwater SBs diversified from the marine SBs ~137 Mya (95% HPD: 258-66 Mya) and further diversified ~80 Mya (95% HPD: 157-31 Mya), when sea level was increasing. Our study reveals the genetic and metabolic underpinnings characterizing the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts of Rhopalodiaceae diatoms.

Article.Title: Conserved Core but Divergent Biochemical Features of RAS-MAPK Signalling in C. elegans
Article.Authors: Bernal Astrain G.; Strakhova R.; Amro J.; Banerjee R.; Teszner E.; Decorso I.; Reiner D.; Smith M.
Article.Abstract: Genetic studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have established core principles of RAS-MAPK signalling. These nematodes encode three RAS proteins: LET-60/KRAS is essential for vulval induction, while RAS-1 and RAS-2 are orthologs of RRAS/RRAS2 and MRAS, respectively, but remain biologically and biochemically uncharacterized. We here present a comprehensive biochemical analysis of all three C. elegans RAS proteins, defining nucleotide cycling and effector interactions. We show that conserved RAS scaffolds are tuned by sequence variation to balance signalling with developmental fidelity. LET-60 has significantly impaired nucleotide exchange and changing its sequence to match human KRAS induces a protruding vulva phenotype in vivo. RAS-1 rapidly exchanges GDP-to-GTP, whereas RAS-2 remains consistently GDP-bound. LET-60 engages the RAF ortholog LIN-45 through a divergent interface, and RAS-1 unexpectedly drives SOC-2:RAS:PP1C holophosphatase assembly in a nucleotide-independent manner. Our findings reveal both conserved and distinctive biochemical features underlying RAS signalling and suggest species-specific tuning of this key proliferation pathway.

Article.Title: Age-related shift towards feedforward motor control under uncertainty
Article.Authors: Kreter N.; Sager C.; Barany D.; Dundon N.; Marneweck M.
Article.Abstract: Humans perform movements in the face of uncertainty on a daily basis. To accomplish these tasks without error, young adults frequently rely on feedback-mediated motor strategies that allow them to update their movement as uncertainty evolves. However, it remains unclear how aging impacts the ability to plan and execute movement under uncertain conditions. Here we use a “go-before-you-know” pointing task completed during functional neuroimaging to examine how aging influences movement planning under uncertainty. Behaviorally, young adults employed a strategy consistent with feedback-mediated control, biasing their trajectories toward the more likely target when uncertainty was low, and intermediate to potential targets when uncertainty was high. Older adults employed a different approach, shifting away from an intermediate reaching strategy, particularly under high uncertainty, suggesting a shift toward feedforward control. Neuroimaging mirrored these behavioral patterns, revealing that young adults encoded task uncertainty and movement direction in sensorimotor regions more strongly than older adults. Overall, these findings suggest that aging diminishes the ability to flexibly encode task-related uncertainty, leading to a shift towards feedforward control strategies.

Article.Title: Distinct genetic perturbations at the endogenous Atf4 locus uncouple polyadenylation loss from transcriptional readthrough
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Wu T.; Chen Z.; Chen D.; Ye M.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transcription termination by RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is coupled to co-transcriptional cleavage and polyadenylation directed by the canonical AAUAAA polyadenylation signal (PAS). A previously characterized Atf4 ΔCDS + ΔPAS allele deleting exons 2-3 induces strong transcriptional readthrough, producing an Atf4 – Cacna1i fusion transcript that suppresses Rps19bp1 and causes severe cardiac defects. To isolate PAS function, we generated an Atf4 ΔCDS allele retaining the PAS and an Atf4 ΔPAS allele preserving the coding sequence but deleting the PAS. The ΔCDS allele produces modest readthrough, whereas ΔPAS does not produce detectable downstream readthrough. Instead, PAS loss permits utilization of a cryptic intragenic polyadenylation site within exon 3, generating a prematurely terminated transcript. These findings demonstrate that PAS loss does not necessarily cause transcriptional readthrough in vivo and can instead promote alternative polyadenylation at an endogenous mammalian locus.

Article.Title: Towards a unified biology of vertebrate number sense
Article.Authors: Zanon M.; Messina A.; Butterworth B.; Vallortigara G.; Brennan C.; Torres-Pérez J.; Miletto-Petrazzini M.
Article.Abstract: Number sense, the ability to estimate and compare numerical quantities, emerges early in development and is widespread across species. Despite decades of work on behavioural and neural correlates of numerosity, the genetic and mechanistic foundations remain poorly integrated. We propose a review and perspective that brings together evidence from vertebrates. Our unique focus relies on how genetic variation, brain lateralisation, and neural circuit organisation across development shape number cognition. We highlight zebrafish (Danio rerio) and chicks (Gallus gallus) as complementary comparative models that can uncover conserved principles and novel mechanisms, opening new avenues for studying the biological bases of numerical cognition and its disorders from the very early developmental stages.
