Here, we show results from what is, to our knowledge, the largest genome-wide association study in East Asians, including 596,778 individuals, with a direct comparison to a European study of comparable sample size. We identified 196 loci, including three previously unreported loci. Subsequent multi-ancestry fine-mapping resolved 521 independent causal signals with high precision, revealing that 74% are shared while the remainder are strictly ancestry-specific. Beyond this shared architecture, we observed population differences in regulatory and pathway-level contributions, particularly involving pancreatic regulation and lipid- or adipose-related pathways. Furthermore, constructing a polygenic risk score using the cross-ancestry meta-analysis yielded the most robust predictive performance (AUC = 0.788). These findings clarify how T2D genetic risk is organized across populations, demonstrating that while multi-ancestry integration maximizes clinical predictive power, well-powered single-ancestry studies remain indispensable for uncovering population-specific biological mechanisms.

Article.Title: Restoring mitochondrial redox balance enhances ribosome-associated quality control to mitigate Alzheimer’s disease pathology
Article.Authors: Rimal S.; Khaket T.; Li W.; Lu B.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and proteostasis failure are early and concurrent features of Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative diseases, yet the mechanistic links between them remain unclear. Restoration of NAD⁺/NADH balance using yeast NDI1, which bypasses dysfunctional complex I, robustly rescues these cellular defects and ameliorates muscular and neuronal phenotypes in the AD models. Mechanistically, NDI1 activates a mitochondrial Sirtuin–VCP axis that prevents the formation of the amyloidogenic, aberrant ribosome-associated quality control products of amyloid precursor protein and promotes their clearance through ATG5-dependent but ATG1-independent autophagy. Disruption of NAD⁺ biosynthesis abolishes NDI1-mediated protection, highlighting the critical role of NAD⁺ availability. NDI1 also modulates the Sirtuin–VCP axis and is protective in human iPSC-derived neuronal AD models. Our findings validate the key pathogenic role of aberrant translational control of amyloid precursor protein in causing proteostasis failure and provide an unexpected mechanistic link between mitochondrial redox balance and proteostasis. These findings have important implications for the mechanistic understanding and therapeutic development for Alzheimer’s disease. Article.Title: Neural representation of the subjective uncertainty of prediction in the human brain
Article.Authors: Sun X.; Gong X.; Luo H.; He T.; Fang F.
Article.Abstract: Prediction is fundamental to human cognition and behavior. It comprises two key components: the objective content and the subjective uncertainty. Taking into account uncertainty in predictive processes is critical for adaptive learning and behavior in dynamic environments. In contrast to extensive research on neural representations of prediction content, how the brain encodes the prediction uncertainty remains poorly understood. Here, we recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals while participants performed a dual-task and used a generative model-based decoding approach to simultaneously decode predicted location and prediction uncertainty. We found that prediction uncertainty could be reliably decoded on a trial-by-trial basis. Importantly, the decoded uncertainty correlated with participants’ reported uncertainty. This correlation emerged shortly before the behavioral prediction response. Here, EaMIC3 was shown to inhibit the apoptosis of infected host cells and facilitate parasite infection by interacting with epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM). Article.Authors: Hou Y.; Jing L.; Sun K.; Chang Y.; Zhao J.; Li X.; Min J.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: Biomolecular condensates spatiotemporally regulate cellular biochemistry through liquid-liquid phase separation. Building on stickers-and-spacers and related grammar frameworks, we highlight a continuum from electrostatic coacervates to viscoelastic networks. We define active anti-grammar as an operational umbrella for localized repulsive or hydration-promoting effects that can counterbalance excessive cohesion when embedded in, modified within or recruited to dense phases. This view predicts measurable changes in partitioning, FRAP recovery, viscosity, aging and fibril-nucleation kinetics. Disruption of the code can drive pathogenic liquid-to-solid transitions and spatial uncoupling with organelle mechanotoxicity. Article.Authors: Krieger E.; Tisdale L.; Bruggemann F.; Li L.; Mele G.; Yan H.; Rich W.; Johnson M.

Article.Authors: Mickle A.; Peñaloza-Aponte J.; Brennan C.; Dale E.
Article.Abstract: Respiratory insufficiency is the leading cause of mortality after spinal cord injury, yet current pacing strategies override brainstem rhythm generators, limiting adaptability and rehabilitation. Article.Authors: Feng C.; He W.; Yin J.; Xu X.; Zhou M.; Wang Y.; Tester M.; Gao X.

Furthermore, projection of generated sequences exposes substrate-fidelity violations in contemporary design models. Article.Authors: Chow S.; Hu H.; Duenki T.; Asakura T.; Sugimura S.; Ikeuchi Y.
Article.Abstract: Brain organoids have the potential to acquire functions through plasticity within their complex cellular ensembles. However, unlocking their intrinsic capacity for functional refinement remains challenging because organoids lack structured sensory input and organized macroscopic circuit architecture. Here, we hypothesized that modular connectivity among cerebral organoids enhances their capacity for stimulus-driven circuit refinement. To test this hypothesis, we connected cerebral organoids and assessed their time-course performance improvement in a source-signal discrimination task. Networks comprising three cerebral organoids, but neither single organoids nor two-organoid networks, significantly improved their discrimination performance after two weeks of repeated stimulation. This improvement was accompanied by the emergence of input-dependent spatiotemporal responses, differential refinement of intra- and inter-organoid functional connectivity, faster response kinetics, and directional propagation of spontaneous activity within the three-organoid networks. Together, these results demonstrate that repeated input to an organized modular network can rewire organoids generated under identical conditions into functionally differentiated modules, thereby generating task-relevant heterogeneity that underlies consistent functional enhancement in vitro.

Article.Title: Targeting chondroitin synthase 1 attenuates hyperplastic arterial remodeling via gene therapy
Article.Authors: Liao D.; Zhao R.; Mizumoto S.; Wong J.; Chng W.; Fajardo V.; Tanudin I.; Motakis E.; Tian J.; Gurung R.; Ng S.; Li P.; Tiang Z.; Aliwarga E.; Tuan L.; Yamada S.; Ackers-Johnson M.; Richards A.; Reversade B.; Foo R.; Chan M.; Koh C.
Article.Abstract: Chondroitin sulfate glycosaminoglycans accumulate excessively in the extracellular matrix during pathological remodeling and exacerbate cardiovascular deterioration. Here we show that chondroitin synthase 1 (CHSY1) is the primary enzyme responsible for chondroitin sulfate synthesis, as identified through in-house single-cell RNA sequencing. Chsy1 knockout mice display markedly reduced chondroitin sulfate levels and are protected against arterial remodeling and fibrosis in two independent disease models, with hyperplasia and inflammation completely abolished in both coronary and carotid arteries. In vitro, CHSY1 inhibition regulates multiple cellular processes such as activation and migration of macrophages, fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition, and hyperproliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells. Cross-referencing transcriptome and proteome analysis reveal that NOTCH3 signaling is associated with CHSY1 modulation. Importantly, in vivo Chsy1 knockdown by RNA interference after disease onset significantly preserves structural integrity and maintains cardiovascular functions. In conclusion, inhibiting CHSY1 is both safe and effective in interfering with CS over-synthesis and preventing vasculopathy, representing a potent therapeutic target for a broad spectrum of diseases driven by hyperplastic arterial remodeling. This study investigates the role of chondroitin synthase 1 in hyperplastic arterial remodeling associated with chondroitin sulfate over-synthesis. Reducing chondroitin synthase 1 via RNA interference regulates multiple cellular processes and pathways, restores vascular compliance and elasticity, and preserves cardiovascular function.

Article.Title: Conserved circadian membrane rhythms arise from divergent cellular mechanisms in pacemaker neurons of mice and Drosophila
Article.Authors: Buhl E.; Nathan C.; Piggins H.; Tsaneva-Atanasova K.; Belle M.; Hodge J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Circadian clocks align physiology and behaviour with daily environmental cycles, requiring neuronal networks that encode and transmit time-of-day information. Whether conserved electrophysiological principles underlie circadian output across evolution remains unclear. We compared the intrinsic electrophysiological properties of identified circadian neurons from a nocturnal mammal (mouse SCN VIP neurons) and a diurnal insect ( Drosophila l-LNv PDF neurons) across the 24-h light-dark cycle using harmonised electrophysiological recordings and matched analytical approaches. Despite ~700 million years of evolutionary divergence and opposite temporal niches, both neuron types exhibited similar rhythmic patterns in parameters, including resting membrane potential, spontaneous firing rate and cell capacitance, indicating a conserved pattern of daily excitability despite different network scales. These shared membrane properties arose through distinct mechanisms: flies exhibited higher input resistance, greater excitability and a greater relative contribution of A-type potassium currents, while mice displayed larger sustained outward currents and post-inhibitory rebound excitation, the latter absent in flies. Rheobase troughs occurred during the inactive phase in both species, while other parameters were stable. These differences likely shape how each neuronal type integrates inputs within its circadian circuits. Our findings reveal conserved functional outputs generated by divergent electrophysiological mechanisms, highlighting evolutionary flexibility in the membrane basis of circadian timekeeping.

Article.Title: CRISPR-based gene drive systems alter the transcriptome in Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes
Article.Authors: Bravo R.; Nguyen C.; Pham T.; Carballar R.; James A.; López Del Amo V.
Article.Abstract: CRISPR-based gene drive systems have emerged as promising strategies for mosquito population control to reduce the impact of vector-borne diseases such as malaria. However, their broader molecular impact on the mosquito transcriptome remains poorly understood. We performed an RNA sequencing analysis of Anopheles gambiae gene drive (GD) mosquitoes under three conditions: males fed with sugar, females fed with sugar, and females fed with blood. Principal component analyses identified sex and diet as the major drivers of transcriptomic variation, although differential expression analyses identified a subset of genes displaying genotype-specific transcriptional alterations. Several changes were unique to the GD mosquitoes across conditions, consistent with a potential contribution of the gene drive cassette beyond target gene disruption. The mRNA transcripts encoded by genes such as histone H1 , ficolin-1 , and E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase XIAP were present in decreased abundance, suggesting a potential impact on chromatin structure, immune function, and protein degradation pathways. These results highlight molecular responses resulting from the engineered gene drive alleles while offering relevant insights into their biological effects and potential implications for field implementation.

Article.Title: Unexpected functional role of the transactivation domain for nuclear import of STAT5
Article.Authors: Ernst S.; Borgen-Möller M.; Küster A.; Schurse H.; Müller-Newen G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (STAT5) is a key transcriptional regulator acting downstream of hematopoietic cytokines and hormones, such as erythropoietin (Epo), thrombopoietin or prolactin. STAT5-mediated gene regulation involves tyrosine phosphorylation at cytokine receptors and subsequent nuclear import. We studied STAT5 nucleocytoplasmic shuttling via live-cell imaging of fluorescent mutants in STAT5 -/- HeLa EpoR cells. Unexpectedly, STAT5 mutants lacking the transactivation domain (TAD) were retained in the cytoplasm following Epo stimulation. Building upon this, we identified a 12-amino-acid stretch in the TAD sufficient to restore nuclear translocation. Further analysis revealed two residues within this 12‑amino‑acid stretch, D754 and D758, to be essential for nuclear import of phosphorylated full-length STAT5. Importantly, a single intact TAD in the STAT5 dimer is sufficient for nuclear import. Our findings reveal a unique role of the TAD in STAT5 nuclear trafficking distinct from other STATs, providing new mechanistic insight and potential targets for therapeutic intervention in STAT5-driven disease such as myeloproliferative neoplasms and leukemia.

Article.Title: Physics informed machine learning predicts binding free energy changes in protein-RNA complexes upon mutations
Article.Authors: Xu W.; Zhang H.; Zhao X.; Yan S.; Zhao Y.; Peng Y.
Article.Abstract: Protein-RNA interactions are central to gene regulation, yet predicting mutation-induced changes in binding free energy (ΔΔG) remains difficult due to sparse, heterogeneous measurements and strong imbalance in mutation types. Here we present Pred-MutPRI, a physics-informed machine learning framework for ΔΔG prediction in protein–RNA complexes. We curated a unified dataset of experimentally measured ΔΔG values with standardized thermodynamic conventions, and introduced thermodynamic permutation (TP) to generate cycle-consistent training pairs that expand substitution-type coverage while reducing mutation-class bias. Pred-MutPRI integrates conventional structure-derived descriptors with weighted atom-level interaction networks that explicitly encode the local binding microenvironment. In addition, it incorporates two compact, information-dense features: a masked ESM-2 entropy term capturing context-dependent sequence constraint, and an AlphaFold3-derived local effective strain descriptor summarizing mutation-associated structural deformation across multiple mutant-structure predictions. With an XGBoost regressor, Pred-MutPRI achieves strong generalization on a sequence-disjoint and structurally low-overlap blind test set (PCC = 0.705) and outperforms existing predictors. The dataset and Python package are available at https://github.com/CCNU-COMPBIO/Pred-MutPRI. Pred-MutPRI is a machine learning method that predicts how mutations affect protein-RNA binding affinity. By combining thermodynamics, structural features, sequence information, and AlphaFold3-derived strain measures, it outperforms existing predictors and achieves strong accuracy on independent test sets (PCC = 0.705).

Article.Title: Coral-associated denitrification is seasonally variable and species-specific
Article.Authors: Hill C.; Tilstra A.; El-Khaled Y.; Garcias-Bonet N.; Bonacker V.; Novoa-Lamprea A.; Rich W.; Ostendarp M.; Fox M.; Carvalho S.; Peixoto R.; Wild C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nitrogen (N) plays a critical role in coral growth, but maintaining an N-limited state is essential for coral-algal symbiosis stability. Coral-associated denitrifiers may help regulate excess N, though denitrification in corals remains poorly quantified. To better understand species-specific and environmental effects on the denitrification pathway, we investigated year-long denitrification dynamics in four Red Sea corals, using acetylene inhibition assays alongside physiological and environmental measurements. All species exhibited measurable denitrification activity, ranging from 0 – 0.8 nmol N cm −2 h −1 for Stylophora pistillata and Acropora sp., 0 – 0.4 nmol N cm −2 h −1 for Millepora dichotoma , and 0 – 2.0 nmol N cm −2 h − 1 for Dendrophylliidae indet. Denitrification displayed seasonal patterns, with higher rates in the spring/summer compared to autumn/winter, and we identified temperature, dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and nitrate availability as key environmental drivers. Lastly, we observed up to fivefold higher denitrification rates in the fully heterotrophic azooxanthellate coral Dendrophylliidae indet, than among mixotrophic species harbouring Symbiodiniaceae. Our findings indicate that denitrifiers use both photosynthetically derived and environmental carbon (C), with DOC central in maintaining tight coupling of C and N cycling in coral holobionts. Additionally, denitrification is modulated by environmental conditions, highlighting its vulnerability to environmental change.

Article.Title: Clathrin adaptors drive phase separation in endocytosis and trafficking
Article.Authors: Draper-Barr G.; Schiller J.; Veith K.; Niebling S.; Ruiz-Carrillo D.; Huang Z.; Tischer C.; Thuenauer R.; Defelipe L.; García-Alai M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) underlies the formation of biomolecular condensates that organize processes, including endocytosis and membrane trafficking. Although LLPS has been implicated in clathrin-mediated pathways, the contribution of adaptor proteins to condensate formation and function remains unclear. Here we show that two yeast adaptors, Ent5 and Sla2, undergo LLPS in vitro and this property correlates with their roles in membrane trafficking and condensate recruitment in vivo. Ent5 condensation is driven by a dynamic helix within its disordered region that acts as a molecular “sticker”. Deletion of this 249-287 helix disrupts membrane-associated condensation and leads to altered coating dynamics in vivo, with Ent5-dependent transport events becoming delayed. In contrast, Sla2 behaves as a driver and as a client of LLPS, with its coiled-coil (CC) region mediating condensation. Together, these findings reveal that endocytic adaptors can promote condensate formation through distinct structural features, coupling clathrin binding and membrane association through phase separation.

Article.Title: Neuroprotective transition metal dichalcogenide nanoflower treatments alleviate pathological cell stress associated with Parkinson’s disease
Article.Authors: Mitchell C.; Matveyenka M.; Brown H.; Aldape J.; Moore P.; Nguyen K.; Walker J.; Pearson B.; Skrehot J.; Warren D.; Kurouski D.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is triggered by irreversible degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain, hypothalamus, and thalamus. Although the molecular etiology of pathology remains unclear, progressive aggregation of alpha-synuclein (α-syn) and mitochondrial dysfunction are two mechanisms implicated in neuronal degeneration. The current study investigates the neuroprotective properties of molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ) and molybdenum diselenide (MoSe 2 ) nanoflowers (NFs) in neurons and astrocytes exposed to α-syn aggregates. It was found that MoS 2 and MoSe 2 transcriptionally downregulated α-syn-induced unfolded protein response, and upregulated autophagy and exocytosis of α-syn fibrils. TMD NFs alleviated α-syn-induced damage of cell mitochondria, simultaneously altering metabolic adaptation, with a decrease in ROS levels observed. Neuroprotective properties were further explored in Caenorhabditis elegans that overexpress α-syn. Nematodes experienced a drastic reduction in the amount of aggregated α-syn which resulted in a significant increase in C. elegans lifespan. These findings indicate that MoS 2 or MoSe 2 NFs could be used as novel therapeutic to decelerate the progression of PD.

Article.Title: Disruption of Lactate Metabolism in the Peripheral Nervous System Leads to Motor‐Selective Deficits
Article.Authors: Bloom A.; Tendulkar S.; Hackett A.; Strickland A.; Sato‐Yamada Y.; Yuan L.; Dong W.; Ippolito J.; Schmidt R.; Sasaki Y.; DiAntonio A.; Milbrandt J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Schwann cells (SCs) myelinate and provide trophic support to axons in the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Disrupted SC metabolism can lead to demyelination and axon degeneration, cardinal deficits in peripheral neuropathy. The lactate shuttle hypothesis proposes that glycolytic support cells supply lactate to axons to sustain their high metabolic demands. This transfer requires lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to interconvert lactate and pyruvate in both SCs and neurons. To test the importance of lactate metabolism in the PNS, we selectively knocked out both LDHA and LDHB in ChAT‐positive neurons, including motor neurons (MNs), Nav1.8‐lineage sensory neurons (SNs), or SCs. Interestingly, motor axons and their synapses progressively degenerate when LDH is deleted from either MNs or SCs, but defects in Nav1.8‐lineage sensory axons and their terminals are not observed when LDH is excised from either SNs or SCs. Deletion of LDH in SCs leads to decreased ATP in peripheral nerves despite marked accumulation of pyruvate and glycolytic intermediates, consistent with energetic deficits due to failed conversion of pyruvate to lactate. Cholinergic neuron‐specific gene expression using ribosome affinity profiling (RiboTag) identified a strong response to metabolic compromise by activating axon‐injury stress programs in LDH‐deficient neurons. Finally, blocking axon degeneration in LDH‐deficient mice by SARM1 deletion preserves axon morphology without ameliorating behavioral and electrophysiological defects, demonstrating functional decline of lactate‐deprived axons that remain physically intact. These results show a differential requirement for SC‐derived lactate by motor vs. sensory axons, suggesting that lactate availability could influence the course of motor neuron diseases.

Article.Title: Astrocytic <scp>EAAT</scp> ‐2 Upregulation Supports Neuro‐Axonal Homeostasis in Chronic Inflammatory <scp>CNS</scp> Lesions
Article.Authors: Reukauf L.; Margineanu A.; Muinjonov B.; Chen J.; Cui Y.; Rosiewicz K.; Radbruch H.; Munro I.; Alisch M.; Siffrin V.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Neuronal loss in multiple sclerosis (MS) is a key factor in the progression of disability. Axonal degeneration within MS lesions is central to progressive MS pathology, yet its mechanisms are not fully understood. Excess extracellular l‐glutamate (GLUT) is neurotoxic due to overstimulation of GLUT receptors. Excitotoxicity, driven by GLUT, is a suspected contributor to several central nervous system (CNS) diseases. Astrocytic glutamate transporters EAAT‐1 and EAAT‐2 play crucial roles in managing extracellular GLUT, yet their role in chronic MS remains underexplored. Using the animal model experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and advanced microscopy in live anesthetized mice, we examined GLUT‐mediated neurotoxicity and protective mechanisms in chronic CNS lesions. By employing genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors, we visualized extracellular GLUT levels and axonal Ca 2+ dynamics within the live mouse brain during EAE. In acute EAE, extracellular GLUT levels were high, while in chronic lesions, normalized GLUT levels together with sustained EAAT‐2 upregulation were consistent with a protective astrocytic response. EAAT‐2 inhibition in chronic lesions led to higher intra‐axonal Ca 2+ levels and morphological changes consistent with neuroaxonal injury, indicating that EAAT‐2 upregulation may counter excitotoxicity and support neuroprotection. Post‐mortem MS brain tissue analysis provided complementary evidence, showing elevated EAAT‐1 and EAAT‐2 expression in chronic MS lesions with expression patterns varying according to lesion type and cellularity. This study highlights astrocytic mechanisms that may contribute to neuroaxonal protection in MS tissue and suggests targeting GLUT transporters as a promising strategy to limit neurodegeneration in progressive MS.

Article.Title: Single‐Cell Integration of Mouse Models of Autism Reveals Conserved Transcriptomic Signatures of Excitatory‐Inhibitory Imbalance and Glial Dysfunction
Article.Authors: Nani J.; Duque V.; Muotri A.; Mecawi A.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The etiological heterogeneity of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) complicates identifying core molecular mechanisms. We systematically integrated scRNA‐seq data from 11 diverse genetic and environmental mouse ( Mus musculus ) models, encompassing > 300,000 cells across multiple brain regions and developmental stages. Using advanced computational harmonization (RPCA), we identified robust convergent transcriptomic signatures that transcend model‐specific variability. Our findings reveal widespread alterations in neuronal communication pathways, specifically increased excitatory‐inhibitory signaling involving PTN, SLIT, and PTPR pathways. Furthermore, cell–cell communication analysis via NicheNet prioritized ligand‐receptor pairs associated with altered circuit excitability, offering a predictive blueprint of dysregulated intercellular crosstalk. Crucially, we identified significant glial involvement characterized by astrocyte function inhibition, marked by Aqp4 and Kcnj10 downregulation related to impaired water/potassium homeostasis and mature oligodendrocyte metabolic dysregulation through Olig family upregulation and enhanced oxidative phosphorylation. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) significantly overlapped with SFARI‐listed high‐confidence risk genes, particularly within excitatory neuronal subtypes. Comparison with human postmortem single‐nucleus data from the prefrontal and parietal cortices demonstrated conserved signatures related to impaired synaptic protein synthesis (GRIN2B, CAMK2A) and oligodendrocyte‐mediated neurodevelopmental deficits (NRXN, DLGAP). This study confirms that E/I imbalance and glial dysfunction are universal cellular pathologies in ASD, providing a robust, large‐scale reference for identifying novel therapeutic targets with single‐cell resolution.

Article.Title: A Müller Glia‐Retinal Pigment Epithelium Apical Network Surrounding Cone Outer Segments in Fish and Mouse
Article.Authors: Sharkova M.; Housset M.; Boudreau S.; Dworkind C.; Amidian S.; Cayouette M.; Hocking J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Homeostasis of the vertebrate retina critically depends on two non‐neuronal cell populations, Müller glia and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Their opposing apical surfaces delineate the subretinal space, a specialized extracellular compartment housing the light‐detecting outer segments of photoreceptors. Although the individual interactions between these supporting cells and photoreceptors have been extensively characterized, Müller glia and the RPE have long been presumed to remain physically separate in the healthy retina. Here, we challenge this assumption and present a revised model of the subretinal space architecture based on detailed FIB‐SEM and confocal microscopy imaging of the zebrafish and mouse outer retina. We demonstrate that both Müller glia and the RPE extend long apical processes that not only contact one another but also collectively ensheath cone outer segments, forming a previously unrecognized tripartite interface. These contact regions are highly elaborated in fish and, while comparatively sparser, are still present in mouse. Developmentally, the growth and interdigitation of Müller glial and RPE apical processes follow the emergence of the outer segment in both species and, in mouse, coincides with the onset of visual function. Although glial–RPE interactions are enriched at cone‐associated sites, their presence is not strictly dependent on cone localization in either species, suggesting they represent a fundamental feature of the vertebrate subretinal space. Together, these findings revise our understanding of the subretinal space cytoarchitecture and reveal a previously unappreciated structural interaction between Müller glia, RPE, and photoreceptors that is conserved across vertebrate species.

Article.Title: <scp>CD47</scp> – <scp>SIRPα</scp> Axis as a Target for Neuroprotection
Article.Authors: Gómez‐López A.; Manich G.; Penas C.; Pampalona J.; Villacampa N.; Almolda B.; Viennois E.; Rojas S.; González B.; Castellano B.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Microglial “Off” signaling is crucial for maintaining microglia in a homeostatic state through the interaction of “Off” neuronal ligands with their corresponding microglial receptors. Dysregulation of “Off” signaling has been reported in both acute and chronic neuroinflammation; however, the influence of inflammatory mediators on this pathway remains underexplored. Here, we investigated whether chronic IL‐6 or IL‐10 overexpression modulates microglia–neuron “Off” signaling after FNA, thereby accounting for the previously observed differences in facial motoneuron (FMN) survival and microglial reactivity in transgenic mouse models (GFAP‐IL6Tg and GFAP‐IL10Tg). To this end, we examined the expression of the neuronal “Off” ligands CD200, CX3CL1, CD47, and CD22, as well as their corresponding microglial “Off” receptors CD200R, CX3CR1, SIRP‐α, and CD45 in non‐lesioned and axotomized GFAP‐IL6Tg, GFAP‐IL10Tg, and WT mice across multiple time points. Our analyses revealed the dynamic regulation of “Off” signaling in both neurons and microglia during microgliosis and FMN phagocytosis and showed temporally restricted strain‐specific differences in CD47 expression across genotypes. Chronic IL‐6 overproduction promoted a more phagocytic microglial phenotype, defined by downregulation of SIRPα and CX3CR1 alongside upregulated CD45 in the microglial population. In contrast, chronic IL‐10 overproduction did not alter the expression of microglial “Off” receptors but induced an IL‐10 dependent accelerated upregulation of neuronal CD47. Our findings highlight the CD47‐SIRPα axis as a key regulator of FMN death via microglial phagocytosis and emphasize IL‐10's neuroprotective potential role through enhanced neuronal CD47 signaling. Overall, this work positions the CD47‐SIRPα axis as a potential therapeutic target to mitigate neuroinflammation‐induced neuronal loss.

Article.Title: Microglial Labeling in Mouse Spinal Cord Injury: A Review of Timing, Efficacy, and Specificity
Article.Authors: Colbert R.; Di Stefano J.; Dooley D.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) is a complex and disabling condition with no curative therapy currently available. The mechanical damage of the primary injury phase is followed and exacerbated by a secondary injury phase, characterized by the release of free radicals and pro‐inflammatory cytokines that lead to chronic inflammation. Microglia, as the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, play a critical role in orchestrating this inflammatory response. Studying their dynamics after SCI not only deepens our understanding of injury pathology but also advances the development of microglia‐targeted immunotherapies. However, trauma‐induced transcriptional and phenotypic changes mean that markers used to identify homeostatic microglia may be unreliable when applied to their reactive counterparts. Another major challenge lies within discriminating resident microglia from infiltrating monocyte‐derived macrophages (MDM), which permeate the blood‐spinal cord barrier (BSCB) after injury. In this review, we examine three key variables for selecting appropriate strategies for labeling microglia in mice: (i) time (in relation to injury); (ii) efficacy (within the chosen murine SCI model); and (iii) specificity (to microglia). We discuss the transcriptional landscape of murine microglia pre‐injury and its alteration post‐injury, evaluate the strengths and limitations of commonly used markers, and highlight emerging tools and approaches for studying microglia in preclinical murine SCI research.

Article.Title: Ifi27l2a Facilitates the Recruitment of Pathogenic T Cells by Retinal Microglia in the Initiation Phase of Experimental Autoimmune Uveoretinitis
Article.Authors: Gao W.; Wu P.; Xie K.; Zhou P.; Jin B.; Zhu H.; Li F.; Wang Y.; Lei B.; Jin X.; Du L.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The mechanisms by which pathogenic T cells enter the immune‐privileged retina at the onset of uveitis remain unclear. To identify regulatory targets that promote retinal inflammation, we established an experimental autoimmune uveoretinitis (EAU) model by immunizing C57BL/6J mice with IRBP 651–670 and dynamically evaluated retinal inflammation after induction; fundus lesions were prominent, with the first 14 days representing the initiation phase, Days 14–28 the amplification phase, Days 28–35 the peak phase, and Days 35–42 the regression phase. We characterized retinal cellular alterations from the pre‐inflammatory stage to the peak stage using single‐cell transcriptomic analysis, and found that retinal immune cells changed in parallel with EAU severity, while immune‐cell interactions were strongest on Day 14, especially between microglia and T cells through multiple chemokine‐related pathways. We then identified key cell populations and candidate targets through integrated analyses and functional validation, and Ifi27l2a emerged as a core gene associated with inflammatory and immune responses in retinal microglia on Day 14. In vitro knockdown of Ifi27l2a in LPS‐activated BV‐2 cells reduced inflammatory mediator production and abolished Th1/Th17 induction. In vivo targeting of Ifi27l2a attenuated EAU severity and restored the balance of T‐cell subsets. These findings indicate that microglia are highly activated before retinal inflammation becomes prominent and that Ifi27l2a regulates this early pathogenic process.

Article.Title: Neuronal Overexpression of Glycogen Synthase Kinase‐3β Accelerates Age‐Related Glial, Vascular, and Inflammatory Remodeling of the Murine Dentate Gyrus
Article.Authors: Prádanos‐Senén A.; Rodríguez‐Moreno C.; Llorens‐Martín M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN)—the lifelong generation of new neurons in the dentate gyrus (DG)—depends on the integrity of the subgranular zone (SGZ) neurogenic niche, which comprises astrocytes, microglia, oligodendroglial cells, and a dense vascular network. Although AHN declines during aging and is impaired in Alzheimer's disease (AD), the cell‐type‐specific alterations within the DG underlying this decline remain poorly characterized. Given the critical role of glycogen synthase kinase‐3β (GSK‐3β) in AD pathogenesis and AHN regulation, we studied how the overexpression of this kinase in dentate granule cells (DGCs) remodels the cellular and vascular composition of the DG throughout life. Using a layer‐resolved approach (SGZ vs. granule cell layer (GCL)) and mice of distinct ages (4–30 months), we quantified glial densities, cellular contacts, vascular architecture, and cytokine profiles in wild‐type (WT) and GSK‐3β‐overexpressing (GSK‐3β‐OE) mice. In the former, aging was associated with a layer‐specific reorganization, characterized by progressive astrocyte loss in the SGZ, midlife increases in GCL microglia, a reduction in oligodendroglial progenitors, and enhanced SGZ vascularization. GSK‐3β overexpression accelerated age‐related changes, triggering premature SGZ astrocyte depletion by 4 months, broader disruption featuring reduced SGZ microglial and mature oligodendrocyte densities accompanied by increased microglial morphological complexity, vascular restructuring, and a shift toward a pro‐inflammatory environment. Therefore, neuronal GSK‐3β overexpression promoted a non‐cell‐autonomous reorganization of the DG, consistent with premature remodeling of the neurogenic niche. These results provide mechanistic insights into AHN failure in AD and point to the modulation of GSK‐3β activity as a strategy to preserve DG integrity.

Article.Title: Red Fluorescent Labeling of Myelin by Membrane‐Targeted <scp>tdTomato</scp> in Transgenic Mouse Lines
Article.Authors: Reinert A.; Winkler U.; Goebbels S.; Komarek L.; Möbius W.; Zanker H.; Schoknecht K.; Bornschein G.; Schmidt H.; Fledrich R.; Stassart R.; Hirrlinger P.; Nave K.; Werner H.; Saab A.; Hirrlinger J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Myelin is a highly complex membranous structure wrapped around axons by oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells in the central and peripheral nervous system, respectively. Fluorescent labeling is widely used to study the structure and dynamics of myelin. Combining structural with functional imaging requires labeling of myelin with red fluorescence, as many functional sensors, including Ca 2+ indicators and genetically encoded metabolite sensors, fluoresce in the green spectral range. However, in vivo tools enabling red fluorescent labeling of myelinating cells and their myelin sheaths remain limited. Here, we generated a set of seven transgenic mouse lines expressing a membrane‐targeted variant of the red fluorescent protein tdTomato in myelinating oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells throughout the nervous system. The mouse lines provide a variety of expression patterns ranging from wide‐spread labeling of myelin to a rather sparse expression, the latter enabling visualization of individual oligodendrocytes and their associated myelin sheaths. In the peripheral nervous system, the pattern of fluorescence in sciatic nerves indicates predominant localization of tdTomato to non‐compact myelin compartments including the inner and outer tongues, paranodal loops and Schmidt‐Lanterman incisures. In summary, our work provides a set of novel mouse lines with myelin labeled by red fluorescence, which are compatible with diverse imaging modalities in the green spectral range enabling integrated structural and functional imaging.

Article.Title: Schwann Cell‐Specific <scp>ATG7</scp> ‐Dependent Autophagy Protects Myelin in a Mouse Model of Krabbe Disease
Article.Authors: Dhimal N.; Sidharth A.; Zhang J.; Rudra T.; Hurley E.; Paez P.; Sim F.; Shin D.; Feltri M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Krabbe disease (KD) is a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by severe peripheral demyelination caused by mutations in galactosylceramidase (GALC), leading to the accumulation of galactosylceramide and psychosine. Although psychosine toxicity is central to KD pathology, additional mechanisms likely contribute to myelin dysfunction. Because Schwann cells (SCs) play a critical role in myelin maintenance, and GALC deficiency disrupts lysosomal function, we hypothesized that autophagy is altered in SCs during KD progression. Using a SC‐specific Galc conditional knockout ( Galc SC cKO) mouse model, we identified early changes in autophagy‐related protein levels and increased autophagosome abundance during the pre‐symptomatic phase, prior to detectable myelin abnormalities. To assess whether autophagy contributes to disease progression, we selectively deleted Atg7 , an essential regulator of canonical autophagy, in SCs. Atg7 deletion alone did not affect myelin or behavior, but its loss in Galc SC cKO mice markedly worsened disease severity. Atg7‐Galc SC cKO mice exhibited significantly thinner myelin and pronounced deficits in motor performance and nerve conduction, accompanied by altered steady‐state levels of autophagy‐associated proteins and functional decline. Notably, Atg7 deletion in Galc SC cKO mice did not further increase macrophage abundance, suggesting that the worsened myelin phenotype occurs without additional macrophage recruitment at this stage. Together, these findings demonstrate that autophagy‐associated changes occur early in KD and ATG7‐dependent pathways play a protective role during disease progression. Modulating ATG7‐dependent pathways may therefore warrant further investigation as a strategy to support myelin maintenance in KD and related lysosomal disorders.

Article.Title: Myelin Maintenance and Addition Regulate Synaptic Plasticity in the Adult Mouse Cortex
Article.Authors: Pepper R.; Makowiecki K.; Pitman K.; Ricci R.; Nicoli A.; Nguyen P.; Blizzard C.; Emery B.; Cullen C.; Young K.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Myelin has the capacity to affect synapse number or plasticity across the lifespan. We report that disrupting oligodendrocyte (OL) and myelin maintenance from P57 ( Plp‐CreER T2 :: Myrf fl/fl mice) induces myelin loss and impairs action potential conduction and gross motor performance. By studying sparsely labeled layer V pyramidal neurons in the primary motor cortex of P57 + 60 mice, we determined that apical and basal dendritic spine densities were normal; however, more were large, stable mushroom spines that generated larger amplitude miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents. When we instead prevented OL and myelin addition from P57 ( Pdgfrα‐CreER:: Myrf fl/fl mice), action potential conduction velocity, gross motor performance, and spine densities were normal; however, basal dendritic spine morphology was changed. Without adult myelination, the basal dendrites of P57 + 60 mice retained the morphological characteristics of dendrites in P57 + 0 mice, which have a higher proportion of thin, plastic spines. These data indicate that existing myelin imposes limits on the proportion of spines that become mushroom spines, allowing neurons to remain plastic, while adult myelination is required for spine stabilization within the basal but not apical dendritic compartment. These data show that myelin regulates synaptic plasticity within the motor circuit and offer a potential mechanism by which myelination can influence motor skill learning and/or recall.

Article.Title: Molecular Control of Neural Stem Cell Quiescence in the Adult Zebrafish Telencephalon: Established Mechanisms and an Integrative Hypothesis
Article.Authors: Hoareau M.; Diotel N.; Rastegar S.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The zebrafish telencephalon is an excellent model for adult neurogenesis under physiological and regenerative conditions, as many pathways regulating neural stem cell behavior are conserved with mammalian neurogenic niches. Resident radial glial cells (RGCs) serve as neural stem cells in the adult brain and are readily accessible in vivo, because forebrain eversion repositions the ventricular zone to the dorsal surface. Recent studies have revealed substantial heterogeneity among RGCs, including activation‐primed cells and deeply quiescent states during homeostasis. Here, we first review the evidence that four mechanisms control quiescence in pallial RGCs: Notch3‐mediated lateral inhibition, the neuronal bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)‐Id1 axis, the nuclear receptor Nr2f1b, and the secreted factor Midkine‐a. The evidence supporting them is unequal, and we state its level for each before asking whether they act together. Notch‐mediated lateral inhibition and neuronal BMP‐Id1 signaling converge on her4.1 , the clearest documented interaction among them, whereas Nr2f1b establishes a deeper dormancy program that resists Notch and BMP inhibition and protects a reserve stem cell pool. Midkine‐a is proposed to reinforce quiescence, pending functional validation. Finally, we propose as a hypothesis that these mechanisms act as partially redundant inputs whose relative contributions determine quiescence depth and vary along the antero‐posterior axis of the pallium. Together, these findings reframe quiescence as a spectrum of actively maintained conditions rather than a passive default state. These mechanisms are conserved across vertebrates, with implications for understanding why mammalian neural stem cell pools decline with age and injury.

Article.Title: Photobiomodulation Ameliorates Alexander Disease Through <scp>AMPK</scp> / <scp>mTOR</scp> ‐Mediated Mitophagy
Article.Authors: Qiu N.; Zhang J.; Yi H.; Dong S.; Han L.; Feng Z.; Gao S.; Shi J.; Liu J.; Wu Y.; Wei X.; Wei Y.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Alexander disease (AxD) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the pathological accumulation of Rosenthal fibers (RFs) and astrocytic inflammation. Despite advances in elucidating its genetic basis, effective therapeutic strategies remain limited. Recent studies indicate that astrocytes in AxD exhibit excessive mitochondrial fragmentation, which may cause mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammatory response. Photobiomodulation (PBM) has been shown to improve mitochondrial function and exert anti‐inflammatory effects, suggesting it may be a promising candidate for the treatment of AxD. Here, we report that exposure to 1070‐nm infrared light exerts therapeutic efficacy in AxD. Specifically, using the astrocytes derived from AxD patients and a mouse model of AxD, we demonstrate that PBM regulates AMPK/mTOR signaling and promotes mitophagy, thereby attenuating reactive oxygen species production from fragmented mitochondria and subsequent inflammatory status. This study suggests PBM may serve as a novel, non‐invasive therapeutic approach for the treatment of AxD.

Article.Title: Macrophage‐Derived, Rather Than Microglial, Cathepsin B Exacerbates Brain Injury After Ischemic Stroke
Article.Authors: Kong W.; Li H.; Wu Z.; Hayashi Y.; Nakanishi H.; Zhao J.; Zhang Y.; Qing H.; Quan Z.; Ni J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Neuroimmune responses critically shape the progression and outcome of ischemic stroke, yet the cell type–specific roles of myeloid populations remain incompletely defined. Cathepsin B (CatB), a lysosomal cysteine protease, has been implicated in neuroinflammation, but its contribution from distinct myeloid subsets is unclear. Transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) was induced in wild‐type and CatB‐deficient mice. Bone marrow chimeras were generated to selectively delete CatB in peripheral myeloid cells or resident microglia. Infarct severity, mortality, myeloid phenotypes, and transcriptional programs were assessed using flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and bulk and cell type–resolved RNA sequencing. CatB expression was markedly upregulated in ischemic brain myeloid cells, with higher levels in infiltrating macrophages than in microglia. Selective deletion of CatB in peripheral myeloid cells, but not in microglia, significantly reduced infarct size, mortality, and pro‐inflammatory gene expression after tMCAO. Transcriptomic analyses showed suppression of inflammatory pathways and preservation of neuronal signaling in mice lacking macrophage‐derived CatB. Cell type–resolved RNA sequencing revealed that CatB deficiency shifted infiltrating macrophages toward a pro‐resolving, tissue‐repair phenotype characterized by increased expression of M2‐associated genes, including Chil3. Consistently, CatB‐deficient macrophages displayed enhanced pro‐resolving polarization in response to ischemic neuron–derived signals in vitro. CatB was also elevated in circulating Ly6C + monocytes after stroke. These findings identify peripheral myeloid–derived CatB as a key driver of ischemic brain injury and a potential therapeutic target.

Article.Title: 4‐Methylumbelliferone Restores Age‐Related Changes in Perineuronal Nets, Memory, and Neuroinflammation
Article.Authors: Cimpean A.; Mizerakova J.; Martinez‐Varea N.; Marekova D.; Machova Urdzikova L.; Fawcett J.; Jendelova P.; Kwok J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Aging‐associated cognitive decline is closely linked to dysregulated glial activity and chronic neuroinflammation, which together constrain neuronal plasticity. Astrocytes and microglia are key regulators of the brain extracellular matrix (ECM), including perineuronal nets (PNNs), whose accumulation during aging contributes to reduced synaptic flexibility. Targeting ECM–glia interactions therefore represents a promising strategy to modulate neuroinflammatory and plasticity‐related processes. Here, we investigated the effects of long‐term oral administration of 4‐methylumbelliferone (4‐MU), an inhibitor of hyaluronan and chondroitin sulfate synthesis, on glial reactivity, ECM remodeling, and cognitive function in aged mice (20–22 months). Aging was associated with PNN remodeling alongside pronounced astrocytic and microglial activation and infiltration of peripheral immune cells. Chronic 4‐MU treatment reduced PNN accumulation to levels observed in younger (10‐month‐old) mice, indicating effective ECM remodeling. Notably, this was accompanied by a marked attenuation of astrocyte and microglial activation and a reduction in immune cell infiltration, suggesting a broad normalization of the neuroinflammatory milieu. Functionally, these glia‐associated changes were paralleled by improved recognition memory, with treated aged mice performing at or above the level of younger controls. Long‐term 4‐MU administration was well tolerated, with no evident adverse effects. Together, our findings identify ECM modulation as a mechanism to regulate glial reactivity and neuroimmune interactions in the aging brain. By targeting hyaluronan‐dependent pathways, 4‐MU links ECM remodeling to suppression of neuroinflammation and restoration of cognitive function, highlighting its therapeutic potential in age‐related neurodegenerative processes.

Article.Title: A Computational Framework for Myelin as a Regulator of Temporal Integration, Neuronal Excitability, and Synaptic Plasticity
Article.Authors: O'Sullivan D.; Pariz A.; Trotter D.; Al Dahhan N.; Knowles J.; Frankland P.; Mabbott D.; Lefebvre J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Myelin regulates neural signaling not only by enabling fast conduction but also by dynamically tuning axonal conduction velocity (CV) and thereby shaping spike timing. While activity‐dependent myelination is thought to optimize neural communication, how changes in myelin translate into altered single‐cell dynamics and plasticity remains unclear. Using a computational modeling approach, we show that disruptions of axonal CV reorganize presynaptic input correlations, leading to systematic changes in postsynaptic excitability, excitation–inhibition balance, and spike‐timing‐dependent plasticity. By spanning CV regimes associated with healthy myelination, demyelination, and excessive myelination, our simulations illustrate how both deficient and excessive CV could induce maladaptive neuronal dynamics. The incorporation of firing‐rate homeostasis into our models further suggests distinct neuronal dynamic consequences for acute versus chronic myelin disruption. Ultimately, these results suggest that axonal CV may serve as a key mechanistic link between myelin plasticity and neural computation, offering a principled framework to interpret the functional consequences of myelin dysregulation in health and disease.

Article.Title: Influence of Small Changes in Intermolecular Distances on Results of Interaction Energy Decomposition for Stacking Interactions, Hydrogen Bonds, and Antiparallel Interactions
Article.Authors: Blagojević Filipović J.; Zarić S.
Article.Abstract: A SAPT (Symmetry-Adapted Perturbation Theory) decomposition analysis was performed for various types of noncovalent interactions (stacking, hydrogen bonds, and antiparallel) for various distances of interacting fragments. Although the total interaction energy does not significantly change within the small range around the optimal distance, the energy contributions can significantly change in some systems. This is particularly pronounced for stacking interactions, while for hydrogen bonds and antiparallel interactions the energy contributions do not significantly change around the optimal distance. Thus, the nature of interactions should be carefully interpreted, as small alterations in distances between the interacting fragments can sometimes lead to significant changes in energy contributions, especially for stacking interactions.

Article.Title: Novel Palladium(II) β-Diketonate Complexes: Synthesis, Dual Antimicrobial/Anticancer Activity, and Molecular Insights into DNA/Protein Interactions
Article.Authors: Trifunović Stevanović M.; Joksimović N.; Petronijević J.; Stojanović S.; Đorđević S.; Stanković J.; Bufan B.; Božić D.
Article.Abstract: This study reports the synthesis and biological evaluation of four novel palladium(II) complexes (B1–B4) with O,O-bidentate β-diketo ester ligands. Spectroscopic characterization confirmed their structures, while biological assays revealed substituent-dependent activity. Complexes B3 and B4 showed the most consistent antimicrobial activity, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 312–1200 μM across the tested microorganisms. B3 exhibited the highest antiproliferative potency, with IC50 values of 2.3, 5.2, and 5.4 μM against K-562, HeLa, and HaCaT cells, respectively. However, its selectivity varied with the cell model, reaching a selectivity index (SI) of 5.17 against K-562 cells relative to MRC-5 fibroblasts and 2.35 relative to HaCaT cells. B2 showed a more moderate activity profile, with some selectivity towards K-562 cells. Flow-cytometric analysis revealed increased sub-G0/G1 populations following treatment, consistent with the induction of apoptosis. Biophysical assays and molecular docking indicated structure-dependent interactions with DNA, while fluorescence studies revealed differences in the apparent binding affinities of the complexes toward human serum albumin (HSA). These findings highlight the influence of ligand structure on the biological activity and biomolecular interactions of palladium(II) complexes, identifying B3 as the most promising candidate for further investigation based on its antiproliferative potency and selectivity.

Article.Title: Platinum-Induced Toxicity and Zinc-Based Interventions: A Systematic Review of Preclinical Evidence
Article.Authors: Tseriotis V.; Ampazis D.; Karachrysafi S.; Papamitsou T.; Kouvelas D.; Stergiou K.; Fouskas V.; Pavliis P.; Hatzibougias D.; Chatzianagnosti S.; Dimaki E.; Konstantinidis I.; Tsiptsios D.; Lallas K.; Sič A.; Keramidas V.; Tastanis C.; Papadopoulou K.; Cheva A.; Arnaoutoglou M.
Article.Abstract: Zinc may mitigate platinum-induced toxicity through antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects. We systematically reviewed preclinical in vivo evidence on zinc-based interventions, focusing on organ protection, mechanisms and antitumour efficacy. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and supplementary sources were searched for studies in rats and mice. Risk of bias was assessed using SYRCLE, and the findings were synthesised narratively. Database searches identified 1552 records; 25 studies were included following database and supplementary screening. The risk of bias was frequently unclear for sequence generation, allocation concealment and blinding. Most studies investigated cisplatin; fewer evaluated carboplatin, oxaliplatin or combination chemotherapy. Zinc interventions included salts, dietary supplementation, organic complexes and nanoformulations, predominantly administered before platinum exposure. Protective findings were reported across renal, reproductive, nervous, hepatic, haematopoietic and cardiovascular systems. Proposed mechanisms included metallothionein induction, enhanced antioxidant defences and modulation of inflammation and apoptosis. Heterogeneity precluded conclusions about formulation superiority. Limited tumour-bearing evidence indicated that zinc-induced metallothionein may reduce cisplatin activity, whereas bismuth zinc citrate preserved tumour control within the tested model. Methodological weaknesses, heterogeneity and scarce tumour-bearing evidence limit confidence in efficacy and oncological safety. These findings support further preclinical investigation rather than clinical implementation.

Article.Title: Quorum Quenching and Quorum-Sensing Interference in Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Molecular Mechanisms, Host Protection, and Translational Barriers
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Zou W.; Pei L.
Article.Abstract: Quorum sensing (QS) coordinates virulence expression, biofilm-associated behavior, and persistence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, making its signaling network a potential target for adjunctive anti-virulence therapy. Quorum quenching (QQ) directly degrades, modifies, or sequesters signaling molecules, whereas broader QS interference encompasses inhibition of signal synthesis, receptor antagonism, and disruption of downstream regulatory interactions. Experimental studies of N-acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL)-degrading enzymes and PqsR antagonists have demonstrated suppression of selected virulence-associated phenotypes, with several infection models showing reductions in host injury or persistence-associated outcomes. The PqsE–RhlR regulatory interface has gained substantial molecular and genetic support as a distinct intervention target, but its pharmacological development remains limited. Responses to QS interference vary with bacterial strain, regulatory network adaptation, environmental conditions, and infection stage. Reductions in virulence-factor production or biofilm biomass do not consistently correspond to bacterial clearance or host protection. Available human studies involving agents with proposed QS-modulatory activity have not established clinical benefits specifically attributable to QS inhibition. Clinical translation requires validated target engagement, efficacy assessment in established and polymicrobial infections, and characterization of delivery, pharmacological exposure, safety, and resistance evolution.

Article.Title: Sugar Depletion in Korean Pine Infected with Cronartium ribicola, Alongside Metabolic Reprogramming by the T6P–Tre Signaling Module
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Wang B.; Yu Q.; Zhang R.; Tan B.; Feng Z.; Wang F.; Li D.
Article.Abstract: In diseased Korean pine trees (Pinus koraiensis), Cronartium ribicola develops aecia only in the bole, where sugar is initially sufficient. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying sugar depletion in diseased Korean pine trees remain unelucidated, hindering sugar-targeted control strategies. Focusing on host responses, this study integrated metabolomics, transcriptomics, and targeted glycomics based on spatial partitioning to investigate sugar metabolic reprogramming in the bole of diseased pines. Multi-omics revealed severe sugar depletion in the blister area, which was significantly correlated with relative C. ribicola DNA level. However, the transcription of sugar synthesis genes was upregulated, while sugar degradation genes were downregulated, indicating decoupling between sugar metabolism and transcription. Concurrently, T6P–Tre-centered reprogramming was identified: Pktppd and Pktpp4, encoding enzymes that convert T6P into Tre, were downregulated, leading to elevated T6P and reduced Tre levels. This T6P–Tre shift likely acts as a signal to activate genes related to sugar accumulation in response to sugar depletion, thereby explaining the observed transcriptional-metabolic decoupling. Targeting the T6P–Tre module to modulate host sugar allocation and restrict sugar availability to the pathogen may offer a novel strategy for the targeted control of Korean pine blister rust (KPBR).

Article.Title: Structural and Biophysical Profiling of HLA Class II Mismatches Using AlphaFold 3: A Computational Study
Article.Authors: Bardash V.; Samchuk O.; Tolstyak Y.; Demydenko H.; Sklyarov E.
Article.Abstract: Conventional linear eplet-matching algorithms (HLAMatchmaker, HLAMM) evaluate primary sequence polymorphisms across human leukocyte antigen (HLA) loci without integrating three-dimensional (3D) steric accessibility and local physicochemical constraints. Here, we developed an exploratory computational antigenicity pipeline using AlphaFold 3 to evaluate 10,000 simulated European donor–recipient pairs across pre-computed, full-length HLA class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) and heterodimeric class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) complexes modeled in a standardized peptide-free conformation. Candidate eplets were sequentially screened using a spatial solvent-accessible surface area threshold (SASA ≥ 10.0 Å2) and an empirical biophysical exclusion gate (5th percentile of absolute net charge |Qnet| ≥ 0.3326 e and hydropathy Htotal ≥ −7.265, calibrated on N = 170 antibody-verified eplets). Across the simulated cohort (n = 10,000), filtration reduced median [Q1; Q3] eplet counts from 19 [12; 26] to 17 [10; 23] for HLA-A, 22 [15; 29] to 18 [12; 24] for HLA-B, 12 [7; 17] to 10 [7; 15] for HLA-C, 15 [10; 19] to 11 [7; 14] for HLA-DR, 12 [6; 17] to 9 [4; 14] for HLA-DQ, and 7 [3; 12] to 6 [2; 9] for HLA-DP. Component ablation demonstrated that 3D steric accessibility (SASA ≥ 10.0 Å2) accounted for the vast majority of eplet exclusions—87.8% in HLA-DR and HLA-DP and 58.2% to 69.1% across HLA-DQ and class I loci—whereas the registry-calibrated biophysical gate acted as a secondary refinement. Within the subset of simulated pairs initially exceeding the arbitrary ≥10-eplet linear cutoff, the proportion dropping below 10 eplets after filtering was low for class I (HLA-A: 4.4%, HLA-B: 8.0%, HLA-C: 13.2%) but substantially higher for class II high-load subsets: HLA-DQ (21.8%), HLA-DR (26.0%), and HLA-DP (33.7% of 3693 baseline high-load pairs). Furthermore, class II loci, particularly HLA-DP, exhibited weakened covariance between heuristic charge and hydropathy indices that persisted after 1:1 count-matched subsampling (ρmatched = −0.268) and partial correlation adjustment (ρpartial = −0.385). This dual-filter pipeline defines a restricted mathematical subset of spatially accessible and biophysically suprathreshold candidate eplets. Because this is a hypothesis-generating in silico framework, multicenter retrospective registry analyses and prospective clinical trials evaluating de novo donor-specific antibody formation, biopsy-proven rejection, and allograft survival are strictly required before clinical translation.

Article.Title: Endocrine Signaling and Tissue Remodeling in Gynecomastia: Implications for Treatment Response
Article.Authors: Deng J.; Tong S.; Liu S.; Zhou H.; Ren M.
Article.Abstract: To critically synthesize evidence on treatment response in gynecomastia using a framework that distinguishes biological response, structural response, and patient-important benefit. We searched PubMed, PubMed Central, and targeted journals through 11 September 2026. Priority was given to gynecomastia-specific human studies; evidence from other breast systems, animal models, and general biomarker methodology was treated as indirect. The randomized anastrozole trial showed an endocrine effect but did not demonstrate superiority over placebo on the prespecified structural endpoint. Receptor expression in surgical specimens provides biological plausibility but does not establish receptor functionality, endocrine dependence, or predictive value. Stromal composition may influence lesion regression, but this remains a hypothesis requiring direct testing. Ultrasonography and elastography may support pretreatment characterization, but current studies do not validate imaging features as surrogates for fibrosis or endocrine responsiveness. Gynecomastia-derived organoids offer a disease-relevant model for functional studies, although donor numbers are small and endocrine responsiveness, cellular representativeness, and reproducibility across patients require further evaluation remain uncertain. Biological response, structural response, and patient-important benefit need not occur together or in a fixed sequence. Further research should link tissue and model findings to pretreatment markers, compare treatment benefits, and establish clinical utility before marker-guided care.

Article.Title: Curcumin Sensitizes Colorectal Cancer Cells to TRAIL-Mediated Apoptosis
Article.Authors: Rimondi E.; Manfredini M.; Nigro F.; Gonelli A.; Milani D.; Celeghini C.; Previati M.; Marcuzzi A.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major clinical challenge due to resistance to conventional cell death-inducing therapies. TRAIL selectively induces apoptosis in cancer cells via death receptors, but its effectiveness in preclinical models is limited by tumor resistance mechanisms. Curcumin, a natural polyphenol, modulates multiple survival and apoptotic pathways and has been proposed as a sensitizing agent to overcome TRAIL resistance. Here, we investigated the combinatorial effects of TRAIL and curcumin in the HCT116 colorectal cancer cell model. Cells were treated with TRAIL, curcumin, or their combination for 24 and 48 h, evaluating apoptosis, viability, and underlying mechanisms. Curcumin significantly enhanced TRAIL-induced apoptosis (p < 0.0001) and further reduced MTT-derived metabolic activity (p < 0.01) compared with TRAIL treatment alone. This effect remained evident after 48 h, although the stability and persistence of TRAIL activity were not directly assessed. Mechanistically, combined treatment enhanced PARP cleavage, γ-H2AX phosphorylation, and BAX and Caspase-3 cleavage, while downregulating anti-apoptotic IAP family members. Notably, cotreatment also promoted pyroptosis, shown by characteristic morphological changes (p < 0.0001) and increased Gasdermin-E cleavage. These findings indicate that curcumin sensitizes CRC cells to TRAIL by engaging both apoptotic and pyroptotic pathways, suggesting a potential approach to counteract both TRAIL and multidrug resistance in colorectal cancer.

Article.Authors: Sinitsina E.; Imatdinov I.; Tuyrin V.; Shipovalov A.; Zaykovskaya A.; Osinkina I.; Yanshin A.; Radchenko N.; Ryzhykau Y.; Sudarev V.; Kuklina D.; Onkhonova G.; Ivleva E.; Agafonov A.; Gladysheva A.
Article.Abstract: The continuous evolution of SARS-CoV-2 necessitates broadly neutralizing antibodies for robust therapeutics. In this study, we isolated 1824 single B cells from a COVID-19 convalescent donor and obtained 91 pairs of nucleotide sequences potentially encoding VH/VL domains. Among this panel, we identified DEV_K57 as a broadly neutralizing human IgG1 antibody targeting the SARS-CoV-2 RBD. DEV_K57 exhibited in vitro neutralization breadth against diverse variants, demonstrating subnanomolar IC50 values. This in vitro efficacy was translated in vivo. In a Syrian hamster model of SARS-CoV-2 Delta infection, DEV_K57 significantly reduced viral RNA and infectious titers in both the upper and lower respiratory tracts, conferring a favorable safety profile with minimal histopathological damage. To elucidate its mechanism, we performed comprehensive biophysical and structural analyses. Biolayer interferometry revealed a high picomolar binding affinity to the RBD Delta. Furthermore, size-exclusion chromatography coupled with small-angle X-ray scattering and computational modeling uncovered a unique, stable dimeric architecture of the DEV_K57 Fab-RBD complex in solution, with a binding interface distinct from previously characterized structures. These findings underscore the value of rapid antibody isolation for pandemic preparedness against future emerging biological threats.

Article.Title: Phylogenetic Analysis of Rare Crepis Species of the Crimean Flora (C. purpurea (Willd.) M. Bieb. and C. callicephala Juz.) Through Plastid Genome Reconstruction
Article.Authors: Emirsaliev A.; Afonnikov D.; Mitrofanova I.; Salina E.; Kochetov A.
Article.Abstract: One of the largest genera within the Cichorieae tribe of the Asteraceae family is Crepis, comprising ∼200 species. The diversity of numerous local forms is of interest for adaptation studies. There are two rare closely related species within the Lagoseris clade of the genus Crepis which occupy highly divergent habitats—C. callicephala Juz. and C. purpurea (Willd.) M. Bieb.—both occurring in the Crimean Peninsula. The habitats differ in environmental conditions and are isolated by location and altitude, restricting opportunities for gamete exchange. The species are similar morphologically but demonstrate different phenological patterns, representing a notable natural model for investigating how isolation and habitat conditions may shape genetic differentiation and local adaptation. We sequenced the total DNA of C. callicephala and C. purpurea. Relying on both short-read and long-read data, we assembled plastid genomes of these species and reconstructed the phylogeny of the subtribe Crepidinae. The assembled plastid genomes are 149,980 bp (C. callicephala) and 150,007 bp (C. purpurea), and the two species were recovered as a closely related pair on a long common branch within the sampled Crepidinae. We also noted an unusual structural rearrangement in the rbcL–psaI locus shared by the studied accessions of both species, affecting the accD gene (encoding the β-carboxyltransferase subunit of acetyl-CoA carboxylase), which has not been reported in other members of Cichorioideae. Together with the shifts in the inverted-repeat boundaries, these features provide molecular data relevant to the taxonomic status and relationship of C. callicephala and C. purpurea.

Article.Title: Multiple Myeloma Measurable Residual Disease: Spotting Three Different Detection Methods
Article.Authors: Tartaglione S.; Tagliaferro M.; Scerpa M.; Basile V.; D’Ambrosio F.; Natali P.; Marino M.; Equitani F.; Maurillo L.; Basile U.
Article.Abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) is the second most common hematologic malignancy. It is still largely incurable, but treatment has changed greatly with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, monoclonal and bispecific antibodies, autologous stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T cells. Most patients now achieve a complete response. As a result, conventional criteria, based on monoclonal protein, serum free light chains and bone marrow plasma cell counts, can no longer distinguish different depths of response. Measurable residual disease (MRD) has therefore become the reference endpoint. The International Myeloma Working Group defines MRD negativity as the absence of clonal plasma cells among at least 100,000 bone marrow cells. MRD negativity predicts progression-free and overall survival, independently of cytogenetic risk and disease stage. The US Food and Drug Administration has also accepted it as an early endpoint for accelerated approval. This review examines the three main technologies now used to assess MRD in MM. Next-generation flow cytometry is standardized through the EuroFlow two-tube, eight-color protocol. It gives same-day results and can be applied to all patients without a baseline sample. Next-generation sequencing of clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangements is more sensitive and can be used on stored samples. It can also follow clonal evolution and the appearance of resistance mutations. Mass spectrometry is performed on peripheral blood. It detects the patient-specific clonotypic immunoglobulin with much higher sensitivity than electrophoretic methods and allows frequent, minimally invasive monitoring. For now, however, it complements marrow-based testing and does not replace it. For each method, we discuss analytical principles, sensitivity, standardization, pre-analytical requirements, clinical validation and limitations, and we briefly consider the growing contribution of artificial intelligence. The review also covers the role of cytogenetics and fluorescence in situ hybridization in baseline risk assessment. Finally, we discuss the limits of MRD testing in a disease that is often unevenly distributed between marrow, extramedullary sites and peripheral blood. Current evidence suggests that combining marrow-based and blood-based assays may identify residual disease most accurately. This combined approach has not yet been validated prospectively, and for now it should be used within clinical trials.

Article.Title: Dual-Metal Oxide on Cellulose Nanofibers for Advanced Supercapacitors
Article.Authors: Bathula C.; Singh A.; Mane S.; Naik S.; Kim H.
Article.Abstract: The effective use of cellulose-based materials in energy applications has attracted significant global attention because of their potential contribution to environmental sustainability. However, the use of eco-friendly materials for energy storage remains challenging because of limitations in cycling stability. In this study, bimetallic oxides such as copper oxide (CuO)–manganese oxide (MnO2) was deposited on cellulose nanofibers (CNFs) through a simple one-step synthesis, and the resulting composite was evaluated for supercapacitor applications. The prepared material, referred to as the cellulose nanofiber/CuO–MnO2 composite (CCM), was characterized using field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). TEM images confirmed the formation of a robust interfacial architecture. The electrochemical performance of the prepared materials was subsequently evaluated for energy storage applications. At a current density of 0.5 mA/cm2, pristine CNF exhibited a specific capacitance of 81.25 F/g, whereas CCM achieved 266 F/g at the same current density and retained 96.1% of its capacitance after 10,000 cycles. These results demonstrate the potential of CCM as an energy-storage material owing to its cycling stability, cost-effectiveness, and environmentally friendly nature, making it a potential alternative to conventional metal oxide-based materials for energy applications.

Article.Title: Licochalcone A Attenuates Oxidative Stress and Inflammation to Promote Second-Degree Burn Healing Through Nrf2/HO-1 Activation in Mice
Article.Authors: Xu M.; Zhou H.; Li S.; Li Y.; Wang Q.; Guan H.; Luo X.
Article.Abstract: Burn injury represents one of the most prevalent accidental traumas worldwide, contributing to substantial morbidity and mortality. Second-degree burns are frequently complicated by bacterial infection, excessive inflammation, and oxidative stress, which collectively impede wound healing. Licochalcone A (LCA), a bioactive flavonoid isolated from licorice, exhibits anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, yet its therapeutic role in burn wounds remains unexplored. Here, we evaluated the effects of a topical LCA-containing hydrogel on wound healing in a mouse dorsal second-degree scald model (100 °C, 5 s) and explored the associated molecular changes. In vivo, LCA-hydrogel treatment was associated with increased collagen deposition, reduced expression of interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), reduced neutrophil and macrophage infiltration, and upregulated Ki67 and vascular endothelial growth factor C (VEGF-C). In hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-stimulated fibroblasts, LCA attenuated reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, improved cell viability and migration, preserved mitochondrial integrity, and restored antioxidant enzyme activities. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses identified 227 co-differentially expressed genes/proteins enriched in the reactive oxygen species pathway. Western blotting showed that the effects of LCA were associated with increased nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) expression and decreased Kelch-like ECH-associated protein (Keap1) expression. These exploratory findings suggest that the LCA-containing hydrogel is associated with accelerated second-degree burn healing, and that the antioxidant effects of LCA are associated with modulation of Keap1/Nrf2/HO-1 signaling, supporting further evaluation of its potential as a burn therapeutic candidate.

Article.Abstract: This study investigated the effects of 1, 10, or 100 μg/mL thymol on bovine secondary follicles cultured in vitro for 18 days at 38.5 °C with 5% CO2. The results showed that 10 μg/mL thymol increased cell viability, antrum formation and follicular development. Transmission electron microscopy showed that granulosa cells exhibited rounded nuclei, elongated mitochondria, and sparse cytoplasmic vacuoles in all treatments, except for those cultured in control medium that had signs of degeneration. Article.Title: Lessons from Plant–Microbe Interactions: Concepts for Improving Plant Nutrition and Stress Tolerance
Article.Authors: Yaish M.; Mithöfer A.
Article.Abstract: Plant-associated microorganisms, particularly plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB), enhance plant nutrition and stress tolerance and offer potential complementary approaches to conventional fertilization and crop protection. However, inconsistent field performance, ecological concerns associated with introducing non-native bacterial strains, and the need for formulations tailored to specific plant genotypes and soil conditions limit their agricultural application. These challenges have stimulated research into complementary strategies for promoting plant growth under favorable and stressful conditions. Here, we review advances and limitations of PGPB-based biofertilizers, focusing on multi-strain consortia, endophytic versus epiphytic microorganisms, and precision agriculture approaches integrating soil microbiome dynamics with plant-genotype-specific formulations. We also examine molecular mechanisms through which PGPB influence plant gene expression, stress signaling, nutrient acquisition, and rhizosphere communication. Building on these insights, we discuss strategies for using beneficial microbial mechanisms to improve abiotic stress tolerance and nutrient uptake. Integrating microbiome-informed biofertilizer development with genetic engineering, crop breeding, and precision agriculture could improve plant resilience. However, successful application requires functional validation and field testing under variable environmental conditions. Such approaches may reduce dependence on external agricultural inputs while improving crop productivity and sustainability. Together, these complementary strategies provide a framework for harnessing plant–microbe interactions to support climate-resilient agriculture and future food security worldwide.

Article.Authors: Alshehri S.; Osman M.; Alnafisah G.; Asiri S.; Arzoo S.; Al-Harbi L.

Histopathological examination of the liver revealed enhanced hepatocellular structure, reduced cytoplasmic vacuolation, decreased immune cell infiltration, and reduced injury scores. Furthermore, NAR was associated with improved antioxidant status, demonstrated by increasing the levels antioxidant mediators such as mRNA Nrf2, GSH, GSH-Px, SOD, and CAT in the liver. Moreover, it suppressed inflammatory mediators, including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and mRNA NF-κB, while elevating the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.
