Article.Title: Engineering Silk and Silk-like Proteins into High-Performance Fiber Materials
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Zhang F.
Article.Abstract: Silk and silk-like proteins emerge as programmable building blocks for high-performance fiber materials because they can integrate mechanical robustness, biological compatibility, environmental responsiveness, and degradability within genetically defined polymers. Synthetic biology now enables precise control over protein sequence, repeat number, molecular weight, and modular architecture, creating opportunities to design fibers beyond naturally harvested silks. However, application-ready protein fibers require coordinated control across multiple length scales, from sequence-encoded motifs and molecular assembly to spinning-induced alignment, hierarchical network formation, and final property profiles. This review discusses recent advances in engineering silk and silk-like proteins into mechanically and functionally optimized fibers. We highlight how crystallite-forming motifs, amorphous domains, terminal domains, and folded or dynamic modules contribute to fiber strength, toughness, extensibility, damping, shape recovery, humidity stability, biodegradation, and recyclability. We further connect these sequence–structure–property relationships to applications in structural textiles, biomedical fibers, smart and protective systems, and sustainable materials. Finally, we discuss future opportunities in scalable recombinant production and data-driven sequence design. These advances are expected to accelerate the translation of engineered protein fibers into practical high-performance materials.

Article.Title: Hassall’s Corpuscles as Dynamic and Functionally Specialized Structures
Article.Authors: Odaka C.; Hub E.; Rot A.
Article.Abstract: Hassall’s corpuscles were first described in 1846 by the British physician and anatomist Arthur Hill Hassall. During histological observations of the human thymus, he discovered distinctive concentric epithelial structures within the medulla, which he termed “Hassall’s corpuscles”. Hassall’s corpuscles are also called Hassall’s bodies. These structures share morphological and molecular features with the epidermis. Since Hassall’s corpuscles express late keratinization markers such as involucrin, keratin 10, and filaggrin, they are considered to be composed of terminally differentiated medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs). Recent fate-mapping and single-cell transcriptomic analyses have demonstrated that Hassall’s corpuscles originate from post-Aire mTECs, and their differentiation has been suggested to be Aire-dependent. Hassall’s corpuscles are now recognized as heterogeneous structures that play a role in central tolerance and regulatory T cell (Treg) development. In this review, we summarize recent advances in our understanding of the development of Hassall’s corpuscles within the mTEC lineage. We further describe that Hassall’s corpuscles undergo dynamic changes in size and number during thymic involution and regeneration. Thus, we propose that Hassall’s corpuscles should no longer be regarded as merely regressive structures but rather as functionally active bodies with critical immunological roles.

Article.Title: Self-Amplifying RNA Vaccines After the First Approvals: Technology, Development Landscape, and Regulatory Science Considerations
Article.Authors: Yi S.; Seo E.; Hong K.; Park P.
Article.Abstract: Self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) is a next-generation nucleic acid vaccine platform that enhances antigen expression through intracellular amplification of replicon RNA without producing infectious virions. saRNA constructs encode an alphavirus-derived replicase comprising nonstructural proteins nsP1–nsP4 and can elicit robust immune responses at low RNA doses. Replication intermediates may activate RIG-I, MDA5, and endosomal TLR3/7/8, contributing adjuvant-like activity. Kostaive (ARCT-154; zapomeran) became the first saRNA vaccine to receive full marketing approval in Japan in 2023, followed by authorization in the European Union in 2025 and the United Kingdom in 2026, demonstrating the platform’s clinical and regulatory feasibility. Development now extends beyond COVID-19 to seasonal and pandemic influenza, rabies, Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever, Nipah virus disease, and individualized cancer vaccines. However, the longer transcripts and additional replicase and subgenomic-promoter elements make in vitro transcription efficiency, full-length RNA content, double-stranded and truncated RNA impurities, lipid nanoparticle encapsulation, and potency testing particularly important. Regulatory assessment increasingly focuses on correct replicase and antigen expression, the magnitude and duration of self-amplification, biodistribution and persistence, and comparability. This review synthesizes the scientific basis, development landscape, manufacturing challenges, and regulatory science considerations of saRNA vaccines.

Article.Title: Converging Paths: Artificial Intelligence for Integrating Biological and Digital Biomarkers in Personalized Longevity Medicine
Article.Authors: Saliev T.; Singh P.
Article.Abstract: Ageing is a multidimensional biological process characterised by interacting molecular, physiological, functional, and environmental changes that chronological age alone cannot adequately represent. The rapid development of epigenetic clocks, proteomic and metabolomic signatures, imaging-derived biomarkers, wearable sensors, and digital phenotypes has created an increasingly rich but fragmented landscape of aging biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a potential integrative framework that can combine these heterogeneous data streams and convert them into multidimensional estimates of biological age, health risk, functional reserve, and potentially treatment response. Recent studies demonstrate that molecular and clinical information can be integrated into composite aging measures, while independent work shows that wearable movement data, retinal imaging, and speech characteristics can provide non-invasive digital representations of aging-related phenotypes. The emerging concept of multimodal aging clocks extends these approaches by integrating physiological, clinical, imaging, and molecular measurements into a common representation of biological aging.

Article.Title: Large-Scale Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis of Mouse Liver Responses to High-Fat Diet Identifies a Reproducible Core and Duration-Associated Variation
Article.Authors: Chung O.; Seong K.; Shim S.
Article.Abstract: High-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice are widely used to investigate hepatic responses relevant to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but reproducibility across experiments remains unclear. We performed a multilevel meta-analysis of 64 mouse liver RNA-sequencing GEO Series (GSEs) comprising 105 HFD-versus-control contrasts and compared the results with three human liver cohorts relevant to MASLD. Among 18,234 mouse genes, 6920 showed significant pooled HFD effects, whereas only 59 met all three study-defined reproducibility criteria: pooled FDR < 0.05, a 95% prediction interval excluding zero, and ≥80% of evaluable GSEs matching the pooled-effect direction (GSE-balanced directional consistency). These 59 genes constituted a high-confidence reproducible subset. Twenty-five Hallmark pathways showed significant pooled enrichment, and HFD duration was associated with 2744 gene-level effects and multiple Hallmark pathways. Mouse–human correspondence was weak, but among 10,658 one-to-one orthologs, mouse directional consistency was associated with the odds of a same-direction human effect (OR 1.075 per 10-percentage-point increase; 95% CI 1.035–1.115; p = 1.5 × 10−4). The hepatic HFD response therefore includes a small reproducible core within a broader duration-sensitive transcriptional response, while greater cross-experiment recurrence in mice was associated with modestly higher directional concordance in MASLD-relevant human liver cohorts, without constituting direct model validation.

Article.Title: Reporter Virus-Based High-Throughput Screening Identifies LM-10 as a Novel Inhibitor Targeting KRM1 for Coxsackievirus A10 Blockade
Article.Authors: Li H.; Gai W.; Yao H.; Gu Y.; Li Y.; Chen M.; Luo G.; Zhou J.; Tang Y.; Wang Z.; Li D.; Cui Y.
Article.Abstract: Enteroviruses causing hand, foot, and mouth disease, including currently circulating Coxsackievirus A10 (CVA10) and Coxsackievirus A6 (CVA6), rely on KREMEN1 (KRM1) for cell entry, making the virus–KRM1 interface a potential target for antiviral intervention. We screened GLMarNP, an in-house library of about 3000 natural products and derivatives. Candidates targeting the KRM1 ectodomain were selected by blind docking, drug-likeness assessment, and scaffold diversity analysis. To enable high-throughput antiviral screening, we inserted eGFP into a full-length infectious CVA10 cDNA clone to generate a reporter virus designated eGFP-A10. The virus was rescued in HEK293T cells and produced robust fluorescence in RD cells over serial passages. Among 29 candidate compounds, LM-10 showed the strongest antiviral activity and exhibited low cytotoxicity. Mechanistically, LM-10 bound KRM1 and acted early in the viral life cycle. Molecular docking suggested that LM-10 binds the KR domain at a site overlapping the VP2 EF-loop contact region. KRM1 also acts as a DKK1 receptor to regulate Wnt/β-catenin signaling. LM-10 did not significantly affect this pathway in the TOP-GFP reporter assay or in transgenic zebrafish embryos. These findings establish a practical CVA10 reporter-virus platform and support steric blockade of the receptor interface as a potential antiviral strategy.

Article.Title: Validation of Reference Genes for RT-qPCR Normalization in Saccharum Genotypes During Smut Infection
Article.Authors: Rocha L.; Contiliani D.; Thomé V.; Monteiro-Vitorello C.; Creste S.
Article.Abstract: Sugarcane and energy cane (Saccharum spp. hybrids) yields are significantly threatened by smut disease, caused by the fungus Sporisorium scitamineum. Gene expression studies are essential for understanding molecular responses in this pathosystem; however, reference gene stability may vary among genotypes, plant organs, and across infection stages, highlighting the need for systematic validation under the specific conditions of each experiment. In this study, eight candidate genes were assessed in the buds of sugarcane IACSP02-1064 (intermediate resistance) and energy cane Vertix 10 (susceptible) during the course of the infection (12, 24, 48, and 120 hpi). Expression stability was assessed using geNorm, NormFinder, and BestKeeper algorithms. For IACSP02-1064, ACAD (Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase family member 10) and GAPDH (Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) were the most stable genes, whereas GAPDH/ACAD and ACAD/UBQ2 (Ubiquitin 2)were identified as optimal pairs. For Vertix 10, GAPDH, UBQ2, and ACAD showed the highest stability, while GAPDH/UBQ2, ACAD/GAPDH, and ACAD/SARMp1 were recommended for normalization. The selected reference genes were further evaluated by analyzing ScSPL19 (SQUAMOSA promoter-binding protein-like 19 from Saccharum spp.) expression, a member of the SQUAMOSA PROMOTER-BINDING PROTEIN-LIKE (SPL) transcription factor family, whose members have previously been reported to respond to smut infection, using the most and least stable reference gene pairs. This analysis revealed differential temporal regulation of ScSPL19 when normalized with the most stable reference gene pair (GAPDH/ACAD). These results support the suitability of this reference gene combination for accurate relative gene expression analysis under the evaluated conditions.

Article.Title: A New Selection Strategy to Enrich Dopaminergic Neurons Facilitates Comparisons Between Patient iPSC-Derived Lines
Article.Authors: Hertz E.; Perez G.; Rytel K.; Kirby M.; Anderson S.; Wincovitch S.; Ahfeldt T.; Blanchard J.; Hao Y.; Li Z.; Andersh K.; Qi Y.; Sidransky E.; Chen Y.
Article.Abstract: Comparative studies of dopaminergic (DA) neurons differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from patients discordant for parkinsonism, especially siblings, provide a valuable model to explore factors underlying Parkinson disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, such studies are complicated by the inherent heterogeneity in differentiation efficiency among iPSC lines derived from different individuals. To address this technical challenge, we devised a selection strategy to enrich DA neurons expressing tyrosine hydroxylase (TH). A neomycin resistance gene (neo) was inserted at the C-terminus of the TH gene, placing its expression under the endogenous promoter. Using iPSC-derived neurons from a healthy individual (HT711), we achieved selective enrichment of TH+ neurons through geneticin selection without compromising differentiation capacity, as demonstrated by Western blots, immunocytochemistry and flow cytometry. We then applied the method to iPSCs derived from two siblings of HT711, one with Gaucher disease (GD) alone and one with both PD and GD. Quantification of multiple DA neuron markers through whole-cell proteomics confirmed their comparable enrichment in the three lines, demonstrating that the new method can be applied to iPSC lines from different individuals to standardize DA neuron cultures. While we focus on methodological developments here, a companion analysis of the same whole-cell proteomics dataset, examining molecular features potentially associated with disease statuses, has been reported separately.

Article.Title: Photobiomodulation Modulates Temporal VEGF Dynamics and Tissue Repair During Diabetic Oral Mucosal Wound Healing in Rats
Article.Authors: Đorđević N.; Dragojević I.; Mijović M.; Todić J.; Marjanović D.; Đorđević A.; Milanović Z.; Rašić J.; Kisić B.; Anđelković Z.; Stašević M.; Kostić M.

VEGF concentrations converged by day 10. PBM remained associated with a higher exploratory tissue repair score after adjustment for healing day, diabetes status, and contemporaneous VEGF, whereas VEGF itself was not independently associated with repair. These findings demonstrate phase-dependent differences in tissue VEGF and suggest that contemporaneous VEGF concentrations do not fully explain treatment-associated variation in exploratory histopathological repair scores.

Article.Title: Precision Radiation Oncology: Molecular Strategies to Enhance Anti-Tumour Responses to Radiotherapy—Beyond Direct Tumour Cell Killing
Article.Authors: Patel V.; Raja A.; Khan M.; Melcher A.; Chong I.; Young A.
Article.Abstract: Radiotherapy remains a cornerstone of cancer treatment, yet treatment response continues to be limited by tumour radioresistance and considerable biological heterogeneity. Although advances in radiation delivery have substantially improved dose conformity and reduced toxicity, increasing evidence suggests that optimising therapeutic outcomes will require greater integration of tumour biology into treatment strategies. This review examines emerging molecular approaches that seek to enhance anti-tumour responses to radiotherapy beyond direct tumour cell killing. We discuss the DNA damage response as a therapeutic target for radiosensitisation, highlighting the evolving role of DNA damage response inhibitors in promoting both tumour cytotoxicity and immune activation. We further examine the mechanisms linking radiation-induced DNA damage to anti-tumour immunity, including immunogenic cell death, cGAS–STING signalling, and remodelling of the tumour microenvironment, together with the opportunities and challenges of combining radiotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibition. Finally, we review emerging concepts in precision radiation oncology, including spatially tailored irradiation strategies, genomically informed radiation prescription, radiogenomics, and the influence of the gut microbiome on treatment response. Collectively, these advances support a shift from anatomically guided radiotherapy towards biologically personalised treatment, integrating molecular, immunological and genomic information with normal-tissue susceptibility to improve the therapeutic ratio and enable more precise, patient-centred cancer care.

Article.Title: Toxicological Evaluations Following 28-Day Oral Gavage Exposure to Polyethylene Terephthalate Microplastic Particles in Mice
Article.Authors: Marcellus K.; Scur M.; Abdulmawjood S.; Wang G.; Prescott D.; Thomas J.; Ross N.; Gill S.
Article.Abstract: The degradation of plastic in the environment can result in the generation of micro- and nano-plastics. As one of the common types of plastics used, polyethylene terephthalate (PET) microplastics are pervasive in the environment. Yet, their potential toxicity remains poorly understood. In this study, we addressed this gap by examining systemic toxicity in C57BL/6 mice following 28-day oral gavage with irregularly shaped PET microplastics at human-relevant exposure levels of 0, 0.3, 1.5, 7.5, or 37.5 mg/kg bodyweight/day. No significant changes were seen in bodyweights, food consumption, organ weights, clinical biochemistry, or hematological parameters. Histological changes were seen in the kidneys of male mice with minimum to mild apoptosis in the outer strip of the outer medulla. Additionally, decreased goblet cells were observed in both male and female mice, albeit in different intestinal sections. However, this change in goblet cell population did not result in overt epithelial damage. Overall, sub-chronic PET microplastic exposure did not cause overt systemic toxicity, but sex-specific minor histological alterations in the kidney and gut were observed. Our findings show only minor effects following short-term exposure, but real-world microplastic exposure is likely to be chronic, thus a longer exposure period may be necessary to fully elucidate the potential impact of PET microplastic-induced toxicity.

Article.Title: A Proof-of-Concept Study: Reference Transcriptome Choice as a Hidden Analytical Variable in Breast Cancer RNA-Seq Analysis
Article.Authors: Zieliński P.; Frąszczak M.; Czech B.; Dobosz P.; Adamiak K.; Mierzejewski P.; Stępień R.; Mielczarek M.
Article.Abstract: Reference genome and transcriptome are fundamental components of RNA-seq analysis and can influence transcript quantification and downstream differential expression results. Although GRCh38 is the current human reference build, GRCh37 remains in use in research and clinical bioinformatics workflows. The extent to which reference transcriptome choice affects transcriptomic inference in breast cancer remains insufficiently characterized. We performed a comparative analysis of publicly available RNA-seq data comprising two MCF7 breast cancer cell-line samples and two healthy breast tissue samples from the European Nucleotide Archive (PRJEB4829). Identical preprocessing, transcript quantification, and differential expression workflows were applied using GRCh37- and GRCh38-based reference transcriptomes. Reference transcriptome-dependent variability was further examined by comparing the same samples quantified under the two reference transcriptomes. Concordance of differentially expressed genes and pathway enrichment was assessed, and sensitivity to reference transcriptome choice was evaluated for genes included in the MammaPrint and Naderi expression signatures and selected hereditary cancer gene panels. The MCF7-versus-normal-tissue comparison identified 15,950 differentially expressed genes using GRCh37 and 16,348 using GRCh38, with 13,899 genes shared between the two analyses. The most significantly enriched Hallmark and KEGG pathways were also concordant between annotations. Principal component analysis showed that the dominant pattern of variation in the MCF7-versus-normal-tissue comparison was associated with biological status. In contrast, when the same MCF7 samples were quantified using different reference transcriptomes, reference transcriptome choice represented a major source of variation. Expression of genes comprising the evaluated prognostic signatures and hereditary cancer panels showed no significant differences in median expression between reference transcriptomes. However, individual cancer-relevant genes, including PTEN, RAD51D, NANOG, and SOX11, demonstrated reference transcriptome-dependent expression differences. In this proof-of-concept analysis, reference transcriptome choice produced measurable differences in RNA-seq quantification and differential expression, while broad biological patterns and the aggregate expression of established gene signatures were relatively stable. Reference transcriptome-dependent variability became particularly apparent when biological heterogeneity was limited, suggesting that reference transcriptome choice can act as a hidden analytical variable in transcriptomic studies. These findings support explicit reporting and version control of reference annotations and highlight the need for validation in larger, independently replicated breast cancer cohorts before drawing clinical conclusions.

Article.Authors: Zaczek-Moczydłowska M.; Kopyciński B.; Biesiada I.; Mishra P.; Matus K.; Ghavami S.; Langer E.; Łos M.
Article.Abstract: Bioactive antiviral biomaterial coatings capable of rapidly inactivating respiratory viruses while preserving cytocompatibility are highly desirable for development protective and high-contact biomedical materials. The morphology and elemental composition of the coatings were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Antiviral performance was quantified by a neutral red uptake cytopathic (NRU-CPE) infectivity assay following 30 and 60 min of virus–surface contact. Coatings functionalized with nAg supported on SiO2 reduced infectious virus recovery by 2.2–5.3 log10, whereas coatings containing Ag-substituted zirconium phosphate achieved reductions of 1.9–4.7 log10, depending on additive loading and exposure time. Interestingly, the unmodified black organic coating also reduced viral infectivity, indicating that both the coating matrix and Ag-based functionalization contribute to the overall antiviral performance. Importantly, all functionalized coatings maintained cell viability above the ISO 10993-5 acceptance threshold (≥70%), demonstrating excellent cytocompatibility.

Article.Title: Genotype-Phenotype Correlation in Cri du Chat Patients Carrying One or Two Copies of the TRIO Gene
Article.Authors: Guala A.; Tognon F.; Minniti G.; Sirchia F.; Kalantari S.; Malacarne M.; Baldo C.; Ferretti A.; Liaci C.; Politano D.; De Icco R.; Merlo G.; Valente E.; Danesino C.
Article.Abstract: Cri du Chat syndrome (CdCS) results from a variable-sized deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p) and is characterized by marked phenotypic heterogeneity. Previous genotype–phenotype correlation studies have primarily focused on deletion size, an approach inherently limited by the large number of genes within the deletion. A gene-centered strategy may therefore offer a better framework for interpreting specific clinical features. Among candidate genes on 5p, TRIO plays a critical role in RAC1-mediated neurodevelopment; furthermore, in related neurodevelopmental disorders, loss-of-function variants are associated with microcephaly, whereas gain-of-function variants are associated with macrocephaly. All data were analyzed in relation to TRIO allele dosage, deletion size, and sex. All patients showed a reduced HC compared with reference curves. However, HC measurements were consistently higher in patients carrying two TRIO alleles versus those carrying only one. Deletion size did not correlate with HC or developmental milestones. Patients with two TRIO alleles generally achieved motor and language milestones earlier, and some differences between males and females, suggested the possibility of sex-specific differences. These findings indicate that TRIO allele dosage might contribute to head size and developmental outcomes in CdCS independent of deletion size. A gene-centered approach could thus improve genotype–phenotype correlations in chromosomal disorders and highlight the importance of considering sex-specific effects in clinical and rehabilitative management.

Article.Title: Wide-Targeted Metabolomics Combined with Network Pharmacology Analysis Reveals Metabolite Dynamics and Optimal Harvest Time Across Developmental Stages in Schisandra chinensis (Turcz.) Baill.
Article.Authors: Qu G.; Sun M.; Wei S.; Yang J.; Li H.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Schisandra chinensis (Turcz.) Baill. (S. chinensis) is a traditional Chinese medicinal plant whose fruits are rich in bioactive constituents, including lignans, organic acids, and flavonoids. Nevertheless, the biochemical dynamics underlying fruit development remain insufficiently characterized, limiting the effective cultivation, harvest, and utilization of S. chinensis. Here, we applied widely targeted metabolomics, together with a dynamic assessment of fruit growth, to profile temporal changes in major metabolites and to identify the optimal harvest window. The results show that the morphological changes in fruit mainly occurred from 70 to 110 days after fruit set; fresh fruit mass peaked at 110 days after fruit set. During the harvest period, the fruits are deep red and firm, showing no signs of softening. Meanwhile, fruit cluster weight, single fruit weight, and fruit longitudinal diameter all reached their peak values. Over the course of maturation, lignan levels declined markedly, whereas terpenoids, organic acids and flavonoids increased significantly. The most pronounced shifts were observed for schizandrin, gomisin N, shikimic acid, citric acid, gamma-terpinene and cyanidin 3-sophoroside, key marker compounds of S. chinensis fruit. Network pharmacology predicts that ESR1, RXRA, GATM, NCOA2, and SONEA are core targets. These findings provide a basis for determining timely harvest and for establishing quality evaluation criteria for S. chinensis.

Article.Title: Kinase Regulation Through Metabolic Control Points Directs Glucose Fate
Article.Authors: Varghese S.; Shivamurthy P.; Pai V.; Soman S.; Ramesh P.; Raju R.
Article.Abstract: Glucose metabolism is organized through interconnected metabolic pathways whose enzymes determine whether glucose is utilized for energy production, storage, or biosynthesis. Although protein kinases modulate metabolic enzymes through phosphorylation, how kinase signaling collectively interfaces with the glucose metabolic network remains unclear. In addition, many reported kinase–substrate relationships are derived from prediction-based resources and lack experimental validation. Here, we systematically mapped kinase associations for 144 enzymes across six glucose metabolic pathways by integrating kinase–substrate databases, quantitative phosphoproteomics from 154 human studies, and protein–protein interaction networks. We developed a multi-layer prioritization framework combining kinase–substrate annotations, phosphoproteomic co-regulation, and interaction-supported evidence to rank kinase–enzyme associations and reconstruct a phosphoproteomic-supported kinase–metabolism network. Prioritization reduced a large initial association space to a refined set of candidate kinase–enzyme associations while retaining broad coverage across glucose metabolism. The resulting network revealed an uneven distribution of kinase associations across metabolic pathways and enzymes, with the highest kinase association density observed at metabolic control points, particularly enzymes integrating branch-point and flux-control functions. Pathway-level analysis further showed that glycogen metabolism exhibited the greatest kinase association density despite comprising relatively few enzymes, while futile-cycle pairs displayed distinct patterns of shared and reaction-specific kinase associations. Network analysis identified a small subset of highly connected kinase hubs together with bridge proteins linking the kinase and metabolic enzyme layers, providing a systems-level view of kinase association patterns across glucose metabolism. Together, these findings indicate that kinase associations are not uniformly distributed across glucose metabolism but preferentially concentrate at metabolic control points that govern pathway routing and glucose allocation. This study provides a systems-level framework for prioritizing candidate kinase–enzyme associations and a resource for investigating signaling–metabolism interactions in metabolic disease and cancer.

Article.Title: Engineering Modification Enhances the Antibacterial Activity of Yak Gastric Lysozyme and Its High-Level Expression in Pichia pastoris
Article.Authors: Fan B.; Zhang A.; Wu Z.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: To broaden the antibacterial spectrum of yak gastric lysozyme (YGL) against Gram-negative bacteria and improve its secretory expression in Pichia pastoris, this study employed a combined strategy of functional short-peptide fusion and host engineering. AW-YGL was subsequently selected for sequential optimization of the host strain, secretion signal peptide, endoplasmic-reticulum-associated molecular chaperones, and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9)-mediated host-gene knockout, followed by physicochemical stability evaluation of the optimized product. AW-YGL exhibited inhibition rates of 65%, 68%, and 67% against Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Salmonella enteritidis, respectively. During expression-system optimization, the GS115 host significantly improved AW-YGL secretion, with total enzyme activity and specific activity in the culture supernatant reaching 3.1 × 105 U/L and 983 U/mg, respectively. Co-expression of the endoplasmic reticulum molecular chaperone binding immunoglobulin protein (BIP) further promoted functional AW-YGL expression, increasing the specific activity to 1560.3 U/mg. On this basis, knockout of the cell-wall-related gene FKS1 further increased the total enzyme activity in the culture supernatant to 6.9 × 105 U/L and the specific activity to 1638.3 U/mg, indicating that stepwise optimization of the signal peptide, folding assistance, and host-cell engineering effectively enhanced AW-YGL secretory expression and enzymatic activity. The optimized AW-YGL retained relatively high activity over defined pH and temperature ranges and showed tolerance to several metal ions and digestion-related proteases. Collectively, C-terminal fusion with hydrophobic short peptides enhanced the inhibitory activity of YGL against Gram-negative bacteria, while the combined strategies of signal-peptide optimization, folding assistance, and cell-wall engineering further improved its secretory expression in P. pastoris. Article.Title: Vascular Complications in Chronic Active Epstein–Barr Virus Disease: Clinical Spectrum, Pathogenic Mechanisms, and Potential Disease Modifiers
Article.Authors: Kim J.; Yang W.; Park M.; Koh H.
Article.Abstract: Chronic active Epstein–Barr virus disease (CAEBV) is a rare, potentially life-threatening EBV-positive T/NK-cell lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by persistent systemic inflammation and multiorgan involvement. Although hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and progression to lymphoid malignancy are well-recognized complications, vascular manifestations—including vasculitis, arterial dilatation and aneurysm formation, intracranial hemorrhage, and vascular involvement of multiple organ systems—remain poorly characterized. Available evidence suggests that persistent activation of EBV-infected T/NK cells, cytokine-mediated hyperinflammation, endothelial injury, and coagulation abnormalities may contribute to CAEBV-associated vasculopathy, whereas the roles of complement activation and thrombotic microangiopathy remain less well established. This review synthesizes the clinical spectrum and proposed mechanisms of vascular complications in CAEBV, with particular attention to the strength of evidence supporting individual pathogenic pathways. Improved recognition of vascular manifestations, application of contemporary CAEBV diagnostic criteria, and further mechanistic and multicenter studies are needed to improve risk stratification and management.

Article.Title: Formation and Properties of the Glassy Matrix: Vitrification Mechanism in Haberlea rhodopensis and the Resurrection Plants
Article.Authors: Tonchev L.; Staykov N.; Gechev T.
Article.Abstract: Cytoplasmic vitrification is the standard explanation for how resurrection plants endure drying, yet the glass is rarely examined in tissue—its composition, glass transition and residual water remain unresolved. We characterize the glassy matrix of Haberlea rhodopensis by integrating transcriptomic and metabolomic data, biophysical modeling and targeted experiments. Sugar-metabolism genes, such as SUCROSE-PHOSPHATE SYNTHASES and SUCROSE SYNTHASES, respond to desiccation with strong concordance across three studies (Kendall’s W = 0.872; 81 genes measured in all three) and, with the metabolites, define a four-component glass-former set—sucrose plus the raffinose family oligosaccharides raffinose, stachyose and verbascose, with sucrose dominant (~92%). Apparent contradictions are plausibly explained: INVERTASE induction is consistent with compartmental separation from accumulating sucrose and declining trehalose with trehalose-6-phosphate (T6P) signaling, not vitrification. A parameterized state diagram traces the desiccation–rehydration path through vitrification and predicts that unfreezable water is locked throughout the glass. Desiccated tissue survived liquid nitrogen (−196 °C), suggesting that freezing tolerance reflects vitrification. Rewetting dried tissue was exothermic, consistent with an amorphous glass. We argue the residual water is functionally bound, that late embryogenesis abundant (LEA) proteins help shape the glass, and hypothesize that natural deep eutectic solvent (NaDES)-forming metabolites provide a transient reaction medium.

Article.Title: Detection of Plum pox virus and Characterization of Oxidative Stress Responses in Stone Fruit Trees of Azerbaijan
Article.Authors: Sultanova N.; Musazade E.; Topkaya S.
Article.Abstract: Sharka disease, induced by the Plum pox virus (PPV; genus Potyvirus, family Potyviridae), represents one of the most serious viral threats to stone fruit production worldwide. This study assessed PPV occurrence in major fruit-growing areas in Azerbaijan and characterized the physiological and oxidative stress responses of infected Prunus species. Symptomatic leaves from orchards in the Quba district were screened by immunochromatographic strips, DAS-ELISA, and RT-PCR. Of 60 trees surveyed, 22 (36.7%) tested positive across all three hosts, confirmed by RT-PCR amplification of a 243 bp coat protein (CP) gene fragment in peach (Prunus persica L.), plum (P. domestica L.), and apricot (P. armeniaca L.). Infection was associated with pronounced oxidative stress: hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and malondialdehyde (MDA) contents were higher in infected trees (6.80–10.60 µmol g−1 FW and 8.0–15.2 nmol g−1 FW) than in healthy trees (3.20–3.90 µmol g−1 FW and 4.5–8.2 nmol g−1 FW). Antioxidant defenses were activated, with increased ascorbate peroxidase (APX) and catalase (CAT) activities and higher ascorbic acid (AsA) and reduced glutathione (GSH) levels. Photosynthetic performance declined markedly: total chlorophyll fell by 17.3–30.8% (greatest in apricot), maximum photosystem II quantum efficiency (Fv/Fm) was lower in infected trees (0.408–0.561) than in healthy trees (0.716–0.728), and total soluble protein was lower in infected trees (7.88–8.45 mg g−1 FW) than in healthy trees (9.38–9.58 mg g−1 FW). Collectively, PPV infection was associated with oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, with activation of enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant defenses, and with reduced photosynthetic performance in Prunus species. These findings advance understanding of host responses to PPV and support sustainable monitoring and management strategies for stone fruit production, aligned with SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 15 (Life on Land).

Article.Title: Statins and the Lifetime Outcomes of MASLD: From Evidence Asymmetry to Outcome Convergence
Article.Authors: Crespo J.; Alonso-Peña M.; Jiménez-González C.; Cayón-González L.; Iruzubieta P.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a systemic disorder in which cardiovascular, hepatic and oncological outcomes shape long-term prognosis. Statins are particularly relevant because their cardiovascular benefit is firmly established, yet they remain underused in MASLD, while their potential liver-related effects remain uncertain. Observational studies consistently associate statin exposure with slower fibrosis progression, fewer major adverse liver outcomes, lower hepatocellular carcinoma incidence and reduced liver-related mortality. However, direct randomized evidence in MASLD remains limited, and available studies differ substantially in disease stage, exposure, endpoint and follow-up. In this narrative review, we critically examine the cardiovascular, hepatic, oncological, randomized, observational, genetic and pharmacological evidence on statin therapy in MASLD. We aim to clarify the apparent discordance between evidence sources, assess whether statins may modify liver-related outcomes beyond their established cardiovascular benefit, and propose a framework for evaluating multidomain therapeutic effects. We propose outcome convergence as a framework for assessing whether a therapy can improve more than one clinically relevant disease domain while preserving independent causal evaluation of each outcome. Statins should therefore be regarded as a candidate, rather than an established, outcome-convergent therapy.

Article.Title: Clinical Distribution and Virulence Gene Profiles of CNF1- and CNF2-Positive Escherichia coli in Calves
Article.Authors: Bednarski M.; Kupczyński R.
Article.Abstract: Cytotoxic necrotizing factor (CNF)-associated Escherichia coli (E. coli) occur in enteric and extraintestinal disease in calves, but the distribution of CNF1 and CNF2 and their virulence profiles remain incompletely defined. We analysed E. coli from 544 calves: 131 healthy, 210 diarrhoeic, 173 with septicaemia, and 30 with central nervous system (CNS) infection. Isolates were classified by PCR detection of cnf1 or cnf2, and only CNF-positive isolates were screened for eight accessory virulence genes. In age-adjusted models restricted to calves aged 2–19 days, overall CNF positivity (aOR 2.83, 95% CI 1.25–6.44; Holm-adjusted p = 0.039) and CNF2 positivity (aOR 3.14, 95% CI 1.18–8.31; adjusted p = 0.043) were associated with diarrhoea, whereas CNF1 was not. CNF2-positive isolates were enriched for f17A, afa8E, and cdtIII, whereas CNF1-positive isolates more often carried papC, sfa/focDE, hlyA, and kpsMT K1. In invasive cases, CNF1 was more frequent in CNS infection than in septicaemia (33.3% vs. 12.7%; adjusted p = 0.034). Among CNF1-positive invasive isolates, kpsMT K1 occurred in 90.0% of CNS versus 9.1% of septicaemia isolates. These findings support distinct CNF2-associated enteric and CNF1-associated invasive virulence profiles; PCR detection does not establish expression, phenotype, causality, or genomic linkage.

Article.Title: Integrating GWAS and Random Forest to Develop a Robust 5-SNP Panel for Genetic Sex Identification in Pacific White Shrimp (Penaeus vannamei)
Article.Authors: Liu J.; Xia Y.; Li P.; Liu M.; Meng X.; Luo K.; Sui J.; Dai P.; Fu Q.; Tan J.; Cao J.; Chen B.; Li X.; Kong J.; Luan S.
Article.Abstract: The Pacific white shrimp (Penaeus vannamei) exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in growth, making early and accurate sex identification crucial for targeted monitoring of sexual development and in-depth research into monosex aquaculture. However, morphological sex identification is unreliable at early developmental stages, and single-marker molecular assays are prone to diagnostic failures caused by genotyping errors or missing data. In this study, we developed a multi-SNP framework for sex prediction by integrating genome-wide association studies (GWAS) with Random Forest (RF) modeling. Analyzing 1244 individuals with a 55K SNP array, we identified 18 genome-wide significant SNPs and 10 candidate genes, including SRRM1 and SPSB3, that may be associated with sexual differentiation. Subsequent multi-marker comparative analyses demonstrated that although the top-performing single marker yielded high accuracy, simulated genotyping errors and missing data caused significant drops in accuracy and elevated no-call rates, whereas multi-SNP panels exhibited substantially improved robustness. A stable performance plateau was reached when expanding the panel to 5 SNPs. The model achieved 100% classification accuracy in the two mixed-sex independent populations, ZJ and HN, and correctly identified all females in the all-female MK cohort. Overall, this study provides a robust multi-SNP tool for sex identification in P. vannamei and highlights the practical utility of machine learning in aquaculture.

Article.Title: Cognitive-Enhancing and Neuroprotective Effects of a Combination Extract of Atractylodes macrocephala and Rumex acetosa Against Scopolamine-Induced Memory Impairment
Article.Authors: Oh D.; Lee H.; Kim Y.; Kim Y.; Bae D.
Article.Abstract: This study investigated the cognitive-enhancing and neuroprotective effects of a mixed extract of Atractylodes macrocephala Koidzumi (AM) and Rumex acetosa L. (RA) in models of scopolamine (SCO)-induced toxicity and memory impairment. In vitro, the 2:1 ratio maximized neuroprotection and p-CREB/CREB expression in SCO-treated SH-SY5Y cells. In vivo, rats received the AR mixture orally for 29 days, with SCO challenges introduced from Day 22. In the Morris water maze, the AR mixture reduced escape latency during the 3-day spatial training period and increased target quadrant exploration during the probe trial. In the passive avoidance test, it significantly prolonged step-through latency, confirming enhanced memory retention. Hippocampal biochemical assessments revealed that the AR mixture attenuated acetylcholinesterase activity, decreased malondialdehyde accumulation, and replenished acetylcholine levels. Furthermore, the formulation suppressed the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6. AR mixture treatment attenuated the SCO-associated reductions in BDNF, p-TrkB, p-CREB, and PSD-95 expression and in ERK1/2 and Akt phosphorylation in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that the AR mixture improves cognitive and biochemical outcomes in SCO-treated rats, accompanied by changes in cholinergic function, lipid peroxidation, inflammation, and BDNF/TrkB-related signaling.

Article.Title: Gene and microRNA Expression Profiling in Experimental Colitis and Human Ulcerative Colitis: Effects of STAT6 Knockout and Corylus avellana Treatment
Article.Authors: Samoilă I.; Țieranu C.; Hermenean A.; Dinescu S.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) are chronic immune-mediated disorders of the gastrointestinal tract resulting from a complex interplay between genetic susceptibility and dysregulated immune responses. To improve the understanding of the molecular mechanisms’ underlying disease pathogenesis, mouse models with experimental colitis and patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) were investigated for the expression of genes and small non-coding RNAs involved in key pathogenic pathways. In experimental colitis, the potential modulatory effects of STAT6 knockout and Corylus avellana treatment were also evaluated. Our findings revealed significant transcriptional alterations in molecular markers associated with inflammation, epithelial barrier integrity, autophagy, and endoplasmic reticulum stress, highlighting their association with the development and persistence of chronic intestinal inflammation. Both STAT6 deletion and Corylus avellana extract treatment modulated several of these alterations, with STAT6 knockout showing a more pronounced effect on the molecular profile associated with experimental colitis. In addition, miRNA expression profiling revealed a panel of dysregulated miRNAs, while bioinformatic analysis identified potential miRNA-gene regulatory interactions, supporting their possible involvement in the post-transcriptional regulation of these biological processes. Overall, the combined analysis of gene and miRNA expression profiles highlights molecular alterations associated with experimental colitis and human UC and suggests potential regulatory interactions that require further experimental validation.

Article.Title: Integrated Multi-Omics Analysis of the Response of Lycium barbarum ‘Ningqi-1’ to Powdery Mildew Infection and Functional Characterization of LbMLO6
Article.Authors: Xu W.; Luo L.; Wang J.; Ren R.; Zhou J.; Wang C.; Qin K.; Li Y.; Li Y.; Zhang X.; Wang J.; Si B.; Duan L.; Dai G.
Article.Abstract: Powdery mildew severely constrains the production of Lycium barbarum L., yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its response to infection remain poorly understood. Here, ‘Ningqi-1’ plants were inoculated with the powdery mildew pathogen and sampled at 0, 12, 24, and 48 hpi for integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic analyses. Quantitative PCR and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing were further used to evaluate the candidate susceptibility gene LbMLO6. Infection induced extensive molecular reprogramming, yielding 1299 differentially expressed genes with sustained changes, 75 DAPs shared across all three time points, and 127 shared differentially accumulated metabolites. These molecules were mainly enriched in plant–pathogen interaction, plant hormone signal transduction, MAPK signaling, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and α-linolenic acid metabolism pathways, suggesting coordinated roles for Ca2+ signaling, reactive oxygen species, defense-related proteins, and secondary metabolism in the host response. Integrated multi-omics analysis identified LbMLO6 as a candidate gene associated with powdery mildew susceptibility, its expression was markedly induced from 24 hpi onward. CRISPR/Cas9-edited LbMLO6 lines showed reduced fungal development compared with the control, particularly during the early stages of infection. These findings provide preliminary evidence that LbMLO6 may be associated with powdery mildew susceptibility in L. barbarum.

Article.Title: Fatty Acid-Binding Protein 3 (FABP3)-Mediated Abdominal Fat Deposition in Broilers via the PPAR Signaling Pathway
Article.Authors: Yuan H.; Zhu Y.; Jin K.; Liu Y.; Lu J.; Zhang R.
Article.Abstract: Excessive deposition of abdominal fat in broilers compromises feed efficiency, carcass yield, processing efficiency, and inflates production costs. Because this trait is governed by multi-tissue crosstalk coupling hepatic lipid synthesis to adipose lipid storage, its coordinated regulation has seldom been addressed. We combined three abdominal fat transcriptomic datasets (GSE42980, GSE49121, GSE104039) with one hepatic dataset (GSE104038), obtaining 2520 meta-differentially expressed genes (meta-DEGs). Functional enrichment revealed a prominent enrichment of lipid-metabolism terms, including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling. Fatty acid-binding protein 3 (FABP3) appeared repeatedly within the Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) lipid-metabolism categories and was therefore taken forward for functional work. Overexpressing FABP3 enhanced proliferation, lipid accumulation and lipogenic marker expression, whereas knockdown reversed these effects. In both adipocytes and hepatocytes, FABP3 raised peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) and fatty acid-binding protein 4 (FABP4) at mRNA and protein levels. Pharmacological intervention showed that the PPARγ antagonist GW9662 suppressed the pro-lipogenic action of FABP3 overexpression, while the PPARα agonist GW7647 reinstated lipid accumulation in FABP3-silenced cells, indicating a reliance on PPAR-pathway activity. FABP3 therefore drives lipid deposition in adipocytes and hepatocytes via PPAR signaling, offering a framework for how the liver and abdominal adipose tissue jointly govern abdominal fat deposition in broilers.

Article.Title: Effects of Hydroxyapatite Pretreated with Two Sodium Fluoride Concentrations on Early Bone Healing in Beagle Dogs
Article.Authors: Suzuki Y.; Bhawal U.; Chowdhry A.; Watanabe T.; Okada H.; Kimoto K.
Article.Abstract: Hydroxyapatite (HA) is widely used as an osteoconductive bone substitute, and fluoride can influence bone-forming cells in a concentration-dependent manner. This study examined how pretreating resorbable HA with low or high concentrations of sodium fluoride (NaF) affects early mandibular bone healing in beagle dogs. Twelve beagle dogs were used in the project, including three in a pilot study and nine in the main experiment. At each observation time point (Days 4, 7, and 14), one dog was assigned to each of the three HA-based treatment conditions (HA, HA + 0.2% NaF, or HA + 4% NaF). Four experimental defects in each dog received the same assigned treatment, while four contralateral defects were left unfilled as controls. The four defects were considered within-animal subsamples rather than independent biological replicates, and all treatment comparisons were descriptive and exploratory. Before implantation, HA was exposed to the designated NaF solution for 3 min and then washed with 100 mL of distilled water. Healing was evaluated by H&E, Azan, Masson’s trichrome and toluidine blue staining, immunohistochemistry, and quantitative real-time RT-PCR. Histological examination showed progressive tissue and matrix organization around the implanted material, with more evident new bone and osteoblast-associated changes in the low-NaF group at Days 7 and 14. Runx2 immunoreactivity was more prominent in the early healing phase, and osteocalcin was more prominent in the later healing phase. Osteocalcin mRNA gradually increased until Day 14, whereas Runx2 mRNA was maximally expressed at Day 7. Both responses were strongest with low-NaF-pretreated HA. High-NaF-pretreated HA retained osteogenic activity but did not produce a response of the same magnitude. These exploratory findings suggest that NaF pretreatment concentration may influence early HA-associated bone healing, warranting confirmation in studies with independent animal-level replication.

Article.Title: Infrared Treatment Alters the Chemical Profile and In Vitro Bioactivity of Jojoba Oil: Antimicrobial, Biofilm Formation Inhibition and Ovarian Cancer Cell Responses
Article.Authors: Qanash H.; Al-Rajhi A.; Bazaid A.; Almarshadi F.; Almimoni N.; Althagafi H.; Almotayri A.; Yahya R.; El-Hawary S.; Aldarhami A.
Article.Abstract: Jojoba oil (Simmondsia chinensis) is widely used in cosmetic and pharmaceutical formulations, yet approaches to enhance its biological activity remain insufficiently explored. This study investigated whether infrared (IR) treatment could modify the chemical profile and in vitro biological properties of jojoba oil. A thermal control matched to the IR temperature–time profile was included to separate bulk heating from IR-specific effects. Crude (untreated) and IR-treated oil (30 min, 50 mW/cm2) were characterized by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), followed by evaluation of antimicrobial, antibiofilm, inhibition of protein denaturation, fibroblast scratch-closure, and antiproliferative activity against SK-OV-3 cells. IR treatment altered the FTIR profile and produced substantial changes in the GC-MS-detectable composition, including the detection of a peak tentatively assigned to 9-hexadecenoic acid, 9-octadecenyl ester (27.45% relative peak area), and 9-eicosyne (8.97% relative peak area); these values represent relative chromatographic abundance, not absolute concentrations. Compared with crude oil, IR-treated jojoba oil exhibited two- to fourfold lower minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC), reaching 7.8 µg/mL against Candida albicans, and inhibited Staphylococcus aureus biofilm formation by 96.8%. It also enhanced fibroblast scratch closure (84.1% vs. 67.0%) and showed greater inhibition of protein denaturation (IC50, 4.43 vs. 6.52 µg/mL). Against SK-OV-3 ovarian cancer cells, IR-treated oil reduced the IC50 from 114.5 to 78.7 µg/mL and produced marked G0/G1 accumulation (97.9%). This response was accompanied by increased BAX (3.67-fold) and CASP3 (5.73-fold) expression and decreased BCL2 expression (0.61-fold). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that IR treatment, beyond a matched thermal control, substantially modifies jojoba oil and enhances multiple in vitro biological activities. The novelty is the linkage between IR-induced chemical alteration and functional biological changes, not the mere combination of assays.

Article.Title: Induction of Carotenoid Accumulation by Salt Stress in a Newly Isolated Dysmorphococcus Strain from Antalya, Türkiye
Article.Authors: Alnsour W.; Johnson X.; Aksoy M.
Article.Abstract: Microalgae are some of the organisms that produce carotenoids, which are high value metabolites. However, algae produce carotenoids under stress conditions and there is a need for more practical and economical ways to increase carotenoid accumulation in algae. Haematococcus lacustris has been one of the most important species for the production of industrial-scale carotenoids in biotechnology. In recent years, new algal species have been shown to accumulate carotenoids as alternative resources of carotenoids; Dysmorphococcus globosus is one of them. In a previous study, we isolated and identified for the first time a D. globosus strain in Türkiye. In the current study, we tested different stress conditions on carotenoid accumulation on D. globosus-KINIK and a Haematococcus sp.-KINIK strain that was isolated along with it from the same water sample. We partially sequenced the 18S rRNA gene of the newly isolated Haematoccoccus strain; it is 96% identical to Haematococcus lacustris. Further studies are necessary to determine the species of our strain. We tested three stress conditions: (i) salt stress by adding 2 g L−1 NaCl, (ii) fresh water stress by replacing growth media with fresh water, and iii) sea water stress by replacing growth media with sea water. Salt stress and fresh water stress have been shown to increase carotenoids in Haematococcus strains in the literature; our Haematococcus strain also responded well to these stresses and accumulated carotenoids. To our knowledge, none of these stresses have been tested for Dysmosphococcus strains in the literature. Our results show that D. globosus-KINIK also accumulates carotenoids under salt stress and fresh water, with salt stress being more effective. We also tested different growth media on the growth of D. globosus-KINIK and showed that it can grow without vitamin supplementation. Our study reveals local strains of carotenogenic algae in Türkiye for consideration for industrial-scale carotenoid production.

Article.Title: Molecular Checkpoints of Nucleic Acid Sensing in Tumor Cells: Linking Innate Immune Evasion to Precision Cancer Immunotherapy
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Cao B.; Lu H.; Wang Z.; Qin Y.
Article.Abstract: Tumor cells possess nucleic-acid sensing systems that detect aberrant DNA and RNA arising from genomic and transcriptomic dysregulation. Cytosolic DNA and RNA sensors, together with endosomal nucleic acid sensors, can induce type I interferons, inflammatory chemokines, antigen presentation programs, and immune cell recruitment. Yet many tumors remain immunologically silent despite harboring potentially immunostimulatory nucleic acids, indicating that malignant cells can restrain these pathways at multiple levels. Nucleic acid clearance, selective RNA editing and remodeling, extracellular second messenger degradation, and epigenetic silencing can suppress these responses. These regulatory layers may favor immune-poor tumor states and limit responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. Therapeutic reactivation must be spatially and temporally controlled, because persistent signaling can undergo maladaptive rewiring. We review these molecular brakes, therapeutic strategies to restore innate sensing, and a proposed biomarker framework integrating sensor competence, suppressor activity, and functional immune output. We distinguish the effects arising within tumor cells from those mediated by sensing mechanisms in neighboring host cells and discuss cellular and spatial context, signaling dynamics, and safety. The proposed framework for matching treatments to patients remains investigational and requires prospective clinical validation.

Article.Title: Expression Characteristics of SERINC1 and TDO2 in Diabetic Kidney Disease: Historical Candidate Reappraisal, Cross-Cohort Evaluation, Single-Cell Analysis, and a Mouse Model Study
Article.Authors: Cui X.; Ren Y.; Ding G.; Chen S.
Article.Abstract: Evaluating candidate molecules in diabetic kidney disease (DKD) requires evidence for both the reproducibility of expression changes and their cellular origin. Using the historically fixed SERINC1/TDO2 panel, we reappraised how these candidates were derived, evaluated both genes in human glomerular transcriptomes and kidney-cortex single-cell data, and examined their relationship with renal injury in a mouse model. The historical WGCNA, LASSO, and SVM-RFE-labelled frozen lists intersected at SERINC1 and TDO2, although the legacy RFE implementation could not be confirmed. TDO2 was increased in both cohorts (Hedges’ g = 2.07 and 0.714; the latter Holm-adjusted p = 0.0182), whereas the SERINC1 reduction was supported only in the discovery cohort (g = −1.90) and not in GSE96804 (g = −0.252; Holm-adjusted p = 0.348). Single-cell analysis showed widespread SERINC1 distribution without donor-level significance after Benjamini–Hochberg correction, and TDO2 was detected in only 50 of 37,331 cells. In streptozotocin-induced mice, SERINC1 decreased and TDO2 increased alongside renal pathology and podocyte ultrastructural changes. Both genes remain candidates for further study, but clinical diagnostic value and shared pathogenic mechanisms are not yet established.

Article.Title: Differentiation of Indigenous Saccharomyces cerevisiae Wine Strains by Oenological and Proteomic Characterization
Article.Authors: Braconi D.; Guerrini S.; Girolamo F.; Costagli S.; Paffetti A.; Armini A.; Draghi S.; Jacomelli G.; Bernini A.; Grasso D.; Galli V.; Ganucci D.; Granchi L.; Santucci A.
Article.Abstract: Indigenous Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains persist within individual cellars and contribute to the character of spontaneously fermented wines, yet the molecular basis of their oenological differences remains largely unknown. In this work, eight predominant strains isolated from spontaneous fermentations in four Tuscan wineries were characterized by technological traits of oenological relevance and laboratory-scale fermentations of both a synthetic must and Sangiovese grape must. In each must, the strains reached similar final ethanol concentrations, although lag phase and maximum fermentation rate differed significantly, whereas the resulting wines differed significantly in glycerol, acetic acid and phenolic alcohol content and in the scores assigned by a trained sensory panel. Four strains spanning the observed range of behaviors were hence analyzed by two-dimensional polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (2D-PAGE) and Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-Of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-ToF MS) at an early and a mid-fermentation stage, yielding 30–46 differentially abundant proteins identified per strain. Strain-specific abundance of proteins involved in glycerol formation, acetaldehyde oxidation and sulfur amino acid metabolism paralleled the corresponding differences in glycerol, acetic acid and hydrogen sulfide production, whereas glycolytic enzyme abundance varied without any corresponding variation in ethanol. Proteomic analysis thus identified candidate molecular correlates of the traits that distinguish strains, suggesting that it could complement traditional screening in the selection of indigenous starter cultures.

Article.Title: Fasting, Systemic Epigallocatechin-3-Gallate Exposure, and Hepatotoxicity
Article.Authors: Sümer A.
Article.Abstract: Green tea (Camellia sinensis) contains bioactive catechins, particularly epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), but traditional infusions and concentrated green tea extracts differ in EGCG content, dosing pattern, product matrix, systemic exposure, and safety. This structured narrative review evaluates how fasting affects EGCG pharmacokinetics and the relevance of increased systemic exposure to hepatotoxicity. Its distinctive contribution is not a further summary of green tea safety but an explicit appraisal of the evidence chain that is generally assumed to connect the two: each link is assessed separately, and the steps that are demonstrated in humans are separated from those that rest on biological inference. Standardized catechin preparations or purified EGCG taken after an overnight fast produce substantially higher peak plasma concentrations and total systemic exposure than when taken with food, although the two randomized within-subject comparisons that establish this effect were small, differed in dose and formulation, and assessed neither hepatic exposure nor liver injury. Evidence linking high EGCG exposure to prooxidant effects, mitochondrial dysfunction, and hepatocellular injury derives mainly from cellular and animal models at concentrations that exceed reported human peak plasma concentrations by roughly one order of magnitude; in mice, caloric restriction renders otherwise non-hepatotoxic EGCG doses hepatotoxic. In humans these outcomes must be kept apart. High-dose, long-term extract use raises serum aminotransferases in a susceptible minority, a laboratory abnormality demonstrated in controlled trials; hepatic adverse events cluster among catechin-rich bolus preparations rather than brewed beverages; and clinically apparent liver injury, documented in registry cases and associated with HLA-B*35:01, is idiosyncratic rather than dose-determined. Progression from the laboratory abnormality to clinically apparent injury has not been established. Fasting therefore increases systemic EGCG exposure, particularly from concentrated preparations, but has not been established as an independent cause of hepatotoxicity in humans. Treating fasting as an exposure-modifying condition rather than a hepatotoxic factor and nutritional state as a graded variable rather than a single category clarifies which precautions are evidence-based and which research questions remain genuinely open. Safety assessments should consider product type, dose, bolus administration, fed or fasting state, concomitant exposures, and individual susceptibility.

Article.Title: Machine Learning-Based Screening and Experimental Validation of PIK3C2A as a Candidate Angiogenesis-Related Molecule in Pulmonary Hypertension
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Zhao D.; Xiao H.; Gao L.; Huang L.; Bai D.; Gou D.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a progressive cardiopulmonary disease characterized by pulmonary vascular remodeling and dysregulated angiogenesis. However, the angiogenesis-related molecular mechanisms underlying PH remain incompletely understood, and reliable diagnostic biomarkers are still lacking. Therefore, To identify angiogenesis-related key molecules in PH through integrated transcriptomic analyses and experimental validation, we aimed to establish a candidate molecular signature and evaluate the discriminative potential of PIK3C2A. Specifically, GSE15197 was used as the primary bulk-transcriptomic discovery dataset, whereas GSE1909 for cross-species validation, and human pulmonary artery single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE210248) for cellular characterization. Moreover, Functional enrichment, Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA), immune infiltration analysis, and three machine learning algorithms—logistic regression, random forest (RF), and Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) were performed to identify model genes. In addition, Single-cell analyses were performed using GSE210248, followed by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) validation of candidate-gene expression in monocrotaline (MCT) and Sugen5416 plus hypoxia (SuHx) rat models. As a result, Forty-three angiogenesis-related differentially expressed genes (ARDEGs) were identified and were enriched in terms and pathways related to angiogenesis, vascular development, extracellular matrix organization, and HIF-1 signaling. Four model genes (DCN, DKK1, PIK3C2A, and UNC5B) were identified and showed moderate-to-high discrimination between PH and control samples in GSE15197. Among these genes, PIK3C2A showed its highest expression in endothelial cells, while complementary immune-infiltration and CellChat (version 2.1.1) analyses characterized the broader immune–stromal context of the angiogenesis-related signature. qRT-PCR further confirmed significant downregulation of PIK3C2A in the lungs and pulmonary arteries of MCTand SuHxinduced PH models (p < 0.05). In conclusion, An angiogenesis-related candidate molecular signature comprising DCN, DKK1, PIK3C2A and UNC5B was identified in PH. Among these genes, PIK3C2A showed preferential endothelial expression and was downregulated in both the MCT and SuHx rat PH models, supporting its further evaluation as a candidate molecule associated with PH.

Article.Title: Treg and Oxidative Stress Biomarker Profiles in Long COVID and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
Article.Authors: Todorova Y.; Dimitrova R.; Kalfova T.; Petrov S.; Bozhkova M.; Ivanovska M.; Dudova D.; Murdjeva M.; Taskov H.; Maes M.; Nikolova M.
Article.Abstract: Chronic immune dysregulation is the possible pathophysiological mechanism in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and long coronavirus infectious disease (long COVID, LC). However, a detailed characterization of regulatory and effector T-cell subsets in these conditions remains limited. To assess and compare T-cell subsets in relation to serum biomarkers of chronic activation and oxidative/nitrosative stress in an attempt to differentiate between LC and ME/CFS patients. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PMNC) from LC patients (n = 89), ME/CFS patients (n = 125), and healthy controls (HC, n = 80) were analyzed using multiparameter flow cytometry. The frequencies of naïve (CD45RA+), effector (CD45RA-), CD31+, CD39+, CD73+, GARP+, PI16+, CD15s/CD161+, and CD147+ Treg subsets were determined in relation to CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell differentiation, activation, and effector subsets. Catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1), glutathione peroxidase 1 (GPX1), malondialdehyde (MDA), nitric oxide synthase 1 and 3 (NOS1, NOS3), zonulin, lipopolysaccharide (LPS), immunoglobulin G (IgG) against lipopolysaccharide (IgG-LPS), Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), and Dickkopf-related protein 1 (DKK1) were measured in serum by ELISA. Clinical symptom scores (HAMA, HAMD, FF, dePol) were additionally assessed. The immune-serum biomarkers distinguishing LC, ME/CFS, and HC comprised Th17, CD15s+CD161−eTreg, and CD161+ Treg. The five-marker signature retained significance after adjustment for age, BMI, and sex. Altered T-cell subsets were strongly associated with markers of oxidative (GPX1) and nitrosative (NOS3) stress but not directly with symptom severity. ME/CFS showed a strong separation from HC across Random Forest (AUC = 0.907) and logistic regression (AUC = 0.924). The modest distinction of LC from HC (AUC = 0.727 and 0.577 respectively) possibly reflected important endotypic diversity, though differences in disease duration, vaccination history, biomarker selection, and other cohort characteristics might add to it. MDA was an independent predictor for three-class classification, ME/CFS vs. HC, and LC vs. HC pairwise comparisons, while GPX1 discriminated between ME/CFS and LC. In spite of shared biomarkers of oxidative stress and T-cell response dysregulation, our results support the hypothesis that LC and ME/CFS differ in the extent of cellular damage and the exhaustion of compensatory mechanisms.

Article.Title: Disentangling Dose and Radiation Quality Effects on Late DNA Damage Response in Human Mesenchymal Stromal Cells
Article.Authors: Korneva S.; Chernyaev A.; Belov O.; Chigasova A.; Osipov A.; Ignatov M.; Yashkina E.; Saburov V.; Vorobyeva N.; Zyuzikov N.; Osipov A.
Article.Abstract: Although ionizing radiation quality shapes the spatial structure and complexity of primary DNA lesions, its contribution relative to absorbed dose in the late DNA damage response (DDR) remains poorly quantified. We analyzed γH2AX and pATM foci kinetics in human mesenchymal stromal/stem cells exposed to 60Co γ-rays, 150 MeV protons, and 14.1 MeV neutrons at doses of 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 Gy, delivered at dose rates of 0.5 Gy/min for γ-rays, 1 Gy/min for protons, and 46 mGy/min for neutrons, respectively. An effective kinetic model was used to describe the time course of the DDR and incorporated an ultraslow component as a model-based index of long-lasting repair burden. Radiation types differed less in early signal amplitude than in decay rate and late persistence. At every investigated dose, the normalized ultraslow fraction followed the order γ-rays < protons < neutrons. This ordering was preserved in per-dose fits, while parametric bootstrapping supported the γ–neutron separation, although the absolute values of the internal fractions were only partially identifiable. RAD51, analyzed independently from model fitting, showed the same qualitative ordering at late time points, supporting the interpretation that radiation quality is more associated with persistent DDR signaling than absorbed dose within the investigated range. These findings suggest that absorbed dose alone may not fully characterize the late cellular response to different radiation qualities and highlight the importance of radiation quality in comparative radiobiology, radiation protection, and the interpretation of normal-tissue responses to therapeutic irradiation.

Article.Title: Non-HLA Autoantibody-Driven Lung Allograft Injury, Clinical Course, Autoantibody Profiling, and Response to Steroid and Belatacept
Article.Authors: Sundlof A.; Taniguchi M.; Gupta R.; Mollaee M.; Cordova F.; Shenoy K.; Geier S.; Liacini A.
Article.Abstract: The presence of HLA donor-specific antibodies (DSAs), both before and after transplantation, is a well-established risk factor for antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) and poor graft survival. However, emerging evidence suggests that non-HLA antibodies may also provoke immune responses, contributing to rejection. Among these, antibodies targeting the angiotensin II type-1 receptor (AT1R) have been linked to adverse clinical outcomes in kidney and orthotopic heart transplant recipients. This case presents an investigation of non-HLA antibodies in a lung transplant recipient diagnosed with AMR in the absence of HLA DSAs, as well as the use of belatacept as part of a combination immunosuppressive regimen to treat AMR in a lung transplant recipient.

Article.Title: Integrated Multi-Omics Analysis Provides No Evidence for Pathogenicity of Balantidium Ctenopharyngodoni in Grass Carp Hindgut
Article.Authors: Zhao W.; Fang L.; Zhou W.; Bu X.; Wu S.; Zou H.; Li W.; Wang G.; Li M.
Article.Abstract: Balantidium ctenopharyngodoni Chen, 1955 is the only ciliate species known to inhabit the digestive tract of grass carp, where it predominantly resides in the spaces between mucosal folds and within the intestinal contents of the hindgut with a high prevalence. Despite its high prevalence, the pathogenicity remains controversial. The intestinal bacterial microbiota interacts closely with enteric protozoa, and such interactions may alter host–parasite dynamics, with consequences for host susceptibility and overall health. In this study, we conducted a feeding experiment with three different dietary regimes to explore the effects of B. ctenopharyngodoni colonization on grass carp, using an integrative approach that combined microbial amplicon sequencing, metabolomics, and intestinal transcriptomics. Our results showed that balantidia colonization was associated with slightly lower body length and body weight, although these differences were not statistically significant. Balantidia colonization was also related to altered microbiota composition and diversity: the relative abundance of Bacteroidetes was more abundant in the balantidia-positive fish with a plant-based diet, while alphaproteobacteria and betaproteobacteria were enriched in the balantidia-positive fish with commercial feed. Although B. ctenopharyngodoni moderately perturbed the microbial profiles and metabolic processes of the grass carp hindgut, intestinal transcriptomic analysis did not detect significant transcriptional changes in immune-related genes between balantidia-positive and balantidia-negative groups. Collectively, under the tested dietary and physiological conditions, our findings provide no evidence of overt pathogenicity, further supporting the view that B. ctenopharyngodoni acts as a commensal ciliate in the grass carp hindgut.

Article.Title: USP1, an MAPK Target with Chaperone-like Activity, Regulates Innate Plant Immunity in Arabidopsis
Article.Authors: Manickam P.; Alhoraibi H.; Veluchamy A.; Almeida-Trapp M.; Rayapuram N.; Hirt H.
Article.Abstract: In eukaryotes, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades are highly conserved signaling modules in transducing extracellular signals perceived by receptors/sensors. MAPKs phosphorylate cytoplasmic and nuclear target proteins, modifying their stability, protein–protein interaction, enzyme activity, DNA-binding affinity, and subcellular localization. A comparative phosphoproteomics analysis of wild-type and mapk mutant plants identified a previously uncharacterized protein, USP1, as a novel MAPK target. In this work, we investigated the role of USP1 in pathogen responses. CRISPR-Cas9-generated knockout usp1 mutants displayed enhanced resistance to the bacterial pathogen P. syringae pv. tomato DC3000, reduced apoplast reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and upregulated defense marker genes such as WRKY29 and FRK1. Transcriptome analyses revealed that immune hormone signaling genes, such as salicylic acid (SA) and jasmonic acid (JA), are differentially regulated. These hormones are responsible for primary defense responses against biotrophic and necrotrophic pathogens, respectively. Accordingly, usp1 mutants show enhanced and reduced resistance to bacterial and fungal infection by Pst DC3000 and Botrytis cinerea, respectively. Biochemical analyses showed that USP1 exhibits chaperone-like activity that stabilizes various proteins, including the MAPKs MPK4 and MPK6. Furthermore, usp1 mutants were defective in flg22-mediated immune priming, indicating that USP1 is required for the establishment of PAMP-induced immune memory. Collectively, our findings identify USP1 as a MAPK-regulated chaperone that plays an important role in coordinating plant immune responses.

Article.Title: Neuropeptide Regulation of Aquaporin Intracellular Trafficking in Marine Teleost Rectal Enterocytes
Article.Authors: Chauvigné F.; Toala-Franco D.; Rey-Alfonso À.; Catalán-García M.; Finn R.; Cerdà J.
Article.Abstract: In marine teleosts, the neuroendocrine regulation of aquaporin intracellular trafficking in osmoregulatory organs such as the intestinal rectum remains underexplored. By using paralog-specific antibodies, here we determined the subcellular localization of seven aquaporin and aquaglyceroporin paralogs in the rectal enterocytes of the marine teleost gilthead seabream (Sparus aurata) and investigated the neuropeptinergic effects of arginine vasopressin (Avp) and oxytocin (Oxt) on channel trafficking. The data reveal that Aqp1aa, -1ab2 and -3a are mainly localized in the cytoplasm and basolateral membranes of the enterocytes, while Aqp1ab1, -10bb and -14 are cytoplasmatic and also present in the apical plasma membrane microvilli. In contrast, Aqp0a localizes in the enterocyte subapical cytoplasm. Treatment of rectal explants with Avp in vitro increases the targeting of Aqp1ab1, -1ab2, -10bb and -14, but not of Aqp0a, -1aa and -3a, to the enterocyte apical microvilli, which involves protein kinase A (PKA)-mediated phosphorylation of the channel subdomains. In addition, we find that the differential interaction of the Aqp1ab-type paralogs with teleost-specific 14-3-3ζ-like binding proteins is associated with the trafficking of the channels to the apical microvilli membranes. Conversely, Oxt treatment does not affect the subcellular distribution of any of the investigated aquaporins, except Aqp14, which is internalized in response to the neuropeptide by a partially independent protein kinase C pathway. These data suggest that Avp-PKA signaling controls plasma membrane trafficking of several seabream rectal aquaporins, possibly to facilitate water and solute fluxes across the enterocyte membrane.

Article.Title: Comparative Metabolomic Profiling of Amino Acids in Dried Blood Spots from Dichorionic and Monochorionic Twins Complicated by Selective Fetal Growth Restriction and Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome
Article.Authors: Chagovets V.; Frankevich N.; Tokareva A.; Novoselova A.; Yushina M.; Hajjar F.; Karapetyan T.; Ryumina I.; Frankevich V.; Sukhikh G.
Article.Abstract: Multiple pregnancy is associated with a high risk of perinatal complications, among which twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) and selective fetal growth restriction (sFGR) are of particular importance. These conditions are specific to monochorionic twins, yet their metabolic consequences in newborns remain poorly understood. Dried blood spots (DBSs) represent a convenient and non-invasive biomaterial for metabolomic analysis. This study included 7 twin pairs with sFGR, 10 pairs with TTTS, and 16 pairs from uncomplicated pregnancies. The amino acid profile in DBSs was determined by HPLC–MS/MS. Statistical significance of variation in normalized intra-pair difference in amino acid levels (ΔS_twins) was assessed using the Mann–Whitney U test with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction. The dynamics of ΔS_twins between birth and the corrected full-term age were analysed. In comparing sFGR group with controls, intra-pair differences for glycine and alanine were altered at birth, and for β-alanine and leucine at the second time point. In the TTTS group, deviations from controls were observed for glutamine (at the second time point) and for alanine, α-aminobutyric acid, and aspartic acid (in terms of dynamics). Direct comparison between the two pathologies revealed differences in citrulline (TTTS vs. sFGR at birth) and in several amino acids over time (valine, leucine, ornithine). Dynamic analysis further showed that placental type significantly influenced the postnatal metabolic reorganisation of valine and alanine. These preliminary observations require independent validation and should not be considered validated clinical biomarkers.
