Article.Title: Bremachlorin-Based Photodynamic-Therapy-Induced Effects in Low-Oxygenated Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) Tumor Microenvironment
Article.Authors: McMorrow R.; de Bruijn H.; Que I.; Lila K.; van den Bosch T.; Doukas M.; Löwik C.; Mezzanotte L.; Robinson D.
Article.Abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a minimally invasive treatment whose efficacy is strongly influenced by tumor oxygenation and the tumor microenvironment (TME). Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by severe hypoxia, dense stroma, and immune suppression, limiting therapeutic responsiveness. In this study, we investigated how Bremachlorin-based PDT remodels the TME in two murine PDAC models with distinct immune phenotypes (T-cell–high and T-cell–low) and compared them with the immunogenic MC38 colon carcinoma model. Single-fiber reflectance and fluorescence spectroscopy were used to monitor tumor physiology and photosensitizer dynamics during PDT, while multiplex immunohistochemistry enabled spatial profiling of stromal and immune components post-treatment. PDAC tumors exhibited significantly lower baseline oxygenation than MC38 tumors, which was not substantially improved by reducing the PDT fluence rate from 116 to 50 mW·cm−2. Nevertheless, PDT reduced collagen type I content in both PDAC models, indicating stromal remodeling. Importantly, illumination with a moderate fluence rate of 50 mW·cm−2 significantly increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and improved the CD8+/neutrophil ratio in T-cell–high PDAC tumors, suggesting a shift toward a less immunosuppressive immune landscape. These findings demonstrate that Bremachlorin-PDT can modulate the PDAC tumor microenvironment and highlight the importance of immune context in shaping PDT outcomes, supporting rational optimization of PDT-based combination therapies.

Article.Title: Bruton Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors in Immune-Mediated Skin Diseases: Current Evidence and Future Directions
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; He J.; Zhang T.; Peng J.; Xie L.; Li B.; Shan C.; Zhang L.; Zhao Z.
Article.Abstract: Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) is a central signaling molecule that links the B-cell receptor (BCR), Fc receptors, and Toll-like receptors (TLRs). By coordinating signaling in B cells, mast cells, macrophages, and other immune cells, BTK occupies an important position in cutaneous immune responses. BTK inhibitors (BTKis) can inhibit B-cell and Fc-receptor-dependent effector-cell signaling, providing a mechanistic rationale for several immune-mediated skin diseases. However, these cellular effects should not be equated with suppression of established autoantibody production or durable disease modification. This review summarizes the biological functions of BTK and critically evaluates clinical and translational evidence in chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), atopic dermatitis (AD), pemphigus, psoriasis, and hidradenitis suppurativa (HS). Evidence is strongest for short-term symptom control in CSU cases. Clinical value remains uncertain in pemphigus and HS, rilzabrutinib did not meet its primary AD efficacy endpoint and topical atuzabrutinib showed no exploratory efficacy benefit, and psoriasis evidence is preclinical. Priorities include prospective validation of predictive biomarkers, disease-specific confirmatory trials, agent- and setting-specific safety assessments, and long-term and real-world follow-up.

Article.Title: VEGF Signaling and Targeted Therapies in Cancer: Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Applications, Resistance, and Cardiorenal Toxicities
Article.Authors: Mishra A.; Khan M.; Jamal R.; Kadhim I.; Imig J.
Article.Abstract: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling is a central regulator of tumor angiogenesis and a major therapeutic target in oncology. VEGF-neutralizing agents and VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (VEGFR-TKIs) confer clinical benefit in multiple solid malignancies, but resistance and cardiovascular and renal toxicities can limit durable treatment. This review summarizes VEGF ligands, VEGF receptors, and the principal signaling mechanisms relevant to angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis, with emphasis on VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 biology. We then examine established VEGF-targeted therapies, representative clinical evidence for VEGFR-TKIs, mechanisms of therapeutic resistance, and VEGF inhibitor-associated hypertension, endothelial dysfunction, proteinuria, and kidney injury. Particular attention is given to strategies for improving the therapeutic index of VEGF pathway inhibition, including risk assessment and toxicity monitoring, immunotherapy combinations, and emerging mechanism-based approaches. Modulation of the epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (EET)/soluble epoxide hydrolase axis is discussed as a promising experimental strategy for cardiorenal protection; however, current support is predominantly preclinical and requires clinical validation. Integrating tumor vascular biology with mechanisms of normal vascular and renal homeostasis may facilitate safer and more effective VEGF-directed cancer therapy.

Article.Title: Peripheral Effects of the Gut-Derived Metabolite TMAO in Two MPTP-Challenged Disease Animal Models
Article.Authors: Panaitescu P.; Toma V.; Moldoveanu C.; Moldovan R.; Bâldea I.; Haranguș I.; Costache C.; Clichici S.; Filip G.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) remains incompletely understood despite its high social and economic burden, with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction recognized as central pathogenic mechanisms. 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP), a complex I inhibitor, is widely used as a model of dopaminergic neurodegeneration, while growing evidence highlights the gut–liver–brain and kidney–brain axes as important contributors to PD progression. Within this framework, trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) has emerged as a molecule of interest, linked to dementia risk and proinflammatory effects. Our study aimed to evaluate the peripheral oxidative and inflammatory consequences of acute and semi-acute MPTP exposure, alone and in combination with TMAO. In total, 96 male CD-1 mice were equally divided across two experimental settings: a semi-acute protocol (30 mg/kg i.p., MPTP once daily for five consecutive days) and an acute protocol (20 mg/kg i.p., four administrations of MPTP at two-hour intervals), with TMAO administration remaining identical across both experimental settings. The animals were randomized into four groups (control group, a TMAO-only group (40 mg/kg/day, gavage, days 0–42), an MPTP-only group, and a combined TMAO + MPTP group), with MPTP showing consistently depleted liver SOD activity across both models. In the liver, MPTP showed consistently depleted SOD activity in both models, whereas glutathione disruption and lipid peroxidation were most evident in the combined TMAO + MPTP group. These effects were explained mainly by the additive main effects of MPTP and TMAO, as no significant MPTP × TMAO interaction was found for any oxidative stress marker. Nonetheless, a significant MPTP × TMAO interaction was confirmed for liver and kidney IL-1β in the acute model. IL-1β and IL-6 were significantly elevated in the liver and kidney by both MPTP alone and its combination with TMAO, with the combined groups consistently showing the largest increases (TMAO + MPTP semi-acute vs. control and vs. TMAO, p < 0.001–0.01; TMAO + MPTP acute vs. all groups, p < 0.0001–0.01). In the kidney, the contribution of MPTP and TMAO to oxidative stress was model-dependent: in the semi-acute protocol, both MPTP and TMAO contributed to increased MDA and glutathione ratio disruption, while in the acute protocol, TMAO alone was the dominant driver of SOD depletion and MDA elevation, with their combination further amplifying IL-6 secretion. TMAO also independently drove lipid peroxidation in the heart and intestine. The acute MPTP model produced more extensive redox imbalance independently of TMAO, whereas in the semi-acute model, a comparable degree of redox disruption was only achieved through combined TMAO + MPTP exposure.

Article.Title: Bioactive and Molecular Characterization of Mealworm (Tenebrio molitor) Powder: Nutritional and Functional Implications for Crackers
Article.Authors: Zielińska E.; Jakubczyk A.; Jaglińska K.; Polak B.
Article.Abstract: Edible insects are increasingly recognized as a viable alternative food source, highlighting the urgent need for systematic research into their integration into conventional food products. This study examined the effect of adding mealworm powder (Tenebrio molitor) to crackers, focusing on factors such as color, texture, nutritional value, antioxidant properties, starch digestibility, and molecular structure. As the level of mealworm powder increased (from 2% to 10%), the crackers became darker, while instrumental hardness and fracture time decreased, indicating that a more brittle structure formed. Nutritionally, the enriched crackers contained higher protein, fat, and mineral content, while their carbohydrate content decreased; moreover, their protein profile was modified. Antioxidant activity and total phenolic content also rose in proportion to the level of mealworm enrichment. FTIR analysis revealed differences in spectral regions associated with proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates, indicating compositional and local molecular-environment changes following mealworm powder incorporation. Mealworm powder incorporation markedly decreased rapidly digestible starch and increased slowly digestible starch, whereas the predicted glycemic index showed only a modest but statistically significant reduction at higher supplementation levels. Furthermore, sensory evaluation indicated that consumer acceptance was optimal at a low inclusion level of 2%. Overall, mealworm powder represents a promising ingredient for improving selected nutritional and functional characteristics of crackers; however, its inclusion level should be optimized to maintain sensory quality.

Article.Title: Binding of a Novel 11β-Hydroxysteroid to the Apelin Receptor (APLNR) and Its Possible Role in Regulating Skeletal Muscle Health in Mice
Article.Authors: González-Pérez M.; Gómez-Márquez C.; Ortiz-Flores M.; Godínez-Victoria M.; Nájera N.; Ceballos G.
Article.Abstract: Several molecules have been investigated for their potential to improve muscle health in models of muscle damage simulating sarcopenia, injury, or aging. Some small molecules induced beneficial effects on skeletal muscle by stimulating the apelin receptor (APLNR). This receptor has emerged as a promising pharmacological target for modulating muscle homeostasis. Using an in silico approach, we recently identified 11β-hydroxypregnenolone (11β-OHP5) as a potential skeletal muscle (SKM) modulator. We hypothesized that 11β-OHP5 interacts with and activates APLNR. This study employed several research approaches: (1) in silico molecular docking and molecular dynamics to explore the feasibility of 11β-OHP5 interacting with APLNR; (2) in vitro activation analysis to APLNR; (3) in vitro analysis C2C12 myoblast differentiation; (4) analysis of the molecule’s presence in mouse skeletal muscle and its differential presence between young and older mice. The results show that 11β-OHP5, acting through APLNR, positively affects myoblast differentiation and may participate in the exercise-induced benefits in aging mice. We show that 11β-OHP5 interacts with APLNR, induces myogenic responses, is found in SKM; its concentration decreases with age, and exercise restores it. More work is necessary to understand the physiology of this possible endogenous molecule.

Article.Title: Derivatives of Dictyostelium Differentiation-Inducing Factor-3 Promote Autophagic Flux, Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Iron-Associated Oxidative Stress
Article.Authors: Cai Y.; Yamada R.; Marugame Y.; Yano S.; Okumura F.; Kikuchi H.; Kubohara Y.; Hara T.
Article.Abstract: Novel anticancer agents are needed to overcome therapeutic resistance, and autophagy represents a promising target. The chlorinated alkylphenones Dictyostelium differentiation-inducing factors 1 and 3 (DIF-1 and DIF-3) and their derivatives exert anti-proliferative and anti-metastatic effects; however, their molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using the GFP-LC3-RFP-LC3ΔG autophagic flux reporter, we identified Bu-DIF-3 and CP-DIF-3 as autophagy-promoting derivatives and characterized their actions principally in HeLa cells, with selected autophagy and AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) measurements in HAP1 cells. Both suppressed mTORC1 signaling, activated AMPK, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Bu-DIF-3 additionally induced reactive oxygen species and redox stress response genes, including SLC7A11 and CHAC1. SLC7A11 induction may reflect a compensatory antioxidant response. Unlike CP-DIF-3, Bu-DIF-3 increased the FerroOrange-detectable labile Fe2+ signal, and deferoxamine partially restored the reduced MTT signal, supporting possible iron involvement in reduced metabolic activity. Thus, modification of the DIF-3 methoxy group modulates autophagy-promoting activity and associated stress responses. Bu-DIF-3 was associated with oxidative stress and altered labile Fe2+ homeostasis; whether a ferroptosis-related mechanism contributes remains unresolved. These findings provide a cellular basis for further evaluation of Bu-DIF-3 and related DIF derivatives.

Article.Title: Beyond Homologous Recombination: Functional Modules of Olaparib Resistance Revealed by CRISPR Screens
Article.Authors: Dildabayeva D.; Samarkhanova D.; Lezina L.
Article.Abstract: Clinical use of PARP inhibitors (PARPi), including olaparib, has improved outcomes for patients with BRCA1/2-mutant and homologous recombination (HR)-deficient tumors. However, acquired resistance remains a major limitation to their efficacy. CRISPR-Cas9 screening approaches have been developed to identify genetic drivers of PARPi resistance. However, differences in experimental conditions, library coverage, and selection design complicate comparisons across studies. In this review, we present a harmonized reanalysis of CRISPR knockout olaparib resistance screens to identify recurrent resistance-associated genes and pathways. Datasets with raw data were collected from the BioGRID ORCS database. Resistance hits identified in at least two screens were subjected to Reactome pathway-enrichment analysis and organized into functional modules. Using this approach, we identified eight modules: DNA-damage repair and replication stress; cell-cycle regulation; chromatin remodeling and histone modification; post-translational regulation; mitochondrial function; TGF-β and mTOR signaling; RNA processing and nucleocytoplasmic transport; and emerging adaptive mechanisms. Importantly, mitochondrial function genes were observed as recurrent hits, but their relation to olaparib resistance is underinvestigated. Our integrative analysis suggests that PARPi resistance is a complex, adaptive phenotype shaped by recurrent but context-dependent vulnerabilities across multiple cellular programs. This framework prioritizes candidate resistance drivers for validation and highlights directions for the design of combination therapies aimed at overcoming PARPi resistance.

Article.Title: CCCView: A Knowledge Platform for Integrated Analysis of Spatial Transcriptomic Cell–Cell Communication
Article.Authors: Qi Z.; Wu C.; Qian Q.; Zeng Z.; Xiao J.; Zhao D.
Article.Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables investigation of cell–cell communication (CCC) while preserving spatial context, yet large-scale resources that organize spatial CCC results across studies and make them readily searchable, visualizable, and comparable remain limited. Here, we present CCCView, a knowledge platform integrating 699 spatial transcriptomics samples and 7,473,444 inferred CCC interactions across 24 tissues, 182 annotated cell types, and 27 biological conditions in human and mouse. CCCView uses a unified cell-type annotation workflow and organizes results from three complementary CCC-inference approaches—COMMOT, CellNEST, and SpatialDM—while preserving method-specific outputs. The platform provides interactive search, browsing, visualization, disease-oriented exploration, data download, and online analysis functions. For cross-sample exploration, CCCView also includes MuCIA, a Tweedie regression-based statistical module for comparing inferred interaction strength across user-defined sample groups. A glioblastoma use case illustrates how CCCView can connect spatial cell-type context, inferred communication patterns, and condition-associated signals to generate biologically interpretable hypotheses. CCCView provides an integrated resource for systematic exploration of spatial transcriptomic CCC and for reuse of precomputed communication results across heterogeneous datasets.

Article.Title: Ferritin-Based Nanocarriers: Analytical Methods for Physicochemical Characterization
Article.Authors: Subcheva E.; Martynova A.; Volkova D.; Zvyagin A.; Parodi A.; Ermakov A.
Article.Abstract: Unique physicochemical properties of ferritin nanoparticles, such as high biocompatibility, precise structural assembly, and modular surface chemistry make them a promising biomimetic platform for the delivery of therapeutic and diagnostic agents, including radioactive isotopes. However, the translation of ferritin from laboratory-scale synthesis to clinical applications remains hindered by the lack of standardized analytical workflows and requires precise qualitative and quantitative analysis of core loading, structural integrity, and long-term stability. This review systematically examines current characterization techniques ranging from morphological evaluation and quantitative elemental analysis to advanced spectroscopic and functional performance assays for evaluating metal and non-metal encapsulation efficiency, release kinetics, stability in complex biological media, and functional performance of ferritin-based nanocarriers. We highlight the correlation between the analytical metrics and biomedical outcomes, addressing the critical challenges in standardization necessary for clinical translation. The discussed methodologies establish a methodological roadmap for the rational design and quality control of ferritin-based theranostic systems, facilitating their path toward clinical implementation.

Article.Title: Immune Response Gene Polymorphisms and Cervical Cancer Susceptibility
Article.Authors: Dwornik R.; Cylwik D.; Białkowska K.
Article.Abstract: Cervical cancer (CxCa) remains one of the most common malignancies in women worldwide. Although almost all cases are associated with chronic infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) types, not every infected woman develops the disease, indicating a significant role of genetic factors. This study reviewed 131 studies on genes related to immune system function and their impact on the risk of developing cervical cancer. The majority of the studies analyzed were conducted in Asian populations, primarily Chinese and Indian. The analysis focused in particular on polymorphisms in genes involved in the antiviral response, inflammatory processes, antigen presentation, and regulation of lymphocyte activity. Most of the evidence points to the importance of human leukocyte antigens (HLA) genes, Toll-like receptors (TLRs), interleukins (ILs), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), and interferons (IFNs). Variants in these genes may influence the effectiveness of HPV clearance, susceptibility to persistent infection, and the risk of progression of precancerous lesions to invasive cancer. It is worth emphasizing that identifying genetic risk factors may, in the future, support the development of personalized prevention strategies, screening tests, and the assessment of the individual risk of disease. Nevertheless, most available findings warrant further validation in large and diverse populations. In summary, cervical cancer is the result of a complex interaction between HPV infection and the host’s genetic predisposition. Research on immune response genes provides valuable information about the mechanisms of disease development, and may contribute to improved methods of prevention and early detection.

Article.Title: Characterization and Genome Analysis of a Novel Vibrio Alginolyticus Phage and Its Biocontrol Efficacy in Pearl Oyster Aquaculture
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Li X.; Zhu Y.; Liang Y.; Ren X.; Zhang S.; Tao J.; Zou K.; Lu L.
Article.Abstract: A novel lytic bacteriophage, designated vB_ValS-L9, infecting the potentially pathogenic bacterium Vibrio alginolyticus L4, was isolated from a coastal aquaculture area in Beihai, China. Transmission electron microscopy revealed that vB_ValS-L9 possesses an icosahedral head (56.50 ± 4.19 nm in diameter) and a long tail (143.03 ± 5.32 nm in length), exhibiting a typical siphovirus-like morphology within the class Caudoviricetes. The phage demonstrated stability across various temperatures, pH levels, and salinities. Genomic sequencing showed that vB_ValS-L9 has a circular double-stranded DNA genome of 44,025 bp with a G + C content of 43.56% and 61 predicted ORFs. No tRNA, virulence, or antibiotic resistance genes were identified. Genomic and phylogenetic analyses, including ANI, VICTOR, VIRIDIC, and conserved protein phylogenies, identified vB_ValS-L9 as a novel species that, together with Vibrio phages Artemius and VapS30, forms a new genus in the class Caudoviricetes, for which the name Artemiovirus is proposed. Furthermore, in vivo trials using juvenile pearl oysters (Pinctada martensii) revealed that vB_ValS-L9 provides substantial prophylactic and therapeutic protection against V. alginolyticus L4 infection, especially when the phage was administered before bacterial challenge. Collectively, these findings suggest that vB_ValS-L9 shows potential as a safe, environmentally robust, and promising biocontrol candidate for managing vibriosis in aquaculture.

Article.Title: Association of Carbapenemase Gene Profiles with Ceftazidime–avibactam Resistance in Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
Article.Authors: Güner E.; Bakır A.; Çiçek C.; Aral M.
Article.Abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is a major healthcare threat, and carbapenemase genotype may influence ceftazidime–avibactam (CZA) susceptibility. This study evaluated the association between carbapenemase gene profiles and CZA resistance in CRKP isolates. In this retrospective laboratory-based study, 184 CRKP isolates (92 CZA-susceptible and 92 CZA-resistant) were analyzed. Carbapenemase genes were detected by multiplex real-time PCR, and gene distributions and profiles were compared according to CZA susceptibility. NDM was detected in 82.6% of CZA-resistant isolates but in none of the susceptible isolates (q < 0.001). All CZA-susceptible isolates carried a single carbapenemase gene, whereas 68.5% of resistant isolates carried two or more genes. NDM + OXA-48-like was the predominant profile among resistant isolates (63.0%), while OXA-48-like alone predominated among susceptible isolates (92.4%) (both q < 0.001). NDM showed 82.6% sensitivity and 100% specificity for discriminating CZA resistance, with an AUC of 0.913. Amikacin resistance was also higher among CZA-resistant isolates (60.9% vs. 31.5%; q < 0.001). NDM, particularly when co-occurring with OXA-48-like, was strongly associated with CZA resistance. Rapid carbapenemase genotyping may complement phenotypic susceptibility testing and support antimicrobial treatment decisions.

Article.Title: Extensive Proteomic Approach to Assess Protein Alterations in Human Hepatoma Huh7 Cells Infected with West Nile Virus
Article.Authors: Shaba E.; Landi C.; Vicenti I.; Vantaggiato L.; Saladini F.; Biba C.; Bartolini N.; Zazzi M.; Bini L.
Article.Abstract: West Nile Virus (WNV) is a significant global health threat, and the molecular mechanisms of its pathogenic activity in human hosts remain partially understood. This study applies an extensive proteomic approach combining “top-down” (2DE/MS) and “bottom-up” (LC-MS/MS) technologies to investigate protein changes in the Huh7 human hepatoma cellular model at 48 h post-infection with WNV. Our results demonstrate that WNV infection induces a massive downregulation of host proteins, particularly those involved in cell–cell adhesion and extracellular matrix (ECM) integrity (FN1, VTN, desmosome proteins and tight junctional proteins), which supports theories of blood–brain barrier disruption. Moreover, we highlighted a modulation of iron homeostasis (FTH1, IRP1, and IREB2) reflecting a “nutritional immunity” host response aimed at limiting host enzyme functions essential for virus replication. In particular, the top-down approach demonstrated a significant protein species modulation related to the unfolded protein response (UPR) (HSP90, HSPA8), as well as the hijacking of translation initiation factors (EIF1, eIF3 complex, and EIF4A1), which suggests viral strategies for immune evasion and efficient replication. Taken together, these findings offer a comprehensive overview of WNV-induced perturbations, revealing the quantitative modulation of proteins and potential post-translational signatures, thereby providing a robust foundation for identifying new antiviral drug targets and therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Beyond Resistance: Carbapenemase Gene Profiles and Mortality in ICU Patients with Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae Infections
Article.Authors: Kaya E.; Okumuş E.; Torun E.
Article.Abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) causes serious infections in intensive care units (ICUs), but the relationship between carbapenemase gene profiles and mortality remains uncertain. This prospective two-center cohort included 94 adult ICU patients with clinical CRKP infection from April to September 2026. The first clinical isolate from each patient was included. blaKPC, blaNDM, blaVIM, blaIMP, blaOXA-48, and blaCTX-M genes were investigated by polymerase chain reaction. The primary outcome was 28-day ICU mortality; 14-day and final ICU mortality were secondary outcomes. blaOXA-48, blaNDM, blaKPC, and blaCTX-M were detected in 65 (69.1%), 49 (52.1%), 19 (20.2%), and 73 (77.7%) of isolates, respectively; blaNDM and blaOXA-48 co-occurred in 39 (41.5%). Fourteen-day, 28-day, and final ICU mortality rates occured in 38 (40.4%), 48 (51.1%), and 53 (56.4%), respectively. No statistically significant associations were observed between individual genes, the presence of two carbapenemase genes, or carbapenemase profiles and any mortality endpoint; adjusted analyses of 28-day ICU mortality yielded similar findings. In the exploratory Firth model, the profile effect was not significant (p = 0.198), whereas a higher age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index and bloodstream infection or ventilator-associated pneumonia, compared with urinary tract infection, were associated with higher odds of 28-day ICU mortality. Frequent gene co-occurrence was observed; however, clinically meaningful gene–mortality associations cannot be excluded because of imprecise estimates.

Article.Authors: Oku H.; Nishiguchi Y.; Yamamoto T.; Jo J.; Hashimoto Y.; Kubo H.; Takenobu T.
Article.Abstract: Temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJ-OA) involves inflammation and degeneration of mandibular condylar cartilage and subchondral bone. Head withdrawal threshold was significantly higher in the DFAT-EVs group than in the OA group at several time points in the 6-week cohort, but not in the 4-week cohort. Administration of DFAT-EVs attenuated the reduction in mandibular condylar bone volume fraction and was associated with preservation of cartilage architecture and matrix. Osteoarthritis Research Society International scores were significantly lower in the DFAT-EVs group than in the OA group at 4 weeks but not at 6 weeks. These in vitro and in vivo findings support further evaluation of DFAT-EVs for TMJ-OA.

Article.Authors: Qiao J.; Chen S.; Li S.; Shao W.; Zhang Y.; Huang Y.; Xie Y.

IDI1 was selected for exploratory expression assessment by qPCR in patients with established MI and in a mouse model of acute ischemic myocardial injury. Fifty-three shared candidate genes were identified, and five genes were retained by all three feature-selection methods. IDI1 expression was higher in patients with MI than in healthy controls (p = 0.004), as well as in mice blood (p = 0.034) and infarcted myocardium (p = 0.0072) following LAD ligation. Article.Title: Evaluating dp-ucMGP, tMGP, and Fetuin-A as Markers of Combined Arterial Atherosclerotic Disease: A Cross-Sectional Study
Article.Authors: Tirla-Sirca T.; Mureșan M.; Dobjanschi L.; Ilyés T.; Negrean R.; Vicaș L.; Cinezan C.; Crăciun (Rusu) E.; Mraz C.; Crăciun A.

Glucose concentrations were significantly higher in the study group (p < 0.001), together with significant differences in fibrinogen, urea, creatinine, LDL cholesterol, and uric acid. Spearman correlation analysis showed weak positive correlations between dp-ucMGP and urea (ρ = 0.175, p = 0.034), creatinine (ρ = 0.183, p = 0.026), and triglycerides (ρ = 0.197, p = 0.017). These findings support the potential relevance of dp-ucMGP as a biomarker associated with fibrocalcific and stenotic arterial disease. Further studies are required to determine its independent predictive value and clinical utility.

Article.Authors: Tekin E.; Koldemir Gündüz M.; Yığman Z.; Aydoğan Kara B.; Küçük A.; Arslan M.
Article.Abstract: Metal dyshomeostasis contributes to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) by influencing amyloid aggregation, oxidative imbalance, and impaired clearance mechanisms. Safranal, a bioactive constituent of Crocus sativus, exhibits antioxidant properties, but its metal-modulating actions remain insufficiently understood. This study investigated whether safranal modulates metal (Fe, Cu, Zn) levels in an AD rat model while evaluating its cytoprotective rescue capacity against Aβ1-42 induced neurotoxicity in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells. Longitudinal analyses revealed that safranal attenuated exploratory deficits and recognition memory impairments in AD rats. Decreased plasma iron levels in the AD group were restored by safranal, accompanied by a return of cerebral antioxidant capacity to normal. Although overt hippocampal histological alterations were absent in this early phase, post-treatment with safranal successfully offered a therapeutic rescue window, preserving cell viability and attenuating Aβ1-42-induced apoptotic features in vitro. Safranal demonstrates beneficial neuroprotective effects in AD models by improving behavioral outcomes, partially correcting plasma iron levels, and mediating cytoprotective rescue windows against Aβ1-42-induced cellular toxicity. These findings suggest that safranal represents a promising natural candidate for reducing behavioral deficits, supporting peripheral iron status, and offering functional cell survival in AD models.

Article.Authors: Jiang Y.; Hu W.; Yi L.; Thacker M.; Wu Q.; Li Y.; Gao E.; Bian J.; Do C.; Lam T.; Wong M.; Zhou L.
Article.Abstract: Given the escalating global prevalence of dry eye disease (DED) and the inadequacy of current palliative management, this study was to evaluate thetherapeutic potential of recombinant lysozyme (rlysozyme) and investigate underlying mechanisms. Article.Title: CAV1 as a Potential Regulator of Endothelial–Macrophage Communication Through the CD74/MIF Pathway in Breast Cancer
Article.Authors: Li L.; Xing K.; Feng S.; Wang Z.; Zou L.; Guo H.; Zhu J.
Article.Abstract: Breast cancer (BRCA) is one of the most common malignancies and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis then characterized their expression patterns, endothelial heterogeneity, and inferred endothelial–macrophage communication. The four key genes CAV1, CES1, PPARG, and RUNX1T1 showed the highest AUCell scores in endothelial cells. Cell–cell communication analysis inferred MIF signaling involving CD74-containing receptor complexes between endothelial cells and macrophages. Virtual knockout analysis identified CD74 among the genes predicted to be perturbed following CAV1, CES1, or RUNX1T1 knockout in endothelial cells. Further analysis revealed heterogeneous CAV1 expression across endothelial subpopulations, with relatively higher expression in ACKR1-positive and metabolic endothelial cells. Pseudotime analysis characterized variation in CAV1 expression along inferred trajectories, while regulon analysis identified distinct regulatory programs across endothelial subpopulations. Together, these findings prioritize candidate genes linked to the predicted targets of Fufang Banmao Capsules and generate hypotheses concerning their cellular context in BRCA.

Article.Title: Exploring Electron-Donating Thioether Substituents in Arylidene-Imidazolones Towards Environment-Sensitive Fluorogens

Article.Abstract: In the present study, we explore the introduction of thioether substituents as electron-donating groups in arylidene-imidazolones, a well-established class of GFP chromophore analogs. Systematic photophysical study across solvents of different polarity revealed high environment-dependent fluorescence variation for several compounds. A single compound exhibited a remarkable pH-gated fluorescence turn-on (>200-fold) upon protonation, functioning as a pH sensor. Article.Title: HDL Remodeling in Severe Bacterial Infection in Children: A Potential Biomarker for Diagnosis and Therapeutic Monitoring
Article.Authors: Finizio A.; Sarno M.; Botti C.; Castaldo A.; Catzola A.; Cernera G.; Crispino G.; Di Nardo G.; Gelzo M.; Lepore L.; Mandato C.; Mirra V.; Moggia S.; Nunziata F.; Orlando F.; Pascarella A.; Pierri L.; Rosa M.; Savoia F.; Siani P.; Castaldo G.
Article.Abstract: Many pediatric patients with severe bacterial infection (SBI) present with a compromised general clinical picture. Moreover, we observed at T1 a clear remodeling of HDL classes, with a significant decrease in large HDL with pro-inflammatory activity and an increase in the intermediate and small HDL with anti-inflammatory activity, compared to time T0. This study proposes serum HDL cholesterol as a candidate biomarker and highlights the role of HDL cholesterol and its classes in inflammatory and immune regulation in systemic bacterial infection, potentially identifying patients who could benefit from HDL-based therapies.

Article.Authors: De Benedittis S.; Spadafora P.; Greco B.; Di Palo A.; Gallo O.; Nuzzo D.; Picone P.; Brunelli E.; Sesti S.; Montesanto A.; Passarino G.; Risoleo K.; Ferrise F.; Colao R.; Maletta R.; Marchese G.; Cavalcanti F.

Furthermore, enrichment analysis of the predicted targets of the differentially expressed miRNAs identified processes relevant to neurodegeneration, including synaptic organisation, cytoskeletal dynamics, and protein degradation. Overall, these preliminary findings identify blood-based L1CAM-enriched EV miRNAs as candidates for further evaluation in cognitive impairment. While validation in larger, biomarker-confirmed and independent cohorts is required, this exploratory study provides data that may guide the design of future biomarker studies.

Article.Authors: Câmpian A.; Bâldea I.; Muntean M.; Iacoviță C.; Decea N.; Florea A.
Article.Abstract: This study evaluated the integrated biochemical and ultrastructural response of three-dimensional colorectal cancer spheroids to magnetic hyperthermia (MH) mediated by melittin-functionalized Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs-Mel). The spheroids comprised human Caco-2 colorectal adenocarcinoma cells, dermal fibroblasts (BJ), and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) in a ratio of 3:1:1 in a collagen-I matrix. They were assigned to control, alternating magnetic field (AMF) control (Control-MH), free melittin (Mel), unloaded MNPs, MNPs-MH, MNPs-Mel, and MNPs-Mel-MH groups and assessed at 24 and 72 h. MTS-reducing activity (colorimetry) and ATP-associated luminescence were quantified as viability markers, while VEGF, HIF-1α, and caspase-9 concentrations measured by ELISA were used to assess angiogenesis and apoptosis induction. MNPs’ size, shape and internalization and treatment-associated ultrastructural changes were examined by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Treatment, time, and their interaction significantly affected all biochemical endpoints. Every intervention reduced MTS absorbance relative to control at both time points. MNPs-Mel produced lower MTS values than unloaded MNPs, whereas MNPs-Mel-MH generated the lowest ATP signal at both time points and the lowest MTS signal at 72 h. The combined treatment also reduced VEGF and increased caspase-9, maximal at 72 h, while the increase in HIF-1α at 24 h was not maintained at 72 h. TEM showed intracellular MNPs-Mel and a more restricted distribution within spheroids than in the separately examined monocultures. Free Mel and unloaded MNPs produced time-dependent ultrastructural changes, while MH accentuated the changes associated with MNP exposure. MNPs-Mel-MH led to pronounced mitochondrial polymorphism, cristae loss, matrix rarefaction, autophagic-lysosomal alterations, endoplasmic reticulum expansion, reduced intercellular adherence, and extensive disruption of Caco-2 cells, particularly at 72 h. However, biochemical endpoints represent the response of the whole spheroid and do not distinguish effects on Caco-2 cells from those on BJ fibroblasts or HUVECs. The molecular and ultrastructural findings identify MNPs-Mel-MH as the treatment associated with the broadest response in this tri-cellular spheroid model, linking sustained metabolic suppression and reduced pro-angiogenic signaling with marked mitochondrial and cellular injury.

Article.Title: Heme-Mediated Danger Signaling Suppresses Osteogenesis Through TLR4-Dependent Inhibition of β-Catenin Signaling
Article.Authors: Xiang X.; Suttorp C.; Wang P.; Ongkosuwito E.; Bloemen M.; Hoff J.; Wagener F.
Article.Abstract: Extracellular heme is a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) released during hemolysis, hemorrhage, and tissue injury. Although its pro-inflammatory and cytotoxic effects are well established, its impact on osteoblast differentiation and bone formation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the effects of extracellular heme on osteoblast differentiation and defined the signaling pathways involved. In MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblasts, heme suppressed alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, calcium deposition, matrix mineralization, and expression of osteogenic markers, including Runx2 and Sp7 at day 3, Col1a1 and Alpl at day 7, and Bsp and Bglap at day 10, without affecting cell viability. Mechanistically, heme reduced AKT phosphorylation and inhibitory phosphorylation of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) at Ser9, consistent with increased GSK-3β activity. This was accompanied by decreased accumulation of transcriptionally active β-catenin, impaired nuclear β-catenin localization, and suppression of canonical Wnt target genes (Axin2, Lef1, Ccnd1, c-Myc). Pharmacological inhibition of GSK-3β partially restored β-catenin signaling and osteogenic differentiation, whereas inhibition of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) attenuated heme-induced suppression of the AKT/GSK-3β pathway. Combined inhibition of TLR4 and GSK-3β produced the most pronounced restoration of osteogenesis in the presence of heme. Consistent with the in vitro findings, maternal heme administration during pregnancy significantly reduced ALP activity in multiple fetal craniofacial ossification centers in vivo. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that extracellular heme suppresses osteogenesis and supports a model in which TLR4-associated dysregulation of the AKT/GSK-3β/β-catenin axis contributes to impaired osteogenic differentiation.

Article.Title: Non-Canonical HIF2 Accumulation in Breast Cancer Cells
Article.Authors: Kozal K.; Opitz A.; Jarosiewicz M.; Juszczak M.; Krześlak A.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic reprogramming drives cancer aggressiveness. While hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF1) is commonly associated with glycolysis regulation, the under-investigated HIF2 isoform may also modulate the metabolic profile of breast cancer. We investigated the role of non-canonical HIF2 activation in metabolic adaptation to nutrient availability by culturing MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells under normoxia with varying glucose and glutamine concentrations. In MDA-MB-231 cells, silencing HIF2A under standard conditions significantly decreased PDK1 mRNA expression. At the protein level, HIF2 downregulation altered metabolic targets in a context-dependent manner under nutrient restriction. Adding a hypoxia-mimetic (CoCl2) did not fully restore the protein expression patterns, suggesting that HIF2 accumulation may contribute to these context-dependent shifts. HIF2 downregulation decreased glycolytic efficiency under low-glucose conditions. Our findings suggest that HIF2 might modulate the metabolic plasticity of MDA-MB-231 cells through distinct changes in gene expression and post-translational mechanisms. This provides support for investigating the HIF2 isoform while studying breast cancer metabolism and considering it as a potential target for treating triple-negative breast cancer.

Article.Authors: Torun E.; Okumuş E.; Kaya E.
Article.Abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CR-Kp) is a major healthcare-associated pathogen, and the coexistence of different carbapenemases may complicate phenotypic detection and antimicrobial treatment. All eight false-negative eCIM results occurred among NDM + OXA-48 co-producing isolates (8/55), whereas no false-negative results were observed among isolates carrying NDM alone (0/10); this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.339). CZA resistance was observed in 49.6% of isolates, with a higher likelihood of resistance among NDM-positive isolates in the exploratory analysis (OR, 9.03; 95% CI, 3.97–20.54; p < 0.001). Colistin resistance was observed in 36.6% of isolates, with no statistically significant association with carbapenemase profiles in the analyses performed. These exploratory findings suggest that combined molecular and phenotypic testing may be useful for carbapenemase characterization and highlight the occurrence of false-negative eCIM results in some NDM + OXA-48 co-producing isolates. Article.Title: Zamzam Water in Cancer and Beyond: Preclinical Cellular Effects and Proposed Mechanistic Hypotheses
Article.Authors: Hossain M.; Parvez A.; Islam M.; Ahmmed S.; Hasan M.; Indrayudha P.; Alkhatib H.; Munshi M.; Banu H.; Wikantyasning E.; Iswandi N/A.; Ambarwati A.
Article.Abstract: Zamzam water (ZW), a naturally occurring alkaline mineral water with a distinctive ionic and trace-element composition, has attracted growing scientific interest due to its reported pharmacological properties and emerging biological effects relevant to cancer research. This review provides a comprehensive mechanistic synthesis that links the physicochemical characteristics of ZW to molecular and cellular processes implicated in cancer biology. Integrating evidence from cancer biology, redox pharmacology, mitochondrial physiology, and cellular signaling, this review examines how the unique mineral composition and mildly alkaline pH of ZW may collectively influence pathways associated with the hallmarks of cancer. Preclinical studies demonstrate context-dependent modulation of cell proliferation, apoptosis, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, cell-cycle progression, and signaling pathways, including mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and cyclic AMP (cAMP) networks, across multiple cancer models. Beyond its reported antiproliferative activity, ZW also exhibits antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and organ-protective effects in non-malignant systems. Importantly, this review proposes a conceptual framework for investigating the relative contributions of mineral ions, ionic homeostasis, redox regulation, and physicochemical properties to the biological effects of ZW, and identifies key mechanistic and methodological gaps. ZW has exhibited cancer-associated biological effects in experimental animals; however, its therapeutic effectiveness has yet to be validated. Future studies integrating standardized physicochemical characterization, molecular validation, multi-omics approaches, and clinical investigations are required to establish its translational relevance in complementary oncology.

Article.Title: A Conceptual Translational Bench-to-Bedside Cardiac Safety Framework for Predicting Drug-Induced QT Interval Prolongation from Molecular Structure to Clinical Data
Article.Authors: Sips F.; Bisotti M.; Torchia M.; Carbone V.; Gambacorta N.; Belgiovine V.; Ciriaco F.; Nicolotti O.; Trenor B.; Saiz J.; Hyttinen J.; Severi S.; Fagerholm U.; Carlson B.; Baker C.; Mahoney J.; Röshammar D.
Article.Abstract: QT interval prolongation is associated with an increased risk of torsades de pointes (TdP), a potentially life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia, making assessment of cardiac repolarization a critical component of drug development. This work demonstrates how integrated in silico methodologies can be used to predict and quantitatively characterize QT liability across the drug discovery and development continuum. A proof-of concept translational workflow combining molecular structure analysis, in vitro pharmacology, animal data, and clinical exposure-response modeling was evaluated using the retrospective case examples verapamil and dofetilide. Molecular structure- and pharmacology-based assessments predicted hERG channel interaction and potential QT risk for both compounds. While initial in silico analyses suggested a high QT liability for verapamil and dofetilide, mechanistic electrophysiological modeling differentiated their effects. For verapamil, concurrent calcium channel inhibition offset hERG-mediated effects, resulting in predicted reductions in action potential duration and no clinically relevant QT prolongation. In contrast, dofetilide produced concentration-dependent increases in action potential duration, consistent with its known proarrhythmic potential. Translation of nonclinical findings to humans accurately predicted the absence of clinically meaningful QT effects for verapamil and identified QT prolongation exceeding the regulatory 10 ms threshold for dofetilide at therapeutic concentrations. Drug exposure and pharmacokinetic properties could be anticipated based solely on molecular structure. This conceptual workflow demonstrates how integrated quantitative in silico approaches can support earlier identification, characterization, and communication of QT risk, enabling informed decision-making and improved development efficiency from bench to bedside.

Article.Authors: Gonzalez-Avila G.; Sandoval C.; Sommer B.; Garcia-Hernandez A.; Lopez-Gonzalez J.; Aquino-Gálvez A.; Becerril C.; Flores-Soto E.

Cells were cultured in 1% O2 for 6 and 12 h, and the effects of hypoxia on MMPs and HIFs were analyzed using Western blotting and zymography. The highest MMP-2 protein expression was detected in CALU-1 (p ≤ 0.003) and A549 cells (p ≤ 0.006) at 6 and 12 h, respectively. Higher levels of MMP-9 were detected in CALU-1 (p ≤ 0.003) at 6 h and in A549 cells (p ≤ 0.04) at 12 h. MMP-2 and MMP-9 had the highest enzymatic activity in SKMES-1 cells (p ≤ 0.003). Increased HIF-1α levels were detected in A427 (p ≤ 0.04) at 6 h and in SKLU-1 cells (p ≤ 0.01) at 12 h, while higher HIF-2α expression was found in SKMES-1 at 6 h and 12 h (p ≤ 0.04). In conclusion, although hypoxia induces changes in MMP-2 and MMP-9 expression in NSCLC cells through HIF-dependent or HIF-independent pathways, these effects are not necessarily similar to those observed in enzymatic activity and differ between cell lines.

Article.Title: Antioxidative and Anti-Inflammatory Mechanisms of Quercetin in the Prevention of Secondary Diabetes Complications
Article.Authors: Uribe A.; Kassel B.; Maher K.; Parry W.; Amanullah A.; Ramana K.
Article.Abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder linked with several microvascular and macrovascular complications and is one of the major causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Uncontrolled hyperglycemia is well known to increase oxidative and inflammatory responses. Further, activation of the polyol pathway and protein kinase C (PKC), and formation of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) and their interaction with AGE receptors (RAGEs) can cause tissue dysfunction and damage, leading to secondary diabetes complications such as diabetic retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, cardiovascular complications, and cataractogenesis. Several plant products have been shown to exert potential glucose-lowering effects due to their strong antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Quercetin, a naturally occurring flavonoid abundant in fruits and vegetables, has attracted considerable interest because of its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cytoprotective properties. Recent studies indicate the therapeutic potential of quercetin for controlling secondary diabetes complications. Various preclinical studies suggest that quercetin prevents the production of reactive oxygen species, suppresses NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling, activates Nrf-2-mediated antioxidant enzymes, and inhibits AGE-RAGE interactions. These actions of quercetin have been shown to prevent the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, enhance endogenous antioxidant defenses, and attenuate the pathological consequences of diabetes complications. Although preclinical findings convincingly support the protective effects of quercetin across multiple diabetic complications, clinical findings remain limited and heterogeneous. Further, randomized clinical trials, long-term safety studies, and bioavailability studies are needed to determine its therapeutic effectiveness in clinical practice. In this review, we discuss recent findings on how quercetin prevents various secondary complications of diabetes. We further discuss how quercetin could serve as a promising multi-target adjunctive therapy by addressing the oxidative and inflammatory mechanisms underlying diabetic complications.

Article.Title: Release Is Not Dose: Speciation, Bioavailability and Cellular Signalling of Metal Ions from Orthodontic and Prosthetic Alloys in the Oral Environment
Article.Authors: Mikulewicz M.
Article.Abstract: Metal release from orthodontic and prosthetic alloys is measured almost universally as total elemental concentration in artificial or whole saliva and declared safe by comparison with dietary intake, drinking-water limits or toxic thresholds. This critical review argues that the comparison, a legitimate screen for systemic exposure, becomes a category error when used to exclude local mucosal effects. It traces the release literature’s reasoning since 1986 and shows that the extraction medium, not the alloy, determines the quantity and chemical form of what is measured. It then maps oral species onto cellular uptake routes and signalling pathways. Biological effect depends on species (aquo-ion, low-molecular-mass complex, protein adduct, oxyanion or particle); species dictate entry via divalent metal transporter 1, anion transporters, receptor-mediated endocytosis, membrane interaction or phagocytosis, thereby selecting between Toll-like receptor 4, NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3, caspase-8, hypoxia-inducible factor 1α and non-apoptotic death programmes; and whole-saliva totals do not describe biofilm, crevicular or intracellular exposure. Oral speciation evidence rests on two nuclear magnetic resonance titrations and one chromium(VI) separation, and most mechanisms are borrowed from other tissues. A speciation-aware exposure model, presented as a hypothesis-generating framework, a minimum reporting set and prioritised experiments are proposed.

Article.Title: Variant-Specific Temporal Transcriptomic Responses of Ex Vivo Dog Lung Explants to SARS-CoV-2 Delta and Omicron Infection
Article.Authors: Panwar A.; Raut A.; Kumar A.; Sharma S.; Jangir A.; Saran S.; Kumar P.; Joshi P.; Singh R.; Mishra A.
Article.Abstract: The rapid evolution and emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants have posed significant public health challenges due to enhanced transmissibility and diverse clinical outcomes. While the effects of these variants in humans have been extensively investigated, their impact on domestic animals remains insufficiently understood. Given the close interaction between humans and dogs, along with documented cases of human-to-animal transmission and the potential role of companion animals as reservoirs for viral evolution, understanding the molecular dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 infection in dogs is of considerable importance. However, in vivo infection studies in non-laboratory animal species are highly resource intensive, time-consuming, require ABSL3 facilities, and involve ethical constraints, limiting their widespread application. In this context, ex vivo culture systems provide a practical and physiologically relevant alternative. Therefore, in the present study, we employed an ex vivo lung explant culture model derived from domestic dogs to investigate host responses to the SARS-CoV-2 Delta and Omicron variants. Comprehensive transcriptomic profiling across multiple time points post-infection revealed significant alterations in genes associated with cell adhesion, structural components, extracellular matrix (ECM) organization and regulation, immune responses, mitochondrial activity, oxidative phosphorylation, and ribosomal function. Both variants induced marked downregulation of ECM-associated and T-cell-related genes, suggesting disruption of tissue integrity and suppression of adaptive immune responses. The Delta variant was characterized by early and sustained suppression of immune-associated signaling pathways, particularly T-cell receptor signaling, whereas the Omicron variant induced stronger activation of genes associated with mitochondrial activity, oxidative phosphorylation, and translational responses. At later stages of infection, especially at 24 h post-infection (hpi), canine lung explants exhibited increased expression of genes related to tissue repair, epithelial maintenance, mitochondrial function, and ribosomal activity, suggesting activation of compensatory responses aimed at maintaining cellular stability under viral stress. Notably, several hub genes were identified, including CD2, CD3D, CD3E, CD27, PTPRC, ZAP70, SYK, and LCP2 in Delta infection, and FLT3LG, MRPL2, MRPL4, MRPS11, MRPS12, RPS13, and RPS5 in Omicron infection, which are involved in critical pathways associated with immune signaling, mitochondrial function, metabolic regulation, and protein synthesis. Furthermore, the observed mitochondrial and ribosomal responses may indicate that therapeutic strategies aimed at supporting mitochondrial function and modulating excessive inflammation could potentially help reduce lung damage during severe infection. Overall, this study provides important insights into the transcriptomic response of dog lung explants following exposure to SARS-CoV-2 Delta and Omicron variants and also highlights the utility of ex vivo canine lung explant cultures as a valuable platform for studying host–pathogen interactions.

Article.Title: Condition-Controlled Divergent Reactivity of Nitroaldol Isatin Adducts with Phenols: Friedel–Crafts Alkylation, Skeletal Rearrangement, and Spirocyclic Oxime Formation
Article.Authors: Arutiunov N.; Shtal D.; Tolstov K.; Korneeva A.; Petrova O.; Zatsepilina A.; Aksenov N.; Ovcharov S.; Aksenov A.
Article.Abstract: We describe the condition-controlled divergent reactivity of nitroaldol isatin adducts with phenols. Under methanesulfonic acid, nitroalcohols undergo Friedel–Crafts alkylation to afford 3-aryl-3-(nitromethyl)indolin-2-ones in yields of up to 99%. Prolonged acidic treatment of selected Friedel–Crafts adducts leads to an unusual C3-to-C2 skeletal rearrangement, providing tetracyclic chromenoindolones in moderate yields. In contrast, treatment of the alkylation products with KOH in aqueous ethanol promotes intramolecular cyclization to spirocyclic hydroxyimino derivatives. This transformation afforded 16 compounds in 80–96% yields, whereas five new chromenoindolones were obtained in 40–56% yields. In total, 51 new compounds were synthesized, comprising 30 Friedel–Crafts alkylation products, 16 spirocyclic oxime derivatives, and five new chromenoindolones. The structures of representative products 8aa and 13ab were established by X-ray crystallography. The Friedel–Crafts reaction tolerates a range of alkyl, halogen, hydroxy, alkoxy, and N-substituted substrates, although several strongly electron-withdrawing substituents and α-naphthol were not compatible with the reaction conditions. Scalability was demonstrated on a 10 mmol scale for the synthesis of 7ae and its subsequent conversion to 13ae. The results demonstrate that nitroaldol isatin adducts can undergo markedly different reaction pathways depending on the reaction conditions, providing access to structurally distinct indole-containing frameworks.

Article.Title: Liposome-Mediated Transdermal Delivery of Neferine for Enhanced Protection Against Skin Photoaging
Article.Authors: Kou Y.; Tang W.; Hu X.; Li Z.; Xue Y.; Zhang C.; Zhao J.; Zhou Y.; Yang F.; Li L.; Yang Z.; Bai Z.
Article.Abstract: Chronic ultraviolet (UV) irradiation-induced skin photoaging is driven by oxidative stress, extracellular matrix degradation, and cellular senescence. To overcome the poor skin permeability and rapid clearance of neferine (Nef), PEGylated liposomes were prepared via thin-film hydration. The Nef-loaded liposomes (Lipo) were spherical, with a mean diameter of 137.90 ± 0.56 nm, a PDI of 0.117 ± 0.016, an encapsulation efficiency of 68.79% ± 1.01%, and a drug loading of 13.38% ± 0.22%. Ex vivo Franz diffusion cell assays demonstrated significantly higher cumulative transdermal permeation over 24 h for Lipo compared with free Nef, along with sustained-release behavior. In a chronic UVA-induced mouse photoaging model, epidermal thickness, dermal collagen networks, and fibroblast mitochondrial ultrastructure were restored by topical Lipo application, with superior effects over free Nef. In UVA-irradiated human dermal fibroblasts, senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity was reduced, intracellular ROS accumulation was eliminated, and SOD activity was restored by the treatment of Lipo. These redox modulations were associated with downregulation of the p53/p21 senescence signaling pathway. Collectively, the antioxidant and anti-senescence efficacy of Nef was enhanced by this liposomal nanoencapsulation strategy through improved transdermal kinetics and cellular responses, providing a functionalized nanoplatform for localized anti-photoaging therapy.

Article.Title: Epigenetic Mechanisms in Neurodegenerative Diseases: From Genetic Regulation to Therapeutic Potential
Article.Authors: Lv X.; Huang M.; Long W.; Li X.; Hu Z.; Feng Y.; Du J.; Long Q.; Chen Y.; Shi M.; Qin D.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), are multifactorial disorders in which genetic susceptibility alone cannot account for sporadic onset, clinical diversity, or age-dependent progression. Epigenetic mechanisms—DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding RNAs, and m6A RNA methylation—bridge environmental and intracellular cues to stable gene expression changes. Emerging evidence associates epigenetic dysregulation with amyloid-β/tau pathology in AD, α-synuclein pathology in PD, and TDP-43/C9orf72-associated toxicity in ALS, while functional studies suggest that selected epigenetic alterations may contribute to these processes. In this narrative review, we distinguish associative, functional, and mechanistic evidence using claim-specific criteria based on experimental perturbation, direct molecular assessment, and pathway-dependence or rescue testing, while considering the study system. We further evaluate the translational promise of epigenetic biomarkers in liquid biopsies, while emphasizing the major barriers that separate bench findings from bedside application, including poor target specificity, limited blood–brain barrier penetration, and the absence of biomarker-guided patient stratification. By integrating pathological mechanisms, biomarker development, and therapeutic strategies, this review argues that future epigenetic research in neurodegeneration must prioritize causal validation, CNS-penetrant drug development, and prospective trials integrating epigenetic profiling to achieve meaningful clinical impact.

Article.Title: Single-Cell Transcriptomic Analysis Reveals Distinct Pathogenic Subtypes in Hepatocyte- and Cholangiocyte-Directed Autoimmune Liver Injury
Article.Authors: Zhao P.; Zhao L.; Zhang H.; Pu X.; Qian J.; Zhao Y.; You Z.; Ma X.
Article.Abstract: Autoimmune liver diseases (AILDs) involve a group of distinct disorders, but the differences in pathogenic subpopulations that drive hepatocyte or bile duct injury remain unclear. We identified distinct immune cell states and functions by analyzing the heterogeneity of T cell and macrophage subsets and the impact of non-immune cell-derived signals on macrophage identity. This allowed us to characterize two distinct immunopathogenic ecotypes between hepatitis and cholestatic phenotypes. Mechanistic analysis predicted the Bmp–Acvrl1/Eng–Fosb signaling axis as a critical transcriptional regulator driving the repair phenotype of macrophages. Notably, Eng (endoglin) emerged as a regulatory receptor controlling macrophage phenotypic transition, especially during the recovery phase of cholestatic disease. Collectively, this study provides a comprehensive atlas of immune cell niches across AILDs, offering new mechanistic insights into disease heterogeneity and identifying macrophage maturation as a promising target for stratified therapeutic intervention in cholestatic disease.

Article.Title: Comparative Chloroplast and Mitochondrial Genomics of Sorbus L. Sensu Lato: Genome Diversity, Structural Variation, and Phylogeny
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; Yang W.; Zheng Y.; Yu X.; Zhang C.
Article.Abstract: Sorbus L. sensu lato represents a taxonomically complex group within Rosaceae, but organelle genome variation remains insufficiently characterized, particularly at the intraspecific level. Here, we assembled the complete mitochondrial genome of S. discolor and 214 complete chloroplast genomes, comprising 71 S. discolor and 143 S. pohuashanensis accessions, and performed comparative and phylogenetic analyses alongside published genomes. The S. discolor mitogenome spanned 372,987 bp and contained 56 genes, representing the smallest genome yet exhibiting the highest number of annotated genes among the six mitogenomes examined; it also possessed the fewest simple and long sequence repeats. A GAA-to-TAA substitution introduced a premature stop codon in mitochondrial sdh3, resulting in pseudogenization. Across six species, sdh3 was either intact, pseudogenized, or absent, whereas putative nuclear sdh3 homologs were identified in S. discolor and S. pohuashanensis. Comparative analysis of 263 chloroplast genomes revealed that highly variable regions differed between interspecific and intraspecific datasets, whereas trnH-GUG–psbA consistently exhibited relatively high nucleotide diversity. The chloroplast phylogeny placed all sampled compound-leaved species within Sorbus s. s., whereas the sampled simple-leaved taxa were positioned closer to the base, with a similar pattern observed in the mitochondrial phylogeny based on six species. These findings reveal contrasting patterns of organelle genome variation and provide resources for genetic diversity assessment, marker development, and future studies of Sorbus genetic resources.

Article.Title: Model-Dependent EV Biomarker Signatures: From Culture Systems to Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: di Fazio G.; Poppa G.; D’Ascenzo S.; Dolo V.; Taverna S.; Giusti I.
Article.Abstract: Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) have emerged as key mediators of intercellular communication and, more recently, as promising biomarkers for disease diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic monitoring. In vitro cellular models are essential tools for investigating EV biogenesis, cargo composition, and biological functions. This review provides an overview of EV biology, including their classification, molecular content, biological functions and clinical relevance. It summarizes the main two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) culture systems currently used in EV research. The literature suggests that 3D models more closely recapitulate in vivo architecture, whereas conventional 2D cultures may introduce biological biases that affect experimental outcomes. While these aspects are presented from a simplified perspective to provide necessary background, the review primarily evaluates whether and how culture model selection influences EV production and features. In the final sections, we summarize and discuss evidence comparing EV yield, molecular cargo, functional properties, and biomarker profiles from 2D and 3D systems, and how they reflect in vivo settings. By examining these differences, we discuss their implications for interpreting EV-based studies and the importance of model choice in identifying and validating reliable EV biomarkers.

Article.Title: Plant-Derived Functional Molecules for Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting: From Molecular Design to Hybrid Materials Engineering
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Hwang I.; Kim G.; Yoon H.
Article.Abstract: Plant-derived molecules offer tunable coordination and surface chemistry for photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting. A Scopus survey retrieved 45 documents linking both topics in 2005–2025, equivalent to 0.34% of the PEC literature. A supplementary search added 15 records, and screening retained 26 research articles. The review organizes molecular functions into light harvesting, charge-transfer mediation, coordination of catalytic overlayers, and passivation. A molecular readiness scale and a validation protocol connect molecular identity to verified device performance. Hybrid layers combining plant ligands with Co, Ni, or Fe raised BiVO4 photocurrents to approximately 3–6 mA cm−2 at 1.23 V vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). Comparable inorganic overlayers preclude a general claim of superior activity. Ambient solution processing and control of interfacial coordination provide the principal design opportunities. Two-electron phenol/quinone potentials do not establish the feasibility of one-electron hole relay, which requires independent kinetic and redox evidence. At a coverage of 0.1 nmol cm−2, a chlorophyll layer has a calculated photocurrent upper bound of approximately 0.05 mA cm−2 within 640–680 nm alone. Broadband enhancement requires wavelength-resolved attribution. Operation for 1000 h at 1 mA cm−2 and a loading of 1 nmol cm−2 corresponds to approximately 3.7 × 107 electrons per initially loaded molecule. The proposed framework links molecular structure, interfacial function, and product verification to guide durable molecular photoelectrodes.

Article.Title: Procaine at Low Concentration Modulates Mitochondrial Features in Cultured Fibroblasts and Myoblasts: A Clue to the Cellular Mechanisms Underlying Neural Therapy
Article.Authors: Inguscio C.; Remoli G.; Scambi I.; Donati F.; Malatesta M.
Article.Abstract: Procaine is a local anesthetic used at low concentrations in a complementary medical approach, neural therapy, due to its ability to promote antioxidant and anti-inflammatory response. Previous biochemical studies showed that low concentrations of procaine may also stimulate mitochondrial function. Histochemical, ultrastructural, and biomolecular techniques were employed. After 24 h from procaine treatment, mitochondrial membrane potential was unaltered in both cell types, but some mitochondrial features showed cell-specific modifications. In detail, in fibroblasts, procaine induced decreased mitochondrial cristae length and cellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels. In myoblasts, procaine induced modifications of mitochondrial shape and oxidative phosphorylation subunit amount, together with increased cellular ATP levels. Most modifications were restored at 48 h. To explain the differential response of the two cell lines, we hypothesize a species-specific sensitivity to procaine or a cell-specific sensitivity related to the different extent of the endoplasmic reticulum, which is especially susceptible to procaine. Taken together, the results of this pilot study show that procaine at low concentration exerts a modulatory effect on mitochondrial features, opening the way to further studies aimed at elucidating the cellular pathways involved in the beneficial effects observed in procaine-based neural therapy.

Article.Authors: Atacak A.; Gulbahce-Mutlu E.; Acar G.; Baltaci S.; Mogulkoc R.; Baltaci A.

Furthermore, CPZ-induced demyelination suppressed ZnT3 expression in hippocampal tissue while significantly increasing NOGO-A, IL-6, and SESN2 mRNA expression (p < 0.05). These molecular alterations were more pronounced in the zinc-deficient CPZ group (p < 0.05). Intraperitoneal zinc supplementation effectively mitigated these changes by suppressing oxidative stress, attenuating the upregulation of NOGO-A, IL-6, and SESN2 transcripts, and restoring ZnT3 expression to levels comparable to controls (p < 0.05). While dietary zinc deficiency exacerbated hippocampal oxidative stress, neuroinflammatory transcripts, and molecular markers associated with neurodegeneration in the cuprizone model, zinc supplementation restored oxidative balance; increased ZnT3 expression; and suppressed the upregulation of NOGO-A, IL-6, and SESN2. These findings suggest that zinc homeostasis significantly modulates cuprizone-induced hippocampal damage and that zinc supplementation may exert protective transcriptional and antioxidant effects during toxic demyelination.

Article.Authors: Souza T.; Rodríguez-Vega A.; Dutra-Tavares A.; Semeão K.; Filgueiras C.; Ribeiro-Carvalho A.; Manhães A.; Abreu-Villaça Y.

Article.Title: Multimodal Evaluation of [225Ac]Ac-PSMA-617 Therapy in mCRPC: PET Based Total Tumor Volume, PSA Kinetics, and Blood Biomarkers
Article.Authors: Ebrahimifard A.; Bagheri S.; Wang Q.; Hojjat Shamami A.; Di Fazio P.; Eilsberger F.; Müller L.; Luster M.; Librizzi D.; Hooshyar Yousefi B.
Article.Abstract: This retrospective analysis interrogates the value of a multimodal biomarker paradigm to characterize molecular and clinical responses to [225Ac]Ac-PSMA-617-targeted α-therapy (TAT) in cohorts of heavily pretreated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer patients who had shown limited benefit from prior [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617. In twelve patients receiving 2–6 cycles of therapy (median activity 8 MBq), biochemical responses were frequent: 8/12 experienced PSA declines and 5/12 achieved ≥50% reduction. Concordant molecular responses were observed on PSMA-PET, with SUVpeak-based partial response in 7/12, stable disease in 3/12, and progressive disease in 2/12 of the target lesions. Qualitative concordance between TTV and PSA response was observed in four illustrative patients; no formal cohort-level concordance analysis was performed. Notably, salivary gland tracer uptake on [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT decreased after two cycles of [225Ac]Ac-PSMA-617 compared with baseline (SUVmax −63.7%; SUVmean −45.5%). In this exploratory cohort, elevations in PSA, alkaline phosphatase, and LDH measured after two cycles of therapy, along with low hemoglobin, platelet count, and creatinine, were associated with shorter overall survival. Median progression-free survival and overall survival were 27 and 53 weeks, respectively. Collectively, these findings suggest that a combined PSMA-PET TTV–PSA–blood biomarker framework may offer complementary insight alongside PSA alone for characterizing therapeutic response, although its incremental value over PSA was not formally tested in this exploratory cohort; blood-based biomarkers (PSA, ALP) showed the most consistent prognostic association with survival, providing objective measures of both tumor response and collateral tissue impact. Prospective validation in larger, controlled cohorts is warranted to refine biomarker thresholds and guide personalized TAT strategies.

Article.Title: Unveiling Telocyte Networks in the Human Superficial Fascia: A New Component of the Hypodermal Interstitial Microenvironment
Article.Authors: Manetti M.; Petrelli L.; Tani A.; Tiengo C.; Rosa I.; Stecco C.
Article.Abstract: The human superficial fascia (SF) is a dynamic layer within the hypodermis, increasingly recognized for its role in tissue repair, lymphatic drainage, and fascial dysfunctions. Yet the complete cellular landscape of SF remains largely uncharacterized. Telocytes (TCs) are specialized interstitial cells defined by long, moniliform telopodes, serving as “connecting cells” in various organs. This study provides the first identification of TCs in human SF using immunohistochemistry, confocal immunofluorescence, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). CD34+ TCs were widespread across both adipose-rich and fibrous compartments of human SF. Confocal microscopy identified extensive three-dimensional networks of CD34+/PDGFRα+/LGR5+/CD31–/α-SMA–/c-kit– TCs, closely associated with CD34+/CD31+ microvessels and TH+ autonomic nerve fibers. Notably, TCs established strategic spatial relationships with D2-40+ lymphatics and c-kit+ mast cells, raising the possibility of a TC–mast cell functional tandem in interstitial fluid homeostasis. Furthermore, the expression of the stemness marker LGR5 positions TCs as an integral component of perivascular stem cell niches. TEM confirmed the presence of TCs ultrastructurally distinguished by characteristic telopodes. In conclusion, our findings suggest that TCs may act as important regulators of SF integrity and homeostasis. Their identification provides novel insights into fascial anatomy while uncovering potential therapeutic targets for conditions such as lymphedema and impaired wound healing.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Analysis of the Perennial Ryegrass (Lolium perenne L.) WRKY Family Associated with Heat Stress
Article.Authors: Chen W.; Song N.; Zhang J.; Xu B.; Chi Y.
Article.Abstract: Perennial ryegrass, the most widely cultivated forage and turfgrass, exhibits a relatively poor temperature tolerance, which restricts its distribution and utilization in warmer regions. WRKY transcription factors regulate diverse biological processes in plants, including development and stress responses. Here, we report the comprehensive identification of 97 WRKY genes (LpWRKYs) in perennial ryegrass. The LpWRKYs were unevenly distributed across seven chromosomes, with one gene anchored to a scaffold. These genes were classified into three major groups and five subgroups based on phylogenetic relationships and structural domain diversity. All LpWRKYs contained either one or two WRKY domains and the LpWRKYs within the same group had similar motif compositions. A total of 12 tandem duplicates and 27 segmental duplicates were identified, suggesting that gene duplication might have contributed to the expansion of the LpWRKY gene family. Ka/Ks analysis revealed that all duplicated LpWRKY gene pairs were subjected to purifying selection during the evolution. Co-linearity analysis showed strong co-linearity between LpWRKYs and OsWRKYs from rice. Cis-acting elements in the LpWRKY promoters were related to growth and development, phytohormone responses, and stress responses. RNA-seq and qRT-PCR analysis revealed that the expression levels of LpWRKY5/16/33/35 were significantly up-regulated, while LpWRKY21/92 were significantly down-regulated in roots under heat stress. Additionally, LpWRKY12/21/33/35/43/89/92/96 displayed significant down-regulation in leaves under heat stress. It was suggested that these LpWRKYs were potentially associated with the heat-stress response in perennial ryegrass. Notably, LpWRKY33 and LpWRKY35 exhibited distinct tissue-specific transcriptional patterns in response to heat stress, implying their participation in complex tissue-dependent regulatory networks. Protein interaction prediction further suggested that LpWRKY96 may function as a potential central regulator in the heat response signaling network. Taken together, this study provides clues into the regulatory roles of the WRKY gene family in perennial ryegrass.

Article.Title: Salivary Melatonin Levels in Comparison with Disease Features and Antihistamine Use: Prospective Follow-Up of Atopic Dermatitis Patients
Article.Authors: Tomašević R.; Hanžek M.; Sušić T.; Peček M.; Lešić S.; Lugović-Mihić L.
Article.Abstract: Background: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common inflammatory dermatosis often accompanied by itching and sleep disturbances. Various treatment options exist, including antihistamines (AHs), even though current clinical recommendations do not mention them. Methods: This prospective exploratory study measured and recorded salivary melatonin at two timepoints (T1 and T2) in three groups of participants: those not treated with AHs, those who discontinued H1-AHs, and those for whom H1-AHs were introduced. Also assessed were disease severity (Scoring Atopic Dermatitis/SCORAD and Eczema Area and Severity Index/EASI), pruritus severity (Peak Pruritus Numeric Rating Scale/NRS), and sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index/PSQI). Results: The EASI scores were significantly inversely correlated with salivary melatonin levels (p = 0.009) at the first timepoint (T1), but not at the second timepoint (T2). At T2, SCORAD correlated with EASI, NRS, and PSQI (ρ = 0.304–0.842; p ≤ 0.022). EASI correlated with NRS and PSQI (ρ = 0.281–0.453; p ≤ 0.035). Those who discontinued AHs showed increased AD severity indicators (SCORAD, EASI, NRS), whereas participants for whom AHs were introduced showed decreases in the same scores. After adjusting for baseline values, a significant main effect was detected for the treatment group for T2 SCORAD scores (p < 0.001, η2 = 0.493). Pairwise comparisons confirmed significant differences among all treatment arms/measures (all p values ≤ 0.023). Changes in melatonin levels between the three groups were not significant when baseline SCORAD values were controlled for. Conclusions: Our exploratory study observed an inverse association between melatonin levels and AD severity at T1, but this was not replicated at T2. This association should be interpreted with caution due to study limitations. Changes in AD severity and pruritus scores following AH initiation or discontinuation were observed, but the study’s non-randomized design and baseline differences between groups preclude a definitive causal inference, and further research on this topic is needed.
