Article.Title: How the Acute Psychosocial Stress Response Ends: A Post-Stressor Transition Model of Glucocorticoid Feedback, Vagal Re-Engagement, and Frontolimbic Context Updating
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Zheng R.; Wu Y.; Zhang M.
Article.Abstract: Objective stressor offset does not mark a common onset of recovery: cardiovascular activation may be waning while cortisol is still rising and threat-related cognition persists. This structured narrative review integrates molecular, autonomic, neural, cognitive, and immune evidence on the post-stressor interval, primarily in adult psychosocial-stress paradigms. We propose the Post-Stressor Transition Model (PSTM) as an operational extension of existing recovery and allostatic accounts, not as a newly discovered biological system. Three regulatory functions organize the synthesis: updating whether threat remains current, changing cardiac autonomic influence, and regulating continuing hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenocortical output. Glucocorticoid receptor signaling, catecholamines, endocannabinoids, oxytocin, and vasopressin contribute across these functions. The framework distinguishes objective offset from system-specific extrema, physiological resolution from demonstrated adaptation, and shared timing from directional coupling. Eight propositions specify outcomes, temporal windows, competing explanations, and prespecified effect bounds. Measurement recommendations address cortisol nonresponse, respiratory influences on heart rate variability, assessment reactivity, and multirate sampling. Hormonal state and development modify candidate parameters rather than define fixed response types. No universal recovery threshold or clinically validated transition profile is claimed. The model is useful only if its additional parameters are identifiable, improve independent prediction, and withstand phase-specific experimental tests.

Article.Title: Propolis Flavonoids: Current Evidence in Animal Models and Future Promise for the Treatment of Ulcerative Colitis
Article.Authors: Hernández-Sánchez K.; Nieto-Yañez O.; Rivera-Yañez C.; Pedroza-González A.; Francisco-Cruz L.; Hernández-Delgado C.; Molina-Gallardo A.; Hernández-Rosas N.; Ruiz-Hurtado P.; Barrera-Ortega C.; Rivera-Yañez N.
Article.Abstract: Ulcerative colitis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory bowel disease with a rising global incidence and a considerable economic burden. Conventional treatments, such as steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and immunosuppressants, are often associated with adverse effects and high costs. In this context, flavonoids—such as those identified in the chemical composition of propolis—are emerging as highly promising therapeutic alternatives. This review highlights how diverse classes of flavonoids, including flavones, flavonols, flavanones, isoflavones, and flavan-3-ols, mitigate colitis through multiple interconnected mechanisms. Their main actions include reducing inflammation by decreasing the levels of proinflammatory cytokines and modulating key signaling pathways; exerting potent antioxidant activity; and improving intestinal barrier integrity by increasing tight junction proteins and mucin production. Numerous studies reporting significant improvements in clinical parameters such as body weight, colon length, and the disease activity index are discussed. Innovation in formulations, for example, the use of nanoparticles, is crucial to improve the solubility, stability, and bioavailability of flavonoids, allowing for their targeted delivery to the inflamed colon. In summary, flavonoids are promising candidates for the development of complementary or alternative treatments for ulcerative colitis. Although further clinical evidence is needed to establish their safety and conditions for use in humans, the available preclinical results are promising.

Article.Title: Fidanacogene Elaparvovec Gene Therapy: Budesonide Treatment of a Late Decline in Factor IX Expression in a Patient with Hemophilia B
Article.Authors: Herbst K.; Pezeshkpoor B.; Klein C.; Albert T.; Lutz P.; Strassburg C.; Spengler U.; Goldmann G.; Oldenburg J.
Article.Abstract: Fidanacogene elaparvovec is an adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy that enables endogenous factor IX (FIX) expression in hemophilia B, potentially eliminating the need for prophylactic FIX replacement. Post-treatment monitoring focuses on FIX durability, hepatic safety, and immune-mediated loss of expression. A 40-year-old man with severe hemophilia B received a single intravenous dose of fidanacogene elaparvovec in the phase 3 BENEGENE-2 trial (NCT03861273). FIX activity was assessed by one-stage and chromogenic assays. Liver enzymes, clinical parameters, and adverse events were monitored. Prednisolone was initiated for liver enzyme elevation and later switched to budesonide in response to declining FIX levels. Follow-up continued for 4 years. FIX activity peaked at week 6 (~30 IU/dL) and remained stable until week 16. Moderate ALT elevation (peak ~70 U/L) responded to prednisolone. Between weeks 22–28, FIX levels declined without ALT elevation. Budesonide (9 mg/day) was started at week 25 for 3 months and gradually tapered, stabilizing FIX activity at 10-20 IU/dL. This level has been maintained for 4 years without bleeding episodes or FIX replacement. Fidanacogene elaparvovec provided sustained, clinically meaningful FIX expression. Budesonide may offer an effective hepatocyte-targeted alternative to systemic corticosteroids while supporting long-term transgene expression.

Article.Title: Insulin Intensification and Simplification Strategies in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes and Overweight or Obesity: A Scoping Review
Article.Authors: Chua C.; Chong W.; Zaman Huri H.
Article.Abstract: Overweight and obesity complicate insulin treatment in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), requiring consideration of glycaemic control, insulin requirements, body weight, and treatment burden. This scoping review mapped insulin treatment modification (ITM) strategies, synthesised their reported outcomes, and identified evidence gaps among insulin-treated adults with T2DM and overweight or obesity. Five electronic databases were searched following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) and updated Joanna Briggs Institute methodological guidance. Thirty-three studies were classified into four ITM domains: add-on therapy to insulin, switching to advanced insulin formulations, simplifying complex insulin regimens with adjunctive therapy, and switching to fixed-ratio combinations. Intensification was generally studied in patients with higher baseline glycated haemoglobin or insulin requirements, whereas simplification was more often evaluated in those receiving complex insulin regimens. Insulin-dominant intensification generally increased total daily insulin dose, while intensification incorporating Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists (GLP-1RAs) or Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitors (SGLT2i) commonly reduced insulin requirements and body weight. Simplification generally reduced insulin requirements and/or injection burden while maintaining or improving glycaemic control, with weight reduction frequently reported. Direct comparisons and obesity-specific subgroup analyses were limited. Intensification and simplification should therefore be considered complementary rather than opposing approaches, with outcomes influenced by therapeutic components and patient characteristics.

Article.Title: Field Density Variation and Metabolite Profiling Reveal Transcriptome Mechanisms Driving Salt-Responsive Root Flavone Accumulation in Scutellaria baicalensis
Article.Authors: Lin Z.; Zhang Y.; Zhao C.; Zhao K.; Ma D.; Zhang T.; Wang M.; Yao H.
Article.Abstract: Root flavones, especially baicalin, baicalein, wogonoside, and wogonin, contribute substantially to the medicinal quality of Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi. In the arid and semi-arid regions where this crop is grown, salinized soils constrain establishment but reshape specialized metabolism. We used field density trials, salt-stress experiments, ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS), and time-series RNA-seq, followed by weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), to ask whether agronomic practices and salt-induced transcriptional changes alter root flavone content. Planting density showed a clear yield-quality trade-off: higher density increased belowground biomass per unit area but reduced individual root growth and flavone content, with 150 plants·m−2 providing a practical balance between population yield and root quality under the tested Xinjiang field conditions. In established seedlings, 0.5% NaCl caused no visible damage over 24 h and specifically raised baicalin and baicalein at 12 h, whereas wogonoside and wogonin (the wogonin-type flavones) remained nearly unchanged. Time-series RNA-seq identified thousands of differentially expressed genes between 2 and 24 h. WGCNA identified a turquoise module (one of the color-named co-expression modules) that was enriched for genes involved in carbohydrate metabolism and cytoskeletal/microtubule processes. Salt-responsive NAC, MYB and WRKY transcription factors co-expressed with core structural genes (PAL, 4CL, CHS, CHI); one candidate, SbNAC86, was up-regulated mainly at 24 h after the metabolite peak, consistent with a potential role in the later phase of the response rather than in triggering the initial accumulation peak. These findings outline the temporal dynamics of salt-induced branch-selective flavone accumulation and suggest candidate regulators for functional validation, with implications for quality-focused cultivation on saline marginal lands.

Article.Title: Metabolic Milieu and Susceptibility: The Combined Benefits of Targeting AMPK and ACE2 for Metabolic Disorders and COVID-19
Article.Authors: Tata F.; Nxumalo M.; Ntanzi N.; Mushebenge A.; Khan R.; Kumalo H.
Article.Abstract: The convergence of metabolic dysfunction and infectious diseases has become increasingly evident, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) emerge as pivotal molecular regulators linking metabolic homeostasis, endothelial integrity, immune modulation, and viral pathogenesis. Metabolic diseases such as diabetes, obesity, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease are marked by insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction, collectively increasing susceptibility to severe viral infections and outcomes. This review examines experimental, computational, and translational evidence exploring the interplay between AMPK and ACE2, focusing on metabolic, vascular, and inflammatory pathways relevant to viral infections. Recent findings show a bidirectional functional relationship between AMPK and ACE2, where AMPK phosphorylation supports ACE2 expression and function, and ACE2 signaling reciprocally enhances AMPK activity, forming a protective metabolic–vascular loop. Disruption of this axis, particularly through SARS-CoV-2-induced ACE2 degradation, exacerbates metabolic deterioration, vascular damage, and exaggerated inflammatory responses. Preclinical and in silico studies show that pharmacological AMPK activators, including metformin and bioactive flavonoids, demonstrate pleiotropic metabolic, anti-inflammatory, endothelial protective, and potential antiviral activities, hinting at the therapeutic potential of modulating the AMPK-ACE2 axis, despite the limited clinical application of flavonoids. The AMPK-ACE2 axis represents an important molecular link between metabolic regulation, renovascular health, and immune defense mechanisms. This evaluation connects AMPK and ACE2 from isolated signaling nodes into a coordinated pharmacological axis with implications for interventions in cardiometabolic and viral diseases. Future research should prioritize mechanistic validation and conduct integrated experimental and clinical investigations to establish AMPK-ACE2 co-targeting as a viable therapeutic strategy for mitigating cardiometabolic disease burden and enhancing resilience against viral infections.

Article.Title: Chitosan-Coated Calcium Alginate Microspheres Loaded with Alpha-Lipoic Acid/2-HP-β-CD Inclusion Complexes Enhance Aqueous Solubility and Enable pH-Responsive Intestinal Release
Article.Authors: Cui Y.; Huang S.; Fu Y.; Zhou Z.; Sun X.; Liu H.; Lai Y.
Article.Abstract: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) exhibits antioxidant and potential cardiovascular protective effects, but its insufficient stability in acidic environments and poor water solubility limit its oral delivery applications. In this study, the stability of lipoic acid in acidic environments was first evaluated through acid treatment combined with mass spectrometry analysis. Subsequently, 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (2-HP-β-CD) and ALA were used to prepare lipoic acid inclusion complexes, which were characterized by phase solubility curves and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The inclusion complexes were further loaded into calcium alginate microspheres, and the properties of the microspheres were evaluated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), morphological observation under different pH conditions, swelling ratio, and in vitro release experiments. Following acid treatment, the liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) response of original ALA decreased, suggesting a reduction in detectable original ALA. The inclusion with 2-HP-β-CD significantly improved the solubility of lipoic acid and altered its crystalline characteristics. The inclusion complex-loaded calcium alginate microspheres exhibit a relatively intact microstructure, display distinct morphological changes and swelling behaviors under different pH conditions, and achieve pH-dependent release. This system may serve as a potential oral delivery platform for improving the aqueous dispersibility of ALA and promoting pH-responsive release under simulated intestinal conditions.

Article.Title: Targeted Nanopore Sequencing for Molecular Characterization of First-Line Drug Resistance and Treatment Outcomes Among Patients in the Republic of Congo
Article.Authors: Dello M.; Mouzinga F.; Ngouama B.; Elion Assiana D.; Boumpouthoud D.; Djontu J.; Mfoutou Mapanguy C.; Ebata-Mboussa E.; Elenga B.; Achimi Abdul J.; Bonsi Tchuandom S.; Okemba-Okombi F.; Ayet M.; Nguimbi E.; Mouanga A.; Adegnika A.; Ntoumi F.
Article.Abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global public health concern, further complicated by the emergence and transmission of drug-resistant strains. Diversity within the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) may also influence disease progression and treatment response. We conducted a longitudinal study among 126 Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra-confirmed TB patients enrolled and followed at the Antituberculosis Center of Brazzaville between July 2023 and November 2024. MTBC species were identified using the Genotype MTBC assay, and resistance-associated mutations in rpoB, katG, and embB were characterized by targeted Oxford Nanopore sequencing and interpreted using the WHO mutation catalogue and TB-Profiler. The overall treatment success rate was 81.7% (103/126). Among 109/126 samples successfully typed, M. tuberculosis accounted for 92.7% (101/109), Mycobacterium africanum for 3.7% (4/109), while mixed infection accounted for 0.9% (1/109) and inconclusive profiles for 2.8% (3/109). Resistance-associated mutations were assessed in 65 of the 126 enrolled patients with high-quality sequencing data. Among these 65 isolates, 32.3% (21/65) harbored resistance to at least one of the targeted first-line drugs, including isoniazid (23.1%; 15/65), rifampicin (15.4%; 10/65), and ethambutol (9.2%; 6/65). Multidrug-resistant TB was identified in 12.3% (8/65). The predominant mutations occurred at rpoB codon 435, katG codon 315, and embB codon 306. Treatment success was lower among patients infected with strains carrying a resistance-associated mutation (71.4%). Isoniazid resistance was associated with reduced odds of treatment success in unadjusted analysis (OR = 0.22, 95% CI: 0.05–0.93; p = 0.04). These findings suggest a considerable burden of genotypically predicted first-line drug resistance and support expanding molecular drug-susceptibility testing beyond rifampicin in TB surveillance and patient management in the Republic of Congo.

Article.Title: Cerebral Metabolism Is More Susceptible to Oxythiamine Exposure Compared to Cardiac Metabolism
Article.Authors: Artiukhov A.; Graf A.; Chistyakov D.; Solovjeva O.; Ivlev V.; Borisova N.; Vasil’ev V.; Maslova M.; Sergeeva M.; Aleshin V.
Article.Abstract: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency is known to cause predominantly neurological and cardiovascular symptoms due to the metabolic function of its diphosphate derivative as a coenzyme. A variety of natural and synthetic thiamine antimetabolites can simulate this deficiency. Oxythiamine may be spontaneously produced from thiamine itself and is known to accumulate in patients with kidney disorders. In this study, tissue specificity of chronic oxythiamine administration was investigated in male rats, focusing on changes in the physiology and thiamine-dependent enzyme activities of the cerebral cortex and heart. While oxythiamine treatment significantly reduced the pyruvate dehydrogenase activity in both tissues, its cerebral effects also included mild downregulation of another thiamine-dependent enzyme, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, indicating higher susceptibility of the cerebral metabolism to oxythiamine exposure. The oxythiamine neurological effects were also reflected in the rats’ altered anxiety-like behavior and heart rate regulation. Further investigation of the cerebral effects of oxythiamine identified elevated 3-hydroxybutyrate and protein acetylation as indicators of perturbed acetyl-CoA utilization in the TCA cycle. Some heart-specific changes, such as decreased glutathione level, were also observed upon oxythiamine treatment. The present results highlight the consequences of chronic oxythiamine exposure. These finding are potentially relevant for understanding the metabolic changes in the brain and heart upon pathophysiological oxythiamine accumulation.

Article.Title: A Time-Course Transcriptomic Resource for Early Embryogenesis in Lethenteron reissneri
Article.Authors: Xu W.; Li J.; Wang G.; Bai Q.; Fu H.; Zhao J.; Yu S.; Zhu T.
Article.Abstract: Continuous developmental transcriptomic data remain limited for jawless vertebrates. We generated an RNA-seq time series spanning 2 h post-fertilization (hpf; fertilization stage) to 10 days post-fertilization (dpf; hatching stage) in Lethenteron reissneri, with 14 developmental stages and three biological replicates per stage. We examined global expression patterns, differential expression between adjacent stages, functional enrichment, and stage-level co-expression, and assessed representative expression trends using reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Gene-expression profiles changed progressively across development. One notable interval was 2.5–3 dpf (late blastula to early gastrula), when upregulated genes were broadly enriched for germ-layer formation, axial patterning, neural development, and morphogenesis rather than the RNA-processing, ribosome-biogenesis, and translation terms prominent at earlier stages. Stage-level co-expression analysis identified a module enriched for development-related terms, and differential expression, functional annotation, and temporal profiles were used to compile a list of 154 candidate developmental genes. This study provides a continuous transcriptomic resource for early L. reissneri embryogenesis and a temporal framework for subsequent studies of lamprey development.

Article.Title: Distinct Clinical Patterns Associated with HLA-DRB1 Genotypes in Pediatric Autoimmune Liver Diseases
Article.Authors: Grama A.; Mititelu A.; Benţa G.; Sucaciu R.; Popescu D.; Mariş B.; Onaciu A.; Agoston Ş.; Pop T.
Article.Abstract: Autoimmune liver diseases (AILD), including autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) and autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis (ASC), are rare but important causes of chronic liver disease in children. Although HLA-DRB1 alleles have been associated with disease susceptibility, their role in modulating the clinical phenotype and long-term outcome of pediatric AILDs remains incompletely understood. We aimed to characterize the distribution of HLA-DRB1 alleles and genotype combinations and describe the accompanying clinical features in a pediatric AILD cohort. Thirty children diagnosed with AIH-1 (n = 14), AIH-2 (n = 6), or ASC (n = 10) underwent HLA-DRB1 genotyping. Clinical presentation, fibrosis stage, treatment response, and associated autoimmune diseases were retrospectively analyzed. The most frequent alleles copies were HLA-DRB1*03 (n = 15), predominantly identified in AIH, and HLA-DRB1*13 (n = 14), identified in both AIH and ASC. Genotype combinations involving these alleles were observed across a broad spectrum of clinical presentations, fibrosis stages, treatment responses, and extrahepatic autoimmune manifestations. In this small cohort, HLA-DRB1*14-containing genotypes were observed in several patients with severe disease features, including advanced fibrosis, cirrhosis, treatment-refractory disease, and ulcerative colitis. Patients carrying HLA-DRB1*11, HLA-DRB1*15, or HLA-DRB1*16 had favorable hepatic outcomes despite severe initial presentation or associated extrahepatic autoimmune manifestations; however, the number of carriers was small. Clinical features varied among patients carrying different genotype combinations; however, the independent contribution of the accompanying allele could not be assessed. Our findings illustrate marked clinical heterogeneity among children carrying different HLA-DRB1 alleles and genotype combinations. In this exploratory cohort, selected HLA-DRB1 combinations co-occurred with distinct clinical patterns. HLA profiling may have a role in future risk stratification and individualized follow-up of children with AILD, but these observations are hypothesis-generating, they do not support genotype-based clinical management and require validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.

Article.Title: Cellular Senescence in Ocular Surface Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zhang L.; Li S.; Gao Q.; Zhang H.; Zhang H.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Cellular senescence is characterized by stable cell-cycle arrest and a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Recurrent desiccating, oxidative, ultraviolet, microbial, and immune-mediated insults may induce stress-induced premature senescence (SIPS) in ocular surface tissues. PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 30 June 2026. Primary human, animal, and in vitro studies were prioritized, and direct evidence of senescence was distinguished from indirect stress-related or SASP-like associations. The p53–p21CIP1–pRB and p16INK4a–pRB pathways mediate senescence-associated cell-cycle arrest. Reactive oxygen species (ROS)–p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) and cyclic GMP–AMP synthase–stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS–STING) signaling act as stress-sensing and inflammatory pathways, whereas mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) and AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) contribute to SASP and metabolic regulation. Transient senescence may support wound repair and immune clearance, whereas persistent senescence may contribute to epithelial and endothelial dysfunction, tear-film instability, immune dysregulation, fibrosis, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Mechanistic support is strongest in selected experimental models; evidence in several human ocular surface disorders remains associative. Cellular senescence is a context-dependent contributor to ocular surface pathology. Senolytic and senomorphic strategies remain predominantly preclinical and require disease-, cell-, and stage-specific validation.

Article.Title: Integrated Single-Cell and Transcriptomic Analysis Suggests a Cuproptosis-Related Phenotype and Potential Therapeutic Target in Acute Pancreatitis
Article.Authors: Xie Q.; He M.; Wang Q.; Li W.
Article.Abstract: Acute pancreatitis (AP) is an acute inflammatory disorder of the exocrine pancreas with limited therapies. Whether cuproptosis, a copper-dependent cell death pathway, contributes to AP pathogenesis remains unknown. We integrated single-cell transcriptomics (GSE279876), single-cell transcriptomics (GSE188819), and human whole-blood transcriptomic data (GSE194331) to evaluate 13 cuproptosis-related genes across cell types, along with pseudotime trajectory, regulatory networks, and cell–cell communication. Findings were validated in caerulein-induced severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) mouse models and acinar cell injury using histopathology, electron microscopy, flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and biochemical assays. Single-cell analysis showed selective activation of a cuproptosis-related signature in acinar cells, with all 13 genes upregulated, most notably GIs and Fdx1. The cuproptosis-related gene signature score increased along with pseudotime, and exploratory transcription factor (TF) and cell–cell communication analyses suggested enrichment of SPI1 and AP-1 (FOS/JUN), alongside MIF/CCL inflammatory signals, which was corroborated in independent datasets. In vitro and in vivo, pancreatic tissues and pancreatic acinar cells in SAP exhibited copper accumulation, FDX1/DLAT upregulation, mitochondrial shrinkage, and cristae loss, which are consistent with a cuproptosis-related phenotype, and were all attenuated by Tetrathiomolybdate (TTM). These findings suggest that the inflammatory microenvironment may be associated with selective activation of a cuproptosis-related program in acinar cells in AP, and that copper chelation with TTM attenuates pancreatic injury, indicating a potential therapeutic strategy targeting copper dyshomeostasis.

Article.Title: Selective Lithium–Magnesium Separation from Brines by Ionic-Liquid Solvent Extraction: Molecular Mechanisms, Extractant Design, and Process Optimization
Article.Authors: Mura M.; Castillo J.; Gálvez E.; Leiva W.; Hernández P.; Galleguillos-Madrid F.; Sepúlveda R.; Toro N.
Article.Abstract: The growing global demand for lithium (Li+), driven by its strategic role in energy storage technologies, faces a critical challenge in its recovery from brines: the selective separation of Li+ and magnesium (Mg2+) ions. Because Li+ (ionic radius ≈ 76 pm) and Mg2+ (≈ 72 pm) have almost identical ionic radii despite their different charge, their coordination and hydration behaviour are difficult to discriminate at the molecular level. The high Mg2+ content in natural brines, such as those from the Atacama Salar, delays the efficiency of conventional extraction processes, which also result in significant Li+ losses. In this context ionic liquids (ILs) are emerging as alternative solvents with tunable properties, low volatility, and high thermal stability, although their environmental performance depends strongly on their chemical structure, toxicity, aqueous solubility, and recyclability, offering advantages over traditional organic extractants. This study evaluates the use of ionic liquids in liquid–liquid extraction systems for the selective removal of Mg2+, analysing operational parameters such as pH, organic-to-aqueous phase ratio (O/A), and extractant concentration. This review critically compares ionic-liquid-based extraction systems by relating Mg2+/Li+ selectivity to extractant structure, coordination chemistry, and key operational variables, while also considering the main limitations associated with their application to high-salinity brines. By linking macroscopic extraction performance to the underlying coordination chemistry, hydration-shell disruption, and computational screening tools such as quantum chemical calculations and COSMO-RS, this approach supports the rational, molecular-level design of environmentally responsible extractants for brines with a high Mg/Li ratio.

Article.Title: Riboflavin Primes Pepper Resistance to Ralstonia solanacearum Through Coordinated Antioxidant Responses and Lignin Deposition
Article.Authors: He F.; Geng Y.; Li H.; Jia X.; Wang P.; Guo Z.; Guo X.; Deng X.; Li Z.
Article.Abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are pivotal regulators of plant–pathogen interactions. Comparative transcriptomic analysis of a bacterial wilt-susceptible pepper cultivar (HS03) and a resistant cultivar (HR01) revealed impaired riboflavin biosynthesis in HS03. Exogenous riboflavin application compensated for this deficiency and conferred significant protection against Ralstonia solanacearum. Physiological and transcriptomic analyses further demonstrated that riboflavin functions as both an inducer of ROS signaling and a modulator of defense-associated metabolism. Riboflavin treatment elicited a biphasic defense response characterized by an early H2O2 burst accompanied by dynamic changes in antioxidant enzyme activities. In particular, the activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and peroxidase (POD) increased markedly at 6 h after riboflavin application compared with control. Following R. solanacearum inoculation, riboflavin-pretreated plants exhibited higher POD, ascorbate peroxidase (APX), and CAT activities at 6 h post-inoculation compared with control. This early antioxidant response induced by riboflavin was followed by increased lignin accumulation and the transcriptional activation of genes associated with cutin, suberin, and wax biosynthesis, galactose metabolism, and tyrosine metabolism at 12 h post-inoculation. Riboflavin pretreatment also enhanced the expression of genes encoding nonexpressor of pathogenesis-related genes 1 (NPR1) and calmodulin (CALM), implicating hormone signaling and calcium-mediated pathogen recognition in riboflavin-induced resistance. Collectively, these results suggest that riboflavin primes pepper defense against R. solanacearum by coordinating early ROS-associated antioxidant responses and subsequent cell-wall reinforcement. Riboflavin may therefore represent a promising environmentally compatible agent for the sustainable management of bacterial wilt in pepper.

Article.Title: Longitudinal Gut Microbiota Changes in Women with Breast Cancer-Related Lymphedema Undergoing a Lifestyle Intervention
Article.Authors: Ruiz-Molina Y.; Padial M.; Rodríguez-Díaz C.; González-Salvatierra S.; Martín-Bravo M.; Plaza-Andrades I.; Aránega-Martín L.; Rodríguez-Pacheco F.; Chicharro-Parras A.; Sasso C.; Queipo-Ortuño M.; Olveira G.
Article.Abstract: Breast cancer-related lymphedema (BCRL) is closely associated with obesity, yet the gut microbiota remains poorly characterized in this population. We longitudinally evaluated gut microbiota profiles in 48 women with overweight or obesity and BCRL who were randomized to either a multimodal lifestyle intervention combining an energy-restricted Mediterranean-style diet and exercise (n = 28) or control care (n = 20). Fecal samples collected at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months (144 samples) underwent 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The intervention resulted in greater reductions in body weight, body mass index, and fat mass over time (group × time p < 0.001, p = 0.001, and p = 0.002, respectively). No significant group × time interaction was observed for alpha diversity or overall microbial community composition based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarity (PERMANOVA R2 = 0.006, F = 0.459, p = 0.324). Exploratory DESeq2 differential abundance analyses identified FDR-significant taxon-specific differences, including higher abundances of Barnesiellaceae and Desulfovibrionaceae in the intervention group and of Prevotella_7 and Lachnospiraceae_UCG_010 in controls (FDR-adjusted p < 0.05). These DESeq2 findings were not confirmed in mixed-effects sensitivity analyses after FDR correction. Prevotella_7 was more abundant in controls at baseline and at 6 months. Participant-blocked group × time models, which were given inferential priority, yielded FDR-significant baseline-to-3-month interaction tests for Izemoplasmatales and Frisingicoccus, although the corresponding shrunken effect estimates were close to zero. Secondary, hypothesis-generating analyses based on supplementation status, supplement adherence, and clinically relevant weight-loss response identified additional taxon-specific patterns associated with supplementation and adherence, including a tentative species-level association involving Bifidobacterium bifidum among supplemented participants, whereas no significant microbiota differences were observed by weight-loss response. Overall, these findings provide no evidence of broad restructuring of the gut microbial community but identify exploratory taxon-specific signals that warrant confirmation in larger longitudinal studies using strain-resolved and functional approaches.

Article.Title: Pyrazolate-Bridged PdCo and PdCu Complexes as Dual DNA-Binding and ROS-Driven Cytotoxic Agents
Article.Authors: Uvarova M.; Kulikova V.; Kozmenko Y.; Revtovich S.; Filippova A.; Shmelev M.; Sokolova D.; Pokrovsky V.; Kaverina A.; Solyev P.; Eremenko I.
Article.Abstract: Heterometallic complexes offer a promising anticancer strategy owing to their simultaneous action on multiple biological targets. In this work, we report the synthesis and evaluation of the antitumor potential of two heterometallic pyrazolate-bridged complexes, [PdCo(phen)(µ-dmpz)2(OOCMe)2] (PdCo) and [PdCu(phen)(µ-dmpz)2(OOCMe)2] (PdCu) (phen = 1,10-phenanthroline, dmpz = 3,5-dimethylpyrazole). The complexes were comprehensively characterized using a combined spectroscopic and analytical approach, including single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SC-XRD), PXRD, FTIR, UV-Vis, and mass spectrometry, confirming their structural integrity in both solid state and solution. Their cytotoxicity was assessed in vitro against colon, A549 lung, and breast cancer cell lines, as well as normal human dermal fibroblasts. The complexes exhibited micromolar IC50 values with selectivity indices up to 7. Using circular dichroism (CD) and fluorescence spectroscopy, it was demonstrated that PdCo binds to DNA, with minor groove binding (Kd = 7.6 μM) being the preferred mode of interaction, dominating over intercalation (Kd = 26.1 μM). Molecular docking simulations confirmed that the dissociated [Pd(phen)(µ-dmpz)2] fragment is capable of binding to DNA. Furthermore, chemiluminescence assays revealed pronounced peroxidase-like and superoxide dismutase-like activities of PdCu and PdCo, implicating ROS-mediated oxidative stress as a second, complementary cytotoxic pathway. Collectively, these findings highlight the dual-action mechanism of the synthesized complexes, combining DNA targeting with ROS-mediated oxidative damage, positioning them as highly potent candidates for further anticancer development.

Article.Title: Eukaryotic Mitogenomes and Their Key Insights: Architecture, Evolution, and Mitonuclear Coevolution
Article.Authors: Mehrotra A.; Sood A.; Kartavtsev Y.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial genomes (mitogenomes) are no longer considered entities solely responsible for cellular bioenergetics, but as dynamic, multifaceted, and synchronized systems that integrate genome architecture, evolutionary processes, and organismal physiology. The present review summarizes the contemporary understanding of mitogenome organization and its diversity, evolution, and associated functions across eukaryotic life, with emphasis on mitonuclear co-evolution and relevance to human health. Moreover, the conserved and lineage-specific characteristics of mitogenome architecture, including its genetic content, topology, and regulatory elements, and their roles in governing the precise replication and transcription of the mitogenome are also comprehensively discussed. Additionally, the review explores the role of evolutionary dynamics, with emphasis on mutation-rate heterogeneity, recombination dynamics, gene rearrangements, and the interaction between mutation, natural selection, and genetic drift in shaping mitochondrial genome diversity and evolutionary trajectories. Comparative approaches have revealed extensive diversity in mitogenome structural organization and composition, which are closely associated with life-history traits of organisms, including metabolic rate, longevity, and reproductive characteristics. Notably, at the functional level, the variability potential of a mitogenome significantly influences oxidative phosphorylation efficiency, reactive oxygen species generation, and the orchestration of cellular signaling cascades. Fundamental to these processes is the existence of coordinated mitonuclear interrelationships, wherein coevolution between mitochondrial and nuclear-encoded genes safeguards bioenergetic functional integrity, whereas disruptions in this coordination may lead to reduced cellular fitness and progression of several diseases. Particularly in humans, mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and heteroplasmy significantly contribute to the development of primary mitochondrial disorders and are increasingly implicated in other complex disease etiologies, including neurodegeneration, metabolic syndromes, and cancer. The paper also summarizes the phylogenetic utility of mitogenomes in the genomic era, accentuating the need to employ integrative approaches that combine mitochondrial and nuclear data. Lastly, the role of emerging technological platforms, including long-read sequencing and multi-omics, is also discussed, since these approaches are expected to transform the current landscape of mitogenome research. Altogether, the manuscript positions mitogenomes as indispensable entities bridging the gaps between evolutionary histories, physiological functions, and personalized precision medicine.

Article.Title: Plasma Lipidomic Phenotype Associated with Pathogenic LDLR Variants in Familial Hypercholesterolemia
Article.Authors: Waś J.; Prejbisz A.; Niedolistek M.; Kowalik I.; Minota I.; Ponińska J.; Drohomirecka A.; Sokołowska D.; Płoski R.; Dobrowolski P.
Article.Abstract: Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is caused by an impaired ability to clear circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) particles due to a defective low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). FH significantly increases cardiovascular risk (CVR). Although conventional lipid parameters are essential for diagnosing FH, they do not fully capture the metabolic impact of inherited LDLR dysfunction. This study aimed to characterize the plasma lipidomic phenotype associated with pathogenic LDLR variants in individuals with suspected FH. Forty-four participants underwent genetic testing for LDLR, apolipoprotein B-100 (APOB), and protein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9). After excluding three carriers of the APOB p.Arg3527Gln variant, the comparative lipidomic analysis included 41 participants. The study included 17 carriers of pathogenic LDLR variants and 24 participants without a detected pathogenic variant in the tested panel. We performed plasma lipidomic profiling using flow-injection analysis coupled with high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry (FIA-MS/MSALL) without chromatographic separation. Lipid annotation and data processing were performed using LipidView software, and lipidomic measurements were expressed as relative signal abundances derived from mass spectrometry (MS) peak intensities. Statistical analyses included Mann–Whitney U tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction across the analyzed lipid features. Exploratory multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were also performed. There were no differences in conventional lipid parameters between genetically confirmed LDLR variant carriers and participants without a detected pathogenic variant in the tested panel. At the nominal level (unadjusted p < 0.05), lipidomic profiling revealed differences in glycerophospholipid (GP) related analytical features between groups. However, no individual lipid feature remained statistically significant after full-family FDR correction. Among (GPs), 69 feature records (16.3%) showed nominal between-group differences, predominantly lower abundance in LDLR variant carriers. The most consistent nominal alterations were observed in features annotated as phosphatidylinositol triphosphates (PIP3) and N-acyl phosphatidylethanolamines (NAPE). Among the analyzed fatty acyls (FAs), 72.7% showed nominally lower relative abundance in LDLR variant carriers. We used exploratory multivariable models to identify GP and FA-related features associated with the detected pathogenic LDLR variant status. The models showed within-cohort discrimination. However, these models were developed and evaluated in the same small cohort after data-driven variable selection. They were not externally validated. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and do not establish diagnostic performance, clinical utility, or functional pathway impairment. Further validation in larger cohorts using targeted lipidomics with chromatographic separation is necessary.

Article.Title: Oral Nitrate-Reducing Bacteria and Nitric Oxide Homeostasis: Functional Host–Microbe Interactions in Oral and Vascular Health
Article.Authors: Altamura S.; Lombardi F.; Ciafarone A.; Palumbo P.; Cinque B.; Cifone M.; Pietropaoli D.
Article.Abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) is a key regulator of vascular homeostasis and host–microbe interactions. In addition to the endogenous nitric oxide synthase (NOS) pathway, the enterosalivary nitrate–nitrite–NO pathway provides an alternative source of NO and critically depends on oral nitrate-reducing bacteria (ONRB). This review examines the oral microbiome–NO axis and its role in nitrate metabolism, NO homeostasis, and oral–systemic interactions. A narrative review integrating microbiological, mechanistic, and clinical evidence on oral nitrate metabolism, ONRB activity, and their impact on oral and systemic outcomes, including dietary and antiseptic interventions. The functional activity and nitrate-reducing capacity of the oral microbiome are key determinants of nitrate reduction and systemic NO bioavailability. Oral dysbiosis, periodontal disease, and antiseptic mouthwash use impair ONRB activity and nitrite production, potentially affecting vascular function and blood pressure. Conversely, dietary nitrate enhances ONRB activity and nitrate-to-nitrite conversion, supporting oral and vascular health. Interindividual variability, partly influenced by sex-related factors, may contribute to heterogeneous responses. The oral microbiome–NO axis represents a functional interface between host physiology and microbial metabolism, linking oral ecology with vascular regulation. Through their activity, ONRB contribute to NO homeostasis, highlighting nitrate bioactivation as an important component of host–microbe interactions with implications for oral and systemic physiology. Recognition of this pathway expands current understanding of host–microbe cooperation in NO homeostasis and may inform future microbiome-based approaches to support oral and cardiovascular health.

Article.Title: Relation-Aware Heterogeneous Graph Learning for miRNA–Drug Response Association Prediction Under Cold-Start Generalization
Article.Authors: Elbashir M.
Article.Abstract: (1) Background: Cancer drug resistance can be influenced by microRNAs (miRNAs), which can alter gene expression and cellular pathways that determine how cancer cells respond to treatment. Potential miRNA–drug response associations can be identified using computational models; however, evaluating these models using edge-based evaluation can result in an optimistic view of model generalization since test miRNAs or drugs can appear in other response associations during training. (2) Methods: This paper presents a relation-aware heterogeneous learning framework that integrates miRNA expression profiles, miRNA–gene regulatory interactions, gene–gene functional associations, drug molecular features, and distinct drug–gene relations in a unified miRNA–gene–drug network. A Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) was used to preserve relation-specific information, and biological paths connecting each miRNA to each drug were used as additional information for the corresponding candidate miRNA–drug pair. A leakage-safe five-fold cross-validation approach was used to evaluate the proposed framework under different settings: edge, miRNA-cold, drug-cold, and double-cold. (3) Results: The proposed framework obtained an AUC and AUPR of 0.9537 ± 0.0044 and 0.9494 ± 0.0069, respectively, under the edge-based setting. The performance remained high under the miRNA-cold-based setting, where the model achieved an AUC and AUPR of 0.9466 ± 0.0061 and 0.9436 ± 0.0049, respectively. A substantial drop in performance was observed under the drug-cold setting, where the proposed framework obtained an AUC and AUPR of 0.6685 ± 0.0354 and 0.6534 ± 0.0569, respectively. The performance was also substantially reduced under the double-cold-based setting. The results also show that the structural resemblance alone is not enough to explain generalization to new drugs, since no significant relationship between cold-start performance and either ChemBERTa molecular similarity or DrugBank target similarity was shown by drug-level analysis. Literature evidence supported 6 out of 20 top-ranked previously unlabeled predictions compared to 1 of 120 randomly selected controls (Fisher’s exact test, p = 2.63 × 10−5; empirical p = 2.80 × 10−5). (4) Conclusions: The obtained results show that the proposed framework can rank candidate miRNA–drug response associations effectively. They also show that predicting response associations under the drug-cold-based setting remains much harder than predicting for similarly held-out miRNAs, which is an important limitation of conventional edge-based evaluation.

Article.Title: pH-Responsive Erdafitinib Liposomes with FGFR3 Targeting for Intravesical Bladder Cancer Therapy
Article.Authors: Liang H.; Li G.; Zhang W.; Wang W.; Li D.; Cheng Y.; Song M.; Xu X.; Lu H.
Article.Abstract: Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) is a key oncogenic driver in bladder cancer (BCa). Here, we report a pH-responsive and erdafitinib-loaded liposomal nanosystem with surface modification of anti-FGFR3 antibodies (Phl-erda@Ab), which demonstrates improved antitumor effects in intravesical instillation therapy. In RT112 cells, we evaluated targeted uptake and antiproliferative activity. The Phl-erda@Ab exhibited sharp pH sensitivity, releasing 49% of the drug payload within 1 h at pH 5.3 while maintaining minimal release at pH 7.4 and 6.5. Liposome retention after intravesical instillation was doubled compared with non-targeted Phl-erda in mice. The Phl-erda@Ab intravesical therapy demonstrated effective antitumor activity, including maximal necrosis, the highest TUNEL-positive apoptotic index, and the lowest Ki67 proliferation index, compared to other groups. No significant pathological damage to major organs was observed. In summary, Phl-erda@Ab enables FGFR3-targeted, pH-triggered intravesical delivery with enhanced intravesical retention, improved antitumor activity, and favorable local safety, providing preclinical evidence to support clinical translation in FGFR3-overexpressing BCa.

Article.Authors: Bakheit A.; Alzaid A.; Almajed A.
Article.Abstract: Gefitinib is an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor used in non-small-cell lung cancer. The quadratic model was significant (F = 83.26, p = 0.0019), and three confirmation experiments yielded prediction errors of 0.515–0.954%, supporting local agreement at the selected conditions. The calculated limits of detection and quantification were 6.89 and 20.89 ng mL−1, respectively, while 50 ng mL−1 was retained as the lowest validated concentration. The method showed acceptable accuracy, repeatability, and selectivity for the investigated tablet matrix. Robustness testing indicated that pH requires careful control around 8.0. Analysis of pooled commercial tablets yielded an assay of 100.21 ± 1.86% of the label claim. TD-DFT calculations supported qualitative interpretation of the electronic transitions. The AGREE score was 0.61, indicating a more favorable environmental profile than the reference spectrofluorimetric method comparator (0.46).

Article.Title: From Gene-Based Breeding to Haplotype-Based Breeding for Rice (Oryza sativa) Improvement in the Genomics Era
Article.Authors: Nguyen T.; Ho A.; Chu H.; Chuong N.; Anik T.; Dong G.; Sulieman S.; Nguyen N.; Jogaiah S.; La H.; Tran L.
Article.Abstract: Rice (Oryza sativa L.) improvement increasingly uses genome-scale variation, but breeding decisions remain trait-oriented and depend on genetic architecture, recipient background, target environment, and selection resources. This review assesses when phased haplotype information adds value beyond causal-gene markers, single-nucleotide polymorphism assays, phenotypic selection, and genomic prediction. Reported configurations for yield, grain quality, nutrition, biotic resistance, and abiotic-stress adaptation are evaluated according to population structure, carrier frequency, effect uncertainty, haplotype-by-background interaction, haplotype-by-environment interaction, linkage drag, transferability, assay availability, and current breeding use. A three-tier hierarchy classifies configurations as Candidate, Validated, or Breeder-Ready. Most reported favorable haplotypes remain Candidate targets, fewer have controlled genetic validation, and few sequence-defined multi-variant haplotypes have documented use in active breeding programs. Practical deployment requires stable sequence nomenclature, accessible donors, diagnostic assays, elite-background and multi-environment evaluation, cost analysis, and donor-segment recovery. Graph pangenomes, phased long-read assemblies, causal reconstruction, and prospective comparisons with current selection methods can improve future assessment. Haplotype information has greatest value when phase improves a defined breeding decision and increases target-environment performance, annual genetic gain, selection efficiency, or cultivar delivery.

Article.Title: Targeting EGR1 Attenuates CCL2 Expression in Inflammatory Keratinocytes and Allergic Skin Inflammation
Article.Authors: Choi Y.; Jung E.; Han J.; Shin S.
Article.Abstract: Early growth response 1 (EGR1) is a zinc-finger transcription factor involved in inflammatory gene regulation, but the extent to which pharmacological inhibition of EGR1 DNA-binding activity influences inflammatory transcriptional responses in keratinocytes remains incompletely understood. RNA sequencing was employed as an exploratory, hypothesis-generating screen using three structurally related EGR1 inhibitors (IT21, IT23, and IT25) to identify candidate genes showing concordant expression patterns across the three pharmacological perturbations. This exploratory analysis suggested broader changes in inflammation-associated transcriptional programs and identified several leukocyte-recruiting chemokines among the candidate genes. CCL2 was selected as a representative candidate for independent biological and mechanistic validation. IT25 treatment and EGR1 knockdown attenuated TNFα-induced CCL2 expression, while promoter–reporter analysis, EGR1-binding site mutagenesis, EGR1 overexpression, and chromatin immunoprecipitation supported EGR1-dependent transcriptional regulation of CCL2 in keratinocytes. Furthermore, topical IT25 treatment attenuated house dust mite-induced atopic dermatitis-like skin inflammation and was associated with reduced epidermal CCL2 expression and inflammatory cell infiltration in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish EGR1-dependent regulation of CCL2 in inflammatory keratinocytes and support further investigation of EGR1 DNA-binding activity as a pharmacological target in cutaneous inflammation.

Article.Title: Nutritional Programming via Maternal Protein Restriction Mitigates Long-Term Consequences of Acute Kidney Injury
Article.Authors: García-Ortuño L.; Barragán K.; Caldiño-Bhon R.; Luna E.; Pérez-Villalva R.; Bobadilla N.
Article.Abstract: The kidney is highly sensitive to prenatal and early-life environmental influences. Maternal protein restriction (MPR) can alter renal development and may modify susceptibility to chronic kidney disease (CKD) following acute kidney injury (AKI). We investigated whether MPR during gestation and/or lactation influences the progression from AKI to CKD after renal ischemia–reperfusion (IR) in rat offspring. Fifty Wistar pregnant rats were fed a control (20% casein) or protein-restricted (10% casein) diet during gestation, with diets maintained or switched during lactation, generating four maternal nutritional groups (CC, CR, RC, and RR). At 280–330 g body weight, offspring from these groups were randomly assigned to left renal IR plus right nephrectomy (CC + IR, CR + IR, RC + IR, and RR + IR) or right nephrectomy alone (CC, CR, RC, and RR). Renal outcomes were assessed in two independent cohorts of rats at 7 days and 5 months after surgery. Offspring from MPR during gestation and/or lactation (CR + IR, RC + IR, and RR + IR) showed reduced susceptibility to AKI-to-CKD progression compared to the CC + IR group, characterized by attenuated proteinuria, absence of glomerular hypertrophy, and minimal renal fibrosis. This protective phenotype was associated with reduced oxidative stress and endoplasmic reticulum stress, as indicated by lower 4-HNE, CHOP, and BiP, together with enhanced post-ischemic repair reflected by lower urinary KIM-1 and Hsp72 excretion. MPR during gestation and/or lactation induces a persistent renal phenotype in the offspring that confers resistance to AKI-to-CKD progression, potentially through modulation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress. These findings highlight developmental nutritional programming as a previously underappreciated determinant of renal resilience in offspring after AKI and provide a basis for investigating nutritional and developmental mechanisms that may be targeted to prevent CKD after AKI.

Article.Title: CYBA Gene Polymorphisms, Lipid Parameters and Atherogenic Indices: A Cohort Study of Healthy Individuals Without Prior Lipid-Lowering Therapy
Article.Authors: Niemiec P.; Nowak T.; Wrona J.; Iwanicka J.; Iwanicki T.; Jarosz A.; Górczyńska-Kosiorz S.; Balcerzyk-Matić A.
Article.Abstract: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the CYBA gene, encoding the p22phox subunit of vascular NADPH oxidases, have been associated with atherosclerosis-related disorders. This association may partly reflect their involvement in lipid metabolism. We investigated the effects of seven CYBA SNPs (rs7195830, rs1049255, rs4673, rs13306296, rs72811418, rs16966671, and rs9932581) on systemic lipid profiles (total cholesterol, HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides) and six lipid-derived atherogenic indices in 220 blood donors who had never received lipid-lowering therapy. Genotyping was performed using PCR-RFLP and TaqMan PCR. Serum lipid concentrations were determined by enzymatic colorimetric methods. For all SNPs, in silico analyses assessed allele-specific binding (ASB) of transcription factors (TFs) and gene expression in cardiovascular tissues. Statistically significant differences in lipid parameters were observed among the rs7195830, rs1049255, and rs13306296 variants. In silico analyses indicated ASB of TFs for rs1049255 and rs13306296 and genotype-dependent effects of rs13306296 and rs4673 on CYBA expression. Notably, the G allele/GG genotype of rs13306296 was associated with the least favorable lipid profile across multiple parameters, preferential binding of thirteen TFs, and increased CYBA expression in aorta and heart tissues. In conclusion, CYBA variants influence the systemic lipid profile and lipid-derived atherogenic markers in individuals untreated with lipid-lowering drugs, potentially through modulation of CYBA expression.

Article.Title: Genome-Informed Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) Assays for Detection and Differentiation of Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum Phylotypes I and III
Article.Authors: Karakkat B.; Huang Q.; Nunziata S.; Yasuhara-Bell J.
Article.Abstract: The Ralstonia solanacearum species complex (RSSC) causes bacterial wilt in a broad range of economically important hosts. The RSSC has been reclassified into three species, of which R. solanacearum sequevars 1 and 2 in phylotype IIB are designated as Select Agents in the U.S. Many rapid tests for “R. solanacearum” target the RSSC and thus cross-react with R. pseudosolanacearum, which is endemic to the U.S. To avoid false positive identifications and unnecessary triggering of Select Agent measures, four portable LAMP-based screening assay variations were developed and validated for specific detection of R. pseudosolanacearum: real-time LAMP assays for detection of R. pseudosolanacearum (1) and differentiation of R. pseudosolanacearum phylotypes I and III in the AmpliFire® Isothermal Fluorometer (2) or Genie® III (3), and a colorimetric LAMP for detection of R. pseudosolanacearum (4). All assays demonstrated high sensitivity (10–50 colony-forming units (CFU)/reaction) and specificity; 100% analytical specificity and selectivity based on 177 RSSC isolates (81 phylotype I, 70 phylotype II, 15 phylotype III and 11 phylotype IV) and 53 non-RSSC bacterial pathogens on relevant hosts and soil, and 100% diagnostic specificity and sensitivity based on testing inoculated plants and a Euphresco sample panel. The assays presented here represent useful diagnostic tools that can be deployed on-site to aid domestic survey and detection efforts.

Article.Title: Integrated Proteome and Phosphoproteome Profiling Reveals Abundance-Independent Phosphorylation Remodeling in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Saleem S.; Sajid M.; Varghese R.; Liu L.; Muralidaran V.; Kroemer A.; Ressom H.
Article.Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by extensive molecular heterogeneity, yet changes in protein abundance alone may not fully capture the regulatory alterations that drive tumor biology. Here, we performed integrated whole-proteome and phosphoproteome profiling of paired HCC and adjacent non-tumorous liver tissues to distinguish protein-abundance remodeling from phosphorylation changes not explained by comparable parent-protein abundance changes. Label-free nano-LC-MS/MS data were processed using quality control, filtering, missing-value imputation, normalization, and paired statistical testing. Whole-proteome analysis retained 3653 proteins and identified 314 significantly altered proteins, including 79 increased and 235 decreased proteins in HCC. Phosphoproteome analysis retained 1682 phosphopeptides and identified 189 significantly altered phosphopeptides, including 81 increased and 108 decreased events. Integrated analysis showed that 132 significant phosphopeptides matched quantified parent proteins; 112 were classified as phospho-only events, and 20 showed concordant phosphopeptide and parent-protein changes. Reactome enrichment of phospho-only parent proteins highlighted immune/inflammatory processes, metabolic remodeling, ER-stress/protein-folding responses, apoptosis, RHO/RHOBTB GTPase-related regulation, and post-translational phosphorylation. Candidate prioritization identified phosphorylation events for future validation. Overall, this paired multi-layer proteomic analysis demonstrates that HCC tissue exhibits both protein-abundance remodeling and phosphorylation-level rewiring, supporting integrated proteome–phosphoproteome profiling as a strategy to resolve regulatory alterations in cancer tissue.

Article.Title: Microplastics and the Kidney: A Narrative Review of Human Evidence, Molecular Mechanisms of Cell Injury, and Future Directions
Article.Authors: La Porta E.; Gentile M.; Quaglia M.; Ducoli S.; Massardo S.; Verzola D.; Mancianti N.; Esposito P.
Article.Abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are widespread environmental contaminants, but their potential effects on kidney health remain poorly defined. As an organ continuously exposed to circulating particles and involved in their urinary elimination, the kidney may represent both a target of MP toxicity and a route of excretion. In this narrative review, we examine current evidence linking MPs to kidney injury, integrating experimental, mechanistic, and human data. Particular attention is given to the early events governing particle–cell interactions. After exposure, micro- and nanoplastics acquire an eco- and biomolecular corona that modifies their surface properties, cellular recognition, uptake, and biodistribution. Following internalization through phagocytic and endocytic pathways, particles may accumulate within endolysosomal compartments and interact with intracellular structures, disrupting cellular homeostasis. In renal cells, these events converge on mitochondrial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species generation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, inflammatory signaling, altered autophagy, and regulated cell death. Several interconnected pathways have been implicated, including Keap1–Nrf2/ARE and NF-κB signaling, MAPK and IRE1/XBP1-mediated stress responses, ACSL4–GPX4-related ferroptosis, and TGF-β1-related profibrotic signaling. Human studies have detected MPs in urine and kidney tissue and provide preliminary evidence linking MP burden with early markers of kidney damage, although current findings remain limited by small study populations and substantial methodological heterogeneity. Patients with chronic kidney disease, particularly those receiving dialysis, may represent a population of special interest because potentially altered renal handling may coexist with repeated exposure to polymer-based medical devices and dialysis fluids. Despite this potential relevance, data on MP exposure and accumulation in CKD and dialysis patients remain remarkably scarce. We finally discuss the limitations of current experimental models and analytical methods and the need for standardized biomonitoring, more environmentally relevant particles and exposure concentrations, and detection strategies capable of reaching the nanoscale, including artificial intelligence-assisted analysis. Overall, available evidence provides a mechanistic basis for MP-induced kidney injury, but its clinical relevance and contribution to human kidney disease remain to be established.

Article.Title: Evolutionary and Functional Conservation of Topologically Associating Domain Boundaries in Rice Genomes
Article.Authors: Geyman O.; Kurbidaeva A.
Article.Abstract: Traditional evolutionary analysis has relied primarily on one-dimensional (1D) sequencing data, but recent advances in three-dimensional (3D) genomics allow for deeper investigation of how genome architecture shapes evolutionary divergence. In this study, we analyze conserved and species-specific topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries across multiple Oryza species to uncover both structural and functional evolutionary insights. Here, we characterize boundary conservation at different levels, from highly conserved to species-unique. We apply TCBF, a relatively novel and underutilized tool for TAD boundary conservation analysis, alongside a suite of complementary analyses, including gene ontology, RNA-seq, sequence conservation, and epigenetic profiling. Our approach not only validates canonical evolutionary relationships reflected in sequence data but also novel patterns unique to 3D genome organization. Most notably, our study uncovers strong associations between highly conserved TAD boundaries and RNA metabolism-related genes, as well as other genetic and epigenetic signatures, and a contrasting absence in minimally conserved boundaries. To our knowledge, we created the first phylogenetic reconstruction derived from topological domain data in plants, which demonstrated a strong similarity between 3D and 1D genomic evolutionary relationships. Overall, our work presents an approach that integrates the 3D genome structure into evolutionary genomics, addressing a critical and underexplored dimension of comparative plant genomics.

Article.Title: Molecular Genetics and Reproductive Genomic Medicine in Cleft Lip and Palate: Current Evidence, Preimplantation Testing, and Clinical Translation—A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Fan R.; Shen H.; Liu Y.; Ji T.; Zhang L.; Ma X.
Article.Abstract: Cleft lip and palate (CLP) is a common congenital craniofacial anomaly with heterogeneous clinical manifestations and complex etiologies. Current evidence indicates that CLP arises from the combined effects of Mendelian syndromic disorders, rare pathogenic variants, common susceptibility loci, non-coding regulatory variants, epigenetic regulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and maternal environmental exposures. Although reconstructive surgery and multidisciplinary care remain central to treatment, families with recurrent CLP or a family history of orofacial clefts increasingly seek reproductive counseling and genetic risk assessment before pregnancy. Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) may provide a clinically meaningful option when a pathogenic variant, chromosomal abnormality, or clearly defined familial haplotype is identified. However, most non-syndromic CLP cases are polygenic or multifactorial, and the application of preimplantation genetic testing for polygenic disorders (PGT-P) remains limited by modest predictive accuracy, population-specific transferability, embryo-number constraints, incomplete penetrance, variants of uncertain significance, and uncertain long-term clinical utility. This narrative review summarizes the clinical phenotypes and genomic architecture of CLP, evaluates the principles and current limitations of preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M) and PGT-P, and discusses psychosocial and ethical issues in reproductive decision-making. We propose that PGT for CLP should be positioned as part of a stepwise counseling framework rather than as a universal preventive strategy. Future progress will depend on standardized phenotyping, multi-ancestry genomic databases, functional validation of candidate variants, transparent risk communication, and shared decision-making that respects both reproductive autonomy and the uncertainty of genomic prediction.

Article.Title: Inflammatory Burden Shapes Antioxidant Adaptation and Immunometabolic Remodeling in LPS-Activated BV-2 Microglial Cells
Article.Authors: Barbalace M.; Rinaldi I.; Mantini M.; Zallocco L.; Ronci M.; Di Cintio F.; Attanzio A.; Prata C.; Malaguti M.; Hrelia S.; Giusti L.; Angeloni C.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of numerous neurodegenerative diseases and is characterized by profound inflammatory, metabolic, and redox alterations in activated microglia. Although lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated BV-2 cells represent one of the most widely used in vitro models of neuroinflammation, a comprehensive understanding of the coordinated molecular adaptations underlying this model remains incomplete. The aim of this study was to characterize the proteomic remodeling of BV-2 cells exposed to LPS 100 ng/mL for 24 h and investigate the relationship between antioxidant and inflammatory responses across increasing levels of LPS exposure. Proteomic analysis identified 89 differentially expressed proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, clathrin-mediated endocytosis, lysosomal function, immunometabolism, and redox regulation. Validation experiments confirmed changes in cytoskeletal and endocytic proteins, including Vimentin, Gelsolin, Disabled homolog-2, and clathrin light chain A, together with modulation of proteins involved in the lysosomal pathways and marked induction of the immunometabolic enzyme aconitate decarboxylase 1. Functional enrichment analysis identified Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) as the most significantly activated upstream regulator, a prediction consistent with engagement of an adaptive antioxidant program. Interestingly, analysis of increasing LPS concentrations revealed that antioxidant responses were not proportional to the inflammatory stimulus. Expression of NRF2-controlled antioxidant enzymes progressively increased for LPS concentrations up to 500 ng/mL, but declined at 1000 ng/mL LPS, whereas pro-inflammatory mediators remained continuously upregulated. This pattern is consistent with the attenuation of antioxidant adaptation under the highest inflammatory burden tested. Together, these findings demonstrate that the BV-2/LPS model is characterized by a dynamic interplay between inflammatory, redox, metabolic, lysosomal, endocytic, and cytoskeletal pathways, providing a more comprehensive characterization to support the interpretation and experimental use of this neuroinflammatory model.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Characterization of the Rboh Gene Family in Populus trichocarpa Reveals PtrRbohB Positively Regulates Adventitious Root Development
Article.Authors: Shi R.; Ding Y.; Guo P.; Shang F.; Cao S.
Article.Abstract: Adventitious roots (ARs) are essential for clonal vegetative propagation of woody tree species. Extensive studies have focused on phytohormone and transcription factor regulatory networks during AR development in poplar, yet the regulatory roles of reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling during AR development remain poorly understood. In this study, we performed a genome-wide identification and systematic characterization of the Respiratory Burst Oxidase Homolog (Rboh) gene family in Populus trichocarpa. A total of 10 PtrRbohs were identified and phylogenetically classified into five subfamilies. Expression profiling revealed distinct tissue-specific and stress-responsive expression patterns among PtrRbohs. Functional validation via CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout showed that disruption of PtrRbohB significantly reduced AR length, diameter, and lateral root density in poplar. Heterologous overexpression of PtrRbohB in Arabidopsis thaliana enhanced ROS accumulation, confirming its conserved function in ROS generation. Furthermore, knockout of PtrRohB down-regulated the expression of several AR-positive regulators and up-regulated that of AR-negative regulators in poplar. Collectively, this study provides the direct genetic evidence that Rboh regulates AR formation in poplar, and identifies PtrRbohB as a key positive regulator of AR development. These findings enrich our understanding of woody plant AR formation and provide candidate genes for molecular breeding of poplar rooting traits.

Article.Title: Urinary Metabolomics in Bladder Cancer: A Scoping Review of Current Evidence and Translation Implications
Article.Authors: Carapito Â.; Amaro F.; Roque A.; Carvalho F.; Pinto J.; Guedes de Pinho P.
Article.Abstract: Bladder cancer (BC) diagnosis and surveillance currently rely largely on invasive cystoscopy, making urine an attractive non-invasive biofluid for discovering metabolic biomarkers, given its direct contact with the bladder urothelium. This review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of the literature on urinary metabolomic profiling in BC, summarising metabolites and metabolite panels associated with the disease, their relevant metabolic pathways, and diagnostic performance. A search was conducted in PubMed, complemented by records from reference lists of relevant reviews. After screening, 30 original studies comparing urinary metabolomic profiles between BC patients and cancer-free controls were included, encompassing diverse analytical platforms and statistical approaches. A wide range of urinary metabolites were reported to be altered between BC patients and controls, of which 52 were recurrently identified in at least two independent studies. Increased levels of taurine, valine, lactate, adenosine monophosphate and adipate were among the most consistent metabolic alterations, whereas the levels of citrate, glycerol, creatinine, and several dicarboxylic acids and acylcarnitines were consistently decreased. Other metabolites, such as hippurate, tyrosine, and histidine, showed variable trends in their levels. These alterations may reflect metabolic processes associated with tumour growth, energy reprogramming, lipid metabolism, and oxidative stress adaptation. Most studies also proposed multi-metabolite panels combining metabolites to discriminate BC patients from controls, achieving sensitivity and specificity up to 100% and AUC up to 0.983, while fewer studies explored panels for tumour stage and grade discrimination, with more modest performance. Overall, urinary metabolomics reveals a broad, biologically coherent set of metabolic alterations associated with BC, but methodological heterogeneity and limited independent validation still hinder clinical translation. Larger, harmonised, prospectively validated studies integrating multi-omics and machine learning are needed to establish robust urinary biomarkers for BC.

Article.Title: TOP2A Overexpression as a Prognostic Biomarker in High-Grade Meningioma: An Integrated Single-Cell and Bulk Transcriptomic Study
Article.Authors: Cai H.; Xie G.; Liu H.; Chen Y.; Li H.; Wan J.; Deng Z.
Article.Abstract: While prior single-cell studies have identified proliferative neoplastic subpopulations, the prognostic and therapeutic implications of TOP2A focal copy-number status have not been defined. This study aimed to delineate the cellular architecture of high-grade meningioma and to evaluate the clinical and prognostic significance of TOP2A expression together with its focal copy-number status through integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic profiling. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was integrated with bulk RNA sequencing (bulk RNA-seq) to resolve the cellular landscape of high-grade meningioma in an exploratory cohort, followed by functional subcluster identification, differential expression analysis, and survival analyses. TOP2A was prioritized for multi-level validation: mRNA overexpression was confirmed in an independent bulk cohort, protein overexpression by immunohistochemistry (IHC), and focal gene copy-number status by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Kaplan–Meier survival analysis was performed to evaluate patient prognosis. Correlations between continuous variables were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. scRNA-seq of an exploratory high-grade cohort revealed a cell-cycle proliferation cluster characterized by high TOP2A expression. In a 160-sample bulk RNA-seq cohort, TOP2A was overexpressed in high-grade and recurrent tumors, and elevated TOP2A mRNA was significantly associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS). IHC on 154 specimens confirmed TOP2A protein overexpression, and FISH on 27 specimens demonstrated focal TOP2A copy-number gain enriched in high-grade cases. Copy-number gain was concordant with TOP2A mRNA levels. Although TOP2A mRNA and protein overexpression were each associated with shorter PFS, the limited size of the FISH subset precluded an independent survival analysis by copy-number status. This study identifies TOP2A mRNA and protein overexpression as a prognostic biomarker in high-grade meningioma, and shows that focal TOP2A copy-number gain is enriched in high-grade tumors and concordant with TOP2A expression. By integrating transcriptional overexpression with copy-number gain, our findings identify TOP2A as a candidate prognostic biomarker warranting prospective evaluation in high-grade meningioma.

Article.Title: Beyond Histocompatibility: Donor Tissue Immune States and Their Role in Heart Transplantation
Article.Authors: Urbanowicz T.; Kowalewski M.; Suwalski P.; Raffa G.
Article.Abstract: Heart transplantation transfers not only donor alloantigens and functional myocardium but also a pre-existing tissue environment shaped by resident immune, vascular, stromal, and parenchymal populations. This review examines the hypothesis that the biological state of donor tissue influences subsequent recipient immunity and contributes to heterogeneity in allograft outcomes. Donor-resident macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, and tissue-resident lymphocytes constitute an immunologically active myocardial niche that encounters ischemia–reperfusion injury and recipient immune effectors immediately after implantation. Experimental and human studies demonstrate the dynamic coexistence and replacement of donor- and recipient-derived immune populations, with recipient cells acquiring phenotypes within the graft microenvironment. We distinguish transient donor-tissue activation from genuine tissue immune memory, which would require persistence of an exposure-induced molecular or functional state and an altered response to a subsequent challenge. Potential mechanisms include trained innate immunity, epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, endothelial inflammatory memory, and persistent stromal–immune interactions. We propose that allograft biology be investigated at the level of the donor–recipient immune pair and outline longitudinal single-cell, spatial, and cell-of-origin approaches to test this concept in human heart transplantation.

Article.Title: Is Aging a Failure to Resolve? Integrating Damage Responses, Regenerative Decline, and Geroscience Interventions
Article.Authors: Chmielewski P.; Strzelec B.
Article.Abstract: Biological aging is accompanied by persistent tissue-damage signaling, chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, cellular senescence, and declining regenerative capacity. Taken together, these features resemble an injury response that is repeatedly initiated but fails to progress reliably through clearance, reconstruction, and functional recovery. This resemblance motivated the proposal that aging is a wound that never starts healing. Here, we develop that proposal into a testable failed-resolution framework in which some age-related dysfunction reflects damage responses that exceed organ-specific capacities for intracellular quality control, efferocytosis, immune termination, matrix normalization, and cell replacement. Its central predictions are that (i) impaired recovery kinetics will forecast functional decline beyond established measures of biological age, (ii) restoring resolution will improve tissue function beyond suppressing inflammatory markers, and (iii) efficacy will depend on treatment phase and tissue-specific failure mode. We specify which age-related processes lie outside the framework and propose measurements spanning damage burden, danger sensing, resolution competence, regenerative reserve, organ function, and recovery after standardized challenge. Supporting evidence is predominantly preclinical, whereas human studies provide mechanistic findings, target engagement, or domain-specific effects. Failed resolution thus offers a falsifiable research program for testing tissue recovery as a therapeutic target in aging.
