Article.Title: A novel single-fish assay for ethanol self-administration in zebrafish
Article.Authors: Morneau L.; Gagné L.; Peterson R.; Bossé G.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a significant public health concern. In Canada, about 18% of individuals aged 15 or older will meet the clinical criteria for AUD at some point in their lives (CAMH, 2023). Treatment options for AUD are limited, and the high relapse rates highlight the urgent need for innovative methods to study and address AUD. Zebrafish (Danio rerio) is an emerging model for exploring the neurobiological impacts of alcohol. Previous studies have demonstrated that zebrafish respond to the rewarding effects of alcohol, but most research methods rely on passive administration, such as immersion, which does not reflect the typical routes of alcohol intake in humans. We previously showed that zebrafish can learn to self-administer drugs of abuse in small groups and conditioned animals are displaying key features of substance abuse disorders. However, group-based conditioning limits our understanding of individual drug preference and intake profile. In this study, we improved upon our previous design by establishing an individual self-administration protocol to measure voluntary alcohol intake and model alcohol use disorder. In this novel assay, individual adult fish learn to discriminate between two zones to self-administer a 5% ethanol solution. Moreover, animals conditioned in this assay can perform progressive ratio and display signs of withdrawal upon cessation of ethanol intake. These results suggest zebrafish can develop ethanol abuse-like behaviour, providing a powerful platform to study genetic predisposition and screen for therapeutic compounds.

Article.Title: Low-dose aspirin versus placebo as adjunctive treatment in bipolar disorder (the Aspirin-Bipolar RCT): Results of exploratory biomarker analyses
Article.Authors: Bruun C.; Long C.; Krogh H.; Zarp J.; Coello K.; Frikke-Schmidt R.; Ostrowski S.; Nielsen F.; Giraldi A.; Vinberg M.; Faurholt-Jepsen M.; Lange T.; Kessing L.
Article.Abstract: Background: Low-dose aspirin (LDA) has anti-inflammatory and immune modulatory properties and has been proposed as an add-on treatment for bipolar disorder (BD). Whether its hypothesized biological targets are engaged in patients with BD remains unknown. Using biomarker data from the Aspirin-Bipolar RCT, we investigated inflammatory and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis biomarkers as candidate mediators of the proposed effects of LDA. Methods: Secondary analysis of the Aspirin-Bipolar RCT including 250 patients (58% female) newly diagnosed with BD randomised to add-on LDA (n = 125) or placebo (n = 125). Biomarkers were measured at baseline (cytokines: n = 236; hair cortisol: n = 201) and 6-month follow-up (cytokines: n = 172; hair cortisol: n = 148). We examined whether baseline biomarkers predicted 6-month mood instability (MI, primary outcome), whether changes mediated the effects of LDA on MI, and whether patients with higher baseline inflammation responded differently to treatment. Higher inflammation was defined as baseline IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α levels all above the median. Missing data was handled using multiple imputations. Results: Baseline biomarkers did not predict 6-month MI. Mediation analyses provided no evidence that the hypothesized biomarker pathways were engaged. Patients with higher baseline inflammation did not derive greater benefit from LDA than those with lower baseline inflammation. Effect estimates were consistently close to zero, with narrow confidence intervals. Conclusion: We found no evidence that the hypothesized biological pathways were engaged or that baseline inflammation modified treatment response. The findings argue against a major role for the proposed inflammatory and HPA-axis mechanisms and are consistent with the negative clinical findings of the primary Aspirin-Bipolar RCT. Article.Title: Further characterization of oral fentanyl self-administration in male and female Sprague Dawley rats
Article.Authors: Yates J.; Allgire E.; Adhikari S.; Neeley J.; Gastright C.
Article.Abstract: Fentanyl is a potent synthetic opioid with high misuse potential and risk for overdose. While primarily associated with the intravenous route of administration, fentanyl is now often found in pills. However, few preclinical studies have assessed oral self-administration of fentanyl. In the present study, different groups of male and female Sprague Dawley rats were tested in a series of paradigms to further characterize oral fentanyl self-administration. Rats were trained to self-administer various doses of fentanyl (2.0-50.0 μg/ml) in the presence or the absence of a drug-paired stimulus and were trained to self-administer fentanyl (2.0 or 25.0 μg/ml) across increasing response requirements. Rats were also assessed for cue- and drug-induced reinstatement of fentanyl seeking, as well as for incubation of fentanyl seeking in the absence of discrete drug-paired stimuli and for resurgence of fentanyl seeking. With one exception, females responded more for fentanyl relative to males. As expected, the presence of a drug-paired stimulus significantly enhanced fentanyl self-administration and reinstated drug seeking. Consistent with previous work, we found that incubation of fentanyl seeking does not occur when a proximal cue is omitted during self-administration training. Oral fentanyl self-administration did not produce the standard U-shaped dose-response function; furthermore, rats showed little motivation to earn fentanyl across increasing response requirements. Drug-induced reinstatement was not observed when rats were trained with a low concentration of fentanyl (2.0 μg/ml). Resurgence of fentanyl (50.0 μg/ml) seeking was also not observed. Overall, additional work is needed to fully characterize addictive-like behaviors using oral fentanyl self-administration paradigms.

Article.Title: Comparison of the efficacy and safety of lacosamide and oxcarbazepine monotherapy in young children aged 1 month to 4 years with focal epilepsy: An ambispective cohort study based on real-world clinical practice in China
Article.Authors: Xiong M.; Yang L.; Zeng Q.; Chen X.; Jiang L.; Li J.; Chen J.; Hu Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: In the context of off-label use, this study aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of lacosamide (LCM) and oxcarbazepine (OXC) monotherapy in children aged 1 month to 4 years with focal epilepsy. Methods: This non-randomized, open-label, real-world study included 134 LCM-treated and 132 OXC-treated children. The primary endpoint was the 12-month efficacy rate (≥50% reduction in seizures). Mantel-Haenszel analysis and E-values controlled and assessed confounding; ANCOVA compared Gesell developmental quotients between groups. Results: LCM efficacy rates at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months were 76.9%, 76.9%, 72.4%, and 64.9%, respectively; OXC rates were 84.1%, 87.9%, 88.6%, and 73.5%, with no significant between-group differences. At 12 months, the adjusted ORs ranged from 0.603 to 0.645, with E-values of 1.55 to 1.60. LCM improved all five Gesell domains from baseline (P < 0.05). The language domain favored LCM after baseline adjustment (difference = 2.59, P = 0.043), but this was attenuated after further adjustment. Epilepsy duration and baseline seizure frequency predicted poorer LCM response. The 12-month retention rates were 75.4% and 84.1%, and adverse event rates were 7.46% and 4.55% in the LCM and OXC groups, respectively; most events were mild. Conclusion: In real-world clinical practice in China, LCM monotherapy demonstrated efficacy and safety comparable to those of OXC in young children with focal epilepsy, suggesting that LCM may represent an alternative option for off-label use in this age group. Its potential benefit for language development warrants further investigation.

Article.Title: Impact of combined CYP2C19/CYP2B6 phenotypes on sertraline dose-normalized concentration and antidepressant switching incidence: A retrospective cohort study in Chinese Han population
Article.Authors: Yan Y.; Luan Y.; Sun Q.; Zhao M.; An F.; Ding K.; Wang J.; Wang Y.; Yu R.; Gao S.; Huang Y.; Duan L.; Wang J.; Yu J.; Zhao Y.; Zhou C.
Article.Abstract: Sertraline, a commonly used first-line antidepressant for major depressive disorder, is primarily metabolized by the polymorphic cytochrome P450 enzymes CYP2C19 and CYP2B6. This large-scale Chinese cohort study (N = 1070 patients; 1414 serum concentration measurements) evaluated whether incorporating CYP2B6 phenotype provides additional information beyond CYP2C19 phenotype in explaining interindividual variability in dose-normalized sertraline concentrations, and investigated associations between combined CYP2C19/CYP2B6 phenotypes and antidepressant switching within 1 year after the last therapeutic drug monitoring assessment. Patients were classified according to CYP2C19 and CYP2B6 metabolizer phenotypes as poor metabolizers (PMs), intermediate metabolizers (IMs), normal metabolizers (NMs), or rapid metabolizers (RMs), resulting in 16 combined phenotype groups, with CYP2C19 NM/CYP2B6 NM as the reference group. Eight phenotype groups had significantly higher model-estimated dose-normalized sertraline concentrations than the reference group. The largest observed fold difference was for CYP2C19 PM/CYP2B6 IMs (fold change, 2.11; 95% CI, 1.84-2.42; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001), whereas the smallest significant fold difference was observed for CYP2C19 NM/CYP2B6 IMs (fold change, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.06-1.26; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002). The combined CYP2C19/CYP2B6 model showed better fit than the CYP2C19-only model (likelihood ratio test χ2 = 28.6, df = 3, P < 0.001). The overall incidence of antidepressant switching was 19.9%. Switching was more frequent in CYP2C19 PM/CYP2B6 IMs (34.3%; OR, 3.33; 95% CI, 1.50-7.41; P = 0.003), CYP2C19 IM/CYP2B6 IMs (26.2%; OR, 2.32; 95% CI, 1.33-4.06; P = 0.003), and CYP2C19 NM/CYP2B6 IMs (25.0%; OR, 2.26; 95% CI, 1.26-4.03; P = 0.006). These findings indicate that incorporating CYP2B6 phenotype provides additional information beyond CYP2C19 phenotype for characterizing variability in dose-normalized sertraline concentrations and support prospective evaluation of combined pharmacogenetic approaches to sertraline dosing and therapeutic drug monitoring.

Article.Title: Molecular mechanisms of amisulpride- and risperidone-induced hPRL in patients with psychiatric disorders: an integrated approach combining network pharmacology and molecular docking
Article.Authors: Chen C.; Liu Q.; Su X.; Li W.
Article.Abstract: Hyperprolactinemia (hPRL) is a frequent and clinically important adverse effect of antipsychotic treatment, particularly with amisulpride and risperidone, which are among the most potent prolactin-raising agents. Clinical observations show a high incidence of antipsychotic-induced hPRL in patients treated with these drugs, with prolactin elevations emerging early and often persisting during therapy. However, the molecular mechanisms by which amisulpride or risperidone, used either alone or in combination, induce hPRL remain incompletely understood. In this study, clinical data were first used to characterize prolactin changes in psychiatric patients receiving combined amisulpride-risperidone therapy. To refine current mechanistic understanding, a network pharmacology strategy was applied to integrate predicted and validated targets of amisulpride, risperidone, and hPRL. Intersection targets were used to construct a protein-protein interaction network and were subsequently subjected to Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses. The enriched pathways were mainly associated with prolactin-related signaling, including the prolactin signaling pathway, the PI3K/AKT pathway, and the dopaminergic synapse pathway. Key hub proteins, including DRD2, GSK3B, HTR2A, IGF1R, JAK2, and MAOA, were then subjected to molecular docking with amisulpride and risperidone. Both drugs showed low docking energies, suggesting strong binding affinities for these core targets. These findings indicate that amisulpride- and risperidone-induced hPRL is mediated by a convergent set of core targets and signaling pathways, thereby providing a systems-level framework for understanding, predicting, and potentially mitigating this adverse effect in clinical practice.

Article.Title: Mechanistic advances in exercise intervention for anxiety and depression via regulation of mitochondrial function
Article.Authors: Yang R.; Tang X.; Shi Y.; Sun J.; Yin Q.; Long Q.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety and depressive disorders are the most prevalent psychiatric conditions worldwide, characterized by complex pathophysiological mechanisms involving neuroplasticity, inflammatory responses, and disturbances in energy metabolism. Mitochondrial dysfunction has been proposed as one contributor, but causal evidence in patients remains limited. Exercise is an evidence-based adjunctive option for reducing depressive and anxiety symptoms, although effect estimates vary. In this narrative review, we comprehensively summarize the current understanding of how exercise may modulate mitochondrial function, including biogenesis, dynamics and energy metabolism, and how these changes could regulate neurotransmitter systems, reduce neuroinflammation, and promote neurogenesis. By integrating findings from both preclinical and clinical studies, we assess the strength of the proposed relationship, outline requirements for causal testing, and discuss the limits of clinical translation. Furthermore, we discuss existing challenges and propose future research directions to optimize exercise-based therapeutic strategies targeting mitochondrial pathways for the prevention and treatment of anxiety and depressive disorders.

Article.Title: A comparative study of modified suanzaoren decoction versus estazolam in chronic insomnia disorder: Clinical outcomes and thalamocortical network changes
Article.Authors: Wang R.; Han Y.; Chen L.; Lv D.; Yao P.; Guo Z.; Guo W.
Article.Abstract: Chronic insomnia disorder (CID) is associated with widespread abnormalities in thalamic functional connectivity (FC). For CID patients with the yin-deficiency and fire-excess syndrome, Modified Suanzaoren Decoction (MSZRD) and estazolam are common treatments, but their longitudinal associations with thalamic networks remain unclear. This study was a non-randomized, patient-preference controlled trial. Eighty-two CID patients with yin-deficiency and fire-excess syndrome received a 6-week treatment with either MSZRD or estazolam based on preference. Additionally, 54 healthy controls (HCs) were recruited for baseline comparison. Clinical scales, polysomnography, and resting-state fMRI data were collected pre- and post-treatment. Using the Human Brainnetome Atlas, the thalamus was parcellated into eight subregions. We examined baseline group differences and longitudinal FC changes, and identified genes associated with the baseline FC alterations for enrichment analysis. At baseline, CID patients showed significantly increased FC in pathways involving the medial pre-frontal thalamus, posterior parietal thalamus, lateral pre-frontal thalamus, and caudal temporal thalamus with multiple cortical regions. After treatment, the MSZRD group showed greater improvement than the estazolam group on subjective and objective measures. While FC decreased in the MSZRD group between the left occipital thalamus and right middle frontal gyrus, and between the right occipital thalamus and right angular gyrus, it increased in the estazolam group for these connections. Enrichment analysis of genes associated with baseline FC alterations identified pathways related to synaptic organization, cytoskeletal stability, and metabolism. These findings provide preliminary evidence that CID is associated with enhanced thalamocortical connectivity consistent with the thalamus-centric hyperarousal model, and that MSZRD and estazolam show different clinical and neural correlates. However, due to the non-randomized design and baseline FC differences, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in future randomized mechanistic studies.

Article.Title: Machine learning integrating high-resolution T1-weighted MR radiomics of subcortical structures with blood biomarkers to identify depressed patients with a history of suicide attempts
Article.Authors: Zheng Y.; Han L.; Zou M.; Wang J.; Yu M.; Cui N.; Lu X.; Lei W.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to develop a machine learning (ML) model combining radiomic signatures from subcortical structures on T1-weighted MR images with peripheral blood biomarkers to distinguish depressed patients with versus without a history of suicide attempts. We enrolled 164 depressed patients, including 60 patients with a history of suicide attempts (DP-SAs) and 104 patients without a history of suicide attempts (DP-NAs), of which 41 DP-SAs and 47 DP-NAs were measured for peripheral inflammatory factors and kynurenine (KYN) pathway metabolites. Radiomic features from subcortical structures were extracted, and a combination of four feature selection methods and four ML algorithms was used to identify the most robust radiomic model for distinguishing the DP-SAs from the DP-NAs. The radiomic scores obtained from the optimal model and statistically significant clinical characteristics in patients with blood data were incorporated into the nomogram. The performance of the nomogram was assessed by a calibration curve and decision curve analysis (DCA). Compared with the other subcortical regions, the right caudate nucleus and bilateral thalamus achieved higher areas under the curve (AUCs) (0.793, 0.762 and 0.693, respectively) for distinguishing DP-SAs from DP-NAs. The model combining multiple subcortical regions demonstrated improved performance, with AUCs of 0.803 and 0.821 in the cross-validation and test cohorts, respectively. Peripheral blood kynurenic acid (KYNA) and KYNA/quinolinic acid (QA) were identified as independent clinical predictors. Owing to the collinearity between KYNA and KYNA/QA, we constructed clinical-radiomic nomograms that integrate radiomic scores with KYNA or KYNA/QA, with C-indexes of 0.919 and 0.914, respectively. Calibration curve analysis and DCA revealed that the nomogram had good reliability and net benefit. The nomogram integrating subcortical radiomic features with blood biomarkers exhibits excellent discriminative performance, providing an exploratory biomarker and preliminary proof-of-concept modelling to distinguish depressed patients with versus without a history of suicide attempts.

Article.Title: The potential role of the gephyrin–CNTNAP4 interface in brain aging: Mechanisms of inhibitory circuit dysfunction and cognitive decline
Article.Authors: Baothman A.; Faheem S.; Al-kuraishy H.; Batiha G.
Article.Abstract: Brain aging is a multifactorial process characterized by progressive deterioration of synaptic integrity, impaired neuronal connectivity, and cognitive decline. Physiological brain aging involves a natural decline in cognitive function due to reduced synaptic connections, and synaptic integrity. However, the brain maintains plasticity, allowing individuals to adapt through lifelong learning and targeted lifestyle interventions. Conversely, pathological brain aging refers to abnormal, accelerated neurological decline that extends far beyond typical age-related changes, characterized by noteworthy brain atrophy, and is a primary driver of neurodegenerative diseases. Increasing evidence suggests that dysfunction of inhibitory neurotransmission represents a fundamental mechanism underlying age-associated alterations in brain circuitry. Among the molecular determinants governing inhibitory synaptic organization, the gephyrin, a principal postsynaptic scaffold protein, and contactin-associated protein-like 4 (CNTNAP4), a synaptic adhesion molecule involved in neuronal connectivity and neurotransmitter regulation, have independently emerged as important modulators of synaptic homeostasis. However, their potential functional interplay in normal and pathological brain aging remains poorly understood. Therefore, in this narrative review, we examine current knowledge regarding the structural and functional biology of gephyrin and CNTNAP4, emphasizing their contributions to inhibitory synapse maintenance, neuronal network stability, and age-related cognitive function. We further discuss convergent mechanisms through which disturbances in gephyrin-dependent receptor clustering and CNTNAP4-mediated synaptic adhesion may promote excitatory-inhibitory imbalance, synaptic destabilization, and circuit dysfunction during aging. Particular attention is given to shared downstream pathways implicated in brain senescence, including mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling, sirtuin-1 (SIRT1) activity, mitochondrial homeostasis, and neuronal autophagy. We propose the concept of a Gephyrin-CNTNAP4 interface as a previously underappreciated framework linking inhibitory synaptic scaffolding with cell-adhesion mechanisms in the aging brain. Understanding this interface may provide novel insights into the molecular basis of cognitive decline and facilitate the development of multi-target therapeutic strategies to preserve synaptic resilience and promote healthy brain aging.

Article.Title: Modulating neuroinflammation with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists: a scoping review exploring their therapeutic potential in schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Otto B.; Zantvoord J.; Siskind D.; Vermeulen J.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation is a key contributor to the pathophysiology and symptomatology of schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), clinically approved anti-diabetic and -obesity medication, have been associated with anti-inflammatory properties. It remains unclear whether GLP-1RA treatment can improve neuroinflammation within psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia. This scoping review synthesizes evidence from clinical and preclinical studies on the anti-inflammatory effects of GLP-1RAs in psychiatric, neurodegenerative and neurological disease models, identifying crucial research gaps and providing future recommendations to guide potential clinical translation. The literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO and included outcomes of cytokine levels within blood and brain samples. Within the 40 included studies, two were clinical (schizophrenia and alcohol-use disorder) and 38 were preclinical models of psychiatric diseases, Alzheimer's -, Parkinson's Disease, Multiple Sclerosis, Epilepsy and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced neuroinflammation. Preclinical studies showed anti-(neuro)inflammatory effects of GLP-1RAs, whereas the two available clinical studies found no significant changes in peripheral inflammatory markers. As these trials were not primarily designed or powered to test neuroinflammatory effects, the clinical findings remain inconclusive. Differences in study design, inflammatory measurements, pharmacokinetics and dosing may have contributed to the discrepancy between preclinical and clinical findings. Future research should prioritize early-phase dose-finding trials in non-diabetic, or -overweight patients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders, evaluating the effects of alternative GLP-1RA regimens on neuroinflammatory markers, safety and clinical symptomatology. This is an essential step to determine their potential mental health-enhancing effects through the modulation of neuroinflammation within schizophrenia spectrum disorders.

Article.Title: Temporal misalignment of brain–heart coupling accounts for multilevel interoceptive dysfunction in schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Zou H.; Li H.; Li C.
Article.Abstract: Schizophrenia involves profound disturbances in the sense of a bodily self. These disturbances increasingly appear to arise from disrupted interoception, the perception of internal physiological signals. However, dominant models that emphasize either intrinsic neural timescales or interoceptive inference tend to treat cardiac signals merely as passive sensory inputs. Here, we propose that cardiac rhythm dynamics may provide a phase-based temporal reference for large-scale neural coordination, potentially synchronizing neural activity across otherwise disparate temporal scales. This scaffolding function is mediated by mechanically transduced pulsatile signals that may influence cortical excitability across distributed networks. Within this framework, interoceptive dysregulation in schizophrenia is reconceptualized as a decoupling of hierarchical cortical oscillations from peripheral cardiac phases. Reduced variability in cardiac rhythms may weaken the stability of temporal references available to higher-order networks. This, in turn, may drive a compensatory increase in the prior precision assigned to ambiguous visceral inputs, thereby blurring the distinction between internally generated and externally driven signals. Such processes may contribute to hallucinations, delusions, and motivational deficits. Emerging therapeutic strategies, therefore, aim to restore temporal alignment across the heart-brain axis. Translating the phenomenology of interoception into quantifiable metrics of neuro-visceral misalignment holds promise as a potential bridge between neurobiology and targeted psychiatric intervention.

Article.Title: Ketamine administration reduced conditioned defensive behaviour and upregulated protein expression associated with neuroplasticity in a planarian model of aversive memory reactivation
Article.Authors: James F.; Ahamed S.; Yang C.; Wilson R.; Canales J.; Vicario C.; Johnson L.; Caruso V.
Article.Abstract: Traumatic memories that are resistant to modification or extinction are a characteristic feature of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The process of fear memory reconsolidation has been identified as a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of PTSD. Ketamine, an NMDA receptor antagonist with dissociative properties, has been identified as a drug with high therapeutic potential for this target, as it destabilises traumatic memory while enabling rapid modification and update of the memory to no longer be threatening. However, its exact mechanisms of action on reducing the impact of aversive memory remains poorly understood. To better understand these mechanisms, a conditioned aversive memory reactivation model using ketamine was carried out in brown planaria (Girardia dorotocephala), an invertebrate model that shows a high degree of conservation in neural anatomy, receptors, neurotransmitters, and learning behaviours, while being comparatively simpler than standard mammalian models. In this study, 15 planaria were randomly assigned to three treatment groups (10 μM ketamine, 1 μM ketamine, vehicle control) and underwent a classical aversive memory reactivation paradigm. Whole planaria were processed for an exploratory proteomic analysis to analyse changes in protein expression associated with the effects of ketamine on the aversive memory reactivation process. Behavioural data showed a significant reduction in defensive behaviours, including scrunching movements F(2,12) = 11.85, p = 0.0014, ƞ2 = 0.66, C-shape movements F(2,12) = 6.59, p = 0.012, ƞ2 = 0.52, and head turns F(2,12) = 9.59, p = 0.0032, ƞ2 = 0.61, in the 10 μM ketamine group on the final test day compared to vehicle controls. Proteomic analysis showed that these behavioural changes were accompanied by a high degree of enrichment in molecular pathways associated with rapid neuronal growth and synaptic plasticity, and changes in cellular mRNA, all markers of learning. These preliminary findings in an invertebrate model improve understanding of how ketamine may facilitate disruption of conditioned aversive memory via rapid neuronal restructuring and augmenting synaptic plasticity.

Article.Title: Cannabidiol attenuates behavioral impairments and deficits in parvalbumin interneurons and their perineuronal nets induced by adolescent stress in adult mice
Article.Authors: Lima T.; Verza F.; Godoy L.; Guimarães F.; Gomes F.
Article.Abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for the development of neural circuits, and exposure to stressors during this stage constitutes a risk factor for psychiatric disorders. Previous studies have shown that adolescent stress in rodents leads to behavioral alterations and functional loss of parvalbumin-containing GABAergic (PV+) interneurons and their perineuronal nets (PNNs) in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and ventral hippocampus (vHip). Although less explored, somatostatin-expressing (SST+) interneurons may also be impaired. Given the reported anti-stress effects of cannabidiol (CBD) in adult rodents, we investigated whether CBD attenuates adolescent stress-induced alterations. Male C57BL/6 J mice were exposed to footshock stress from postnatal day (PND) 31-40 and subsequently received CBD (30 mg/kg, i.p.) for ten days (PND 41-50). After a 15-day drug-free period, animals started being evaluated in adulthood using behavioral assays for anxiety (elevated plus maze, light-dark box), sociability (social interaction), social memory (social discrimination), and cognition (novel object recognition). Adolescent stress impaired social discrimination and object recognition memory, and CBD attenuated these deficits, while sociability and anxiety-like behavior remained unaffected. Consistent with the behavioral findings, stressed animals exhibited reductions in PV+, PNN+, and PV+/PNN+ cells in the mPFC and vHip, as well as a less marked reduction in SST+ cells in the vHip, and CBD attenuated these stress-induced cellular alterations. Our findings suggest that CBD may attenuate behavioral and molecular alterations associated with adolescent stress exposure, particularly those involving PV+ interneurons and their PNNs, highlighting its potential to mitigate stress-induced deficits.

Article.Title: Altered intrinsic neural timescales in cocaine use disorder
Article.Authors: Tang X.; Di T.; Sheng J.; Sun Y.; Zhang M.; Luo W.
Article.Abstract: Cocaine use disorder (CUD) is a major public health challenge, but its neurodynamic and molecular mechanisms remain unclear despite evidence of structural and functional abnormalities. This study mapped whole-brain intrinsic neural timescales (INTs), reflecting temporal integration of neural activity, using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging in 44 CUD patients and 44 healthy controls. In the primary analysis with global signal regression (GSR), CUD showed increased network-level INTs in the visual, somatomotor, dorsal attention, frontoparietal control, and default mode networks compared with HC. In the sensitivity analysis without GSR, the visual and somatomotor network differences remained significant. Within the CUD group, regional and network-level INT variation was associated with individual differences in flanker-task performance, despite the absence of significant between-group differences in behavioral performance. Notably, the spatial distribution of INT differences was associated with normative maps of gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptors and the noradrenaline transporter. Atlas-based models showed modest discrimination and limited validation, while outcome-informed cluster-based models yielded higher but exploratory estimates. Importantly, classification performance in a mixed-source evaluation sample was close to chance, indicating limited generalizability. Together, these findings reveal widespread alterations in intrinsic neural timescales in CUD and highlight the relevance of spatiotemporal brain organization to addiction.

Article.Title: Circuit organization of Tac2-expressing neurons from established functions to testable hypotheses
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Hu S.; Cao H.; Mu M.
Article.Abstract: Tac2-expressing neurons participate in behavioral and neuroendocrine functions through regionally specialized circuits. Building on a 2021 review of the Tac2/neurokinin B (NKB) pathway, we examine how cell- and projection-specific studies have refined this organization. Fear-memory and isolation-stress studies provide convergent evidence for NKB-neurokinin 3 receptor (NK3R) signaling, whereas other studies establish functions of Tac2-expressing populations without demonstrating peptide dependence. We distinguish interventions targeting neurons, the Tac2-encoded peptide, NK3R, and NK3R-expressing cells, and assess classical-transmitter evidence separately. We then integrate descriptive Allen Brain Cell Atlas MERFISH visualizations with regional circuit knowledge to formulate hypotheses for the medial habenula, dorsal tegmental nucleus, and spinal trigeminal nucleus interpolaris. Established reinforcement in a Tac2-driver-defined habenular subset motivates tests of output specialization; tegmental and trigeminal expression patterns motivate hypotheses about orientation-arousal coupling and sensory gating. Atlas annotations identify candidate molecular phenotypes, not validated transmitter release or behavioral functions. Together, the literature supports a region- and state-dependent account of Tac2-expressing populations and defines where additional molecular evidence is needed to establish NKB-NK3R mechanisms.

Article.Title: Cellular senescence in ageing and neurodegenerative disorders: Molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies
Article.Authors: Verma A.; Goyal A.; Agrawal N.; Yadav H.
Article.Abstract: Cellular senescence has been increasingly associated with neurodegenerative disorders, potentially linking ageing-related cellular impairment with mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and disrupted intercellular signalling. The present study aims to explore the increasing relevance of cellular senescence among key cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, neural progenitor cells, microglia and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells across neurodegenerative ailments such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and multiple sclerosis. This review discusses the findings of pre-clinical and clinical studies which suggest that senescence-associated features may contribute to neurodegeneration. Further, it provides an overview of the biomarkers used in the identification of senescence in the CNS. Also, the review examines senotherapeutic treatment approaches, highlighting their actions on different CNS cell types and the growing clinical evidence. It also points out the challenges in translating these approaches to clinical application, such as targeting specific cell types and the lack of suitable biomarkers. Collectively, present findings suggest that senescence-associated alterations may contribute to neurodegeneration, although their effects appear to vary across cell types and diseases.

Article.Title: Serum metabolic characteristics and potential biomarkers of first-episode schizophrenia: An exploratory machine learning-based metabolomics study
Article.Authors: Peng X.; Liu B.; Meng W.; Huang J.; Zhang Q.; Chen L.; Li K.; Tong H.; Zhang X.; Zhang J.; Rao W.
Article.Abstract: Metabolomics studies in first-episode schizophrenia (FES) remain limited and heterogeneous. This study aimed to characterize the serum metabolomic profile of FES, identify metabolic biomarkers, and develop machine learning-based predictive models. In this exploratory study, serum metabolomic profiles were compared among healthy controls (HCs; n = 10), untreated FES patients (n = 10), and the same patients after second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) treatment. Candidate biomarkers were evaluated using six machine learning algorithms. Bayesian network analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) were further applied to explore the network relationships. Cross-dataset integrative analysis was additionally performed using an external public dataset comprising patients with schizophrenia (n = 30) and HCs (n = 30). Disease-associated candidate biomarkers included PG(16:0/18:1), PC(20:4/15:0), PC(22:5/15:0), PG(18:1/18:1), and PE(16:0/16:0), whereas treatment-associated biomarkers included PG(16:0/18:1), PC(20:4/15:0), PC(22:5/15:0), cholesterol sulfate, DG(20:4/22:4), and Phe-Thr-Asn-Lys. All selected candidate biomarkers achieved Area Under the Curve (AUC) values above 0.9, with performance varying across algorithms. In the Bayesian networks, disease served as a direct parent node of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score and all biomarkers, whereas treatment shared direct edges with the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) score and all biomarkers except cholesterol sulfate, which was indirectly connected via Phe-Thr-Asn-Lys. WGCNA identified metabolite modules significantly associated with disease status (r = -0.88, p < 0.01) and treatment (r = 0.75, p < 0.01). Cross-dataset analysis identified phenylpyruvic acid, SM(d18:1/22:1(13Z)), and 2-octenoylcarnitine as shared differential metabolites with modest-to-moderate discrimination. These exploratory findings reveal potential serum metabolic signatures of FES and provide a basis for the development of objective biomarkers for diagnosis and SGAs treatment monitoring, warranting validation in larger independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Rabies and distemper exhibit distinct patterns of axonal damage and apoptotic cell death in the central nervous system of dogs and foxes
Article.Authors: Pfetzing S.; Freuling C.; Puff C.; Kammeyer P.; Rozza D.; Teifke J.; Kleinschmidt S.; Baumgärtner W.; Müller T.; Ulrich R.
Article.Abstract: Rabies is a fatal zoonosis caused by the rabies virus (RABV), which enters the central nervous system via a retrograde axonal pathway with histopathologically often very subtle but fatal polioencephalitis. Distemper is characterized by neuronal and/or axonal damage, as well as leukoencephalitis with demyelination in dogs and polioencephalitis without demyelination in foxes. This study aimed to compare the neuropathological lesions and the amount of axonal damage and apoptosis in the central nervous system of dogs and foxes infected with RABV or canine distemper virus (CDV), alongside non-infected control groups. Staining with hematoxylin and eosin, luxol fast blue-nuclear fast red, and immunohistochemistry for lyssaviral nucleoprotein, CDV nucleoprotein, β-amyloid precursor protein (a marker for early axonal damage) and active caspase-3 (a marker for apoptosis) was performed on archival formaldehyde-fixed, paraffin-embedded brain specimens. Dogs and foxes infected with RABV showed no change in the number of active caspase-3-immunoreactive cells and β-amyloid precursor protein-immunoreactive axons and no demyelinating areas. In contrast, CDV infection was characterized by an increase in active caspase-3-immunoreactive cells and β-amyloid precursor protein-immunoreactive axons in both species, and additionally demyelinating areas in the dog. These results suggest that RABV effectively evades recognition by intrinsic neuroaxonal antiviral mechanisms on its route to the central nervous system.

Article.Title: A non-destructive workflow for simultaneous reconstruction of nuclear and dendritic architecture in intact brain tissue
Article.Authors: Higgins J.; Schneemann A.; Cavanagh B.; Egan S.; Henshall D.; Mamad O.
Article.Abstract: Neurons display elaborate dendritic and axonal structures which serve as input and output sites for the transmission of information across the nervous system. Changes to the structure and complexity of both are commonly reported in genetic and acquired brain diseases with neuropathology studies also reporting changes to nuclear architecture. However, a methodological limitation has prevented direct study of this relationship: resolving nuclear geometry conventionally requires physical sectioning that severs dendrites, whereas tissue-clearing approaches that preserve dendrites introduce anisotropic dimensional distortion. No existing method simultaneously quantifies nuclear geometry and dendritic morphology within the same intact neuron at sub-micrometre resolution. We exploit a property of Golgi-Cox impregnation that has historically been treated as a staining artefact. Namely, the consistent exclusion of precipitate from the nucleus, which appears as a geometrically precise, low-attenuation void within the high-contrast soma in X-ray microscopy (XRM). Using this void as a label-free nuclear imaging channel, we performed compartment-level morphometry on mouse neurons across two independent XRM scans at sub-micrometre voxel resolution (0.619 and 0.726 µm isotropic), and full whole-neuron reconstructions including nucleus, soma, and dendritic arbour. Across 26 CA1 neurons, nuclear morphometrics were consistent: median nuclear sphericity 0.893, median soma-to-nucleus centroid offset 1.35 µm, median perinuclear cytoplasmic thickness 3.96 µm, and median nucleus-to-soma volume ratio 4.2%. Nuclear metrics did not differ significantly between scans after correction for multiple comparisons. This feasibility study establishes Golgi-XRM for simultaneous, non-destructive reconstruction of nuclear geometry and dendritic architecture as a tool for investigating nuclear positioning as a disease-sensitive variable.

Article.Title: RAAS/HPA axis abnormalities and hypothalamic connectivity in hypertension: A multimodal MRI study
Article.Authors: Huang R.; Lu J.; Li J.; Ma J.; Wu J.; Jin J.; Li J.; Meng F.; Fu D.; Hua X.; Xu J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Hypertension is associated with brain remodeling and an increased risk of cognitive impairment. Although endocrine hormones play a central role in blood pressure regulation, how endocrine abnormalities are associated with brain network reorganization and cognitive function in hypertensive populations remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis abnormalities are associated with distinct multimodal brain alterations and cognitive profiles in hypertension. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 47 hypertensive adults underwent endocrine profiling, neuropsychological assessment, and resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) and T1-weighted structural MRI on a 3.0 T scanner. Image analyses included amplitude of Low-Frequency Fluctuations (ALFF), Voxel-based Morphometry (VBM), and hypothalamic seed-based Functional Connectivity (FC). Based on plasma levels of angiotensin II (Ang II), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), and aldosterone (ALD), patients were classified as endocrine-abnormal hypertension (EH; n = 20) or non-endocrine hypertension (NEH; n = 27). Group differences and endocrine-imaging associations were examined. Results: Compared with the NEH group, the EH group showed poorer performance on memory and language measures. The EH group also showed reduced ALFF in frontal regions and increased ALFF in the cerebellum, together with reduced gray matter volume in posterior cortical regions. Hypothalamic seed-to-voxel FC was reduced in the EH group with frontal, temporal, and occipital cortical regions and increased with cerebellar regions. In whole-sample analyses, hypothalamic-vermal connectivity was negatively associated with global cognition and language performance, cerebellar ALFF was negatively associated with episodic memory performance, and right superior frontal gyrus ALFF was negatively associated with circulating ALD levels. Conclusions: Endocrine abnormalities in hypertension are associated with a distinct pattern of brain alterations characterized by prefrontal hypofunction, posterior cortical gray matter reductions, and altered hypothalamic-cortical and hypothalamic-cerebellar connectivity, accompanied by poorer performance on memory and language measures. These findings suggest that hypertensive patients with endocrine abnormalities may represent a subgroup with greater brain and cognitive vulnerability.

Article.Title: Alpk1 activates JAK2/STAT3 signaling to enhance M1-microglial activation in epileptic rats
Article.Authors: Chen J.; Cui H.; Zhao M.; Du X.; Chen W.
Article.Abstract: Background: Epilepsy is a chronic brain disorder characterized by recurrent, highly synchronous abnormal neuronal discharges leading to cerebral dysfunction. This study investigates the role of alpha kinase 1 (ALPK1), a pattern recognition receptor, in epilepsy. Methods: ALPK1 expression and distribution were analyzed using the GSE190452 dataset and a pilocarpine-induced rat model. An adeno-associated virus delivering Alpk1 shRNA was injected intra-hippocampally into model rats, followed by seizure monitoring. Pathological changes were assessed via hematoxylin and eosin and Nissl staining. Primary microglia and BV2 cells transfected with Alpk1 siRNA were stimulated with kainic acid. Immunofluorescence, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction, and Western blot were used to evaluate M1 microglial marker and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was performed to identify potential signaling associated with Alpk1 function. Results: ALPK1 was widely distributed and highly expressed in epileptic microglia. Alpk1 knockdown alleviated seizure symptoms in rats, including hippocampal damage, Nissl body loss, reduced Racine scores, and decreased daily seizure frequency and duration. Both in vivo and in vitro, Alpk1 knockdown downregulated the M1 marker inducible nitric oxide synthase and pro-inflammatory cytokines (tumor necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6). GSEA indicated Alpk1 activates Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) / signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) signaling. Stat3 overexpression reversed the inhibitory effects of Alpk1 knockdown on M1 activation and inflammation. Conclusion: ALPK1 is highly expressed in epileptic microglia. Silencing Alpk1 alleviates M1-microglial activation and inflammation in epilepsy by inhibiting the JAK2/STAT3 signaling.

Article.Title: Research progress on Drp1 in the pathological mechanisms and therapeutic interventions of stroke, based on the imbalance in the dynamic equilibrium of mitochondrial fission and fusion
Article.Authors: Lin Z.; Chen B.; Fu Y.; Luo Y.; Chen L.; Zhang M.; She R.; Wang L.; Li S.; Pu Y.; Tang H.; Bai X.
Article.Abstract: Ischemic and haemorrhagic strokes together constitute the leading cause of death and disability worldwide, and their pathological mechanisms involve an imbalance in mitochondrial dynamics. Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a key GTPase driving mitochondrial fission, is overexpressed in response to post-stroke pathological signals (calcium overload, oxidative stress, and inflammatory factors), leading to fragmentation of the mitochondrial network and subsequently triggering energy depletion, reactive oxygen species (ROS) bursts, and various forms of programmed cell death. This article provides a comprehensive review of the molecular regulatory networks and cell-type-specific effects of Drp1 in ischemic and haemorrhagic stroke, covering key processes such as neuronal apoptosis, inflammatory polarisation of glial cells, and disruption of the vascular endothelial barrier. The literature was synthesized based on a thematic rather than a formal systematic approach, with emphasis on high-quality mechanistic studies and preclinical evidence published over the past decade. Building upon a summary of preclinical evidence for the protective effects of pharmacological inhibitors such as Mdivi-1, P110 and Drpitor1, the paper provides an in-depth analysis of the bottlenecks currently facing translation, including core challenges such as the narrow therapeutic time window, insufficient blood-brain barrier permeability, the need to strike a balance between physiological and pathological fission, and the lack of biomarkers. Finally, this paper outlines next-generation intervention strategies based on nanodelivery systems, precise temporal regulation and multi-omics integration, emphasising a paradigm shift from 'complete blockade' to 'fine-tuning', thereby providing a theoretical basis for the development of innovative Drp1-targeted therapies for stroke.

Article.Title: Mechanomarker-informed identification of Alzheimer’s disease based on lateral ventricular deformation
Article.Authors: Cunniff L.; Weickenmeier J.
Article.Abstract: Structural magnetic resonance imaging reveals lateral ventricular enlargement as a prominent structural change in normal aging, with accelerated expansion in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. In this study, we characterize ventricular shape changes and corresponding mechanical loading in cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects in their seventies, using longitudinal magnetic resonance images over a two-year interval. Surface-based deformation metrics were computed to capture localized displacement magnitude, curvature changes, surface area stretch, and maximum principal wall strain, both relative to the population average at baseline and relative to each subject's baseline over the two-year follow-up. Longitudinal displacement over two years increased markedly with disease progression, rising 114 ± 15% from CN to AD. Area stretch exhibited a more modest 6 ± 1% increase, while maximum principal wall strain nearly doubled, increasing 110 ± 16% from CN to AD. Curvature change remained minimal when averaged globally, although localized deformations along ventricular edges suggest subtle region-specific alterations. The significant differences between mechanics-related features for individual disease groups highlight the value of deformation-derived mechanomarkers that go beyond the more commonly reported volumetric analyses. As such, our mechanomarkers demonstrated a predictive value for disease classification, especially in the direct comparison of CN and AD. Our results highlight the potential of ventricular mechanomarkers as non-invasive, MRI-derived biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of neurodegenerative progression, providing insight into the mechanical loading resulting from structural brain shape changes.

Article.Title: Clusterin interference decreases cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury by suppressing TFR1-dependent ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Zhou X.; Yuan H.; Huang W.; Huang G.; Ye X.; Gao H.
Article.Abstract: Ferroptosis plays a crucial role in the pathological process of cerebral ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury, but the specific regulatory mechanism of Clusterin in this process remains unclear. This study aims to investigate whether interfering with Clusterin can alleviate cerebral I/R injury by regulating neuronal ferroptosis. A cerebral I/R injury mouse model was established and the adeno-associated virus (AAV-sh-Clusterin) was stereotactically injected into the brain. Brain tissue damage was evaluated using TTC and HE staining. The expressions of blood-brain barrier proteins (Occludin, ZO-1) and inflammatory factors (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6) were detected. Downstream differentially expressed genes were analyzed through mRNA transcriptome sequencing. The expression changes of iron death-related indicators (Fe2 +, MDA, GSH, NRF2, GPX4, ACSL4, SLC7A11) were evaluated by means of biochemical methods and WB/qPCR. Subsequently, an in vitro oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R) model of HT22 cells was constructed to analyze the effects of Clusterin interference on the proliferation and ferroptosis of HT22 cells. The interaction between Clusterin and TFR1 was detected, and a rescue experiment was carried out by overexpressing TFR1. Clusterin was significantly upregulated in both in vitro and in vivo models. Interference with Clusterin effectively reduced the volume of cerebral infarction, upregulated the expressions of Occludin and ZO-1, and inhibited the inflammatory response. Besides, interference with Clusterin significantly decreased the ferroptosis level in mouse brain tissue. There is a protein interaction between Clusterin and TFR1, and the rescue experiment indicated that overexpression of TFR1 could counteract the inhibitory effect of sh-Clusterin on ferroptosis and the proliferation protection effect of HT22 cells. In summary, interfering with Clusterin by inhibiting TFR1-dependent neuronal ferroptosis significantly mitigates neuronal damage and inflammatory responses induced by cerebral I/R.

Article.Title: Structural connectivity between the retrosplenial cortex and hippocampus in the healthy human brain: A diffusion tensor tractography study
Article.Authors: Yun S.; Cho I.
Article.Abstract: Background/purpose: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) and hippocampus are important regions involved in spatial navigation by integrating vestibular information into spatial representations. Although functional interactions between these regions have been demonstrated, there is currently a lack of evidence regarding the structural connectivity between the RSC and hippocampus in the human brain. This study aimed to reconstruct and characterize a tractography-derived pathway between the RSC and hippocampus in healthy adults using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tractography. Methods: Thirty healthy adults were recruited. The seed region of interest (ROI) was defined in the RSC with reference to both sagittal and axial planes, and the target ROI was placed within the hippocampus on the axial plane. The structural characteristics, including fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, and tract volume were analyzed. Results: A tractography-derived RSC-hippocampal pathway was identified bilaterally in all participants. Conclusion: This study characterized a tractography-derived RSC-hippocampal pathway in the healthy human brain. Our findings provide insight into RSC-hippocampal structural connectivity and suggest a potential structural substrate for interactions between these regions in spatial information processing.

Article.Title: Multiband ALFF in patients with major depressive disorder treated with esketamine and sertraline: A preliminary study
Article.Authors: Hua Z.; Shu Y.; Li L.; Xia S.; Xiao J.; Li J.; Ji Y.; Li H.; Peng D.; Wan A.; Wu G.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: This study investigated changes in multiband amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in patients with major depressive disorder following a 2-week combination treatment regimen of esketamine and sertraline, and examined the associations between ALFF changes and clinical symptom improvement. Methods: Forty patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) received esketamine (0.25 mg/kg, intravenous infusion, three times per week) combined with sertraline (50-150 mg/day, oral) for 2 weeks. The Hamilton Anxiety Scale, the Hamilton Depression Scale, the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation, and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment were administered at baseline and week 2, and resting-state functional MRI data were collected. ALFF values were calculated for the typical band (0.01-0.08 Hz), the slow-4 band (0.027-0.073 Hz), and the slow-5 band (0.01-0.027 Hz) using DPABI 5.1. Clinical scores were compared between baseline and week 2 with paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests according to the Shapiro-Wilk test. Whole-brain ALFF maps were compared with voxel-wise two-tailed paired t-tests in all participants (Gaussian random field correction; voxel-level p < 0.001, cluster-level p < 0.05), and the extracted mean ALFF value of each surviving cluster was then compared between time points at the region level with a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test according to normality; normality was therefore assessed only for the extracted regional values, not at the voxel level. Partial correlation analyses, with sex, age, education, baseline clinical scores, and mean framewise displacement as covariates, were conducted to examine associations between ALFF measures and clinical outcomes. Three families of ROI × frequency-band × clinical-outcome tests were defined according to the question addressed (baseline ALFF versus week-2 outcome; post-treatment ALFF versus concurrent outcome; change in ALFF versus change in clinical score; 32 tests per family, 96 tests in total), and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction within each family (q < 0.05) was the primary multiplicity control, with Bonferroni correction within family (adjusted α =0.0016) and FDR across all 96 tests treated as a single family as sensitivity analyses. Results: After treatment, HAMA, HAMD, and BSI scores decreased and MoCA scores increased (all p < 0.001). ALFF values in the left inferior frontal gyrus increased in the typical and slow-4 bands, whereas ALFF in sensorimotor and visual cortical regions decreased across multiple bands (GRF-corrected, voxel p < 0.001, cluster p < 0.05). Treatment-related increases in L-IFG ALFF in the typical band were negatively correlated with reductions in BSI scores (partial r = -0.500, uncorrected p = 0.004); however, this association did not remain significant after FDR correction across the 32 ΔALFF-Δscore tests (q = 0.114) or after Bonferroni correction (adjusted α =0.0016), and no ROI-clinical correlation survived correction in any family. It is therefore reported as a nominal, exploratory finding. Post-treatment ALFF in the L-IFG, right precentral gyrus, and right middle occipital gyrus showed nominally significant partial correlations with concurrent symptom scores; none of these remained significant after FDR correction within the corresponding family (smallest q = 0.153). Baseline L-IFG ALFF was not independently associated with treatment outcome after covariate adjustment. Conclusion: A 2-week combination treatment regimen of esketamine and sertraline was associated with frequency-specific ALFF changes in prefrontal, sensorimotor, and visual cortical regions in patients with major depressive disorder. No ROI-clinical correlation survived correction for multiple comparisons across the three families of tests; the nominal association between L-IFG ALFF change and suicidal-ideation reduction is exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and requires independent replication before prefrontal ALFF modulation can be considered a candidate marker for monitoring treatment-related neurofunctional changes.

Article.Title: Salidroside regulates hippocampal neuronal autophagy in ASD mice via the SIRT2/FoxO1 pathway
Article.Authors: Ning X.; Yu Z.; Liu L.; Xie X.; Guo L.
Article.Abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by neuronal dysfunction and impaired autophagy. Salidroside (SAL), a bioactive component derived from Rhodiola, exhibits neuroprotective activity; however, its effects and mechanisms in ASD remain largely unknown. Here, we examined the effects of SAL on valproic acid (VPA)-induced neuronal injury and ASD-related behaviors and assessed the role of the sirtuin 2 (SIRT2)/forkhead box O1 (FoxO1) pathway. VPA-induced HT22 cell injury models and ASD mouse models were used in this study. HT22 cells were exposed to 2 mM VPA and treated with 20 μM SAL, with AGK2 applied for SIRT2 inhibition. ASD mice received SAL administration from postnatal day 21 for 14 days, and AK-7 was used to further evaluate SIRT2 involvement. VPA exposure decreased HT22 cell viability, caused neuronal damage, increased autophagosome accumulation, and induced ASD-like behaviors in mice, including impaired social interaction, enhanced repetitive grooming, and reduced exploratory activity. SAL treatment improved cell viability, alleviated neuronal damage, attenuated autophagy-related changes, and improved behavioral abnormalities, whereas these effects were partially blocked by AGK2 or AK-7. Furthermore, SAL reversed VPA-induced alterations in autophagy-related proteins, including decreased Beclin-1 and LC3 expression and increased p62 expression, while restoring SIRT2, FoxO1, NeuN, and MAP2 levels and reducing the Ac-FoxO1/FoxO1 ratio in HT22 cells and hippocampal tissues. These findings indicate that SAL protects against VPA-induced neuronal injury and ASD-related behavioral deficits, which are associated with changes in the SIRT2/FoxO1 pathway and autophagy-related processes.

Article.Title: Resting-state functional connectivity alterations and neurodevelopmental outcomes in neonates at high risk of hypoxic–ischemic brain injury
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Peng C.; Liu L.; Niu F.; Yang J.; Ji Y.; Hou X.
Article.Abstract: Background: High risk of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury during the neonatal period may disrupt early brain maturation, yet its impact on large-scale functional network organization and later neurodevelopment remains insufficiently understood. Methods: Resting-state functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to characterize cortical functional connectivity in neonates at high risk of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury and controls. Functional connectivity, multivariate pattern analysis, and graph-theoretical approaches were applied to examine group differences in network organization and their associations with developmental outcome. Results: Compared with controls, high-risk neonates showed reduced functional connectivity predominantly within the frontoparietal network. Seed-based multivariate pattern analysis identified the left parietal lobe as the strongest discriminator between groups. Within the frontoparietal subnetwork, the high-risk group showed reduced clustering coefficient and increased global efficiency, suggesting reduced local segregation and atypical network reorganization. Clustering coefficient was positively associated with later Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3) scores in both groups, consistent with a general developmental relationship. In contrast, higher global efficiency and lower nodal clustering in the left prefrontal cortex were associated with poorer developmental outcomes only in the high-risk group. Conclusions: Neonates at high risk of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury show early alterations in frontoparietal functional organization, some of which are associated with later neurodevelopment. Resting-state fNIRS-derived connectomic measures may therefore have potential for early risk characterization, although further validation in larger independent cohorts is needed.

Article.Title: Glibenclamide treatment improved intraspinal blood volume, tissue sparing, and functional recovery after cervical spinal cord injury in rats
Article.Authors: Prasse T.; Jensen D.; Chandran P.; Odarenko A.; Hyde J.; Ng M.; Eysel P.; Bredow J.; Ugiliweneza B.; Hofstetter C.; Bruce M.; Khaing Z.
Article.Abstract: Limiting the expansion of the primary injury after a traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) can offer improved functional outcomes. Glibenclamide (glyburide) has been shown to limit intraspinal bleeding and promote vascular stability after SCI in rats, but its impact on intraspinal hemodynamics has not been investigated. Here, we hypothesized that acute glibenclamide treatment would improve intraspinal hemodynamics after a cervical contusion SCI in a rat model (200 kdyn). Intravital ultrafast contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) imaging revealed that glibenclamide treatment significantly increased total blood volume (i.e., tissue perfusion) at 72-hours post-injury (hpi) compared to vehicle treated controls (p < 0.05, Cohen's d >1.2). Histological data confirmed that glibenclamide treatment significantly lowered caspase-8-positive cells in the white matter at 72-hpi (p < 0.05, Cohen's d>1.2). Weekly forelimb locomotor scoring revealed significant functional improvements in animals treated with glibenclamide at 4-weeks post-injury (wpi) (p < 0.001, Cohen's d>1.2), which continued through to 8-wpi compared to vehicle treated animals (p < 0.05, Cohen's d>1.2). Glibenclamide intervention significantly reduced lesion size by 8-wpi compared to controls (p < 0.05, Cohen's d>1.2). This study is the first to report in vivo improvements in intraspinal blood volume associated with glibenclamide treatment after acute cervical SCI in rats.

Article.Title: The brain before the herd: Pre-Decision EEG prediction of herd-consistent investment choices among bilingual investors
Article.Authors: Loang O.; Jiyang H.; Azar A.
Article.Abstract: This study examines whether pre-decision electroencephalographic (EEG) activity provides incremental information for explaining and predicting herd-consistent investment choices when social and fundamental signals conflict. A controlled 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 within-participant factorial experiment involving 80 English-Mandarin bilingual Chinese investors who met a predefined English-proficiency threshold equivalent to IELTS 6.5 or TOEFL iBT 80 and had prior experience in U.S. equity markets manipulated language, information format, social-media sentiment, and information consistency. Herd-consistent choice was conservatively defined as alignment with the social signal when it contradicted fundamental information. Behavioural and single-trial EEG responses were analysed using mixed-effects models, while machine-learning models were evaluated through nested participant-disjoint validation. The findings indicate that Mandarin-language presentation and short-form financial information are associated with greater conformity to social signals under informational conflict. Conflict between social and fundamental information also elicits stronger frontal-midline theta activity, consistent with heightened demands on cognitive control and conflict monitoring before choice. Pre-decision P300 and theta provide distinct predictive information beyond contextual and participant characteristics, indicating that attentional updating and conflict processing contribute differently to subsequent herd-consistent decisions. These findings support a process-based account of investment conformity in which information architecture, social influence, and pre-decision neurocognitive processing jointly shape herd-consistent choices.

Article.Title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation alleviates depressive- and anxiety-like behaviors in adolescent stressed rats via SIRT1/NRF2-mediated modulation of hippocampal redox and neuroimmune homeostasis
Article.Authors: Zheng Y.; Jiang Y.; Wang X.; Rong P.; Sun L.
Article.Abstract: Aims: This study aimed to identify key molecular changes in the hippocampal subregions underlying the antidepressant effects of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) in a rat model of chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) during adolescence, and to explore the potential involvement of the SIRT1/NRF2/GPX4 signaling pathway in regulating oxidative stress and related ferroptosis- and pyroptosis-associated signaling. Methods: To investigate the antidepressant mechanism of taVNS, a CUMS rat model was established. One hundred postnatal day 21 male Sprague-Dawley rats were used. In Experiment 1, rats (n = 10 per group) were randomly assigned to Control (Con), CUMS model (Mod), CUMS + taVNS (taVNS), and CUMS + tnVNS (tnVNS) groups. After 21 days of CUMS exposure, rats received a 21-day taVNS or tnVNS intervention. In Experiment 2, rats (n = 10 per group) were randomly assigned to Con, Mod, taVNS, taVNS + DMSO, taVNS + ML385 (NRF2 inhibitor), and taVNS + EX527 (SIRT1 inhibitor) groups, with inhibitors administered intraperitoneally for 14 consecutive days. Behavioral tests, including sucrose preference test (SPT), open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), and passive avoidance test, were performed. Hippocampal tissues and plasma were collected for ELISA, western blot, and immunofluorescence analyses. The expression of SIRT1, NRF2, GPX4, KEAP1, NLRP3, Caspase-1, GSDMD, COX-2, and β-actin was assessed, along with oxidative stress markers (MDA, SOD, CAT, GSH), inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-18, IFN-γ), and immunofluorescence staining for Iba-1/NeuN, PSD95/MAP2, BDNF/TREM2, and 4-HNE. Results: Compared with the Con group, CUMS-induced rats exhibited significant depressive- and anxiety-like behaviors, increased oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, and decreased expression of SIRT1, NRF2, and GPX4 in the hippocampus. taVNS treatment significantly reversed these behavioral abnormalities, reduced MDA, IL-1β, and TNF-α levels, and increased SOD, CAT, and GSH activities. taVNS also upregulated SIRT1, NRF2, and GPX4 expression, while downregulating KEAP1 and COX-2, and showed a downregulation trend in GSDMD-related pyroptotic effectors, without statistically significant changes in NLRP3 or Caspase-1 protein levels. Immunofluorescence showed that taVNS reduced Iba-1-positive microglia, increased NeuN/Iba-1 ratio, restored MAP2 and PSD95 expression, and decreased 4-HNE levels in the CA1, CA3, and DG regions. However, administration of ML385 or EX527 attenuated these protective effects, as evidenced by worsened behavioral performance, increased oxidative stress and inflammatory markers, and reduced expression of NRF2 and GPX4. No significant differences were observed between the taVNS and taVNS + DMSO groups. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that the SIRT1/NRF2/GPX4 signaling pathway in the hippocampus is a critical regulatory node underlying CUMS-induced oxidative stress and the associated alterations in ferroptosis- and pyroptosis-related signaling in adolescent rats. taVNS exerts its antidepressant and anxiolytic effects by activating this pathway, thereby attenuating ferroptosis- and pyroptosis-related signaling, alleviating neuroinflammation, and enhancing neural plasticity.

Article.Title: NOTCH1 and ADORA3 define a novel transdifferentiation-related prognostic index for prognostic stratification in glioblastoma by integrating clinical factors
Article.Authors: Zheng Z.; Li Y.; Zhang Y.; Huang C.; Li C.; Lin J.; Yu H.; Gao H.
Article.Abstract: Background/objectives: Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits aggressive progression and poor prognosis, partly driven by glioma stem cell-endothelial transdifferentiation (GSC-ET), an alternative vascularization mechanism associated with therapeutic resistance. However, robust prognostic models based on transdifferentiation-related genes remain lacking. This study aimed to identify key GSC-ET-associated genes and develop a personalized prognostic framework integrating molecular and clinical factors. Methods: Transcriptomic and clinical data from patients with primary IDH-wildtype GBM were obtained from CGGA, TCGA, Gravendeel (GSE16011), and Murat (GSE7696) cohorts. Survival analyses and Cox regression were performed to identify prognostic transdifferentiation-related genes. A glioblastoma transdifferentiation (GTN) index was established based on candidate genes and integrated with clinical variables to construct a prognostic risk model. External validation, immune infiltration analysis, and functional assays were conducted. Results: Among 12 transdifferentiation-related genes, NOTCH1 and ADORA3 were identified as independent adverse prognostic factors in GBM. A GTN index derived from these genes effectively stratified patient survival and was validated across external cohorts. Integration of the GTN index with age and chemotherapy status generated a risk model with favorable predictive performance and clinical utility. Immune analyses revealed distinct associations between NOTCH1/ADORA3 expression and immune cell infiltration. Functional experiments demonstrated that silencing either gene suppressed tube formation, reduced CD31 expression, and impaired LDL uptake in glioma cells. Conclusions: NOTCH1 and ADORA3 are associated with GBM prognosis, and their silencing reduces transdifferentiation-related endothelial-like phenotypes, supporting their inclusion in an integrated prognostic framework.

Article.Title: Hippocampal ALKBH5 contributes to depression-like behaviors in a mouse model of inflammatory pain
Article.Authors: Deng S.; Zhu J.; Zhou H.; Tang X.; Gong W.
Article.Abstract: Background: Chronic pain and depressive symptoms frequently coexist and mutually reinforce each other, severely compromising patients' quality of life, yet the underlying central molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. ALKBH5, an m6A demethylase, has been implicated in the regulation function of central nervous system. However, whether ALKBH5 contributes to depression-like behaviors induced by chronic inflammatory pain remains unknown. Methods: The Complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA)-induced inflammatory pain model was employed in this study. ALKBH5 expression and behavioral performances were examined in CFA-treated mice. To further validate the role of hippocampal ALKBH5 in this model, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated shRNA was delivered to knock down ALKB5 in the hippocampus. Results: ALKBH5 protein levels were significantly unregulated in the hippocampus of CFA mice. Adenovirus-mediated knockdown of hippocampal ALKBH5 markedly alleviated CFA-induced depressive-like behaviors, possibly due to the reduced expression of iNOS. Conclusion: our findings identify hippocampal ALKBH5 as a key regulator of depression-like behaviors in chronic inflammatory pain and suggest that targeting ALKBH5 may provide a novel therapeutic strategy for alleviating affective disorders associated with chronic pain.

Article.Title: Diffusion MRI assessment of white matter microstructure and free-water fraction in drug-naïve children with SeLECTS
Article.Authors: Zhou X.; Chen Y.; Luo Y.; Kuang Y.; Deng C.; Lai H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS) is a common childhood-onset focal epilepsy syndrome. Although seizures are typically self-limited, some children may show neurodevelopmental or cognitive vulnerability. Diffusion MRI may provide insight into white matter alterations in SeLECTS. Objective: To evaluate white matter diffusion differences in newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) and white matter free-water fraction (FW-WM), and to explore within-patient associations with selected seizure-related and cognitive variables. Methods: Fifty-three newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS and 53 healthy controls with a similar age and sex distribution were prospectively enrolled in this cross-sectional case-control study. Diffusion MRI was acquired at 3.0 T, and white matter diffusion differences were assessed using TBSS and FW-WM analyses. Voxelwise between-group differences in fractional anisotropy (FA) were tested with age and sex as covariates and corrected using threshold-free cluster enhancement-based family-wise error correction. FW-WM was compared between groups using age- and sex-adjusted general linear models, with additional adjustment for years of education in a sensitivity analysis. Exploratory within-patient associations between imaging measures and selected clinical or cognitive variables were assessed using partial Spearman correlations with false-discovery-rate correction. Results: Children with SeLECTS showed lower FA than healthy controls in multiple TBSS-defined white matter regions after correction for multiple comparisons, mainly involving commissural, projection, and association pathways. No between-group differences in mean, axial, or radial diffusivity survived correction for multiple comparisons. FW-WM was higher in the SeLECTS group after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted mean difference = 0.0085; 95% CI, 0.0023-0.0147; P = 0.008), with similar results after additional adjustment for education. In exploratory cluster-level analyses, mean FA in a left-sided cluster involving the posterior internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, and sagittal stratum was inversely associated with disease duration after FDR correction (r = -0.413; P = 0.003; q = 0.010). No imaging-cognition or within-patient FW-WM-FA association survived FDR correction. Conclusions: Newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS showed white matter diffusion differences, including lower FA in distributed TBSS-defined regions and higher FW-WM. These findings support diffusion MRI-based characterization of white matter alterations at diagnosis, before antiseizure treatment. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify their clinical and developmental relevance.

Article.Title: High-frequency rTMS attenuates cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury and modulates mTOR-related signaling and brain–gut–immune phenotypes in MCAO/R rats
Article.Authors: Xue H.; Wang J.; Hua X.; He K.; Jin X.; Liu L.; Hu J.
Article.Abstract: Background: High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) may promote neurological recovery after ischemic stroke, but its protective effects after MCAO/R and associations with neurotrophic factors, mTOR-related autophagy markers, systemic inflammation, and gut microbiota phenotypes remain unclear. Methods: Cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury was induced by right MCAO/R. Rats were assigned to Sham, MCAO/R, and MCAO/R + high-frequency rTMS groups. rTMS was initiated on postoperative day 3. Neurological and motor functions were assessed behaviorally. Western blotting, immunofluorescence, ELISA, and 16S rRNA sequencing were used to examine related proteins, inflammatory cytokines, and gut microbiota, followed by multivariate and correlation analyses. Results: High-frequency rTMS improved neurological and motor functions, reduced infarction and histopathological injury, decreased TUNEL positivity, and increased the number of Nissl-positive neurons. It upregulated FGF-2, BDNF, and the p-mTOR (Ser2448)/mTOR ratio, attenuated abnormal changes in Beclin-1, LC3-II/LC3-I, and p62, and reduced serum TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels. 16S rRNA sequencing showed altered gut microbiota β-diversity and genus-level composition, with several genera associated with motor or inflammatory indices. Conclusion: High-frequency rTMS alleviated cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury and promoted neurological recovery after MCAO/R, accompanied by enhanced neurotrophic support, improvement in mTOR-related autophagy marker abnormalities, and lower serum pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Gut microbiota alterations were also observed following rTMS treatment, although their functional significance remains exploratory.
