Article.Title: Cross-organ crosstalk in brain-aging–related sarcopenia: Caudate iron accumulation impairs muscle health via blood-brain barrier dysfunction
Article.Authors: Ye F.; Li N.; Hao L.; Yu F.; Peng Q.; Deng J.; Hu X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Brain aging and sarcopenia represent multisystem manifestations of aging. Although emerging research supports the brain-muscle axis, the causal evidence and mechanisms remain unclear. Methods: Multi-stage genetic analysis investigated cross-organ regulation between brain Quantitative susceptibility mapping(QSM) and muscle health, with replication at each stage. High-Definition Likelihood inference(HDL) and Mendelian randomization(MR) assessed associations between regional QSM and lean body mass(LBM). Single-cell disease relevance score(scDRS) nominated cell types involved in brain-muscle crosstalk. Transcriptome-wide association studies(TWAS) prioritized candidate genes at the tissue level. Candidate genes were replicated at the cellular level through SMR analysis and colocalization, and then exploratorily characterized by simulated knockout. Based on 669 blood-brain barrier(BBB)-related biomarkers, mediation analysis explored mechanisms linking caudate QSM to LBM. Results: Increased caudate QSM was associated with lower LBM. Caudate vascular cells were involved in the brain-muscle crosstalk. CYBRD1 in the caudate nucleus was associated with LBM across different TWAS methods. SMR and colocalization indicated that CYBRD1 expression in pericytes was positively associated with LBM, grip strength, and physical function. After simulated knockout of CYBRD1, the perturbed genes were enriched in BBB function and structure pathways. Elevated right caudate QSM was associated with decreased plasma TYRO3 levels, which partially mediated the negative effect of right caudate QSM on LBM. Conclusions: Elevated caudate QSM was associated with muscle atrophy, partly mediated by BBB dysfunction. This brain-muscle axis suggests brain iron management and BBB homeostasis as potential intervention directions for brain aging-related sarcopenia.

Article.Title: DEW-MEGA-PRESS of phosphorylethanolamine and glutathione: Reproducibility and feasibility in individuals with autism
Article.Authors: Saleh M.; Melch M.; Triolo E.; Bloy L.; Blaskey L.; Brodkin E.; Roberts T.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: To demonstrate double-editing (DEW) MEGA-PRESS editing of phosphorylethanolamine (PE) and glutathione (GSH) in vivo, estimate measurement variability, and conduct a feasibility study on individuals with autism. Methods: 13 participants with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), with an average age of 28.00 ± 4.81 years, and 14 typically developing (TD) participants, with an average age of 29.33 ± 5.36 years, were enrolled in the study. DEW-MEGA-PRESS at a Siemens 3 T MRI scanner was used to edit both PE and GSH (ONPE/ONGSH = 3.98/4.56 ppm). Within-subject variability was examined in 15 participants (11 TD and 4 ASD) using repeated scans conducted at 4 and/or 12 weeks after baseline. Finally, differences in PE and GSH between the two groups were assessed using linear mixed-effects models. Results: In vivo experiments show excellent separation between the PE (3.22 ppm) and GSH (2.95 ppm) signals. Within- and between-subject reproducibility assessments revealed coefficients of variation (CV) of 9.0/18.5% for PE and 7.4/10.3% for GSH. Although GSH showed no statistically significant differences, PE levels were significantly higher in ASD than in TD (p < 0.05), and only TD showed a decrease in PE with aging (p < 0.05). Conclusion: In vivo experiments demonstrate excellent separation between PE and GSH, and good within-subject reproducibility, supporting the stability of the approach. Between-subject variability exceeded within-subject variability for both chemicals, suggesting that biological differences between individuals dominate over measurement noise and supporting the feasibility study assessing differences between TD and ASD.

Article.Title: Cuproptosis in cerebrovascular diseases: Mechanisms and advances in targeted therapeutic strategies
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Xu R.; Zhang H.; Gao Y.; Liu Z.
Article.Abstract: Cuproptosis is a recently identified form of regulated cell death. It is primarily driven by abnormal mitochondrial copper accumulation. Ferredoxin 1-dependent copper reduction promotes the pathological aggregation of lipoylated proteins involved in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the loss of iron-sulfur cluster proteins. This process induces proteotoxic stress, ultimately causing the collapse of mitochondrial energy metabolism. Evidence from transcriptomic analyses, single-cell multi-omics studies, and in vivo and in vitro models suggests that copper dyshomeostasis may be involved in cerebrovascular disease. Specifically, it may contribute to oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and neurovascular unit dysfunction in conditions including acute ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, vascular cognitive impairment, and cerebral small vessel disease. This review outlines the regulatory networks governing cerebral copper homeostasis, summarizes the molecular machinery of cuproptosis, and examines its crosstalk with apoptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and disulfidptosis. We discuss the potential molecular pathways by which cuproptosis may contribute to cerebrovascular injury, its possible role in modulating the local immune microenvironment, and emerging interventional strategies. Furthermore, we critically evaluate current therapeutic approaches and weigh their preclinical progress in light of current empirical limitations. Finally, we assess the translational potential and practical challenges of targeted nanomedicine platforms. By synthesizing these findings, this review provides a hypothesis-generating framework for future mechanistic and interventional research. These insights highlight the need for mechanistic validation, cuproptosis-specific biomarkers, and direct cerebrovascular efficacy and safety studies before clinical translation.

Article.Title: Multiscale white- and gray-matter diffusion abnormalities and their associations with serum ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy: A free-water elimination diffusion MRI study
Article.Authors: Zeng T.; Lin C.; Chen L.; Wang X.; Hong C.; Mao M.; Huang H.; Shen A.; Fu L.
Article.Abstract: Background: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) involves complex brain edema, but conventional diffusion models may be confounded by extracellular water and cannot readily distinguish tissue-specific abnormalities from fluid-related effects. This study used a free-water elimination (FWE) diffusion tensor imaging framework to characterize multiscale white- and gray-matter (GM) diffusion abnormalities in HE and to examine their associations with serum ammonia and clinical measures. Methods: Patients with HE and healthy controls (HCs) were prospectively enrolled in a cross-sectional observational case-control study. FWE-DTI was used to derive conventional diffusion metrics (FA, MD, AD, and RD), tissue-specific metrics (FAt, MDt, ADt, and RDt), and the fractional volume of free water (FW). White-matter (WM) and cortical GM alterations were evaluated using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) and GM-based spatial statistics (GBSS), respectively. Conventional peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD) quantified global WM diffusivity heterogeneity. Within the HE group, voxel-wise multiple linear regression models assessed associations of diffusion metrics with serum ammonia, MELD, PHES, and MMSE, adjusting for age, sex, and TIV. TFCE with 5000 permutations and FWER correction within each statistical map was applied. Results: Compared with HCs, patients with HE showed elevated PSMD and widespread diffusion abnormalities across the WM and cortical GM skeletons. Increased FW was observed in the WM skeleton. Within the HE group, higher serum ammonia was associated with lower AD, ADt, and FW in WM and with lower AD, MD, RD, ADt, MDt, and RDt in cortical GM. Exploratory analyses identified positive associations between PHES and selected white- and GM diffusion metrics and between MMSE and selected WM diffusion metrics; no significant MELD-related associations were detected. All reported voxel-wise associations survived TFCE-based FWER correction. Conclusions: The findings indicate coexisting white- and GM diffusion abnormalities in HE and distinct within-HE associations between serum ammonia and selected diffusion metrics. FWE-derived metrics provide complementary estimates of free-water fraction and tissue-specific diffusion, but their cellular basis, temporal evolution, and causal interpretation remain uncertain. These findings require validation in larger longitudinal cohorts using multi-shell diffusion MRI and complementary biological assessments.

Article.Title: The stems of Syringa pinnatifolia alleviate insomnia based on the brain-gut-microbiota axis mediated by 5-HT in mice and rats
Article.Authors: Wuken S.; Jurat J.; Liu C.; Yang G.; Liang Y.; Ulzhi Batu T.; Sun J.; Liang X.; Gao X.; Chai X.
Article.Abstract: The peeled stems of Syringa pinnatifolia Hemsl. (SP) have long been used for the treatment of insomnia in Inner Mongolia, China, but their hypnotic constituents and underlying pharmacological basis remain poorly defined. In this study, we investigated the hypnotic activity of SP and identified its active fraction and major constituents using an equal mass to equivalent effect transmission (EMEET)-guided fractionation strategy. SP extracts and fractions were evaluated in pentobarbital-induced sleep tests and a PCPA-induced insomnia model in mice and rats. The phenolic fraction (Ps) significantly shortened sleep latency, prolonged sleep duration, and reduced hyperactivity in insomnia animals. Further fractionation and pharmacological evaluation identified alashinol F (F), alashinol G (G), and (-)-secoisolariciresinol (K) as major constituents contributing to the hypnotic activity of Ps. Mechanistically, Ps decreased serotonin transporter (SERT) expression and increased tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH) expression in the hypothalamus and colon. Ps treatment was also associated with decreased hypothalamic 5-HT2C and PLCβ1 expression, restoration of Gαq/11 expression, and alterations in gut microbial composition, including changes in Bacteroidetes, Prevotella_9, and Blautia. Collectively, these findings identify the major hypnotic fraction and active lignans of SP and suggest that its sleep-promoting effects are associated with coordinated regulation of serotonergic signaling and the gut microbiota.

Article.Title: PI3K/AKT signaling contributes to prenatal nicotine exposure-induced developmental impairment of the pontomedullary respiratory network in neonatal rats
Article.Authors: Du Y.; Liang S.; Bian M.; Wang Y.; Xu Z.; Wang Q.; Tu F.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: Prenatal nicotine exposure (PNE) disrupts the development of the pontomedullary respiratory network and increases susceptibility to respiratory dysfunction after birth. However, the role of PI3K/AKT signaling in PNE-induced impairment of neuronal development within the pontomedullary respiratory network remains unclear. In this study, a rat model of PNE was established to investigate neuronal development, apoptosis, microglial activation, and PI3K/AKT signaling within respiratory-related nuclei of the pontomedullary network in neonatal rats on postnatal day 2. PNE induced neuronal morphological abnormalities and reduced NeuN-positive neuronal populations in the VIIn/pFRG, XIIn, and NA/pre-BötC regions. These changes were accompanied by increased TUNEL-positive cells, elevated caspase-3 and caspase-9 expression, enhanced microglial activation as indicated by increased Iba-1-positive cells, and increased PIK3CA expression and the p-AKT1/AKT1 ratio. Pharmacological inhibition of PI3K/AKT signaling with wortmannin partially attenuated neuronal development impairment, apoptosis, and microglial activation. PNE was also associated with reduced neonatal body weight and length. These findings provide pharmacological evidence that dysregulated PI3K/AKT signaling contributes to PNE-induced developmental impairment of the pontomedullary respiratory network, potentially through processes involving neuronal apoptosis and microglial activation.

Article.Title: BH-CMA: A cross-modal attention network based on brain-heart collaboration for stress cognitive state decoding
Article.Authors: Zhao W.; Li P.; Yang J.; Ying S.; Yao D.; Qin Y.; Liu T.; Xie J.
Article.Abstract: Accurate recognition of stress states under different cognitive loads is important for adaptive human computer interaction and physiological stress monitoring. However, unimodal measurements provide incomplete central or autonomic information, while indiscriminate multimodal fusion may obscure the distinct temporal and spatial organization of electroencephalography (EEG) and heart rate variability (HRV). This study proposes BH-CMA, a compact cross-modal attention network based on brain-heart collaboration for stress cognitive state decoding. Modality-specific encoders preserve the frequency, temporal, and scalp spatial organization of EEG and model the temporal dynamics of HRV. EEG representations then guide cross-modal temporal attention to retrieve complementary autonomic information from synchronized HRV. A linear preserving residual classifier further combines stable discriminative information from the original physiological inputs with nonlinear corrections learned by the deep branch. BH-CMA was evaluated using data from 28 participants under four conditions defined by acute stress induction and cognitive load. Leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation showed that BH-CMA achieved an accuracy of 58.07%, a Macro F1 of 55.54%, and a Macro AUC of 81.74%. Compared with EEG alone, BH-CMA increased mean Macro F1 by 4.15%, with higher Macro F1 in 23 of 28 participants. Masking HRV also reduced Macro F1 in 21 participants, supporting the contribution of HRV information to classification by the multimodal model. BH-CMA achieved significantly higher Macro F1 than its internal linear prediction mode. Gains were larger for cognitive load discrimination, with the largest recall gains in HCS and ASH. BH-CMA provides a compact framework for cross-subject stress cognitive state decoding using coordinated EEG and HRV information.

Article.Title: Atypical cortical asymmetries in toddlers with congenital heart disease before surgery
Article.Authors: Li H.; Du X.; Cheng L.; Yang F.; Ma S.; lu F.; Zhu M.; Wang H.; Yang M.; Mo X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Patients with congenital heart disease (CHD) may exhibit atypical structural asymmetry in the brain, while the altered structural lateralization and its relationship with cognitive function have not been fully revealed. Methods: We performed a cross-sectional structural imaging study of 109 toddlers of CHD, including 80 with mild CHD, 29 with moderate-severe CHD in our hospital and 56 normal controls (NC). Surface-based image analysis was used to compute lateralization index (LI) for cortical surface area (CSA), cortical thickness (CT), and cortical volume (CV) in CHD groups and NC group across 34 bilateral regions. Group comparisons were conducted using generalized linear models, and partial correlation analyses were performed to examine associations between LIs, clinical variables, and developmental quotients (DQs) assessed by the Gesell Developmental Scale. Results: Compared to the NC group, both the mild and moderate-severe CHD groups showed overlapping altered lateralization regions in the caudal anterior cingulate gyrus, pars opercularis, superior temporal gyrus, cuneus cortex, medial orbitofrontal gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate cortex (p_FDR < 0.05). Moreover, the LI of CT in the pars opercularis was negatively associated with personal-social skills DQ in the CHD group (r = -0.327, p＜0.001 uncorrected; p_FDR = 0.021). Conclusions: Mild and moderate-severe CHD groups showed comparable alterations in cerebral asymmetries, predominantly involving perisylvian and default-mode network regions. Notably, the association between the LI of CT in the pars opercularis and personal-social skills DQ highlights a potential structural correlate of neurodevelopmental risk in CHD.

Article.Title: Recent advances in research on the amygdala complex in sleep and anesthesia awakening: A hub for the integration of emotion and arousal
Article.Authors: Wang K.; Li X.; Yu R.; Sun S.; Deng D.; Zhang Q.; Zhang T.; Zhang Y.; Ding R.; Shen J.; Ku X.; Wang Z.; Fan S.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: The amygdala complex (comprising the lateral, central, and medial amygdala) has traditionally been regarded as playing a central role in emotional learning and fear memory. However, recent studies have revealed its critical functions in the regulation of sleep cycles and recovery from anesthesia. This review proposes a new theoretical framework that views the amygdala complex as an "emotion-arousal integration network" that integrates internal emotional states with external environmental demands to dynamically regulate overall arousal levels and states of consciousness. This review first outlines the neuroanatomy and cellular composition of the various subnuclei of the amygdala, then systematically elaborates on the role of the basolateral amygdala in the regulation of the physiological sleep-wake cycle, and explores its new role in promoting the recovery of consciousness during general anesthesia. Building on this foundation, the review further analyzes the complementary roles of the central and medial amygdala in sleep regulation, as well as how functional imbalances in the amygdala lead to sleep and emotional symptoms in conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder. Finally, the review outlines potential clinical translation strategies based on amygdala circuits and neurochemical mechanisms, and discusses current research challenges and future directions.

Article.Title: Altered functional topology related to the development of wearing-off in Parkinson’s disease
Article.Authors: Gao T.; Zhou C.; Guo T.; Tian J.; Guan X.; Wu J.; Xu X.; Zhang M.; Pu J.; Zhang B.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Wearing-off (WO) is the most common medicine-related complication that develops in later stage of Parkinson's disease (PD), whereas the underlying mechanism still remains unknown. Here, we aimed to decipher the mechanism underlying the WO in PD patients. Methods: Twenty-six PDWO (PD with WO), 26 PDnW (PD without WO) and 34 healthy controls were included and functional and structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were employed. Functional network was constructed based on the matrix of each subject's functional images and attributes of functional topology (e.g., global and local metrics) were calculated. Intergroup differences in white matter and grey matter were compared to potentially explore the structural abnormalities. Partial correlation analysis was performed to demonstrate the relationships between the altered imaging findings and clinical variables. Results: Wearing-off in PD patients was independently associated with levodopa equivalent daily dose (LEDD) /weight. Functional degree centrality (DC) having negative correlation with WO severity was significantly decreased in supramarginal gyrus in PDWO. Functional DC in precentral gyrus was significantly lower in PDnW compared with healthy controls, which was correlated with dopaminergic medication profiles. No apparent evidence about structural abnormality was found in PDWO and PDnW patients. Conclusions: The occurrence of wearing-off in PD patients was independently associated with LEDD/weight. The functional disruption in supramarginal gyrus might reflect the development of wearing-off, and we speculated the attenuation of levodopa related plasticity in precentral gyrus had an association with the susceptibility of wearing-off in PD patients. Further research are needed to validate and extend these preliminary findings.

Article.Title: Dexmedetomidine attenuates sepsis-associated inflammation and encephalopathy by modulating the MeCP2/NLGN1 pathway
Article.Authors: Hu B.; Wang Y.; Yang Y.; Wei H.; Yang J.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a common and serious complication in septic patients that significantly reduces quality of life. Besides its sedative and analgesic effects, dexmedetomidine has been suggested to have potential neuroprotective benefits. This study aims to determine whether dexmedetomidine guards against cognitive dysfunction in a murine model of sepsis and to investigate the possible role of the MeCP2/NLGN1 signaling pathway in this neuroprotection. Methods: An animal model of SAE was established by cecal ligation and puncture (CLP). Sham-operated mice underwent the same surgical procedure but without ligation or puncture. Mice in the Dex-treated group received intraperitoneal administration of Dex (25 µg/kg) once daily for three consecutive days, starting immediately after CLP. Selective knockdown of MeCP2 in the hippocampal CA1 region was achieved via adeno‑associated virus (AAV)‑mediated RNA interference. Between postoperative days 14 and 17, a series of behavioral tests-including the open field, novel object recognition, and Y-maze tests-were conducted to evaluate locomotor activity and cognitive function. Hippocampal expression of MeCP2 and NLGN1 proteins was analyzed by Western blot. Immunofluorescence staining was used to assess microglia activation and neuronal activity. Levels of inflammatory cytokines in the serum and hippocampus were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). In addition, dendritic spine density and morphology were assessed using Golgi staining. Results: In mice subjected to CLP, cognitive deficits were associated with increased levels of inflammatory factors in both the serum and hippocampus, aberrant microglial activation, upregulation of MeCP2 protein, and downregulation of NLGN1. These alterations contributed to reduced neuronal activity and a decrease in dendritic spine density. Selective knockdown of MeCP2 in the hippocampal CA1 region reversed NLGN1 downregulation and ameliorated cognitive dysfunction, confirming the pathogenic role of the MeCP2/NLGN1 pathway in SAE‑associated cognitive impairment. Treatment with Dex attenuated the inflammatory response, normalized MeCP2/NLGN1 expression, and reversed the aforementioned pathological changes. Conclusion: The neuroprotective effects of Dex, which include the attenuation of neuroinflammation and improvement of synaptic plasticity and cognitive function in SAE mice, are associated with the regulation of the hippocampal MeCP2/NLGN1 signaling pathway.

Article.Title: Investigating the therapeutic mechanism of leech in vascular dementia: An integrated approach combining network pharmacology and experimental validation
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Xue X.; Luo H.; Chen D.; Yang S.; Huang X.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Vascular dementia (VaD), the second leading cause of dementia following Alzheimer's disease, results from the reduction in cerebral blood flow. Medicinal leeches (SZ) in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), a classic remedy for promoting blood circulation and improving blood stasis, have shown capabilities to relieve neuroinflammation and repair the blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity. However, the efficacy and the underlying mechanisms of medicinal leeches in treating VaD remain unclear. Objective: This study aimed to explore the efficacy of medicinal leeches in treating VaD and its molecular mechanisms. Methods: An in vivo VaD model of rats was created via a two-vessel occlusion (2VO) ischemia protocol. Learning and memory functions in rats were assessed via the water maze test, Y-maze test, and novel object recognition test. The neuronal injury in rat hippocampus was assessed by H&E and Nissl staining. Network pharmacology (NP) and molecular docking depicted a "SZ-Compounds-Targets" network and visualized the binding pattern between core components of medicinal leeches and key targets of VaD, respectively. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), ELISA, quantitative PCR, and Western blotting were performed to validate the involvement of the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway in leech treatment against VaD. Results: Medicinal leeches alleviated the cognitive deficits and neuronal injuries in VaD rats. Seven key targets were predicted as the leading contributors to the neuroprotective potential of medicinal leeches against VaD. Enrichment analyses further showed that the Toll-like receptor and NF-κB signaling pathways were enriched in the key targets of medicinal leeches. Experimental assays showed that expression levels of TLR4, MyD88, p-p65, and pro-inflammatory mediators were significantly elevated in VaD rats, which were further enhanced by LPS induction. Encouragingly, leech treatment significantly downregulated their levels. Conclusion: Medicinal leeches can effectively alleviate the learning and cognitive impairments, neurological pathology in the hippocampal CA1 region, and the loss of BBB integrity in VaD rats. Moreover, medicinal leeches can suppress the neuroinflammation in VaD rats through inhibiting the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway.

Article.Title: Neural connectivity patterns associated with high-altitude residence duration: An exploratory cross-validated multimodal MRI study
Article.Authors: Guan F.; Xie W.; Wang F.; Ma H.; Li Y.; Zhang Y.; Peng K.
Article.Abstract: Living at high altitudes (HA) poses challenges to the brain due to hypobaric hypoxia. However, most neuroimaging studies have focused on group-level comparisons, leaving the brain features associated with individual differences in HA residence duration incompletely characterized. We therefore used a data-driven, individualized, multimodal machine learning framework for exploratory cross-validated association analysis to estimate individuals' HA residence duration after adjustment for age and gender. The analysis included 217 healthy migrants at HA and incorporated whole-brain anatomical morphometry, structural connectivity (SC), and functional connectivity (FC). Resting-state FC showed the highest estimate-target correlation among the unimodal models (r = 0.34, permutation p = 0.01, out-of-sample predictive R² = -0.15, MAE = 41.04 months, RMSE = 52.39 months). Combining FC and SC produced a numerically higher r and lower MAE and RMSE (r = 0.36, permutation p = 0.01, out-of-sample predictive R² = 0.00, MAE = 38.37 months, RMSE = 48.86 months) than FC alone, but the difference in correlation was not statistically significant. The FC model thus showed a statistically significant but modest cross-validated association with the residualized target, but its accuracy was insufficient to support clinical prediction or monitoring of HA residence duration. Meanwhile, FC within the somatomotor network (SMN) showed a positive contribution to model estimation, while FC between the SMN and the default mode network (DMN) showed a negative contribution. Positive contributions were observed for SC between the DMN and the frontoparietal network and for FC between the DMN and the dorsal attention network. SC between the thalamus and the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) showed a positive contribution to model estimation. Whether these residence-duration-associated connectivity patterns reflect within-person changes over time requires longitudinal investigation. As no behavioral validation was performed in this study, the functional significance of these connectivity patterns remains to be determined.

Article.Title: Napping during night shift preserves normal neural activity in nurses with sleep deprivation: Evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging study
Article.Authors: Gao Z.; Huang Z.; Lin H.; Chen H.; Lin J.
Article.Abstract: Background and purpose: Neuropsychological studies suggest that napping during night shifts may benefit nurses' brain functions and clinical performance. However, in vivo neuroimaging evidence remains scarce. This study aims to use resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) to investigate how night-shift napping modulates neural activity in nurses experiencing sleep deprivation (SD), addressing a critical gap in understanding the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying nap-induced recovery. Methods: rs-fMRI was administered to 24 nurses during three sessions: rested wakefulness (RW), SD, and napping (NAP). Within a biological day, RW represented normal sleep duration, SD indicated an absence of sleep, and NAP referred to naps lasting less than two hours during the night. Amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF) analysis was performed to assess spontaneous neural activity and reflect brain function. One-way repeated measures analysis of variance, followed by post hoc paired t-tests, was used to examine ALFF differences. Results: A comparison between RW and SD revealed a significant SD-related reduction in ALFF, predominantly affecting the bilateral frontal and temporal cortices, insula, subcortical structures, and cerebellum, and a notable ALFF increase predominantly involving the bilateral occipital cortex, motor and sensory-related areas, parietal lobe, and several temporal regions (FWE-corrected P < 0.05). When comparing RW with NAP sessions, the spatial extent of ALFF alterations was significantly reduced (FWE-corrected P < 0.05). Additionally, comparison between SD and NAP sessions showed that NAP effectively mitigated the ALFF disturbances induced by SD. Conclusion: Night-shift napping may serve as an effective strategy for restoring disturbed neural activity and thereby preserving cognitive and perceptual brain functions. These findings provide novel neuroimaging evidence supporting napping as a neuroprotective strategy for sleep-deprived nurses.

Article.Title: Frontal midline theta reduction during attentional reconfiguration links local cortical dynamics to network-level connectivity changes
Article.Authors: Ohgomori T.; Shiraiwa K.; Naito Y.; Ishii R.; Takeda M.
Article.Abstract: Attentional reconfiguration during transitions between task contexts induces a transient reduction of frontal midline theta (Fmθ), a well-established neural marker of focused attention. However, it remains unclear whether this transient reduction reflects changes in local cortical activity associated with specific visual information processing or a more general reorganization of network-level connectivity. Thirty-six healthy young adults performed a rule-switching 2-back task that required attentional shifts between color-based and position-based processing. Electroencephalography was recorded using a 19-channel system and we compared changes in power spectral density, current source density, and lagged linear functional connectivity between epochs immediately before and after attentional reconfiguration using exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography technique. Statistical analyses were conducted using permutation-based non-parametric methods. Transient reductions in Fmθ power and the number of Fmθ-positive epochs were consistently observed across both rule-switching patterns. In contrast, α band activity showed condition-dependent spatial modulation: parietal α suppression emerged selectively during shifts toward spatial processing, whereas occipital α suppression was observed during shifts toward color processing. Moreover, Fmθ reduction was significantly associated with parietal (but not occipital) α suppression. Connectivity analysis revealed robust increases in long-range θ-band coordination following attentional reconfiguration across conditions. These findings suggest that transient Fmθ reduction during attentional reconfiguration reflects at least two partially dissociable processes: θ-band connectivity changes consistent with network-level reconfiguration associated with attentional reconfiguration in general, and local cortical dynamics selectively related to spatial information processing.

Article.Title: Association between structural disconnection and early cognitive impairment after acute ischemic stroke: A network-based statistical study
Article.Authors: Fang Y.; Liang W.; Li T.; Du Q.; Liu Y.; Chen S.; Li G.; Pan C.; Zhu Z.
Article.Abstract: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) affects up to 75% of patients acutely and strongly predicts dementia, yet the acute-phase structural network signature remains unclear. We included 589 first-ever acute ischemic stroke patients (≤ 7 days) and classified them into PSCI and non-PSCI groups using the acute-phase MoCA. Individualized structural disconnection matrices (135 nodes) were constructed from DWI lesion masks and the HCP-842 normative tractography atlas (derived from 842 healthy adults), representing indirect disconnectome estimates rather than patient-specific DTI tractography. Network-Based Statistic (NBS) identified group-different subnetworks, followed by binary graph-theoretical analysis. In exploratory full-sample analysis, a left-lateralized subnetwork of 25 nodes and 42 edges (PFWE < 0.001) showed prefrontal-striatal radiating disconnection converging on the left caudate nucleus, and greater subnetwork disconnection strength correlated with worse acute MoCA (r = -0.27, P < 0.001). To address circularity, repeated internal discovery-validation analyses using five random 70/30 splits showed that the direction of the SubNet_Total_SDC-MoCA association was reproduced in held-out test sets, where SubNet_Total_SDC was negatively associated with MoCA (partial r = -0.265 to -0.150, test-set ΔR² = 0.014-0.056). The left caudate nucleus was reproducibly identified as the anatomical convergence point across all training samples. These findings suggest that acute PSCI is associated with a cortico-subcortical radial disconnection pattern converging on the left caudate nucleus under the present parcellation.

Article.Title: Niosome-encapsulated hesperidin accelerates antioxidant defense and TRPM2 protein expression to restore cognitive function in a rat model of depression
Article.Authors: Otarkhani M.; Hatami H.; panahi Y.; Yavari S.; Hatami S.; Azami M.; Eslami A.
Article.Abstract: Aims: Hesperidin is a potent antioxidant; however, its therapeutic efficacy is hindered by limited bioavailability. Furthermore, the role of TRPM2 in oxidative stress-induced depression remains to be elucidated. This study investigated the therapeutic potential of niosomal hesperidin in a reserpine-induced depression rat model, focusing on learning and memory performance, oxidative stress markers, and TRPM2 protein expression. Methods and materials: 36 rats were randomly divided into six groups: Control, depression (Reserpine), free hesperidin, Niosomal hesperidin, treatment with hesperidin, and treatment with niosomal hesperidin. Reserpine 0.5 mg/kg was administered intraperitoneally for 14 days. Then, rats received hesperidin (20 mg/kg, 14 days) and niosomal hesperidin (20 mg/kg, 7 days). The novel object recognition and shuttle box tests were performed. Finally, glutathione peroxidase levels, serum superoxide dismutase, and western blotting for TRPM2 protein expression were measured. Results: SOD activity and GPX levels increased in the reserpine-induced rats treated with hesperidin and niosome hesperidin (P < 0.05). TRPM2 protein expression decreased in niosome-hesperidin-treated groups compared to the depression group (P < 0.0001). The discrimination index increased in the reserpine-induced rats treated with niosome hesperidin compared to the depression group (P < 0.001). The total time spent in the white box increased in the shuttle box in the reserpine-induced rats treated with niosome hesperidin compared to the control group (P < 0.05). Conclusion: Niosomal encapsulation accelerates cognitive recovery and modulates antioxidant capacity and TRPM2 protein expression. Thus, niosomal hesperidin represents a promising nanocarrier strategy for managing depression-related cognitive dysfunction.

Article.Title: Impact testing system for an anthropomorphic craniocerebral model with enhanced mechanical fidelity
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Zhang Y.; Li R.; He K.; Chen Z.; Ren H.; Lei Z.; Zhou L.; Liu Z.; Liu Y.; Yang B.; Holzapfel G.; Jiang Z.; Sun T.; Tang L.
Article.Abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide, yet direct observation of the internal mechanical response of the human head under impact is severely constrained by the lack of high-fidelity craniocerebral models and suitable testing platforms. To bridge this gap, we developed an impact testing system featuring an anthropomorphic craniocerebral model with enhanced mechanical fidelity relative to earlier simplified head models. This system integrates a transparent anthropomorphic skull, a mechanically biomimetic brain phantom with highly realistic mechanical properties, artificial cerebrospinal fluid, and dedicated impact loading and measurement modules. It accommodates impacts from multiple directions and at varying velocities. Combined with a custom-built digital stereo-image correlation technique, the system enables millisecond-resolution reconstruction of surface displacement and strain fields, successfully capturing critical phenomena such as relative rotation and regional strain concentration within the brain phantom. Comparisons with simulations from human brain finite element head models (FEHM) confirm that the system provides a reliable experimental benchmark for evaluating and validating different finite element models. Looking ahead, further enhancements-such as integrating co-cultures of human neural cells into the brain phantom-could establish this platform as a transformative tool for fundamental research in brain medicine and neuroscience, offering unprecedented capability to investigate mechano-neuroelectrophysiological coupling in the human brain under impact conditions.

Article.Title: Glycosylation in neurological disorders: Mechanisms, crosstalk, and therapeutic implications
Article.Authors: Wu W.; Wang W.; Xu L.; Yao Y.; Zhao X.; Zhong J.; Hu J.; Wang L.; Zhu Y.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: Neurological disorders pose a major global health challenge for complicated pathogenesis and a lack of effective curative treatments. As a post-translational modification, glycosylation has emerged as a multifunctional regulator in the nervous system, influencing key processes including receptor activation, cell adhesion, and immune surveillance. Its dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared mechanism across various neurological disorders. This review synthesizes the molecular mechanisms of glycosylation within a novel framework of four neurological disorder categories: neurodevelopmental disorders, proteostasis disorders, neuroimmunological disorders, and acute nerve injuries. Furthermore, we advance the concept of glycosylation as an integrator of mechanistic crosstalk and demonstrate its pivotal role in bridging and amplifying intertwined pathological cascades. This integrative perspective aims to reframe the understanding of disease pathogenesis and inspire innovative diagnostic paradigms and therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Personalized brain-based anesthetic-state detection with portable fNIRS and AI
Article.Authors: Minoccheri C.; Joo P.; Hu X.; Affendi H.; Elayyan F.; Harville A.; McDonald N.; Botero T.; DaSilva A.
Article.Abstract: Portable functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) may support brain-based monitoring around local anesthesia, but between-patient variability and patient-overlapping validation can limit generalization. We examined affected-tooth classification before versus after anesthesia, exploratory Pre-session affected-versus-healthy classification using both resting-state and held-out healthy-tooth reference schemes, and validation inflation. We analyzed fNIRS data from 25 patients during percussion before ("Pre") and after ("Post") anesthesia. The primary cohort comprised 13 patients with complete pain abolition; 156 affected-tooth epochs were classified using Pre-session healthy-tooth responses as patient-specific references. Leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation tested each patient using models trained on the others. A random forest using a fixed, data-informed three-feature oxyhemoglobin (HbO) panel achieved mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) = 0.752 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.624-0.865; one-sided exact conditional p = 0.0057). Fold-nested selection yielded AUC = 0.740. Referencing improved estimates for two of four classifiers. In Pre-session analyses, resting-state and split-half referencing increased affected-versus-healthy AUC from matched raw values of 0.513 and 0.524-0.731 (12 patients) and 0.782 (21 patients); both gains survived eight-comparison adjustment. Because tooth blocks followed a fixed order, these pain-related estimates may include block-position effects. Across 32 feature-based configurations, pooled-epoch cross-validation exceeded LOSO by a mean of 0.159 AUC (95% CI 0.078-0.252); inflation was also positive in all three aligned waveform models. These results support proof-of-concept held-out-patient classification of pain-related affected-tooth responses before versus after anesthesia, exploratory referenced affected-versus-healthy classification before anesthesia, and patient-disjoint validation for estimating performance in new patients.

Article.Title: Mobile EEG Reveals Age-Dependent Cognitive-Motor Interference with Increasing Motor Task Complexity- a cross-sectional study
Article.Authors: Wollesen B.; Winter L.; Gramann K.; Protzak J.
Article.Abstract: This study examined age-related differences in behavior and brain dynamics underlying cognitive-motor interference (CMI) during motor dual-tasks (DT) with increasing motor task complexity. Behavioral performance and electrocortical activity were assessed in 19 younger adults (11 males, 8 females; 25.5 ± 2.3 years) and 11 older adults (6 males, 5 females; 72.6 ± 4.6 years) using mobile electroencephalography (EEG). Participants performed an oddball choice-reaction task under three conditions: sitting, standing, and treadmill walking. Event-related potential (ERPs; P1, N1, P3) amplitudes and latencies, response times, postural sway, and gait parameters were recorded to evaluate CMI. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVAs with within-subject factors of motor condition and stimulus type and age group as a between-subject factor. Older adults exhibited reduced step length compared to younger adults, but no DT-related changes in gait or postural sway were observed. Response times were generally slower in older adults and increased from sitting to standing and walking whereas younger adults showed slowing only from sitting to standing. Early sensory ERP components (P1, N1) demonstrated increased amplitudes with higher motor demands. The P3 component was reduced in amplitude in both groups during walking, with delayed latencies in older adults. For both groups, P3 latencies were associated with prolonged response times. Our findings suggest that this slowing during walking reflects altered cognitive resource allocation, characterized by delayed central information processing and enhanced early visual processing, rather than impaired peripheral motor coordination.

Article.Title: Altered white matter functional activity and connectivity in pretreatment breast cancer: exploratory associations with affective symptoms
Article.Authors: Wu S.; Zhang Z.; Chen N.; Cheng S.; Xu W.; Xu Z.; Jia X.; Wei F.; Cheng Y.; Mao G.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Resting-state fMRI studies in breast cancer have predominantly focused on gray matter, with limited attention to white matter functional organization. This study investigated white matter functional activity and connectivity before treatment and their associations with anxiety and depressive symptoms. Methods: Female patients with breast cancer (BC) were recruited from Zhejiang Provincial Tongde Hospital from November 2023 to December 2025. Amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF) and fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (fALFF) were used to compare local white matter functional activity between the BC and healthy control (HC) groups. Seed-based functional connectivity (FC) analysis was then performed to investigate whole-brain white matter FC alterations. Correlations between clinical scale scores and rs-fMRI indices were analyzed. Results: Compared with HCs, patients with BC showed altered ALFF/fALFF in the anterior and posterior corona radiata, internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, body of the corpus callosum, pontine crossing tract, left superior cerebellar peduncle, and left superior longitudinal fasciculus. Seed-based analysis revealed decreased FC within the bilateral anterior corona radiata and between the body of the corpus callosum and right anterior corona radiata, and increased FC between the left superior cerebellar peduncle and left posterior thalamic radiation. Higher ALFF in the body of the corpus callosum and reduced FC between this region and the right anterior corona radiata were associated with higher Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores at an uncorrected threshold. Neither association survived FDR correction. Conclusion: Patients with BC showed altered white matter functional activity and connectivity before cancer-related treatment, suggesting that pretreatment brain functional alterations may also involve white matter functional organization. The relationship between these white matter changes and anxiety or depressive symptoms remains exploratory.

Article.Title: Fetal Brain Volumes in Complete Vascular Ring: A Cross-Sectional MRI Study
Article.Authors: Ren J.; Chen C.; Zhu M.; Zhang X.; Li Y.; Dong S.
Article.Abstract: Background: The association between complete vascular ring (CVR) and prenatal brain development remains poorly characterized. Objective: To compare global and regional fetal brain volumes between fetuses with CVR and controls, accounting for gestational age (GA), fetal sex, and estimated fetal weight. Methods: In this retrospective single-center study, 70 prenatally diagnosed CVR fetuses and 200 GA-matched controls with normal brain anatomy (22-37 weeks) underwent 1.5-T fetal MRI. Motion-corrected three-dimensional brain reconstructions were generated by slice-to-volume registration, and 19 regions were automatically segmented using a deep-learning pipeline. Linear regression included continuous GA, group, their interaction, fetal sex, and estimated fetal weight. Regional-to-intracranial volume ratios and sensitivity analyses incorporating maternal body mass index were evaluated. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Results: At the 28-week reference age, adjusted supratentorial brain, cortical gray matter, white matter, thalamic, lentiform nucleus, brainstem, and lateral ventricular volumes were smaller in the CVR group (all false-discovery-rate-adjusted P<0.05). Intracranial volume did not differ significantly. Thalamic, lentiform nucleus, brainstem, and lateral ventricular proportions were also smaller. No group-by-GA interaction survived correction in the primary model. Conclusions: CVR was associated with differences in selected fetal brain volumes, including regional differences relative to intracranial volume. Larger longitudinal studies with postnatal follow-up are needed.

Article.Title: Lung-brain-axis-mediated mechanisms of sepsis-associated encephalopathy secondary to lower respiratory tract infection: a narrative review
Article.Authors: Cheng X.; hen Qi G.; Zhao S.
Article.Abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) represent one of the most frequent causes of sepsis. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE), a serious complication of sepsis, markedly increases patient mortality and the risk of long-term cognitive impairment. The emerging concept of the lung-brain axis offers a novel framework for understanding the pathogenesis of SAE. Unlike general reviews covering all-cause sepsis-associated encephalopathy, this review specifically focuses on SAE secondary to LRTI, and discriminates its unique epidemiological, clinical and mechanistic signatures from SAE triggered by abdominal, urinary or bloodstream infection. This review systematically summarizes the epidemiological characteristics of SAE induced by LRTIs, the anatomical and immunological basis of lung-brain interactions, and key pathological mechanisms including neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, neurotransmitter imbalance, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Additionally, it highlights advances in biomarker research and clinical management strategies. By integrating evidence from molecular‑biology and neuroimaging studies, this article describes how pulmonary infections drive brain dysfunction via neural, immune, and endocrine pathways. These findings provide a theoretical foundation to support early diagnosis and targeted therapeutic interventions.

Article.Title: Apelin-13 exerts neuroprotection through activation of APJ/mTORC2 axis in microglia after Intracerebral Hemorrhage in mice
Article.Authors: Fan H.; Sun H.; Hu Z.; Lin W.; Chen Y.; Yao Y.; Zhang A.; Ren R.; Wu Q.
Article.Abstract: Background: Apelin-13, a bioactive peptide that acts via the APJ receptor, exhibits potent anti-oxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory properties. However, its role in intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains poorly understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of Apelin-13 and the underlying mechanisms in a mouse model of ICH. Methods: A mouse model of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) was established and randomly allocated to receive either recombinant Apelin-13 (rApelin-13) or phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). To investigate the role of the APJ/mammalian target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) axis in Apelin-13-mediated neuroprotection, the APJ antagonist ML221 and the mTORC2 inhibitor JR-AB2-011 were administered. To further elucidate the underlying mechanism, microglia-specific knockdown of Rictor was achieved via intracerebroventricular injection of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) carrying CD68-promoter-driven shRictor. Assessments included brain water content, short-term neurobehavioral tests, Western blot analysis, quantitative RT-PCR, and histological staining. Results: Following ICH induction, the expression of Apelin-13 was upregulated and primarily secreted from neurons. Exogenous administration of rApelin-13 significantly attenuated neuronal apoptosis and improved short-term neurological function in mice after ICH in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, rApelin-13 enhanced M2-like polarization of microglia in the post-ICH brain. Notably, the neuroprotective effects of rApelin-13 were abolished by inhibition of mTORC2.

Article.Title: Epidural Spinal Cord Stimulation Promotes the Expansion of Endogenous Neural Stem Cells and Neuroprotection via the PI3K/AKT/ mTOR Pathway after Spinal Cord Injury in Rats
Article.Authors: Li G.; Shen F.; Li J.; Fan Z.; He S.
Article.Abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) often leads to severe motor and sensory dysfunction, yet no effective treatment currently exists. Epidural spinal cord stimulation (ESCS) is a treatment for chronic neuropathic pain in the trunk and extremities, and exerts a significant effect on the recovery of motor function, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. The present study aimed to investigate the effects of ESCS on the endogenous neural stem cells (eNSCs) proliferation and neuroprotection as well as the underlying mechanisms following SCI in rats. In the present study, results showed that ESCS improved hindlimb motor function and markedly increased the numbers of surviving ventral horn neurons of the spinal cord at 7 and 28 days after SCI. ESCS significantly reduced the apoptosis of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord on day 28 post-SCI. Moreover, ESCS remarkably increased the expressions of NSCs markers nestin and sox2, as well as the proportion of nestin/sox2/DAPI-double positive cells (eNSCs) at 7 days after SCI. Notably, ESCS induced only a negligible number of Sox2/NeuN/DAPI double-positive cells at 28 days after SCI. LY294002, a selective inhibitor of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) markedly decreased the ratios of eNSCs and surviving ventral horn neurons after ESCS treatment. Finally, ESCS increased the protein levels of phosphorylated-protein kinase B (p-Akt) and phosphorylated-mammalian target of rapamycin (p-mTOR) at 7 days after SCI, and LY294002 significantly attenuated the effects of ESCS on p-Akt and p-mTOR. This report suggests that ESCS treatment after SCI enhances the expansion of eNSCs and neuroprotection via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway.

Article.Title: Interpretable Machine Learning Model Based on Radiomic Features of Hippocampal Subfields for Classifying Zoster-associated Pain
Article.Authors: Wen X.; Peng R.; Wang M.; Yu M.; Liu S.; Zhang D.; Ren C.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), the most common complication of herpes zoster (HZ), is difficult to prevent due to limited understanding of the mechanisms underlying the transition from acute to chronic pain and the lack of objective neuroimaging biomarkers for individualized risk stratification. In this study, we aimed to develop interpretable machine learning models based on hippocampal subfield radiomics to classify zoster-associated pain (ZAP) patients and identify neuroimaging biomarkers reflecting microstructural alterations in hippocampus associated with ZAP. High-resolution 3D T1-weighted MR images were obtained from 28 PHN patients, 25 HZ patients, and 21 healthy controls (HCs). We extracted radiomic features of ten hippocampal subfields and used five machine learning classification algorithms to identify the most contributive subfield and robust model for classifying ZAP patients. Furthermore, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was used to interpret the optimal model. In distinguishing ZAP patients from HCs, the SVM_Linear model based on the left subiculum radiomics achieved the highest performance with an AUC of 0.740, whereas the Logistic_L1 model based on the right CA4-DG and left SR-SL-SM radiomics showed the best performance with an AUC of 0.799 in distinguishing PHN patients from HZ patients. SHAP analysis revealed that SmallAreaEmphasis from the right CA4-DG subfield was the dominant feature for identifying PHN patients, followed by ClusterShade from the left SR-SL-SM subfield. Furthermore, both features showed strong associations with disease duration. These results suggest that hippocampal subfield radiomics can effectively stratify ZAP phases. Specifically, right CA4-DG radiomic features may serve as effective neuroimaging biomarkers associated with disease chronicity and have the potential for early risk stratification and intervention of ZAP.

Article.Title: EFFICACY OF EUGENOL AGAINST N, N′-DIMETHYL-4,4′-BIPYRIDINIUM DICHLORIDE (PARAQUAT)-INDUCED NA⁺/K⁺/CA²⁺ DYSREGULATION AND BEHAVIORAL DEFICITS IN RAT MODELS
Article.Authors: Obinna U.; Augustine I.; Victoria C.; Emeka I.; Ejiofor A.; Tamunoibelema C.; Samuel O.
Article.Abstract: Background: Ion level disruption causes mitochondrial aberration and alters cytochrome c activity. Purpose: To evaluate the efficacy of eugenol in Na+/K+/Ca2+ Cytochrome C dysregulation and behavioral deficits in Wistar rats. Methods: Forty male Wistar rats were acclimatised for two weeks and assigned to five groups of 8 rats. Group A received feed and normal saline. Groups B, C, D, and E received 10mg/kg paraquat (PQ), and then C, D, and E received eugenol at graded doses of 200, 400, and 600mg/kg. PQ was administered for 28 days at 1-day intervals, before the rats were treated with eugenol for 14 days via the oral route. Social interaction and depression-like behaviours were studied using a sociability chamber and a tail suspension box. Results: In Group B, interstitial Na+/K+ increased, while Ca2+ significantly decreased. In the treated groups, Na+/K+ and Ca2+ levels decreased and increased significantly, respectively. Cytochrome C, Caspase cleavage, and Full-length cytokeratin-18 were significantly increased in the untreated Group B and were reduced by eugenol (p<0.05). In the PQ-untreated Group, social interaction and immobility were impaired, but eugenol attenuated these behavioral deficits. Dopamine levels and gamma-glutamyl transferase activities were lowered and increased in Group B, respectively, while eugenol increased and reduced them (p<0.05). Microscopically, paraquat caused a significant loss of dopaminergic neurons, formation of Lewy bodies, and Pyknosis in the substantia nigra. Conclusions: Overall, eugenol shows valuable therapeutic potential against pesticide-induced neurotoxicity and associated ion dysregulation.

Article.Title: Temporally differentiated modulation of emotional face processing by attentional resource availability: An ERP study
Article.Authors: Yang L.; Liang J.; Li Y.; Li S.; Li Y.; Fang X.; Chen J.; Luo W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The interplay between top-down attentional control and bottom-up emotional capture remains debated, particularly in the late positive potential (LPP) time window. In the present study, we used mass-univariate analysis to examine whether task difficulty itself modulates late-stage emotional processing in an implicit task. In a dual-target rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) paradigm, perceptual load was manipulated at T1, and at T2, fearful, happy, neutral, or face-absent stimuli were presented in a face-detection task. Emotional differentiation emerged during 148–372 ms and was not influenced by perceptual load, suggesting that emotional features were extracted relatively automatically. During the early LPP (400–600 ms), emotional differentiation was detected under low but not high load, suggesting that inconsistencies in emotion-related LPP effects reported in previous implicit-task studies may stem from differences in task difficulty. During the late LPP (600–800 ms), however, fearful expressions remained distinguishable from neutral expressions even under high load, indicating that resource limitations did not eliminate late emotional differentiation. Together, these findings provide compelling evidence that the availability of attentional resources differentially shapes the processing of emotional information in implicit tasks.

Article.Title: The gentle grip of beauty: Neural bases of motor inhibition during aesthetic appreciation
Article.Authors: Barbieri P.; Frascaroli J.; Varesio G.; Piovesan F.; Bechis L.; Sarasso P.; Ronga I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A century-old tradition characterizes aesthetic experiences as intense contemplative moments in which we suspend practical concerns and devote our full attention to the object at hand. In line with this tradition, recent theories suggest that aesthetic experiences involve heightened sensory processing accompanied by a suppression of motor activity. Yet, while the link between aesthetic appreciation and perceptual enhancement has received considerable attention, the role of motor inhibition remains largely unexplored. The present study addressed this gap by investigating whether the aesthetic appreciation of images can modulate behavioral and electrophysiological markers of motor inhibition. In Experiment 1, significantly slower reaction times following the observation of preferred images were found. In Experiment 2, EEG responses associated with motor preparation and execution were significantly reduced in trials involving preferred compared with non-preferred images. Time-frequency analysis revealed significantly decreased alpha power (associated with attentional engagement toward visual perception) and increased beta power (associated with inhibited motor preparation) for preferred than non-preferred images. Overall, our results provide new evidence for the existence of a relationship between aesthetic appreciation and motor inhibition and position aesthetic experience as a valuable case study for exploring the adaptive coordination of sensory and motor systems in response to environmental demands.

Article.Title: Deep learning mitigates batch effects in Raman spectroscopy
Article.Authors: Sjöberg J.; Lita A.; Larion M.; Petre I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Raman spectroscopy is widely used for its ability to provide rich molecular-level information from biological samples. However, the high sensitivity of Raman spectra can also unintentionally encode extraneous information, such as patient identity, instrument-specific signatures, environmental conditions, and sample handling protocols. This hidden structure, referred to as the batch effect, poses increasing challenges in machine learning applications, where it can lead to model overfitting, poor generalization, and even privacy risks when datasets are shared. In this work, we investigate the presence and impact of the batch effect in a Raman spectroscopy dataset derived from glioma tumor samples. We show that deep learning can accurately predict patient identity from individual spectra, revealing strong bias patterns in the data. To mitigate this issue, we explore several approaches and introduce an algorithmic framework based on adversarial deep learning. Our method effectively reduces the influence of confounding sample-specific signals while preserving information relevant to tumor classification. These findings highlight the need for careful bias control in Raman-based AI pipelines and provide tools to support more robust applications in biomedical spectroscopy.

Article.Title: Morphological and permeability changes of the intestine in patients nourished exclusively with parenteral nutrition: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Pérez-Cordón L.; Molina-Montes E.; Serra-Prat M.; Yébenes J.; Campins L.; Marin S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract While evidence from animal models suggests that total parenteral nutrition (TPN) induces alterations in the intestinal mucosa, effects on humans are not clearly established. To analyse alterations in morphology and permeability associated with TPN in human intestinal mucosa, we conducted a systematic review following PRISMA recommendations. MEDLINE and Embase databases were searched from inception to May 2025 for literature on adults receiving TPN for any condition irrespective of the nutritional comparator. Outcome measures were intestinal morphological and permeability assessments. Meta-analyses conducted to synthesise the evidence were based on the random effects model because of heterogeneity in design characteristics. Of 1071 studies identified, 20 were included (morphology:10, and permeability: 13). Synthesis showed no significant short-term changes in villus height, crypt depth, or mucosal thickness over time after TPN. Villus height (mean difference: -87.51 µm [95%CI: -106.56, -68.46]) and crypt depth (mean difference: -44.48 µm [95%CI: -77.62, -11.34]) were significantly lower in patients on TPN compared to healthy volunteers or patients with dyspepsia. The lactulose/mannitol (L/M) ratios were significantly increased during TPN compared to baseline values (mean difference: 0.04 [95%CI: 0.02, 0.07]), and were also significantly higher for TPN compared to the enteral diet (mean difference: 0.03 [95%CI: 0.02, 0.05]). The overall strength of the evidence was low to moderate. Clinical status may have influenced the inconsistencies found in morphological outcomes. A possible association between altered permeability and TPN was observed; however, surgery and inflammation may have also contributed. The clinical significance of these findings and the effects of TPN duration and composition remain unclear. Prospero registration number CRD42022265814.

Article.Title: A multi-source earth observation and artificial intelligence framework for unsupervised water-use anomaly screening in Mediterranean agriculture
Article.Authors: Kakoulli E.; Antoniades A.; Neophytides S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Reliable screening of agricultural water-use anomalies over large areas remains challenging because verified event labels and field observations are rarely available. We present AI4WaterGuard, a multi-source Earth Observation and artificial intelligence framework for unsupervised water-use anomaly screening across Cyprus. Using 617,862 records from 1,974 centroids across six hydrological years, six primary detector families were assessed under nested temporal cross-validation with training-consistent scaling, validity-aware scoring, and harmonised temporal support. Among the five centroid-sequence detectors, the convolutional neural network autoencoder showed the strongest response to the strong-reference controlled synthetic proxy, achieving Average Precision of $$0.893\pm 0.130$$ and Proxy F1 of $$0.880\pm 0.100$$ . The spatially explicit convolutional long short-term memory variational autoencoder was evaluated at finer land-pixel-sequence granularity and interpreted descriptively. Across five perturbation patterns and three severities, the convolutional neural network autoencoder achieved an equal-scenario mean Average Precision of 0.342, declining to 0.088 for weak perturbations. These synthetic metrics quantify controlled-proxy sensitivity, not field-validated detection performance. Operational post-processing on 1,157 WorldCover-eligible centroids combined threshold sensitivity, 1,000 exact-count randomisations, a primary Top-50 inspection-prioritisation queue with a nested Top-20 high-priority subset, and common-cadence spatiotemporal events. The resulting screening priorities require independent administrative and field evidence to establish physical cause or legal status.

Article.Title: Contributing factors for surgically treated Hallux Valgus: a nationwide population-based cohort study in Taiwan
Article.Authors: Kuo T.; Chen Y.; Chung C.; Cho D.; Wang S.; Kuo C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Hallux valgus (HV) is a prevalent deformity of the first metatarsophalangeal joint that can progress from a cosmetic concern to a painful, function–limiting condition requiring surgical correction. However, population-based data focusing on severe HV in Taiwan remains limited. Therefore, this study aims to examine national trends and systemic disease associations among patients undergoing HV surgery. Data from the National Health Insurance Research Database of Taiwan (2008–2021) were analyzed. Severe HV was defined by receipt of corrective surgery (procedure codes 64132 and 64133). Exposures were claims-defined comorbidities (≥ 10 outpatient visits or ≥ 1 hospitalization), and individuals with prior HV surgery were excluded. A non-exposed cohort was assigned random index dates. Propensity-score matching (1:1) was applied, and hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models. Of 25,767,574 individuals in the NHIRD, 2,392,429 with index dates outside 2008–2020, 9,065 with prior HV surgery, and 8 men in the breast cancer analysis were excluded, leaving 23,366,072 eligible individuals (3,377,791 with and 19,988,281 without the study comorbidities). After 1:1 propensity-score matching, the matched cohort comprised 6,755,582 individuals (3,377,791 per group) with excellent post-matching covariate balance. The annual prevalence of severe HV increased steadily over the study period and was consistently higher among women and older adults. Several comorbidities were associated with significantly higher risk of HV surgery, most notably anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury (adjusted HR 7.37, 95% CI 2.62–20.75), rheumatoid arthritis (RA; adjusted HR 5.31, 95% CI 3.52–8.00), Sjögren’s syndrome (adjusted HR 4.25, 95% CI 1.94–9.30), and osteoporosis (adjusted HR 3.52, 95% CI 2.90–4.27). Increased risks were also identified for obesity (adjusted HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.42–4.44), gout (adjusted HR 2.58, 95% CI 1.93–3.45), thyroid disease (adjusted HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.46–1.99), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD; adjusted HR 2.44, 95% CI 1.83–3.25), and breast cancer (adjusted HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.10–1.93). Severe HV requiring surgery was associated with multiple systemic comorbidities, suggesting that factors beyond a localized forefoot deformity may be involved. A surgery-based case definition identifies clinically meaningful disease but may be influenced by healthcare access and treatment preferences. These findings may inform risk-stratified counseling; however, causal relationships and the benefit of early preventive strategies require confirmation in prospective studies.

Article.Title: Enhancing ferric-reducing antioxidant activity through terpene mixture optimization
Article.Authors: Qasem A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The present study investigated the antioxidant potential of three terpenes p -cymene, thymol, and β-ionone—through their ferric reducing power (FRAP). Individually, p -cymene demonstrated the strongest activity with an EC 50 of 123.03 ± 2.05 µg/mL, followed by thymol (EC 50 = 153.16 ± 2.84 µg/mL), whereas β-ionone exhibited the lowest ferric reducing capacity (EC 50 = 931.46 ± 5.37 µg/mL), revealing significant variation in their antioxidant efficacy. To assess combinatorial effects, twelve randomized mixture trials were performed, each representing the mean of three independent repetitions, yielding FRAP EC 50 values ranging from 79.76 to 931.46 µg/mL. Statistical analysis identified significant contributions from linear terms (β 1 , β 2 , β 3 ), binary interactions (β 12 , β 13 ), and the ternary interaction term (β 123 ), indicating that both individual and combined effects shaped the overall antioxidant response. Analysis of 2D and 3D mixture plots suggested that an EC 50 around 79.70 µg/mL could be obtained by combining all three terpenes. Furthermore, desirability analysis predicted an optimal FRAP EC 50 of 58.23 µg/mL, achieved with a mixture comprising 17% β-ionone, 42% p -cymene, and 41% thymol, with a global desirability of 99.9%. These findings demonstrate that strategic blending of structurally related terpenes can substantially enhance ferric reducing capacity, providing a robust framework for the development of potent natural antioxidant formulations.

Article.Title: Blockchain-assisted revocable capability credential authentication for cross-domain UAVs
Article.Authors: Xu S.; Guan Y.; Li S.; Li J.; Zhao Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cross-domain UAV operations require secure and privacy-preserving authentication across multiple administrative domains. However, existing schemes still suffer from centralized authorization, exposure of mission attributes, insufficient revocation consistency, and limited auditability. To address these issues, this paper proposes a blockchain-assisted revocable capability credential authentication protocol for cross-domain UAV edge networks. The main innovation is to shift cross-domain UAV authentication from identity- or location-centric verification to revocation-aware lifecycle verification of mission capabilities. In the proposed framework, a Domain Authority committee jointly issues blinded capability credentials through distributed key generation and threshold BLS signatures. UAVs then prove mission-policy compliance using Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs without revealing sensitive capability attributes. Meanwhile, the blockchain maintains credential active states, revocation versions, and audit-root evidence for cross-domain consistency and accountability. A ticket-based AuthResume mechanism is further designed to reduce repeated authentication overhead while preventing outdated tickets from bypassing revocation. Formal security analysis, BAN logic, and Scyther verification show that the protocol supports credential unforgeability, revocation enforcement, auditability, mutual authentication, freshness, and session synchronization. Solidity smart contracts were deployed on the Sepolia testnet, and experimental results demonstrate acceptable FullAuth overhead and lightweight repeated access through AuthResume.
