Article.Title: Motor imagery vividness does not predict the ability to judge object weight from observed hand actions
Article.Authors: Székely O.; Buckingham G.; Davies J.; Chambers C.; Preatoni E.; Bultitude J.
Article.Abstract: Observing others' actions and imagining oneself performing the same actions (motor imagery) have been linked in the literature in several ways. They have been shown to have overlapping neural representations, both seem to relate to one's ability to move, and both have been shown to positively affect movement rehabilitation. Whether these overlaps reflect a direct functional relationship between motor imagery and the ability to derive relevant information from observed kinematics (action understanding) has not yet been investigated. A previous study found that individuals with low self-reported imagery vividness exhibit weaker motor system engagement during action observation than those with typical imagery vividness. The present study provides the first behavioural test of the relationships between motor and general visual imagery vividness and a quantifiable behavioural measure of action understanding-specifically, the ability to judge the weight of objects based on observing someone else lift them. To test the research question across the full imagery spectrum, our recruitment strategy included a high proportion of individuals with very low imagery vividness (often referred to as 'aphantasia'). An online sample (N = 392) completed a weight judgement task alongside a matched speed judgement control task. Neither motor imagery vividness (Vividness of Movement Imagery Questionnaire-2) nor general visual imagery vividness (Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire) predicted action understanding, with a Bayesian analysis suggesting moderate evidence against any relationship. Overall, our findings suggest that self-reported motor and general visual imagery vividness are functionally independent from action understanding of manual interactions.

Article.Title: Non-conscious knowledge of complex regularities supports instrumental conditioning: A registered report
Article.Authors: Jurchiş R.; Preda A.; Costea A.; Skora L.
Article.Abstract: Instrumental conditioning (IC) consists in actively learning to approach rewarding stimuli and to avoid punishing stimuli. This central process for adaptation requires a relatively high computational capacity because it entails the integration of knowledge regarding stimuli, behaviours, and outcomes. Recent studies using subliminal exposure show that IC occurs only for consciously perceived stimuli, suggesting that IC may require awareness. In the present study, we investigated whether IC could occur when implicit processing is stimulated not by subliminal exposure but by employing predictive regularities that are complex and difficult to detect consciously. In a novel IC task based on the artificial grammar learning task, participants gave approach (Go) or avoidance responses (No-Go) to strings from two grammars. Unbeknown to them, one of the grammars was associated with rewards while the other was associated with punishments. Trial-by-trial measures assessed participants' awareness of the grammar structures and of their judgments regarding the predictive value of the strings. In both an IC phase and a delayed responding phase, we found that participants (NIC phase = 187; Ndelay = 160) responded adaptively when they were aware of the regularities and, also, when they were not. Importantly, we found reliable evidence that non-conscious regularities produced adaptive responding only when they produced conscious judgments regarding the predictive values of the stimuli. When judgments of predictive values were not conscious, data were insensitive or more consistent with chance performance. This suggests that IC may be produced by a combination of unconscious learning and conscious integration.

Article.Title: Cortical tracking reveals disrupted syntactic processing dynamics in aphasia
Article.Authors: Rafferty M.; Saltuklaroglu T.; Paek E.; Reilly K.; Bowers A.; Stone T.; Jenson D.; Albornoz A.; Casenhiser D.
Article.Abstract: Sentence comprehension requires the rapid construction of hierarchical structure and the integration of non-adjacent dependencies under working-memory constraints. Many people with aphasia (PWA) show difficulty comprehending syntactically complex sentences, yet the neural mechanisms underlying these deficits remain unclear. We examined cortical tracking of two distinct syntactic computations-hierarchical constituent closure (node count) and dependency integration cost-using EEG during a sentence-picture matching task. PWA and neurologically healthy controls listened to subject- and object-relative clause sentences varying in semantic reversibility. Neural alignment with each syntactic predictor was quantified using a conditional mutual information approach controlling for speech acoustics. Node count tracking was stronger for reversible sentences across groups, consistent with increased structural parsing under thematic ambiguity, and node count peaks were wider for PWA than controls specifically for reversible sentences, suggesting more prolonged constituent closure processing. Integration cost tracking was greater for object-relative clauses and exhibited delays under higher retrieval demands. PWA showed significantly earlier integration cost peaks overall, and earlier integration cost latencies predicted poorer comprehension accuracy for reversible object-relative clauses-the condition placing the greatest demands on dependency formation without semantic support. This relationship was consistent at the trial level, with all PWA showing shorter latencies for incorrect than correct responses. Integration cost latency predicted online comprehension accuracy but not performance on a standardized clinical assessment, suggesting that the timing of neural alignment with integration cost captures online dependency-resolution demands not fully reflected in global clinical measures. These preliminary findings highlight the potential of neural tracking measures to reveal structure-specific processing differences in aphasia.

Article.Title: From pre-stimulus preparation to the “Aha” burst: Unraveling the dynamics of perceptual insight with multi-method EEG
Article.Authors: Wang T.; Xian M.; Si Y.; Zhang Z.
Article.Abstract: How does the brain transform a confusing perceptual input into a sudden "Aha" experience? To investigate the neurocognitive dynamics of perceptual insight, we employed an embedded Chinese character task in which twenty-six eligible participants judged whether a source character contained a previously presented target. Targets were embedded either in a hidden/intersecting manner or in an unhidden/non-intersecting manner, allowing us to compare successful recognition under different restructuring demands. Matched invalid counterparts were also included as control conditions. Behaviorally, the hidden condition was associated with greater solution difficulty, followed by stronger "Aha" experiences-characterized by heightened surprise and suddenness-upon successful recognition. Electrophysiologically, relative to the unhidden condition, the hidden condition was associated with a more negative frontal N2 and a less positive parietal late positive component (LPC), consistent with differences in conflict-related and restructuring-related processing. Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) further showed that neural activity reliably distinguished valid-hidden from valid-unhidden trials during a post-stimulus interval (430-480 msec). In addition, lower pre-source alpha power for hidden relative to unhidden trials predicted stronger hidden-relative-to-unhidden increases in Jolt and overall Aha scores. Together, our findings suggest that successful recognition of hidden targets is not merely more difficult perception, but is associated with a distinct phenomenological and neural profile. More broadly, perceptual insight appears to unfold dynamically, from pre-source neural-state differences to later stimulus-driven processing stages during successful recognition.

Article.Title: Anterior temporal lobe mediates associative and taxonomic neighborhood effects in lexical processing
Article.Authors: Xiao C.; Arheix-Parras S.; Riccardi N.; Johari K.; Desai R.
Article.Abstract: Processing a word's meaning activates some of its semantic neighbors that are related associatively or taxonomically. While prior studies have shown that both types of neighborhoods influence lexical processing, their underlying neural bases remain unclear, particularly regarding the involvement of the Anterior Temporal Lobe (ATL). This study used HD-tDCS to examine the role of the left lateral ATL in how associative and taxonomic semantic neighborhoods influence the lexico-semantic processing of abstract and concrete words. Participants (N = 42) performed a semantic concreteness judgment task on words, with and without left ATL stimulation, where neighborhood sizes were varied. A strong facilitative effect of concreteness was found in both real and sham conditions, consistent with the traditional concreteness effect. Both associative and taxonomic semantic neighborhoods influenced semantic judgments. Critically, ATL stimulation slowed responses to words with sparse neighborhoods, regardless of whether neighborhoods were defined associatively or taxonomically. Furthermore, the neighborhood effects were more readily apparent for abstract words, with significant interactions between stimulation and neighborhoods observed only in this subset. Together, the findings highlight the independent effects of associative and taxonomic neighborhoods in lexico-semantic processing and show that the ATL modulates the activation of both associative and taxonomic semantic neighborhoods, challenging models that characterize it solely as a taxonomic hub.

Article.Title: Cortical and network architectures in limb and oral apraxia
Article.Authors: Nishio Y.; Itabashi R.; Kataoka Y.; Yazawa Y.; Mori E.
Article.Abstract: To characterize the distinct network principles underlying limb and oral apraxias, we investigated the structural brain lesions and white matter disconnections associated with limb apraxia (LA), buccofacial apraxia (BFA), and apraxia of speech (AOS) within a single cohort. In 136 patients with acute left-hemisphere ischemic stroke, LA was assessed using pantomime of tool use and communicative gestures, BFA via non-verbal orofacial movements, and AOS through perceptual evaluation of speech production tasks. We employed voxel-based, region-of-interest-based, and connectome-based lesion-symptom mapping to directly contrast the cortical damage and network disruptions associated with each deficit. LA was associated with damage to the inferior parietal lobule and widespread white matter disconnections within posterior networks, involving both intra-hemispheric and inter-hemispheric pathways. BFA was uniquely linked to an anterior lesion pattern centered on the ventral premotor cortex, driven by intrafrontal white matter disconnections. Furthermore, AOS emerged primarily as a focal cortical symptom linked to circumscribed lesions in the mid-precentral gyrus, with minimal structural disconnection. These findings demonstrate that LA emerges from disruptions within a widely distributed posterior network, whereas BFA involves an anterior intrafrontal network, contrasting with AOS which reflects a focal primary motor execution deficit. These data indicate that the neuroanatomical organization of apraxia is governed by the specific class of actions rather than simple effector specificity.

Article.Title: Early neural face perception is not modulated by emotional prosody prime congruency
Article.Authors: Mueller C.; Itier R.
Article.Abstract: Faces and voices are some of the most salient sources of information for identifying others' emotions. However, little research has focused on how emotional prosody modulates the earliest stages of face perception at the neural level. This study investigated priming effects of emotional prosody on the time course of subsequently presented emotional faces using event-related potentials (ERPs). Auditory prosodic primes (spoken sentences filtered to remove semantic information) expressing happy, neutral, or angry emotion were presented and immediately followed by a face expressing a congruent or incongruent emotion. After each trial, participants (n = 58) rated the face on valence and arousal. ERPs time-locked to face onset were analyzed at all time points and electrodes using data-driven mass univariate statistics. A significant main effect of face emotion was found spanning the N170, P2, and early EPN components. A significant main effect of voice emotion was found from approximately 50-100 msec and 150-400 msec, interpreted as increased attention in V1 and other non-face visual areas due to arousing vocal stimuli, especially angry ones. Critically, these factors did not interact, suggesting that face-voice congruency did not affect early perceptual face processing in this context. Behavioural results, however, showed that voice emotion influenced ratings of face valence and arousal, suggesting that voice prime and face information are integrated only at later cognitive but not early perceptual stages. Thus, prosody primes influenced visual processing before and after facial expressions were decoded, but face-voice congruency did not modulate early face emotion processing.

Article.Title: Assessment of pragmatic language in Turkish-speaking children: Development and psychometric evaluation of the PLSAS scale
Article.Authors: Keleş-Karaşahin Ç.; Özaydın L.
Article.Abstract: The scarcity of locally developed assessment tools for understudied languages remains a significant issue in research on language disorders. This study aimed to examine the validity and reliability of the Pragmatic Language Skills Assessment Scale (PLSAS), developed to assess pragmatic language skills in Turkish-speaking preschool children aged 36-72 months. PLSAS, represents the first original pragmatic language assessment tool specifically designed for this population and seeks to address an important gap in the literature. Data were collected face-to-face from 121 preschool teachers in Turkey regarding 519 children enrolled in preschool education. Separate subsamples were formed to examine criterion validity, discriminant validity, and test-retest reliability. Criterion validity was assessed using the Social Communication Skills Checklist. Structural validity was evaluated through Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA). EFA revealed a three-factor structure (Communicative Intentions, Discourse Management Skills, and Context) comprising 23 items and explaining 69.49% of the total variance. CFA findings indicated good model fit. Internal consistency coefficients demonstrated excellent reliability (Cronbach's α = .96; McDonald's ω = .96). Test-retest results supported temporal stability. Criterion validity analysis showed a strong positive correlation with the Social Communication Skills Checklist (r = .717, p < .001). Furthermore, discriminant validity analysis indicated that the scale significantly differentiated between typically developing children and children with developmental disabilities (ASD and intellectual disability) (t = 17.508, p < .001). PLSAS is a valid, reliable, and sensitive instrument for assessing pragmatic language skills in Turkish preschool children.

Article.Title: Covert consciousness in behavioral coma
Article.Authors: Edlow B.; Fecchio M.; Freeman H.; Rapalino O.; Cash S.; Young M.
Article.Abstract: Approximately 25% of patients with severe brain injuries who appear unresponsive on the bedside behavioral examination are covertly conscious-able to volitionally modulate their brain activity using task-based functional MRI or task-based EEG. Since the first description of covert consciousness in 2006, nearly all reports of covert consciousness have been in patients who were behaviorally awake, with their eyes open. These observations led to a widespread assumption that cortical activation associated with consciousness required a foundation of subcortical connections to produce wakefulness. We report the case of an 80-year-old woman with acute severe traumatic brain injury, whose level of consciousness was evaluated in the intensive care unit with a multimodal diagnostic protocol integrating behavioral, task-based fMRI, and task-based EEG assessments. Despite behavioral evidence of coma on every behavioral examination, the task-based fMRI and task-based EEG assessments both indicated the presence of covert consciousness. These observations suggest an unexpected phenomenon whereby awareness (i.e., volitional brain activity) can be dissociated from wakefulness (i.e., eye opening) in the human brain. The possibility that individuals who outwardly appear comatose may harbor covert consciousness carries both clinical and ethical weight, and unsettles long-held assumptions, embedded in the very term coma, that patients diagnosed as such are uniformly unaware and insensate.

Article.Title: Mapping peripheral misreaching in a large cohort of stroke patients
Article.Authors: Smits A.; Lugtmeijer S.; Hartung S.; van Grinsven E.; Ramsey N.; Raemaekers M.; de Haan E.; van Zandvoort M.
Article.Abstract: Peripheral reaching to objects outside the direct line of sight supports motor flexibility. Deficits in this ability are the hallmark of optic ataxia, yet impairments may exist along a continuum and warrant investigation in larger, unselected samples. This study examined peripheral misreaching and its neuroanatomical correlates in stroke patients. Peripheral reaching was assessed using a standardized reach-to-grasp task in 86 ischemic stroke patients and 22 mean age-matched controls. Group-level analyses assessed effects of target location and reaching hand, and case-control comparisons quantified deficit prevalence. Lesion symptom mapping examined associations between lesion location and peripheral misreaching, and structural disconnection mapping assessed the impact of structural connectivity damage. At group level, stroke patients showed significantly greater peripheral misreaching than controls, with group differences emerging at older ages. Peripheral reaching deficits were present in 31 out of 86 stroke patients and were most pronounced in the contralesional field. Ipsilesional deficits were also observed, particularly after left hemisphere lesions. Lesion symptom mapping across 77 stroke patients with available MRI data associated left-field peripheral misreaching with the right supramarginal gyrus, while structural disconnection mapping implicated the right optic radiation. No lesion-behaviour associations were observed for right-field peripheral misreaching, though right hemisphere lesion volume correlated with misreaching in this condition. These findings indicate that peripheral reaching deficits after stroke are more common and heterogeneous than previously recognized. The involvement of the supramarginal gyrus suggests a broader role in visuomotor control, including attentional and proprioceptive processes. The right hemisphere dominance in lesion-behaviour associations raises questions about hemispheric specialization.

Article.Title: The effects of Foreign Accent Syndrome on bilingual speech production: Multilevel evidence from a controlled-case study
Article.Authors: Contreras-Ruston F.; Navarra J.; Elvira-García W.; Sierpowska J.; Rico Pons I.; Paipa A.; Peñaloza C.
Article.Abstract: Foreign Accent Syndrome (FAS) is a rare motor speech disorder with altered speech patterns perceived as a foreign accent. The effects of FAS on the first (L1) and second-acquired (L2) languages in bilinguals have not been examined in depth and knowledge about its neural correlates is limited. Additionally, possible disruptions in auditory-motor feedback processes supporting speech monitoring and voice adaptation are rarely assessed. This study reports on P1, an L1 Catalan- L2 Spanish bilingual with FAS. We sought to characterize FAS in her two languages using a multilevel approach combining perceptual, phonetic, neuropsychological, auditory-motor voice feedback-based adaptation and structural neuroimaging analyses. Results showed that P1’s L1 and L2 speech production were perceived as foreign by native bilingual listeners. Phonetic analyses revealed segmental and suprasegmental disturbances in both languages resulting from focal left motor cortex damage. Voice adaptation to auditory noise revealed an abnormal pattern, with differences between L1 and L2, suggesting altered auditory-motor integration. Notably, P1’s speech rate, fluency and eloquence were more affected in her L1, suggesting decreased automaticity in this language. She also presented domain-general executive control deficits and increased L1 to L2 switching, as she found L2 production easier. These findings suggest differential effects of FAS on the L1 and L2 speech production of P1, with increased L1-L2 switching as a potential compensatory strategy to decrease executive control burden in L1 production and facilitate more fluent communication. Our findings highlight a potential role for disrupted auditory-motor speech and voice integration in the manifestation of bilingual FAS.

Article.Title: Assessing Brain-Behaviour Coupling in Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Insights from Reliable Change Indices and Monte Carlo Simulations
Article.Authors: Fujiyama H.; Wansbrough K.; Lebihan B.; Tan J.; Levin O.; Mathersul D.; Tang A.
Article.Abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NiBS) studies frequently report exploratory brain-behaviour correlations following the application of NiBS. However, these analyses are typically underpowered and rely on ratio-based change scores with known statistical limitations. We addressed these limitations by pooling individual data from three independent studies (N = 69) and combining empirical analysis with a Monte Carlo simulation framework. All studies applied 20 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) targeting the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG) during a stop signal task. Changes in preSMA–rIFG EEG imaginary coherency (ImCoh) and stop-signal reaction time (SSRT) were quantified using reliable change indices (RCI), z-standardised within studies for pooled mixed-effects regression. We found no meaningful association between tACS-induced ImCoh change and SSRT change (r = .013, marginal R 2 = .004), with project-wise correlations being small, non-significant, and directionally inconsistent. While sensitivity analysis using ratio-based change scores converged on the same null result (r = .014), the simulation framework revealed that ratio-based scores show near-complete failure to recover true brain-behaviour associations across all plausible effect sizes. Conversely, RCI-based scores preserved directional accuracy and provided well-calibrated Type I error control, despite moderate attenuation under realistic noise conditions. These results highlight the severe statistical limits of detecting individual-level brain-behaviour coupling following 20Hz tACS. Rather than ruling out a true biological association, our findings demonstrate that standard sample sizes and typical measurement noise create substantial 'blindness' to realistic effect sizes, underscoring a broader need for more reliable metrics and adequately powered designs in NiBS research.

Article.Title: From affect to rules: A conceptual model of compensation in prodromal behavioral frontotemporal degeneration
Article.Authors: Bertoux M.
Article.Abstract: Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) is typically described in terms of progressive loss of social and behavioral control. However, the earliest stages of the disease may also involve active, developed forms of compensation that remain largely invisible to standard assessment. These strategies are rarely characterized, yet they may offer a unique entry point into the mechanisms by which social functioning is temporarily preserved despite emerging degeneration. Here, I report a longitudinal single-case study of a young C9orf72 repeat-expansion carrier followed from the prodromal stage to established moderate bvFTD. Based on more than a dozen hours of semi-structured interviews initiated at symptom emergence, thematic analysis identified five compensatory subthemes. Together, these strategies suggested a coherent shift in the architecture of behavioral control that remain largely invisible to standard medical or neuropsychological assessment. As implicit, flexible, and internally sustained regulation became less reliable, functioning appeared to rely on control processes that were more explicit, environmentally distributed, routine-based, and effortful. These observations can be organized around three broader principles: explicitation, externalization, and stabilization. The case suggests that early preservation in bvFTD may reflect not only residual capacities, but also an active and fragile reorganization of social and behavioral control. By foregrounding the patient’s own compensatory work, this study provides a hypothesis-generating conceptual framework for understanding how everyday functioning may be maintained during the prodromal-to-dementia transition, and highlights qualitative longitudinal single-case designs and participatory research as a powerful tool for identifying hidden forms of adaptation in neurodegenerative disease and refine theoretical models of social behavior.

Article.Title: Stretch‐Induced Muscle Responses Under Threat Versus Safety
Article.Authors: Visser Y.; Bramson B.; Medendorp W.; Roelofs K.; Selen L.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT When in a stressful situation, making fast and accurate decisions is crucial. Previous work has shown that sensorimotor decisions can improve under threat. However, it is unclear if these improvements are achieved by improvements in perceptual or motor performance. Here, we present two hypotheses for how threat might influence motor preparation and use muscular stretch reflexes to test both. The task‐unspecific hypothesis predicts that threat promotes motor preparation irrespective of the reach target, through tonic upregulation of the short latency stretch reflex. In contrast, the task‐specific hypothesis predicts that threat increases sensory processing for a specific reach target, leading to direction‐selective up‐ and down‐regulation of the long latency stretch reflex. Participants were asked to reach to one of two targets that appeared shortly before a perturbation eliciting a stretch reflex; they performed this task either under threat of an electric shock or under safe circumstances. Skin conductance and heart rate results show that the threat manipulation significantly increased sympathetic activation, but not parasympathetic activation. Supporting the task‐specific hypothesis, the EMG findings demonstrate a direction‐selective modulation of the long‐latency response of stretch reflexes, starting ~100 ms after perturbation onset. Our results suggest that stress affects action preparation through upregulation of cortical visuomotor circuits.

Article.Title: Advances and Applications in Population Voltage Imaging
Article.Authors: Dorst M.; Fuzik J.; Grimm C.; Kannan M.; McCluskey K.; Šarauskytė L.; Szücs G.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT This brief review summarizes the most recent progress in in vivo voltage imaging in the neurosciences, as an extension to the work presented at the voltage imaging session of the 2025 FENS regional meeting in Oslo. First, we outline the latest advances in genetically encoded voltage indicators. Next, we examine technical innovations that have reshaped imaging platforms and lay the groundwork to investigate neural activity in real time across large fields of view and in deep tissue. Finally, we highlight a selection of compelling applications that have emerged over the past 5 years, illustrating how voltage imaging evolved from a proof of concept to being deployed to answer pending neuroscientific questions.

Article.Title: Dynamic Phase Synchrony in Cortical Networks Underlying Conscious Awareness of Flicker
Article.Authors: Uchiyama Y.; Takahashi T.; Nomoto K.; Fujiki S.; Fukushima T.; Katsuyama N.; Kawase T.; Koganemaru S.; Kansaku K.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Flickering light sources, such as fluorescent lamps, evoke neural oscillations in the occipital cortex aligning with the flicker frequency; however, this flicker often remains outside conscious awareness. This discrepancy suggests neural mechanisms gating flicker perception. While functional magnetic resonance imaging studies have indicated the involvement of large‐scale frontal and parietal networks in conscious flicker perception, their low temporal resolution limits insights into the underlying dynamic interactions. Using electroencephalography and physically identical stimuli near the critical flicker‐fusion frequency, we investigated the temporal dynamics of phase synchrony and power distribution. Flicker perception was characterized by an early increase in higher beta‐band (19–28 Hz) synchrony, followed by an increase in gamma‐band (29–48 Hz) synchrony between fronto‐parietal and parieto‐occipital regions at approximately 300 ms post‐stimulus. This was accompanied by a global expansion of gamma‐band power from occipital to fronto‐parietal areas—effects not observed during fused perception. Conversely, alpha‐band (8–14 Hz) synchrony between anterior and posterior regions showed a more pronounced reduction specifically during fusion. These findings suggest that frequency‐specific coordination and global information sharing across large‐scale networks may underlie conscious flicker perception. The emergence of broad gamma‐band synchrony at around 300 ms may reflect the integration of local sensory signals into distributed cortical networks. Early beta‐band synchrony may facilitate the initiation of this process through top‐down modulation, whereas attenuated alpha‐band synchrony during fusion may reflect insufficient engagement of these networks. Such dynamic interplay within distributed networks is suggested to be involved in shaping the temporal resolution of visual awareness.

Article.Title: TMS‐Derived Neurophysiological Measures of Corticospinal Excitability, Intracortical Excitability, and Interhemispheric Interactions Associated With Post‐Stroke Motor Recovery: A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Pereira G.; da Silva M.; Baptista A.; de Araujo J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Motor recovery after stroke is associated with changes in corticospinal integrity, intracortical excitability, and interhemispheric interactions. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) provides neurophysiological measures of these processes, but their relationship with motor recovery across randomized controlled trials remains uncertain. This systematic review synthesized evidence from randomized controlled trials investigating TMS‐derived neurophysiological measures associated with motor recovery following TMS‐based neuromodulation after stroke. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Embase were searched for studies published between January 1, 2016, and July 10, 2026. Eligible trials enrolled adults with ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, assessed at least one TMS‐derived neurophysiological measure, and reported a motor or functional outcome. Study selection followed PRISMA 2020, risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. The search identified 1441 records; after removal of 519 duplicates, 922 records were screened, 55 full‐text reports were assessed, and 16 randomized controlled trials were included. Motor evoked potential (MEP) amplitude, MEP status, and resting motor threshold were the most frequently reported measures. Several trials found that changes in corticospinal excitability accompanied improvements in upper‐limb function, activities of daily living, gait, or balance. One trial found greater motor gains among participants with preserved baseline MEPs; however, the contemporary randomized‐trial evidence is insufficient to establish MEP status as a predictor of differential response to neuromodulation. In contrast, short‐interval intracortical inhibition, cortical silent period, and interhemispheric inhibition were assessed in very few trials, whereas intracortical facilitation was not directly evaluated in any eligible RCT. Most studies raised some risk‐of‐bias concerns, and one study had high overall risk. Certainty was moderate for clinical motor recovery, low for MEP‐ and motor‐threshold‐based measures, and very low for intracortical and interhemispheric measures. Overall, MEP‐derived measures and resting motor threshold were the most frequently reported neurophysiological domains, whereas baseline MEP status was evaluated in only one stratified trial. Standardized TMS protocols are needed to clarify their monitoring, prognostic, and treatment‐response value.

Article.Title: Posttraining Dorsal Premotor cTBS and Devaluation‐Based Action Control: No Detectable Difference From Vertex Stimulation
Article.Authors: Mejías Martínez G.; Obeso Martín I.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The neural basis of recently learned stimulus–response associations involves interactions between premotor, supplementary motor, sensorimotor, and striatal regions, but the causal contribution of premotor cortex to their posttraining expression remains unclear. Thirty‐five right‐handed volunteers learned six stimulus–response–outcome mappings in a single experimental session. Continuous theta‐burst stimulation (cTBS) was then delivered over a right dorsal premotor target or a vertex active‐control site before participants completed outcome‐devaluation, slips‐of‐action, and baseline tests. The primary behavioral analyses showed no detectable group differences in reaction time or response accuracy during the outcome‐devaluation or slips‐of‐action tests. Baseline performance was also comparable between groups, providing no evidence that stimulation affected retention of the recently learned mappings. Under the present limited‐training protocol, posttraining cTBS over the right dorsal premotor target did not produce detectable behavioral differences relative to vertex cTBS. However, given the modest between‐subject sample, the variability of devaluation‐based measures, and the possibility that vertex stimulation affected adjacent medial motor regions, smaller or shared stimulation effects cannot be excluded.

Article.Title: Dual‐Task Interference Impairs the Acquisition of Standing Balance Skills
Article.Authors: Tor Ö.; Berberoğlu U.; Demirci S.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Cortical areas, including the primary motor cortex (M1), are engaged during motor learning; however, their role in acquiring balance skills remains uncertain. By incorporating a concurrent cognitive task that demands attentional and cortical resources, this study investigated whether early balance learning depends on cortical engagement. Twenty‐five healthy young adults were divided into a control group ( n = 13; four males; age: 21.38 ± 1.98 years) and a dual‐task group ( n = 12; three males; age: 21.91 ± 2.11 years). Both groups underwent a balance training session consisting of five sets of three 40‐s trials on a balance board. The dual‐task group counted backward by threes from a random number during training. Throughout the training, the tilt angle of the balance board was recorded in both the anteroposterior (AP) and mediolateral (ML) directions using an accelerometer mounted on it. Balance performance was quantified using the tilt angle, standard deviation of the tilt angle, and the tilt‐angle speed. Balance improved in both groups, as shown by significant reductions in standard deviation of the tilt angle in both directions, and tilt angle and tilt speed were reduced across both groups in ML. Conversely, only the control group demonstrated significant improvement in AP tilt speed between the first and third, second and third, and first and fifth sets ( t = 3.7, p = 0.003, d = 1.45; t = 2.8, p = 0.044, d = 1.11; t = 3.2, p = 0.016, d = 1.26, respectively). Furthermore, the control group showed a significantly lower tilt speed than the dual‐task group in the third set ( t = 2.1, p = 0.044, d = 0.92). In conclusion, the present findings suggest that performing cognitive tasks concurrently with balance training may disrupt the acquisition of balance skills. This disruption cannot be attributed solely to increased cognitive demands but also to heightened attentional demands, which cause competition for shared cortical resources and potential interference with balance learning. These findings highlight the role of cortical structures in early balance learning and could inform future studies aimed at optimizing rehabilitation training protocols.

Article.Title: Chronic Postnatal Chemogenetic Activation of Forebrain Excitatory Neurons Modulates Astrocyte‐Associated Function and Metabolism in Adult Male Mice
Article.Authors: Pradhan A.; Pati S.; Saba K.; Chaudhari P.; Tiwari P.; Kapri D.; Balakrishnan A.; Patel A.; Vaidya V.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Early adversity increases vulnerability for adult psychopathology. Across multiple preclinical models of early adversity, there are reports of astrocyte dysfunction and disrupted amino acid neurotransmission, along with maladaptive behavioral responses in adulthood. Disrupted G protein‐coupled receptor signaling is known to phenocopy specific consequences of early‐life adversity. Enhanced Gq signaling in the forebrain excitatory neurons in early postnatal life programs anxio‐depressive behaviors in adulthood, accompanied by altered neuronal glutamate and GABA metabolism in mouse models. We hypothesized that enhancing Gq signaling in forebrain excitatory neurons in early postnatal life may also impact astrocyte function in adulthood. Our results show that postnatal hM3Dq‐mediated chemogenetic activation of CaMKIIα‐positive forebrain excitatory neurons not only increases anxiety‐like behavior but also evokes bidirectional transcriptional regulation of multiple astrocyte‐associated genes in the neocortex and hippocampi. While Gfap , Aldh1l1 , Eaat1 , and Eaat3 mRNA levels were reduced in the neocortex, they were enhanced in the hippocampus, and a similar pattern was noted for GFAP protein levels. Chronic postnatal chemogenetic activation of CaMKIIα‐positive neurons did not alter astrocyte cell density in both the neocortex and the hippocampus. Using ( 1 H‐( 13 C)) NMR spectroscopy, we observed a significant decline in astrocyte‐specific glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter turnover, and a reduction in astrocyte metabolic flux within the neocortex and hippocampus in adulthood in animals with a history of postnatal chemogenetic activation of forebrain excitatory neurons. Our findings indicate that chemogenetically driving Gq signaling chronically during the postnatal window in forebrain excitatory neurons results in persistent changes well into adulthood, with enhanced anxiety‐like behaviors and disrupted astrocyte function and metabolism, phenocopying specific changes in astrocyte function noted following early adversity.

Article.Title: Emergence of Deviance Detection in Cortical Cultures Through Maturation, Criticality, and Early Experience
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Yaron A.; Akita D.; Shiramatsu T.; Chao Z.; Takahashi H.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Mismatch negativity (MMN) in humans is widely interpreted as reflecting deviance detection (DD) within predictive processing frameworks. However, the developmental processes by which DD emerges and matures during early cortical development remain incompletely understood. Here, we longitudinally tracked the development of DD in dissociated cortical cultures grown on high‐density CMOS microelectrode arrays from Day In Vitro (DIV) 10 to DIV30 (Study 1) and compared cultures with and without early structured stimulation at DIV31–35 (Study 2). Cultures were stimulated with oddball and many‐standards control paradigms while spontaneous and evoked activity were recorded. In Study 1, stimulus‐evoked responses at early stages were largely confined to fast components corresponding to direct stimulation effects. From DIV15 onward, robust late responses emerged, and deviant stimuli evoked stronger responses than frequent and control stimuli, marking the emergence of DD as defined in this study. By DIV30, responses became stronger, faster, and more temporally precise. Neuronal avalanche analysis revealed a transition from subcritical to near‐critical dynamics across development. Cultures exhibiting power‐law–like statistics showed larger DD indices, although DD was also observed in non‐critical networks. These findings indicate that critical dynamics are not required for DD, but critical‐like states are associated with more robust and differentiated DD responses as networks mature. In Study 2, both groups shifted toward power‐law–like avalanche distributions, with no significant difference in their developmental trajectories. At DIV31–35, stimulated cultures had earlier peak responses and lower DD indices than controls, but these group differences were not significant. Together, these findings indicate that dissociated cortical cultures can exhibit DD under simplified in vitro conditions and that its developmental trajectory is associated with network maturation and self‐organization toward critical‐like dynamics.

Article.Title: Insulin Enhances Nitroglycerin‐Induced Hyperalgesia Through Insulin‐Responsive Receptor Signalling Involving the Trigeminovascular System and Meningeal Mast Cells
Article.Authors: Torun I.; Celik H.; Kilinc E.; Kurtoglu M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Migraine headache prevalence is lower in patients with diabetes, but the underlying mechanisms remains unclear. This study explored the influences of hyperglycemia, insulin and insulin receptor (IR)/insulin‐like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF‐1R)–related signalling on migraine‐related mechanisms in in vivo and ex vivo rat models. In in vivo experiments, migraine‐relevant responses were induced by systemic injection of nitroglycerin (NTG), whereas hyperglycemia was induced by streptozotocin (STZ). The effects of hyperglycemia, insulin and the dual IR/IGF‐1R inhibitor BMS‐754807 were investigated. In ex vivo experiments, the effects of insulin and BMS on basal and capsaicin‐induced calcitonin gene‐related peptide (CGRP) releases from migraine‐associated tissues (peripheral meningeal afferents and trigeminal ganglion, and central brainstem trigeminal nucleus) were directly tested. Mechanical hyperalgesia was evaluated by von‐Frey, CGRP and c‐Fos levels by ELISA and meningeal mast cells by toluidine‐blue staining. In in vivo NTG group, insulin further lowered the pain threshold and further enhanced CGRP and c‐fos concentrations in trigeminal tissues and mast cell activation in the meninges. Hyperglycemia alone or in the NTG‐treated group did not change these parameters. In ex vivo experiments, direct administration of insulin stimulated CGRP release in meningeal and trigeminal ganglion, but not trigeminal nucleus, tissues and further enhanced capsaicin‐stimulated CGRP release, confirming the in vivo effects. The in vivo and ex vivo effects of insulin were reversed by BMS. Hyperglycemia did not modify the NTG‐induced responses. However, insulin facilitates migraine‐related responses by enhancing trigeminal CGRP signalling and meningeal mast cell activation through IR and/or IGF‐1R‐related signalling. Modulation of insulin‐responsive IR/IGF‐1R–related signalling within the trigeminovascular system may represent a potential target for future therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Towards a Brain–Computer Interface (BCI) for Improving Phonological Processing in Developmental Dyslexia: An Exploratory Study
Article.Authors: Zheng X.; Araújo J.; Busson Q.; Goswami U.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) have immense potential regarding the provision of therapies for disorders of development, but to date have typically been created for non‐linguistic disorders such as ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder). Here, we present a BCI designed to improve linguistic phonological processing during natural speech listening, aimed at participants with developmental dyslexia. Phonological ‘deficits’ are considered a core feature of dyslexia across languages and are present from infancy in those later diagnosed with dyslexia. Here, a non‐invasive EEG–BCI relying on auditory inputs and visual feedback was developed to optimise brain patterns related to phonological development in infants and children. The BCI focused on neural patterns identified using Temporal Sampling theory, which has found the theta/delta ratio during natural speech listening to be a key neural associate of impaired phonology. As a first step, the BCI was tested with adults. Adults with and without dyslexia played the BCI for 16 sessions and received pre‐ and post‐testing regarding phonological awareness and single word and non‐word reading skills. Learning was assessed both online, as in most BCI studies, and offline, enabling removal of a greater number of potential EEG artefacts. Significant associations between offline BCI scores (a measure of BCI learning) and improvements in non‐word reading were found for all participants who learned the BCI, both dyslexic and control. BCI learning also showed significant associations with improvements in real word reading and amplitude rise time discrimination. The data are interpreted with respect to Temporal Sampling theory.

Article.Title: B Lymphocytes in Acute Ischemic Stroke: From Immune Tolerance to Neuroprotection and Autoimmunity
Article.Authors: Zouali M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Whereas the pathobiology of stroke is traditionally thought to be mediated mainly by innate immune cells, the recent discovery that immune tolerance to brain‐specific antigens takes place in the meninges suggests that the CNS makes use of unique pathways to respond to brain‐derived antigens. By virtue of their adaptive and innate‐like functions, B lymphocytes can play multiple roles in stroke. Following acute ischemic stroke, B cells home to the site of injury and produce cytokines that can either promote or exacerbate inflammation. They also secrete autoantibodies against neuronal and/or vascular components, potentially aggravating the damage and contributing to long‐term neurological deficits. Clinical studies indicate that stroke patients can develop B‐cell responses that potentially contribute to dementia. In animal models, age‐associated B cells were found to worsen inflammation and contribute to autoimmunity. Through the production of antibodies and cytokines, B cells play a role in affecting the permeability of the blood–brain barrier, thereby compromising its integrity. In addition to contributing to adverse outcomes by enhancing inflammation and producing harmful autoantibodies, B cells have been demonstrated to exhibit protective effects, helping to resolve inflammation and promoting tissue repair. In mice, the absence of B cells results in delayed recovery, suggesting that B‐cell migration to different regions of the brain imparts reduction of poststroke cognitive impairment. Gaining further insight into the multiple roles of B cells in stroke could lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies and biomarker development.

Article.Title: Effects of Cerebellar Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation on Motor Learning in Healthy Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
Article.Authors: Liu R.; Yue T.; Vicario C.; Luo X.; Guo F.; Qi F.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Cerebellar transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) may enhance motor learning, but findings vary across tasks and stimulation protocols. This systematic review and meta‐analysis quantified its effects on motor adaptation and motor skill learning in healthy adults and examined potential moderators. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and Embase were searched from inception to 17 August 2026. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024596088). Randomized controlled and crossover studies comparing cerebellar tDCS with sham stimulation and reporting practice‐dependent or time‐dependent changes in motor performance were eligible. Twenty studies comprising 739 participant observations were included. The random‐effects model showed that anodal cerebellar tDCS significantly improved motor learning (SMD = −0.52, 95% CI −0.90 to −0.14, p = 0.007; I 2 = 83%), with negative values favouring tDCS. Although meta‐regression identified no significant moderators, exploratory subgroup analyses yielded significant SMDs for online stimulation (−0.66), 2 mA (−0.44), 25 min (−0.93), a 25‐cm 2 electrode montage (−0.99), motor skill learning (−0.49) and outcome assessments at < 24 (−0.52) and ≥ 24 h (−1.11). Leave‐one‐out sensitivity analysis and trim‐and‐fill analysis did not materially change the pooled result, although Egger's regression test indicated small‐study effects. These findings indicate that anodal cerebellar tDCS can facilitate motor learning and support further investigation of stimulation protocols, longer term retention and clinical applications. Nevertheless, the magnitude and generalisability of the effect require confirmation in larger, adequately powered trials.

Article.Title: State of the “Art” in Freezing of Gait: Drawing on Perspectives of Individuals With Parkinson's Disease
Article.Authors: Pötter‐Nerger M.; Spee B.; Zeitzschel M.; Siems N.; Gulberti A.; Howe E.; Ehgoetz Martens K.; Gilat M.; Nieuwboer A.; Bloem B.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Freezing of gait (FoG) in Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as a multidimensional phenomenon encompassing motor, cognitive, and emotional domains. The impact of FoG is enormous, but can be difficult to articulate. Traditional clinical assessments typically fail to capture its subjective and affective impact. This qualitative study explored drawings from individuals with PD to better understand the lived experience of FoG. Specifically, we collected artworks created by individuals who experience FoG. We studied the personal perceptions and emotions associated with FoG drawings in two ways: by asking participants to narratively explain their artwork and a qualitative curation by an international panel of experts of neurology, neuroscience, neurorehabilitation, neuroaesthetics, art, and empirical aesthetics. Five overarching themes emerged: (1) “Captured feet,” depicting sensations of being glued, tethered, or rooted to the ground; (2) “Chaos,” reflecting disrupted motor control during environmental or cognitive overload; (3) “Emotional explosion,” expressing fear, anger, helplessness, and loss of control; (4) “Freezing and falls,” highlighting instability and existential threat; and (5) “Released from freeze,” portraying therapeutic relief, restored movement, and joy. These visual narratives reveal that FoG is more than just a motor block. Rather, it is an embodied experience of immobilization, emotional escalation, and vulnerability, contrasted by profound relief when mobility returns. Artistic expression offers unique insights beyond structured assessments, fostering empathetic clinician–patient communication, and supporting a more holistic, person‐centered approach to PD care.

Article.Title: Mismatch Responses to Prosodic Changes in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: A Longitudinal Approach
Article.Authors: Themas L.; Schaadt G.; Lippus P.; Padrik M.; Kask L.; Vaher U.; Männamaa M.; Kreegipuu K.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Developmental language disorder is characterized by difficulties in auditory processing and prosody discrimination. Estonian word prosody features a unique three‐way quantity distinction, characterized by changes in syllable duration and pitch contour, which differentiate word meaning and grammatical cases. In this study, we examined the Mismatch Responses longitudinally in 23 children with developmental language disorder and 25 age and biological sex matched typically developing peers (age at first measurement 4;6–6;5 years; age at second measurement 5;6–7;5 years). A multifeature paradigm was used in which all stimuli were meaningful words; two deviants differed from the standard, one in syllable duration and the other in both syllable duration and pitch contour. We also tested the discrimination of these prosodic features with behavioral tasks at both measurements. For duration discrimination, an early positive mismatch response diminished from first to second measurement, while a subsequent negative mismatch response increased. Significant longitudinal changes were observed in the typically developing group but not in children with developmental language disorder, while direct comparisons of maturational trajectories did not reveal significant group differences. For the duration and pitch contrast, in both groups and at both assessments, no mismatch response was detected. Additionally, no association was observed at the individual level between maturational changes in mismatch responses and behavioral discrimination at either measurement. These findings provide insights into the maturation of prosodic change detection processes and contribute to a better understanding of developmental language disorder and its manifestations.

Article.Title: Freezing of Gait: A Therapeutic Perspective
Article.Authors: LeWitt P.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Despite improved definition of the problem and better understanding of its phenomenology, freezing of gait (FoG) remains a therapeutic enigma for clinicians and neuroscientists alike. Patients with Parkinson disease (PD) or other neurological disorders experiencing FoG are similarly frustrated, despite the benefits that levodopa and other medications provide for control of PD's primary motor features. For those burdened by episodes of FoG, current therapeutic options are quite limited. Some patients achieve improvements from pharmacotherapy—for example, by adjunctive use of an oral dopaminergic agonist or by subcutaneous infusion of apomorphine. If needed, deep brain stimulation sometimes offers symptomatic improvements. Certain interventions devised by physical therapists (or discovered by patients themselves) can improve FoG. However, successful pharmacotherapy for FoG has lagged behind, though the future holds some promising leads for therapies acting on dopaminergic, adenosinergic, noradrenergic, glutamatergic, and cholinergic circuitry.

Article.Title: lickcalc : Easy Analysis of Lick Microstructure in Experiments of Rodent Ingestive Behaviour
Article.Authors: Volcko K.; McCutcheon J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Lick microstructure is a term used in behavioural neuroscience to describe the information that can be obtained from a detailed examination of rodent drinking behaviour. Rather than simply recording total intake (volume consumed), lick microstructure examines how licks are grouped and the spacing of these groups of licks. This type of analysis can provide important insights into why an animal is drinking, for example, whether it is influenced by taste or affected by the consequences of consumption (e.g., feeling ‘full’). Here, we present a software package, lickcalc , that allows detailed microstructural analysis of licking patterns. The software is browser based and is hosted at https://lickcalc.uit.no , or the repository can be downloaded and installed locally. Lick timestamps can be loaded from a variety of formats, and different analysis and plotting options allow quality control of data and the determination of critical parameters for microstructural analysis, including the number and size of lick bursts. Data can be divided into epochs for detailed examination of changes across the session. Batch processing and custom configurations are supported. In this manuscript, we demonstrate the use of the functions exposed by lickcalc by analysing data comparing lick patterns between mice on a protein‐restricted and a control (non‐restricted) diet. We show that lickcalc allows quality control of the data and the uncovering of subtle differences in lick behaviour that are not apparent when just considering the total number of licks. This software makes microstructural analysis accessible to any researcher who wishes to employ it while providing sophisticated analyses with high scientific value.

Article.Title: Exploring Hippocampal Neural Network Dynamics in Rodents Using Virtual Reality: A Narrative Review on Systems, Spatial Coding, and Applications
Article.Authors: Ezgin N.; Kurul F.; Cetin A.; Hrnčić D.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Virtual reality (VR) provides a highly controllable, immersive, and interactive platform for investigating hippocampal mechanisms underlying spatial learning and memory. In rodent models, VR‐based paradigms have elucidated how hippocampal subregions including CA1, CA3, and the dentate gyrus support spatial representation, pattern separation, and memory consolidation. Within VR environments, place cells, grid cells, head‐direction cells, and boundary vector cells exhibit characteristic remapping dynamics, reflecting both the experimental advantages and sensory constraints inherent to VR. Although VR enhances reproducibility and integrates seamlessly with advanced methodologies such as two‐photon calcium imaging and optogenetics, reduced vestibular and multisensory inputs can limit the fidelity of spatial coding. This review synthesizes current evidence on hippocampal–retrosplenial interactions, synaptic plasticity, and multisensory integration in VR, highlighting mechanistic insights into spatial cognition.

Article.Title: Altered Timing of Self‐Voice Processing in Parkinson's Disease
Article.Authors: Contreras‐Ruston F.; Criscuolo A.; Callén A.; Cucurell D.; Navarra J.; Kotz S.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Parkinson's disease (PD) affects voice and speech production, often resulting in reduced vocal intensity and monotonous speech. Recent studies suggest that these changes can be partially explained by altered sensory feedback processing in speech production: individuals with PD (IwPD) may fail to monitor and adapt sensory feedback when producing speech. We investigated PD voice production using a voice playback paradigm and focused on the sensory attenuation typically observed in event‐related responses (ERPs) to the self‐generated voice. When sensory feedback is intact, the P50, N100, and P200 responses to a self‐generated voice are attenuated compared to an externally generated voice. Twenty‐three IwPD and 23 matched healthy controls (HCs) completed the voice playback study with three conditions: self‐generated voice (auditory‐motor [AMC]), externally generated voice (auditory‐only [AOC]), and motor‐only. Linear mixed models assessed group differences in ERP morphology. Groups differed in the N100 latency response: IwPD showed a greater shift in latency between AMC and AOC than healthy controls. Regarding the P200, a significant group‐by‐condition interaction indicated that IwPD, unlike healthy controls, produced larger amplitudes for the self‐generated than the passively listened to voice. Taken together, these findings suggest that the processing of one's own voice in IwPD is altered in terms of temporal precision rather than in the N100 suppression effect per se. This effect was accompanied by an enhanced P200 attentional response. These response patterns in IwPD are indicative of likely progressing difficulties in regulating one's own voice, characteristic of Parkinson's disease.

Article.Title: Optimized Cardiorespiratory State at Tone Onset Enhances Sensory Responses but Not Associative Learning in Healthy Adults
Article.Authors: Santhana Gopalan P.; Nokia M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Previous studies suggest that when a tone‐conditioned stimulus (CS) predicting an airpuff towards the eye is presented at diastole during expiration, both sensory responses to the CS and trace eyeblink conditioning (TEBC) are enhanced. However, not all participants learn and individual variation in the body–brain relationship remains overlooked. We studied whether timing the CS based on an individually optimized bodily state enhances sensory responses and TEBC. We assumed so, as sensory response magnitude reflects attention and stimulus salience: A salient CS should facilitate TEBC. Forty‐one young adults and 19 older adults completed a passive auditory task while electrocardiogram, respiration and electroencephalogram were recorded. The cardiorespiratory state associated with the largest N1–P2 response was identified individually. Optimal states varied across participants and did not differ between age groups. Participants underwent TEBC at their optimal state (Personalized) or at diastole during expiration (Control). As expected, the CS evoked a larger N1–P2 response in the Personalized than the Control group. However, conditioned responding, peak performance, and learning rate, or the proportion of good learners did not differ between groups. Older adults learned more slowly, made fewer conditioned responses, and were less aware of the tone‐airpuff association than young adults. These findings tentatively suggest that enhancing early sensory processing of the CS may not improve TEBC, although the low reliability of the individually determined optimal state limits this conclusion. Future studies should examine whether timing external stimuli to specific bodily states effectively influences behaviour in tasks that rely on rapid sensory processing.

Article.Title: Rhythms in Decoding Do Not Signal Pulsing Information
Article.Authors: van Ede F.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Emerging studies report that information decoded from brain activity may pulse at specific frequencies. As such inferences take root, I clarify that trial‐level decoding time courses inherit background brain rhythms even when information content is stable. This cautions against conflating rhythms in decoding with rhythms in information content.

Article.Title: The FOG‐COA Protocol: Validation of Freezing of Gait Clinical Outcomes Assessments in Parkinson's Disease
Article.Authors: Howe E.; Ginis P.; Ehgoetz Martens K.; Gilat M.; Mancini M.; Mckay J.; Nonnekes J.; Mammen J.; Adams J.; Cella D.; Nieuwboer A.; Horak F.; Lewis S.; Hausdorff J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The development and evaluation of novel treatment options for freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease have been limited by an ambiguous definition and lack of standardized clinical outcome assessments (COAs) that 1) reliably assess FOG severity, 2) are responsive to change, and 3) capture patient‐relevant impact. To address these gaps, working groups from the International Consortium on FOG (ICFOG) developed a clinician‐rated outcome—the Giladi Protocol for assessing FOG severity (GP‐FOG), and a patient‐reported outcome—the FOG Quality of Life questionnaire (FOG‐QOL). The FOG‐COA project will evaluate the conceptual framework and psychometric properties of these COAs to determine their fit‐for‐purpose in clinical trials. A total of 105 freezers and 35 non‐freezers from seven international centers will complete the GP‐FOG in the dopaminergic OFF and ON states during two separate visits (7–14 days apart). FOG annotations from video recordings will be used to assess criterion validity. OFF and ON GP‐FOG scores from two trained raters at Visit 1, as well as within‐rater scores across visits, will examine reliability. Responsiveness will be evaluated by comparing effect sizes between OFF and ON GP‐FOG scores. Patient meaningfulness will be assessed through the association between patient‐perceived FOG severity and GP‐FOG scores. Participants will complete the FOG‐QOL at each visit to assess test–retest reliability and validity against the NFOGQ and PDQ‐8. A subset of freezers will undergo cognitive interviews to identify relevant daily life FOG impacts and evaluate FOG‐QOL meaningfulness. Collectively, this work will advance standardized, sensitive, and meaningful FOG‐COAs, supporting regulatory‐grade endpoints and the development of a multi‐dimensional outcome framework.

Article.Title: Aging in Autism: An Event‐Related Potentials Study of Auditory Change Detection
Article.Authors: Bessé M.; Morel‐Kohlmeyer S.; Houy‐Durand E.; Prévost P.; Tuller L.; Bouazzaoui B.; Taconnat L.; Capdeville J.; Angel L.; Gomot M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Autistic individuals are often thought to exhibit reduced tolerance for change, which may stem from atypicalities in sensory processing, particularly in the detection of environmental changes. Within the predictive coding framework, this intolerance may reflect altered generation and updating internal predictions in response to sensory input, leading to increased prediction errors. Mismatch negativity and the P3a component are event‐related potentials (ERPs) indexing automatic auditory change detection and involuntary attention shift. While studied in autistic children and young adults, little is known about how these components evolve during aging, an important gap as 21 million autistic adults over 60 are expected by 2050. This study examined mismatch negativity and P3a responses in 43 autistic adults (aged 21–64) and 60 nonautistic adults (aged 20–69) using a passive auditory oddball paradigm with standard (1000 Hz) and deviant (1100 Hz; p = 0.15) tones. Electroencephalography recording revealed no significant differences between autistic and nonautistic individuals on mismatch negativity and P3a amplitude or latency. However, mismatch negativity amplitude decreased with age over frontal site, similarly across both groups. No age‐related effects were found for mismatch negativity latency or P3a measures in either group. These findings suggest that, from adulthood onward, the neural mechanisms underlying automatic change detection and preattentional processes are similar in both autistic and nonautistic adults, and that their overall time course of aging appears comparable, supporting the parallel aging hypothesis. Nonetheless, future research should explore how these preserved neural responses relate to behavioral reactivity to change in autism.

Article.Title: Amyloid‐Induced Network Resilience and Collapse in Alzheimer's Disease: Insights From Computational Modeling
Article.Authors: Nguessap E.; Depannemaecker D.; Ferreira F.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Alzheimer's disease is marked by progressive synaptic loss and cognitive decline, with amyloid‐beta accumulation playing a central pathological role. Although the molecular effects of amyloid‐beta are well‐characterized, the cascade from local synaptic dysfunction to large‐scale network collapse remains poorly understood. We present a biophysically grounded computational model that integrates small‐world network topology, Izhikevich neuron dynamics, short‐term plasticity, and amyloid‐beta‐induced synaptic pruning to investigate how amyloid burden degrades functional brain connectivity over time. Crucially, we simulate the evolving network dynamics across disease stages, revealing how firing rate, synchrony, variability, and Fano factor evolve in response to progressive structural degradation. Our results demonstrate a two‐phase deterioration: Initial compensatory dynamics followed by abrupt disintegration of coordinated activity. This temporal dissociation mirrors clinical observations and offers mechanistic insight into Alzheimer's disease progression. We further identify a critical accumulated amyloid dose beyond which network collapse becomes inevitable, preceded by early‐warning indicators such as declining global efficiency and the spectral radius of the network connections. Network topology, synaptic time constants, and repair mechanisms strongly influence resilience, with small‐world networks showing delayed collapse and greater functional compensation. Finite‐size scaling reveals that larger networks experience earlier and sharper phase transitions. Ultimately, by establishing a mathematical link between microscopic synaptic degradation and macroscopic network failure, our findings suggest that if experimental proxies for the spectral radius can be identified, they would serve as highly sensitive early‐warning indicators of impending network collapse. This theoretical framework offers new mechanistic targets for the early detection and therapeutic monitoring of neurodegenerative diseases.

Article.Title: Modulating Microglial Activation Through GLP‐1 Pathways: A New Frontier in Neuroinflammation Research
Article.Authors: Lakshmi S.; Singh V.; Vanangamudi M.; Taj T.; Shahin DH H.; Nath R.; Dutta G.; Avvari S.; Sridhar S.; Panigrahy U.; Noushida N.; Chaudhary P.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Microglia are the immune cells resident in the central nervous system (CNS) and are involved in CNS homeostasis and in responses to injury and disease. Microglia, upon activation, become pro‐inflammatory (M1) or anti‐inflammatory (M2), with M1 being neurotoxic and M2 participating in tissue repair. The activation of microglia in neuroinflammation and pain hypersensitivity is important in the neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's (PD) and Alzheimer's disease ( AD ). Recent investigations have identified GLP‐1 receptor agonists (GLP‐1 RAs) as potent pharmacological agents that can regulate the activity of the microglia. GLP‐1RA attaches to the GLP‐1 receptor found on the microglia to cause a phenotypic shift to the anti‐inflammatory M2 form, which, in turn, reduces neuroinflammation and increases neuronal protection. Experimental evidence shows that GLP‐1 RAs are effective at reducing hypersensitivity to pain, improving cognitive performance, and attenuating inflammatory effects in preclinical models of AD , PD, and multiple sclerosis (MS). All these facts suggest that GLP‐1 RAs are a significant treatment option in chronic pain and neurodegenerative disease management, as they can change microglial polarization and suppress neuroinflammation.

Article.Title: Structuring the World: Statistical Learning From the Top and From the Bottom
Article.Authors: Tabas A.; Fiser J.; Lengyel M.; de Hoz L.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Statistical learning is the brain's primary strategy for transforming continuous, noisy, and ambiguous sensory inputs into structured internal representations. This process is studied through a diverse array of perspectives spanning different species, sensory systems, levels of analysis, and methodological frameworks. Here, we present four such perspectives. Two of them approach the problem from the bottom, examining the neural substrates of the biological implementation. The first line describes implicit contextual learning in the rodent auditory midbrain, showing how neuronal frequency tuning adapts to predictable statistical regularities over days. The second line shows that explicit knowledge modulates belief updating as early as the human auditory midbrain and thalamus, revealing a functionally specialized subcortical inferential hierarchy. The other two research lines approach it from the top, examining the computations the brain performs. The third line compares statistical computations across species and human development, uncovering fundamental differences in probabilistic chunking strategies between honeybees, human infants, and adults. The fourth line provides a computational framework for continual learning in which experience is organized into structured internal models through ongoing contextual inference. We then examine what each line can contribute to the others. We argue that, if the brain evolved statistical learning under pressure to behave optimally, this optimality must have been achieved globally through the constraints and synergies that emerge from the interplay between subsystems and levels of analysis. The neuronal mechanisms implementing a computation are shaped by the computation they perform, while that computation is itself constrained by the available physiology: a mutual dependence that can only be understood by bridging across perspectives.

Article.Title: Beyond Dissemination: From Critical Science Literacy to Citizen Neuroscience
Article.Authors: Raschle N.; Federici E.; Hauser T.; Dresler M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Neuroscience increasingly informs education, mental health, and public policy, yet its real‐world impact remains limited, with misunderstandings and neuromyths persisting. We argue that the societal impact of neuroscience communication depends less on the volume of information disseminated than on whether it cultivates critical science literacy, namely, the ability to evaluate how neuroscientific knowledge is generated, modeled, and constrained and to understand the inferential steps linking data to conclusions and their limits of generalization. In the context of neuroscience, we refer to this as critical neuroscience literacy to emphasize the domain‐specific challenges of interpreting brain‐based evidence. The primary barrier is not insufficient dissemination alone, but systematic misinterpretation of neuroscientific inference once findings leave the laboratory. We advance three claims: first, that public misunderstandings often reflect limited insight into scientific reasoning and practice rather than simple information deficits about scientific results; second, that citizen science and dialogical engagement function as mechanisms for practicing such reasoning rather than as outreach add‐ons; and third, that neuroscientists share responsibility for shaping the interpretive conditions under which findings are translated, particularly in education, health, and policy. Importantly, this self‐referentiality is not merely descriptive. Interpretations are associated with beliefs, expectations, and environments that may themselves be linked to neural and behavioral change. We outline implications for training, incentives, and professional norms within the neuroscience community.

Article.Title: Reduced Brain Complexity During the Execution of a Sequential Arm Movement Following an Augmented‐Feedback‐Based Practice: A Multiscale Entropy Analysis
Article.Authors: Piskin D.; Margraf L.; Weigelt M.; Baumeister J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Motor learning is accompanied by adaptive changes in neural processing, yet the extent to which feedback‐based practice alters the complexity of cortical activity during movement execution remains unclear. The present study examined learning‐associated changes in brain complexity during the execution of a sequential arm movement following augmented‐feedback‐based practice. Thirty‐eight healthy young adults practiced a sequential arm movement with augmented feedback across five sessions. Cortical activity was recorded with electroencephalography during the first and last practice sessions. Multiscale entropy was used to quantify brain complexity across 50 time scales. Behavioral measures indicated improved movement accuracy and reduced dual‐task costs across practice. At the cortical level, a significant global decrease in entropy was observed from the first to the last practice session. Further analyses revealed that the differences were confined to coarse temporal window and midline frontal electrodes Fz and FCz. In addition, changes in coarse‐scale entropy at FCz were negatively correlated with reductions in absolute error. Together, the present findings suggest that augmented‐feedback‐based practice is accompanied by a refinement of cortical complexity during movement execution, particularly in large‐scale frontal dynamics. Multiscale entropy may therefore provide a sensitive framework for capturing learning‐related neural adaptations that complement conventional electroencephalographic measures and advance the understanding of motor learning at the systems level.

Article.Title: mir‐57 Influences Posterior Motor Neuron Axon Morphology in Caenorhabditis elegans
Article.Authors: Waduge N.; Tatnell H.; Davis G.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Organization and specification of the nervous system start in the embryo and are largely controlled by a cluster of transcription factors known as HOX genes, which control body patterning and morphogenesis at the transcriptional level. However, this entire process requires the influence of multiple pathways, including cell signalling, genomic and post‐genomic pathways. These include the Wnt (wingless) pathway, which controls neuronal development and polarity, and the small miRNA pathway, which regulates genes post‐transcriptionally. In this study, we investigated mir‐57 , the homolog of human miR‐10 in Caenorhabditis elegans and its role in influencing motor neuron function. mir‐57 is expressed posteriorly throughout development and enriched in motor neurons. Absence of mir‐57 results in decreased movement and abnormal axonal projections of posterior motor neurons. Moreover, the Wnt pathway genes cam‐1 and mom‐5 are mir‐57 targets and show elevated expression at the post‐transcriptional level in mir‐57 deletion mutants. Taken together this study suggests that mir‐57 influences Wnt receptor expression to maintain posterior motor neuron axon morphology.

Article.Title: Idiosyncratic Eye‐Movement Patterns to Faces Are Associated With Differences in Neural Processing: Evidence From Behavioral and Event‐Related Potential Responses
Article.Authors: Zhong N.; Hsiao J.; Chan A.; Hayward W.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Although faces are homogeneous stimuli, individuals adopt different eye‐movement patterns when looking at them. Do such differences in eye movements reflect distinct patterns of neural processing of faces? We conducted two experiments to investigate how face‐viewing preferences affect face‐sensitive event‐related potentials (ERPs). In both experiments, participants were separated into two groups: an upper‐focused group who fixated mainly on the eyes of faces and a lower‐focused group who fixated more on the nose and mouth. Participants then completed two fixation number‐controlled blocks in Experiment 1 or two fixation duration‐controlled blocks in Experiment 2, in which the initial fixation location was restricted to the left eye or the nose. In both fixation number‐controlled and duration‐controlled blocks, the upper‐focused group performed better and elicited a larger P1‐to‐N170 peak‐to‐peak amplitude for the eye‐fixation condition than the nose‐fixation condition. In contrast, the lower‐focused group performed evenly and elicited comparable P1‐to‐N170 amplitudes between fixation conditions. In addition, the P1 component was larger for the nose‐fixation condition than the eye‐fixation condition, and this difference was bigger for the lower‐focused group than the upper‐focused group. On the other hand, the P1 appeared to have no relation to behavioral performance. These findings show how individual differences in fixation patterns for faces map to differences in neural processing of those faces, and in turn provide evidence for the intricate relationship between sensory and neural processing of visual information.
