Article.Title: Associations of affective states and cognitive functions with eating behavior in healthy young Korean adults
Article.Authors: Jung J.; Goto Y.; Lee K.; Lee Y.
Article.Abstract: Altered eating behaviors have been identified in various psychiatric disorders; however, the psychological and cognitive correlates of eating-behavior traits in healthy young adults remain unclear. This cross-sectional study investigated whether affective states and cognitive functions are associated with eating behaviors in young Korean adults, hypothesizing that both affective and cognitive factors would be linked to maladaptive eating tendencies. One hundred healthy adults (50 men and 50 women, average age 21.88 ± 0.19 years) were recruited from March 2021 to June 2022. Eating-behavior traits were assessed using the Adult Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (AEBQ). Affective states were evaluated using the Autism-Spectrum Quotient, Depression Anxiety Stress Scale (DASS), Buss-Perry Aggression Questionnaire, and Big Five Inventory. Visual working memory, reward sensitivity, and salivary biomarkers, including cortisol and serotonin, were also assessed. AEBQ-based eating-behavior traits were more consistently associated with affective states than with cognitive-function indices or salivary biomarkers. Total AEBQ scores were positively associated with total DASS scores. Contrary to the initial hypothesis regarding cognitive functions, reward sensitivity and visual working memory showed no significant associations with AEBQ subscales. Salivary serotonin and cortisol were also not significantly associated with AEBQ subscales. These findings suggest that AEBQ-based eating-behavior traits in healthy young Korean adults may be more closely related to affective states than to cognitive-function indices or salivary biomarkers. Given the cross-sectional design, the findings should be interpreted as associative rather than causal or predictive.

Article.Title: Affective reactivity to a remote computer-based Trier Social Stress Test during a planned quit attempt: associations with short-term cigarette smoking lapse risk
Article.Authors: Arce N.; Wee C.; Kirkpatrick M.; Black D.
Article.Abstract: Background: The Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) elicits affective responses and has been linked to smoking behavior. However, its remote use during a planned quit attempt-when stress reactivity may influence early lapse-remains understudied. Objective: To quantify affective reactivity to a remotely administered TSST on a planned quit date following overnight abstinence and evaluate associations with cigarette use and lapse within 48 h. Methods: This secondary analysis used data from a randomized controlled trial of adult smokers completing a remotely administered TSST following overnight nicotine abstinence. Urge, anxiety, and stress were assessed using visual analog scales and summarized using area under the curve (AUC) metrics. Smoking outcomes included cigarette count and lapse within 48 h. Associations were estimated using generalized estimating equations. Results: In adjusted models, anxiety reactivity-but not urge or stress-was associated with cigarette count and lapse. Greater anxiety exposure (AUCtot) and change above baseline (AUCab) were associated with higher cigarette count (IRR=1.0004, 95%CI:1.0002-1.001, p=.002; IRR=1.01, 95%CI: 1.002-1.01, p=.002) and increased odds of lapse (OR=1.001, 95%CI: 1.0001-1.002, p=.03; OR=1.02, 95%CI: 1.001-1.03, p=.03). Effect sizes were small. Conclusions: Anxiety reactivity under nicotine deprivation was associated with increased cigarette use and lapse 48 h post quit attempt, suggesting individual differences in stress-evoked anxiety may serve as a behavioral marker for early lapse. Remote TSST administration appears feasible for eliciting affective responses on a quit date.

Article.Title: The ratio of GABA/Glu as a biomarker in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Article.Authors: Cheng X.; Wang L.; Diao C.; Wang Y.; Xue Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) lacks objective laboratory biomarkers for diagnosis and disease monitoring. Given the potential role of excitatory-inhibitory imbalance in ADHD pathophysiology, this study investigated the clinical significance of serum gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glutamate (Glu), and the GABA/Glu ratio in children with ADHD. Methods: A total of 145 children with ADHD and 120 healthy controls were enrolled. Serum GABA and Glu levels were measured by ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and the GABA/Glu ratio was calculated. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to assess diagnostic performance. Correlations between neurotransmitter indicators and SNAP-IV subscale scores were analyzed in the ADHD group. In addition, changes in serum GABA, Glu, and GABA/Glu ratio were evaluated after 12 weeks of methylphenidate treatment. Result: Compared with healthy controls, children with ADHD showed significantly higher serum GABA levels and GABA/Glu ratios (both p < 0.001), whereas serum Glu levels did not differ significantly (p = 0.059). The GABA/Glu ratio demonstrated the best diagnostic performance, with an area under the curve of 0.87, sensitivity of 76.55%, and specificity of 85.83%. Serum GABA levels were positively correlated with both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity scores, while the GABA/Glu ratio showed the strongest correlations with both symptom dimensions (all p < 0.001). After 12 weeks of treatment, serum GABA levels and the GABA/Glu ratio decreased significantly, whereas serum Glu remained unchanged. Conclusion: The serum GABA/Glu ratio may serve as a promising biomarker for the auxiliary diagnosis, severity assessment, and treatment monitoring of ADHD. However, further independent validation is required before clinical application.

Article.Title: Impact of a high-fat fructose diet from early life to young adulthood on spatial memory deficits in male rats: Assessments using the Barnes maze and Morris water maze
Article.Authors: Izadi M.; Salimi M.; Eskandari F.; Zardooz H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Chronic intake of a high-fat-fructose (HFF) diet may result in oxidative stress and inflammation, ultimately leading to cognitive impairments. To assess potential spatial memory deficits resulting from HFF diet consumption from birth to young adulthood and the impact of 4-phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) treatment, two spatial memory assessment tests were utilized: the Barnes maze (BM) and the Morris water maze (MWM) tests. Methods: After delivery, dams and their pups were randomly assigned to either the control (Ctrl) or the HFF diet group. After weaning, male pups were subdivided into the four groups based on the diet and treatment: Ctrl-DMSO, Ctrl-4-PBA, HFF-DMSO, and HFF-4-PBA. They continued their respective diets for five weeks, followed by a ten-day drug injection period. Behavioral tests, including BM and MWM tests, were performed on the sixth and seventh days of drug treatment, respectively. Finally, plasma corticosterone levels, as well as hippocampal levels of interleukin-1beta (IL-1β) and oxidative stress markers, were measured. Results: Early life to young adulthood consumption of HFF diet caused hippocampal IL-1β and malondialdehyde (MDA) contents, alongside a decrease in glutathione (GSH) level. These alterations were accompanied by memory impairment, decreased time spent in the target area, and increased latency to first in the HFF-DMSO group. 4-PBA administration improved the adverse changes in HFF-fed rats. Based on the behavioral findings, the BM appeared to be more sensitive than the MWM in identifying spatial memory impairments. Conclusion: Overall, a prolonged HFF diet consumption led to inflammation and oxidative stress in the hippocampus, which was associated with memory impairments in young adult male rats. The findings indicate that 4-PBA may represent a promising therapeutic approach to mitigate the negative biochemical and behavioral effects of such dietary exposure. Furthermore, the BM test is recommended as a useful tool for assessing potential spatial memory deficits in dietary intervention studies.

Article.Title: The PPC neurons modulate memory generalization via NR2B-type NMDA receptors in mice
Article.Authors: Deng Y.; Song D.; Huang T.; Wang C.; Qiu Y.; Li H.; Qing H.; Quan Z.
Article.Abstract: Generalization, the ability to apply learned rules to novel situations, is a fundamental cognitive process, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. The posterior parietal cortex (PPC) is considered a key hub for extracting abstract rules from specific experiences, yet its precise role in generalization requires further elucidation. In this study, we developed a five-hole operant paradigm to demonstrate that mice exhibit robust memory generalization, as reflected by graded success rates across tasks of varying difficulty. Fiber photometry revealed that PPC neurons are selectively activated during correct choices in generalization tasks. Chemogenetic inhibition of PPC neurons significantly impaired this generalization ability, particularly for the most difficult tasks. local infusion of NMDA receptor antagonists into the PPC, but not AMPA or acetylcholine receptor antagonists, specifically disrupted generalization, indicating a critical role for PPC NMDA receptors. Importantly, blockade of the NR2B subunit of NMDA receptors reproduced this impairment, whereas NR2A antagonism had no effect. Together, our findings establish that PPC neurons and NR2B-containing NMDA receptors within the PPC are essential for memory generalization in mice, providing new insights into the circuit and molecular mechanisms underlying adaptive behavior.

Article.Title: Progressive weight loss is attenuated by THC treatment in rats with activity-based anorexia
Article.Authors: Joyner S.; Eckel L.
Article.Abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder with limited effective pharmacological treatments. Given the role of the endocannabinoid system (ECS) in regulating energy balance and its possible involvement in AN pathophysiology, cannabinoid-based interventions may hold therapeutic potential. Using the preclinical activity-based anorexia (ABA) model, we investigated whether Δ⁹-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) could attenuate the progression of ABA-induced weight loss. Female rats were exposed to the ABA paradigm, which combines restricted food access (2 h/day) with unrestricted access to running wheels. After 3 days, when ABA rats had lost 10-12% of their baseline body weight, they received daily injections of either THC or vehicle. Rats were removed from the paradigm after losing 23% of their body weight or on the morning of day 8, whichever occurred first. THC treatment significantly attenuated weight loss and prolonged survival in the paradigm. These beneficial effects of THC were mediated by a selective suppression of excessive dark- and light-phase wheel running with no additional effects on food intake. These findings provide the first evidence that initiating THC treatment after significant weight loss in the ABA paradigm can halt the progression of weight loss through a selective decrease in energy expenditure. Importantly, treatment was initiated after (rather than before) the emergence of ABA-induced weight loss, thus enhancing the translational relevance of the model and our findings. Together, these findings suggest that pharmacological activation of the ECS may represent a promising treatment for individuals with AN.

Article.Title: Enhancing training efficiency in non-human primates: A structured approach to the delayed matching-to-sample task
Article.Authors: Kim Y.; Won J.; Jeon C.; Lim K.; Bae G.; Jeon E.; Seo J.; Seong J.; Yeo H.; Kim K.; Gwon L.; Kim M.; Nguyen T.; Jung Y.; Min J.; Jang H.; Moon G.; Park J.; Lee Y.
Article.Abstract: Touchscreen-based cognitive tasks are widely used to assess learning and working memory in non-human primates (NHPs); however, systematic evaluations of training efficiency and factors influencing task acquisition remain limited, often resulting in prolonged training periods and substantial inter-individual variability. This study investigated cognitive task acquisition and performance in cynomolgus monkeys using a touchscreen-based training system. Monkeys were sequentially trained on two-choice discrimination (TCD), matching-to-sample (MTS), and delayed matching-to-sample (DMS) tasks with varying training frequencies. TCD performance showed considerable individual variability regardless of the schedule. In contrast, training frequency significantly influenced MTS acquisition, with faster learning observed in monkeys trained four to five times per week than those trained two times a week. There was a trend for older monkeys, which had previously been individually housed, to require more trials to reach the MTS learning criterion. All monkeys completed working memory assessment, revealing notable individual differences, with some monkeys tolerating delays of up to 300 s, whereas others declined after 20 s. In addition, adaptive task modification through the introduction of short delay intervals during MTS training facilitated learning in monkeys that initially struggled with task acquisition. These findings highlight the importance of training intensity and individual variability in cognitive training outcomes and address a methodological gap by providing empirical evidence for optimizing DMS training protocols, support the DMS task as a valuable tool for assessing non-human primate memory.

Article.Title: Sex differences in onset times of cutaneous thermal sensations across non-noxious to noxious heat intensities
Article.Authors: Roh S.; Lee J.
Article.Abstract: Sex differences in thermal perception are well documented, but how these differences vary across heat intensities remains unclear. This study investigated sex differences in perception of cutaneous warmth, hot, and pain sensations across contact temperatures ranging from near-threshold to clearly noxious levels. Eight healthy males and eight females were exposed to contact heat stimuli at 42, 46, and 50°C using a Peltier stimulator (6.25 cm2) applied to the left anterior thigh. Onset times for each thermal sensation were recorded, along with heat flux. At rest, skin temperature was significantly higher in males than females (30.2 ± 1.0°C vs. 28.8 ± 0.5°C, P<0.01). Onset times for warmth and hot sensations did not differ between sexes at any temperature. In contrast, females perceived heat pain earlier than males at the contact temperature of 42°C (110 ± 33 s vs. 180 ± 77 s), whereas this sex difference diminished at higher temperatures (46 and 50°C). The temporal distinction between hot and heat pain sensations was evident at 42°C but diminished at higher intensities. Heat flux did not differ between sexes during the initial phase of heating, but heat flux was lower in females during prolonged exposure (P<0.05), suggesting a more rapid rise in skin temperature toward contact temperature. These findings indicate that sex differences in heat pain perception are most pronounced near the nociceptive threshold and diminish with increasing heat intensity. The results highlight the importance of considering both stimulus intensity and temporal dynamics when evaluating sex differences in cutaneous thermal sensitivity.

Article.Title: Pancreatic mu opioid receptors regulate metabolism and ingestive behaviors
Article.Authors: De Gregorio D.; Castro D.
Article.Abstract: The mu opioid receptor system has long been recognized for its role in regulating ingestive behaviors and food palatability. However, beyond their robust expression in the brain, opioid receptors are also found throughout the body, including the stomach, intestines, and pancreas. Previous studies suggest that opioids may directly regulate glycemia through actions in the endocrine pancreas, but whether these metabolic effects are linked to their influence on ingestive behavior remains unclear. Here, we used metabolic, ingestive, and genetic approaches to determine how the mu opioid receptor (MOPR) regulates in vivo phenotypes via its actions in endocrine pancreas. Glucose and insulin tolerance tests in male Oprm1 KO mice had enhanced glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity. Conditional deletion of MOPRs in alpha cells had no effect. To test if loss of MOPRs influence overt ingestive behaviors, we measured 24-hour ad libitum food consumption using Feeding Experimental Devices (FEDs) in wild type, Oprm1 knockout (MOPR-deficient) and GCG-Cre x Oprm1fl/fl mice (10-12 weeks old). We found that Oprm1 KO male, but not female, mice exhibited increased mass and food intake, and dysregulated ingestive microstructures relative to wild type controls. Conditional deletion of MOPRs in alpha cells only recapitulated some of the phenotypes related to ingestive microstructure. These findings suggest that MOPR regulation of ingestive behaviors extends beyond typical neural circuits of reward to include peripheral metabolic organ mechanisms.

Article.Title: Treadmill exercise partially attenuates bisphenol A-associated behavioral alterations with coordinated multi-omics changes in mice
Article.Authors: Guo X.; Yang J.; Hao Z.; Tang Z.; Yuan J.
Article.Abstract: Environmental chemical exposure may influence behavior through coordinated physiological changes, but whether lifestyle-related interventions can modulate these effects remains insufficiently characterized. In this study, a mouse model combining chronic bisphenol A (BPA) exposure and treadmill exercise was used to investigate behavioral outcomes and related multi-level physiological changes. Male mice were exposed to BPA by oral gavage at 200 μg/kg/day for 90 days, with or without treadmill exercise intervention. Spatial memory was assessed using the eight-arm radial maze, and exploratory/anxiety-like behavior was evaluated using the open field test. BPA exposure was associated with increased reference and working memory errors and reduced center-zone exploration, without marked changes in total locomotor activity. Treadmill exercise partially attenuated these BPA-associated behavioral alterations. Multi-level analyses revealed coordinated changes in gut microbiota composition, serum metabolite profiles, and hippocampal gene expression, with the BPA plus exercise group showing a partial shift toward control-like patterns. Integrative correlation analysis, together with exploratory feature-prioritization analysis, highlighted several candidate microbiota-metabolite-gene association patterns, among which the Rikenellaceae_RC9_gut_group-taurocholic acid-Cdkn1a pattern showed relatively higher consistency within the current dataset. Western blot analysis further provided protein-level support for group-related changes in hippocampal Cdkn1a expression. Overall, these findings suggest that treadmill exercise is associated with partial attenuation of BPA-related impairments in spatial memory and exploratory behavior, accompanied by coordinated microbial, metabolic, and hippocampal transcriptional changes.

Article.Title: Cortical responses to food stimuli in eating-disorder symptoms: An EEG study of approach-avoidance motivation
Article.Authors: Suiçmez Z.; Volkan E.; Ülsever H.
Article.Abstract: Eating disorders involve disturbances in body perception with substantial psychological and physical consequences. Neurobiological and motivational processes may help explain why these symptoms emerge and persist. This study examined cortical responses to food stimuli, indexed by frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) within an approach-avoidance framework, to clarify their relation to eating-disorder symptoms in a nonclinical sample. Eighty adults aged 18-40 completed an EEG task with food images varying in calorie content (low vs. high) and freshness (fresh vs. rotten), alongside self-report measures of eating-disorder symptoms and cognitive flexibility. Regression analyses showed that FAA was associated with global symptom severity and, more specifically, with dietary restraint; after controlling for age, sex, and BMI, only the association with restraint remained significant. Frontal asymmetry may therefore index individual differences in restrictive eating rather than serve as a general neurophysiological marker of eating-disorder pathology. The behavioural data supported the task itself: participants clearly distinguished stimuli by calorie content and freshness, rating fresh foods more favourably and responding faster to rotten ones, consistent with heightened salience for aversive food cues. Cognitive flexibility, by contrast, was not related to eating-disorder symptoms in this sample. Taken together, these findings suggest that FAA may reflect motivational processes underlying restrictive eating tendencies in nonclinical populations and support the use of task-based neurophysiological paradigms for studying these processes.

Article.Title: Comparative evaluation of two chronic stress models in zebrafish for advancing depression research
Article.Authors: Tripathy C.; Dhaygude S.; Vijay V.; Mondal A.; Soren K.; Kumar A.; Chakravarty S.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a debilitating neuropsychiatric disorder, and the failure of many antidepressants in clinical trials reflects the limited predictive validity of preclinical models. Therefore, a comparative evaluation of animal models that recapitulate the behavioral and molecular features of depression is essential for improving translational relevance. This study evaluated the utility of two chronic stress paradigms in zebrafish for modeling depression-like states. A modified Chronic Stress model termed Chronic Aggression Stress (CAgS) was developed and compared with the established Chronic Unpredictable Stress (CUS) model. In the CAgS paradigm, zebrafish were subjected to daily encounters with an aggressive cichlid for five days, while the CUS paradigm involved ten distinct stressors administered unpredictably twice daily for 10 days. Behavioral outcomes were assessed using the novel tank test, scototaxis, and threat response test. Molecular changes were examined by RT-qPCR, western blotting, and immunofluorescence. Both stress models induced robust depression-like phenotypes in adult zebrafish. CAgS produced consistent behavioral deficits, including reduced locomotion, increased anxiety-like behavior, and enhanced passive defensive responses across sexes, whereas CUS elicited divergent behavioral trajectories. At the molecular level, CAgS triggered a pronounced pro-inflammatory state characterized by elevated microglial activation and disrupted neurotrophic signaling. In contrast, CUS produced a more heterogeneous response, including sex-specific regulation of inflammatory cytokines and neurotrophic pathways. Both stress paradigms also showed astroglial activation and altered cellular proliferation. These findings demonstrate that both CAgS and CUS paradigms induce depressive-like phenotypes in zebrafish, with CUS uniquely revealing sex-specific behavioral and molecular alterations, highlighting their complementary utility for investigating depressive pathophysiology.

Article.Title: Dynamics of feeding behaviour and meal patterning in protein-restricted mice
Article.Authors: Taghipourbibalan H.; McCutcheon J.
Article.Abstract: Of the three dietary macronutrients, protein plays an especially pivotal role in physiological functions. Nevertheless, the behavioural control of protein intake is poorly understood. In this study, we used Feeding Experimentation Devices (FED3s) to examine the structure of ingestive behaviour in mice given access to diets varying in protein content. Adult C57BL/6NRj mice were contact-housed in pairs in custom-made cages with perforated dividers, each having access to an individual FED3 unit. Mice were given ad libitum access to either 20 mg control, non-restricted (NR) pellets (20% casein) or 20 mg protein-restricted (PR) pellets (5% casein) from FED3s on free-feeding mode. Each pellet retrieval event was timestamped ∼24 h/day. All mice experienced both diets for 7 days with order of diet presentation counterbalanced (i.e., NR→PR and PR→NR). Analysis of dynamics of pellet intake per day revealed that mice that were initially protein-restricted first showed a decrease in pellet intake before increasing on later days and exhibiting a persistent high level of intake once non-restricted diet was available. The group that was initially non-restricted exhibited a blunted response to the same diet manipulation. In addition, we clustered pellet retrieval data into discrete clusters of feeding events and used a mathematical approach to determine the boundary of meals (2-5 pellets), separated from "snacks" (1 pellet) and "feasts" (>5 pellets). We identified alterations in meal patterning in response to diet manipulation with protein restriction increasing "snacking" and leading to increased meal number, and reduced meal size. Moreover, restored access to NR diet, elicited "feasting". These effects depended on the sequence of diets the mice experienced, such that the effects were stronger in initially protein restricted mice compared to those initially non-restricted. In summary, our findings show that manipulation of dietary protein levels affects meal patterning in adult mice.

Article.Title: Time-dependent sleep disruption at simulated 7000 m in rats: Delineating the compensation-to-decompensation transition
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Yan W.; Ma W.; Zhang Y.; Li X.; Ma Y.; Fang J.; Li W.; Wang R.
Article.Abstract: High-altitude exposure disrupts sleep, but the temporal dynamics remain poorly defined. This study characterises time‑dependent changes in sleep architecture, HPA axis function, inflammation, and central sleep‑regulatory molecules during subacute hypobaric hypoxia. Male Sprague‑Dawley rats were exposed to simulated 7000 m for 1, 3, 5, or 7 days (H1d-H7d). Sleep was recorded by wireless EEG/EMG. HPA axis hormones, inflammatory cytokines, and sleep‑regulatory molecules were measured in serum, hippocampus, and hypothalamus. Multi‑dimensional integration was performed using principal component analysis (PCA). Hypoxia progressively reduced total sleep time and sleep efficiency, increased REM sleep percentage, and fragmented wakefulness, accompanied by declines in SWS delta power and REM theta power. The HPA axis exhibited peripheral-central dissociation: serum ACTH increased, whereas hippocampal ACTH and CORT were suppressed. Peripheral inflammation followed a time‑dependent pattern: an early IL‑6 surge (H1d), sustained Th1 suppression (IL‑12), and delayed IL‑10 elevation (H7d). Hippocampal BDNF, GABA, and histamine progressively declined; hypothalamic PGD₂, orexin A, 5‑HT, and histamine similarly decreased, while dopamine increased at H5d-H7d. PCA indicated a temporal separation between H3d and H5d, suggesting a transition from compensation to decompensation (mean Q² = 0.43). Subacute hypobaric hypoxia is associated with a time‑dependent transition from compensation to decompensation, characterised by sleep architecture collapse, HPA axis uncoupling, phased inflammation, and progressive loss of central sleep‑regulatory molecules. These findings offer a descriptive framework for understanding high‑altitude sleep disorders.

Article.Title: Memory impairments induced by neonatal excitotoxicity are associated with altered expression of NMDA receptor subunits NR2A and NR2B
Article.Authors: Castañeda-Cabral J.; López-Pérez S.; Contreras-Marín S.; Castro-Torres R.; Ureña-Guerrero M.
Article.Abstract: N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors are typically composed of two NR1 subunits and two NR2 (A-D) subunits. These receptors are overactivated during excitotoxicity, which can alter the expression of their subunits. Neonatal treatment with monosodium glutamate (MSG) induces a long-lasting neurodegenerative process triggered by excitotoxicity and involving multiple alterations in neurotransmission systems. This study aimed to determine whether neonatal MSG treatment modifies the protein expression of NR1, NR2A, and NR2B subunits, and whether these changes are associated with memory impairments in adulthood. Male neonatal rats received 4 g/kg MSG subcutaneously on postnatal days (PD) 1, 3, 5, and 7. At PD 60, protein expression of NR1, NR2A, and NR2B was assessed in the cerebral motor cortex (CMC), striatum (STR), hippocampus (Hp), and entorhinal cortex (EC) using Western blot. Memory performance was evaluated between PD 55 and PD 60 using the Barnes maze and novel object recognition tests. NR1 expression did not show significant changes in any brain region analyzed. NR2A expression was significantly increased in the CMC (p< 0.001) and decreased in the STR (p< 0.01). In contrast, NR2B expression was reduced in the CMC (p< 0.05) and increased in the STR (p< 0.01) and Hp (p< 0.05). MSG-treated animals exhibited impairments in short-term spatial and working memory. These findings indicate that neonatal excitotoxicity induced by MSG leads to long-term, region-specific alterations in NMDA receptor subunit composition, which may disrupt glutamatergic signaling and contribute to cognitive deficits in adulthood.

Article.Title: Intermittent Fasting as a Therapeutic Strategy in Alzheimer’s Disease: Understanding of Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor Modulation
Article.Authors: Shrirame D.; Tatode A.; Dabhade D.; Taksande J.; Taksande B.; Kakade O.; Umekar M.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques, tau tangles, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress, and it causes cognitive impairment and neuronal loss. The pharmacological treatment is of limited effectiveness, therefore the interest in novel approaches such as intermittent fasting (IF). IF, a nutritional regimen of periodic caloric restriction, has shown a potential to modulate neurodegenerative alterations by metabolic and molecular mechanisms. This review presents the implications of IF in the etiopathogenesis of AD, specifically in controlling brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). BDNF is a major neurotrophin that plays a key role in synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and cognition. Evidence indicates that BDNF is drastically decreased in AD, therefore enhancing disease progression. IF enhances BDNF expression via mechanisms such as improved mitochondrial function, increased ketone body production, and reduced systemic inflammation. Preclinical studies indicate that IF not only upregulates BDNF but also alleviates key AD pathologies, including Aβ deposition and tau hyperphosphorylation. Additionally, clinical data highlight the cognitive benefits of IF and its role in modulating metabolic health, although studies specifically linking IF, BDNF and AD in humans remain limited. This review underscores the need for further research to determine optimal IF protocols and clarify its long-term impact on AD progression. IF's ability to modulate BDNF and other neuroprotective pathways positions it as a promising non-pharmacological intervention for AD management. By bridging metabolic health and neuroprotection, IF offers potential therapeutic synergy for mitigating AD's complex etiopathogenesis.

Article.Title: Food restriction and hyperactivity differentially shape microglial Iba1 immunoreactivity across feeding-, cognitive-, and reward-related circuits in the activity-based anorexia model
Article.Authors: Camoglio C.; Dedoni S.; Scherma M.; Siddi C.; Nilsson I.; Fadda P.
Article.Abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is characterized by marked metabolic, behavioral, and neurobiological alterations. Although neuroinflammation and microglial activation have been suggested to contribute to its pathophysiology, preclinical evidence remains inconsistent and appears to depend on the experimental conditions and brain regions examined. Here, we asked whether the two core components of the activity-based anorexia (ABA) paradigm, food restriction and voluntary hyperactivity, are associated with distinct regional patterns of Iba1 immunoreactivity across neural circuits involved in energy balance, cognition, and reward, and whether these alterations relate to the behavioral and metabolic severity of the model. Using the ABA rat model, we quantified the percentage of Iba1-positive area in the prefrontal cortex, dorsal and ventral hippocampus, anterior cingulate cortex, nucleus accumbens, caudate putamen, amygdala, and the arcuate and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. ABA animals displayed an overall reduction in Iba1 immunoreactivity, with significant decreases in the hippocampus and paraventricular nucleus. Conversely, food restriction alone increased Iba1 coverage in the arcuate nucleus, whereas voluntary physical activity selectively enhanced Iba1 immunoreactivity in reward-related areas, particularly the nucleus accumbens. These findings indicate that starvation and hyperactivity induce distinct, region-specific changes in Iba1 immunoreactive coverage, potentially reflecting alterations in microglial responses that may differentially affect hypothalamic, cognitive, and reward-related circuits implicated in AN pathophysiology.

Article.Title: Gene-Environment Interaction in Transgenic Rats overexpressing human DISC1: Effects of Early Social Isolation on Behavioral Domains
Article.Authors: Pedroso-Fidelis G.; Avila F.; Nani J.; Porta L.; Bertagna N.; Rodolpho B.; Lee R.; Cruz F.; Hayashi M.
Article.Abstract: Early-life social isolation (SI) is a well-established environmental stressor associated with persistent behavioral alterations relevant to psychiatric disorders. Whether SI interacts with neurodevelopmental brain abnormalities to modify behavioral vulnerability remains unclear. We investigated the effects of post-weaning SI in transgenic rats overexpressing full-length human Disrupted-in-Schizophrenia 1 (tgDISC1), a model characterized by DISC1 protein aggregation, impaired dopamine homeostasis, and abnormal neuronal migration. Male wild-type (WT) and tgDISC1 rats were housed individually or in groups from postnatal day 21 for 28 consecutive days and evaluated using behavioral tests assessing stress-coping, self-care, locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, contextual fear memory, and social behavior. SI reduced grooming behavior, shortened the latency to the first immobility episode in the forced swim test, and decreased contextual freezing regardless of genotype, whereas locomotor activity and anxiety-like behavior were unaffected. Genotype-dependent differences were observed in anxiety-related measures, showing distinct performances in the Open Field and Elevated Plus Maze tests. In the social interaction test, SI selectively altered social preference, revealing a significant gene × environment interaction, indicating that neurodevelopmental brain abnormalities specifically modulated the effects of early-life SI on social behavior. Together, these findings demonstrate that early-life SI induces selective behavioral alterations, whereas DISC1-related dysfunction selectively influences the behavioral consequences of SI in the social domain rather than conferring generalized vulnerability. These results highlight the value of multidomain behavioral phenotyping in gene × environment models and identify social behavior as a sensitive marker of DISC1-related susceptibility to early-life stress, with implications for the developmental origins of psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Mechanistic insights into Aβ effects on neural stem cell proliferation and differentiation
Article.Authors: Zhao Y.; Yang Y.; Zhang L.; Hu B.; Yang Z.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: Amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation impairs hippocampal neural stem cell (NSC) function, but whether Aβ biases NSC lineage commitment toward the astrocytic lineage remains unclear. In this study, primary hippocampal NSCs from neonatal Sprague-Dawley rats were treated with 60 μM Aβ25-35 fragment, close to the 48-h half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50 ≈ 57.8 μM) determined by a CCK-8 assay. After 48 h, the proportions of Nestin+ and 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU)+ cells were significantly decreased (P < 0.01 and P < 0.001, respectively). After 7 days of differentiation, the proportion of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)+ cells was significantly increased (P < 0.001). GFAP+ cells exhibited an increased number of processes but shortened process length. Western blotting confirmed decreased Nestin and increased GFAP protein levels (both P < 0.01). Network-based bioinformatics screening identified 124 overlapping genes between Aβ-related targets and NSC-associated genes, with the PI3K-Akt pathway most highly enriched; validation showed a reduced p-Akt/Akt ratio (P < 0.01), decreased p-GSK-3β (Ser9) and β-catenin levels (P < 0.001), and upregulated total GSK-3β (P < 0.05). Taken together, these findings indicate that Aβ25-35 inhibits NSC proliferation and promotes astrocytic lineage differentiation, at least partly through suppression of the PI3K/Akt/GSK-3β/β-catenin pathway.

Article.Title: How crocodiles lost a forebrain circuit
Article.Authors: Pritz M.
Article.Abstract: Why do brain circuits differ among species of the same or different classes of vertebrates? Answers to this question are critical in determining brain organization and evolution. Investigations in mammals and in certain model systems have been the main focus of these studies. Among the areas that have commonly been investigated are cell death, synaptic pruning, and synapse organizing proteins. Whether these same or even other factors sculpt similar circuits in other vertebrates such as reptiles is unknown. The present study examined the development of a well defined circuit in crocodiles and compared it with a similar circuit in mammals. In mammals, cortical areas project directly back to the same dorsal thalamic nucleus that provides its input. However, in reptiles, pallial regions in receipt of dorsal thalamic input do not project directly back to dorsal thalamic nuclei. Instead, pallial areas in reptiles project to the basal nuclei, similar, in part, to the striatum of mammals. The basal nuclei then project back to the dorsal thalamus. This suggested the possibility that this circuit might have been lost in reptiles or perhaps added in mammals. To determine which of these two possibilities might be the case, the development of this circuit in Alligator embryos and juvenile crocodiles was investigated. The results indicate that cell death caused the loss of this circuit in crocodiles and is the likely explanation for this difference. However, a distinction between neuronal death and axonal re-modelling could not be determined.

Article.Title: Neuroprotective potential of safinamide against LPS-induced neuroinflammation and cognitive dysfunction in mice
Article.Authors: Kasaraneni R.; Gurram P.; Narne S.; Babiker M.; Salah A.; Narayanarao Alla N/A.; Rebello A.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation, a key pathological hallmark of neurological diseases, contributes to neurodegeneration, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive decline. Safinamide shows toll-like receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory effects in cellular models; however, it's in vivo neuroprotective and neuroinflammatory effects remain unexplored. In the present investigation, the anti-neuroinflammatory impact of safinamide was evaluated in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced mice using behavioral, biochemical, and histopathological assessments. LPS was administered intraperitoneally from days 8 to 15 to induce neuroinflammation, followed by 15 days of safinamide treatment at 10 mg/kg and 20 mg/kg. Safinamide 20 mg/kg significantly improved spatial and recognition memory, as evidenced by the percentage alternation in the Y-maze and recognition index in the novel object recognition test. Furthermore, safinamide significantly reduced the levels of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), phosphorylated NF-κB (p-NF-κB), NLRP3, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), and malondialdehyde (MDA), and increased levels of glutathione (GSH), catalase, and superoxide dismutase (SOD). Histopathological analysis revealed decreased amyloid-β deposition and preservation of neuronal architecture. These findings suggest that safinamide modulates neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress pathways and exhibits promising neuroprotective potential against inflammation-associated cognitive impairment.

Article.Title: Sivelestat sodium improves post-resuscitation brain outcomes possibly by inhibiting cell pyroptosis via inactivating the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway
Article.Authors: Ying P.; Zhou T.; Hu Y.; Luo Y.; Xu J.; Wu X.
Article.Abstract: Sivelestat sodium (SS) is shown to protect vital organs against regional ischemic stimuli. We investigated its effects on brain outcomes after global ischemic stimuli resulted from cardiac arrest (CA) and resuscitation. Adult pigs were randomly divided into sham (S), cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and CPR + SS groups. The animals were subjected to 9 mins of CA followed by 6 mins of CPR. After resuscitation, a dose of 10 mg/kg of SS was intravenously administered for 60 mins. Post-resuscitation brain injury and neurological function were regularly evaluated. Brain hippocampus tissues were harvested to measure histopathological injury, cell apoptosis, pyroptosis-related proteins and proinflammatory cytokines, and the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway. Consequently, post-resuscitation brain injury and neurological dysfunction were observed in those animals experiencing the CA/CPR procedure. However, they were significantly milder in the CPR + SS group than in the CPR group. Hippocampal histopathological injury and apoptosis were observed after resuscitation in the CPR and CPR + SS groups. Nevertheless, SS treatment significantly decreased both of them compared with the CPR group. Furthermore, pyroptosis-related proteins were upregulated, its-related proinflammatory cytokines were increased, and the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway was activated in post-resuscitation hippocampus in the CPR and CPR + SS groups. Likewise, SS treatment significantly reversed the changes of pyroptosis-related proteins and proinflammatory cytokines, and the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway compared to the CPR group. Thus, SS treatment was effective in improving post-resuscitation brain outcomes, and its protective role was possibly related to the inhibition of cell pyroptosis through the inactivation of the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway.

Article.Title: Endpoint-specific interactions between aerobic exercise and benfotiamine in chronic noise-induced prefrontal cortical dysfunction in mice
Article.Authors: Ziari H.; Shaki F.; Seyedabadi M.; Safarzade A.; Amiri F.
Article.Abstract: Chronic environmental noise can impair brain redox and inflammatory homeostasis, but the effects of combined non-pharmacological and metabolic interventions remain unclear. This study investigated whether aerobic exercise and benfotiamine, separately or combined, attenuate noise-induced behavioral dysfunction and prefrontal cortical injury-related changes. Male Swiss albino mice were assigned to Control, Noise, Noise + aerobic exercise, Noise + benfotiamine (200 mg/kg/day), Noise + aerobic exercise + benfotiamine, or Noise + N-acetylcysteine (500 mg/kg/day) groups (n = 9/group). Noise-exposed mice received broadband industrial noise at 90 dB sound pressure level for 4 h/day for 28 days. Behavioral despair-like phenotypes, cortical redox status, inflammatory gene expression, and histopathology were evaluated. Noise increased immobility in the forced swim and tail suspension tests, elevated reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, malondialdehyde, protein carbonyls, and pro-inflammatory transcripts, and reduced glutathione and antioxidant capacity. Both interventions attenuated multiple abnormalities. Aerobic exercise produced prominent behavioral effects and increased interleukin-10 expression, whereas benfotiamine strongly reduced reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, and interleukin-1β. Significant exercise × benfotiamine interactions occurred for both behavioral tests, reactive oxygen species, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-10, but not for several other endpoints. The combined intervention frequently produced the most favorable absolute values, although significant interactions were generally subadditive rather than synergistic. Aerobic exercise and benfotiamine therefore provide broad but endpoint-specific protection against chronic noise-associated prefrontal cortical dysfunction.

Article.Title: Repeated ketamine administration induces cross-tolerance to sodium salicylate but not to morphine in male rats
Article.Authors: Moghimian M.; Fathi A.; Ebadi A.; Mansouri S.; Shafaei-Bajestani N.; Abtahi-Evari S.; Gholami M.
Article.Abstract: Cross-tolerance profiles provide critical insights into shared neurobiological substrates among analgesics. This study evaluated whether repeated sub-anesthetic ketamine administration induces cross-tolerance to morphine or sodium salicylate. Thirty-six adult- male Wistar rats (180-200 g, n = 6/group) received either normal saline or ketamine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) once daily for 8 consecutive days. Antinociceptive thresholds were assessed daily using the hot-plate test (52 ± 0.5 °C) at 45 min post-injection and expressed as the percentage of maximum possible effect (MPE%). On day 9, acute cross-tolerance challenges were conducted using morphine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) or sodium salicylate (300 mg/kg, i.p.). Serum malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity were measured on day 8 to evaluate systemic oxidative status. Repeated ketamine administration produced a progressive decline in MPE%, demonstrating marked antinociceptive tolerance by day 8. On day 9, morphine maintained full antinociceptive efficacy in ketamine-pretreated rats, indicating no cross-tolerance. Conversely, sodium salicylate-induced antinociception was significantly blunted, confirming cross-tolerance. Biochemically, ketamine pre-treatment did not elevate serum MDA and preserved SOD activity substantially better than morphine. In conclusion, repeated sub-anesthetic ketamine administration induces antinociceptive tolerance and selective cross-tolerance to sodium salicylate, while sparing morphine responsiveness. These behavioral adaptations parallel a favorable redox balance, highlighting distinct pharmacodynamic mechanisms governing ketamine interactions with opioid versus non-opioid regimens.

Article.Title: RGS6 is a key regulator of itch in female mice
Article.Authors: P. Blount A.; Gavagan S.; Jawhar L.; Sutton L.
Article.Abstract: Pruritus, commonly known as itch, is a protective somatosensory sensation whose dysregulation is a common feature of many pathologic conditions and can severely impact quality of life. Despite its clinical relevance, itch perception is among the least well known of all somatosensory modalities. G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) in pruritic circuits are key modulators of itch, however the intracellular regulators of GPCR signaling in itch circuits remain largely unexplored. Regulators of G protein signaling (RGS) proteins are vital modulators of GPCR signaling and may influence itch processing in histaminergic and non-histaminergic circuits. Here we report that RGS6, a member of the R7 RGS protein family, modulates itch through both histaminergic and non-histaminergic mechanisms in female mice. Using global knockout mouse models, we show that this anti-pruritic phenotype is specific to RGS6, with no comparable effect in RGS7, highlighting functional specificity within the R7 RGS family. This study uncovers a regulatory role of RGS6 in modulating pruritus in females and provides critical insights into mechanisms fundamental to acute and pathological itch.

Article.Title: A drug repurposing-based mechanistic study of ilepcimide against febrile seizures
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Zhao J.; Yang L.; Tian K.; Cheng S.; Cai Z.; Kong D.; Zhang W.
Article.Abstract: Febrile seizures are the most common childhood paroxysmal neurological disorder. Although ilepcimide is used for pediatric epilepsy, its efficacy in febrile seizures remains unknown. Here, we investigated the effects and mechanisms of ilepcimide in a juvenile mouse model of febrile seizures using network pharmacology, molecular docking, brain slice electrophysiology and patch-clamp recordings of transfected cells. Ilepcimide prolonged seizure latency and reduced EEG spike-wave frequency. Network pharmacology linked its targets to glutamatergic synaptic signaling. Molecular docking further predicted that ilepcimide could target two subunits of AMPA receptor. In acute hippocampal slices, ilepcimide suppressed CA1 pyramidal neuron firing, increased rheobase, and prolonged action potential half-width. In HEK293T cells expressing GluA1/GluA2, it prolonged AMPAR deactivation and desensitization time constants. These results suggest that ilepcimide protects against febrile seizures through a multi-faceted mechanism: modulation of glutamatergic transmission, reduction of hippocampal excitability, and altered AMPA receptor gating. This study offers new target predictions and experimental evidence supporting the extended use of ilepcimide in pediatric febrile seizures.

Article.Title: Voltage-sensitive dye imaging reveals chronic peri-infarct hyperexcitability after MCAO in mice
Article.Authors: Kato J.; Dezawa S.; Tominaga T.; Higo N.; Takashima I.
Article.Abstract: Plastic changes in the peri-infarct cortex are thought to play a key role in post-stroke functional recovery, yet the circuit-level mechanisms underlying such reorganization remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated chronic changes in perilesional cortical excitability and synaptic organization using a mouse model of middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO). Evoked cortical activity was assessed by voltage-sensitive dye (VSD) imaging following direct cortical stimulation. The ischemic hemisphere exhibited significantly greater response amplitude and broader spatial spread than the non-ischemic hemisphere, indicating enhanced perilesional cortical excitability. Immunohistochemical analyses focused on superficial cortical layers, the primary source of VSD signals, revealed significant increases in both excitatory (VGLUT1-positive) and inhibitory (VGAT-positive) synaptic markers, with a greater increase in excitatory inputs, resulting in a shift in the excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) balance toward excitation. Reduced NeuN-positive neuronal density was also observed, suggesting concurrent neuronal degeneration. These findings demonstrate chronic peri-infarct hyperexcitability after MCAO and suggest that altered synaptic E/I balance may contribute to persistent changes in cortical network responsiveness. This circuit-level reorganization may represent an important mechanism underlying post-stroke plasticity and a potential target for therapeutic modulation.

Article.Title: Peripheral endotoxemia is associated with microglial activation, neuronal apoptosis, and amyloid precursor protein accumulation
Article.Authors: Niu L.; Yang C.; Li Y.; Qu C.; Guo L.; Wu H.; Zhao L.; Zhang J.; Lu F.; Zhu J.; Liu M.
Article.Abstract: Chronic microglial activation and the resulting neuroinflammatory cascade drive Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression. Systemic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) triggers robust microglial responses and is linked to neurodegenerative disorders, yet the full spectrum of neuroinflammatory and neuronal changes associated with chronic peripheral endotoxemia remains incompletely characterized. We hypothesized that sustained peripheral endotoxemia establishes a neuroinflammatory environment characterized by microglial activation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuronal apoptosis, accompanied by amyloid precursor protein (APP) accumulation. We analyzed public transcriptomic datasets for inflammatory signatures associated with LPS exposure in BV2 microglia (GSE18740) and mouse brain tissue (GSE3253). HT22 neurons were exposed to conditioned medium from LPS-stimulated BV2 cells, and apoptotic markers were measured. Adult rats received repeated systemic LPS injections over six months to model chronic endotoxemia; brain sections were then analyzed by immunohistochemistry for CD68 (microglial activation), cleaved caspase-3 (apoptosis), and APP. Inflammatory-related pathways were consistently upregulated across datasets. Conditioned medium from activated microglia increased neuronal apoptosis. Both LPS-treated microglial cells and HT22 neurons cultured with BV2-conditioned medium exhibited increased reactive oxygen species production and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential. The endotoxemia model exhibited cortico-hippocampal microgliosis, elevated cleaved caspase-3, and APP accumulation. These results support the hypothesis that peripheral endotoxemia probably propagates microglial hyperactivation, which subsequently promotes neuronal apoptosis and APP accumulation. Whether modulation of the inflammation-related pathways identified here can attenuate this microglia-mediated neurodegeneration warrants dedicated investigation.

Article.Title: Nrf2 overexpression ameliorates cognitive deficits and neuronal damage in APP/PS1 mice via attenuation of Aβ deposition and neuronal ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Zhu X.; Bo J.; Qian Y.; Diao F.; Liang H.; Fan L.; Su Y.; Li W.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-beta (Aβ) deposition, yet the mechanisms underlying Aβ-induced neuronal damage remain elusive. Emerging evidence implicates ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death, in AD pathology. We hypothesized that dysfunction of the Nrf2 pathway critically links Aβ deposition to neuronal ferroptosis and cognitive decline. In this study, AD progression in APP/PS1 mice was associated with progressive cognitive impairment, Aβ accumulation, and neurodegeneration. Aged APP/PS1 mice exhibited marked suppression of the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway, accumulation of reactive oxygen species, and prominent hallmarks of ferroptosis, including elevated DMT1 and TfR expression, accompanied by reduced GPX4 and xCT expression. Remarkably, genetic overexpression of Nrf2 significantly ameliorated cognitive impairment, attenuated neuronal and synaptic loss, and concurrently reduced Aβ deposition, oxidative stress, and neuronal ferroptosis. These findings demonstrate that Aβ accumulation is associated with impaired Nrf2 signaling during AD progression, leading to oxidative stress, neuronal ferroptosis, and cognitive dysfunction. Collectively, these findings suggest that activation of the Nrf2 pathway exerts robust protective effects against AD-like pathology, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic strategy for AD.

Article.Title: Maternal separation reshapes layer-specific PV-PNN architecture in the mouse barrel cortex
Article.Authors: Zhan X.; Miao J.; Chu P.; Tan P.; Chen C.
Article.Abstract: Early-life adversity alters inhibitory circuit maturation across developing brain systems, but most studies have focused on corticolimbic regions involved in emotional and cognitive regulation. Whether early adversity also reshapes inhibitory extracellular matrix architecture in primary sensory cortex remains less clear. Here, we examined the effects of maternal separation on parvalbumin-positive (PV+ ) interneurons and Wisteria floribunda agglutinin-labeled perineuronal nets (PNNs) in the mouse primary somatosensory barrel cortex (S1BF), a highly organized sensory region in which laminar position carries clear developmental and functional significance. Mice underwent daily maternal separation from postnatal day 1 to 14, and PV/PNN anatomical features were analyzed in young adulthood. PV density, PNN density, PV/PNN co-labeled cell density, and PNN-only density were quantified across layers 2/3, 4, and 5/6 of S1BF. Maternal separation did not alter PV+ interneuron density in any cortical layer. Instead, its effects were selective to PNN-related measures in layer 4, where both PNN density and PV/PNN co-labeled cell density were significantly increased. By contrast, PNN structures not associated with PV cells remained unchanged, indicating that the increase in PNN density was predominantly associated with PV-labeled interneurons. These findings show that maternal separation does not produce a generalized loss of PV-PNN architecture in barrel cortex. Rather, early adversity selectively enhances PV-associated PNN organization in the principal thalamorecipient layer of S1BF. This layer-specific pattern suggests that early-life stress may alter the timing or distribution of plasticity and stabilization within primary sensory circuits, with potential consequences for how tactile information is filtered and integrated during cortical maturation.

Article.Title: Single-housed, but not pair-housed, male and female rats demonstrate social conditioned place preference
Article.Authors: Bensing P.; Bowers C.; Moosa I.; Leong K.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the factors that modulate social reward has important implications for conditions characterized by social dysfunction, including autism spectrum disorder and social anxiety disorder. Social isolation is particularly relevant, given rising rates of subjective loneliness and social disconnection in the United States. The present study investigated the impacts of isolation on social reward by testing the effects of single- versus pair-housing on social conditioned place preference (sCPP) in adult male and female Sprague-Dawley rats. Across a ten-day paradigm with eight conditioning days, rats were trained in a two-chamber apparatus in which one chamber was repeatedly paired with a same-sex, weight-matched littermate, while the other chamber served as an unpaired control. Pair-housed rats were co-housed with their conditioning partner for the duration of the study. Single-housed, but not pair-housed, rats of both sexes developed a significant preference for the social-paired chamber. These findings indicate that housing condition modulated sCPP expression in adult male and female rats.

Article.Title: Prior trauma shapes the effects of psilocybin on stress sensitization in mice
Article.Authors: Ottofaro S.; Maltman J.; González-Maeso J.
Article.Abstract: Exposure to traumatic events induces persistent alterations in defensive behavior that extend beyond associative fear memories, including heightened responses to novel stimuli (stress sensitivity) and sustained defensive states in neutral contexts (stress sensitization). While serotonergic psychedelics such as psilocybin have been shown to facilitate fear extinction in associative paradigms, their effects on trauma-induced non-associative stress adaptations remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a behavioral paradigm in mice that dissociates contextual fear recall from stress sensitivity and stress sensitization within the same subjects. Male C57BL/6J mice were exposed to an acute foot-shock stressor, followed by assessment of trauma recall, administration of psilocybin (1 mg/kg) or vehicle, and subsequent evaluation of responses to a novel auditory stimulus and context. Trauma-exposed mice displayed robust associative fear and increased freezing in response to a novel auditory stimulus, consistent with enhanced stress sensitivity. However, psilocybin did not significantly alter this stimulus-evoked response. In contrast, psilocybin produced bidirectional, experience-dependent effects on stress sensitization - it reduced baseline freezing in non-traumatized mice but increased freezing in trauma-exposed animals when re-exposed to a novel context in the absence of a stimulus. Together, these findings demonstrate that psilocybin does not uniformly attenuate trauma-related behaviors, but instead modulates non-associative defensive responses in a manner dependent on prior experience. This work highlights the importance of distinguishing between associative and non-associative components of fear and suggests that psychedelic-induced plasticity may amplify latent trauma-related states under certain conditions.

Article.Title: Left DLPFC activation in the association between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Wu Y.; Yang M.; Xi M.; Si S.; Zhang W.
Article.Abstract: The prevalence of depressive symptoms among college students continues to rise. It has been shown that individuals with higher psychological resilience generally exhibit fewer depressive symptoms. The aim of this study is to examine potential associations between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students and to explore the statistical mediating role of brain activation in this relationship. 140 college students received functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) scans while completing a verbal fluency task (VFT). Psychological scales, oxyhemoglobin (HbO) concentration, partial correlation and mediation analyses were processed. Partial correlation analysis showed that psychological resilience was significantly negatively associated with depressive symptoms. The activation of HbO in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC; CH23), right DLPFC (CH3), and right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; CH6) were significantly positively correlated with psychological resilience and negatively correlated with depressive symptoms. Further mediation analyses demonstrated a significant indirect association between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms through activation in the left DLPFC (CH23). The findings suggest that the left DLPFC may be involved in the relationship between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students. Future longitudinal or intervention studies are needed to further clarify the causal relationships among these variables.

Article.Title: Efficacy of chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine on seizures induced by pentylenetetrazole kindling
Article.Authors: Roudini F.; Kohsari I.; Derakhshan M.; Nazemi S.; Azhdari-Zarmehri H.; Mohammad-Zadeh M.
Article.Abstract: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced kindling is an established model for investigating seizure mechanisms and evaluating the efficacy of antiepileptic drugs. Novel drug delivery systems, such as nanoparticles, offer improved therapeutic outcomes by enhancing brain bioavailability and reducing adverse effects. This study investigated the effects of chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine nanoparticles on seizure activity in PTZ-kindled mice compared with the free form of the drug. Male BALB/c mice were divided into three groups: PTZ-kindled control, PTZ + free carbamazepine, and PTZ + chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine. Seizure stage, Stage latencies 1 and 4, seizure duration, and mortality were assessed using a modified Racine scale. The results showed that while free carbamazepine temporarily reduced seizure stage, its effect diminished over time. In contrast, the chitosan-encapsulated formulation significantly reduced seizure stage, seizure duration, prolonged latencies, and completely prevented seizure-induced mortality. Characterization of the optimized nanoparticles revealed a mean particle size of 65 nm, a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.21, a zeta potential of -34.5 mV, and an entrapment efficiency of 55.35 %, indicating favorable stability and delivery properties. Overall, this study demonstrates that chitosan‑based nanoencapsulation of carbamazepine enhances its antiepileptic efficacy in a PTZ‑kindling model, suggesting its promise as a potential therapeutic strategy for epilepsy.

Article.Title: Varlitinib attenuates neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neurodegeneration in experimental Parkinsonism
Article.Authors: Lim H.; Park J.; Lee W.; Park G.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation mediated by microglial activation plays a critical role in Parkinson's disease (PD), with the NLRP3 inflammasome contributing to dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Varlitinib, a clinically developed pan-human epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor, has been investigated as an anticancer agent; however, its therapeutic potential in PD remains unknown. BV2 microglial cells were stimulated with α-synuclein and 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium and treated with varlitinib. Varlitinib significantly improved cell viability, reduced lactate dehydrogenase release, and suppressed IL-1β and IL-18 production. Co-treatment with the selective NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 produced no additional anti-inflammatory effects, suggesting that NLRP3 inflammasome signaling contributes, at least in part, to varlitinib's actions. In a 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine-induced mouse model of PD, varlitinib significantly improved motor performance, reduced microglial activation in the substantia nigra and striatum, and preserved tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons. Collectively, these findings support varlitinib as a potential drug-repurposing candidate for PD.

Article.Title: Analysis of the participation and influence of the cerebellum in emotion and emotional memory processing in mice through c-Fos expression
Article.Authors: Prati J.; de Russo T.; Lepesteur Gianlorenço A.
Article.Abstract: The cerebellum's involvement in non-motor functions, such as emotional and cognitive processes, has been gaining attention. The functional topography of the cerebellum remains inconclusive, and both clinical and preclinical studies have aimed to identify it to achieve a better understanding of cerebellar neurophysiology and its influence on other brain structures in different functions. The aim of this study was to analyze activation in cerebellar lobules IV-V, VI and VII under different context and temporal conditions of an inhibitory avoidance (IA) task, and to assess the association between c-Fos expression in these lobules and in other brain regions involved in emotional and memory processing. Thirty-three naïve Swiss Albino mice were exposed to the IA box for 1, 4, and 8 days. After the final exposure of each group to the evaluation apparatus, euthanasia was performed, followed by transcardiac perfusion and brain removal. Immunofluorescence analysis of c-Fos in pre-established structures was performed. Significant c-Fos/DAPI ratio was observed in cerebellar lobules IV-V and VI in animals that performed IA task for 4 days. No significant difference in c-Fos expression was found in the other regions of interest. Spearman's Correlation Coefficient test did not indicate any associations between the c-Fos/DAPI ratios across the regions of interest. These results suggest that cerebellar lobules IV-V and VI may be differentially recruited during the IA task, although their specific involvement in emotional and emotional memory processing remains to be determined.

Article.Title: Anillin functions in distinct glial subtypes to support larval locomotion in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Huynh M.; Dang T.; Thao Dang T.; Yoshida H.
Article.Abstract: Anillin (Ani)/Scraps has a well-characterized function in cytokinesis and has recently been shown to play a role in the nervous system. Ani is expressed in neuroblasts, axons, and neuromuscular junctions in the Drosophila larval nervous system, and pan-neuronal ani knockdown impairs both larval and adult behaviors. However, despite the expression of ani in glial cells, its function in these cells remains unclear. In the present study, we therefore investigated the role of ani in Drosophila glial cells by performing pan-glial ani knockdown and assessing the subsequent effects on larval and adult behaviors. Ani was expressed in a subset of glial cells, including in the central and peripheral nervous systems, and expression levels varied across individual cells. Pan-glial knockdown of ani significantly impaired larval and adult locomotion, larval learning ability, and adult activity; however, it did not affect lifespan. Although ani depletion decreased the number of glial cells in the central nervous system, it did not disrupt neuropil formation. In the peripheral nervous system, ani knockdown increased the total length of neuromuscular junctions. Subtype-specific knockdown analyses suggested that Ani functions in endoreplicating subperineurial and wrapping glia to support larval locomotion. The results also suggested a possible role for Ani in astrocyte-like and ensheathing glia, although the evidence is inconclusive. In contrast, Ani did not appear to have an obvious role in cortex glia or actively proliferating perineurial glia for larval locomotion. Together, these findings indicate that ani exerts both canonical and non-canonical roles in Drosophila glial cells.

Article.Title: Increased CCR2-immunopositive myeloid cells in the putamen and cerebellar white matter with blood–brain barrier disruption in multiple system atrophy
Article.Authors: Okada N.; Togawa N.; Ishimoto T.; Ayaki T.; Maki T.; Matsumoto R.
Article.Abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, and autonomic dysfunction. Recently, a close relationship of neuroinflammation to MSA pathogenesis was identified. Studies in mouse models of MSA have indicated that peripheral-type myeloid cells and endogenous microglia promote neuroinflammation in MSA. However, their distinct roles in MSA pathogenesis remain unknown. We performed immunohistochemical analyses of brain tissues obtained at autopsy from patients with MSA and age-matched controls to examine the putamen and cerebellar white matter with antibodies against CCR2 (a chemokine receptor expressed by monocyte-lineage cells), TMEM119 for microglia, and fibrinogen for blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage. The CCR2-immunopositive area was significantly increased in both regions in MSA patients compared to controls (putamen, p = 0.0043; cerebellar white matter, p = 0.0438); however, the TMEM119-immunopositive area showed no significant between-group difference (putamen, p = 0.4220; cerebellar white matter, p = 0.8152). The densities of CCR2-immunopositive areas in the putamen and cerebellar white matter were positively correlated (Pearson's r = 0.7325, p = 0.0248). In the putamen, fibrinogen immunoreactivity and perivascular leakage were increased and showed a distribution similar to that of CCR2 immunostaining (p = 0.0398). These findings suggest that CCR2-immunopositive myeloid cell accumulation in regions with BBB dysfunction may involve recruitment of peripheral monocyte-lineage cells.

Article.Title: Neural mobilization combined with a polylactic acid conduit enhances functional and morphological recovery following median nerve repair
Article.Authors: Cardoso F.; Pestana F.; Taboada T.; Silva B.; Campos N.; Souza D.; Oliveira J.; Abreu C.; Mendonça H.; Almeida F.; Blanco Martinez A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Peripheral nerve transection repaired with a poly(lactic acid) (PLA) conduit remains associated with incomplete functional recovery. Neural mobilization (NM) may enhance nerve regeneration, but its optimal timing and effects remain unclear. This study investigated how NM timing affects nerve regeneration and functional recovery after median nerve transection and PLA conduit repair. Methods: Nineteen young adult female Wistar rats underwent median nerve transection and repair using a 10-mm PLA conduit to bridge an 8-mm gap. Animals were assigned to control (no mobilization) or NM groups initiated 1, 5, or 30 days after surgery. Mobilization consisted of scapular depression and forelimb movements for 10 min, three times weekly. Recovery was assessed using von Frey and grip strength tests, electrophysiological, histological, morphometric, and muscle analyses 8 weeks after surgery. Results: NM effects were time-dependent, with mobilization initiated 5 days after surgery producing the most favorable functional and electrophysiological outcomes. This timing improved grip strength, mechanical sensitivity, and CMAP amplitude without affecting latency. NM also enhanced axonal regeneration and increased the proportion of myelinated fibers, but did not significantly affect angiogenesis, myelin thickness, or muscle atrophy. Conclusions: Initiating NM 5 days after nerve repair may represent a favorable therapeutic window following severe peripheral nerve injury. NM at this time point improved functional, electrophysiological, and structural outcomes, although it did not significantly affect muscle atrophy or myelin thickness. These findings support NM as a time-dependent therapeutic approach and provide a basis for further investigation of its translational potential future clinical studies and applications.

Article.Title: Selective vulnerability of the spinal cord in a rat model of asphyxia-induced cardiac arrest
Article.Authors: Lee S.; Shin H.; Kim R.; Lee J.; Sabuj M.; Kim I.; Ahn D.; Tae H.; Kim S.; Yoon J.; Lee J.; Park B.
Article.Abstract: Spinal cord injury after cardiac arrest (CA) can cause devastating neurological deficits, including paraplegia. Although lumbar spinal cord injury is clinically important, regional comparisons remain limited. In this study, we examined region-associated vulnerability of the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord using a rat model of asphyxial CA (ACA). Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent sham surgery or ACA, and thoracic and lumbar spinal cord tissues were collected 24 h after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) from ACA survivors with hindlimb paralysis. Histopathological analysis demonstrated significantly fewer surviving neurons in the lumbar compared with the thoracic spinal cord after ACA. The lumbar spinal cord also showed higher BAX/BCL2 ratios and cleaved caspase-3 expression, together with increased phosphorylation of NF-κB and mitogen-activated protein kinases, including p38, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK). Exploratory transcriptomic comparison between ACA-L and ACA-T identified 292 upregulated and 187 downregulated DEGs. Enrichment analyses indicated that upregulated DEGs were associated with extracellular matrix-receptor interaction, focal adhesion, integrin signaling, and PI3K-Akt signaling, whereas downregulated DEGs were associated with nervous system development and myelination. Collectively, these findings demonstrate region-dependent molecular and histopathological alterations at 24 h after ROSC, with a more pronounced injury-associated inflammatory and apoptosis-related profile in the lumbar spinal cord of paralyzed ACA survivors.

Article.Title: Phosphatase of regenerating liver-1 is associated with inflammatory pain, spinal GluN2B upregulation, and microglial activation
Article.Authors: Jin W.; Li L.; Yang J.; Xu X.; Xiao Q.; Li J.; Ke C.; Wu Y.
Article.Abstract: Central sensitization in the spinal dorsal horn, characterized by enhanced neuronal excitability and sustained neuroinflammatory responses, is a key mechanism underlying persistent inflammatory pain; however, the upstream molecular regulators coordinating these processes remain incompletely understood. PRL-1 knockdown attenuated pain hypersensitivity and was accompanied by reduced expression of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor subunit GluN2B. In addition, PRL-1 knockdown was associated with decreased microglial reactivity and lower levels of proinflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-6. Article.Title: Xylazine reduces methamphetamine-induced hyperlocomotion in rats through κ-opioid and α2-adrenoceptor mechanisms
Article.Authors: Wiah S.; Lami A.; Rawls S.
Article.Abstract: Xylazine, a veterinary anesthetic, is an adulterant in fentanyl and heroin that worsens opioid-related adverse effects. Two recent evidences - one epidemiological and the other pharmacological - have emerged regarding xylazine. Epidemiologically, xylazine co-use with methamphetamine (METH) is increasing; for example, in a recent toxicology report, xylazine was detected in 30% of human METH samples. Pharmacologically, xylazine is not only an α2-adrenoceptor agonist but also a full κ-opioid receptor agonist. Here, we determined effects of xylazine (1, 2.5, 5 mg/kg) on METH (1 mg/kg)-induced hyperlocomotion and investigated α2-adrenoceptor and κ-opioid receptor mechanisms. For co-administration with METH, xylazine dose-dependently reduced hyperlocomotion evoked by METH. In rats pretreated with the α2-adrenoceptor antagonist yohimbine (1 mg/kg), xylazine did not reduce METH-induced hyperlocomotion. Pretreatment with the competitive κ-opioid receptor antagonist LY2456302 (30 mg/kg) also attenuated xylazine's suppression of METH-induced hyperlocomotion. In xylazine-naïve rats, neither LY2456302 (30 mg/kg) or yohimbine (1 mg/kg) affected METH-evoked hyperlocomotion or spontaneous locomotor activity. Article.Title: NRN1 inhibits neuronal apoptosis and improves motor recovery after spinal cord injury via binding to FZD2 to activate the GSK-3β/Nrf2 pathway
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Hao J.; Shui C.
Article.Abstract: Neuritin 1 (NRN1) is a neurotrophic factor known to protect neurons from damage and cell death; however, its role and mechanism in cervical spinal cord injury (CSCI) remain unclear. In this study, we investigated the function of NRN1 using oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD)-treated PC12 cells and a rat model of CSCI established by anterior cervical screw compression. In vitro, NRN1 overexpression promoted neurite outgrowth, attenuated oxidative stress, and inhibited apoptosis in OGD‑exposed PC12 cells, while NRN1 knockdown showed opposite results. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence confirmed that NRN1 interacts with FZD2. In OGD-treated PC12 cells, overexpression of FZD2 reversed the neuronal damage induced by NRN1 silencing, reducing oxidative stress and the number of apoptotic cells. Furthermore, NRN1‑mediated neuroprotection was dependent on activation of the GSK‑3β/Nrf2 pathway, since pharmacological inhibition of Nrf2 with ML385 abrogated the protective effects of NRN1. In vivo, decreased expression of NRN1 was observed at the site of spinal cord injury in rats. Notably, intramedullary delivery of adeno‑associated virus (AAV) encoding NRN1 restored NRN1 levels, significantly improved motor function, reduced neuronal apoptosis, and alleviated oxidative stress in spinal cord tissue. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that NRN1 exerts neuroprotective effects against CSCI by binding to FZD2 and activating the GSK‑3β/Nrf2 signaling pathway, suggesting that targeting NRN1 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for promoting motor recovery in CSCI patients.
